If you ever liked Minesweeper you will love Hexcells! It's played on a hex grid, but has a similar mechanic of combining information to deduce the locations of the blue hexes (mines). The information you get is more diverse than Minesweeper.
What is especially noteworthy here is the outstanding level design. The game consists of 35 or so levels that gradually escalate in difficulty, while never requiring the player to outright guess. I repeat: Every puzzle can be logically deduced with the information available. I recommend playing it without guessing, since figuring out the logical deductions is immensely rewarding.
The two sequel games (Hexcells Plus, Hexcells Infinite) have the same mechanic but additional levels. Hexcells Infinite also has randomly-generated levels in addition to the hand-crafted ones. All three are fantastic games that any puzzle lover will enjoy!

TL;DR: The game is simply "okay" but suffers from several flaws that ultimately sour the experience.
First and most important of all, the game's biggest issue is that the AI has some big time cheats that are obvious as night and day. Right from the beginning of the game, some AI opponents will be able to generate, maintain and throw a ridiculous amount of enemy troops at you with seemingly no maintenace costs that you cannot simply cannot compete with.
It will not matter what you do and there is no strategy, if you run into an aggressive AI that has these cheats early on you may as well restart as there is no way you'll be able to generate enough income to support a large enough army to fight them, nor will you be able to replenish fallen troops fast enough with the turn limit. Trying to negotiate peace through diplomacy has the AI asking for ridiculous demands you won't be able to meet and it's essentially a slow progression to the game over screen. And all of this is hoping and praying that you don't run into a SECOND AI that looks to take advantage of you while you're busying trying to do whatever you can to simply survive the first aggressive encounter. In my second game, I happened to run into three. All of this is on normal mode, by the way.
If the developer can fix their cheating AI, it will be a much better game but for the moment it's just a frustrating experience of RNG - maybe you'll land next to some weaker, less aggressive AI to start, and maybe you won't. How many turns and how much time do you want to waste to find out?
As for other game elements, I can only say they're... well, "okay". Battles are simplistic and the AI will often do some really strange things in the battle for no real reason. Feels a bit too much like RNG again to me. I've had battles where I felt like I should never have won and other battles that I lost that had me raising my eyebrow in a 'how did THAT happen' way. And the other super annoying thing is you'll constantly have battles where you have superior numbers against a smaller force that simply don't end with the enemy being destroyed because 3-4 guys will manage to run away. Every. Single. Time. So you get to waste turns upon turns trying to hunt down those few man units. Fun... I guess? Not really. It's a game, it needs to have some satisfaction too.
Other weirdness that I've experienced for battles is enemy AI that seiges your towns that simply don't do anything. They'll just sit there in one or two hexes for ages, not attacking, not pillaging, just... waiting. For what? I dunno. They'll move if you try to reinforce your town or attack them from your sieged village but until then, they'll just sit there. Staring. Playing patty cake. I mean a dozen or more turns I watched them just sit there doing nothing. Is this intended? A bug? Do they not know how to attack towns with walls? I have no idea.
In other areas, the UI really needs work. I figured most of it out but the tutorials won't help you out and just be ready to left click-right click-double click everything in the beginning to try to figure out how to do stuff on your own. Elements like 'culture' and 'authority' are never really explained and are kind of left to you to figure out how important they are. Authority seems to be related to how many settlements you can have early on, yet the game will not stop badgering you to make new settlements and create new settlers - all the while, your unrest is shooting up because you don't have enough 'authority' via research. Again, a mechanic never really explained so I'm kinda doing it for them here. I haven't played enough to figure out what culture does but, uh, guess it's a thing that... well, who the hell knows to be honest, they don't give any indication either.
As for the good, the visuals aren't bad for the kind of game it is and the music is fine too. It's a ROTK-like game from a studio that isn't KOEI and there aren't too many of those so I can give it props for that too. But all in all, this game just leaves me feeling wanting for more. Virtually everything feels rough around the edges and not fully fleshed out yet. As a veteran of ROTK games, this game begins to scratch the itch but ultimately just makes me want to dust off the PS2 and put my ROTK X disc in. Maybe it will change with further updates, and I sure hope it does.
However, at this time, I don't think I would recommend this game to anyone but to others like me who are just looking for anything to fill the void of this style of game and is willing to overlook the many flaws. I will probably still continue to play it but once the itch is fully scratched, I can't see myself coming back to this unless some real changes are made.

My peasent say they are over worked, so the game wants you to do nothing, I guess that is a choice.
And there are generals but they are just another unit, they are not needed. The game revolves around you chasing individual peasant units around. The game does not incourage you to form armies because there is no benefit, execpt it requires less clicking to move your units. It  would improve greatly if you could only form armies with a general. That is not some revolutionary concept.
The technology tree is neat. That is a pro I guess.

While by no means a bad game, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is plagued by uninteresting characters, a less than stellar story, and many questionable and/or outright poor game design choices. Most of my play time in this game is in The Handsome Collection on the Xbox One, but that doesn't change my thoughts on the game at all. Many of the levels are incredibly frustrating to navigate or just deal with in general, and the necessity of grinding means you'll be spending a lot of time in these poorly-designed areas. The difficulty curve is incredibly erratic as well, so while one level may be very easy the next could be borderline impossible and invoke a Dark Souls level of bashing your head against the wall repeatedly until it breaks. The Grinder is a pathetically easy mechanic to break, and makes it incredibly trivial (if slightly tedious) to get the rarest loot in the game. The game just doesn't have nearly as much depth to it as Borderlands 2 did, and I'd only recommend buying it if it's deeply discounted and you have a lot of patience.

So I've played this for a fair while now since buying it.
i have to say i love this game the battle AI needs a little TLC but it is definitely a nice game.
the economic side is a little easy. but the battles are quite unique you give orders to your armies during your turn at the end of the turn they proceede to carry out those orders. (still needs a bit of work to do this better especially with the time it takes for units to decide what action to take .)
but they play out and you feel more like the ruler of the nation than anything. outside of your plan you don't get a lot of control over your army mid battle. so if you're an armchair general who thinks you're great at planning. and not so much in the execution of your own plans i think this is for you.
the AI isn't super aggressive so it is quite possible to play without ever going to war i spent 300 turns at peace with the same 3 AI , my first official war was due to defending an ally.
and i gotta say i really enjoy it. it is missing a few things like coordination with your allies to make the most out of your planning during your turn.  but i'm hoping that'll be something added down the line.
this is an Early Access game so of course bugs are to be expected but the game is extremely stable i haven't had it crash once in the time i've played so far.
the sieges are long drawn out affairs they're almost like a real siege . first you have to bust through the walls with siege equipment, and eliminate the enemy units . it can take several turns to fight one >.> which the AI factions like taking advantage of your sieges an sending a small army to try an steal victory out from under your feet. which is a tad annoying.
but i have to say that this is slowly becoming one of my favourite turn-based strategy games. imo it is way better than some of the other games in the genere and i think with proper support it'll be a hit.
oh and the map is gigantic. it really does feel like you're fighting in China. because even at 500+ turns i had barely explored any of the map even after spending 25 turns crossing the enemy. but don't get me wrong every step of the way there are NPC cities an factions who are growing an building their empires along side you. with each army able to have 6 units in it, and you able to keep as many armies as you can financially maintain.
the battles can be large affairs of thousands of troops , and units going at it. and the game is well optomized so it doesn't take much processing power , the game loads quickly saves quickly for the size of the map and the amount of things in the game.
the diplomacy is a little simplistic , with your basic treaties  Non-agression - Defensive Alliance - Trade Embargoes - Agree to attack on xturn.
with the ability to force nations to become your vassal or to recognize your right to be the "emperor. '
the game is open-ended with some victory conditions so you can play as long as you want. even if you are like me and tend to avoid aiming for a 'win' goal and simply wanna play run/build your empire perhaps do a little roleplaying with your characters and armies(you get a few generals/governors that help you run your empire a little more efficently).
the Dev is active on the forum and gives input and responds to feed back  with a positive demeanor so if you were to have a problem with bugs, they are usually quick to respond an offer assistence.
i highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys planning their next move. and watching the battles play out.

Overview:
The game is about a man who is unable to sleep due to all the parties and decides the best course of action is to start murdering every partygoer he sees at every party he spots. The goal of each level is to methodically kill everyone at a party without being caught by the police, using traps, items, a knife, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dance moves to pick off everyone, one by one.
Pros:
+ Nice Soundtrack!
+ Gives that warm feeling you get when you slowly, but surely, work out a problem. In this case, slaughtering your fellow man.
+ Lots of events, items, and other ways to kill to keep the killing from being monotonous.
+ Different Characters to spice up the way you play.
+ Story is interesting, if slightly predictable.
+ Has lots of sight gags sure to make you chuckle a bit.
+ Nice, clear visual design.
+ Level editor and Workshop support, meaning you could theoretically play forever.
+ Feels very rewarding if you use clever tactics, the game acknowledging and rewarding the sneaky, the quick, or the brutal.
Neutral:
+/- All the items vary in usefulness from very useful to completely pointless.
+/- A slight amount of RNG is at play with the layout of some traps or characters changing a little bit if you constantly ♥♥♥♥ up, likely forcing you to change tactics rather than plan out a gameplan from the start.
+/- A lot of the top workshop levels make unlocking the other characters♥♥♥♥♥♥easy.
+/- Characters will typically blame whoever is nearby of killing someone if they spot a body. This obviously includes you.
Cons:
- A bit buggy, including a bug where some partiers will be constantly be alerted despite the police having left and not calling them back or bodies being left unattended by the medics or police.
- Later story levels can get a bit frustrating and tedious as they reduce the amount of traps in the area and make calls more and more useless, forcing you to rely on stabbing everyone up.
- If somehow, you aren't at fault for a killing and someone sees a body near you, no matter the cause of death, you're still  getting labeled the killer.
- AI doesn't seem particularly smart, not remembering when you're the killer after calling the police, even if they called the police on you before.
- Some items (like the sword) feel utterly pointless since they don't add much to gameplay.
- This game cries out for Co-Op or some other form of Multiplayer rather than the TwitchPlaysPokemon-ish feature where you can stream the game and people can affect your game from Twitch.
Overall: 7.5/10
Its definitely flawed, but if you look past those flaws, you can have a lot of fun with this title. Its really cathartic in a way and it feels satisfying to finish a level using all the tools at your disposal. Definite recommendation.

Stellaris is not Masters of Orion nor does it try to be.
As it might be quite obvious to most, Stellaris has more in common with the other Paradox titles which created a genre of their own, called "Grand Strategy".
In this genre, you do not care so much about the details, but instead you deal with bigger decisions, so for example in Stellaris you do not tell your admiral how to fight, he will do that on his own, but you do decide how many ships of each type to build.
This genre has always been notorious for being very complex and difficult to learn and while Stellaris might be considered the easiest one to learn of Paradox's titles, it is no exception.
Some leeways are made due to the genre, so everyone starts as a small 1 system empire with just a handful of ships, not very overwhelming at all, with the focus squarely be on exploration and identifying the best way of expanding your fledging empire. Before too long, though, the focus shift and the game becomes more similar to Europa Universalis, with most of the known galaxy colonized by one or another empire, alliances will form, Federations will be born and wars will be massive affairs involving 6 empires on each side.
Paradox, as always, put great support in their product and you can be sure there will be content patches and expansions released for this game for a long time to go, but the complexity of the game comes with its own set of problems. Bugs, bugs, bugs! Things do not always work as intended and because of the before mentioned complexity is hard at times to realize if you just hit a bug or if that feature is working as intended, but you just did not know it was supposed to work like that.
Since release, Paradox has tried to inject meaning in the most boring part of the game, the midgame, and they did so with random events and more random things you can find in the galaxy, like pirates systems, space dragons and colony-based events.
Eventually, you will hit the end game and here once again Paradox has tried to shake things up from the usual endgame of games of this type, ie. the time when you already know you "won", but you need to defeat two more empires to do so. Here instead you will find many scifi tropes, from interdimensional aliens to AI revolts or massive super powerful fallen empires reawakening and going to war with one another, the end game is a time of action and possible defeat!
Finally, as in all Paradox games, do not expect much of an ending screen, no big fanfare and cinematic showing how great you are, these games are more about the journey than the destination.
In the end, even with all the bugs and issues, Stellaris is a great game and a perfect introduction to Paradox's Grand Strategy genre than any other.

The mix of general survival, inventory management, crafting, and resource harvesting creates a delicate touch within the game.  It feels as a roguelike game, difficult, but that ONE thing that killed you could have been avoided. The game feels like a survival journey as much as an RPG, with limited amounts of health potions and gradual biome progression. However, the biomes don't seem to get any harder on their own, with the only increase in area difficulty being that the biomes gradually swap each other out in an attempt to get you to go to the harder zones. The game is about risk versus reward in an aspect, as running into a difficult biome will also grant you access to plenty of treasure chests or high amounts of valuable ores. However, said biomes often end up having enemies hard enough to take out your level 30 character in a mere 4 hits without any health potions to rely on.
Overall, the game has its ups and downs, but the mix of aspects in the game end up making it worth buying.
Better than the sequel, that's for sure.

This series is criminally overlooked.
If you enjoy games like sudoku, you will thoroughly enjoy Hexcells. While a naive comparison, the game plays similarly to a very advanced Minesweeper. By the second act, though, you'll have discovered the futility of that comparison; this game is on an entirely different level and has an elegance in the solutions that random Minesweeper puzzles cannot ever hope to achieve.
The soundtrack is quite relaxing. It's really fun when you get on a "roll" of solving the puzzle, too, because you generate little ditties as a reward.
The entire Hexcells series contains puzzles that are among the greatest I've ever solved. I highly recommend the entire collection, and also very strongly recommend that you start with this one. Don't worry if you breeze through this installment; I put a little over three hours into this one and Plus took me over 15. All of the concepts you'll need to beat the series are introduced here, too, so there are no surprises down the road -- it's almost like a tutorial.
Definitely worth your purchase.

Probably the most freeform spell casting game I've ever played. You get access to a number of different magical elements and can then create different (usually lethal) effets by combining various elements on-the-fly. The effects will also differ depending on how you then release the spell (just straight up casting, casting it as AoE, enchanting your weapon) and so on.
The different elements interact, for the most part, in a very reasonable way, which is probably the only reasonable thing in this game. It's full of weird nonsense language, friendly fire, tons of ways to die, quirky humor and lots of enemies to blow up.
Some highlights are:
- The ability to create healing mines which then explode and throw you (or a teammate) off the screen to your doom.
- The ability to electrocute yourself to death, just because you tried using lightning while you were wet.
- The ability to die from setting yourself on fire.
- The ability to drown because you accidentally thawed the frozen river you were crossing on foot.
- The ability to cross streams with a teammate and cause an explosion that kills you (or someone else).
- The ability to cast meteor showers that kills almost everything on screen, including yourself.
- People who are not vampires.
It's messy, it gory, it's full of accidental death and it's a ton of fun, especially in 2-4 player multiplayer.

I love the multidirectionality of Hexcells: solving a single cell can affect three lines of cells, as well as the set of surrounding cells. At first, it felt much like a hexagonal version of Minesweeper. When the lines were added, I was reminded of nonograms / paint-by-numbers puzzles. Then, as the puzzles continued, my mind became so occupied with the intersecting logic that I stopped trying to compare it to other games at all.
It may be worth skipping this and going directly to Hexcells Plus. First, if you get easily addicted to logic puzzles, Hexcells Plus will keep you thinking for much, much longer. Second, Hexcells Plus' difficulty ramps up slowly and consistently, never adding more than a few techniques at a time. The puzzle difficulty from the original Hexcells increases smoothly at first, but jumps dramatically in the second half. It's a great challenge, but also changes the rhythm of play.

I've rated this review negative, but I wouldn't say it's a bad game. Quite the contrary, I think it has great potential (yes, it's the three words that doom a game: "has great potential") but it's been acted out badly. So, an snap review after a few hours of gaming, here we go!
GAMEPLAY
Oriental Empires is a Civ-like game set in China with Total War-esque battles fought out and predetermined tactics for your troops' useage. This is a great idea for a strategy 4X, but there are a few problems - namely, and in order of importance,
1: AI
2: Battle Endings
3: UI
So, the AI - this game's main problem. The AI is an absolute cakewalk! I mean, I may have some bias as an avid (if somewhat amateur) Paradox player, but on my first game on a random map, normal difficulty, I got a Son of Heaven victory at around turn 20 - Han submitted as a vassal after a brief and easy defensive war and I just paid off the other nearby Dynasty/Civ to recognise me as Emperor! This is considering that it is a 300 turn game (average), and I won in about 7% of that time! IN MY FIRST GAME! ON NORMAL MODE!
Next, battle endings - while battles are epic, the ends are basically your (usually victorious) units running around for ages. It's annoying.
Finally for Gameplay, the UI - it just dosen't tell you anything! You aren't accurately told people's opinions of you, you don't know why you can't settle in certain places... TELL ME!
On the other hand, the blend of TBS GSG and RTS is great, and works to make battles both more impactful and more player-controlled, if not totally in your hands. This helps you win the great victories you never could in Civ because "arbitrary rules", and adds to both historicity and immersion.
5/10
GRAPHICS
Basically, they're nice, but not AAA by any means - more variation in animations, soldier uniforms, and texturing would be lovely. On the other hand, zooming in to your cities and seeing all your little subjects at work is cool...
7.5/10
STABILITY
While mostly stable, the game does have the odd game-breaking glitch - examples include being unable to move the map, and the map simply not loading on Game start. To be completely fair, it is early access, so I'll forgive it.
7.5/10
OVERALL
65% needs so much improvement, yet has so much potential!

While by no means a bad game, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is plagued by uninteresting characters, a less than stellar story, and many questionable and/or outright poor game design choices. Most of my play time in this game is in The Handsome Collection on the Xbox One, but that doesn't change my thoughts on the game at all. Many of the levels are incredibly frustrating to navigate or just deal with in general, and the necessity of grinding means you'll be spending a lot of time in these poorly-designed areas. The difficulty curve is incredibly erratic as well, so while one level may be very easy the next could be borderline impossible and invoke a Dark Souls level of bashing your head against the wall repeatedly until it breaks. The Grinder is a pathetically easy mechanic to break, and makes it incredibly trivial (if slightly tedious) to get the rarest loot in the game. The game just doesn't have nearly as much depth to it as Borderlands 2 did, and I'd only recommend buying it if it's deeply discounted and you have a lot of patience.

I've played this to death, so when I ask myself "Play Deus Ex?" the answer is now "Nah.", and this would negatively color my judgment. But if I really ask myself, I'd have to say that this is by far my favorite game of all time. I must have done more than 20 complete play-throughs, and that's a conservative estimate.
This is (so far) the best execution of what happens to be my favorite kind of game: The lone wolf 1st person 3D experience. An immersive setting with story background and world simulation where I can (within tight limits) do whatever I want. Bonus points if I am somewhat a special/superior character, however borderline pathetic that may sound.
So much for the review of this game.
Games that satisfy some of the above criteria:
And quite a few more. BUT NOT ENOUGH! Seriously, this kind of gameplay - if it's well done, you will get my money. I'm thirsty enough to even dwell on crappy such products like Far Cry 3/4 which are very obviously a theme park and very obviously uninspired.
While I'm making wishes - what I very much desire to come into existence:
. No wait you don't know what I mean: Did you ever create a monster grinder in Minecraft? What's great about that is that the world's elements and simulation are intuitively used to create a considerably different additional element in the world. All of a sudden, you have a ginormous machine in which you constantly hear monsters die, and you get their drops in a central outlet. So, what do I mean when I say "mix of Deus Ex gameplay and Minecraft"?
The best way to demonstrate this is to point out a key difference between Deus Ex: Human Revolution and its predecessors. In DX:HR, the automatic turrets can not just be hacked (which is cool but possible in all DX games), but you can
which allows to create new strategic situations. This is emergent gameplay! I must say that DX:HR's use of this aspect is a bit underdeveloped, but anyway: That's an example of you using elements in the world intuitively to alter the game's situations.
So, what if you could build traps (camera wired with explosives; if certain characters are seen, the explosives go off)? Or you could take a terminal and reprogram/reconfigure it somehow. A fully destructible environment would be cool, too: Realize that so far, when this has been done, the destruction was just far too easy. In reality, if you'd explode a LAM on a wall of the 'ton hotel, it would wear down the wall,
even knock out a small part of it, but overall you'd do little damage. And shooting a whole magazine into a wall would not make a hole in it.
So, what if a realistic form of destructibility and ability to construct (Requiring the right tools and considering weight limits, so no way you can carry around a wall.) were part of the game? What if the machinery you deal with in the end of Deus Ex (1) is somewhat really functioning with its water pumps and such, instead of the buttons just being facade that drive the story? What if in Doom 3, if a firefight damages the pipes and cables around you too much, a side-mission emerges completely naturally/logically: Before you can progress, you have to repair stuff.
Do you have any idea how incredibly high the replayability of THOSE games would be? Deus Ex with its fixed world is already high in this regard, but with a more modular world, we'd do real damage to the game market economy :)
An additional bonus would be this: 3D game worlds are only facades. Maybe you don't notice, but when you explore a new game world, you actively try to find out which types of doors (or whatever element) are real and which types are only decoration. This factor alone considerably lowers immersion, because even if visually nothing negatively changes to you, you're still looking at the world through these filter glasses instead of just
. But if the game world would consist of Minecraft-like objects (Not necessarily cubes. E.g. a placed computer terminal object could have its corresponding shape.), you'd know that everything is real, every "door block" (or whatever) would fundamentally be like any other door block. And you'd know that the wall is not paper thin with a hall-of-mirrors void behind it, but there is always substance.
Minecraft survival is great (Let's ignore creative mode here, and let's also mostly ignore the ability to build.), and 1st person story shooter games are great, what's still COMPLETELY MISSING (Seriously, WTF? Do you realize how crass this is?) is games that mix the two properly. We have plenty of multiplayer destructive environment shooters, but we don't have such a thing as a single player experience in a realistic environment with story and not too much fighting. That's a completely unwritten book. An entire genre waiting to be created, ground waiting to be broken, gaming history waiting to be written.

Stealth game with unusual narrative: you become a murderer who simply wants a sleep... by killing those noisy party-goer neighbors.
The stealth mechanics, 1980s electronic music and the pixel graphic remind me of Hotline Miami, except that this one's story is rather simple and the missions are rather short (I beat the game in 7,5 hours). However it is still as challenging (and frustrating) as Hotline Miami, making you trying and trying all over again.
As the other reviewer has said, it takes a while to figure out the game mechanics, especially figuring out the AI behavior and line of sight. Sometimes you thought you're well hidden behind a barrier, but turns out the barrier isn't an actual inobstructable wall--so the AI's vision passed it through. As soon as you figured it out though, it wouldn't be too hard to use it for your tactical advantage.
The game has a number of unlockable characters and the Steam Workshop contents are quite numerous. Not to mention as the game randomizes the trap location each time you play the missions, it opens up different ways to beat the missions, making the game has its own replay value.
If you've always been bothered by noisy neighbors, try this one.

Deus Ex is truly a masterpiece. Despite the name there is no Deus Ex Machina effect whatsoever - everything is logical and consequential and every detail is a piece of whole - user's password can tell you about his life more than you can hear from anyone, organisation name contains a key to it's entrance, and internet adresses hint major plot twist. The world of demolished Lady Liberty is surprisingly and eerily real both in it's behaviour and as a very possible future of ours. It also one of the most stylish worlds out there. Without overusing design cliches and descending into self repetition it keeps cold, metallic demanaur faintly lit by distant LED lights and blue ROM module colloids from the start to the end. And the wonderful tracker soundtrack by Alexander Brandon and Michel van de Bos is making perfect - transcendent.
As for the gameplay. On the first glimpse arsenal is quite poor - less than ten types of firearms, couple of throwables, few melee choices and array of tools - but what this game about is you, as a player, as a character. Main tool in your arsenal is your head - numerous ways to approach the objective are only multiplied by your skills and the most useful tool in game - augmentations, which allow you to perform superhumane tasks such as invisibility, wind speed combined with impossible jump height or even projectile-stopping nanite shield - everything is in your hands. But beware that you are limited not only by supply of bioelectricity, but also with finite augmentation possibilities. The brighter you burn the faster you expire and one possibilities take take place of anothers. So at the end your head - is your main tool and weapon
.

Below is a comparison to Overwatch:
So what is the difference between Paladins and Overwatch you ask? Don't say Paladins is an Overwatch clone and don't say Overwatch is Paladins clone please, being in the same genre, both games are bounded to have similiarities. Just like so many moba characters are similar.
The gameplay:
Comparing both games, Overwatch's TTK is lower than Paladins. This means that the same mistake in Overwatch may not be as punishing as Paladins. For example, if you walk around the wrong corner, in Overwatch, you are probably dead before you know it. In Paladins, you can probably react and escape with some health, or even outplay the enemy team. If you prefer fast pace games, Overwatch would definitly be your game, however, Overwatch does have a ridiculus amounts of 1-2 hit KO, which can be extremely furstrating.
To counter the enemy team, in Overwatch, you simply switch heroes. This can be frustrating at times as the game can resort to a hero swap fest. In Paladins, if you mess up the draft phase, you are semi-screwed, however, you can use instead an item system where you buy items to counter hero comps. Sometimes, in Paladins, you may just face that one situation where you can't do anything, but in general, Paladin's way of countering compositions take more strategy.
Out of combat health regeneration is something that Paladins have while Overwatch avoids, rather, Overwatch went for the health packs. In Paladins, if you stay out of combat for long enough, you start recovering health, while Overwatch, you don't recover health and have to depend more on healers and health packs.
Graphics:
Paladins' graphics are more on the fantasy side while Overwatch's graphics are on the Sci-fi side. In terms of graphics, I say Overwatch definitely has the upper hand. Though be warn though, if you are just a casual gamer and your PC or laptop isn't the best for gaming, you may find yourself having to lower that quality on Overwatch just to get those precious fps.
Price:
Overwatch costs $40 whereas Paladins is free. Though for the sake of comparison, since Overwatch comes with all heroes, we will assume you also buy the founder's pack. So in the end, Overwatch will cost arond $20 dollars more if you want both games to have all heroes unlocked. It isn't really hard to unlock champions in Paladins to be honest, what you will find hard is the essence grind for all your legendary cards. The card system is slightly pay-to-win, though end-game, everyone's going to be on a leveled playfield.
Overall, Overwatch is a polished, beautifully made game at the moment, however Paladins' progress in improving in my opinion is definely better than Overwatch. I go with Paladins because I like the game mechnics more and in the near future, I'll say Paladins will completely surpass Overwatch.

Deus Ex is truly a masterpiece. Despite the name there is no Deus Ex Machina effect whatsoever - everything is logical and consequential and every detail is a piece of whole - user's password can tell you about his life more than you can hear from anyone, organisation name contains a key to it's entrance, and internet adresses hint major plot twist. The world of demolished Lady Liberty is surprisingly and eerily real both in it's behaviour and as a very possible future of ours. It also one of the most stylish worlds out there. Without overusing design cliches and descending into self repetition it keeps cold, metallic demanaur faintly lit by distant LED lights and blue ROM module colloids from the start to the end. And the wonderful tracker soundtrack by Alexander Brandon and Michel van de Bos is making perfect - transcendent.
As for the gameplay. On the first glimpse arsenal is quite poor - less than ten types of firearms, couple of throwables, few melee choices and array of tools - but what this game about is you, as a player, as a character. Main tool in your arsenal is your head - numerous ways to approach the objective are only multiplied by your skills and the most useful tool in game - augmentations, which allow you to perform superhumane tasks such as invisibility, wind speed combined with impossible jump height or even projectile-stopping nanite shield - everything is in your hands. Crayfish, also known as crawfish, crawdads, freshwater lobsters, or mudbugs, are freshwater crustaceans resembling small lobsters, to which they are related; taxonomically, they are members of the superfamilies Astacoidea and Parastacoidea. They breathe through feather-like gills and are found in bodies of water. Some species are found in brooks and streams where there is fresh water running, while others thrive in swamps, ditches, and rice paddies. Most crayfish cannot tolerate polluted water, although some species such as Procambarus clarkii are hardier. Crayfish feed on living and dead animals and plants.
The name "crayfish" comes from the Old French word escrevisse (Modern French écrevisse). The word has been modified to "crayfish" by association with "fish" (folk etymology). The largely American variant "crawfish" is similarly derived.
Some kinds of crayfish are known locally as lobsters, crawdads, mudbugs, and yabbies. In the Eastern United States, "crayfish" is more common in the north, while "crawdad" is heard more in central and southwestern regions, and "crawfish" further south, although there are considerable overlaps.
The study of crayfish is called astacology.
In Australia (on the eastern seaboard), New Zealand and South Africa, the term crayfish or cray generally refers to a saltwater spiny lobster, of the genus Jasus that is indigenous to much of southern Oceania, while the freshwater species are usually called yabby or kōura, from the indigenous Australian and Māori names for the animal respectively, or by other names specific to each species. Exceptions included Western Rock Lobster of the Palinuridae family found on the west coast of Australia; from the Parastacidae family Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish found only in Tasmania, and the Murray crayfish found on Australia's Murray River.
In Singapore, the term crayfish typically refers to Thenus orientalis, a seawater crustacean from the slipper lobster family. True crayfish are not native to Singapore, but are commonly found as pets, or as an invasive species (Cherax quadricarinatus) in the many water catchment areas, and are alternatively known as freshwater lobsters.

Supports are great with healing but getting a different kind of support would be vastly interesting, like one that can help with cooldowns or can place faster traveling areas like a zipline from capture point to a safe distance. A strong strength character able to provide area knockback and do just pure melee or a bit like Zhin. A VERY cool little 4X game. It takes a zoom system similar to a game like Ruse, the core gameplay tenets of a Civilization, and adds some flair of its own for a really interesting combination. Coming in as a fan of Romance of the Three Kingdoms games, I'm excited to be able to experience this setting from its roots in the early bronze age all the way through its early post-imperial age, and it's doing a good job of really pulling me into the setting.
The addition of characters (including your leader and potential heirs) and real-time military engagements, complete with a plethora of behavioral options for each of your military units, make for a couple of strong layer additions to the traditional 4X formula. Both elements are executed elegantly and feel "right" in the context of the game's other systems.
Battle is a unique combination of 4X turn-based placement strategy, operational settings and a little luck, as stacks of units form armies that spread across the surrounding area of the map in real time when contacting enemies, behaving in battle according to the behaviors you've set for each unit. I've yet to get to diplomacy or mid-game economics and policy, but according to everything I've seen of the game so far, I don't expect them to disappoint.
And just to top it all off, it LOOKS really great for a 444 MB download. It does a superb job of recreating period architecture and regional flora. Seasons come and go, and each is rendered beautifully. On my graphics settings, it's far from graphically groundbreaking, but it looks magnificent in a way all its own.
Even more impressive is how it manages to scale everything - buildings, mountains, individual people in units - in a way that makes everything look realistically proportioned against everything else, something most 4X games don't even bother attempting. It makes the micro/macro zoom feature so beautiful. I love being able to observe the vast empire I've built from up high, then step down on the literal ground level to look at a particular city or battle up close. How many 4X games do you know that let you walk the streets of your cities? :)
Definitely worth my money. I can't wait to see it at its fully completed state, it's already a fantastic addition to my library.

Pros:
*It's a platforming Roguelike, you can play it with a mouse and keyboard (I prefer this method) OR you can play it via controllers (Still good, just don't play slime girl with it, she's better with keyboard and I'll explain why later) and it's concept is pretty simple one to grasp.  You jump on stuff, shoot bad guys, jump on more stuff, shoot more bad guys... collect powerups via chests, stores, POW guys.  Navigate a Randomly generated series of rooms, kill boss- do this 7ish times.
*Thematically, it's fun - I love the character designs, all characters play rather differently (or different enough), the game has some bit of attitude in it's rather extensive lore...(though I feel like with the way you unlock pieces of lore I would hope there is a deeper rooted backstory).  The designs are somewhat refreshing, overally aesthetically this game is kinda cool.
*You die a lot, but you get persistant upgrades with an exp bar that does not reset on death.  After horribly maiming yourself a dozen times the game does start to pick up speed while being challenging yet not COMPLETELY dependant on upgrades.  If you're some gaming prodigy you probably can knock this game out in a few goes - also you don't have to die in order to get the permanent upgrades and you can technically farm a level a little bit.  (Farming sucks as a mandatory mechanic but I accept it as an option for the sake of having the option)
*Couch CoOp - If you can give your friends a 5 minute crash  course in how to play, you can essentially get a team going.  Provided you have friends.
*If you don't have friends because you smell bad and nobody loves you, there is online multiplayer.
*Power Ups that you gain and find in the level are substantial enough to feel a difference in power when playing.
*Blue Projectiles only hurt enemies, Red only hurts players, Yellow Hurts everyone - This is important and anice simple way to keep track of the onslaught of bullets sometimes.
Cons:
*Single Player can get boring or broken sometimes - It feels like it's fun for a couple of sessions but then you find the need to put it down and do something else after maybe dying a couple of times or playing a couple of levels.
*Tiny as hell graphics, I love the design choice but at the same time it's hard to tell what is what on the screen.  Also some enemies are tiny as hell and hard to read.  The game does amazingly well in clearly displaying projectiles as "HEY THIS IS RED OR YELLOW DON'T TOUCH IT" but the Melee attacks from the enemies don't really have any indicators to show they are attacking and as tiny as some of these enemies are... you sometimes simply can't tell.
*Couch CoOp is fine, however one thing I don't care for with the controller inputs is with the mouse and keyboard we have some sort of crosshair or aiming mechanism- witht he controller we don't.  Also I would prefer there be a shoot button than just leaning the right thumbstick.  It's alright for anyone with rapid fire but it makes characters with an actual reload rate a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play especially solo.
*Multiplayer online is dead, extremely dead.  There is no one- but then again with the price point what it is- I don't see the multiplayer scene expanding any time soon...or ever.
So in reality, it's a good game for what it is- but I think honestly the price really hindered what could have been easily a developed cult classic with some fine tweaking.

While certainly a bit rough round the edges in the graphical department these days, Deus Ex still manages to impress a decade and a half on from its release. It's an incredibly ambitious game, and most of the ambition comes from its narrative themes. The setting is the near future-ish 2050s; world governments have all but practically collapsed and the corporations have taken over, themselves controlled from the shadows by secret societies pushing their agendas of peace through a subtle form of dictatorship. Within this new world order is the trans-humanism culture, where people are able to get augmented and become relatively nuanced cyborgs. But of course, augmentation isn't open to everyone who want it and isn't agreed with fundamentally by certain sects of society, so this sets up a multi-way conflict as to where the future of trans-humanism goes. And as a deadly virus has been unleashed in North America, a new threat has emerged on top of the battle of humanity's future, and at the start of game, you the protagonist are sent by a shady government organisation to investigate who's behind the virus outbreak and why.
Thus begins a globe-trotting adventure of lengths rarely seen in most action-adventure games or even RPG main storylines of today. Your character, which you can bizarrely choose your own name for, is JC Denton, a clone stuffed full of augmentations and looking like a cross between Riddick and Neo from the Matrix. As this is an RPG game, Denton starts off merely passable at most things and needs to work at his skills by leveling up. Experience points can be garnered from completing objectives, exploring the spacious maps and hub worlds, performing admirably on missions and completing side quests. There are skills which boost your hacking, lockpicking and computer abilities, your aptitude with various weapon types, your resistance to damage and environmental hazards and your ability to swim, which should be avoided because it's rarely necessary. The RPG mechanics are relatively basic but allow you to approach the game in different ways and afford multiple playthroughs.
The way you play does influence the story to a certain degree, though I wouldn't say it goes to the level Alpha Protocol ever did. That game was a landmark game mainly because it handled the concept of choice so well in a video game. Deus Ex offers a certain level of choice+consequence but overall, the main story progresses linearly enough to focus on it's core narrative threads, with you for the most part along for the rollercoaster ride. The world is set up in a way which makes it sensible, at least in the beginning, to play as a pacifist and avoid conflict as much as possible. Indeed, you are rewarded with experience and more gadgets if you choose this route. However, as the story takes a more complicated turn, violence usually erupts even if you will it not to, and it'll soon make sense to approach situations with with some running-shooting-grenading action (especially when super-soldiers turn up about 2/3rds of the way through the game).
The game is more fun, I found, by sneaking and playing pacifist for the first act of the game before going a bit more gung-ho for the remainder. Once I'd levelled up a bit and was strong enough to wield assault guns, snipers and energy swords, I found myself enjoying the rather simple yet fun classic-FPS style gameplay. Deus Ex came out in that little golden age of FPS games which tried something new with the genre, like System Shock 2 and Thief, or improved massively on the labourious and tedious gameplay of early 90s shooters by developing physics and polishing up the environments to be more than just a load of rooms connected together. As such, the solid FPS mechanics soon mesh well with the RPG elements once you've gotten strong enough in your appropriate skills so you aren't missing a dude from 5 inches away.
The core gameplay is still relatively solid despite it's age, then. However, AI is rubbish, and most enemies and civilians stand about doing nothing, having no patrol routes or routines. I forgive it for that though, it was 2000 and I believe even as it was, the game needed a supercomputer to run at any playable speed back then. There are some rather annoying quirks with the non-lethal crossbow. Hit an enemy and he flails around for almost a minute, giving him ample opportunity to get a colleague of his to raise the alarm. Yeah, not that stealthy at all, which leaves only the prod or the baton as reliable alternatives for stealthy runs, which with practice you CAN take the entire level's worth of enemies down with silently.
The majority of the environments aren't that impressive these days. It's mostly dull, brown city streets and grey/blue secret underground bases that you find yourself in. The one thing which broke the monotonous Invisible War storyline was the fact you went to Antarctica and not just in secret bases underneath the damn place. Of course, unlike its sequel, there are many alternate entrances, shortcuts and secret areas in the original's maps. Outside the main narrative, a big and very interesting world is ready to comprehend off the beaten track, through emails, conversations with NPCs and books lying around.
So really, the main question is does Deus Ex stand up after 15 years of technological innovation? On the gameplay front alone, it's a little quirky but certainly not dated, as I felt that after playing most modern games and even it's amazing prequel, Human Revolution, that it's classic-FPS groundings with RPG stat building working alongside them is still a relatively fresh idea. It's story, meanwhile, is excellent and unique in every way and however much it ages, it's message and warnings of a possible real life scenario and more-accurate-than-most depictions of a society tearing itself apart remains as clear today as it did back in 2000. It scores points as well by being a computer RPG which broke away from the standard fantastical mould to try something new, morally complex and daring at the dawn of (we believed) an exciting new era as the millenium kicked off.
So Deus Ex remains a grand exploration into the concept of pushing the boundaries of what it means to be human, and also manages to be a damn fine game as well. Recommended? You betcha.

Verdict: An old school legend.
Arguably one of the greatest PC titles of its time, the influences of Deus Ex are still seen to this day.
While I have only recently played this game I was immediately sucked in to it despite its various flaws which, fortunately, are far from game breaking and are more or less symptomatic of less complicated times. The game rewards stealthy approaches where players may make use of tools to circumvent obstacles or, for the less patient, blast their way through the opposition. Although it is far more difficult to survive head on battles as the player character is fragile and weapons typically don't do the trick until skills as well as stat improving mods are invested in.
Level design is superb with many hidden nooks for secrets items to be found and the story holds a depth not seen often even in today's bustling gaming industry. Those familiar with Deus Ex: Human Revolution will find plenty of hallmarks here as conspiracy theories and hundreds of sub plots run rampant in a dark cyberpunk near-future.
I'd definitely recommend this title to those looking for a solid old-school experience and to fans of the franchise looking for more. Your money will be well spent.

Rogue Stormers does not hold your hand. There are no long tutorials telling you how to play the game. From the outset, prepare to kill or be killed. Some enemies are easy. Others require a lot of fire power. You get upgrades, and you got to choose whether to keep one or gamble on something else. You even got to decide about trading your health for upgrades.
The best experience is mouse and keyboard. Controller has a weird layout and needs getting used to, and you'll nonetheless  lose accuracy.
One funny detail is that the goblins come from an organization called Goop -- which, funny enough, is the "alternative medicine" company that Gwyneth Paltrow runs. I'd like to think, that in this universe, Goop enthusiasts ingested the wrong homeopathic herb, which turned them into a horde of killer goblins.
Another thing I love about this game is that you can play on almost any hardware released within the past 5 years. I managed to get it to run on my crappy HP Stream 11, which is runs a Celeron processor and has only 2GB of memory. It also runs great on my Lenovo ThinkPad T440p that runs on Ubuntu. And, of course, it also runs great on my desktop PC that runs on an i7 processor, with 16GB of RAM, and a GTX 1050 Ti.
Which brings me to the graphics. For a game that works on low end hardware, the artwork is beautiful. I enjoy the character models, the setting, and the various weapons effects.
Over all, this is a fun game. I rate it a 4/5.

Rogue Stormers is a side-scrolling, rouge-like, twin-stick shooter with 5 different playable characters; each with their own weapons and abilities. As you play with each character, you level them up and gain different perks, which themselves can be upgraded. The controls feel smooth, the colors are vibrant, bosses creative, and I can't complain about the music (though I listen to my own most of the time.) As for the difficulty of the game, I suppose it’s kind of hard (to begin with anyway.) You’re not going to beat the game in your first couple runs. Keep in mind that you are leveling up and gaining perks during your runs. Therefore your runs will get easier with that character over time. In each run, there’s also a bit of luck involved. Since the levels are procedurally generated, sometimes you will come across better items early and sometimes not. Though I don't think it makes the biggest difference, it doesn’t detract from the fun either. Similar to other rouge-likes, you have one life. If you die, you begin again from the first stage. Personally, I like this feature. After all, there are only 8 stages. Beating them all in one go, without checkpoints, is what feels accomplishing. As you play through each level, you can come across keys, chests, and stores. One thing that stood out to me in this game was the respawning of enemies. Being accustomed to Rogue Legacy before this, I was unsure how I felt about that. But to sum up, considering the game is $20.00 and so far I got over 20 hours of gameplay out of it, I'd say it's a justifiable price. The Summer sale of 2017 is currently going on, and at only $4.00 for this game, I'd say it's an easy yes to pick up.

This is, in a nutshell, a great little timekiller.
Basically you have a number of playable characters with which you go through a series of levels. You kill hordes of goblins and orcs. At the end of each level is a boss waiting for you. Every character has its own gimmick. They have varying stats as well as different weapons. They each have an ability with a specific cooldown period. One shoots a large barrage of little rockets, another gets a short period of immensely boosted firerate, to name two examples. To complement your play style, you find some secondary weapons, which get damaged and eventually broken as you sustain damage.
During your journey, you are given various powerups, either found in chests or purchased from item stores in each level. Every boss also drops one or two powerups for you. These last for the duration of your entire run. When you start a new game, they are gone and have to be collected over again. On the other hand, you get perks for each character through leveling them up. Needless to say, perks stay with your character forever, making them grow gradually stronger for every next run.
When you complete a level and go for the next one, you can stop and return later. Leaving a level uncompleted, however, will make you start from the beginning of that level. That is so even if you may have completed more than half of the level. This is how saves work in this game. You have to complete your current level or else you will start it over with the powerups from the previous level. This is not an issue though. At least for me. If you read through the other reviews, you can see that other people found it unpleasant. You decide. Reconsider getting this game, if you want a more precise spot-on save system. Levels are short and they gradually grow a little longer as you approach the final level. But all in all, you should be able to clear even the longest one in 15 minutes tops.
Now let's go on with some pros and cons:
+ Good variety of playable characters
+ Fun platforming
+ Pleasant visual appeal
+ Fairly good replay value
- Might get tiresome to play the same set of levels and kill the same range of enemies over and over again. The game could definitely use an expansion.
- Same with the selection of powerups available. It really wouldn't hurt to double the number of available upgrades. Off the top of my head, I can already think of interesting replacement weapons. They could be unlockable powerups or even readily available for new heroes. How about an activated version of the flail that is not just spinning around but swung around manually, for example?
In the end this game is worth the price tag and doesn't come with too many issues. It all comes down to lack of variety, which might be the only issue that will bother most people.

This is my favorite Total War game to date. A great setting, excellent gameplay, and good mechanics all rolled into one.

The Kingdoms expansion adds a lot more to the game, allowing you to play campaigns in the Batic, the Middle East (Crusader States), and even the Americas.
The game is also highly modable and has a ton of amazing mods you can download which offer so many new experiences. I'd recommend giving the Third Age mod and the Westeros: Age of Petty Kings mod each a try.
I highly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in the Middle Ages or strategy games. Really a first class Total War game.

Hexcells is an excellent game, I just made the mistake of playing the sequel
.
Hexcells, as the name implies, is all about hexagonal cells. Using logic you need to determine which of the orange hexes are blue underneath. You do this by using Minesweeper-like logic where a non-blue hex will tell you how many adjacent hexes are blue.
All the puzzles are completely logical and do not require guess work, which is a critical part of any good puzzle game.
As you progress through the 6 words some extra tricks are introduced that make the puzzles more complicated and more fun (for people who have already played Plus, everything you've seen there except the numbered blue hexes and the ?-hexes).
Should you get this game?
Generally: yes.
If you've already played Plus: As long as you don't expect to be challenged.
If you can only afford one of the Hexcells games: Maybe

Some compare Hexcells to Minesweeper, but it is not quite the same.  With Minesweeper, winning fells like the luck of the draw rather than a logic exercise.  Luck adds a certain flair to other types of games, but with puzzle games like this, it does not do the game any favors.  Fortunately, Hexcells does not make the player rely on luck to complete puzzles.
Hexcells forces you to use reason and logic to solve a puzzle.  The goal of each puzzle is to clear the orange hexagons to reveal a certain pattern.  The numbers in each cell indicate how many surrounding cells are part of the pattern (this is where the similarity to Minesweeper comes in).  As you progress, new elements are added.  These elements are reminsicent of Picross.  There is a number above the column that indicates how many cells in that column are part of the ultimate pattern.  There are also numbers in brackets that tell you how many cells are connected.  The puzzles also get larger.
This is a relaxing puzzle game that is definitely worth the time if you enjoy logic puzzles.  It took me about 4.5 hours to complete 30 puzzles.

I backed the Indie Graphics Bundle when it was a project on Kickstarter, back in the middle of 2012.
Like sound tracks on Steam, you are not really buying any sort of application, here. You're buying content that you download through Steam and then access directly. What you'll get here is a wide variety of graphics that can be used in  numerous projects in and out of game development.
In total, you (currently) will get more than 27,000 images in the colelctive three-pack bundle exceeding 9gb of content. There are a variety of art styles and countless subject matters, so if you take a browse before buying, something is sure to fit your needs. A lot of the work is intended to be mixed and matched, so you can many more whole things out of smaller components.
I don't know if I'll use any of the content in a final product, but I find myself referring to the bundle quite often for placement holder art. Incredibly useful if you're a coder and engineer, but not an artist. No more grey blobs or copy pasted clip-art for months, while you wait for your project to reach the point where you can involve an artist.
That is also where the cost comes in. Some may see the price (currently $99 USD) and scoff, but I think those people are ignoring that you are given the license to use this in your projects, without paying further for it. Have you ever commissioned artwork? Or even gone to an existing royalty-free clearing house to buy a limited license to some artwork you found on there? They usually come with a lot of strings and you can easily pay $40-100 for just *one* piece of artwork.  I paid more than this entire bundle costs, before, just to get a custom avatar drawn (head only). Hell, I paid nearly that much to have my logo (seen attached) designed. In this bundle, I paid maybe half of a penny per image.
If you don't know if you need or want this art bundle, then you probably don't. But you
if you do. And for the price, it's hard to pass up.

I didn't understand that the key in this game is to experiment, find a playstyle and weapon-combination that fits for you and most importantly try different routes to reach your goal. But once I understood all this, my experience with this game changed entirely... It became my favorite game of all time!
It is extremely satisfying each and every time you complete your objectives in this game. This is for one main reason, which games of today seem to have forgotten:
YOU completed the mission on your own, without being handheld by the game the whole time.
You found your own route and tactic to reach the objective and complete it. You don't just get a minimap in this game, or follow a questmarker till you reach your objective. No, you have to gather information, maps or drawings. You have to make notes, complete sidequests and search for hidden (and a bit less hidden) areas and paths. Long story short, you really feel accomplishment because you were the one who did all these things, you weren't just following a marker.
The gameplay of this game feels a bit old at times, but it is still fun and rather deep. You have a ton of different weapons, and they all fit to different playstyles. They all work pretty good, except for a few hit-detection issues with certain weapons. Augmentations are also a major part of the gameplay, but I'll let you figure out that part yourself :)
You can complete a level however you want, and there are a TON of ways you can play. You can be stealthy, a ruthless killing machine or an invisible hacker, or you can go with one of the countless different variations in between. It is a ton of fun, as you can play exactly as you like.
I don't have much to say about the story, because it is epic, exciting and thought provoking, and I am afraid to spoil anything for potential new Deus Ex players. Just believe me, it is good, and it changes according to your actions and choices throughout the game. It was mindblowing when it came out, and even today it stands out as one of the best stories gaming has to offer.
This has already dragged on for too long, as I expect most people to have heard more than enough about thIs game to know it is an old masterpiece and a legend in the gaming industry. I really hope that more people will experience this gem for the first time after reading this review. It is, and will probably keep being my favourite game of all time! :)
P.S. The game also has a superb soundtrack, really good stuff!

There are some things that only videogames can do. For me, Putt-Putt® Joins the Parade was emblematic of all of them. Where most games do their best to be something else – to tell a story like a novel, to impress with cinematic techniques like a film – Putt-Putt is pure game, a complete and darkly fascinating vision that makes no concessions to the modern conception of how games should be. Instead, it was an exploration of how games could be; how bleak, how twisted, how focused and – most famously – how challenging. Most developers take pains to protect you from failure. Humongous Entertainment turns it into an artform.
Putt-Putt® Joins the Parade is a brutal and demanding point and click action-RPG set in a world full of monstrous, disturbing things that are trying their hardest to end your life as quickly as possible. Using whatever weapons and armor you can scavenge, buy or forge, the challenge is to inch your way through this damned and deadly place, now and then coming across gigantic bosses that take especial valor and tenacity to kill. The eventual aim is to make it out alive, but there are about 50-60 hours of creative cruelty between you and that goal.
You will die, a lot. You will die on the end of a sword, on the edge of an axe, crushed by a boulder, impaled on fangs; you will be poisoned, eaten, stabbed, assassinated and pushed off cliffs. Death is everything in Putt-Putt. It's education, it's progress, it's the recurring stylistic and thematic motif that runs through all of its spectacularly varied, decaying and depraved environments. The first thing that you have to understand about this game is that survival is in itself a tremendous accomplishment. It can be punishing, cruel, sadistic and uncompromising. It can also be the purest, most thrilling adrenaline rush in gaming – it can take over your life and reward you like nothing else can. Exactly because your chances of success are so slim, each victory feels monumental.
The reviewer's job is difficult when it comes to a game like Putt-Putt. I simply can't unreservedly recommend that you buy it. It's not a game that you play to relax. It doesn't care in the slightest about whether you're enjoying yourself, and it doesn't give a fig for your notions of entertainment or your mental well-being. If you just play games for fun, this isn't for you, and no amount of insistence on my part is going to change that.
But if you're interested in the limits of the videogame form – to see just how focused, how pure and how uncompromising in its vision a game can be – Putt-Putt is unmissable. If you take the time get into Putt-Putt's mindset, to begin to understand the twisted way in which it operates and taste the rewards behind its cruellest challenges, this is one of the most thrilling, most fascinating and most completely absorbing experiences in gaming.

This pack is a MESS! I've read other reviews stating that the files are all over the place and that's pretty much true. There's no logic in the overall system on how the assets are stored, other than a general categorisation, while some assets could also belong to other categories. That means that you need to browse a lot when you're in need of assets for your game.
Then the comment that this pack also includes ALL assets from the other 2 packs (Character Creator - Graphics Pack & Space Galaxy - Graphics Pack) which I both reviewed as good. Those 2 packs hold around 6500 assets and this one just a bit over 20K. So for a bit over double the price you get a lot of extra assets!
Like those other 2 packs, these assets are NOT meant to copy/paste 1 on 1 into your game (though the platform tiles would allow you to). You do need to put in some extra work to model them into what you want them to be and make the game look more 'your own' than just a cheap copy/paste result with assets that have been used in other games.
Couple of (negative) comments on the pack though
- Why on earth are there over 1500 assets of crystal gems that are all looking quite the same while it's only 13 different gems?
- Why are there hammer parts in the weapon creation pack (good pack in general IMO) while there's no wooden stick to connect them to (can make it myself, but WHY?)
- Why make icon packs and give them all different dimensions?
- Why make an platform pack that feels incomplete (though in general is well made)
Also worth to note, the pack is NOT worth the default price of €135. But I picked it up on the Stream Summer Sale for €34, which is more around the worth of the pack...

So,let me explain a few thing before we dwelve into the review,mmkay?
This game is an elderly piece,espically since it came out start of second millenia (in gaming years anything 5+ years is elderly).So you will expect issues if you're not used to millenia age game (i.e right mouse button is use instead of "e" or etc.).Easily fixable in keyboard and mouse settings,so your modern age controls are there :).Although,this is clunky and glitchy on modern systems (download New Vision mod instead of Revision ((TRUST ME)) ).
So how's the game?
Damn good! The story is rough to get into from the first mission,the introduction will confuse you,but you will understand everything by fourth mission.JC Denton has no emotion,but that's the player,he's suppost to represent YOU! It dosesn't break immersion as you (suprising for a anicent game).
Summary of the plot?
You're JC Denton,or whatever you picked your name as,but you will be always called JC Denton.JC is a starter for  U.N.A.T.C.O (United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition Operations) based in Liberty Island.JC is an nano-augmented agent,the prototype per say for the new generation of augmentations,your brother Paul is also augmented like you.You can see the diffrence between generations,as Agent Navarre and Agent Hermann are mechanically augmented (you will meet them in UNATCO Headquaters).So what is UNATCO's job? Their job is to protect and distribute the vaccine Ambrosia,manufactured by VersaLife,due to a massive plague,known as "Grey Death".Thing is,a domestic terrorist group known as "N.S.F" (National Secessionist Federation,they want to seced from the Union) keep stealing the shipments.As the best duo for the job,you and your brother are signed to deal with these missing shipments,but something seems off about your brother.As you get deeper to the roots about the NSF,your brother uncovers a massive conspiracy involving an secret society called "Majestic 12" who is possibly behind the dystopia that has ravashed the world and even the "Grey Death".
Gameplay?
Gameplay is an FPS/RPG hybrid with an optional stealth mechanics (IMO,stealth for advanced players).You have your skills and augmentations,now you can't get every skill mastered and every augmentation available,you have to decide on the skills and augmentations you want for your playthrough (I.E skills:Lockpicking,Electronics;Augs:Regeneration,Cloak).So it makes it very interesting on how you choose,and makes multiple playthroughs possible by learning about diffrent augmentations to use.As for the maps,they look small,but in turn they are very big when it calls for the little nooks and crannies that are in the map,play again to find that recoil upgrade!
Graphics? The game looks old,still up to date?
*sigh*
The game runs on a modified Unreal Engine 1 engine.Of course it looks dated,but the New Vision mod helps by adding new textures to certain things that needs visual upgrades (avoiding the Revision mod).I've gotten past everything by focusing more on gameplay and story.
Worth it?
Oh yes,definetly! This game is worth multiple playthroughs,due to being so big and complex! I'm on my whatever number playthrough.Absolutley worth the very cheap purchase!
Multiplayer? Mods?
Gamespy shut down the multiplayer back in 2014,but a community-made patch has fixed this and it is better than ever!
As for mods,there is mod support,but I have no clue on the current state of that,only ones I know that were popular was Nameless Mod and Malkovian.So don't expect and total skyrim-esque mods.

I remember buying this game on the developer's site and as soon as it arrived on Steam, I was excited to play it again. Although there weren't any additions or changes made (other than a bug that was fixed from the direct only version), Lucky Rabbit Reflex! (LRR) is as great a game as I remember. ^^
LRR is basically a visual novel with dating sim elements. You play as the new female student starting her final year of college (in the US, it would be the final year of high school) in a new school. There are a total of 6 guys that you can date although only 4 of these guys you'll find in the school. The other two you'll have to search elsewhere. Also, there are a total of 5 girls that you can become BFFs with. The dating sim elements include, of course, asking each of the guys on a date on Saturdays or asking one of the girls to hang out with them as well as stat grinding. There are 4 different stats you can grind but you must make sure that the stress level doesn't get too high or else the MC will be more likely to fail at raising certain stats.
Although the art itself did put me off from buying this game for a while, the story and gameplay more than made up for it. I liked that you can achieve multiple endings with most of the guys. Four of the guys have three different endings-a best end, a good end, and a dual end. The dual end happens if you're trying to romance said character and another certain guy at the same time. I haven't seen this possibility in many VNs/dating sims. Also, one of the guys is a secret character so you have to figure out who it is and how to romance him although the developer's site does have a walkthrough of this game if you're trying to achieve a certain ending or pursue a possible character. So basically, what really hooked me to this game was the multiple playthroughs you can have although I liked the story that I read for each dateable male character. Each one of them had me hooked to his story although I'll admit that I liked certain ones more than others.
Overall, I'd highly recommend buying LRR if you're a fan of VNs, dating sims, etc. A lot of play time can be had from this game so it's well worth the money. ^^

Recommended if you enjoy a fairly straightforward otome visual novel / stat raising game.  Detailed enough to get to know the various characters and doesn't feel too short.  Not a lot of surprises, but I thought it was good - I don't always need or want harrowing and dark, and these characters actually seemed to act more like normal people (of 17-19) than in many games.
Pros:
+ Enough unique features/plots in the different storylines to be interesting as you try to complete the different endings
+ Likeable characters
+ Generally well-written (and the dialogue was more realistic than usual)
+ UK setting (I really enjoyed the setting and the slang - so many games are set either in Tokyo or the US)
+ The endings (Best, Good and "Dual") were quite well done; I thought the "dual" endings were a neat touch
+ The intro to the game pokes fun at itself...
Cons:
- The artwork takes getting used to; many people have criticized the strange chins and it *is* a distraction (but I found many of the CGs were fine)
- Parts of the game are pretty repetitive
- Not sure why you can "fail" when attempting to improve a skill, since you can just save and reload
Overall:  Glad I bought and played it, sorry I'm just about done.

A stealth game with a very simple premise: Kill everyone. However there are some challenges and incentives to make it more interesting, like cops and bouncers trying to stop you, or hiding the bodies to avoid the next victims from panicking. However all of this is pretty optional, and unless the game or a challenge asks for certain requeriments you can strategize the stages however you like. Is not a really difficult game once you know your resources and character behavior. It also has a small RNG to build the stages and provide different assets from one playthrough to another, giving you more options to kill although might conflict with achievement hunting. Finally, the community can work on their own stages, giving even more play time.
However the game is not perfect, and has some techincal issues. The AI is a bit iffy, with victims getting stuck running into walls, to certain areas able to exploit the cops' behavior. It also has some graphical glitches with dead characters looking alive. There's also some small issues with achievement unlocks i think, as i got the All Achievements one when i still have a few left, while others might or might not be unlocked by community stages.
Overall a fun game which shouldn't take much time to beat all its stages, but with various options and possibilities to goof arround. If anything it might seem chaotic in the most convoluted stages to the point you might not notice enemies or even lose where your character is. But in an hour of playthrough you'll be entertained despite any several retries to get certain kills.
