There is a lot this game does right, and it felt lovely playing it for a while. But for me there are too many things that need to be improved before i recommend this game.
Improve Diplomacy:
I like how the enemy AI is very opportunistic, attacking you when it senses a weakness, but other than that it's very dull and has no depth whatsoever. And no meaning either. I paid an enemy 700 gold (was cheap) for 50 rounds of peace only to have him declare war on me again 5 turns later. He should atleast get some penalty or diplomatic consequences from other nations. It feels like no matter what i do diplomatically, it won't effect my strategy. I can go to war if i want. Or not. It doesnt really change much except how many units i have to manage.
Improve Battle Mechanics:
And managing these units is just as dull. The different unit strategies are cool and seem to work so-so ok in battle... but in siege mode it's chaos! I don't really know what's going on sometimes. Nothing makes sense and it doesn't feel like a siege at all. How can my archers light their palisades on fire before i reasearched the fire arrow? And how can a couple of peasant rebels who JUST spawned this turn, prevent my main army (who luckily happened to be one turn away from the turned city) from marching toward the city to reclaim it? No matter what I command, my army will be distracted like a moth by a light and chase after those peasants only to have them withdraw and everyone return to where they started at the beginning of the turn. Over and Over, until my main army joins the rebels. I could have crushed the peasants and the turned city but now i've somehow lost everything. The AI priorities are seriously messed up. They shouldn't auto engage like that (or auto pillage farms!). Also, very often during battle you'll have 1 unit fighting the enemy unit while your other units stand and watch, but it KINDA works if you chose 'outflank'. So the strategies seem to work, but the units scatter all over the place because they don't really follow the route designated by you until AFTER the battle.
Improve City Management:
City Managment is confusing. What it needs most is some sort of citizen/work management. I completely crippled a city because i built 2 gold mines there first. Then I had no more citizens to build a farm and couldn't grow more citizens. I had to demolish a gold mine and rebuild. Instead of being able to momentarily turn off the gold mine's production. I also don't understand how to give my farmers a break, like the game often recommends me to, when i can't turn off farms or manage anything. Unhappiness just grows silently in the background and i can't really tell where it's coming from except for the very vague info you get. Make it more clear overall, more viewable and more managable.
Steam Workshop: If you can't fix this game, maybe the modders will. They will definitely make it more interesting long-term.
The game could be really good, and i hope they fix it as it IS early access after all. It would be a shame if it didn't improve. The Civ/Total War hybrid idea is awesome and it feels very nice establishing the first few cities and getting the trade routes up and running and all, a very good pace somehow, but then it just gets dull. It lacks overall depth. The game doesn't reward you for your choices / strategy. You just earn money and build. Neither other nations, nor your army, nor citizens seem to react to anything you do.

A First Person Time Travel Puzzle Game!
Puzzle design:
Pretty decent actually. Not amazing, but way better than a lot of other puzzle games I played. Most of the levels are fairly straight-forward, but some will make you stop and think and make you feel like you accomplished something after completing them. There are almost no annyoing levels ("do this simple trick 10 times!" "backtrack the same path back and forth multiple times!") and most levels are short and can be solved in less then a minute if you know the solution already. The tutorial levels are probably the weakest one in the game since they are super hand-holdy (the game actually walks you through the first few levels step-by-step).
Mechanics:
The time-travel mechanics work fairly well. The animations could be sped up a bit and unfortunately sometimes your clones get out of sync when you rewind time (which is a freaking shame in a time-travel puzzle game). You can avoid those problems by playing carefully and not rushing every move you do, so it is not game breaking.
A lot of levels also include a gun (and enemys to shoot). This is not a shooter though. The gun and the enemys just server as an additional puzzle mechanic and it works quite well for that.
Audio/Video/Performance:
The game is certainly not a high-quality-big-budget product. The graphics are servable and the voice acting is not annoying, so it does not hamper the puzzle experience. The game runs very well and should be fine on lower-spec machines as well.
Story:
The story seems interesting but is kind of disconnected from the gameplay. It's a dialoge between the protagonist and another character. However they mostly talk about how you got here and now what you are doing here. This results in a situation where you could just listen to the story without even playing the game and it would make totally sense.

I'm not much for writing reviews, but Nier:Automata deserves every ounce of praise given to it and more.
What is it?
-- It is hack/slash RPG with a simple combat system that shows remarkable depth over time.
-- It is a arcady bullet-hell game at times.
-- It is a story driven game that will drive you to tears and heartbreak.
-- It is an open world that begs to be explored and appreciated.
-- It is home to one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard.
It is one of the most satisfying games, story and gameplaywise, that I have ever had the experience of playing.
If I am to be fair, Nier:Automata is not without its flaws:
-- I had some studdering/fps issues at times even after using Borderless Gaming (which I highly recommend for this game).
-- The keyboard controls (especially dodging) are rather sh*tty, I did not have much choiced but to use a controller.
-- Aiming without a lockout is rather poor.
-- The game can be too easy sometimes, but the difficulty jump between normal and hard is unfair. (Think 5x more damage from all enemies)
But all of these flaws are either avoidable or ignorable. They did not ruin the game for me in the slightest.
Nier:Automata is a melting pot of various ideas and genres, and successfully manages to combine them while setting itself apart from everything. Yoko Taro created a beautiful world, story, and characters. If I were to compare this game to anything, it would be to a black hole. The game pulled me into its world and never let go until I beat the game. And, mild spoiler:
I apologize. I have been rambling. I don't write reviews well, but I had to try for this game. It touched me and will forever hold a special place in my heart. This is undoubtably, one of the single best games I have ever played. You will not regret buying this game.

*Cue the very long review, with pros and cons and everything inbetween. Get comfy :p*
NOTE: There are 4 curriencies in this game, I meantion two of these in the review:
Crystals: Currency you get with real money. They are not needed to advance in the game or get better, they just mean you may be able to get something for 50 crystals that may cost 7500 Gold (Example)
Gold: This is something you earn after every game. Once you get the hang of the game, you could be earning enough gold to buy a new champion after around 5-6 games (You eventually forget about how long it takes, as you get into the habit of trying to master level up your champions! :D
Essense: This i sagain earned after each game in what seems to be small quantites. Also earned in chests if you recieve a card you have already got (It is replaced with essense vard after a chest opens and the cards are revealed). These are used to buy cards for your champions (explained below in "Pro's:"). And with the rarity system on the cards, some cards can cost more than overs, but offer very useful effects)
Credits: This is an in-MATCH currency. You earn this during the match, and you start with a small amount at the very start. These are used to purchase perks for your champion during that match. Use your champion to their purpose (Front line's on the objective, Flanks flanking the enemy, etc etc) and you will earn credits faster.
------------------------
This is honestly a great game. You will always have the people saying the same thing as they do for other games of similar nature. "Clone of Overwatch". Ignore all reviews or comments like this, as for every similarity, there is a difference between this game and Overwatch (I mean... seriously, how many games can you think of where there aren't a similar game on the internet? It's called game rivalry, it's common for all games, and Paladins is a huge worthy rival of Overwatch - and it's also free!. I have already sunk 36.4 hours into this game to date, and I am not going to be leaving the game anytime soon.
Pro's:
- Great game, some games lasting around 10 minutes, some lasting 25 minutes, all depending on the teamwork of both sides.
- Great community: The community is not toxic. You have a lot of good players who aren't try-hards getting angry at every small thing. Just have fun, even if you're a novice, you'll get the hang of the game quickly. You will always get the one player once in a while that gets fed up or is toxic, just ignore them. But they are very rare, so you likely won't see many people like that often.
- In-game perks: During each map, you will find while in the team spawn point you can spend Credits (earned during the game) on perks that can take advantage, or help cover weaknesses in your champion, as long as you pick wisely. There are four categories of perks, holding 4 perks per category (That's 16 perks altogether, 4 perks you can pick in total per game). Each perk holds 3 tiers, each tier costing more Qredits (As you would expect). You can only pick one perk in each category, so pick wisely.
Examples: category 1: Resilience (See stealthed enemies a little further away), Blast Shield (Slight reduced splash damage) and Haven (Slightly reduced direct damage) and another perk I have forgot (oops).
- Card system: Each champion also has their own large set of cards. These cards allow you to create 5 unique loadouts for each champion. You have in total 6 loadouts per champion (Including the default basic loadout which you start with). This allows you to earn cards in chests, or buy them with essence (One of the in-game currencies). This can allow you to adjust your champion's abilities to take advantage of your playstyle. Do you find yourself using a champion's abilities that allow you to escape quickly or give you a surprise advantage? Use cards that increases the ability duration (For example increasing duration of stealth) and allows speeds up the cooldowns with each kill/elimination (Assists). There are a lot of cards to choose from, and each champion has their own large collection of cards depending on their abilities. Experiment, and enjoy the customisation.
Cons:
- First of all, please remember this is still a beta status game (BETA: A game that is still in development. "Pre-release" so to speak) Bugs may or may not sometimes be present. Sometimes these can be tiny bugs you may not even notice. Sometimes it may be a random bug that won't effect gameplay but you may notice. It's not that common, but do not slate the game personally if you come across it. Just report the bug to the developers so they know to fix it. The developers work hard to fix all bugs while adding features in each patch, while also getting new features in like new champions, champion skins and maps.
- Through steam, I do find that the game can take around 2 minutes to load. It'll load up the launcher, press play then it may go back to steam but say it is "Running", then about a minute later of waiting it will load up on it's own. This could just be my laptop being the laptop it is, and I can't validate if it happens on other computers. If it happens with you, just be patient, it will be worth it and WILL load up!
- It can take a long time to gain essense sometimes, meaning you have to grind it slowly so you can buy a few more cards for a champion. Also means earning enough for legendary crads can be a very long grind. (However I guess they are legendary rarity for a reason! So i guess it can't be too easy). I think the game developers should add a few more ways to earn essence, as they have for quests but even then, it could still be better. We'll see what they do in future patches :p
Overall:
This is a great game and people should at least try it out and find out for yourself if it is for you. It is free to play, so what have you got to lose?
You may just find yourself addicted to it after a few hours when you start getting the hang of the champions and their abilities, creating your own playstyle.
Just please! Use your champions how they are meant to be used!! If they're a flank champion, work on using their abilities to get behind your enemies and hit them with the element of surprise. Damage champions, or course cause as much damage as possible. Support champions, keep healing your teammates! Heals for everyone will give your team a very large chance of winning. Front line champions, shield your teammates! Use your shield abilities wisely ON THE OBJECTIVES and make sure your teammates aren't under fire as much as possible!
Use your champions to their purposes as explained above, and you will earn Credits faster and get them higher tier perks easier ;) Also your team will appreciate it.
Try the game out, it deserves the recognition.

You begin with one character unlocked and earn four others as you play. They each come equipped with their own specific primary weapon, an activated special power, and some passive traits. There's also a bevy of secondary weapons you can find, each with their own strengths and weaknesses (except the Eruptor, that thing is awful all the time!) that add to your own lethality and ability.
As you kill things you'll level up your character and unlock new permanent traits. When you die, you lose all of your pick-ups but the level-up perks persist between games and are independent to each character, and while they're somewhat random you do later gain the ability to reroll some of them to more useful things.

Half-Life Deathmatch: Source is a Source engine port of the multiplayer portion of Half-Life. It was released on Steam on July 2, 2005. The game is given to players for free as part of their purchase of Half-Life: Source.
As a port, the game possesses several differences with the original multiplayer component of Half-Life, such as the Colt Python lacking the zoom feature.
Half-Life Deathmatch: Source (or simply HLDMS) has game play similar to that of the original multiplayer component of Half-Life. Players are spawned at random points across one of many maps and battle each other in an all out free-for-all. To acquire weapons and ammunition (as well as health and energy), players must search the map for various caches of them. Players get point (Frags) by eliminating other players. The player with the most frags at the end of a match wins that match. If a player has the same amount of frags as another player, but a higher number of deaths than the other player, the player with more deaths will be ranked lower.
HLDMS Never saw the same success as other multi player source engine games, even though a good number of custom maps and some custom game modes have been made by the community.

Putt-Putt Joins the Parade is the first in a series of windows into the human condition through talking animated cars. Putt-Putt's endeavors to enter said parade offer a reflection of our own mortal wants and desires: Greed, nepotism, a need for acceptance in the face of adversity, how the color of your skin effects others opinion of you, surving in a capitalist society, working for mimimum wage, and generally understanding the value of a dollar. Putt-Putt has all sorts of valuable lessons to dole out upon unworthy ears willing to shell out a gold coin or two just to listen through a rusty keyhole.  Even when you finally acheive your hopes and dreams, your parade, if you will... It's never quite what you expected. This tale of caution is worth your 30-45 minutes. Please digest it's meaning fruitfully.

Call of Duty®: Black Ops is the second best Call of Duty (After COD 3 IMO).
This game has a compelling and factual story line based on the timeline of the Cold War and Vietnam War. The campaign story veers into Zombies, which does make copmplete sense and adds to the lore of the game.
This game has by far, in my honest opinion, one of the best multiplayers ever (or at least it used to - when ranked lobbies had more players). Guns are balanced and upgrades/attachments are unlocked at the right moments, prestige was something to look up to and challenging (unlike the newer games - where an easy grind can get you to high levels).
I have played this game on Console (PS3) and decided to get it on PC to remember the game and play it when I'm travelling; if you play on console and purchase the PC version to play, you will be disappointed. The graphics are the same thing, the sounds are also the same.
BUT, the PC port of the game does come with some minor visual bugs and glitches in the campaign and zombies portion of the game; and the multiplayer only hosts unofficial and unranked lobbies and servers in Europe and U.S. Since there are no dedicated servers, the game fails to deliver stability in the connection between players.
The slight issues above are not due to my setup or internet connection;
Internet (Lan - Cable):
- 120 Mb/s Download
- 8-11 Mb/s Upload
PC:
- Intel i7-7700HQ 2.81 GHz, x64 based processor
- GeForce GTX 1050 4 Gb
Personally, I asked for a refund. However, if you have never played it, I do recommend you get it.
All in all, I do recommend this game. However, if you come from the Console version, do not get it. This game is well balanced in all aspects, and if unranked lobbies and the occasional hacker don't annoy you, then go ahead and grab this for the experience.

This game is already quite good.  It's basically Civ with a Total War element for smart people.  To all the people giving this game a bad review... GET GUD SCRUB!
Seriously though, I think people are disliking the game because it's difficult and not particularly intuitive yet.  That being said, it's lack of intuitiveness comes from it playing like Civ games, BUT HAVING MECHANICS THAT ACTUALLY REQUIRE YOU TO USE YOUR BRAIN.  What a concept!
For instance, building every building in your city isn't wise (or possible).  As buildings come with steep upkeep, you actually have to plan out your Empire a bit economically to get the most out of it and turn a profit.  If you space out your cities too much, they will be too far for trade between cities (logical right?).  If you are making silk in every city, then you're trade caravans won't be trading silk between cities (makes sense, huh?).  So therefore you won't get the lucrative trade multiplier on your goods.  Therefore, you need cities specializing in goods and then trading between them to make the most money.
The game is highly logical in its mechanics and the way it plays.  Sieges take multiple turns.  Peasants get unruly if you're constantly using them to do back-breaking labor.  Etc. Etc.
It's not without its flaws.  The game has a number of bugs, especially once you get hundreds of turns in.  Though, none have been game-breaking.  They're mostly just annoyances that cause you to reload and then it's back to normal.
I think with more development this game will extremely outclass Civ and Total War.  Albeit, the intellectual nature of the game's mechanics and it's Ancient China theme will likely not appeal to a huge market.
TL;DR If you like Civ/Total War and are someone who enjoys a challenge and has a brain, get this game.  You'll love it.  If you're a pleb, then don't.

“It's 3am. Your neighbors are having a loud party. Stop them.”
Welcome to Hotline Miami’s slow and methodical little brother. With 1980’s style lights, colors and killer electronic soundtrack – the game will easily leave you wanting more. It’s 2015’s best indie game with fine-tuned mechanics and eye pleasing pixelart.
A narrated story following the case of the Party Hard killings, Detective John West, follows the trail a murderer just trying to get some sleep. Using Hitmans tactic to divide and conquer the room, it’s a hack-and- slash for the patient minded players.
Given a plethora of environmental “accidents” to trigger that randomly appear for each level, you can blow up or poison parts of the party to thin the herd. If those methods don’t pan out for you, there are random power-ups to
give you a hand. Drop a sick dance move, smoke & stun grenades, poisons, running shoes, disguises and even TNT. Use with caution however, some power-ups cause negative effects like a SWAT team raiding the party, or a casualty at your feet and the blame gets placed on you where the crowd beatings ensue.
As good as it is it doesn’t come without faults. The voice actors in the cut scenes are awful, and the repetitive screaming sounds from the crowd upon finding a dead body can find you muting the sound all too quickly. More often than not I found myself having glitch out the police being called, never to return to clean up the bodies and leaving the room in a constant panic loop.
Thankfully the game doesn’t take itself too seriously trying to be something it isn’t and is just pure fun. Now Party Hard offers player created levels, and Twitch.tv streaming to employ your viewers to influence your game in a way you can’t foresee.
The good outweighs the bad, and is definitely worth every penny.

Though you see elements of Civ V and Age of Empires games at times, don’t expect the game to be true to either franchise. Instead, what you find is an experience that comes across as a comic book combined with a board game from another era, and spawned into digital format; born again in some alternate continent’s code of conduct. If you are looking for something different in the world of 4X, this may be for you. At this time, it released in Early Access, only because the multiplayer is not finished. So, only single player is available at this point.

In a beautiful world of mountains & rivers, laid out on a map that allows you to panoramically zoom to any degree in or out, the Empires of the Far East come to life in the beautiful scenes that seem to be reminiscent of charcoal drawings. It’s an art style sure to be appealing to everyone. When you zoom in, you become a part of the village & the daily lives of the people. Yet, when you zoom out you see the whole countryside and can plan & plot combat moves & colonization. If you continue to zoom out, you can even see other empires and the cities they are building. All of this beautiful scenery is augmented with lovely tunes from the Orient that are as high-quality as those made by Kairis for Paradox Studio’s lovely music dlc’s. The tunes are lively & provide ambience that certainly makes the gameplay enjoyable.
With simplified graphics reminiscent of This War of Mine, Oriental Empires makes the story come alive on a map in an imaginative way that can be intensely pleasing for many people. It could be seen as quaint, or maybe retro. It certainly calls to mind playing old Stratego & Risk boardgames. This may not appeal to some gamers, especially the simple characters, who appear as 2d in the bottom corner, & fight in stiff 3d scripted forms. It’s certainly not a Triple A title, but it manages to bring a sense of atmosphere to the world of the Orient.
The storyline progresses through 5 eras of Chinese & Mongolian history. You are able to play as different factions, and you have some control over when you move into the next era, based on which tech you choose. The techs are limited, but provide story-rich choices to the way you will develop your nation. Some narration appears between eras, and the voice acting is as great as the music. But, don’t expect a Western game set in the East. The game itself & the story are very Oriental in design.
The combat allows you to plot all your moves, & then watch them play out before you. This forces you to plan for contingencies. You are able to change the way the units face at waypoints. You are able to select their fighting stance; whether defensive or offensive, in a variety of strategies. And, unlike most games, it seems often that the best method is to avoid conflict, and defend your villages. I’ve seen the raiders act just like huns; pillage, burn, run, &  while you chase after them, another unit is coming in behind to raid your unprotected village. The mechanics are not cookie cutter, and seem to be unique to the game, despite the fact that many components are shared by other 4X games.
The tutorial needs work, though there are no bugs at all that I’ve seen. I like the way the advisor stays in the corner greyed out until you need her. Also, all of the overlays are unobtrusive, since they can be toggled individually to allow for great screen shots, which is very important to many people. I wish some of the bigger 4X titles could learn that idea. The biggest problem I see with the game for some is that you need to read the text info provided behind the question mark, in something similar to an infopedia to play the game. It’s one of those TL;DR things that some just won’t care to deal with. But, for me, I read everything from street signs to cereal box small print anyways. In the case of this game, you will probably need to read the more info area to proceed. Also, the advisor seems to offer advice periodically, just sometimes that advice seems to come after you need it instead of before.

*Art style is very engaging
*Combat is fun & fresh
*Gameplay is realistic for the Far East territory
*Interface is user-friendly with total control
*Tutorial is scant leaving a learning curve
*Graphics are simplistic
*In EA until MP is complete

Putting the massive weapon customization aside, the gameplay is very smooth. I love the gameplay. Not once do I feel halted by silly animations. Nothing stops the action from going in Loadout. Loadout is a fast paced 3rd person shooter with a large variety of weapons and character customization.
Personally though, I feel there are some things that take away from the game as well in a competetive stand point. While the game entirely focuses on weapon customization, it's also what breaks it.
Never have I really felt that my kills are "legit"
It is most commonly the case that people who have played the game longer and have better gear that will dominate the competition. The weapons have a leveling system and with time, you can make your parts stronger. Pair a person who has a level 9 slug rifle with a new player.
There is no question who has a much higher advantage. Balance does not exist what so ever. The game was fine when first released because people were just starting and didn't have all the high leveled gear. Now that people have finally put more time into it, it is entirely noticeable that the balance went out the window.
The game at its core is fantastic. The gameplay is smooth, very well optmized, and just fun to play.
ALTHOUGH. A big problem I've been experiencing which I hope is fixed is the fact that being in a party with your friends is almost meaningless. 9 times out of 10 you will be on seperate teams against each other instead of being able to communicate with your teammates. This is NOT how a "party" system should work. I want to be in a party to play with my friends, otherwise I would just go play matchmaking by myself. I am completely aware that custom games will be a thing eventually so possibly this will fix that issue.
Overall I give Loadout a 7/10
The gameplay is great, but it's the balance that really turns me off about the game. If you put a lot of time into the game, prepare to steamroll anyone who's played less than you.
Keep in mind this is just a personal gripe with the game. I'm sure future updates could possibly fix balance issues. I would still reccomend it to people who would enjoy a humourous, graphic, and fast paced shooter.

I tried really REALLY hard to like this game. The concept behind it is awesome, but the execution of this third person shooter is flawed to the core and will eventually frustrate players to the breaking point.
First off, props to the developers for giving the player so much creativity to how they build their weapons. Now shame on the developers for making so many of those weapon designs completely useless. This is one of the game's biggest disappointments, when you spend a good amount of time and in-game currency to unlock a boatload of weapon parts then realize that none of those parts are actually useful. I spend about 10000 blutes, the in game currency, just trying to make a viable shotgun, but nothing I made in that regard could kill a enemy at full health in any less then 4 direct hits at point blank, which is pathetic. The only creation I made that was remotely reliable was literally just the default assault rifle with a 1.5x scope on it. Absolutely everything else I tried to do to this gun made it worse for how I played. Same goes for the default rocket launcher, which in my entire time playing, I only kept used a part which increased how fast the rocket flew when it fires.
Sure I hard the parts to make a gun that could do something interesting like make dozens of glowing fire balls shoot off in a corkscrew pattern and then bounce off the walls until they hit someone. That would be interesting sure, but it wouldn't kill anyone because any player who knows what they're doing just makes the same damn gun as everyone else, that same damn sustained telsa beam gun.
The sustained beam gun already kind of sends the message that you don't want to properly time your shots, but with the way that telsa will arc and hit an enemy even if the shot only hits a surface near them, using a telsa is also sending the message that you don't want to have to aim either. So everyone and their dog are using these "no timing or aiming necessary" weapons and anyone who wants to get creative gets slapped in the face by a whole team of lightning-laser♥♥♥♥♥♥
So balance in weapon design is an issue, this I could deal with if the overall presentation of the game wasn't so obnoxious. I can deal with goofiness and I can deal with a cartoonish art style, but everything about Loadout just screams immature. I feel like it is try to cater to a demographic so desensitized and jaded that anything less then absolute gratuity get's completely ignored. I don't know if I'm just turning into an old man or if maybe I just think a game where an actual avatar costume item that's just a pixilated♥♥♥♥♥♥swinging around is kind of ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.
Lastly we have the heart beat that plays when you're low on health. I respect that this game doesn't have rebounding health like every other shooter to come out in the last 8 years. It does make the experience feel a little bit more like Unreal or Quake, but for the love of god who honestly needs an auditory indicator this grating? I would have traded this annoying, relentless pounding for annying, relentless flashing around the edges of the screen any day of the week. I think the fact that there's no option to disable it or adjust it's volume specifically is inexcusable and it all just adds to how much the game annoyed me over all.
All in all, this game's just disappointing. It's a kickass idea that's weighted down by metric tons of balancing issues and stupid design and presentation decisions. Maybe after a year or two more in the oven this game will have been tweaked enough to be enjoyable, but I predict that the devs just going to cash cow for as long as they can off the people who are more willing to forgive this game for it's jagged edges.

This game is amazing, one of my favorites. Lots of cool factions, events that shake up the campaign (the Black Death, for example), lots of cool units, and much more. Settlements are divided between castles and cities which make the game more interesting and fun.There are a lot of little details that go a long way to making the game interesting and giving it some character. For example, after a battle, if you have prisoners you can decide whether you want to release them, execute them, or attempt to ransom them. I'm not much for writing reviews, but Nier:Automata deserves every ounce of praise given to it and more.
What is it?
-- It is hack/slash RPG with a simple combat system that shows remarkable depth over time.
-- It is a arcady bullet-hell game at times.
-- It is a story driven game that will drive you to tears and heartbreak.
-- It is an open world that begs to be explored and appreciated.
-- It is home to one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard.
It is one of the most satisfying games, story and gameplaywise, that I have ever had the experience of playing.
If I am to be fair, Nier:Automata is not without its flaws:
-- I had some studdering/fps issues at times even after using Borderless Gaming (which I highly recommend for this game).
-- The keyboard controls (especially dodging) are rather sh*tty, I did not have much choiced but to use a controller.
-- Aiming without a lockout is rather poor.
-- The game can be too easy sometimes, but the difficulty jump between normal and hard is unfair. (Think 5x more damage from all enemies)
But all of these flaws are either avoidable or ignorable. They did not ruin the game for me in the slightest.
Nier:Automata is a melting pot of various ideas and genres, and successfully manages to combine them while setting itself apart from everything. Yoko Taro created a beautiful world, story, and characters. If I were to compare this game to anything, it would be to a black hole. The game pulled me into its world and never let go until I beat the game. And, mild spoiler:
I apologize. I have been rambling. I don't write reviews well, but I had to try for this game. It touched me and will forever hold a special place in my heart. This is undoubtably, one of the single best games I have ever played. You will not regret buying this game.

Rogue Stormers is a side scroller platformer shooter. It has RPG and roguelike elements as well. It can be quite fast paced and difficult. The gameplay will remind you of games like Metal Slug, Contra etc. The game also reminded me of Shoot Many Robots which is one of my favorite 2D shooter games.
The game looks gorgeous with very nice art-style, which Is dark and gloomy and really makes you feel like you’re in some kind of creepy atmosphere. The game runs very smooth. The FPS get locked to whatever Hz frequency you choose in the graphics menu’s resolution option. So in theory if your monitor can support 144Hz refresh rate you should get 144 FPS lock. For me, my monitor goes to maximum 72Hz so my FPS was locked to that.
The game features very nice almost rock music. It’s very nice and engaging music and suitable for the pace of the game. The hit and enemy sounds are also pretty good and overall the music and sounds are very nice in this game. I especially like the opening theme music of this game.
The gameplay is simple run and gun. You can move around with WASD keys and shoot with your mouse. All the keys can be re-assigned on the keyboard so that’s a good thing. You have a jetpack of sorts which lets you jump a bit higher and dash through air or ground as well, this dash ability is very useful in dodging the enemy bullets. You have a main gun which shoots infinite bullets, a secondary weapon can be picked up in-game. There are many types of secondary weapons available, such as droid which go and shoot random enemies, huge projectile bullets weapons etc. These secondary weapons also have a health bar and once depleted these can no longer be used. The secondary weapons also run out of ammo and recharge automatically over time.
Your main goal is to go through randomly generated level and get to either the wall and take it down and in every other level you get to face a boss. Every time you die you start at the beginning so the game can be pretty unforgiving. That’s where the RPG elements come in, when you do levels over and over again you gain XP and eventually start leveling up. Once per level you get to choose a perk which is permanent. So by making lots of runs and leveling up you keep piling on perks which help you out with the game’s later levels. The perks can improve your weapons or give you bonuses such as if your currency is low you get 10% more damage from your guns etc.
You start off with 60 HP (or if you have perks which increase HP you will start with that perk bonus added) and in order to beat the game you must do it in one run without dying. This can be difficult as the game gets pretty hard as lots of enemies and projectiles are being thrown at you. Your only ways to gain health are either if an enemy drops a little health kit and you pick it up, it’ll grant you some health or the other way to get health is the mini slot machine. You gamble a number of coins (usually 100 and 250) and you can get random things. It can be a big health pack or multiple big health packs. It can be 10 coins, or 750 coins. Other than that you can also get secondary weapons and or temporary bonus like e.g. when you get hit a giant spiked ball goes around you damage any nearby enemies etc. You can also find these temporary bonuses in chests. These chests come in different types e.g. one chest requires you to give up 30 HP to open, another one requires keys to open etc.
When you kill enemies sometimes they drop souls which you can collect. These are basically experience points which help you level up. Many types of enemies in the game as well. From tiny goblins to huge monsters who attack with all sorts of projectiles, turrets, flying snakes, goblins in balloons etc.
There’s more than one main character and ever character has their own unique ability. Level cap seems to be 60 for heroes. You start off with Brekht and eventually unlock other characters every 2 stages. Each hero has their own abilities and health/bonus stats. Brekht for example starts off with 1 key and 250 gold, his unique ability is rapid fire for a few seconds. If you’re playing co-op this effect will affect all the players playing the game. Game can be played single player, local co-op or online co-op.

*Cue the very long review, with pros and cons and everything inbetween. Get comfy :p*
NOTE: There are 4 curriencies in this game, I meantion two of these in the review:
Crystals: Currency you get with real money. They are not needed to advance in the game or get better, they just mean you may be able to get something for 50 crystals that may cost 7500 Gold (Example)
Gold: This is something you earn after every game. Once you get the hang of the game, you could be earning enough gold to buy a new champion after around 5-6 games (You eventually forget about how long it takes, as you get into the habit of trying to master level up your champions! :D
Essense: This i sagain earned after each game in what seems to be small quantites. Also earned in chests if you recieve a card you have already got (It is replaced with essense vard after a chest opens and the cards are revealed). These are used to buy cards for your champions (explained below in "Pro's:"). And with the rarity system on the cards, some cards can cost more than overs, but offer very useful effects)
Credits: This is an in-MATCH currency. You earn this during the match, and you start with a small amount at the very start. These are used to purchase perks for your champion during that match. Use your champion to their purpose (Front line's on the objective, Flanks flanking the enemy, etc etc) and you will earn credits faster.
------------------------
This is honestly a great game. You will always have the people saying the same thing as they do for other games of similar nature. "Clone of Overwatch". Ignore all reviews or comments like this, as for every similarity, there is a difference between this game and Overwatch (I mean... seriously, how many games can you think of where there aren't a similar game on the internet? It's called game rivalry, it's common for all games, and Paladins is a huge worthy rival of Overwatch - and it's also free!. I have already sunk 36.4 hours into this game to date, and I am not going to be leaving the game anytime soon.
Pro's:
- Great game, some games lasting around 10 minutes, some lasting 25 minutes, all depending on the teamwork of both sides.
- Great community: The community is not toxic. You have a lot of good players who aren't try-hards getting angry at every small thing. Just have fun, even if you're a novice, you'll get the hang of the game quickly. You will always get the one player once in a while that gets fed up or is toxic, just ignore them. But they are very rare, so you likely won't see many people like that often.
- In-game perks: During each map, you will find while in the team spawn point you can spend Credits (earned during the game) on perks that can take advantage, or help cover weaknesses in your champion, as long as you pick wisely. There are four categories of perks, holding 4 perks per category (That's 16 perks altogether, 4 perks you can pick in total per game). Each perk holds 3 tiers, each tier costing more Qredits (As you would expect). You can only pick one perk in each category, so pick wisely.
Examples: category 1: Resilience (See stealthed enemies a little further away), Blast Shield (Slight reduced splash damage) and Haven (Slightly reduced direct damage) and another perk I have forgot (oops).
- Card system: Each champion also has their own large set of cards. These cards allow you to create 5 unique loadouts for each champion. You have in total 6 loadouts per champion (Including the default basic loadout which you start with). This allows you to earn cards in chests, or buy them with essence (One of the in-game currencies). This can allow you to adjust your champion's abilities to take advantage of your playstyle. Do you find yourself using a champion's abilities that allow you to escape quickly or give you a surprise advantage? Use cards that increases the ability duration (For example increasing duration of stealth) and allows speeds up the cooldowns with each kill/elimination (Assists). There are a lot of cards to choose from, and each champion has their own large collection of cards depending on their abilities. Experiment, and enjoy the customisation.
Cons:
- First of all, please remember this is still a beta status game (BETA: A game that is still in development. "Pre-release" so to speak) Bugs may or may not sometimes be present. Sometimes these can be tiny bugs you may not even notice. Sometimes it may be a random bug that won't effect gameplay but you may notice. It's not that common, but do not slate the game personally if you come across it. Just report the bug to the developers so they know to fix it. The developers work hard to fix all bugs while adding features in each patch, while also getting new features in like new champions, champion skins and maps.
- Through steam, I do find that the game can take around 2 minutes to load. It'll load up the launcher, press play then it may go back to steam but say it is "Running", then about a minute later of waiting it will load up on it's own. This could just be my laptop being the laptop it is, and I can't validate if it happens on other computers. If it happens with you, just be patient, it will be worth it and WILL load up!
- It can take a long time to gain essense sometimes, meaning you have to grind it slowly so you can buy a few more cards for a champion. Also means earning enough for legendary crads can be a very long grind. (However I guess they are legendary rarity for a reason! So i guess it can't be too easy). I think the game developers should add a few more ways to earn essence, as they have for quests but even then, it could still be better. We'll see what they do in future patches :p
Overall:
This is a great game and people should at least try it out and find out for yourself if it is for you. It is free to play, so what have you got to lose?
You may just find yourself addicted to it after a few hours when you start getting the hang of the champions and their abilities, creating your own playstyle.
Just please! Use your champions how they are meant to be used!! If they're a flank champion, work on using their abilities to get behind your enemies and hit them with the element of surprise. Damage champions, or course cause as much damage as possible. Support champions, keep healing your teammates! Heals for everyone will give your team a very large chance of winning. Front line champions, shield your teammates! Use your shield abilities wisely ON THE OBJECTIVES and make sure your teammates aren't under fire as much as possible!
Use your champions to their purposes as explained above, and you will earn Credits faster and get them higher tier perks easier ;) Also your team will appreciate it.
Try the game out, it deserves the recognition.

has been aptly described as a modern version of
. There are several key differences, however:
randomly generates its levels, while each level in
was created by hand. This gives it the advantage that every level is solvable using pure logic, no need for guessing.
is also more lenient when it comes to making mistakes: it counts how many mistakes you make, but they do not result in a game over. Instead, you must solve each level with a minimum of mistakes in order to earn a perfect score.
Creating each level by hand also has the disadvantage of limiting the game to a finite number of levels. There are so few in fact that it only took me two hours to complete every level with no mistakes. Because of this I would not recommend spending more than $2 on it.

The puzzles are very good but never reach the full complexity afforded by the rules. If you like this game and finish it wanting more, there are two sequels available.

Really enjoyable casual puzzle game; challenging without being frustrating, although seasoned puzzle enthusiasts might consider it to be a bit too easy. Common complaint is that it is short, but for the price I still see this as a good value title. There are around 30 logic puzzles, still offering several hours of challenges to exercise your mind. Concept is most like the classic Minesweeper that was included with Windows OS back in the day. You need to use logic to determine if there is a 'number' or 'vacant' hex in the adjacent cell from the already revealed hexes.
The simple designs, grows in complexity as you progress through larger levels with new rules being added & for the purists there is also the challenge of completing each puzzle without any mistakes. Graphics are bright yet clean & basic, but suitable to the game. Sounds are relaxing & controls are easy (just left & right mouse buttons).
Other than the exceptional
, this is one of the best puzzlers I have played in recent years & look forward to trying out the sequels (which I am told are a much harder challenge too!).

Oriental Empires feels like a blend of Civilisation and Total War series. Happily sank two whole evenings into it already and plan to explore more factions. Definitely recommend it for strategy game fans, despite one or two issues (as detailed below)
To elaborate a bit on the above points, I found unlike a lot of strategy games, the movement and combat system doesn't punish mistakes. Being able to set up all your moves, then only have them executed at the end of the turn allows for much easier planning, and means if you make a mistake, you can undo it. Ultimately, that makes executing complex strategies much easier. Related to that, the combat system, even though there's no direct control of the battles, does a good job of simulating interactions between multiple armies on the battlefield.
Where I really struggled with this game was in building up an empire beyond the first 3 or 4 cities. A chance famine combined with a random flood event can throw cities into peasant uprising, with relatively few options for redressing that. Equally, making money in order to expand my empire, in order to make more money was a real struggle - Creating a trading network and carefully investing in building more economic buildings didn't always result in increased revenue. Makes it hard to expand to more than 3 or 4 cities, and some of the solutions I've found are counter-intuitive to say the least.
Really happy with this game, despite my frustrations with some aspects of the empire building. Definitely recommend it though to any strategy game fans!

This game is fascinating for its innovative ideas. It is similar to Civilization V or Total War at a first glance. However, you will realize that the idea behind is totally different after you tried it for a while. Although some new conceptions introduced in this game still need to be improved，this game is definitely worth the price, considering that it is only in early access stage.
Pros:
1. Realistic (complicated) economy and society mechanism. The mood of the people can be affected by so many factors, which make the game very challenging but intriguing. As a lord, you have to SERIOUSLY make effort to satisfy your people by providing them enough food, proper labor works, entertainment and religion, etc. The punishment of mistreating your people is heavy. Peasant will become bandits to rob your farm, and your army will rebel to overthrow their lord. The wrath of the people is unstoppable.
2. Innovative edict system and classes. Two classes exist in this game: noble and peasant. Not responsible for labor work, the noble class provide well trained warriors, particularly useful in early stages. The edict you issue usually benefit only one class and irritate the other. Making balance between them is important. Generally, comforting the noble class is much easier than pleasing the peasants. However, those filthy nobles can betray you if their city locates too far from your capital to be controlled, especially when your faction leader died and his successor is young and weak.
3. Weather system. It is amazing how the whether is changing over time and OVER THE MAP. I have tried two factions, one is Han in the east and the other Shu in southwest. Apparently, the weather in southwest is much more terrible. I have experienced more heavy rains, which ruined my infrastructures and reduced the population. In addition, earthquakes occur more frequently in the southwest area.
4. Fascinating details when zooming the map. You can overlook and manage your cities the same way as playing Civ V. But when you zoom in, the detail of your soldier is just as good as that in a Total War game.
5. Completely new stories. As far as I know, Total War have never dabbled in Chinese history before. Although there is Chinese civilization in Civ V, it lack the depth and details compared to Oriental Empires.
However，lots of problems exist since the game is unfinished.
Cons:
1. I encountered few minor bugs during my 11 hours of gaming. The map will scrolling unintentionally in rare cases (but went normal in next turn). Luckily, I haven't experience any crash or serious bugs that prevent me from continue the game.
2. The AI, in both diplomacy and combat (Biggest problem currently). The AI in this game indeed needs to be improved. First of all, my enemies are all being nice and friendly to me. They are willing to pay a lot to please me, which make me feel bad for them in most cases. Until now, the only faction that dared to declare war on me is Zhou. After I successfully defended my cities, Zhou surprised me by begging me for peace and paying me 1 coin (Are they trying to insult me???).
I also want to point out that the AI does not match the graphical details displayed during the combat. I would strongly suggest the developers to grand players the access to control their units during the battle.
3. Tuning of the game is needed. In current version, the upkeep fee for buildings is too high, and as a result, the number of buildings are severely limited. Also, natural disasters cause too much damage to farming lands and anger the peasants so easily. It could be very difficult for new players to handle those accidents.

4. More contents are needed. Although the game includes four type of technologies, there are too few eras (including bronze, warring state and imperial age only). How could a three thousand year history be concluded by merely three eras? More content are needed for sure. Also, more instructions and detailed descriptions should be helpful.
In summary, this game demonstrates lots of details of the evolution of civilizations in some very innovative ways. It focus more on management of states than on combat. This early access game is not perfect and have significant drawback in AI. However, I am attracted by the ideas presented and have high expectation on the developers. Hope they can finish and release the complete version soon.

No game has ever had me say, "How?" and "What the f**k?" more than Party Hard.
Don't get me wrong, the concept is great and the game can be fun to play. I can see why people love it, however I found the experience more annoying and frustrating than fun during my playthrough and here's why...
-The line of site is almost completely broken in this game:
Victims and cops can see you and bodies behind objects and walls that should be impossible to see. Not to mention, the game tries to balance this by making their line of sight moderately short range taking away from the fun. I think the game could be much improved with longer lines of sight and improved obstructions of said line of sight. As of now it's pretty much flipping a coin on each kill unless you're totally secluded from everything else.
-Traps and placements are randomized every time the mission starts:
Now this is actually a cool and interesting feature but I'm afraid its a double-edged sword. More than often you find yourself spawning with barely any ways to kill or distract crowds with a near to zip chance of succeeding. Of course, there's players who seek this challenge and like to pull it off. I just feel an average player with moderate skill like me is going to find themselves restarting the mission over and over until there's at least one worthy trap.
-Every other map has a totally broken trap/phone call that can clean house hands free with zero work:
This is very unfortunate because maps with traps like these tend to lack good design and are thrown in there like a cheat to skip the mission. It's mind blowing not a single victim/guard cares if your phone call brings people to the party and are obvious threats knocking people out and killing left and right.
-The police/guards make no sense at all in this game, especially considering their methods of public safety:
Upon arrival the police almost always run over people killing them instantly. I'm sure most people wouldn't write this off as a bad thing because who cares, free kills. Wrong, I think it's beyond stupid as you can't even use this feature to your advantage like luring crowds into the street and getting the cops to run them over. The swat beat everyone down if they're called but for some reason you get "BUSTED" for being beat down like anyone else. (The people beat down aren't even arrested.) Finally, the guards... These guys beat you down just for showing up. I can understand if they're at the front door serving as a bouncer like in the second mission, but otherwise it's a dumb mechanic. How would they know if you're invited or not with all the people and partying going on.
-Horrible blame and accusation system:
I can't even state how many times I was busted for doing nothing wrong at all. If anyone at all dies near the player everyone assumes its the player and calls the cops over for an arrest. Countless times I've been walking on the brinks of the map to try ang get away from people dying and cops who are passing by will stop to arrest me for walking away like everyone else. Sometimes it's its not the cops and just random people who will call the cops for no reason. An interesting yet broken feature is the ability for victims to accuse and call cops on other victims. This leads to the most random arrests I've ever seen and it doesn't help the player's experience as it can't really be triggered on purpose similarly to police running over victims...
-Handful of small bugs that aren't "game breaking" but result in the player's death all the time:
Typically, the cops are supposed to leave and ignore any more crimes the second they have someone over their shoulder or have bagged all the bodies but I've been arrested with people over their shoulder's twice in my time playing. Is it a feature? Possibly. It sure doesn't look like it. These police have pretty broken behavior and do random things they shouldn't more than often.
Conclusion:
Overall the game is fun yes, but success is a crap shoot and mostly RNG. When I say it's RNG I mean RNG... Going back to replay the game with end game knowledge and skill barely helps in this game. The game offers a mediocre story with TERRIBLE voice acting. The only real replay value in this game comes from the steam workshop allowing the player to download other player's missions and play them. Note, there ARE unlockable characters in this game with some really good pros but, they have horrible cons that render them useless. People say this game is a "stealth" game but it really isn't at all.
I would recommend waiting for a sale to pick this game up. I think it's worth a playthrough but isn't an amazing game you'll be playing a lot. Heck, I'll probably forget about this game a week or so from now. I don't mean this in a bad or rude way, the game just didn't leave a memorable impact on me at all.
Side Note for Hotline Miami fans:
People compare this game to Hotline Miami all the time, but the two are nothing at all alike aside from being a masked killer who cleans house. If you're looking for a good alternative to Hotline Miami 1&2, I would recommend Deadbolt and not this. Deadbolt features a 2D world with one hit kills. It provides better challenge that requires planning very much like Hotline Miami.
Final Rating: 4/10

Quick overview: This game is incredibly fun to play, provided that you're willing to look past a few pre-release bugs. While I wouldn't recomend that you buy it imediatly, I would definatly keep an eye on it and buy it later once the major bugs are removed.
8/10 would buy again.
Best part: Civ like play with added depth and detail that make this game unique.
Worst part: The battles are incredibly complex, and most of the time I feel like I'm just throwing troops to the slaughter.
In depth review:
This game most certainly has it's bugs, but considering its only a pre-release I expected as much. Everything from troop movement to events will do something strange now and again, but this in know way interfered with the enjoyment of the game in my view.
Everyone seems to agree that it's very similar to Civ in regard to troop movement and placing the cities so I won't go into that as much.
The other comparison is to Total War which seems to be a bit more of a debate. The realism and detail is right up there with Total War, but the game play is drastically different. The battles that take place in Oriental Empires take place once you end the turn, and you have no control over the troops movements once the battle starts. You can give them "orders" however the troops don't always follow them persay, and it seems to be a jumbled mess a lot of the time. this made it very frustrating when trying to take cities or fending off bandits or rebels. But the frustration made me feel more like a general giving orders and watching as the chaios of battle ensues.
Oriental Empires is also a very interesting way of teaching the culture and History of China. Going into the game I knew nothing of either, so I really can't verify whether or not this game is acurate, but I'm definatly interested in finding more about this time in Chinese history.
In regards to the art and music, both are incredible. The music is suething during peace times and exciting when battles are enitiated. Also, being able to scroll all the way down to the peasents on the farm is facinating. Watching battles take place as if I were apart of it was awesome.
All in all I really did enjoy this game.

Party Hard is an unexpectedly addictive indie gem that taps into some primal part of our prehistoric lizard brains. A little remeniscent of Hotline Miami and the SNES Metal Gear games, the high contrast colors, thumping beats and constant euphoric injections gel very nicely to fuel you with adrenaline when you pull off successful sneaky combos.

The story is over the top and predictable but this isn\'t a game which focuses on narrative. The mechanics are solid and provides a refreshing experience. While it shouldn\'t be a slow game, some patience and planning is required.
Overall an enjoyable game that\'s easy to put down and pick up when you\'ve an hour to kill. Definitely play this with a controller and headphones with the bass up. A little tidbit that\'s nice is that the game also takes over your Alien FX lighting system for Alienware rigs to sync with the catchy soundtrack to create your very own mini disco.

Medieval II is, quite simply, one of the finest games I have ever played. It's the game that got me back into strategy games after a long hiatus, and that introduced me to what is now one of my favorite game series ever.
But will you like it?
Well, let's start from the beginning.
Medieval II is a combination turn-based and real-time tactics strategy game that takes place in Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East during the Middle Ages. You can play as one of 17 different factions in the campaign mode (plus four others in skirmishes) that have a wide variety of playing styles, strengths, and weaknesses. As 450 years go by, the Old World is thrown into chaos- or Total War, as the narrator would say- as it endures Crusades and Jihads, rebellion and betrayal, infighting among the Christian nations, two monstrous hordes from the East, and that terrible calamity known as the Black Death, all while the slow wheel of time turns and technology continues to advance from the simple spear to the crossbow to the terrible might of gunpowder. The Kingdoms expansion essentially adds four entirely new games, with campaigns in more localized areas of the normal TW map with over a dozen new factions to play from, in scenarios that all present very different challenges.
You will spend half of your time on the grand campaign map, a sort of political overworld where you manage the large affairs of your empire and move about your units. Here is where alliances are made and broken, provinces are developed, units are recruited, money is managed, and the dark tasks of espionage and assassination are undertaken. While a battle might change the course of a war, this is where you make sure that you have every chance of winning it in the first place.
But most people play Total War for the battles. With the capacity to have thousands of units on the field at any given time, they're as much spectacle as strategy, as the ordered chaos of the battlefield threatens to overwhelm even the greatest captains. With a rich unit roster and a wide array of special abilities, your armies will be versatile and able to employ any number of tactics, from slowly whittling enemy numbers down with a stream of arrow fire to forming a defensive circle to protect your captain to employing a devastating hammer and anvil strike with your cavalry to launching diseased cow carcasses at their generals. Morale, terrain, weather, and energy levels all play important roles in how well your soldiers will be able to fight, and how well you will be able to govern the events of the battle.
While there are some common strategies that can be undertaken for any nation or situation, no two campaigns or battles are the same, as the game can and will throw out surprises for you that you'll have to think quickly about to overcome. You may think you're doing well as France, fighting off England and preparing to make an invasion of the isles, when suddenly those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in Portugal declare war on you and blockade all of your provinces, forcing you to stretch yourself out along two fronts. And while you may be able to overcome this obstacle, His Holiness the Pope probably won't take kindly to your conquests against your Catholic brethren, and may excommunicate you. All eventualities need to be prepared for in Total War if you want to survive.
While this game is nearly a decade old, it still has a sizable and dedicated community of players to turn to if you want to fight a battle, try out a mod, or just get some friendly advice on how to deal with the Timurids. And as one of the easiest TW games to modify, it also has one of the best mod communities you'll be able to find, with an active base of players uploading and supporting their mods to this day. I highly recommend Stainless Steel, an expanded version of the base game with more provinces, factions, and units, and better AI, and also Third Age, a total conversion mod for Lord of the Rings that in my humble opinion is arguably the best TW game ever created, despite being a mod. If those two don't suit you, I'm sure you can find others that will.
As for performance, the game still runs fine almost a decade after release, and still looks great. I can start a battle with 5,000 troops on the field and have little to no lag on my less than stellar computer. The score is also one of the finest I've had the pleasure of listening to in any game, and fits it very well.
So, what are you waiting for? Go get the game! Europe won't conquer itself!

Having never been a platformer fan (let’s say I’m more into strategy and turn based stuff) It's the first game of its kind I can get anywhere with. The difficulty is solely based on the amount of mistakes one does but that's about it; every level is manageable when you concentrate.
The atmosphere has a bit of a dark, hellish comic flavour, a bit like old-school dungeon game; the main colour scheme is blood red and acid green most of the time.
The atmosphere is futuristic and primitive at the same time, orcs and medieval stuff in a sci fi atmosphere with jetpacks and zeppelins, bombs, guns, etc.
The kills are gore and fun, you can interact with your environment, use it to your advantage, there’s a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of equipment & upgrades to find, etc.
It feels a bit like Trine, but hellish & goblinish instead of pretty & fairy-esque. Somewhat reminds of Metal Slug as well, with the added dark fantasy factor.
Pro's
Regular and interesting upgrades for your character through level-ups that persist through death are a great feature, also making the regular fails not a total waste of time, as you still gain currency in order to improve your skills.
The music is great & fitting, the sound effects are alright.
The mechanics are great, it's possible to dodge pretty much everything with a bit of hindsight, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t gameplay where you necessarily need to DIE to know what’s coming to you. It's nicely balanced.
The Bug & Game Support has been excellent over the past few months from what I’ve seen.
Con's
You get to see the first few levels quite a lot before being able to pass them (or maybe it’s just me), so that was the bit that annoyed me; though I’d like to note that even though you restart the same level, a few things change every time to keep every retry interesting.
Unlocking characters takes a bit of time, but at least it’s rewarding.
Secondary weapons: I would love some detailed infos for min/maxing. I feel often enough like: weapon A isn't much different from weapon B, so did I just waste 250 gold on it?!
Those few cons didn’t really prevent me from having a good time playing Rogue Stormers. It’s really tons of fun, alone or in coop, everytime I pick it up (perfect party game. Yes I only have one friend. Stop judging me).

I'll be honest, after Quell and Quell Reflect I felt a little burnt out and didn't have high hopes. But this game immediately reinvigorated my interest in the series and is easly the best installment so far.
While the core gameplay remains the same, this game features a new look, from the reworked and much improved menus to the various tilesets. The amount of content included has significantly expanded. Not only are there a lot more regular levels, the developers also added 24 hidden levels. There are dozens of new mechanics which gradually introduce a diversity so far unseen in the series. Levels never feel same-y or boring due to various new blocks, bubbles, mechanics and goals.
There have been several fixes of old annoyances when it comes to menu handling and transitions. The progression is very gentle and captivating and better balanced than either predecessor. The sound effects are great. The keyboard handling is as solid as ever. I've never had any kind of technical problems.
The game also introduces a melancholic storyline told in voice-over for the first time. I didn't much care for it and I feel it didn't add anything to the game. It just felt out of place and shoe-horned in. The initial load time including splash and title screens is very long for such a simple puzzle game and started to annoy me over time, but that's pretty much the only downside I can come up with.
If you want to buy only one Quell game, make it this. I do recommend picking up the trilogy collection, but there is no denying that Memento is the pinnacle. It has the most content, is the most visually appealing and stylish, is better balanced, more diverse and over-all the most enjoyable game of the series so far. This is an easy recommendation at full price for any puzzle fan.

Unlike the first two "Quell" games ("Quell" and "Quell Reflect"), I'm going to not recommend "Quell Memento."  Like them, the game is beautifully done.  Unfortunately, the developer continued the trend of adding more and more to the game and ended up over-complexifying it.  As Scotty said in "The Search for Spock:"
"The more they overthink the plumbing, the easier it is to stop up the drain."
And that's what happened here.  "Quell" was mostly fine with just a bit that was too complex (the green dots).  "Quell Reflect" added a few more things and made many of the puzzles too complex.  I considered it borderline OK.  With "Quell Memento," the developer added many more behaviors.  Some are fine, but a few of them just gum up the works.  If he had just left the puzzles as interesting and pleasing, I'd have been happy.  But, when a good percentage of them lead to hair-pulling and need walk-throughs to complete them, it's just not fun any more.  So, sadly, unless you're really, really good at complex puzzles, I've got to not recommend it.

I played this when it came out and it was way ahead of it's time - it has to have been one of the earliest choice-and-consequence games ever made. It even has multiple endings. Until today, I remember this game with such clarity, it was revolutionary at the time and I will never forget the second time I played it and early on, something different happened than the first time I played - my mind was totally blown. I never did manage to recreate the first event.
It's a surprisingly large world and often there are multiple solutions for how to tackle an objective if you explore and find the multitude of secrets this world hides. The combat's a bit clunky now but the weapons provide great variety, meaning you sometimes have to get creative to finish an objective and you don't have what you need. I can still remember judging other games, with e.g. inventory, and other games came up short. This game made an impression that has lasted to this day - I couldn't believe it when I found it on Steam, I bought it immediately - initially for nostalgia's sake but when I played it again, it was as amazing and immersive as I remembered.
Astonishingly, it works on Windows 8.1 and though the graphics are poor by today's standards, it is still a fascinating game with excellent gameplay. It will always hold a place of enormous fondness in my heart and I absolutely recommend it. I just played it through again, about 14 years after the first time, and I enjoyed it every bit as much as when I bought it.

This is my first ever game review. The only reason i did this because i wanted this game to better whenever it come to full release.
In its current state, i rate it 6/10. Here is why
1. Gameplay is civ-like. It's not like it borrow simple mechanic from civ but i can tell most core mechanic are civ like except the turn mechanic. Building cities, resource, etc is very civ like. It borrows from civ, but not entirely improve on it.
2. Battle is clunky. Not only the animation feels clunky, but say the battle formation and battle plan sometimes not executed correctly e.g i set two units with charge battleplan against one enemy unit with onel ine formation. Only one unit charge, the other unit charge in some seconds after.
3. Ui and guides/ tutorial is minimal. Minimal, not simplistic. No minimap for now so you wont know where u are early in the game. You can get hold later after you understand the whole map as a basis, but if you wanted to go to the other side of the map, it will take time instead of just one click away. This game is guides/tutorial also so minimal you will learn by doing it yourself instead of reading or playing tutorial.
4. Inconsistency. This come from the minimal guide and hint in the game e.g you can sometime build a shrine in a steppe hill and sometime you cant. No reasoning whatsoever in the game you wont know until you build a settlement next to it. This also applies to building road, public orders and leader character.
I would say that the game is good in it earlier hours but gets boring at later time. It is good if you like civ but cant wait for civ 6 or wanted to play 4x games with other culture instead of europe. In its current state, i wouldnt reccommend if you are looking for replayability. But if youre curious, it is not a bad game, just unpolished. Also, the price it offer is not bad, around 20$ but i get for around 13$ (IDR Rp 159.000) on iceberg weekend sale so that's quite a good deal.

I had waited for a game like this, covering ancient Far East Asia (Mongolia-China) and after playing a few hours on it, I will admit... I was thoroughly impressed. There are hiccups of course... the game just got released in an early access so.... what do you expect?
Level of Detail: 4/5, You can literally zoom into you're towns and cities, seeing every building and the citizens doing their own thing. Farmlands actually have moving people ploughing away and bands of wild horses just graze around in their pastures. Nearly everything is possible to zoom into and see... from great monestaries to the tiny little country-side Gers and Mansions. You can also see your troops, they are individually unique (for the most part) although their combat mechanics are quite basic (charge to enemy, poke him with spear, then poke again).
Gameplay Mechanics: 4/5, You're peasants build farms, mines, roads, shrines, pavileons, monastaries and chop down trees. You can select various buildings to build in your cities to improve trade, defense, peasant/noble happiness, available food and military buildings to improve your forces. You can engage in diplomacy, form alliances or vassals, ask nations to accept you as the Emperor or simply form a non-aggression pact. The Technology Tree is split into 4 groups, each can be researched at the same time. They unlock various Edicts (that you can choose to decree to give great bonuses) as well as many other economic, military and social technologies.
The AI: From my playthrough, I would say the AI is decent, they would do what you'd expect them to do.... chomp down on the weak, or suck up to the strong... but I did encounter some interesting times such as an allied nation working with me to take down a peasant rebellion... but rather than taking the city himself, his forces allowed me to take it. The AI have also given decent amounts of money to aid me in difficult financial situations. I have noticed however... that the AI seem to have an almost unlimited amount of wealth as wars CAN last a very long time unless you severely out-number and out-gear the enemy faction.
AI Bandits and Rebels also take opportunties to raid your farms but are slightly... stupid when it comes to a fight, they are willing to dive head-first into a fight that severely outnumbers them.
End of my review, I personally think it is a fantastic game and recommend any and all to at least try it... it is NOT a combination of total War.. it is more like Endless Legends, Civilizations and Nobunaga's Ambition combined.

I love the ability to customize games.  (Remember this:  Continental map, huge, All China terrain, and seed of 666666.)
The one down side is that the battle AI still needs tweaking.  I mostly play on easy mode (most games I like hard) because of this.
I've read several of the negative reviews.  Either the writers had unrealistic explanations, or they didn't delve deeply enough into the game (yes I'm including the one with almost 60 hours of gameplay).  There's a lot of depth here and economic strategy can be just as important as military.
Polish is needed in several areas.  HOWEVER you should recall that the game has only been out on Early Access for a week.  It's highly playable now, but, if you like a completely polished game, wait 2-3 months.  Even with its flaws, it's already a lot of fun.
