First of all it is more like Civilisation then TW. The battles are real time but you don't give orders to your units during the battle, you give them standing orders before it. Epoch goes from early Bronze age up to the Imperial age, with gunpowder and paper money etc. Aparently there is a difference between Farmer factions and Herder factions, but the Herder factions are locked until you have played the game for 200 turns so I don't know what the difference is.
Its good as it is although I have two complaints. One is that there is an effect when you work a city, work as in Build buildings, cultivate farms, contruct roads and so on, where you build up a malus negative effect on the moral of the peasants of that city. The problem as it stands is the malus grows and grows as long as you work the city, and its only by leaving the city to stagnate that the malus decreases. And the problem is that it slowly increases and slowly decreases, so 50 turns of building need to be compensated by 50 turns of nothing. It needs to be rebalanced.
The second problem is the balancing of battles, its not a major problem but as it stands you ocasionally get a semi-elite unit holding out against a full stack of milita. Another minor problem is the lack of bridges, although they functionally exist it just looks like you have build a road on the riverbed.
Of the positives: the variety of units is quite impressive. Millita, Noble, Trained, Convict and Palace are the recruitment catagories, which alone is special. Then several types of Melee Infantry, Foot Missile, 3 Types of Chariot, Cavalry and Missile Cavalry. All having different strengths and weaknesses. For instance I found that, although Heavy Spearmen are cheap and effective in the Field, when you put them up against Noble Dagger-Axemen (baring in mind that this unit is obsolete at this point in the game) in a seige, the nobles will hold out and kill more of the spearmen then have casualities inflicted on them.
The Grand Campaign is all the Factions present in their historial locations on a large map of China and Mongolia. The map is, from my playing of RotK and Grand Strategy games, rather acurate. The Factions have variety, although some are samey, they make up for this in the Grand Campaign by there vastly different starting positions. The other form of game, the Custom game, has several options for map type and environ composition, and full customisation for which factions will be present and will not be present. I honestly cannot think of anything more to ask from a random map generator, except the incusion of a map editor.
In conclusion I find this game in its current form to be well worth it's current asking price. Any more features to be included after the writing of this review will be considered by me to be more icing for a well iced cake, perhaps even a cherry on top. I am hoping the devs will be added new factions, such as Korean, Japanese and Thai tribes, as well as perhaps a new epoch.

Still a fairly bland shoot-em-up.
Edit: Tried out the new version of the game. The game is now trying to be like Risk of Rain, which is a good game, but it fails to really deliver interesting gameplay. The game changed names from Dieselstörmers to Rogue Stormers to most likely match the Rogue-like gameplay of, "start a new game/character and play until you die, then restart from the beginning."
The enemies' attacks can often go through walls and floors, but not always, even if the attacks look the same. Standing behind what should be cover from attacks becomes dangerous because of this. The enemies are boring (simplistic AI) and will jump through walls and floors to get to where they need to be to attack you. This often leads to an enemy being inside a solid floor shooting through it at you, while you are unable to kill it.
The camera is locked to the area you are in, so you can't look down into a hole before jumping in, which leads to a suicidal enemy immediately blowing you up before the camera even has time to scroll down.
The characters you can play as are not very different at all. The primary weapon is different and there is a single unique active ability each character has. The active abilities are poorly balanced. Essentially the long cooldown abilities are terrible. They aren't powerful enough to justify the long cooldown, when the short cooldown abilties will kill all the enemies on screen anyways.
The random chests in the world have no logic to their set up. You may play through the first mission and there will be only chests that require keys to open them, but you won't find any keys. The next mission you might get keys out of every single chest that you spend health or gold to open, but no chests that need keys. You might find only chests that require gold to open, but not find enough gold in the mission to open a single one. You might find only chests that require sacrificing health to open, but find no healing station things to recover health, so you can only open one.
The bosses are extremely easy. You can kill most of them by just brute forcing it. Stand still, shoot at the boss, and it'll be dead before it even hits you twice.
If this was the game that first showed up on Early Access, then this would be a promising start to the game's development, as all these things could be fixed during development, before release. Unfortunately, a release date was announced and this is pretty much the game that it will be.

Rogue Stormers is another game part of the recent wave of rogulikes / roguelites that has brought about many fine titles like Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy, Hero Siege and Enter the Gungeon. It is not a dual-stick shooter, however, but rather a side-scrolling shooter, gameplay-wise comparable to titles like Metal Slug and, to an extent, the aforementioned Roge Legacy or Castlevania, though obviously with less focus on melee combat.
It does offer a few unique twists though, such as complete free-aim and a plethora of secondary weapons. You won't have to worry about ammunition either, and can fire from all barrells pretty much full throttle :D
The game offers multiple playable characters with individual special abilities (all but one of which you will have to unlock by playing & progressing), plenty of unlockable pasisve perks and powerups, and secondary weapons. The latter two of which you will have to collect anew in each run, while the others are permanently unlocked (hence the roguelite moniker).
Personally, I find this game quite enjoyable and well worth the price of admission. A great pickup game to do a run or three when the fancy strikes. While the gamepad controls took some time getting used to, the keyboard + mouse scheme should feel fairly intuitive to most gamers. The comic artstyle and the over-the-top lore (if you want to call it that) might not be everyone's cup of tea, but it's the type of game where gameplay counts most and this the game does very well!
The game's co-op modes offer great fun as well, both locally and online, and from what I've seen (admittedly, I'm not overly involved), the devs seem to be on the ball as well, delivering patches and update to accommodate the community feedback.
tl;dr
I would recommend Rogue Stormers to any fan of side-scrolling shooters / action-based roguelites / co-op pickup games. Well worth the price!

Rogue Stormers:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The Medieval city of Ravensdale is under the control of the terrible High Priest, Hector Von Garg, and his large army of goblins. The city needs to recruit troopers - no, shall we say, heroes, to eliminate the despicable Hector Von Goop. . .  Sorry, I meant Hector Von Garg!
Rogue Stormers is an action/rogue like / twin stick shooter game where you take control of one of five characters available and save the city of Ravensdale. When you launch the game, you will be introduced to Hector and his fellow minions with a fun cut-scene. Then you will be able to choose which of the three following modes you want to play - single player, couch or online co-op. So far, I have been playing only single player as so many people seem to play online co-op.  You will start with one character available out of five and your goal is to successfully reach and beat the level seven. You will be able to unlock other heroes when you successfully beat two, four, six and the last level (seven). This game is extremely challenging and it will take you time to unlock each one of them.
You will arrive, really crash-landing on the first level, with some sort of a yellow drilling capsule (that‘s what it looks like to me). Your objective is to find where the boss is located and beat him to go to the next level. As I mentioned above, this game is really challenging and you will encounter different types of goblins, some of whom will be really easy to eliminate and others rather tough. As you move through the levels, you will find chests. Some you will be able to open straight away but others will need a key or a large amount of gold to open. The contents might consist of blue orbs (which are xp), booster items, secondary weapons, gold and even health keg to regenerate your health. Occasionally, you might come across other drilling capsules from fallen heroes (I assume) on each level; just check them out as they usually have great goodies too. Most of the goblins will appear from the Transgoop station and they usually come in a large group at once. As you eliminate them, some will leave behind either gold, health keg or even xp at the place they have fallen. Religiously collect all of the blue orbs and try to fill your xp bar. Each time you reach another Xp level, you will be rewarded with a new random perk (which you will keep) upon your glorious death. Oh, by the way, when you die, you will start from the beginning again. Very tough and unforgiving game.
In regards to the gold, you can use it at the jackpod (supply) or at the shop which is located on each level. At the end of each level, you will see how many goblins were shredded to pieces and how many points you receive for your efforts. This always make me laugh.
Graphically, the artwork is very nice. Smooth animations and the game runs well. For the controls, you can either use your gamepad or your mouse and keyboard.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	5 character classes
-	Fun and fast gameplay
-	Great re-playability
-	7 challenging and well-designed levels
-	Heaps of upgrades
-	Achievements and Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	You might get a bit frustrated at times
-	Hard to find an online game
I really like this game! If you like a hardcore type of challenge, you’ll find plenty to chew on in Rogue Stormers!
8/10

First, I'd like to be clear that I received this game for free, from a high score event at PAX East 2016;
Rogue Stormers is a fantastic mix of Metal Slug, Rogue Legacy, and Risk of Rain - The smooth run and gun of Metal Slug (and saving prisioners who have had items the whole time!), the random level layout of many rougelike games, the small upgrades persisting after death of Rogue Legacy, and the random non-persistant occassionally wacky power ups from Risk of Rain all make for a very enjoyable game.
The atmosphere is great; it manages to be funny, quirky, and a little brooding in a combination that helps make it enjoyable to mow down tons of enemies. The boss battles are varied and enjoyable, with a difficulty that doesn't let you run to the end of the game your first go, but makes you feel like you are chipping away at it more than running into a brick wall.
The most impressive part of the entire game, for me, is how I enjoy playing it solo even though it is better with a group - many games like this give you a boring or tough time going solo, and it is only enjoyable with multiplayer - not Rogue Stormers. It is certainly worth looking into, I highly recommend it!

What I like:
- The visual style is weird and great - a mishmash of steampunk, feudal Germany, fantasy and sci fi resulting in werewolf dudes in space armor shredding goblins in the face amidst a steampunky brauhaus.  Weird enough to make you go "huh?" but also cool enough to make you go "...that's pretty awesome."
- Tight, responsive controls and very few deaths where I feel cheated by b.s. kills.  If I die, I feel like it was my fault, not some rubberband AI or unavoidable things.  It's HARD, like 1990s SHMUP hard, but it feels like it should be.
- Collecting the upgrades, perks and powerups is random and expensive(the gold drops seldom feel like there is enough), but most of the things collected are worth it, and even things I didn't particularly care for, I could see how they would benefit players of a different playstyle than mine.
- Different characters, unlockable = YES.  I wish there were more characters, and it's hard as hell to get some of them now, but that's a minor gripe.
- Metroidvania style map system makes backtracking and taking the chances of clearing everything out before the boss a risky and fun affair.
Things I DON'T like:
- Framerate/v-sync issues.  I don't own a powerhouse rig, but I definitely have one that will run fullscreen modern FPS without missing a beat, Wolfenstein: New Order runs on full rez and epic quality with almost no issues.  This game has so much going on - I don't know if it's rendering background as detailed as the foreground or if there are simply too many particles or light effects, but this game ABSOLUTELY CHUGS on full quality, and even on lowest quality I get kinks and screen tears.
- I wish there were more visual variation between players during multiplayer.  A colored halo, a circle around the feet, a larger arrow over the head or something, but in all the SHMUPpy chaos it gets really tough to figure out who you are, and often. Many a time have I confused myself for a friend in local multi and end up getting shredded.
- As much as I like the psychedelic visual style, I wish there were more variation in the roguelite elements.  I often see the same patterned rooms(roof you can't reach without a squid*, lightning pits with symmetric blade spinners, platforms you can't reach under the lightning platform) and the enemies don't change much in style.
- Some elements in game you just have to figure out.  For instance, the *squid in the rooftops.  It took me about 15 plays finding him to realize that you had to shoot him but get close so he grabs you with his tentacles - this game is arcadey enough that I don't think it would be detrimental/take me out of the experience with some on-screen prompts with the more esoteric parts of gameplay.
For it's faults, this game is still fantastic and a hardcore challenge, especially in local multiplayer, and highly recommended - I tested it out at PAX East and was entranced immediately, and the Steam version does not disappoint.  If they fixed JUST the framerate issues, I would give this a 9/10, but as it stands it's more of a 7/10 - which is still fantastic.  Highly recommended.

Green Cat is a simple platformer with a gun and instant death. The game is a piece of art as it looks great and sounds great even without music. As platforms assemble they make noises which essentially become the music. Its one of those things that is too difficult too soon. Its a needlessly difficult game, the enemies seem to have random actions which makes them dangerous and there are tricky jumps just a few minutes into playing the game.
You start out on a hovering platform and need to press a button to generate the next stage. Then when you reach the next hovering platform you need to press that button again to generate the next stage. Why do I bring that up? Because the game neglected to remind me, so I'd just wait for the next stage. I'd even go back through the stage only to discover it deteriorates as time goes by as incentive to keep going.
These stages are quick, maybe a few seconds if that. By the fourth stage you're jumping from narrow platform to narrow platform. By the fifth its modified to include jump blocks that launch you into the air. Then on the sixth you're launching yourself higher on narrow platforms. It all needs to be perfect even if its mere seconds of perfection. To compensate for difficult design the game gives you infinite lives.
Even with a gun, its tough to call it a shooter as you will find enemies after the first few stages and what you do find multiplies when you shoot them. So its more like they're obstacles. Here's the problem with jumping over enemies, they don't collide with you, the invisible square around them collides with you. That makes it a bit frustrating as small enemies still have big hit boxes. The same goes for projectiles and the enemies will fire three at once in a random spray to make the game even tougher.
To give you the illusion of more control you do have a weak double jump that still seems to get me killed trying to dodge things where invisible boxes still hit me. There were also times where enemies would spawn on me. Its an exercise in frustration that I'm uncertain if its by design or just bad game development.
I highly recommend looking at the game for its color, simplicity and sound... but avoid playing it unless you want to maneuver around the game's flaws.

This game is hard really hard but it's addicting as hell. So far the game is playable but some improvments could be made to make it even better and some of these are in every game. First I shall say why it's a great game because what's the point of saying what could be improved if I haven't talked about the game in general. It's a rogue like 2D platformer (less platformy) the game is perma death and you have to start over when you die which is easy and it's not friendly. The survival aspect consists of a hunger bar, a health bar you fill these with health postions which a few and far between and eating food which you find by killing each live stock animal type. On most areas you will have a small slime which will do a tiny amount of damage a higher level mob which is harder a live stock animal and at times you can run into a boss. Inbetween each area there is a safe village which you can sell and buy and craft higher level items. The rest is cutting trees, crafting and mineing however this is no clone of Terraria or Minecraft. You can unlock equipment and perks and new characters by getting further in the game so even if you die if you got further on your next run you will likely unlock some new item or hat which makes it worth playing over and over. Multiplayer is hamachi based typical 4 player co op and all that jazz. Combat is quite weighty which adds a degree of skill (timing and dodging). It would be nice to have a save point of sorts since runs can be lengthy. Maybe make it more friendly for newer player instead of looking up videos and tutorials online. Apart from that the game is great and I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of challanging, simple (to a degree), co op, rogue like, platformer experience with some survival elements mixed in.

Description:
An endless run-and-shoot platformer that draws inspiration from the 8-bit era. You play as a green cat with a gun, leaping across platforms in space and defeating enemies and obstacles in your way as you collect diamonds and rack up your score.
Positives:
+ Very nice graphics and smooth animations.
+ The controls respond excellently.
+ The designed levels are well done.
Negatives:
- There's no music, only loud 8-bit inspired sound effects which become grating after a while.
- After thirty or so levels, they're no longer designed and become automatically rendered from around six or seven types of levels, making the rest of the game very tedious.
- The above in itself wouldn't be a huge problem if some of the stages weren't literally impossible to clear. A time limit set upon the game causes the blocks in the stages to start disappearing after a while, starting at the beginning of the stage and soon enough catching up with you. At some stages, even running at full speed, it's completely impossible to clear the stage before it disappears on you.
- The hitbox appears to be huge. Sometimes I get killed even though I feel I haven't even been close to an enemy or projectile.
- The gun is practically useless, as well as the Rocket and Mega Shoot upgrades. The spinjump takes care of most enemies, while the gun only splits the jellies in half, for example. The only powerup I personally found useful was the Donut.
There are a few other nitpicks about the game, but this would be it as a whole. I'm sorry, but it felt more like a chore than a fun game.

I'm very optimistic about this game, and will be following its development with great interest. I have only had the time to give it a very preliminary try, but was already impressed by its innovative combination of well-known aspects of some of the best-loved strategy games. The city-management appears distinctly CIV-like, as does the settling of new cities. Map interface and movement of units on it seems mostly indepted to Total War -franchise, but with some differences. Technology tree and research comes across as a combination of both CIV and TW, and the simultaneity of several branches or fields of research not only feels intuitively 'right', but also confirms my hunch (based on such games as Stellaris) that this is the way to go in grand strategy.
As for the setting - it astonishes me that it has not yet been treated by more franchises or studios. Originally, I hoped for TW series to feature the Warring States period, but this does not seem the way the company wants the franchise to develop. A pity, as such. So while I'm waiting for Paradox to have their go at the Warring States of China, Oriental Empires is a really wonderful game to have. Thank you and good luck to the developers!

This is not only *by far* the best game in the Quell trilogy, but also one of the best puzzle games I've ever played.
For the first time in the trilogy I was actually looking into getting perfect moves for all puzzles, and in order to 100% the game I only had to get help on a dozen levels or so.
Memento has the most puzzles, the most interesting puzzles, the most 'ah AH!' moments, the most mechanics, the most diversity in using those mechanics, the most songs, the most details, I could go on and on. Since it also boasts an actual story (do what you want with it), it just feels like the first two were prototypes and this is the real game they wanted to build.
I would like to insist on the puzzle designs. Memento slowly introduces many, many new mechanics over the entire game, and never forgets to add a few tutorial puzzles, which also give you breathing room after some harsher earlier stages. But it never tries to impose these new mechanics on you -- sometimes it'll just abandon them after a few puzzles, because the game simply wants to surprise you; it doesn't try to force mechanics that don't make sense into a particular puzzle.
You can feel that the developers had a lot of fun creating the levels, and hopefully you'll have just as much fun discovering them. Take your time, enjoy the view and have a nice cuppa.

If you have played Quell or Quell reflect then all you need to know is
- This game is of the same quality of the other games but longer
- There's new elements and more puzzles. The puzzles are not a copy of the old ones
- This game takes a couple of seconds to start. Something that I rarely noticed in the other games
You don't need to have played the previous games. You can start with this one.
If possible, though, I'd recommend playing the whole collection in the proper order: Quell, Quell Reflection and Quell Memento.
--------------------------------------------------------------
- The levels are well designed with a difficulty going from easy to hard (but not too hard) levels
- No timer at all
- You can play as as little as you want and continue where you left off or go back to previous levels to complete unfinished objectives
- A few levels are hard to finish but a perfect number of moves but there's no penalty for retrying them (there's even an achievement for that!) so you can be persistent or use coins that you obtain by perfecting levels
- Finding and getting the jewel in every level gives you a different objective. There are also 24 secret levels and the clocks in it
- Good fun for the price
It's very well done too:
- Graphics, music and sound are nice and polished
- Graphic options work as the should (several fixed resolutions, full screen, windowed mode)
- Music and sounds can be muted separately
- Movement can be controlled with keyboard
- Resetting a level or going to the next one can also be done with keyboard

It's not a game that I can even remotely recommend in its current state, as while I can see potential here, I don't know if this game even knows what potential it has, or where it really wants to go. This is a game I REALLY want to like, but I just can't in this condition.
I was in great debate in buying this, because while I was ALL for it seeing the trailers and footage, the reviews made me wary. A lot of the recommended reviews always seemed to recommend this tentatively, while the negatives had no problem voicing why. I feel I completly understand the first ideal. Again, I see really interesting potential, but if this current iteration is "launch" quality, I think we might never get there.
First off, this framerate completely eats when moving horizontally, which is not only murder to a side-scroller, it's not easily deflected by "your computer sucks!", as I purchased the 4-pack for friends and each of them experienced the issue.
Granted, that was hardly the first sign something was wrong. The game downloaded vastly different amounts of data on each of our PCs. My install total was slightly over 4 gig. Another friend had to install over 5. Another only 2. The one who's download consisted of only 2 gigs was then unable to start the game at all and gave up in frustration immediately. The rest of us dropped off after seeing the odd issues.
Enemies spawning into walls while their shots went through them.
Items in co-op appearing for other players and then vanishing when they attempt to take them.
The frankly ridiculous amount of shots it took to kill ANYTHING, even the standard mooks, in this Contra inspired game.
Boasting 5 character classes, and having them all locked behind a progression wall, forcing us all to have to play the same character.
The fact the game would LOCK you into keyboard controls in an invite-only multiplayer match, because it took the "shift-tab" input for the interface as a signal that you suddenly wanted to use a keyboard instead of a controller. The only way to fix this, mind you, is to spam buttons on your controller ONLY as you're loading into the match. Once you're in the room, you're stuck with what it gave you, and have no way to change it.
(I was recently made aware this was just fixed, so there might be hope yet. Too late for me, though.)
These all frustated my group so much they all immediately swore never to play it again, and refunded my gifts back to me.
These are the kind of alpha/beta level bugs that easily should have been ironed out or addressed in Early Access, but the stories I hear of this game having changed its name and direction so often in Early Access, is immediately telling by the condition of this launch title. I know we live in the age of digital media, and developers can fix their issues, or change their games with a simple upload now, but to be out of early access, claims this is representative of the final product. Unless it completely changes from this state, I can't recommended this at all, unless you have faith this really is just another beta stage.

TL;DR - minesweeper, short, needs polishing, nice for 1$
This puzzle game is basically "minesweeper" in hex form. Yes, there are some additions. Yes, the levels have "shapes". But it's basically "minesweeper".
It's not too hard - took me just over an hour to finish. It's kind of fun for those who like this sort of thing.
However, it's not polished enough:
- The controls are confusing (right-click "opens" the cell, left click sets the "mine" - the opposite of minesweeper) so that most of the mistakes I made were from mixing up the buttons
- whenever you move the mouse over a hex, it "reacts" similar to a wrong click. That is very confusing when you play "fast", as you get the "you did wrong" feedback all the time making you hesitate
- The "extra" information ("the mines are all adjacent" for example) are often unnecessary (meaning you could have solved the puzzle even without it)
- - best example for this is the appearance of {5} in a cell - meaning "five neighbors have mines, all adjacent to each other". This is silly, as it's the ONLY way to put five neighbor mines in a hex grid!
- - but there are other examples of this information just serving nothing help at all. I would expect puzzles with this sort of "extra information" that doesn't always appear to be unsolvable without it. This isn't the case here.
- You can't easily fine the levels you didn't finish "perfectly" if you want to try and redo them.
So that's it. I payed 1$ for the game, and it's OK for that price. I wouldn't pay more, nor would I recommend anyone else pay more.

Minor spoilers below.
One of the most beloved classics, Deus Ex's gameplay hasn't aged too well (although Deus Ex: Revision helps) but I still recommend it to anyone who loves Human Revolution, Mankind Divided, or games with similar themes (Metal Gear Solid franchise).
It was one of the earliest hybrid FPS/RPG games, taking after the System Shock games but being far less linear and more ambitious.  Overall I'd say it has a slightly more "choice and consequence" than Human Revolution, with unforeseen consequences happening much later in the game resulting from not so obvious choices unlike today's games.  Both this and Human Revolution have a "button press" style ending although it isn't literally just a button press like Human Revolution is.
One of the major distinguishing factors between Deus Ex and Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the overall style the games go for.  Deus Ex has a sort of 80s action style, evident in the soundtrack and protagonist dialogue (man of few words who tends to deliver one liners).  Human Revolution and Mankind Divided on the other hand have a more serious and grim tonality.
Despite this different in style, both games end up feeling quite similar.  Vaguely similar gameplay, similar emphasis on exploration (improved in Human Revolution courtesy of more detailed levels and even bigger, content heavy hubs contrary to popular belief, at the cost of less total levels), similar environments and similar story themes.
As far as story goes, Deus Ex is undoubtedly more complex than Human Revolution and most other games in existence.  It has so many plot elements going on at once, yet it never burdens itself or becomes confusing.  The dialogue isn't excellent, and it does have numerous moments of absurdity but not any worse than most films (e.g., we're supposed to believe that Denton easily bribes is way into a top secret facility, or how you travel to Area 51 right after nuking it and there's no radiation anywhere).  If this game were to be remade with largely revised dialogue and without the things I just described, it would be one of the best video game stories ever, but as it stands it is still well above average.  One of the reasons this game was named "Deus Ex" was because it tries to make it a point to not rely on Deus Ex Machina.
As most would expect by now, Deus Ex does make use of environmental storytelling, although Human Revolution actually does a better job at this thanks to even greater levels of detail.  There is so much interaction in all levels of both games, and so much exploration.  When exploring and interacting you will find lots of reading material, whether it's newspapers (or Human Revolution's oddly more advanced equivalent), computers, datacubes, excerpts from books with thematic similarities, etc.
There are often debates about whether or not this game is better than Human Revolution.  Truthfully, both games are so good that everyone who likes one game should try the other.  Human Revolution has slightly better character development and dialogue, it has one of the best persuasion systems ever made, it has much better stealth gameplay primarily due to the AI (in Deus Ex, if one person sees you or is wounded without even seeing you, every enemy in the vicinity knows your precise location for the next 20 seconds or so).  Many like to praise Deus Ex's level design (the openness and interactivity) but Human Revolution is not only more detailed, but its hubs (Detroit and most of all Hengsha) are MUCH larger with far more content (side quests).
Both games showcase lots of dynamic physics effects to boost environmental interaction.  Deus Ex does not have a cover system like Human Revolution does.  It has first-person shooter mechanics with leaning.  Compared to Human Revolution it has more activated/hotkeyed augmentations which is nice.  You are certainly more powerful and advanced in this game than in Human Revolution, which makes sense considering Deus Ex takes place over 20 years later.  Denton has nano-augmentations rather than mechanical.
The AI can really take a lot of enjoyment out of both stealth and combat, and so does the primitive clunky aiming/crosshair system.  Also it's terrible that cameras are invulnerable in Deus Ex... one of few synthetic limitations it has.  Furthermore this game's balance is off; harder difficulties simply make the player more vulnerable but not so much the other way around, although this is fixed by Deus Ex: Revision which is another reason to play that instead of just this.  The mini-crossbow is worthless because it only grants an instant knockout if you hit the enemy in the back of the neck; if they aren't knocked out, then they along with all nearby enemies know your precise location for the next 20 seconds and rush you.  Deus Ex lacks in effective non-lethal stealth weaponry unlike Human Revolution.  The riot prod is really good, that's it.
If you can deal with the terrible AI and clunky combat, then install this game and then install Deus Ex: Revision over it.  Play Deus Ex: Revision exclusively.  Read my review of that if you want to know more about it.

Absolutely not recommended.
I would love to see either a CIV or TW game set in ancient China like this, which is why I bought this game. However, this is neither of those things, although it tries so hard to be both. The combat is automated, which is very frustrating because the mechanics are very vague and the AI is completely incompetent. Vagueness is a key part of the experience of this game, because although the UI gives some information about things like combat effectiveness, replenishment, trade values, unrest etc, there is no DETAIL. For instance, I know from the UI that army "readiness" depletes through movement or combat, and is restored by resting. What is readiness, you ask? I haven't got a clue. It was never explained. A similar one is how combat is initiated - we're told that this happens when armies cross paths during the execution phase, but it's unclear how close armies have to get to each other to actually fight.
For more detail on the terrible combat mechanics, I'd recommend checking out some of the other review below, as I'd just be reiterating what they said, but if you don't fancy that and want the short version: it's terrible. The AI has no idea how to use different types of units - it will let your archers/cavalry just stand still and be cut down by infantry, while your own infantry stand around scratching their balls. Enemy factions will take your cities with armies which are 1/10 the size of your garrison.
This game was disappointing because I really really wanted it to be good. This is a setting which is underdone in strategy franchises and I was hoping this game would be the thing I'd been looking for, but sadly in this state it is just confusing, frustrating and unbalanced. And if I'm honest it feels as if the game was planned as something better than this, but funding got cut half way through, leaving the developers to try and polish what mechanics they already had into something resembling a game, leaving many of the planned features out of the finished product.
Not recommended in this state.

If you really like wasting time, here you go. If you're an achievement hunter looking for a game that might frustrate you enough to stop caring about achievements, here's an idea.
There isn't really a "game" here. You buy a lemonade stand, use the profits to buy another lemonade stand, keep buying lemonade stands, eventually use the profits to buy other things. The joy is in the big numbers, upgrades, eventually getting other things on the Moon and Mars...maybe some hope of eventually finishing the game...100something hours later?
If that sounds interesting, eh, there's just a screen showing the overall profits of your businesses. You don't really see the businesses in action, control fine details, customize, or anything like that. Buy Lemonade Stand. Get profit. Buy more businesses. Get profit. Repeat. Repeat. Repeat.
I had already beat all the planets on mobile and for some reason decided to do it here as well. I honestly regret that decision.
The game is well-made and has adorable designs and funny little bits throughout. It also hits a weird human chord of greed and senseless accumulation of meaningless numbers. I thank the game designers for finding that weird middle ground. I have nothing against them or their game-making.
But I can't recommend anyone play it just because of the huge time suck of actually finishing it. It feels like a chore and not like fun very, very quickly. I am still playing because I have admitted to myself that I can't stop until I have every achievement, no matter how done with it all I am at this point. If you're looking at it, whatever, pick it up if it piques your interest, and try not to get sucked in.
The thought of spending real money on this (other than a tip of sorts to the game devs, which I fully support) really boggles my mind.

This game is terrible in its current state. There is no tutorial, no intuitive interface that tells you why rebels spawn or why there is a limit to the number of units you can recruit despite having enough money. Rebels keep spawning without any warning as to what threshold of disorder will trigger their spawn and when you send armies to intercept them, they keep sending you on a wild goose chase while the enemy faction builds up its army to attack you. All this while, how your unit recruitment cap works is a mystery and you end up fighting an intense war very early because enemy factions spawn too close to your capital and refuse peace.
There are background numbers that you have to manually search for to see their effects but these are obfuscated in the primary UI. There is also no indication how fast units will heal and whether they can replenish in enemy regions or not. There is no indication of effective range by which enemy units can be intercepted or reinforcements may join a fight. Although researching certain techs allows you to build bazaars for more money, they cost a ton to build relative to your early income. A huge problem is the mechanics to build up your economy do not scale appropriately to the mechanics to build your military and civil buildings. While this game is not directly comparable to Total War, the costs of early tier 1 economic buildings and units in Total War are reasonably scaled to allow sustainable recruitment during the early game when income is very limited. I have no problems with enemies attacking me early on as long as scaling as decribed above is sustainable and balanced to match the game stage you're in. This is not the case in Oriental Empires.
I can see the game intends to create many interesting mechanics, but how these mechanics are related to one another is extremely vague and the lack of a clear intuitive interface aggravates the lack of a tutorial. Unless the UI is improved to present key mechanics info you need to know, provides adequate and clear warnings on rebel/disaster thresholds, and scales expenses appropriately with game stage you're in, avoid this game at all costs.

First and foremost, I have been a big NieR fan since the release of the "first game" in the NieR series. Despite not owning a console to play the game on, NieR Gestalt's soundtrack and story was so intriguing that I could not help but pour in hours watching playthroughs on Youtube and reading up on the lore via wikis in my free time. Yoko Taro's brilliantly unique story-weaving in conjunction with Keiichi Okabe's masterfully-crafted melodies really touched a special nerve within me, and ever since, I've been yearning for a new creation from the duo that I could partake in.
And here we are -- Automata. And welcome Platinum Games to fulfill my thirst for fluid hack and slash combat. What an emotional roller coaster this was, and how glad I was to be able to finally play this game (even on my sad potato computer). Once again, Yoko Taro asks the hard to answer philosophical questions that challenge the minds of the players, throws the player straight into the blistering conflict, and forces them to make the tough decisions that will haunt them for some time long after the playthrough. Keiichi Okabe delivers a worthy successor to the NieR: Gestalt symphonic masterpiece and brings back some of the older soundtrack with a futuristic twist. Certainly exceeded all of my expectations given how wonderful the first soundtrack was.
I am glad that this series is finally getting some attention, as opposed to being constantly labeled as a "cult classic". Yoko Taro deserves more recognition for his work, and hopefully more people will experience the other games that he has developed. Of course, these games may not be for everyone, but it would be a real shame not to at least give it a try. Hats off to you guys, you've pulled it off!

I started playing Magicite about exactly when it hit version 1.0.  Since then, every update has only improved an already amazing game.  A brutal roguelike, this game punishes you for every mistake in combat, but gives you the tools to dodge, attack from a distance, and obtain a larger health pool, so that (most of the time) you can only blame yourself.  This isn't to say you can't get an overwhelming amount of bad luck.  Facing down two tyrannox, a bee, and a couple boars while dodging spiked blocks can (and likely will) happen to you right off the bat at some point, but most of the time, you get a fair chance to prepare or avoid such things.
The crafting in Magicite is simple, minimal, essential, and for the most part, intuitive.  Once you understand that you can only combine two items, experimentation will likely result in figuring out how to make fires, cook food, make basic tools, and basic potions.  Very few things in the game are not obvious from basic crafting practice (drums and enhancing a certain rare sword).  Overall, it encourages enough item collection to enhance your character without feeling like a terrible grind.  The longest you ever have to grind is for enough sticks for arrows if you want to be an archer, but you'll need two easily obtained stacks at most.
As for your character choices, you can customize a setup for your preference, but you usually have to choose to be a spellcaster, an archer, or a melee fighter.  Currently, melee is the easiest to power up your attack for, but also by far the hardest to play (because you are constantly in danger).  Archer's are the easiest to play, but require the most maintenance (you always need ammo), and spellcasters are somewhere in-between (not always easy to access the items for your basic staves, and a bad run of it with skills can make going out-of-mana a true hazard).  However, despite being locked into a less-than-obvious class choice, unlockable races, hats, and companions (companions being one of the most valuable, and most difficult, set of unlockable items) ensure you will have a lot of choices after you start playing through multiple times.
Finally, multi-player.  This game needs work on its multi-player, but it's already fun (if you can set it up).  Currently it only supports LAN games normally, so some external networking effort is required to play over the internet.  In addition, playing with multiple people has a few bugs (that are being worked on) and some imbalances (which are currently not being addressed... yet).  Only the host can see the crystal nodes needed to ease the defeat of the final enemy (and, in fact, the only decent way a melee player can attack it).  Often you won't find enough ore for everyone to upgrade their armor (or melee's weapons), and there is only really enough for one archer's arrows (which is just as well, since they have it easier).  Food also becomes a lot more scarce, because you have multiple people growing hungry, and while the enemies have more hp in a multiplayer game, they do NOT drop more food or become more plentiful.  That all said, playing with a friend can be a very fun and rewarding experience.
All in all?  Buy this game.  Play this game.  Love this game.

Minor spoilers below.
One of the most beloved classics, Deus Ex's gameplay hasn't aged too well (although Deus Ex: Revision helps) but I still recommend it to anyone who loves Human Revolution, Mankind Divided, or games with similar themes (Metal Gear Solid franchise).
It was one of the earliest hybrid FPS/RPG games, taking after the System Shock games but being far less linear and more ambitious.  Overall I'd say it has a slightly more "choice and consequence" than Human Revolution, with unforeseen consequences happening much later in the game resulting from not so obvious choices unlike today's games.  Both this and Human Revolution have a "button press" style ending although it isn't literally just a button press like Human Revolution is.
One of the major distinguishing factors between Deus Ex and Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the overall style the games go for.  Deus Ex has a sort of 80s action style, evident in the soundtrack and protagonist dialogue (man of few words who tends to deliver one liners).  Human Revolution and Mankind Divided on the other hand have a more serious and grim tonality.
Despite this different in style, both games end up feeling quite similar.  Vaguely similar gameplay, similar emphasis on exploration (improved in Human Revolution courtesy of more detailed levels and even bigger, content heavy hubs contrary to popular belief, at the cost of less total levels), similar environments and similar story themes.
As far as story goes, Deus Ex is undoubtedly more complex than Human Revolution and most other games in existence.  It has so many plot elements going on at once, yet it never burdens itself or becomes confusing.  The dialogue isn't excellent, and it does have numerous moments of absurdity but not any worse than most films (e.g., we're supposed to believe that Denton easily bribes is way into a top secret facility, or how you travel to Area 51 right after nuking it and there's no radiation anywhere).  If this game were to be remade with largely revised dialogue and without the things I just described, it would be one of the best video game stories ever, but as it stands it is still well above average.  One of the reasons this game was named "Deus Ex" was because it tries to make it a point to not rely on Deus Ex Machina.
As most would expect by now, Deus Ex does make use of environmental storytelling, although Human Revolution actually does a better job at this thanks to even greater levels of detail.  There is so much interaction in all levels of both games, and so much exploration.  When exploring and interacting you will find lots of reading material, whether it's newspapers (or Human Revolution's oddly more advanced equivalent), computers, datacubes, excerpts from books with thematic similarities, etc.
There are often debates about whether or not this game is better than Human Revolution.  Truthfully, both games are so good that everyone who likes one game should try the other.  Human Revolution has slightly better character development and dialogue, it has one of the best persuasion systems ever made, it has much better stealth gameplay primarily due to the AI (in Deus Ex, if one person sees you or is wounded without even seeing you, every enemy in the vicinity knows your precise location for the next 20 seconds or so).  Many like to praise Deus Ex's level design (the openness and interactivity) but Human Revolution is not only more detailed, but its hubs (Detroit and most of all Hengsha) are MUCH larger with far more content (side quests).
Both games showcase lots of dynamic physics effects to boost environmental interaction.  Deus Ex does not have a cover system like Human Revolution does.  It has first-person shooter mechanics with leaning.  Compared to Human Revolution it has more activated/hotkeyed augmentations which is nice.  You are certainly more powerful and advanced in this game than in Human Revolution, which makes sense considering Deus Ex takes place over 20 years later.  Denton has nano-augmentations rather than mechanical.
The AI can really take a lot of enjoyment out of both stealth and combat, and so does the primitive clunky aiming/crosshair system.  Also it's terrible that cameras are invulnerable in Deus Ex... one of few synthetic limitations it has.  Furthermore this game's balance is off; harder difficulties simply make the player more vulnerable but not so much the other way around, although this is fixed by Deus Ex: Revision which is another reason to play that instead of just this.  The mini-crossbow is worthless because it only grants an instant knockout if you hit the enemy in the back of the neck; if they aren't knocked out, then they along with all nearby enemies know your precise location for the next 20 seconds and rush you.  Deus Ex lacks in effective non-lethal stealth weaponry unlike Human Revolution.  The riot prod is really good, that's it.
If you can deal with the terrible AI and clunky combat, then install this game and then install Deus Ex: Revision over it.  Play Deus Ex: Revision exclusively.  Read my review of that if you want to know more about it.

This is, and always will be, one of the best and most revolutionary games of all time. It is one of many places where I need to call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on metascore, because it deserves more than 90. I would not go as far as to say it deserves a full ace, but about 96-97? Sure.
Back when it came out, it was the biggest deal. Sure, Half-life laid the foundation for FPS games, but this game is no mere FPS. It is an RPG, and an excellent one at that. Comparing it to other old-school RPGs, it would always come out on top for me.
The best feature of this game is, it does not stop you from finding your own solutions to problems. Say there is a laser tripwire that sets of an alarm. You can solve this problem in so many different ways. You can run through and shoot your way through. You can hack the control panel. You can find one of usually at least two ways around it. Or, alternatively, you can stack up some boxes and jump over it. The game will not stop you.
Also, everything you do actually matters. It matters if you go lethal or peaceful, it matters if you talk to people or not, it matters if you explore and it affects the game, and the story. It is up to this day, one of the most sublime non-linear RPGs on the market.
The story is very good, provided you are into conspiracy theories. The hero, JC Denton will struggle with or against UNATCO, the UN, US government, NSF and even the Illuminati. To avoid spoilers, I will just say that the conception is just fantastic, but you need to experience it yourself.
The graphics don't hold up today, unfortunately, but a true connesieur will be able to look past that, as lack of graphical fidelity is the case with many games of the past age. The soundtrack makes up for it, though. This is one of many cases where music from a game is a real piece of art.
You would do yourself a great service if you bought this game and played it to completion. It bears the name of a classic with pride, and does not disappoint. After a little bit of tinkering it will run at 1080p, and the controls are fully customizable, so you should make do with those somewhat clunky mechanics.
It is really that good. And dirt cheap too. Take my word, and pick it up.

Quell Memento is the third game in the Quell series, and is unique in several ways. Some of the things it includes with the two previous Quell games are the amazing level of polish, and the spectacular soundtrack. This game also retains the challenging puzzle aspect of the other games, but manages to add so much new content that it feels like a whole new world.
In Quell Reflect several new mechanics had been added over the original game, Quell Memento takes those mechanics and multiplies them three-fold. Adding in whole new puzzle types, and at least a half dozen new mechanics, this game is a whole new experience on the old puzzle game we’ve all grown to love.
It just takes to the second shelf before you start seeing some of the major new mechanics (Illumination), and it does not take long until you start seeing why these can be so challenging!
Another aspect new to Quell Memento, and one of its strongest components is that the game has added a sort of storyline to it. For the first time in the series the game has a voice over that talks as you reach new stages. This story helps put the entire Quell series into perspective, and gives the game a life of its own. When I first played Quell Memento I was truly touched when I reached the end.
The Quell series is truly spectacular, and I cannot recommend these games enough, Quell Memento is the final installment in the series, and if you’ve played either of the others, you owe it to yourself to pick this game up today.

While the game is getting a huge amount of praise, the PC port is really bad.  Riddled with bugs and performance issues for some users and completely unplayable for others.
AMD users are finding the game crashing to a white screen which can only be fixed by rolling back drivers.  Some nVidia users are finding the screen freezes and, though you can hear the game is still running by the sounds it makes, it does not recover.  Because the game has no save point for a SUBSTANTIAL amount of time at the beginning, these users have no way to progress in the game.
The developers have been aware of the issue for some time but, over two weeks from release, they have still not released a patch and it seems unlikely they will do so.
With the Steam refund deadline rapidly approaching and with no word on a patch from the devs, I was forced to refund this game.
Edit 5/1/2017: A month from launch, the game has been patched.  It did not fix the issues reported here.
Edit: 7/8/2017: Three months from launch, this issue has still not been resolved.

This game is one of the best games I have ever played. I heard about this game when it first came out, liked it, forgot about it, but came back when it went on sale a few weeks ago. You can already see at the time of this review, I have less than 100 hrs in the game, but I know it will soon rise. This game is fantastic, a blast to play, and just fun to mess around.
Pros-
-This game has insane customization at the start, and you can make a very detailed empire with unique traits. Personally I tried something new and created 2 more human nations along with the 2 usable generated human nations, and made them fight in my galaxy.
-The expansion is great, I have so much fun expanding my empire, colonizing new worlds and building bases
-The story is actually pretty good. Along with your own journeys, countless side projects and missions are available, deepening your obsession with playing this game.
-the beginning of this game is great and you won't be left bored
-the amount of customization for ships, research, and descisions is endless, and I love all the descisions.
-the game is easy to learn because of the tutorial bot, but can be easily deactivated without being a nuisance.
Cons-
-The mid-game is a little boring. Its not bad, just not great. beginning game is a blast but mid-game feels a little empty. Wars are fun but you feel like a little something is missing. at this time players begin to realize and feel the pain of their previous mistakes in traits, actions, or wars. This made me end up restarting a few times to get the empire I truly wanted.
- Wars are great, but sometimes feel a little bad. Once I went to war with a seemingly "equivalent" force, but in actuallity their force was far larger than mine, and I was crushed.
- Migration. migration usually works just fine but has a couple issues. Once even though my empire had free migration, fine migration stats and everything needed for migration, no one came. I waited generations for other species to migrate but little to none actually did. My species were fast breeders, and migrated across the galaxy. It got to the point where my species had 300 MORE populations than any other species in the galaxy, and more of my species lived in one empire than the native species. Also something should be done about species that look the exact same. If im human and a human empire starts a migration treaty with mine, sure the humans will have different traits but there should be something that shows me the difference in their pops when I click on a planet.
Overall this game is absolutely fantastic and I would highly reccomend it to anyone who likes stategy or is new to strategy games, its a fun game to play for hours.

Rogue Stormers is a 2.5D platform shooter. I guess the best way to explain it, it's a little bit like Contra or Metal Slug, with 3D textures. The game gets the "Rogue" aspect from the different layouts of the stages presented, but in all honesty, the stages are so generic, that after playing it for awhile, no matter what the layout of the map, it starts all looking the same. I have to admit, I have a chip on my  shoulder. My friend and I were looking for a game to play co-op together. We found this and I bought a bundle and gave one copy to him. My game wouldn't launch. And I'll admit I was pissy about it. To further add fuel to the fire, when I posted in the forums, a developer (I guess?) said that Monday morning they'd look into it. I didn't like this, the game just launched a few days ago and people were already having problems and instead of getting someone to look into right away, they were going to wait until Monday. Regardless of the situation, their studio, their employees, I didn't like the response.
I had initially filed for a refund, which was denied because I had to get the gift copy back first. But according to my friend, his copy installed and played fine. Annoyed with this, I spent the next 3 hours screwing around with my PC. Eventually I ran Rogue Stormers as admin, I got a error, this error was related to a missing .DLL file for Microsoft C++ 2015.
I already had that installed, so I uninstalled it and tried to re-install it. Nope, no dice, the new package refused to install. After updating all 16 Windows updates, it finally installed properly and the game finally worked. I don't like having to screw around like this for my PC games. The fact all my other games played just fine, but Rogue Stormers demanded special attention♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
So we finally started playing. The first thing that annoyed us was there's only initially one character to select from. Why couldn't they have included more then one? I mean, seriously, it'd be like buying popsicles from a icecream truck and the guy splitting off the other side and only giving you half. Jesus.
The difficulty of this game (in co-op at least) is just frigging ridiculous. After playing for nearly 4 hours, we could get no further then level 2. And you know what's even worse? The progression is TERRIBLE in this game. Every time you die, you have to start over all the way from the start, you loose any power-ups or gold you've found, but you can level up and gain these perks that carry over from game to game. In this sense, you can gradually get better and more powerful as you play the game.
The biggest issue with the perks system is, your perks don't carry over to other characters you unlock. This is a huge problem because of the insane amount of time and XP it takes to level up. Theres5 or 6 different characters, which means you'll end up having to grind out possible millions of XP in order to have each character unlock perks. This is INSANE. The sheer amount of grinding for XP involved is just stupid. Why weren't the perks spread across the entire account instead of making them character specific?
Guess what, after playing the game for almost 4 hours, we both gained 2 LEVELS. Can you even imagine that? Think about playing Final Fantasy, or even playing NetHack, now imagine the game hates your guts, is so hard it's borderline stupid and it takes you 4 hours to gain 2 levels. You can't even choose from a perk tree, it's randomized like a god dang slot machine, so a lot of times you might just be finding the junk perks anyways.
There's other complaints about the game I want to address:
1. Random people joining private servers.
2. The host controlling the other players screens for perks, ect.
3. Graphical Glithces where the screen will just go insane for a few seconds.
4. For some reason, being invited to a game resets my controls to keyboard and mouse from controller.
The bottom line is, I already went into this game upset with having to work with it to play it. When we first started playing this game, we were trying to be open minded and learn how the game played and the mechanics. After almost 4 hours playing, we stopped. We were annoyed and upset, we felt like we made no progress and felt like we wasted our time.
Video games are supposed to be time wasters, but they are supposed to be time wasters you enjoy, ones where you feel like you made at least some sort of progress. Rogue Stormers doesn't do that, it treats your valuable time as garbage and spits in your face.
Not only that, it doesn't deserve the "Rogue" title. It's a generic 2.5D shooter at best with some half-arsed features tacked on. Do yourself a favor and do ANYTHING else with your money then spend it on this garbage.

What can I say about Party Hard?
It's got spelling errors, some bugs that will screw you over during a level, and generally some wonky achievements that will either unlock or will not.
But it still works. Unlike Hotline Miami, where it's always about the speed and the efficiency of the kill, Party Hard wants you to slow down and be stealthy about your wanton murder sprees. You need to use traps and items to wipe out the groups of party goers while picking up the introverted stragglers who wander off into an empty room, back alley, or balcony to take a breather from the party.
It is definitely a challenging game and there will be times where you'll say "this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t", but once the gameplay clicks and you get the hang of running away from your crime scenes and learn just how far away you need to be from someone in order to stab this person without them freaking out, you won't be able to stop.
It's definitely not one of the best gaming experiences ever, but it's a decent title worth spending 3 - 4 hours playing (which you will beat the campaign in that amount of of time).
Disclaimer: Bought this on Steam when it came out, bought and completed it on the XBOne version.

Early access builds of Rogue Stormers were not very good, and notably did not have a cast of varying characters. This release build? Much improved, though at some level I lament the loss of weapon-customization, which was never actually implemented to my knowledge. I first became aware of the game during its initial kickstarter campaign, when it was still called DieselStormers. I purchased it from the humble store and didn't have a chance to finally play it until about a year ago, when it was still in a very rough and bland state.
Now what we've got is a tactical, side-scrolling run-and-gun platformer with rogue-lite level and item randomization, and a stylish medieval-meets-dieselpunk presentation. The city of Ravensdale is coming apart at the seams thanks to the rampaging orcish hordes of the corpulent high priest Hector von Garg. The populace faces opression, indiscriminate violence and horrific mutation thanks to the mysterious "Goop" drilled up from deep below ground. But there is hope: the Rogue Stormers, five playable rocket knights: Brecht carries a Contra-style automatic rifle and can buff the team's fire rate, Presto has a flamethrower and can throw up a shield that also doubles his flamethrower's range, Camille has a rocket launcher and can fire a swarm of missiles, Stabbygale has a shotgun and can throw a glaive and pulls in enemies, and El Cazador has a sniper rifle and can fire a huge round that pierces through enemies. You begin with only Brecht, and unlock the others after finishing the second, fourth, sixth and the seventh and final stage, respectively. You also unlock new upgrades that can drop after completing certain challenges.
Your Stormer's primary weapon has infinite ammo and does not need to reload, and you can carry a secondary weapon that recharges over time. The variety of secondary weapons is considerable: Contra-style spread shot, rapid-fire volley gun, mines, attack drones, the rare health grenades, plasma shots, a melee-range claw, sentry guns and even an orbital strike, among others. You can execute a short dash that allows you to go through enemies and dodge their shots. Combat is less fast-paced then other platform shooters, instead rewarding the careful and thoughtful shooter. Enemies and their shots are usually avoidable, and you are rewarded in the long term for conserving your health as much as possible.
Enemies are aggressive, numerous and at times tiresome to kill, but you are rewarded not infrequently with gold, XP orbs, and precious, precious health pickups. Gold can be used to roll at vending machines for health, gold, keys, upgrades and secondary weapons, and also to purchase upgrades directly from shops. Aside from the vendors there are also treasure chests. A few aren't locked, but often will only contain gold or keys instead of an upgrade, but the locked ones, which require a key, 500 gold or 30 health and are color-coded accordingly, always seem to contain an upgrade.
Said upgrades are similar to those found in other Rogue-lites such as Binding of Issac or Starward Rogue, or the perk cards of Ziggurat. They provide significant boosts to your stats, adding anything from additional maximum health or secondary weapon recharge speed to extra jumps and various abilities that trigger when you take damage, but are lost when you die. However, pick up enough experience drops for a level up, and after finishing a stage or dying, you are given a choice of two random perks, such as a small boost to your damage or movement speed, or a small amount of health restored whenever you purchase something. These perks are incremental compared to the dropped upgrades, but notably, these perks are retained after you die, making subsequent runs just a little bit easier- a welcome addition, considering I have finished only one of five runs thus far. Completing a run earns you a token that can be used to re-roll a perk choice.
I should mention there are some technical problems. The few times I tried online coop the host lag was significant, and there is a persistent issue with enemies getting stuck in walls and items spawning in them so they can't be picked up, though this was infrequent enough not to ruin a run and has since been patched out.

Paladins is game full of diverse character that all have their own unique play styles. You are bound to love playing at least a couple. The card and item systems are great, letting you play champions in different ways, and adapt to the enemy teams weaknesses or where they are beating you. I do have a few complaints though. The game isn't actually free. If you want to access all the characters you either need to spend tens of hours in-game to get enough gold, or spend 20 dollars. Most people "main" play offense or flank, and the next (but very small) category is front line. Healers though, they seem confused. Almost all healers have mostly offensive abilities, and a weak heal on a 6-15 second cooldown. You never forget your abilities as tank or DPS, but as healer you will sometimes forget that you can heal, and it really throws you off.
All around, this game is a 7.5/10 for me. Definitely not perfect, but a lot of fun and can be highly addicting.

Paladins is a fun, FPS MOBA game that is
Yes, you read that right - free to play! While a lot of people see this as a direct competitor of Overwatch; it definitely shares some elements of it's rival. For example, each game has similar/identical game-modes, each game has a pre-defined set of champions (in Overwatch, heroes) and each games has a handful of maps.
I'll list what I like about Paladins below:
Paladins has been in beta for around eighteen month. It's probable that you'll experience a match crash or two that will force you to the main menu.
The Paladins community isn't as nasty or..robust as Overwatch or other FPS MOBA games are. You'll still get the random try-hard every few games that may seem demanding of you but this game is 95% fun. Sod that guy and play it the way you want to!
Communication in your team is key. Use the chat system in matches to try and mix things up for the enemy and talk with your team - that is, if you don't have a microphone.
Other than that, I love this game and will continue to play it wholeheartedly!

Lets Break it down
First off I'd like to say that this was one of my first CoDs, So i am a bit biased, but I have my reasons because 1. Im a cod player, After playing this one, I played every single other cod game. 2 This is the game that got me into zombies.
Campaign:
If you like good storylines and great gameplay, This brings it all. The storyline is very compelling and immersive and honestly the vietnam setting was just absolutely amazing. Also if you like the cold war era, this is the game for you
Multiplayer:
Don't get me wrong, I like to dabble into multiplayer, but for PC.. Its not the best. The lack of true dedicated servers and just chaos(And not in a good way) But it can be fun if you grab some friends or even try to get into some of the modded servers.
Zombies:
By far, to me, the best selling point of this game. If you love a deep storyline and insane map designs, then you will love this. It's a good game for casual zombies players to get started, or if youre new. Id say Kino is definitely one of the best on disc maps ever made on top of Five, which isnt that great but its still fun to play as JFK. If you buy DLC, grab some friends and try dabbling in the easter eggs. Its really fun, however if you dont fancy doing easter eggs with other people, then there's mods that will allow you to do all the easter eggs on this game solo.
So if you are looking for a jam packed game, then this is it. However Im not a fan of the steep price tag on steam, so I would suggest going out to a store and getting a disc copy or buying through a third-party site.
Rating: I definitely rate this a 9/10 game, its not perfect, but its highly enjoyable.

Gorgeously simple.  Clean and elegant to look at, Hexcells plays like a cross between minesweeper and sudoku; in fact the feel of Hexcells is so similar to those style of puzzles that anyone who likes them will like this.  It won't take long to scoot through the game, but the puzzles are genuinely enjoyable and in the later levels you can spend a good few minutes stalled, hunting for the clue you've missed and deciding whether or not to just take a punt and click a tile.  In fact that's the best thing about this game: unlike minesweeper and many sudoku, you don't at any point need to guess; the entire solution is workable from the initial position of the tiles.  So if you don't get it ... well, it's on you.  If you can pick this up for a few dollars, it is definitely worth the time.

Treyarch in my opinion shouldn't be put underneath Ininity Ward. I love MW, but Treyarch just keeps on bringing brilliance to it's games. First lets talk about the campaign. The story is without a doubt well written. It takes place during the Vietnam and Cold War era and it's a story covered in mystery. You want answers just as much as the characters do.
The story takes place in an interrogation room. Your character is being ordered to decode a group of numbers, and find out what they mean. From there it's a trip down memory lane as you go into flashbacks that tell out what led you to this predicament. It's a great story. Now lets talk about presentation. The graphics, sound editing, and music are all simply top notch stuff. One thing I love about Treyarch is the small amount of extra gore and violence they include in their games.
The violence in this game shows how the MW games are a little squeamish. Sure they killed an airport of civilians, but did you blow their limbs off in that game? Nope. The sound editing is also just great, really shows off a lot of talent. The music is superb as well. Now that I am done with the singleplayer stuff lets talk zombies and multiplayer. If you are a guy/girl/whatever who feels invincible, and you like to beat down noobs while taking their cash in wager matches then multi is for you. Or you can just play zombies until you get tired of dying before round 20. Is the game perfect? No. A problem that has annoyed me throughout my online experience is when game lobbies are closed. Then again, it could be worse.
Overall I highly recommend this game, but really do I need to? Everyone has bought the thing already. Plus it's 2017 soooo... maybe go with Black Ops 3. Still great game though.

One of the only F2P shooters I've actually enjoyed. It's not perfect, but it is really a blast to play with its tight gameplay and unique art-style.
I love that it isn't shying away from a massive amount of crude content (gross gore effects and nudity), because it really makes it stand out, ultimately, making it even more enjoyable.
Best of all, no renting of awesome weapons with a huge amount of in-game cash, or owning a gun through micro-transactions. Once you buy an weapon part with in-game cash, it is yours.
If there are any accusations that this is a Pay to Win game, they are completely wrong and here's why:
Blutes, which are used to upgrade your arsenal, can only be earned through playing the game.
Spacebux, however, can only be bought. Spacebux are used for your cosmetic needs.
It's as simple as that.
About the cosmetic items. None of them are free, and some of the items cost a RIDICULOUS amount of money.
It's a little overboard, but at least they give you nothing but something to look at.
This means you'll end up seeing most people using the same default characters a lot.
I'm a little disappointed with the soundtrack. It's pretty generic and it only exists withing the menu, so I had it turned off pretty quick.
A bit disappointed with the overall lack of personality, aswell.
By looking at the screenshots, it looks like it's all over the place, but it feels kinda disjointed and not always present.
Maybe that's just me, though. I feel like it's not quite up to par with TF2 level of personality, yet.
Anyway, in conclusion, play it if you're into arena shooters (for example, Quake) and you don't mind a bit of silly fun.

I bought this game one sale (I don't think games should cost more than $30 but that's just me) several weeks ago.
I have to say, It was very enjoyable. The fact that the game is moddable also helped prevent the game from being stagnant, making it more interesting.
I started playing this game without any basic knowledge other than the universal keys of a grand strategy game for scrolling around the map. The learning curve of this game isn't very steep. The gamer could learn the basics of the game at least within 1 hour of playing the game.
I like how the game doesn't show the tech tree because it forces me to decide which tech branch I should prioritize and when choosing for the tech that would be best at the time or would be best in the future. I am a bit dissapointed that, in the vanilla game, you are unable to colonize barren planets (w/o the need for terraforming them). There should be a tech for that at least, without need to use a mod.
The diplomacy section of the game definitely needed working initially but with the recent patches made it much better and a bit sensible. I don't have the Leviathans pack so I am not sure about those changes.
The war section of the game, I like how paradox made it difficult for the game to just bulldoze through the civs after making it to some point in the game. The strict 100 warscore helps with that. Although, I'm interested if instead of being a strict 100 warscore, maybe attaching severe consequences for going over 100 warscore (taking more than you should have).
The recent patches also made battleships-only fleets obsolete (more vulenerable against corvettes). Definitely a plus and more realistic.
I also like how the AI attempts to counteract your ship weapons and defences after a couple of battles. Although, sometimes the AI does not tend to defend their system well with defense stations, platforms, and/or fortresses. These tend to happen only for xenos popping up during crisis events. I wouldn't mind additional crisis events either or increased difficulty because after reaching a particular point between mid- to late-game it all becomes a bit too easy, especially within a Federation.
The governing portion of the game, I am not so sure about how easy it is to handle seperatist planets/sectores (just put a bunch of assault troops on them and you're good). Needs a little bit more difficulty, I think....maybe.
I like how you are able to genetically alter particular populations within the empire for a reasonable cost.
The Sector AI needs more working, even with generous resources, these AIs tends to not build the structures that goes towards the prioritized resources (energy, minerals or research) for the sector. When dealing with massive unhappiness, Sector AIs doesn't build structures that alleviates the unhappy pops. These also goes towards xeno empires which I have notices after a planet invasion.
As I said, the game continues to be very enjoyable thanks to the large community who continues to play and publish their own mods.
