Rogue Stormers is probably the best game you didn't even realize that you already had.  Seriously, break it open and play it now and you're going to be asking "where the hell did this game come from and why wasn't I playing it?"
Let's go back for a moment.  When it first started out - Dieselstormers (its prior name) got dropped into EA too early and unfinished.  The premise was ok, but the overall gameplay was pretty bland, and probably kept you entertained for half an hour before you put it aside and went yup, done that, been there.
It stayed that way for a while, getting some updates but never really enough to make it awesome.  Most people set it aside and largely never thought about it again.
But here's the kicker - Realizing this, someone at BFG with large metal gonads actually convinced the team to revamp the game and give it this cool Rogue-style rework.  They added a full set of levels with all sorts of really creative critters, a bunch of bosses, and just boatloads of new content.  I mean like a really amazing LOT of new content.  It just kept getting added and added and added!
What came out the other side is a damn good game.  There is a definite Risk of Rain air to it, coupled with much shinier art, an arsenal of unique character classes that change the gameplay, and a whole collection of twisted new items / power-ups that get unlocked as you progress.
The end result is a blast, and totally worth your time to go back and give a serious playing.  Unfortunately there's a good chance the media will miss this transformed gem now since it fumbled its initial release, but that didn't keep the developers from just pouring love into this game for years, and the end result really shows it.  If you don't already own it, buy this game.  If you do own it, play this game, again.  You'll be glad you did!

This game is awesome.
While reviews may be mixed and some can be rather scathing this is actually a very well done game.  It is done in the old style ala total war medieval 2 and civ 2 with more freeform and hardcore systems.  The city building seems to be a bit more like the upcoming civ 6 with a decentralized system rather than an internal system which allows the enviroment to vary your play a fair bit.  The map is dynamic in resources and "goody huts" which take place as encounter oppurtunities instead of huts.  However being a historical game the geography remains unchanged each game and depending on your faction choice your starting city will always be in the same place.  Cities expand thier borders not through culture or even through growth but instead through construction.  You have to build farmland to expand your city borders and the maximum distance of this is based on the settlement size which like medieval 2 is tied to population and the act of upgrading the town which also controls the number of buildings that can be supported and how many troops can be recruited at one time.  In this regard it is very much total war.
That being said here are some breakdowns of things people have not noticed and have led to poor reviews:
1. the game released like 3 days ago to early access and is very much playable despite this more so than most early access games ive played even years after they were released to early access.
2. technology is performed by a 4 field system in which you constantly research 1 tech from each field at a time and some things in one field have pre-reqs in another field. some factions excel or suck at researching certain fields and events can cause the speed of research to rise and fall.
3. combat is slightly unrefined but is also highly adaptive if you use it correctly.  I left some units in defend stance and told them to attack some archers who wanted to burn down my walls.  Sat there for a few minutes wondering why i lost 10 men and they just stood there.... yeah totally my fault.  More on combat later.
4. techs provide a variety of benefits but can be broken down into 4 main effects. culture, authority, military and trade.
Culture allows you to combat unhappiness by having a unfiied culture.  Events and tech increase these.  Authority let's you beat down those snobby nobles who dont like being controlled and effectively increase your city limit. Combat are techs that directly affect your combat options by adding or changing units.  Trade affects your ability to produce goods for internal trade or external trade.  Little tip on that research pottery first as it has no upkeep and provides pottery for internal trade early on.  Trade grows the longer it is operational so at first you lose money due to upkeep but pottery is pure profit.
Now combat.  It seems this is most misunderstood even among those who spent all morning watching my stream.  Combat has a lot of variety in troop types and capabilities.  Spending time researching the movement speeds, morale levels, defense ability and attack ability is well worth it.  A low morale unit will break long before being killed.  Attaching a general to the army stack helps with this.  A unit that is high in defense ability will perform better in qa defense position but if you place them in defense and other units in attack the other units will move forward on the field and leave the defenders behind.  I hope they add a control for this to force like archers to stay behind defenders or they did and i haven't discovered how yet.  Facing also matters as a unit facing the wrong way will send less men into battle then one facing the right way.  All moves are planned in advance including facing so choose wisely.  Sieges are very realistic as well as I have had an army of 1000 men sit outside my city because they were all infantry and had no way to get through the walls and gates.  Archers can set the walls and gates on fire but upgrading from wood pallisades to rammed earth makes the walls immune to fire.  This doesnt stop archers though.  When attacking a town the number of openings determine how many units can hit the town at one time.  Each broken gate gets attacked and if you damage the walls your units can enter there as well.  With rammed earth archers can only burn the gates not the walls so you need stone throwers to break the walls open and create more openings.

Oriental Empires strongly reminds me of a Total War game, except for the very important fact, that it does not present battles as a separate sub-game. Oriental Empires lets you assemble armies from a sizable choice of units. You get to choose formations and move them on a large map of hex tiles, with all your cities, farms, mines etc.
Battles are fought when two armies meet. You can seamlessly zoom in on the action all the way and watch the individual men battle it out with the enemy. But you cannot interfere.
I am fine with this. I personally want my strategy game to focus on the strategic level of a campaign and not have me fight single battles.
However, the battles here confuse me. This is very much due to the  the presentation, the UI,  obfuscating rather than clarifying what is going on. Possibly the underlying systems are also more complicated that they need to be.
Example: When are armies close enough to trigger a battle? It's more than one hex tile, maybe two or three. I cannot exactly tell, because of the way movement is handled. During your turn you issue the movement orders, but the execution happens after you end your turn. Then all units from all factions move at the same time and battles get resolved. This looks cool, but apart from pure visuals of the fighting men you do not get any additional information. Why do only some of the troops in my army attack? I have no idea, I have set the tactics for the army to full assault. Additional armies can join a battle if they are close enough. Again, how close?
Things get really hard to understand when the battle is about a city. I had a large army camping in a city and wanted to engage a small enemy army approaching in the following turn. However due to their movement range plus the battle range – yes, they do not actually have to reach the city to take it – my army got surprise attacked and wiped out. Wait what? How did my large army with my excellent commander lose?
Undefended cities have four gates and I did not assign troops to these locations but kept them in the basic garrison position. Then during the battle the two enemy units attacked one gate each. And my army met them there with one unit each. For some reason my weakest unit was selected to fight their strong unit and that was that.
Now, I do not say, that all those systems are bad, I do not understand them enough. But I have my doubts. I really want a game to better present what is going on and why. Why can I not get additional information during battles? Let me click on stuff to tell me stuff.
Apart from the battles the game appeals to me more. There is a technology tree to research, cities to settle and to build up, land to develop and an economy to cater for. But overall, while this is fun, it is more on the Total War level of complexity than a civilisation, and in any case it relies on you being able to win battles, a lot.
I will check back with the game when it is completely done. I want to see this setting of ancient China done well. Maybe?

At its current state, Oriental Empires is not worth the investment
************************************************************************
(Edited Spelling)
Summary:
The ideas are there, but there are tons of factors that make those ideas near impossible to experience.
The game seems to be designed to bloom at some point, making the one more turn feel come to mind. Yet there are a lot in the way, dragging the experience down to a slow, slow drag.
Almost like the developer is buying time, letting the gamer live on dreams and imagination alone.
I have to wait 200 turns to test other factions?
When I do get there, will the clunky animation, path-finding problems, lacking diplomacy and economic options be solved?
It would make for one of the best games of 2016, but the early access stamp whispers of yet another game being left in development: until pigs fly.
************************************************************************
Full Review:
It's a fun game, and it has potential, but potential has come to  mean nothing for consumers.
Empty promises being the standard in the industry.
What I hear, is that the game is only lacking multiplayer, and that the single player experience is more or less complete.
Now, ironing out bugs and polishing, are what we can expect. Yet there are some flaws that go beyond polishing and bug reports.
If the problems are somehow fixed, I will of course make this a positive review, but as things stand, the game is lacking, and left as is, it is simply just another good idea that wasn't given the time and love it needed. It needs to go back into the forge.
What needs to be mended:
*Combat*
Combat needs to be reworked on many levels. It feels rushed and slapped together.
The combat AI is really bad. Making total war vanilla combat AI look amazing in comparison.
Path-finding is a big, if not the biggest problem. Units will run around aimlessly, run the wrong way: making the choices of "battle plans" (harass, charge, flank etc) seem to have no, to little impact at all. You don't control your soldiers like in total war, battles are fought in a cinematic fashion as you end your turn. You can decide what way your troops face, number or ranks, and each units “battle plans”. In theory it is awesome, but what unfolds looks like a pc game to movie by Uwe Boll with the budget of a bag of chips.
Beside clunky, limited animations and god awful path finding, combat also has some really bad design decisions lingering. Near game breaking.
As an example: single units can take a settlement of four units.
A city has four gates, but if a fight is lost at only one of those gates, the battle is over and the city is lost. Now if I have three good units, with one sad sack bamboo spear peasant mob tasked with guarding one gate, I feel hatred for the game when said, "sad sack mob" is defeated by a unit that could never best even one of the other three units guarding the other gates.
What the hell are the other soldiers doing?
Another example:
A large amount of solders should be able to interfere with one unit mobs in near hexes, in friendly territory at the very least. Having a large army of trained soldiers, just watching enemies burn the rice fields around them is always frustrating. It's their lifeblood, their money, and their people being savaged. Units jogging around the city, rice paddy hopping (in hexes), to catch looters is ridiculous. It makes no sense. As long as soldiers are present outside the city walls, or garrison, they should be able to defend the rice fields.

Why you might ask?
There is a meter measuring revolt risk in percentage. When you draft the peasants to fight off the looters, the meter increases. When the fields get burned around the sad sack mob you call an army, and the city lacks food, the revolt risk increases to the extreme. Then if you manage to handle all the damn looters, and ask the peasants to re-cultivate the burned out rice fields, the meter increases as they feel overworked. Making a few single unit looters, a very likely reason for a revolt and the city being lost.
If you're lucky you manage to re-cultivate in time without any revolts:
I swear, you will see bandits popping up as the revolt risk is high. And what do you think they do?
Paddy hex hopping until either your population, or your sanity turn against you.
*Actual look and feel of the combat*
This is important, as it is a very big part of the game. Cinematic war, you only look to see your men fight, you can't control them during the fighting, so this being poorly polished gives the game a really ugly feel.
Units facing the wrong way and shooting arrows through their backs. Chariots spinning to unheard disco tunes.
Soldiers running through each other. Zooming in to see fighting being clunkier than a made-for-tv-movie-vhs-tape that someone paid you to see. Units are either marching, or having no idea what animation they are supposed to do, as the swing, stop, spin, and run to the horizon, only to come back like nothing happened. Is this an example of a compete single player experience? The combat looks awful. Animations are lacking.
If this was an alpha, and not a game that will soon be released I would understand, but this feels like a cash grab. Is multiplayer with or without the civilization management?
If it's only the fighting and war part of the game, the clunky animations and sad sack combat animations will spell doom for multiplayer in a heartbeat.
*Diplomacy*
The ghosts of total war whisper my name.
It's limited to the extreme. This is a game about building a civilization and waging war. Add more options!
The diplomacy ai is clearly a b-stard child of total war sneaking into the production.
I ask for peace, and I'm refused by a stronger enemy. I get it, I'm there for the taking. What I don't get is why that enemy would ask for peace the next turn and add one single gold coin to the bargain. "I could destroy you, and that is crazy,  here is a gold coin, call me maybe".
*Economics and the Tech Tree*
A lot of buildings cost too much to maintain. Soldiers too. Having markets and bazaars costs more than the economy they provide. While the maintenance of each building makes for a beggar king. The Tech Tree is there to suck the years out of your life with very little change. There's a lot of interesting text to come with each advancement.  Fun to read once, but providing little impact.

Basically just a free visualiser to go with your own music. Problem is that other than blocks that move back and forth, the backgrounds aren't really in sync or dependent on your music at all, and while they fit a frantic techno beat, they seem really out of place when it comes to easy listening music or music like 'wheels on the bus go round and round'.
Also because of the intense amount of flashing lights, I have serious concerns for people who suffer with epilepsy since I could see no public warning on the Steam page or inside the game direct.
The game gives you two modes. First ‘Arcade’ which requires you to move left and right targeting blocks with an automatic firing system. Technically if you just leave the computer running for 3 hrs you will earn enough coinage to buy all the modifications (extra video backgrounds, lighting, FX). This will further reward you with the one achievement which comes with the game. For other gamers who want to actually do something, a second mode called ‘dodge’ is offered, which requires you to come close, but not hit, the blocks travelling towards you. With every block you come near too you are rewarded with 7 coins, with every block you hit, you will lose 25 coins. The speed of the blocks travelling towards you are also in sync with the speedy beat of the particular music you are listening too.
Personally not too impressed with this. It's a concept, idea which never really went anywhere. Nobly Mathew Brown saw this fact and offered the product for free and instead started concentrating on the Hexcell niche where he has progressed his expertise.

Paladins is game full of diverse character that all have their own unique play styles. You are bound to love playing at least a couple. The card and item systems are great, letting you play champions in different ways, and adapt to the enemy teams weaknesses or where they are beating you. Team builds are important, and all classes are crucial to winning.
I do have a few complaints though. The game isn't actually free. If you want to access all the characters you either need to spend tens of hours in-game to get enough gold, or spend 20 dollars. Most people "main" play offense or flank, and the next (but very small) category is front line. Healers though, they seem confused. Almost all healers have mostly offensive abilities, and a weak heal on a 6-15 second cooldown. You never forget your abilities as tank or DPS, but as healer you will sometimes forget that you can heal, and it really throws you off.
All around, this game is a 7.5/10 for me. Definitely not perfect, but a lot of fun and can be highly addicting.

This is one of the best games I've played, and I've played and finished it in 2016, 16 years after its release. I first played Human Revolution. Whilst the hacking system is better in HR, this original game is also fantastic.

You can play it as an action shooter if you like. The reason I clocked up 40 hours on one play through is mainly because I'd reloaded if I wasn't happy with my play style, or if I messed up my stealth.
The augmentations are a blast! The Ai's pretty funny as well.
I'd recommended this game to fans of Metal Gear Solid, Splinter Cell, and BioShock. Even Half-Life fans would enjoy this because of it's story. The RPG elements are simply that, you don't need to go around grinding to level up or anything.
The lore and the story of this game are spot on. The world isn't thrown in your face, it's yours to explore, and the story is enough. I get irritated with a lot of games now trying to be action movies. This game doesn't do that, it's a good honest title.
TAKE NOTE:
Make sure you safe frequently and often -- don't rely on binding quick saves. Mine corrupted, and it seems a common issue. Make manual saves, I'm afraid e.g. <level name> suffixed with 'after guards', 'before aug', etc. I had gigabytes worth -- they take up a lot of space!

First of all, this is not interesting as a videogame, but more like an utility. Sound Shift works better when you just want to visualize your music (bass preferably) with some stunning shapes, colours and animations.
It features two playable game modes and one interactive visualizer, which makes patterns and changes the visuals at the sound of your beats.
The ARCADE mode is about shooting at some objectives and earning points.
The DODGE mode is about moving along the track avoiding such objectives, losing 25 points when you hit them and winning 7 when you pass close to them.
The points will get saved on a total credits section, which will be used to buy new visuals, effects, colors and patterns.
Maybe you will see a bit of delay between your music and the visualizer. This is caused by the way this works, it reproduces the visuals on real time just by hearing the song, so don't expect a good sync with the music, since it makes it all at the same time.
The achievement is easy to get but it can take a while if you don't do some tricks.
I think it is worth a try, after all, it's free and lightweight too, so don't worry about freeing up space on your drive and just install it!

17 years later and still my all time favourite game. Deus Ex is a cyberpunk first person action adventure that takes place in 2052. You play as JC Denton, one of the first of a new breed of nano augmented agents working for UNATCO, the  worlds leading anti terrorist organisation.
I have never been so engrossed in a storyline and genuinely interested about characters backgrounds as i have in Deus Ex. The game has you going from tackling a few simple missions to unravelling some sinister conspiracy theories which are still relevant topics to this day. The characters are superbly well written and voiced for the most part despite some dodgy accents with some of the side characters. But at least they’re memorable. JC is a fantastic protagonist that shows little emotion except for some dry humour sometimes in not the most appropriate times. His lack of emotion gives the player a platform to think for themselves and produce their own thoughts and feelings whilst still having great dialogue and an interesting backstory. Along the way your travels take you to many memorable locations such as Hong Kong and Paris. And whatever ending you choose you are left thinking what an epic experience that was.
The level design is also another thing that makes this game so great and i don’t believe the diversity of playing styles the game offers has been matched to this day. Many many locations in throughout the game are approachable from different angles and using different tactics. There may be a building that you can sneak around the back and find an alternative entrance, use the sewer grates to gain underground entry, you may choose to hack a computer or find a login for it. You can pick locks, deactivate tripwires, use explosives or just shoot your way through if. There are many skills and augmentations (special abilities) offered to the player and the possible combinations are almost endless. Combat can be tricky to get used to for new players but once you get some skill points into what you want to use the gameplay is very fun. Also their are lots of hub areas throughout the game whilst not fully open world they provide lots to explore and discover.
The soundtrack in this game composed by Alexander Brandon, Michiel Van Den Bos and Dan Gardopée is nothing short of a masterpiece. It does a great job at drawing you into the game and some of the tracks are just legendary. The old saying was every time you mention Deus Ex, someone reinstalls it. But it should never be uninstalled!

Loadout immediately caught my attention, and quickly found its way into my heart. It somewhat reminds me of some older shooters, like quake 3, but with a fresh 3rd person view, and much more sillyness. The gamemodes are unique and easy to understand, and it puts a nice emphasis on teamwork. The combat and movement is easy to grasp, and very engaging, but still skill based, offering room for improvement and some necessary practicing. And, of course, the weaponcrafting is very detailed and offers huge diversity, appealing to all syles of gameplay, and letting players play whatever role they want, whether it's support, area denial, sniping, or just plain ol' firepower. But, I feel that in a game called Loadout, you should have some loadouts. I'm all for leveling up, and I think its important in games, but I feel that giving players only 1 single loadout to begin with and for the next five levels is a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥rather than a goal to work towards. I think having even just 2 loadouts to begin with could really make starting the game a lot easier. But, all in all, Loadout feels like a classic FPS, controls like a platformer, and plays like a modern objective-driven FPS, with a fantastic, ridiculous weapon crafting system. 9/10, would play again!

Overall, this is an amazing game. If you're going to try 100% this game you've got a good 200 hours ahead of you. For such a cheap game, that is amazing. It's well worth the time! The DLC adds plenty of excellent things that make the game bigger and better. Get it with the base game.
Achievements: With 84 achievements, this game has plenty to complete. It's a massive challenge to 100% this game... You'll find yourself wanting to give up with how hard it gets but you'll enjoy it so much you'll want to keep playing!
Worth: This is such a cheap game for what you get. Just buy it now! It's worth whatever price it's at. Otherwise, wait for a sale where it's a brilliant price! Get the DLC as well.

Party Hard is a pixel graphic strategy/stealth-em-up game. The idea of the game is you're a guy trying to get some sleep, your neighbours are having a house party, so at 3am you go around there and kill them all, even the DJ. From that you go on an anti-party psychopathic rage around America crashing parties and killing everyone in your path.
There's small (skippable) cut scenes between levels which help set the narritave, but aren't important to watch if you just fancy killing 40 odd people on a rooftop party instead.
The gameplay itself can be quite slow, but not to the point of where it's boring, to me it makes it feel more like the character you're controlling is cool, calm and collected; although it can be annoying when trying to outrun Police/FBI/Bouncers. There's a sprint bar which depletes *very* quickly, a slight shame if you're waiting to speed up your murderous rampage. Different 'events' can and do happen per level which can be a help or hindrance. SWAT might turn up, FBI might turn up, Pest exterminators might even turn up. Level design is nice and the mechanics are good, I think the odd thing could do with a slight tweak, but it still perfoms solidly.
The soundtrack to the game is pretty decent, and will end up staying in your head for hours after you've exited out of the game. The sound effects suit the game to a tee.
At the time of writing this I had completed the 'main' story within 7 hours, that's with several restarts on one level, so I suspect it could be completed within 5-6 hours. There's scope for replayablilty with extra unlockable characters with different abilities and probably even better a level editor and steam workshop thus allowing for arguably endless playability.
All in all, it's a decent, humourous game; a solid little indie title which I would recommend to anyone.

First and foremost, I have been a big NieR fan since the release of the "first game" in the NieR series. Despite not owning a console to play the game on, NieR Gestalt's soundtrack and story was so intriguing that I could not help but pour in hours watching playthroughs on Youtube and reading up on the lore via wikis in my free time. Yoko Taro's brilliantly unique story-weaving in conjunction with Keiichi Okabe's masterfully-crafted melodies really touched a special nerve within me, and ever since, I've been yearning for a new creation from the duo that I could partake in.
And here we are -- Automata. And welcome Platinum Games to fulfill my thirst for fluid hack and slash combat. What an emotional roller coaster this was, and how glad I was to be able to finally play this game (even on my sad potato computer). Once again, Yoko Taro asks the hard to answer philosophical questions that challenge the minds of the players, throws the player straight into the blistering conflict, and forces them to make the tough decisions that will haunt them for some time long after the playthrough. Keiichi Okabe delivers a worthy successor to the NieR: Gestalt symphonic masterpiece and brings back some of the older soundtrack with a futuristic twist. Certainly exceeded all of my expectations given how wonderful the first soundtrack was.
I am glad that this series is finally getting some attention, as opposed to being constantly labeled as a "cult classic". Yoko Taro deserves more recognition for his work, and hopefully more people will experience the other games that he has developed. Of course, these games may not be for everyone, but it would be a real shame not to at least give it a try. Hats off to you guys, you've pulled it off!

Well our first day of going back into the game is complete, but feel I should give it another day tomorrow. At this point I figure I should drop some thoughts.
-using alt tab seems to let the game still dominate the screen, making it a bother to tab out and talk on skype among other things.
- health is not very plentiful and feels like it should be a little more.
- I'm not a fan of EVERY character other than your starter being locked wit the only unlock option for the others to finish the other various levels that in the begining, you're probably NOT going to complete and get your first character in one sitting.
- You level up, yet it feels like even the stage is getting MORE difficult for leveling up, and the scaling of how much damage they can take according to who's with you can really break the game.
- Sadly I still think converting everything to rogue like and losing all progress is something being over used and done in the likes to sell games with the buzz word rouge like, but I suppose that's a personal feeling.
- In some cases durring online games the lag spikes really yank and unsteady the pace of everything from platform movements to character placing.
- For some reason the camera can start yanking left and right on some stage lay outs, like the game confused it's self with a lay out and makes it nearly impossible to work some of the platform elements. Even if not, why the screen would yank the cam off of you left and right to the point you're nearly off the entire screen is an odd bug.
-If you're paused while online, nothing updates, but the game continues. As such you could be brought back to life and getting killed, and you'll have no idea as the ONLINE pause menu seems to treat the game as if it's still in offline one player mode. Your friends continue on, may even bring you back, and if no one says anything, you will die again, costing the team.
- another hard hitting point, unless you're friends with someone on steam or skype to talk, you're NOT going to be communicating with ANYONE in this game. It's not the worse thing in the world, but it exasperates the problem above.
+ However, I do still like ragdolling and gibbing baddies all over.
+ The enemies are interesting
+ Character designs are interesting,
- but I feel with the difficulty curves where they're at many players won't ever get to use most of them...
+ It's nice to see that the button mapping owrks now. It's a little cumbersome and in it's self in a few details has a bit of a learning curve but it's manageable for most of us.
+ It's nice that the odd design choice to allow peple to run around when they're already dead, potentialy holding up the survivors, has been fixed.
----------------------
Over all the game has vastly improved, but it still has more bug fixes to go, and some of the design choices still feel to really wall people off from some fun at a rate that does not feel progressive. You can get better at the game, you see yourself better at the game, but then the first and second level still climb in difficulty as you lvel up, further hindering the reasoning it feels to such leveling up. Unlocking new items for potential drops is cool with the news paper clipping bit, and the choice of upgrade that seems to happen whenever is kind of neat too, but I don't really feel like I'm able to progress much, and behold my first charachter unlock remains hidden away behind finishing stage 2 which has yet to happen for me either by just hard luck, difficulty cranks of the stages already present, or the odd scaling of various other players just trying to have fun with others actually making for miss matches that hinder their survival chances instead of helping.
Within this nugget hides a diamond in the rough. If the game could support mid game drop in and out game play when levels are in progress, that would be good. If you had some more charachter choices to suit different play styles from the get go, or at least a bit faster as I had stabagale in the earlier version after a bit of play, that also would've helped. But there are still design choices and bugs that are holding it back. Great game pay concepts, fun action, guns blazing, and the little return of the old character models as stormer interns is a grand fun experience to watch get ragdolled. But I'm just not able to play with any new characters yet, progress, and the game seems to almost punish me for keeping at it longer.....
Maybe I just am not good enough at the style of game now, maybe I'm missing something, but I would've thought that after out manuvering my fellows, other players finally coming in later after mine was the only room public on a saturday afternoon for a while, and over all seem to be the leading element of various players of how to deal with obsticles and enemies alike that maybe, MAYBE, I would've gotten past STAGE 2 after about what felt like three hours or so.
At least a character unlock under a different unlock design like previous builds perhaps.
But again, I just might not be good at it, but I can say I saw just about nothing but wolf people out there, and supposedly one goo girl who quite out after getting killed early who was the only high level of us all to even have another character.
So yeah, improved, but it feels like it needs more. I'll try again tomorrow.

Going on year two and the game has gone thorugh many changes, sadly not for the better. The concept of the origional game holds place in people's hearts yet sadly converted into a rouge like that doesn't quite capture what the kickstarters wanted. These things might be forgivable if more progress has been made, but in reality the screen to re map even a game pad, or have three pre set control methods is there in the menu, but doesn't work properly for your controller re mapping pleasure.
The characters, weapons, and world design has some interesting imagination to it, but it's drowned in issues that sufficate the entire package into making a lot of people even think the game was abandoned, which is said NOT to be the case. Yet sadly the last notable update that was made recently has only further made the game unstable and thus more crash happy.
As of this writing, the game is pretty broken. Between crashing, re mapping menues that don't truly re map all buttons for controller, a hard to justify loading time for even it's launcher, and the over all heart break that is many people who hoped for a shooter with some slight RPG building elements seeming more turned into a die once start from scratch mentality with everything, makes it feel like a game that's stepped backward into alpha, tripped over it's own feet in trying to do something popular, and cracked it's crown until it forgot what it was.
Despite all this, I keep it a bit harsh but real, because I do keep hope for the tittle in it's concepts and world design. If they got back to their roots, and really knuckled down into the work, this game could be a loot grab smash that would set some bars for others, teaching games like shoot many robots, how to do it right with a much more thought out plot and concept that's more identifyable with imagination. But until they dare to get back to those roots, or at least really start making progress forward again, this game has fallen into a kind of developer hell.
It feels like it indeed has been abandoned by a chunk of it's origional ideals and developers. Don't spend much on it now, not in it's current state, but do put it on your wishlist and following so you can see if it turns it all around, because the idea of the game it was MEANT to be ORIGIONALY is indeed quite the interest with what could be very solid game play.
But right now it has a long way to go, a lot of growing up to do. Still I'll be checking back on this one, because I want them to take these harsh thoughts and not give up, but move forward with them.

Well I played this game for a decent amount of time. I've put in the effort to go through all the main endings and my biggest disappointment was that: I was expecting to ride a very emotional roller-coaster.
I was disappointed as I was expecting a good story to have me crying or even watery-eyes at the story. But after the 2nd playthrough, any of the big reveals were...lack-luster. I wasn't found baffled or surprised as it all felt like it had small impact.
The only case I felt as that really yanked at my heart-strings was with the side-story of side character rather than the main 3. I found the whole build around Adam and Eve boring. They had very little screen time for me to even acknowledge them. They weren't there to harrass you, or even just taunt you through the game. It was just one boss fight after another. And the only reason we ever knew their motives was because of cutscenes randomly thrown in just so we know what they were thinking. It felt just kinda boring to me. 9S was this curious person who had actual personality but was shunned every step of the way for having one.
2B was callous, cold, and calculating. But that's the only the ever side we see. Sure, there is the moments where she calles 9S "Nines". But at the end of the first playthrough, 9S' body is killed once again. And we see 2B crying.
And this bothered me so much because we take this cold stiff character, that wasn't even acting like the cold but caring type, just COLD.
And then she just sorta breaks down and I'm expected to accept that? Even after the other endings, explaining why she broke down the way she did. I felt like it was...kinda just weird on the writing. The moments I was meant to feel emotions were taken away out of sheer ignorance because at that time, I did not know enough about these characters to care or even feel remotely attached.
But enough with my complaints on Story.
In short, I found the Story to be lacking. Uninteresting as how it breaks things down.
The gameplay was interesting. It wasn't really new by any means if you've played Bayonetta or even Metal Gear Rising. Different angle but same result. Due to the weapon classes, it allows variety in attacking so that was appreciated.
As for voices, music, graphical setup. Voices were good, I like both Japanese and English versions. Both well excuted.
Music is AWESOME. Plain and simple.
As for graphics, other than there is no Full screen windowed mode or that it goes from Full Screen to Windowed mode when I tab out (which I do a lot.) Gets a bit frustrating having to move through the settings again and again.
I never ended up experiencing any serious problems like Data Loss, White screens or anything else. It ran smoothly and was overall fun to play.
Despite my problems with the story, I still say this game is worth a buy. If I was to give a rating, I would give it a 8/10

Can I start by saying: Wow. I cannot believe we have actually got a grand strategy game based on China. That is a rare thing to happen. That's with considering the vastness and depth of Chinese history, culture and the sub continent as a whole.
Now to the review. When you first start this, you may find this game rather boring. Theres only a few things to do: Build farms, choose technologies, let your troops explore. What doesn't help with this is the clunky way troop movements work. I am quite suprised that there isn't just a skip button, if you're not interested in the movement/battles. However, when you start being able to do a lot more things the game becomes surprisingly addictive. You will get the similar feeling from any CIV or TW game where you say to yourself: "Just one more turn".
The only thing I find a little annoying is that the eras seem to not last long and money seems a little too low. Now I like a challenge, but currently for me, it makes more sense to constantly to ask the AI for non-aggression pacts and grow my own economy rather than build vast armies. This is beacuse my budget has only just got to 200+ per turn and still to expand a city takes 2000 so that's 10 turns (With a mximum of 300) to do that. But to be fair, this is also a common problem I have had with TW. I just like to have the ability to build a sizable force and while also having the AI be able to match or do better than that. I don't like running round the map with single units or just garrsoning everywhere. This compounds the effect when they predominantly advertise the game as a wargame. What helps TW is mods and I do hope this game will be able to conjure up a massive mod culture as well.
I would also like to see a bigger expansion of the imperial age of China. If they made a fall of samurai style expansion (ofcourse either built into the game or with savegame conversion) to this game, dealing with imperial powers picking at China, while also trying to westernise (while also trying to keep a hold on power), that in short would be my favorite game.
Apart from that I think this game has a lot of potential considering it is early access and I look forward to future updates. Now a quote from Sun Tzu "知彼知己，百战不殆，不知彼而知己，一胜一负，不知彼不知己，每战必殆"

It's bad. Real bad.
At a bird's eye view, it's a Civ clone, but only in that you can build cities at various hexes on the map and make your way through a simplistic tech tree that effects one or two stats.
When looking deeper, it is an empty shell of a Civ game, chalk full of bad design decisions, illogical behavior, bad AI, and the most abysmal combat I've ever seen in a strategy game.
Battle is automated. The player has no control over what occurs during battle. That alone takes half the potential strategy out of a strategy title. They make you watch the battle take place in a scene like total war reenacted by your kid sister with stick figure dollies.
During those battles you'll see:
Troops run through each other, run away into the terrain, run in circles...
The AI runs through your full stack army with one troop and takes your city...
Your movement gets blocked by continual spam of beaten up worthless units....
and other various nonsensical behavior.
You'll be saying "WTF?" at your monitor over and over, not understanding the mechanics of movement, retreat, and combat, because they don't make sense and they don't match what the help says.
I made videos and asked on the forums to get to the bottom of it.
Just as an example of one "WTF?", in the last video, the developer explained to me that when an AI unit attacks a city, it doesn't matter that I have an army that outnumbers and out-stats the enemy attacker, that a single one on one unit battle takes place at the gate and if the randomly selected unit of mine loses, my entire army dies and I lose the city...
so 40 men, can take 10,0000 and will, completely obliterating your army and your game. You can't do anything about it, because you have no control over combat, you cannot retreat because a single man can block your army of 10,000 from moving. It leaves the player no options.
When I heard that, I lost all faith in the game. Such a shoddy, nonsensical design, means someone on the team over there is making decisions like that, that actually get into the game. Early Access or not.
I don't mind difficult games. I yearn for them, but being nonsensical is not the same as being difficult.
...and then there is this really scary blurb:
"What is the current state of the Early Access version?
“The English language single player version of the game is feature complete, although it may still contain some minor bugs. The game has had several months of beta testing to achieve a reasonable state of balance and tuning, but it’s likely that this can be improved further with feedback from Early Access players.”"
If they don't realize what poor shape the game is in after testing, I don't know what hope there is,

Stellaris, a game, I would say, is a mixture of other Paradox games like Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis and Sid Meier's Civilization games. You get to create your own race with its own ethics, morals and allegiances. In an ever expanding universe the selfish idea of humanity being alone in this vast and massive space becomes a myth as other races now meet with first contact and must look eye to eye with each other.
We may look at other countries on Earth with different cultures as strange and weird. Now imagine that you, an independent individual with freedom and human rights, meets with an avian creature with beliefs that it is better than you in every way and that there is no way to convince it otherwise. The idea of enslaving you and all other humans is the most common ideology for that creature and not just a very extremistic thought, it is a common tolerance for it and its entire kin. In Stellaris you must stand the test of time in an infinite and immortal universe and unite with likeminded people like humanity has done endless times in the past. But that was on Earth, now the political battlefield is between galaxies and races that look like birds, reptiles, cockroaches even flipping MUSHROOMS!
Conquer you enemies, study the arts of massive weapons of galactic destruction and find allies as ancient empires will remind you that you are not the first to rise nor the first to fall. And something worse is awaiting out there, something incomprehensible...
Stellaris is in my opinion a more "easy to understand" Crusader kings or Europa Universalis. There are still many options and tabs that you need a basic understanding of, but it has been made so that you learn all of it by pressing buttons and looking around at tabs. It has been made more user friendly, although some might say it has become more casual.
There are many events to experience throughout the game and the first twenty hours, AT LEAST, are an endless amount of excitement as you progress, meet other factions, study new technology, new planets, anomalies... start a new war for liberation, conquest, humiliation or even political demands.
With patience, a fascination for science fiction or grand strategy in general, this game is certain to be a favorite.
Some of the problems I encountered with this game are sadly spoilers but whatever, they are part of the fright in this game.

I've been looking for a game exactly like this for awhile. I'm a huge fan of Spelunky, and was looking for an equivalent game that was more weapons oriented.  Nuclear Throne is a fun option that I really enjoy, but I was looking for a roguelike action game with more modern graphics, and with a side scrolling -- rather than top-down - orientation.  Risk of Rain is another possibility, but again, I'm not a big fan of the pixelated graphics, and I always disliked the fact that one couldn't aim diagonally or vertically in that game.  Dieselstörmers is far closer to what I was looking for
Dieselstörmers plays best with dual sticks.  Although the left stick does aim, the fact that you're also using it to move creates inaccuracy, and using both sticks, you can walk and dash backwards while shooting.  You shoot automatically whenever using the right stick.  As far as I can tell, you never swap out your primary weapon, but you'll find more  powerful secondary weapons in short order.  You also have a cool-down ability that enhances your weapon's capabilities.    You can find temporary upgrades to weapons and armor that expire when you die, but whenever you complete a mission, you receive a permanent "perk", that stays with you as you repeatedly die.   I'm generally not a huge fan of permanent upgrades in action roguelike games, as I prefer a game that one can complete in a single run.  One shouldn't have  to die hundreds of times in order to earn enough gold to buy sufficient upgrades to complete the game (as with Rogue Legacy).  That said, this game doesn't seem to verge too far in that direction. Gold doesn't purchase permanent upgrades -- only the completion of missions does, and if one were to complete the game in a single run, they'd have access to the same "perks" as one who dies multiple times.
I'm hoping to see more variety in secondary weapons, as I've only counted about four or five in the first two missions.  I'm hoping that will expand in subsequent levels or in future updates to the game.  The game is not complete yet, so I'm excited to see what features they add in the future.

I agree with a prior review.
I understand this is an early access game.
These are the issues:
The Combat AI is in need of major work. Formation settings don't hold. An archer unit assigned to harrass engages enemy in melee instead of backing off to attack ranged. While the infantry sits idly by and watches the whole situation unfold. Archer unit gets wiped out - like that wasn't expected. Archers against armored foot soldiers don't tend to fair so well. Units walk towards another unit and then walk away for no apparent reason. Two armies will walk right through each other and not even engage. There should be a group army command that tells all the units to act as a whole, instead of ordering the whole group do something and then sit and watch the individual units do whatever they want. When units from other factions attack each other on your territory, they walk right through your walls like they aren't even there. (Pathing issues).
The above issue is probably why Civ is like it is.
The excessive amount of rebels that are constantly waiting to attack your cities is well excessive. And when your city starts a rebellion... you lose the whole city, without being able to suppress the revolt. I was attacked by multiple large units of rebels from the first day in the game with no units. The rebel units were stronger than the actual faction armies.
The automated features don't appear to work. I set the AI to growth and nothing gets done, no farm building, no buildings, nothing. I had to manually control multiple cities by myself (which I can do), but auto governing actually working would be nice.
There should also be a retreat option when in combat and a verification of your formation prior to entering battle. Field commands are needed to make the battle a little more controllable.
I love the concept of this game and do believe it has potential. The price is a bit high for this early of access, and is not really something someone should spend their money on just yet. Give it time to get better and then buy it. Till then just follow.
The company should not require the money to make a good game, they should make a good complete game to get that money. Because if you put out a quality product... people will buy it.
I will recommend this game, but advise you should wait for it to get better.

As an early backer I was able to watch this game grow over the last year and I must say it's making great progress. The devs are never afraid to play with new ideas and weed out those that don't work well - even though it means discarding a lot of hard work. They are also doing a great job at listening to the community. I was lucky enough to test the upcoming build at this year's Gamescom and it's another huge step forward. While the long-term motivations (character leveling, permanent upgrades, etc.) are still a work in progress, the game in its current state is already good for a few hours of couch co-op fun. The random level generation works well, graphics and SFX look and sound great and the gameplay is well balanced. The different characters' primary weapons add variety and the secondary, collectible weapons are real game-changers and not just gimmicks, especially when you play alone or with just one other person.
A few visual aids are missing that make it hard to understand what's going on at first: A clear description of what the different weapons do; different icons for collectible weapons to make them easily recognizable; a minimap to show already explored areas; a noticeably placed hint to when a character is low on, or out of health - all that would be helpful. And, of course, more levels, more badguys, more bosses. But if I understood the devs correctly, or extrapolate from my experience with the game's past progress, I'm sure we can expect all of that in a future build.
I believe that the game's current state is a good representation of what we can expect from the final product. Being early access, the game is obviously still short and lacks some polishing; but that which is there is already great fun. If you are going to Gamescom this weekend, make sure to stop by at area 10.1 and see for yourself.

Sound Shift is an enjoyable, almost no skill demanding visualiser. Despite that, it does not fit with every kind of music and it certainly is no rhythm game. There are two game modes, an additional visualiser mode without gameplay and 20 visual effects to unlock with points earned in the two game modes.
Arcade, shooting blocks, is kept simple and forgiving making it the ideal mode to relax to. Dodge, dodging blocks, though feels a bit clunky and more challenging to control, requiring more attention. The unlockable visual effects are an exceptionally engaging way to alter your experience during the rides. Players with the right music at hand and in the mood to get lost in a tunnel vision can use those effects to enhance the sensation.
Playing Sound Shift with trip hop was my approach to the game. I tried a few different genres and uptempo tracks but came to the conclusion that the gameplay doesn't mirror my inner drive for a faster pace. Rhythm has a vanishingly low effect on gameplay, which doesn't necessarily diminish the enjoyment. There are certainly better games for twitch gameplay.
Sound Shift is great if you're up for light-headed tunnel vision listening to chill music.

First of all I would like to thank Iceberg Interactive for making a game about Chinese history, for a Chinese total war fan I have to say this is what I've been yearning for years. It is easy to understand why there wasn't one: market does not have such demands, people know about sumurai more than about the Shi culture(of which bushido derived from) of ancient China. Now it's time to review the game itself!
P:   a. It's amazing how accurate they restore the historic figures back to life, like, all those military and civilian units, they dress exactly like what I saw from history books, I mean exactly. The colors, the cloth texture, the tools and weapons, helmets and hats, and even the hair buns!! so for all y'all players out there what you saw is exactly how Chinese looked like 3600 years ago!! This is espiceally amazing when you consider the fact that many of the historical materials and books about that period were either long lost or damaged, because most of them were written on oracle bones and bronze wares! bruh seriously all the civs back then except Shang and Zhou can't even write.
b.  The buildings, the houses, you are looking at a Chinese city 3600 years ago and man that is just amazing.
c.  The concept is really new and ambitious, you don't get to micro-managing battles like what you did in Total War series anymore. Instead, you drew plans and sit back and watch them play out. A lot of hidden object games play at horror to hold their player’s attention, throwing up spooky faces behind windows or jamming items to find in skeletons. Left in the Dark leans harder on these tropes than most, electing to base its plot around a mysterious slasher villain and a derelict ship full of his victims. It feels like a premise that’s hard to foul up (at least by hidden object standards) but that’s one challenge accepted and slam-dunked here by a distant, poorly-defined plot. Despite the persistent efforts to startle, I found the hardest part of this one to be staying awake.
You play an unnamed detective (which should be your first red flag) summoned to Port Providence over the appearance of said derelict ship. The vessel went missing years ago and has suddenly reappeared with nary a sign of its crew or cargo. Once aboard you find your nameless self at the disinterested whims of a hooded killer brandishing a meat hook. Solving the mystery of the ship and the killer will take you from the bowels of the boat to a distant deserted island, collecting dubious junk and solving simple puzzles along the way.
Do I sound a little down on the game? In retrospect it seems hard to pick out parts that were really worth any sort of attention. Design-wise the game follows the template of so many other hidden object games, with a network of scenes to traverse and click for inventory items, HOG scenes to click for more items, and roadblocks to use those items on to pass. The HOG scenes are a good encapsulation of what you’re getting in this game, as they task you to find 12 items with no gimmicks and can be passed almost entirely through random clicking. This is no exaggeration, out-of-place objects are obvious and few enough in number to just click on one at a time until you clear the scene. There’s an achievement for solving a HOG scene in under a minute, and I think I fulfilled that requirement with every single one.
Don’t expect the puzzles to do much for you, either. All you’re getting here are the tired old rotating ring picture and swapping fuses and such. I’ve seen plenty of neat gimmicks in HOGs at this point and Left in the Dark doesn’t borrow any of them, placing it much closer to your average budget offering than what Artifex Mundi normally puts out. That just leaves the story to carry your clicking, and that’s probably the worst part of the game right there. Aside from some sparse notes about an old family and a tragic fire, you’re not going to get any kind of explanation about the ghost ship or its shrouded killer. The various parts of the mystery don’t actually seem to be connected at all, and the big killer reveal at the end basically has to explain why you would even care about who it is. They don’t even make much of a case for it, either.
The graphics are certainly adequate for a game of this caliber, featuring enough detail and color to keep me from ever missing anything of note. The sound is fine as well, aside from the normally awkward voice acting. So that’s about as far as you can get with this one, an adequate hidden object game that doesn’t do a single thing to excel in any way. It’s not bad, certainly not as bad as some HOGs I’ve downvoted, but in a field as crowded as this one being just OK really isn’t OK. Left in the Dark is one of those better-than-nothing HOGs, the kind you only resort to once you’ve played everything else. That’s about as nice as I can be to a game that nearly put me to sleep more than once.

is a Hidden Object Game (HOG). So there's your typical 'point and click adventure game'-style gameplay where you collect items and use them on objects in the game world in order to advance. And then there's a lot of puzzle-solving, including the genre's typical 'hidden objects puzzles' (HOP) that show you a scene cluttered with objects and require you to spot specific items in that scene.
The HOPs are 'old school' in that they require you to just find and click on the items listed at the bottom of the screen (whereas newer HOGs mix it up a bit by requiring you to combine items or use one item on another to acquire the hidden object). But
's HOPs are of great quality, finding that golden mean between requiring the player to go pixel hunting and placing the 'hidden' objects so plainly in sight that no searching is required and the player doesn't feel challenged at all.
The other puzzles of
are very decent. If you're looking for puzzles that'll have you stumped for hours, this isn't your game. But most puzzles do offer a challenge and will require some thinking to solve them, at least.
As is typical for HOGs, you can select a difficulty mode for
that determines whether interactable spots in the game are highlighted from time to time, or not. The difficulty mode also determines how often you can use a 'hint' if you're stuck in the game or in a HOP, and whether or not you can skip a puzzle entirely.
You play an unnamed female detective who's asked to investigate a ship that went missing but has now reappeared without its crew or cargo. The game adds elements from a classic ghost story and from a classic slasher story to the mix, and there you have your mysteries to solve.
The story won't win any awards but it's decent enough to keep a HOG going. Or, in other words, to keep the player motivated to keep on puzzling. The writing is also decent, although I do feel I should mention one gripe I found with the writing, because it's just so strange: people call you 'Madam Detective', ok, but you're also
as 'Madam Detective', even when people write about you in a newspaper. That's just strange. Even the developer refers to the main character as 'Detective' in the game's description, again as if that's a name and not a profession.
The graphics of
are fine for a HOG. Like in most HOGs I think the scenes look very nice but static. I don't understand why they don't add ambient moving objects a bit more often. It would lighten up the scenes so much more with so little effort, really.
The music is atmospheric and of high quality. The sound effects are sharp and spot on. The voice acting is mediocre, with the exception of the protagonist's voice actress who sounds a bit more convincing than her male colleagues. Turns out she's Kristin Price (although credited in this game as Kristin Price-Wilson), the same actress who voiced the protagonist female detective in the Artifex Mundi HOG series 'Enigmatis' and who did a terrific job in those games, as well.
has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
The 13 Steam Achievements are a nice mix of some story-related achievements, a few achievements awarded for not skipping puzzles and not using hints, and several missable achievements that are awarded for various optional tasks, so a completionist will want to use a guide.

While the game is getting a huge amount of praise, the PC port is really bad.  Riddled with bugs and performance issues for some users and completely unplayable for others.
AMD users are finding the game crashing to a white screen which can only be fixed by rolling back drivers.  Some nVidia users are finding the screen freezes and, though you can hear the game is still running by the sounds it makes, it does not recover.  Because the game has no save point for a SUBSTANTIAL amount of time at the beginning, these users have no way to progress in the game.
The developers have been aware of the issue for some time but, over two weeks from release, they have still not released a patch and it seems unlikely they will do so.
With the Steam refund deadline rapidly approaching and with no word on a patch from the devs, I was forced to refund this game.
Edit 5/1/2017: A month from launch, the game has been patched.  It did not fix the issues reported here.
Edit: 7/8/2017: Three months from launch, this issue has still not been resolved.

A huge amount of different factions and hundreds of different units means that each faction will have their own battlefield strategy. The game consists of Chinese empires that start with a pre placed city. This city lets you construct buildings for gold and build farms, roads, etc. for free. The cities also use a happiness system involving complex scenarios like blood rain, labor unrest, insignificant authority etc.

I heard from a lot of people that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel isn't as good as the first or second Borderlands games, but honestly I'm finding that's not true at all. This game is just as good as the previous two. The class are fun, the story is engaging, and the weapons are just as great. It works nearly identically to Borderlands 2 as far as gameplay goes, with the exception of the additional oxygen feature.
I thought at first that the oxygen feature would be tedious, but it's honestly not that big of an issue. There's no micromanaging involved, and oxygen areas are easy to come by. The butt bounce it provides is tons of fun, especially with an elemental Oz kit, and the option of much-quicker resurrection of teammates using your oxygen supply is invaluable in a team setting.
There were only a few things I found wrong with the game. The soundtrack isn't nearly as good as the previous titles' soundtracks. Though I haven't yet finished the game, there doesn't seem to be as wide as range of areas to explore, especially compared to Borderlands 2 and its DLCs, but the story is interesting enough to make up for that for me. It's interesting to see the character development that Jack goes through on his descent toward Handsome Jack. The addition of Cryo-- or ice elemental-- weapons is fantastic as well, especially when pared with the DLC Aurelia Hammerlock class, which has a whole skill trees devoted to Cryo damage.
Overall, if you loved the previous Borderlands games, this one is a great addition to your collection. Don't pass it up, especially if you can snag it during a sale.

What is this game?
It's a Civilization-style 4X game with a more robust combat system set in Ancient China. It has tech trees, diplomacy, multiple factions with their own advantages and drawbacks, and much more. It is nearly feature-complete next to a Civ game, but it doesn't have much in the way of a religion/missionary/holy war system (since that really doesn't apply well to Chinese history).
There is a bit of a learning curve. You are forced to do battle a lot in some maps, so get it out of your head that you can do the ol' Civ 4 single-base strategy and sit in a corner on your own hoping no one bothers you. You will be harassed by bandits and your territory will be encroached on. If you expand too quickly or overwork your people you'll get revolts.
If you're a fan of Civilization and Ancient China and you always wished the Civilization games had a better combat system, but were always put off by the depth and length of the Total War combat system, then this is a game made for you.
As for me, this game almost literally seems made for me. I'm a lifelong fan of 4X's and have a master's degree in Chinese Studies. I LOVE this game. It may be my new favorite.
But here are some Cons to keep in mind:
1. It's in early access so AI has some issues
2. Once revolts start happening it's hard to recover at the moment
3. There are some balance issues... chariots in particular are not as good as they should be
4. There is a semi-steep learning curve (watch a YouTube tutorial or Let's Play first)
5. The tech tree is a lot more complex-looking than Civ 5's, but it isn't really. It's cool once you get used to it.
6.  Some typos and awkward grammar in the tooltips
7. Diplomacy AI seems to need a few minor tweaks, and there should be more indicators about how the other factions feel about you
8. The game looks beautiful but some of the factions recycle diplomacy screens, so that feels a bit cheap.
For early access I give it 8/10 with hope that it may one day rise to true greatness. I say buy it now, though, because it's really awesome for the price and I want to see some DLC for this bad boy.

This Game is pretty great. The only problem I got was getting into the game because many mechanics are different from what you'd expect them to be. I decided to make a short list about the pro's and con's:
+ It looks beautiful - Zooming in and seeing every single face is awesome and I love the details
+ The battle mechanics - I adore how they decided to make the combat in this game, sth like that in Civ would be amazing
+ Tech's - The Tech-tree is divided into 4 parts, each work on their own but are still connected to each other
+ Limited buildings - Yeah, I personally like that. You just can't build every building in one city because it has limited space
+ Setting and Music - Both are awesome, nothing more to say to that. Never seen a game that is set in that period.
+/- Whether you like or dislike the difficulty in this game is up to you. I for myself find it rather "hard" especially early game
+/- I had a few crashes lately but haven't seen anyone complaining about that so I dont know if it's just me
+/- As I said earlier, the game is hard to understand at first. I had several games I messed up by doing stuff wrong that I didn't know are actually wrong or different. I have about 300 hours at Civ 5, about 1000 hours in Total War Games, and this game often beeing selled as "mix" of both (which is actually wrong) I went in with the same strategies - My fault tho.
- No Total War/Civ Mix - The game has alot in common with Civ (Hexagons, 4k game etc) but not much with TW. I'd rather say it is a "Civ with new mechanics and awesome combat".
- The combat is sometimes weird - units dont attack each other because sth is in the way, they dont do what they are told to sometimes. The Battle AI struggles alot when facing two armies at once.
So in conclusion, the Game is really good and I'm looking forward to the multiplayer. Some minor negative points but still worth a shot since you can always refund if it isnt what you expected it to be.
tl;dr The game is good, try it out. Especially when you like Civ 5.

I bought Hexcells on sale because it was $1.01, and the gameplay looked like precisely the sort of thing I would enjoy as a fan of both Minesweeper and Betrapped!
The preview images and videos tell you all you need to know about how to play the game. The rules are simple, and the premise is a fresh take on the Minesweeper gameplay with another layer of complexity for those of us who like a bit more challenge in our logic puzzles.
I was not disappointed. But, had I paid full price, I would have found the shortness of the game (I completed it with perfection in 70 minutes) and the static nature of the puzzles to be offputting.
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game at full price unless you are a major fan of the genre, but at the sale price, it's a buck well spent. Hopefully the upcoming Hexcells Infinite will offer a more extended play opportunity.
Pros - Clear in-game instructions. Excellent concept and implementation. Pleasant ambiant music.
Cons - A finite number of puzzles. No 'free play' mode or randomized puzzles, so no replay value. A bit on the short side.

This is the ultimate epitome of a first-person role-playing game. Even its very few flaws do not result in any considerable frustration, and the fluidity in gameplay and mechanics outbalance the blemishes, thanks to its excellent insertion of the augmentation system and its relevance to mission progression, or its meticulously designed maps, or its well-balanced and concise skill chart. Stealth would need a little improvement in terms of AI response and timing of critical moments (e.g. the player finds situations in which, after being flat-out spotted, the only urgency is to hide behind a crate so that the sin is forgiven), and it must be said that this is the game’s most apparent problem. In sum, the challenge that the stealth element poses is greatly reduced by the enemy’s poor response and follow-up actions to spotting. Another problem is the shallow issue of graphics and general animation. Naturally, this is a minor aspect to worry about, but it could be argued that textures, as well as said animations, are not en par with games from the same period, such as the posterior Return to Castle Wolfenstein, or even the preceding System Shock 2; both more visually appealing than Deus Ex.
It could be argued that story, writing and player’s choice are the pillars that hold the game up there on the eRPG Olympus. The main premise encompasses themes such as global conspiracy, scientific/pharmaceutical agendas, corporate domination of geopolitics, and the confines of biological manipulation. The approach to such themes demonstrates the maturity and profound research done by main writer Sheldon Pacotti, and the ideological directions that the game can take will depend solely on the player, without any biases ultimately affecting the general mood. Main missions are no-nonsense tasks that are as intimately related to the plotline as a story-driven gaming narrative can get, and the side missions are an additional flavour to the lore that periodically unravels with each book or data vault accessed. Everything works in perfect unison.
The long and versatile campaign can be played several times and still not be exhausted from all the plot possibilities that arise should the player simply pick a different choice when dealing with a major objective. The choices shall always be there, whether the headway involves breaching into a building to reach a quest target’s whereabouts, or choosing the fate of the populace from a destitute area portrayed in a grim future. Additionally, the story carries convincing alternate chronicles for the fictional geopolitical scenario that it proposes: the protagonist J. C. Denton travels to multiple locations in different real-world countries and, either through news segments found on papers casually lying about or through dialogue, is able to make sense of the plot and the dystopian intricacies that it articulates. In fact, every piece of plot-related data is cleverly placed and communicated, and even the interpolations are executed meticulously and with later lore to back it up as the player advances through the missions. The several twists in the narrative never wane, precisely because every bit of adversity is accounted for during gameplay and is there to integrate the political dilemma posed by the storyline.
Remarkably orchestrated, Deus Ex excels at virtually every aspect of gaming development, which paved the way for the title to become such a successful franchise afterwards. Incorporation of several gameplay dynamics may be its most notable quality – quite a novelty for a late-90s/early-2000s game, and a virtue that it shares with the likes of the aforementioned System Shock 2, for instance –, even though story and writing may be its greatest one *for an RPG*. In terms of audio production, besides some decent voice acting, the beautiful soundtrack conveys the game’s cyberpunk aesthetics, and the synth-based music is an aural delight composed by Unreal genius Alexander Brandon and Michiel van den Bos, among others. Deus Ex is a genuine gem of its time and onwards; a complete package for those who crave for a mature action-RPG experience and/or for those who want a taste of high-quality sci-fi in a videogame.

This is what I'd call one of the few examples of Early Access done right. The developers have put continuous effort into the game, leaving us with updates and major in-game changes every now and then, showing their interest, passion and support for the game and the community. As the game itself needs a lot of work when it comes to optimization, graphic customization options and mechanics, it's been a victim of improvements from the very beginning.
Graphically the game is one of a kind - messy, vibrant, colorful, with tons of small details that almost aren't noticeable in the background amidst the action - the urban scenario presents itself to you in a unique way that gives this game its own visual signature, almost making you wish this weren't a 2D platformer and that you could explore the scenario in a depth that only a three-dimensional world could provide.
With the amount of titles in the market that follow the classing roguelike mechanic, it's hard to make a game satisfying based solely on the act of killing monsters, but Dieselstormers isn't too far from providing us this awesome sensation. I feel like the campaign itself needs to be explored more, maybe by giving a bigger objective to work with in order to make the player feel he has a bigger purpose, rather than just stepping into the world shooting anything that tries to kill him. The current diversity in weapons and enemies does create a fun enough challenge for anybody who needs to blow off some steam for a couple of hours. If you and your friends are getting this game, you'll be able to experiment the Multiplayer that in its current state is a bit stale, unless you find your own friends to play with; it's the easier way to have fun in this crazy adventure where there's still room for a ton of improvement.
There's not much else I can comment on apart from a few glitches I encountered; it's important to mention that some have already been fixed throughout development. Being this an Early Access game it's expected to house glitches, and I have no doubt all will be taken care of in due time.
Looking at Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams, another title brought to us by Black Forest Games, I look forward to the future of Dieselstormers. I have faith in this company and I strongly recommend you give this game a try if you wish to support its development while still having fun in the process.

If you ever play Shoot Many Robots or at least any game in the Metal Slug series and enjoy any of them, you will find this game quite enjoyable for just being an Early Access title. The game got a lot of potential now that it got a bit of a Rouge-like elements in it. It has a medium pace gameplay so it good for keeping the balance in a Side-scrolling Rouge-like Action game, the pace sure rise higher when you play it in multiplay mode, but right now having people to play with is not that easy (since the game is new).
The graphics feel quirky (weird in a good way), personally I feel it has a good bright and colorful theme with some mechanical stuffs and monsters (which is a unique theme). But some stuffs can be hard to see since sometime the color tone are similar and they overlap each other. Also the guns graphic is well made, some is extremely well designed and fun to play with.
The sounds could use some improvement, more gun sounds, more BGMs, more monster noises, etc... Basically more diversity in sounds and more sounds effects. But for moment I think the sounds is decent.
The gameplay can be expand more, I would say some user customable mode and difficulty could suit this game really well (bosses rush, god mode, extreme mode, etc...). Some noob-friendly tutorial is needed too since the start could somewhat be a little boring since you are being throw in the game with no real explaination - which is important and the game can slip in some of the small story in the tutorial too. I think with just some small tweak the game could get more fun for each stage playthrough (again, Shoot Many Robots is a great example of this). Overall the gameplays should get expand more with some detail touch, so many other great things can be done in the future.
I'll be sure to update this review when the game is updated in the future, but for now I recommend you to give DieselStormers a chance.
