I really wanted to like this game, but it just fell short of generally everything that Borderlands 2 did well.
The writing in this game in comparison to either of the past Borderlands games is just dull and boring. The jokes may get a half smirk out of you, but truly, nothing more. It tries far too hard to be "lol random xd!!" and comes off as purely childish. And the voice acting of it all.. Some characters are voiced well, but there are many instances where it felt like the voice actor was reading from a script with no rehearsal whatsoever, with an extremely monotone voice. Sloppy.
The quests are nothing more than "go here, pull this," and "hit this," which usually consists of traversing a large portion of the map to make you feel like you're actually spending time *playing* the game.
Moon combat felt alright at first until it (very quickly) became hampering to the overall combat experience of the game. It's merely a gimmick that didn't even perform well as a gimmick. In BL2, I'd be happy to take on a group of Loaders or Threshers, but I can't find any enjoyment in the encounters in this game, a lot of which stems from the floaty combat.
I'll admit the addition of laser guns is a welcome, and they're pretty fun when being used, but their addition can't make up for the lackluster experience that is the rest of the game.

(This first (but added after initial review): Since I am became convinced that the faults of this game are by design and not fixable (and since the developer seems to think that single player is done - making it unlikely that structural changes to core mechanics will even be attempted) I tried to get a refund. I didn't get it because I played the game for more than 2 hours. My fault for giving the game a second/third chance, I guess. If you don't want to run into the same trap just be aware that you have to make up your mind in the first two hours)
If single player is indeed done and they are just working on multiplayer, then this is a bad game.
Building buildings is a bad idea more often than not because the huge upkeep costs will ruin you. Even things like market places, which usually help build a working economy, seem to hurt your growth more than they help.
The battles are very frustrating. There is no way to lock down enemy armies and they almost always survive the fight. Also the AI (which does all the moving and fighting for you) makes very dumb things... like ignore the enemy bandits that are pillaging your city (right next to your army) and instead attack the neutral player next to your OTHER city several hexes down. I've had to spend like 20 moves just hunting one bandit and I didn't even defeat him, he just retreated to somewhere else. I would really like to publicly execute that general and his entire army for incompetence, but the game doesn't even give you THAT option.
Armies that lose their battle don't retreat to your city directly behind them, but instead to somewhere ~1.5 moves away from your city. Which puts you in trouble for next turn because your city is alone with whoever just routed you and you can't get back.
And when you got an economy going by cleverly NOT building your cities, then peasant revolts turn 3 of your 9 cities in two turns (one of them your capital - which was fine a few turns before, so no idea what happened there). No warning or anything. And of course the peasants can afford military that you could only dream of (instant full stacked armies). Plus, what would you even use to reconquer? Your capital is the city that was built up to create armies.
I mean not that a warning would help. You can't really do anything. I mean you could build a building for a few turns and then raze it after, but the helpful effects are negligible and the costs huge (and the whole idea of building a temple for a few turns to make the  peasants happy and then razing it for economic reasons is idiotic), Seriously, I had a very strong economy at one point, built an Taoist temple in every city, to make my peasants happy, and that alone completely tanked my entire economy.
All in all the game continually expects you to make decisions, but all the data required to make those decisions is hidden from you. Like silk for example. Is it a good idea to produce silk? No idea. At this point I think it is probably ALWAYS a bad idea. Building it in every city will definitly ruin you. Maybe it will be feasible to build it once in your empire after you reach a certain size? Or maybe the only point when it is ever feasible is when you have a map buff for silk in one of your cities? But how would you know when? So right now I just avoid it... I mean what's the point of having so many buildings when almost all of them are designed as noobtraps?
I am hoping that they will still work on single player because all in all this *could* be a very great game.
The similarities with Civ end with the hexes, but the game is pretty much a carbon copy of TW games (right down to the end of turn gong) without user controlled battles (which I enjoyed less every TW game after Medieval II, so not a big loss there) and with faster turns (which is a HUGE plus).

I really thought I would like this game seeing that I loved Don't Starve's penchant for thoughtful grueling unfairness. To my surprise I initially found this game boring but mad a 180 turn the more I played it. It does have some odd design choices but is fun overall.
Firstly let me state what I like about the game. The art design is wonderful, the pixel design on the characters, beasts and environment is exquisitely done. The lighting effects adds a level of charm that makes me love it even more. The game itself runs buttery smooth with limited to no screen tearing. The sound is nice and somewhat tribal\adventurous while the platforming is as tight and non floaty as it could ever be. Now with that said it pains me to write about my dislikes however it must be done.
My first gripe comes from the crafting system as it is knee deep laborious to craft items. I understand that certain items must be crafted before others but there must be a faster way to expedite the process like a recipe book or something to store the knowledge once you've created any item which allows you to instantly create the item next time. I get that crafting is a major hook of the game but as it stands, it wastes too much time and can cause your demise if you're in a tough situation.
Another gripe of mine is a none issue to those who're fine with playing platformers with keyboard. But, for those of you who are like me and love playing via gamepads beware there's no gamepad support. I often mis-pressed keys but that's simply as result of my ineptitude with using keyboard for platformers and not a knock on the game's actual controls as the controls themselves feel fine. With that said the controls can be remapped to suit your needs. If you really dislike playing plaformers with keyboard like me you might want to wait until the developer implements gamepad support. As of this review (26-Jun-2014, v1.1.5) it's not there yet.
Also I think I found a bug, when the game starts the audio is extremely low even though it's set to 10 (max) lowering and raising it from there returns the sound to audible levels.

This is ... not a good game.
It would have been okay when it originally released in 2000, but the interesting story and characters are severely hampered by bad gameplay. The controls feel like steering a shopping cart, the UI is bad, and the foes are all bullet sponges (even the unarmored and unaugmented humans) in a world that hordes ammo like it was the zombie apocalypse.
I really like everything about this game EXCEPT PLAYING IT. Interesting characters, complex conspiracies (poorly executed, but if they were doing it well you'd probably miss it), a dystopian future that is distressingly more plausible every day, choices and consequences, multiple options for resolving tactical challenges, lots of exploration and rewards for doing so, a strong emphasis on story, and the ability to alter the fate of the game world. Unfortunately, playing it is a tedious chore that is sometimes actually painful, and never fun.
Great ideas, and the writing is good, but the only reason this gets praise still is nostalgia. People played it as children, loved it when they had nothing better to compare it to, and still remember it fondly.
Stay away.
If you want to play in this universe, Human Revolution is nearly as solid a story and has significantly better gameplay.
Edit:
Clarification about why I say the gameplay is bad.
I sat down to play DX, and discovered that I could barely interact with the world, that the control scheme was just bad.
So, I did my research. I learned that it used the same engine and similar features as System Shock 2 (another beloved classic). So, I tracked down SS2 and started playing.
SS2 is violent, twitchy, and unforgiving. It also has an interesting discovery-based narrative (the story happened before you show up) that I found compelling. I put in the work, adjusted the controls, tweaked my upgrades to match my prefered play style, and beat SS2. I even had a lot of fun doing it.
With all my training, I came back to DX. I adjusted the button layout to match my trained reflexes, put on my patience hat, and settled in to enjoy DX.
Deus Ex still controlled terribly.
System Shock 2 is older, less ambitious, and less well regarded than Deus Ex. SS2 also has smoother, more responsive gameplay, a more useful UI, and does a much better job of making the protagonist feel like an augmeted badass (regardless of playstyle).
That's why I say DX has terrible controls. Because an older game, using the same engine, did it better.

Sounds Shift takes any song played by your system and uses it to estabilish the rhythm and speed of the whole game: you'll get two game modes where you either shoot at targets ( both static and moving) or have to dodge them while moving close enough to gather points.
While sporting decent visuals and being fun in quick burts its gameplay is sadly too shallow to have any kind of staying power making Sound Shift a pretty bland and forgettable experience.
-once you unlock a few visual mods (and the ability to mix them) the game will look quite pretty
-being able to choose any song played on your system, regardless of source, gives you lots of freedom
-gathering the points to unlock all visual and effect mods will take a few hours
-very simple gameplay with little variation and basically no way to fail, it can get dull fast
-no leaderboards, no high scores or any kind of purpose to gameplay except gathering points
-doesn't work too well with low tempo songs as your fire rate is also tied to the music
-the lack of mouse support was a big surprise for me, keyboard or controller work decent enough but lack the smoothness a mouse would have and this is something that the "dodge" mode sorely needs
Sound Shift isn't an horrible game at all, it's pretty decent actually and the first few songs'll be fun as you slowly gain points and unlock new visuals: but after an hour you'll realize there's basically no variance in what you're playing as there's just one flat path and only a few types of blocks coming your way.
The game is also infinite as it goes on and on until you quit, the fact it streams whatever your system is playing rather than single tracks means you can forget about online leaderboards or even just local high scores: after a bit I felt as if it simply lacked purpose and even more so once you've unlocked everything thus making gathered points useless.
Ultimately I can't recommend Sound Shift due to how bland the gameplay feels, there's simply much better rhythm based games out there: still it might be a decent purchase (especially at its 1$ sale price) for players looking for a simple game to play during a break or people wanting a very easy game to try and get into the genre.
Short but sweet, absolutely worth the small price of entry if you like puzzle games. In other words, Hexcellent.

Imagine Terraria and Spelunky. Two great games. And then combine them.
So what comes out? Another great game!
Magicite is a rogue like survival game with RPG Elements, where you farm minerals and materials,and try to craft better weapons and gear once you are in a town. (There's always a level --> town --> level --> town --> etc.). Really important is Inventory management, since you only have limited space and you still need space to craft materials together. So if you just harvest everything you will soon run out of inventory space. This can be annoying for beginners,since they don't know what materials exactly are important,but it's also a strength of the game: It is really fun to just combine different things with Shift - Click and experiment to see what comes out! (If you don't like experimenting there's always the Wiki to help you out!)
Once you understand the depth of the game you will notice that you can specialize yourself on one "class":
- A Warrior (High ATK,DEF stats and melee weapons)
- A Ranger (High DEX stat and a Bow with different types of Arrows)
- A Mage (High MAG stat and 3 different Magic Weapons as it is right now)
It is really fun to farm ores and materials to craft better gear for your character,
because every new item you craft has a noticeable impact on your character (wheter it is damage or HP or DEF).
Another strength of Magicite is the "unlock system": Once your run ended (by death or by beating the game), you get the chance to unlock certain characters or hats. Different characters have different starting conditions,which can influence your run and different hats give you different bonuses.
Keep in mind: Most unlockables only have a chance to get unlocked so even though you reached certain goals, the unlockables are not guaranteed. This can be sometimes frustrating,if you have a 50 minute run (definetely a possilble time) and you die because of stupidity and unlock nothing new.
What kinda weakens the whole experience,is that Magicite doesn't really seem finished.
There is a final boss and the current version is over 1.0 but it seems like there could be way more.
Because once you actually understand the whole crafting mechanism,it seems really simple.
(Important to point out here is,that the game is still being worked on and new content WILL come in future updates)
There are some points that I didn't really talked about, so I will list a summary of all Pro's and Con's:
- Super Mega Awesome Soundtrack (seriously this is important to mention,it creates a perfect atmosphere)
- Lovely Pixeldesign / Graphic
- Feel your character becoming stronger,so every Level Up and new Item feels like progress
- Acquire 3 individual Skill out of 3 different "Skill - Pools" at level 5, 10 and 15
- It's fun experimenting with different strategies to see what works best for you
- Challenging bosses and an epic final boss
- Constant Time pressure that creates tension (Some might argue that this is a Con,I personally like it)
- It's really fun to play overall, once you understand how the game works
- Multiplayer

Hexcells is the illegitimate love child of Minesweeper and Picross. Using a series of number clues, you must logically remove and mark hexagons in order to fill out the pattern hidden underneath. If you've played either of the two before mentioned games this will be entirely intuitive, with numbers within a hexagon corresponding to the number of blue tiles (ie. mines) surrounding said hexagon, and the numbers on top of a column signally the number of blue tiles within it (with a few special signals providing additional info).
What Hexcells adds over vanilla Minesweeper is the more puzzle oriented design of its levels, each being individually designed to test your skills of deduction with cleverly disguised patterns that are often far more obvious than they first appear. Solving them is abundantly satisfying, and makes it rather hard to go back to the randomly generated boards of its spiritual predecessor.
But this is also the cause of my biggest complaint, that being the times when logic is thrown out the window and you are all but forced to guess in order to move forward. This is frustrating because you're allowed but one mistake before forfeiting your perfect rating, essentially requiring you to memorize patterns and replay levels or cheat and use screenshots of the completed puzzle to go back and perfect the stage. It's odd that a game essentially designed to entirely do away with the use of luck to solve puzzles falls into such a disappointing pitfall, but I can only assume it was an oversight by the developer as for the majority of the game it's entirely possible to intelligently complete stages, which I suppose is why these moments of guesswork stand out so strongly.
Although it just barley misses the mark, the overwhelming opinion I took away from Hexcells is that of a strong new logic puzzle that has the potential to perfect itself in future iterations, and may one day sit beside the likes of Picross and Sudoku. If you have any appreciation for the games I've compared it to, I wouldn't hesitate to check Hexcells out. It's budget priced so you've got very little to lose, and may find yourself similarly enamored by what at first seemed but a cheap knockoff.

The puzzles are mostly the same types we meet in other Artifex Mundi titles, this time with decreased difficulty. The genre-defining hidden object scenes are excellent, as always, but a little too empty: a few of them are almost completely cleared out after two visits.
Play time is also short– around two hours–, which is compensated by the low price range. So if you want a good alternative for a movie ticket, Left in the Dark may provide an entertaining afternoon.

Welcome to Party Hard, where you play as a man with the stamina of someone who's never ran before in his life against a group of party people who have each been trained to run a marathon. Where pushing people into open flames is A-Okay, but standing 5 feet away from a dead body is not. Party Hard is a unique stealth game that has you kill groups of about 50 people without alerting the cops. Although the mechanics may seem tricky at first, a bit of patience and experience makes this game very enjoyable. There are about 10 maps to the story, each lasting about 10~15 minutes (depending on luck and skill). After a few frustrating mistakes, being able to complete a difficult level is extremely satisfying. The game itself is not very long, but with the level editor, you are able to create and play on maps made by other players. Overall, I'd say this game is worth the price if you enjoy stealth games, but could probably be held off on until a sale comes by if the video and screenshots dont really catch your eye.

The tagline you see in most of the reviews here on steam is that this is “CIV + Total War set in China”. I’d say the first part of that tagline is inaccurate – this game does not much resemble Total War. If you really want a Total War style game set in China get Koei’s Romance of the Three Kingdoms series, with the caveat that those games are based on historical fantasy and not actual history. That said, Oriental Empires is a good game with interesting design plus a unique setting.
Gameplay: In the Grand Campaign you explore a semi-random (resources are distributed differently each game but the map is fixed) map of China that starts in 1500BCE. There are many historically-flavored factions but the differences between them are small at the time of this review and each start with the same setup – a capital city in a fixed, historical, location, a settler, a commander and a faction leader who can also command. The biggest difference between factions is starting location.
As you explore you’ll find resource deposits or points of interest your named characters can interact with similar to Elemental or Endless Legend. These points of interest can be positive or negative but at the moment variety seems limited. I’ve only encountered trait increase/decrease, money gain/lose, technology shortcut and map reveal events. I hope they add more variety and take more from Endless Legend/Elemental by including short quests.
You’ll also encounter the other factions (no minor factions are present). After meeting a faction you can enter into diplomacy with them but I find the balance within the system to be poor. It doesn’t feel great when nations you meet quickly declare war, march about for a few turns, then accept peace if you offer them 1 gold. Maybe they just wanted the pride of saying they beat you, but with no buff/debuff apparent based on the outcome of a war it seems more likely that they haven’t finalized the faction relationship system yet. After the initial “we hate all our neighbors” round, it is easy to establish peace with everyone near you, especially if you start by offering to recognize a strong neighbor as Emperor – a decision I hoped would carry stronger penalties than a single point off my “authority”. The peace network seems to endure indefinitely (80+ turns in my second game), leading to a rather slow-paced early-mid game where you simply tech, settle new cities and explore.
As you found new cities and grow your existing ones, you’ll want to balance a few different factors. Expansion is limited by two resources – you have a “recruitment pool” of units that refreshes periodically (Similar to Medieval 2) so you can’t simply spam settlers and you have the previously mentioned “authority” attribute, which must be higher than the number of settlements you own or you will face penalties to unrest. Authority can be increased via the research tree. Unrest is divided into “noble” and “peasant” unrest with the former being influenced mostly by authority and Edicts – special commands you can issue which enact empire-wide policy decisions and advance you into different ages. Peasant unrest is influenced by how many turns you’ve been giving your peasants tasks constructing buildings, farms, etc. and can be reduced by not issuing such orders for a few turns. If unrest gets too high you start to get bandit spawns, and if the unrest continues you may face a rebellion. There are two types, peasant and noble. If you approach a rebellious stack with your own army composed of 50% or more of the same class of unit there is a chance your army will defect! Your faction leader’s army will never defect however. I quite like this mechanic as it gives a strategic factor to what type of army you send rather than simply picking your strongest units.
Cities themselves can be fairly easy to manage– there’s no “upkeep” for the city or population itself so just building farms and growing the population is a decent way to make a profit. Each settlement has a number of slots for buildings (expanding the settlement increases the number of slots) and some of these require upkeep. Don’t build more high-upkeep buildings than you can afford in the early game. There are also tile-based buildings, including mountain shrines, mines and river quays. Production buildings don’t seem to turn a profit until you’re able to integrate them into a trade network and be warned that trade, while profitable, takes a bit of time to build up. Trade is limited by distance but upgraded trade buildings can reach farther. Also, some Edicts have a high maintenance cost while others can introduce new taxes, both significantly affecting your income.
Your cities are precious and can be lost to rebellion fairly easily (cities can rebel) but are generally secure from all but a concerted effort from enemy factions once you build defenses. Walls are very strong in this game and can only be overcome by ranged units and, later on, artillery. This defensive strength does contribute to the mid-game stagnation I’ve noticed – cities rarely change hands and wars are more about pillaging land and defeating armies than capturing territory.
Armies in this game are composed of a few different types of units (no unique units for factions at the moment) basically divided into noble, peasant or trained/professional class infantry, cavalry and archers. Noble and peasant units can be recruited for free from cities and as mentioned there is a replenishing recruitment pool in each city which is influenced by building choices, technology and population. I tend to specialize only a couple of cities in recruitment as it costs a lot to maintain the buildings and units are only equipped with advanced weapons and armor when recruited. Professional units are useful for all purposes though they carry a high cost while peasant units are cheap and plentiful but weak and nobles are strong but limited in number. Units on the map can be stacked up to 8 on one tile and are influenced by the traits of a character if his bodyguard unit is part of the army.
Combat in this is not Total-War style as so many have mentioned. Multiple stacks can participate in a battle, and battles take place on the regular game map (think Endless Legend). Battles are not manually controlled but you can set tactics and army-facing beforehand, giving you some influence over the course of the battle. The system reminds me of Endless Space. I’d like to see more factors come into play like bonuses for professional armies vs. peasants and so on, plus a clearer UI for setting up tactics.
Exploration, City Management and War will take up about 90% of your time, but the other 10% isn’t wasted. Research in this game is conducted simultaneously via 4 mostly-separate research trees. I like the system but most technologies and bonuses are straightforward stat boosts or unit/building unlocks. I’d like to see more gameplay elements tied into research. As a note, unlike many other 4X games a full suite of diplomatic options are available from the start and don’t need to be researched.
Overall Feeling: This is a slower 4X game than many others in the genre. There is a large emphasis on internal city management and minor wars compared to competitor’s emphasis on technology or outright destroying opponents. If you’re looking for an “exciting” 4X or total war style strategy on the battlefield you may find yourself disappointed. If you want a historically flavored nation-building game with diplomatic and military options, focused more on strategy than tactics, you may have a winner on your hands here. I for one have enjoyed my time playing Oriental Empires immensely and would recommended it provided you are 1) interested in the setting 2) looking for a slower-paced, city focused 4X rather than a combat-oriented one.

Speedball 2 HD, is a modern retelling of the Amiga classic. All the original Amiga coding has been sliced, gutted, reworked and repackaged with a new graphics system, which does add some shinier visuals while keeping the 2d view element.
Unlike some other so-called HD remakes. The gameplay systems and features offered has seen a big improvement.
Namely, Strategic play modes, changable on the fly: Attack, Defence, balanced.
League/cup mode.  What is essentially a career mode, allowing you to make transfers, upgrade skills and compete for league and cup supremacy.
6 brand new speedball arenas.
And more.
Trophies and Achievements to collect, as well as trading cards
The game supports the use of joypads and controllers, although there's no real issue with standard keyboard input controls in terms of playing. Some people have said that due to the stoic 8 way control system of the original the updated version can seem like it assists throwing/scoring/passing functions. However i think this is still well balanced and doesn't have a noticable affect on the gameplay as a whole.
All the rough, violent, fast paced fun is there with extra features to keep you interested.
While the game does feature a multiplayer mode, this is local multiplayer only. Which is the games one major downfall. It'd have been nice to be able to matchmake, take your team online and generally play with the world.
Overall, highly recommended game :) Well worth the price.

It's not the worst I've played... But to call it a game is a stretch.  Heres my breakdown.
The Good:
Lightweight. Despite being pretty to look at, it's not that intencive.  This is Unity at it's most streamlined, I think.
Uses external audio, so you can literally use anything.  Go for it.  Literally any website, format of audio/video, or anything like that is usable.
The Bad:
Movement controls. What made Audiosurf so playable was the quick, mouse-based controls.  It made moving left to right easy, sharp, and accurate.  This is simply clunky in comparison.  Even with a gamepad, the analogs just don't feel "good".
Uses external audio.  While it can use anything, it's also not user friendly.  Being lightweight isn't an excuse to force the player to use another program to play music/media.
The Ugly:
Firing controls.  Firing is music-based.  And the special secondary weapon is time-based.  Everything is automatic.  Which means theres no chance to actuallly use skill, because the only thing you can do is go left or right.  Sniping blocks or even destroying all of one block becomes a chore as you pray that this riff causes enough shots, and hoping that you don't "run out" when you have a strong on 10c blocks.
Zero consiquence for missing blocks.  This makes some sense as firing is automatic, random and skill-less, but theres literally no insentive to play this.  Just fire up a random playlist and let it play itself on repeat while you're at work and sleeping.  I bet you'd have all the upgrades in a few days or so.  Idle games can be fun, but this could be so much more...
Uses external audio.  Yes.  It's greatest flexibility is it's greatest weakness.  Being able to read off the audio output is a nice feature, but it shouldn't be the ONLY way to play.  It ruins immersion, and really makes it feel more like what it is; Not a game, but a semi-interactive visualizer.
I'd recomend it simply because it is pretty, and makes music fun to watch... But as a game, it's kind of a flop.

Hexcells is a singleplayer puzzle game, in the vein of Minesweeper, except using a hexagonal grid. Tiles will contian numbers, which indicates the number of tiles which they border which need to be flagged - you mark those tiles, and logically work to clear the board. In later levels, there are other rules which apply (totals for columns, requiring the markers to be contiguous or explicitly non-contiguous, etc).
Hexcells is a rather easy game - I was able to complete it in roughly an hour and a half without difficulty. Hexcells Plus, another game by the same developer, takes what was started in this game and makes it into a much harder, more complete experience. If you're looking for a nice, simple puzzler that's similar to Minesweeper? Sure, this game will scratch that itch. It's not difficult, though. If you're looking for more of a challenge? Feel free to take a pass and go straight for Hexcells Plus.

Sound Shift is a game based on the generation of a play environment by the interpretation of music. It doesn't have an in-built music player, I played it by putting on some music using Itunes in the background, then starting up the game. I also tried this successfully with Spotify, so it will probably work with your preferred streaming service too. If you start the game up without some kind of "audio output", the game will give you a message which instructs you to "play some music".
Sound Shift has two modes; Arcade and visualiser. Arcade is a simple game where you shoot at moving white blocks with your ship at the bottom of the screen. Firing is automatic and hitting blocks generates credits of various values. Your ship also powers up over time and when full, it fires a larger bullet, emptying out your reserves. All the time, your music generates visuals on screen.
The second mode is a traditional music visualiser, generating patterns on screen to the beat of the music you play. You can change how it looks using the Function keys on your keyboard.
The credits you earn in the shooting game can be spent in the mods section to unlock changes to how the visualiser works.
When you start up the game, it gives the impression that it can only be played using a gamepad but it does have keyboard support (WASD or Cursor keys, plus F1-F6).
Sound Shift is something to do whilst listening to your music but game-wise, Audiosurf or Beat Hazard are currently much more diverse and engrossing examples of this kind of game. I enjoyed listening to some good music while playing around with this. Has potential and is currently cheap.

Call of Duty: Black Ops blew my mind back in middle school, as I reveled in the campaign, sucked at multiplayer but loved bots with friends, and spent hundreds of hours on Zombies. Today, it stands as one of the best CoD games ever made.
The campaign was an absolute monster. Awesome voice acting, amazing visuals, crisp detail and overall a solid story told. The music, set pieces, and atmosphere made it a top 3 CoD campaign for me, easy.
The multiplayer was fun and uniquely set a new standard for the franchise's most popular mode. BO's maps were fun, original, and lended themselves to the variety of weapons available. Unlike Modern Warfare, Black Ops didn't overly suffer from broken killstreaks and poor weapon balance.
The Zombies mode is one that I have probably spent 1000 hours on on the xbox 360 back in its day. BO sparked my love for the mode (that quickly became an obsession) after a night at my cousin's house playing Kino and listening to Avenged Sevenfold. It was all over after that, and I'm still known today as someone who loves CoD/Nazi Zombies. I went on to buy loads of season passes/Zombies DLC, and loved them, all because of Black Ops.
I really miss the days when this was the cutting edge CoD. You can leave all those jetpacks and stuff in the vault, and just give me some classic Cold War carnage. That's what Black Ops delivers, and it does it well.

Lovely logic-based puzzle game that is essentialy Minesweeper meets Picross (but much better than that sounds). It took me a couple of hours to play through but had me completely transfixed the whole time.

You're at full health, fully armed, spells in pocket. You come to a nice clearing, people are standing around happy, talking, smiling. Nothing is wrong, and that is exactly what is wrong. It's a God Damn Goblin ambush!! The townsman are fighting, chaos ensues! As I try to separate them with a hefty water spell, my incessant button mashing gets the best of me, and 12 soaked humans, and goblins catch the wrath of my full charged lighting spell. Purple flame and streaks exhibit everywhere, and the next thing I know everything in the village has met a catastrophic death. Whoops.
I move on, move forward, pretend nothing happened, and hope the evidence isn't enough. As I lay on a woodcutters stump, my heart gets heavy about the carnage I just witnessed. How many babies, how many families? Those demons will follow me surely throughout life and into the next. The next village over thinks I'm a hero. They congratulate me. An hour later, after a quick toke on the tobacco, sentries spot Goblins and a Troll heading toward the village. Things get dark, morose.
I pray they don't know my true nature, the outsider, the lone wolf, the one with the spells that crisp the Earth and I'm completely indifferent to the result. 10/10 would vigilante again.

Update[03/06]: Post-release review
This game has been through a couple of different iterations. We had a mission-based sidescroller, we had a rogue-like with generic characters with generic weapons and now we have a full crew of characters.
A bit of history: this fact (passing to roguelike) has caused a lot of controversy in the community of the game. Some people liked the idea of a mission-based sidescroller with weapon customization way more than the current roguelike approach which is more hardcore.
But in my opition this change turned out to be for better. This whole idea even though it sounds good in theory - in practice it just didn't work. It was an attempt to take Diablo-like loot system and put it on top of a 2D shooter. Lack of diversity left the game content-less and somewhat boring for me in just 20 or so hours (now I have 120 and counting), I only continued to play from time to time to do achievements which were boring to complete because the diversity was completely exhausted by that time. There were also a lot of balancing issues and it was a bit hard to coop when people had different progress.
So now the game offers a unique experience with each of the 5 characters, random generation and loot (secondary weapons and upgrades) keep the game relatively fresh from run to run, progressive unlock of those upgrades makes sure diversity doesn't kick in too fast.
Gameplay wise there's not much to say - it's very fast-paced and quite challenging. The controls (which are the bane for a lot of platformers) are quite good. The only real problem in my opinion is that doesn't explicitly follow the "fair" roguelike spirit (which means you can complete the game flawlessly). Sometimes there're hazards which are de facto unavoidable, even though it's realtime and theoretically everything is avoidable. This might annoy the hell out of you and put you on tilt if it happens too frequently in a short timespan. Fortunately the game is quite generous on health pickups so overall it's acceptable, dying due to only truly unavoidable damage is almost impossible.
Among other pros I'd say the awesome style of the game, this "fantasy meets steampunk" theme just rocks.
Being released in the end of April this game had quite a number of technical problems but as for now almost all of them seem to be fixed (ilol'd from inivisible non-interactable barrels draining CPU when you are in the rooms with them).

Magicka was quite the entertaining game that I didn't expect it to be. I expected a short 5 hourish game that would be fun for like the first 2 hours. I was very wrong. I ended up playing through the whole adventure mode of Magicka with a friend, so in co-op, and it was quite a bit of fun.
To start, Magicka has great graphics and spell effects and animations. Everything about the game looks good. Another thing that makes Magicka so good is that there are so many different orb combinations to make different spells, effects, and Magicka. When I mean there are so many different combinations, I mean that there are legit possibly over 100 differnt unique and tiered spells and Magicka you can cast. Not only that, but each spell combination often features its own unique graphical effect and animation. Couple this with some other weather and terrain, the game has a really a super in depth spell casting system.
Magicka has a pretty random story, but it is pretty funny in places. The gameplay is pretty entertaining and the difficulty level increases perfectly for the most part. Although some times there are some abnormally easy bosses while some of the mob fights were annoyingly hard. Overall, Magicka does a very good job with checkpoints too so you do not feel super punished when you screw around and die. As I mentioned before, I played this game with a friend. I strongly recommend that you play Magicka with a friend or two or three because there are so many little things that make playing with more people more fun. For one, the revive is a clutch coop spell and there are so many more spells that can be comboed.
Overall a good and fun game that you should play with your friends. I really did not find any flaws to this game apart from the occasional crash.

If you're half decent w/ the Halo series, you'll enjoy this game a lot. If you like Team Fortress 1 or 2, you'll enjoy this game a lot. If you love the fast-action paced game series of Call of Duty, you'll enjoy this game a lot.
For me this game was like a duck taking to water. With loads of customization to offer, it allowed for my creative intellect to go crazy. Instantly I was hooked.
What I REALLY liked about this game:
It's like League of Legends in that everything is free with time invested into this game. Sure, they offer you "vanity packs" through real world money if you want to show off cool avatars, skins, more weapon slots, etc, but nothing paid by real world money effects the game outside of cosmetics. Not only that, but if you simply want to stick with one particular weapon set/duo, you'll unlock all the gizmos to that weapon set/duo extremely fast. If you want to diversify and try to create many different weapons in the game, sure it'll take you a lot longer, but it still won't cost you a dime.
What I thought might need improvement:
Although the creators of the game claim there are tons of weapon combinations, I found this to be a bit exagerated. While they do have many different customizations available per type of weapon, you only build off four main weapons: Rifle, Launcher, Pulse, and Beam. It would be great to see more choices in types of weapons as four really isn't something to get too excited about. In the future I would like to see more close-ranged weapons like plasma swords from Halo or perhaps weapons like the Needler. I know I'm taking ideas from Halo, but let's face it, they have a lot of fun weapons to choose from. Another thing they could add is pistols.
One more improvement I would like to see them change is to have everyone have an overshield by default. The minute you get passed level 5 you'll notice around 80-90% of everyone running with an overshield. When I noticed this trend I decided to buy one immediately and once I did I saw the reason why. If I could recommend anything in this game, it would be to rush the overshield. You'll automatically see a clear increase in your k/d ratio. If they were to make it by default, I believe it would more level out the playing field and winning would then be primarily by map knowledge as well as skill based instead of random losses versus someone else because you couldn't take their shield down fast enough.
Overall I give this a 4 out of 5. It's a heck of a lot of fun and if you're into shooters you'll love this game. Currently I've been playing this game like it's crack. I've been hooked on it for a week straight now and I can't seem to stop playing. Haha!

Short summary: Risk of Rain meets Metal Slug.  A rogue-lite that consists of minor platforming exploration while blasting orcs & various murderous contraptions on the way to each randomly-generated level's boss.  I am having a lot of fun after having not played for a little over a year.  Much positive progress has been made.
Features: 5 characters, each with their own primary weapon & special ability.  7 randomly generated maps with a fixed boss somewhere in each.  Playing provides XP to the characters, whose levels & perks gained from them will carry to every new run.  Power-ups include single-run items a la Risk of Rain or Rogue Legacy.  These can provide stat boosts or unique effects.  Secondary weapons can be found that provide more firepower but at varied cooldown speeds.  Supply drops, purchasable power-ups, and key-unlocked chests/rooms are scattered through each map.
Gameplay: There is a good bit of risk/reward in choosing whether to continue exploring the map & risk dying/excess damage, or to simply move onto the boss at the risk of being underpowered.
I really like the combat.  It's your typical dual-stick style run-with-keyboard, aim-with-mouse sidescroller similar to the controls of Bastion or Crimsonland.  Very smooth, which is really needed due to how hectic things can get.  A short-cooldown dash helps with maneuverability.  As a game control preciseness and intuitiveness freak, I regard it highly overall.
There is a little bit of story flavor included as unlockable scrolls phrased as newspaper articles which explain what's going on between the good guys and Baron von Whatsisface.
Graphics:
The game looks great, that's for sure.  From BFG reps on the Community boards, it is an upgraded version of the engine than ran Giana Sisters.  Sadly, it's not optimized and is therefore heavily taxing very good systems based on Community reports.  With my underpowered CPU I'm running at 1280x1024 and it still looks great.  Unfortunately, when things get really heavy the game no longer stays at a steady framerate while slowing the whole game down; it will just chug and sometimes characters and items will jump crazily.  I think this is mostly due to things spawning off screen and not the overall demand of particles & graphics.

My one word review.
Disappointing.
How the game was advertised and pitched: Hotline Miami style pixel murderspree with crazy parties and quirky exciting scenarios. Sheer insanity and fun!
How it actually plays.  A slow, tedious test of patience and frustration. Most of the people you'll end up killing just from slowly walking at them and hitting E when there aren't any witnesses and then dropping their body somewhere, wash, rinse, repeat. If something goes wrong there isn't really any gameplay afterwords, which is where I'd expect a game about chaos to excel in the "what happens when unexpected things happen" but alas.
If you get spotted a police office gets a homing beacon to your position and you can escape by hopping back and forth across a barrier the cop can't cross for some reason. Then the cop gives up and calls a repairman who "fixes" the barrier so you don't do that again, you bad, bad, little murderer. There is one or maybe two other similar hopping points on the level which function largely as extra lives.
The special events for the most part don't really to be the focus of the game at all and are mostly downplayed relative to just shanking people. Many events only kill a single person and give away your location. Others like poisoning food get similarly poor results without you being spotted but do force you to wait for excessive periods of time to the results.
As a result I entered with high hopes but left with a largely unmemorable experience. I think it'd be possible to make this game good still but it would require a lot of work on the core game loop and mission design so I'm dubious we'll ever see it.
Disclaimer I only played through the first level and tutorial but I watched some let's plays to make sure I wasn't missing really cool stuff later on and it continued to meet my expectations. I also checked with a friend who had beaten most of the missions and he was similarly disappointed. I would stay away. Watch the trailers, imagine how the great game would play out in your head, and then move on.

When you're asked to investigate a boat that came back without its crew, you discover that someone killed them and is trying to trap you. However, a ghost appears to you and guide you to find the truth behind her family death and the disappearance of many sailors...
Left in the Dark: No One on Board is another Artifex Mundi's game, though they're only the publisher here. However, as you're used to me and many others saying it, Artifex Mundi is always choosing good games. Left in the Dark isn't perhaps the best title out there but it's still very enjoyable.
While the story has a correct plot, it's just a shame that everything is chaotic. Indeed, you're first investigating murders before having a ghost guiding you to the culprit and even discover that people thought dead are alive. I liked however the fact that it's a woman being the detective, in a time where I'm pretty sure it was though to be an active woman (it's maybe the 19th century but women were more seen as wives and mothers than a real asset for the society).
The gameplay is pretty standard: use items that you find lying around (or hidden somewhere), clear hidden objects scenes and solve puzzles. I must say that while the puzzles are really easy, the hidden objects scenes are a little harder than expected as some of the items aren't really visible and that the translation was sometimes a little bad. As I've said, you're in the 19th century but I don't why I was feeling that some objects were kinda anachronic. The only puzzle that could be a problem is the lockpick one, as you have to put your cursor on the lockpick to make sure it's working, however, the item in itself is moving, so if your cursor is too far, you will have to restart.
The graphics are more than acceptable, though I was under the impression that some of the backgrounds seemed rushed. It's the same feeling as in the hidden objects scenes. The characters aren't really seen, but the look of the detective is really great: somewhere with a steampunk inspiration, very badass.
The soundtrack is good too, so, are the voice actings.
Left in the Dark is a good game, though it's not the best Artifex Mundi, even when it was released. I would recommend to wait for a discount (and Left in the Dark has been often in the situation) or a bundle (it's also often bundled).

Pros:
+Great humor, and breaks the fourth wall sometimes just because it can.
+Lots of items.
+Lots of replay value due to the amount of items and enemies.
+Alternate ways through the progression of floors later on.
+Good soundtrack.
Cons:
-Laggy on older computers, even though it says the requirements are just a measly 2.5GHz computer. (I run it on a Pentium 4 E2180 Dual Core 2.0GHz, so don't refrain from trying this game when I say this and you have a fast PC.)
-Sometimes, I keep getting the same few items near the beginning of each run, making the items I might get predictable, and I might get one or two different items every 2 or 3 runs.
-Some rooms have unfair structures to them, where you are almost forced to take a hit.
Overall, I recommend this game if you don't want to shell out the cash for Rebirth. Also, if you plan on getting this game along with the Wrath of the Lamb DLC, I must warn you, the Wrath of the Lamb DLC makes the game much harder, but it does come with much more content as well. Also keep in mind the Wrath of the Lamb DLC cannot be disabled, so you are stuck with the harder enemies. (There may be a way to disable it I am not aware of in the games files, so sorry if I missed it) However, Rebirth is better in almost every imaginable aspect. Rebirth runs much better on older computers, has a nice retro look to it, and has MUCH more content, as well as a few entirely new features. Some may argue that Rebirth lacks a soundtrack as great as its predeccesor, but they both have there own charm in the soundtrack.

The moment you start the game you will notice the many limitations imposed by the Flash platform. From the performance issues to the restricted audio channels to the minimal graphical settings to the lack of many options in general. It's pretty obvious that the developer's design scope went well beyond what Flash has to offer. Because of this overall hindrance, it's also easy to be impressed by what has been accomplished even though the glaring flaws are present throughout.
The Binding of Isaac is a simple game. It's important to realize this past the voices of all its fans. The main appeal is playing the game over and over in order to unlock items and achievements. In short, achievement hunting is what this game is all about. There is nothing more to it. Its difficulty is not the biggest hurdle, however. While there is a total of 198 items to unlock, the frequency in which the majority of them appear is quite rare. You will play the game hundreds of times, yet you will see a small percentage of those 198 items in most of your playthroughs. In other words, even though there are nearly 200 items available, you will only enjoy about 20 or 30 of them on a regular basis. This undermines the existence of those 198 items, as you will very rarely come across most of them. Which brings up another problem related to the items. There are only about ten or so that are truly game changing, and when it comes to the bosses of The Cathedral and The Chest, there are only about two or three items that are truly helpful against them. When one considers these serious issues with the item pool, it unfortunately means that The Binding of Isaac has some balance issues, particularly at end-game.
For a game that is so widely praised and loved, it surely deserves credit. What the developer was able to accomplish is meaningful and popularized an entire genre. The Binding of Isaac remains fun for the most part, albeit frustrating at times. Beating some bosses ensures progression by unlocking other parts of the game, which means the struggle and victory are always sweet and exciting. Completionists will have much to work towards. The challenge is half the fun, and if that's an aspect of gaming that is important to you, there are a couple hundred hours waiting for you in The Binding of Isaac.

The year is 2382. The Bruggan Fanatics, the most powerful fallen empire in the galaxy, had awoken six years ago and had set their sights on the main federation, Celeste Entente. The Federation fought a brutal and brave war against the fallen scourge, but in the end they lost the war and their systems fell under the iron grip of the Bruggans. Having witnessed the destruction of the only powerful federation, I began to search the galaxy for assistance and built forts and dozens of ships in hopes of halting the Bruggan's brutal and relentless war spree. The further I moved south, the more empires I began to find. Eventually, my searches led me to yet another hyper advanced and powerful federation, as well as another fallen empire. Having decided to seek the help of the new federation, I began to fund their armies and grant them technologies to grow and prosper. Just as the federation was about to begin their advance on the Bruggans, hostile ships were detected approaching our galaxy. Long story short, the new threat to our galaxy from the outside, the Prethoryian Scourge, obliterated the Federation. Even the new fallen empire, who was far weaker than the Bruggans, only managed to contain the scourge. Having realized my only known hope of defeating the Bruggans layed dead and cold in the southwest, I begin to prep my empire for the inevitable: total and futile war against the Bruggans. When they invaded they swept my systems like the locust swarm of a crop field. Within two months the Bruggans had managed to push my fleet and all my armies into Sol. A few months passed and the Bruggans attacked Earth, destroying the galaxy's only hope of survival and ending the near 200 year reign of the Human Assembly Systems.

It says its an Early Access game, but I feel I am getting a completed game. Great job developers!
Some 3 hours into the game, allow me to sum up the pros and cons I can find.
Pros:
-Great details and graphics (cities, boats, units, etc.)
-Total War like combat, albeit it is not as smooth
-Its pretty easy to get on with the game, but it requires some thinking on a deeper level on the later stages of the game, especially when you are choosing between getting an extra 10% unrest (which can be deadly...I am currently facing this problem...) or an amazing economic boom.
-They do offer a very friendly "easy" mode in which other countries will incline to sign non-aggression pacts with you and allow you to develop and get on with the game
-There are some historical accuracy, I haven't got much further so I don't know how accurate it can get
Now some cons:
-Some bugs, when you load sometimes the cities' names are misaligned and another city's name is aligned onto one of my cities...
-The unit AI can be some what weird, when garrisons exit a city they don't exit from one gate, so this causes a serious problem which for example, if an enemy is attacking from the North, and you order your garrison to go out into the fields and battle them, the individual units exit through different gates, if it happens to be an archer unit exited from the North, it would get slaughtered by the enemy while your heavy infantry has to circle around all the way from the South gate. I do hope this can get fixed.
-The economic system is kind of funny. In the early stages you basically just have to build A LOT of cities to make sure you are ahead of other countries in terms of economy. There is very little trade system involved, there are 'internal trade' but that does not help with your economy (or maybe its just me). Later there is an edict to impose some tax, and suddenly your income can skyrocket to 500/turn in contrast to the
but in return this adds 10% peasant unrest.
-The character system is odd, there are just random chances characters emerge...I would suggest an overhaul of the character system so it is more like Shogun 2 Total War.
I personally think this game has its potential, and its pretty fun to play it even in its current stage. This is what I am going to play for 4X games before Civ VI is released.
I personally would like to see DLCs for this game in which the tech tree is expanded to at least the 1800s and you get to battle Western Civs (or play as Western Civs). That would definitely be fun to play. I encourage the developers to take this game to the next level.
Edit 9/23: Some new thoughts...
-Frame rate fluctuates crazily
-Some buildings and upkeep feels overpriced...

Oriental Empire is the kind of game that I've wanted for a while. Yes, I would like to see some more out of it - and perhaps some tweaks as well: but with the short time I've spent playing it I've had a lot of fun! I've done everything from build an extensive trade network stretching from one side of the map to the other, engage in vicious primitive wars (Bronze age) and emerged victorious, and paid close attention to the little details in the map that make this game what it is.
But what is this game?
I would personally say that this game is a mixture of Civilization and Total War. You kind of get the best of both worlds. The randomized maps and building system of the Civilization games, with the up close and personal combat of Total War! Mind you you can't control your unit movements once they've engaged in a battle (so more like Civ?), but you can set their stances before they engage, as well as what kind of formation they will be fighting it. This combat makes for some epic clashes that can take place in an extensive battlefield that could stretch from the front gates of a city to the far outskirts of it!
Though this all sounds really cool I think they're missing out on a few things: the big one being more on-the-map activity! This would be physical buildings with civilians working around them (maybe at the forge, barracks, ect.), a variety of different people - not just farmers, more animals roaming around (not just standing there), and natural disasters that we can actual see. The one thing that they did do very well is the on-map destruction caused by warfare! I also wouldn't mind seeing more commodities. The map feels very bare - with useful resources seemingly few and far between. Maybe as you advance through the ages more resources reveal themselves?
However though it could improve, this Early Access title delivers with little/no bugs - and a fantastic time!
Right now I'd give it a 8/10!
Short list of features I'd like to see:
- Dynasties
- More resources
- More on the map activity
- more diplomatic options
- unique play styles from different AI
- more empire customization
- Variety of different citizens (not just farmers and soldiers!)

Don't Starve Together is quickly becoming one of my favorite games in my library. It has a way of making you lose track of time with your friends in the best of ways. If you enjoy the genre, this is definately a game you need to pick up.
I personally own both the original singleplayer Don't Starve and Don't Starve Together, and I would recommend you pick up both if you find yourself liking one of them, along with the DLC for the singleplayer. The reason I say this is because while most of their mechanics are the same, they do have quite a few major differences. I was debating on getting both of them when I made my purchase for the reason of thinking they'd just be the same thing. They are not.
Don't Starve Together is probably the best sandbox game I've ever picked up. You get your own servers, (or you can join someone else's, if you don't like to host) and can choose literally everything about your world; how long (if at all) the seasons are, what monsters and resources will spawn and how often, and how often disasters hit, if at all. If you want a challenge, you can give yourself just that. Want a casual experience with a few friends, where you never really have to worry about dying? You can have that too. There are way too many different things for you to actually do and control that I can't list them all here without running on for paragraphs worth of block text, you just have to see for yourself.
This game never lets you run out of things to do. When you finally discover everything there is to discover, and have built up the best of bases you can reset your server and start all over from scratch, in an entirely new world with entirely new rules. In just the time I've played I've constantly been discovering new or more efficient ways to obtain certain items or craft certain things. Still think you've run out of content? There are community made mods, that provide even more hours of gameplay. Not to mention, you get free chests and costumes the more you play, that you can trade or sell on the Steam Community Market.
There is nothing more fun than getting into a new server with a group of your friends and fending for yourself in the wilderness together on a voice chat, hearing the screams of terror mixed with the laughter of each other's pain as you run into monster mobs you aren't strong enough to fight, or as you accidentally die to a bee you didn't see. The only downside to the multiplayer, is there is no split screen. Anyone who wants to play with you has to own this game, so you can't make this into a party game unless everyone brings their laptops.
I simply can't find something about this game that I dislike. The art style is amazing, and highly appealing for the genre. The music is interactive, and very fitting for the world and the activities/fights you go through. It's not your typical survival sandbox, everything is very creative and vibrant, while still making complete sense. It's filled with immersion, and makes a great game for Discord communities or streamers looking to interact together. The developers are constantly updating with events, new costumes, and extra content. This game will never get old.
Pick this game up, even better when it's on sale with an extra copy for a friend. You won't regret the fun you'll have.

WARNING: If you do not like battles where you have no direct, manual control over the tactical outcome, do NOT get this game. Just don't. There are too many 4x games out there where people get it and leave a negative review because they are expecting old school tactical battles. Save yourself the trouble and prevent confusion at the same time.
That said, this is a great 4x game for people interested in the setting. The map is massive, and there are a lot of strategic options that give each playthrough a little something different to try. The economic/trade system is abstracted, but it makes intuitive sense and there's some good depth to it, which is what I look for when building trade empires.
The tech tree is mid-sized, but I didn't find a tech that I didn't want to use; not a lot of superfluous tech and while specializing in the early game seems important, you'll have it all researched by the "endgame".
Other than that, it plays somewhat like Civ and/or Endless Legend so if you you liked those games, don't care about tactical battles (or find them tedious), this is a good, solid title to get your hands on.

I am so happy about it, even though it's only a game. (Yes, I know the game Romance of 3 kingdoms, but they are different. In this game, I think we could experience more Chinese culture and history while Romance of 3 kingdoms is more like an epic, a novel full of lengendary heros. Heros are more important in that game instead of history and culture.)
As for the game, I think it seems like the combination of Civilization series and Total War series.It looks very complicated, a real strategy game. And as for Chinese history and culture in the game, the details are accurate. It starts from the first dynasty of China, Shang, and goes to dynasty Zhou, and then waring state period, including all the major states in the real Chinese history, even Xianbei. For culture part, you could develop Taoism, Buddisim, Confucianism and even YinYang which really suprises me since not many western people know it.  And for the video performance, it's really cool. You could zoom in and out in the game and check all the details of your city and your people. You could see the farmers working in the field and the merchant working in the city, all in details.
I just played the game for half an hour and didn't fight in any war right now but I am quite looking forward to it since in Chinese history, people developed lots of strategies about how to fight in the war, how to defeat enemy effectively and wisdomly. The famous and well-known example is the book 'the Art of War' by Sunzi, who was born in Spring and Autumn Period, 550BC. So I am quite curious about that whether we could use strategies in the war and get some benefits from them, use militory wisdom to defeat enemies effectively .

I think this game would become a masterpiece if there are more improvements in the future. For example, the game would be better if it has a mini map, an open CG and more tutorials for beginners because it is kind of complicated at the first glance. And there are also translation problems, comparing to the history facts. For example, in the game there is one tribe which is called 'Dog Rong'. Actually this is kind of funny since it looks like the combination of English and Chinese pinyin,'Dog' is English while 'Rong' is Chinese...Actually, it is 'Quan Rong' in Chinese, even though 'Quan' in Chinese means 'dog' in English. In the game, there are lots of these phenomena, the combinations of English and Chinese pinyin makes the game funny for the people who know Chinese history.
And also I suggest that it would be better if this game has Madarin version because in China, there are many steam players right now. All of them will be very happy to play such a game. This will also solve the traslation problem. English speakers do not need to read Chinese pinyin which might be hard and inconvenient for them since they might not know how to read Chinese pinyin, not to mention the meaning of Chinese pinyin. For example, in English version, the game could use 'Go' instead of 'Weiqi', 'Taoism' instead of 'Daoism'. They are same things, but clearly, Go and Taoism would be better for English speaker to undertand what they are.
Anyway, I will recommend this game to the players who love strategy game and the players who are interested in Chinese history and culture. Excellent work.

Now before I begin, I must say this is a fun game, and a good concept. You play several different levels and each level gives you different items. Those items are always materials you need to make your own gun. You can also find extra materials throughout each stage. As you progress, you get better guns, and can kill bigger and badder enemies. The game somewhat resembles Shoot Many Robots, but with more customization of guns, and no armor or any other sort of gear. Just guns.
That being said, this game definately has its flaws. One of the main things about this game that I had a problem with was that there are very little explanations for what you are doing. What is that glowing ball that they call an arc? Why am I fighting? Each stage has a difficulty level but I don't know my own level, if I even have one. Another thing that bugged me was the stages. They all felt randomly generated, but not in the good way. Some stages just felt like no human in their right mind would think the layout was a good idea.
The game does try and give you slight explanations for everything, but it doesn't really make much sense. If you look by the lack of explanations, then we can look at the gameplay. I do like the gun customization, but I don't like that there is no other gear to get. You won't get any armor or customization items besides the guns. The only thing that makes you and your co-op partners distinguishable from each other is the color. Everything else looks exactly the same.
Overall, the game is fun, but it doesn't have what you would expect from a full fledged game. lt is in early access, and is the reason why I still recomend it. I can see a great future for this game once the problems all get fixed.

Pretty much like Civilization 4/5, only instead of some goofy animation of one dude/mechanical killing another, you get taken down to a map and engage in RTS action. You can compose armies of many unit types of the time period, and each one has an information card telling you about that unit and a description of their historical use. You can play as 5-ish factions initially, though you can unlock more.
Just like Civ4/5, while on the overmap you can upgrade cities/castles and engage in trade/sabotage/war/diplomacy with other nations, only you can't build new cities, only take over others, though you can repurpose them to Towns(Money Makers) or make them into a Castle(Troop Maker), though both can make money or troops, their respective ones do it better.
For those who have played Rome: Total War, Medieval is extremely similar, except during a different time period. There are improvements, such as improvements and supporting modern resolutions without mods.

At last a game portraying the Warring State period in China. Or as close as it gets.
First impressions :
This is Early Access but the game feels more polished than some strategy game release lately.
Great potential, fresh ideas, could be amazing in MP, i didn't play enough to assess long term replayability though (which is critical for 4Xs)
UI :
Interface is clean, and user friendly although usability is not on par with CIV, it takes some hours to get used to it.
GFX :
Graphics are uneven, it's great to zoom down to ground level and see buildings and people almost on scale, and overall the game look pretty. Terrain is not so good and tile improvements feel cheap (ie compared to Civ5). Each turn is a new Season which is quite cool visually (similar to RotK XI), unit details is a bit lacking especially texture feel cheap. Overall, despite these minor issues, it's still quite eye-pleasing. My major gripe with the GFX are the animations, they are choppy and the soldiers feel as rigid as the terracota army. Clashes between armies are not very epic bccause of that, and there can be a bit of benny hilling around too.
Economy :
Economy is interesting and engaging, it's actually fun to manage at least at the beginning, I don't know how well it scales towards the mid-late game. You have to be mindful of the satisfaction of the Nobility and the Peasants, who both can rebel against you. Nobles will contest your authority while Peasants will mostly complain if overworked/not fed enough etc. Raising armies can be very expensive, and limited income mean you have to carefully decide what to do in the early game, it feels good to develop the land and see your investments pay off after a while when trading routes are booming and your populationg growing fast.
War :
There are several type of units to train, most unlocked through technology. Units can stack on a single tile, where you can group them into formations and give them different behaviors for battle. The interface for managing units is a bit confusing so i hope they improve that.
When you finish a turn all units move together simultaneously so you can intercept or escape enemies, if units are close enough they will engage in battle. Battles atm feel a bit wonky, especially when there is not  a lot of units around. It's hard to tell why they are attacking X and not Y or why they stop moving instead of engaging the enemy. Overall the system feels pretty interesting, but i hope it will be more fluid and understandable in the future.
Diplomacy :
Typical 4X diplomacy, similar to total war. Basically you have non agression pacts, defensive treaties, alliances, vassalage, tribute, etc. They didn't reinvent the wheel here.
Technology :
There is 4 trees that you can research in parallel, and there is a sizeable amount of techs in each of them, although there doesn't seem to be a lot of choices, i think gamers will find quickly a critical path to follow in most cases.
AI :
The AI seemed competent, although a bit weak. In my first game, most neighbors were seemingly scared of me and giving me money for non-agression pacts (kinda like in Warhammer TW at release). And when I attacked one of them he left 2 cities undefended which i could easily take (you can just march into a city if there is no garrison), before bringing his main army.

is a sports game with simple controls, and yet enough complexity of gameplay that it
be decent.  Maybe the original actually was a decent game; I wouldn't know since I've never played it.  This one, though, has issues. More problematic is the fact that you directly control one of the Speedball players on your team, but the game automatically determines which player you control, and switches you around so frequently that it can seem impossible to keep track of what's happening and where you are, and react quickly enough (sometimes control even switches to a player who's off-screen). The best part of this game by a long way is the Prologue. It's a brilliant high paced blending of different action arcade game genres, moving from one to the next beautifully. Honestly, that part of the game blew my mind.
Then, the rest of the game happens. It's like someone else made the Prologue then went on holiday for a few weeks. Whilst he's away some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ has turned it into a plodding open world game that's at best an average RPG where you spend most of your time picking up items off the floor. And when it finally does go back into an arcadey mode it feels so out of place after the hours of trudging around. Sometimes it just doesn't seem to work or make sense at all and does nothing but hinder and confuse (boss at fairground for example).
Certain things just don't make sense such as: Why is there fishing in this game? Wtf is the point in that? And why is the prologue so much more hardcore than the rest of the game? No saves (and you can be 1 hit by the double buzzsaws). This would be fine (oh, it's one of those hardcore games) BUT in the rest of the game you can save every 5 seconds! What's the point in the bodies everywhere? What are they even adding except to break the immersion? And what's the point in that idiot following me around the whole game like Tails?
If the rest of the game was like the Prologue, this could very well be a classic game. As it is, it's just a missed opportunity.

For those a fan of the original you may find yourself looking at playing this and expecting a simple update to the classic, you may be slightly disappointed. The overall feel of the game is the same but a few issues prevent it from truly recreating the feeling of the original.

The aiming seems to now be somewhat automated whereas before you would have to aim to one of the 8 directions available on the joystick, this does make the game easier for newcomers and I can see why this is the way it is. Player selection seems to be a bit clunky at times, suddenly your control is moved to another player and you'll end up performing actions you didn't intend. The menus are certainly a lot more simplified than the original and it seems as though a lot of the control you have over your squad and their training is lost.

I would say overall this game is definitely easier than the original (Steel Fury used to be a very strong opponent but now you can wipe the floor with them) But it's still got something about it that makes me want to play it, I would still recommend this to people just don't go into it expecting to feel and play just like the original.

This game has largely the same factions as the manga Kingdom and plays a lot like Endless Legends/Civ/Total War. I've been following it since it was first announced like two years ago and I think the current result is pretty good, but not perfect.
Pros:
- fresh setting (as far as I know this is the only other game on Steam besides RTK13 that is set in China)
- seamless zoom on a map with Total War level graphics
- the combat is simple and easy to understand without feeling like a rehash
- costs less than half that of a major game these days
- the AI doesn't seem to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like in some games and can be quite aggressive (if you don't have walls and garrisons your cities will be taken)
- the main devs designed Medieval 2 and judging from the direction this game is going they know what they're doing
- factions can be unlocked rather than hidden behind a paywall
Cons:
- the game stutters a lot
- the battle animations are pretty bad and nothing on par with Shogun 2 (but only a bit worse than Rome 2)
- construction is hard to understand and not all the math is displayed to the player properly
- there's not really a tutorial and reading the guide sucks
- the implementation of the tech tree is uninspired and boring
- UI is missing features like a mini map, also when a faction declares war on you it's hidden away in the event box, which can be frustrating
- turns take a bit too long, i'd like a third speed
- some factions are locked which is weird because some of the factions among them like the Qin are quintessential to the setting, it would be like if you had to play as Carthage in Rome Total War to unlock Rome, so that's quite frustrating, imo only the nomad and barbarian factions should require unlocking while the main Warring States should be the default factions
- faction abilities are quite underwhelming, they're basically stat buffs
- the game doesn't represent all of China, not just Tibet and Xinjiang are missing, but also a lot of southern China, which would be fine if the game only took place during the ancient era, but it's quite weird playing in the imperial age and not be able to expand to Guangxi or Guangdong
- no zoom to mouse cursor option
- no edge scrolling
