If you want to learn more about Handsome Jack's origin story, this game provides context. Other than that, it didn't feel as fun or relatable as Borderlands 2. A lot more female characters and accents this time around, yet none of the characters really stood out. I played through Athena's story, and it felt lackluster. Then again, most, if not all, character back stories in the Borderlands lore are lacking.
Oxygen system felt more of a nusciance than anything else. Didn't experience asphyxiation at all during the game, but the system just felt annoying. The majority of the game is spent in low gravity anyhow, so oxygen is somehow relevant? Speaking of, with a lot of the game in low gravity, a lot of the movement comes out slow and floaty. Even though Borderlands 2 had this, its more prominent in this game. Be expected to spam double jumps and slams just to seem fast.
Mechanically, without slag, there's less reliance on damage amp and moreso on various effects. There wasn't a time when I was boned without the proper elemental effect, because the game does its job on making sure you're not without the right elemental type. Quests will allow for fire/cryo/electric/etc. weapons if needbe, so there's no need to hunt for a certain element.
The map definitely feels smaller this time around, and to get around this, the side quests feel heavily back-tracky. A lot of the time, side quests will pop up in areas that you've already cleared in the main story, multiple times. Not much to explore, so might as well do it repeatedly. With a lack of multiple TPs in areas, I saved, quit, and then resumed a lot just to hop to fast travel points. Sucks, but beats having to jump all over the place.
If you're a fan of the series, play this for continuity. If you enjoyed Borderlands 2 for the writing but not the overall series for the world and lore, skip over this.

You probably don't need me to sum it up for you, as I'm sure many other people have summed this game up far better in the 16 years it's been out for. To put it bluntly, Deus Ex is a stealth game, and a damn good one, at that. It offers an unprecedented amount of freedom and lets you take on your objectives in whatever way you want, or just not at all.
So many unexpected consequences and little variations, multiple playstyles and different augmentations to support each one mean that every playthrough can be completely different.
The only real problem is the AI. They're forgetful and seem to lack basic combat sense. Also, the tiny inconvenience of not being able to move a body without looting it. I don't want to have to clear room in my inventory to pick up a flamethrower that I'm not using so I can move a body.
Other than that, the game lets you play completely non-lethally with the exception of glitching past one boss, and you've gotta almost bend the game over your knee and show it who's your daddy just to get through areas non-lethally. It's not like the later entries where non-lethal ghost runs are built into the game. You've really gotta ♥♥♥♥in' work for it this time.
That's about it, I guess. The game mechanics still hold up very well and the story is even more engaging than most modern games, so Deus Ex gets a literal 100/10. Would play again, many times(have played again, many times). As long as I don't have to deal with those ♥♥♥♥ing spiderbots. ♥♥♥♥ those things. Oh, and the ♥♥♥♥ing greasels. ♥♥♥♥ them too.

Hexcells is basically a collection of puzzles, the kinds of which are a dime a dozen in GAMES magazine or Dell's puzzle magazines.
This particular kind starts like hexagonal minsweeper, then adds new kinds of clues that aren't unlike Picross. The visuals are minimal, but pleasing and the ambient music mixes well with the sounds generated by your progression towards the solutions.
The BIG problem is that it's way too short and easy. None of the 29 puzzles presented any kind of challenge to me, and we all know that I'm no Puzzle got (Remember my Spacechem debacle). I was really taken aback when I discovered the "1", "2", "3" entries in the menu didn't bring me to different puzzles but were just save slots. I couldn't believe it was that short. The puzzles may be handcrafted, ensuring that there never is need for guessing, but they aren't all that elegant for it. Not only are the puzzles easy, but they also contain way too many redundant clues.
Another minor problem is that, by default, the mouse buttons used to open a cell or indicate it's part of the pattern are reversed from Minesweeper, which caused a couple of mistakes from my part.
Now, I've already begun playing the sequel, Hexcells Plus and the puzzles there aere much more challenging, which is a good thing.
Anyone with a certain level of puzzle exprience should probably skip this one and go straight to Hexcells Plus.

They are solitary creatures who spend their time making and mending shoes and have a hidden pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. If captured by a human, they often grant three wishes in exchange for their freedom. Like other Irish fairies, leprechauns may be derived from the Tuatha Dé Danann.[1] Leprechaun-like creatures rarely appear in Irish mythology and only became prominent in later folklore.
Modern depictions of leprechauns are largely based on derogatory 19th century caricatures and stereotypes of the Irish.[2]

Short, but sweet puzzle game. It might not be the most original -- this is pretty much a hexagonal variation of Minesweeper with some slight changes -- but it's not like the game pretends to be something more. For what it is, it's quite enjoyable, albeit short; at the current price it might not be the best buy.
The ambiance and sound are exquisite and fit the style of the game, and puzzles require thought. Guesswork will deduce points from your score -- the more mistakes you make, the less points you get -- and more levels are unlocked at a certain number of points, so you can't just click your way to victory.
Not much replayability, except maybe trying to get Perfects in every level to get the 'chieve. (Usually you can make one or two errors, but not more) Levels don't change however, so there's pretty much no point replaying them once you've beaten them all.
If you like Minesweeper, but don't like how random-generated puzzles sometimes require guessing and every error ends in a failure, this might be a good buy. Avoid if you hate puzzlers.

Very cliché game that doesn't really do anything particularly good.
This is a Hidden Object Game. Gameplay consists of searching for different objects in locations available to you, to you use at other locations, minigames (that name the subgenre) where the player completes a checklist of random objects to locate in a fixed screen and other puzzles.
The gameplay is a bit poor. HOG games already make for excellent casual games, for having linear gameplay, shallow story and plain difficulty curve. One could stop playing a HOG for a month to retake it later with very little loss. So content and duration should compensate for the lack of other qualities. But one way or the other, much of the gameplay in this genre (for what I have experienced) is spent navigating the map searching for an active zone that has been activated and will grant you an object that you need in other part of the map. How random are those objects and the locations where you find them also impact the game. That randomness is good for a casual game but not really for a game trying to make an impact.
The game is short. I finished the game in less than three hours (the rest of the played time comes from the first installation and idling for cards). It doesn't have much content (few HOG minigames, easy puzzles, even if had one or two I hadn't yet seen in a HOG [yes, HOGs have all very similiar puzzles]). And the content it has (and I include the story when I say content), has the same shallowness and randomness. See a pair of examples in the spoiler.
The main character is Madam(e?) Detective. Yes, that's her name. Maybe it's a template technique to allow the player to put in the shoes of the main character. In other HOGs you never see the main character; in this one, you can see her in some cutscenes. But, yeah, ok, Madame Detective, pleased to meet you, I'm Mister Reviewer.
Art is kind of solvent, nothing out of the ordinary. Locations, objects and animations have the standard Artifex Mundi quality. Cutscenes are ok. I even recognize that I tried this particular game for the close-up of Madame Detective featured in the video, where she looks more interesting than she proves to be.
Music and sound effects are unremarkable (did the game have any music at all?).
The game is not bad per se, it's decent even. But it doesn't really provide anything new. So it's plain. Even bad games often have new, risky mechanics that don't really work and may be interesting for a while.
Pros:
+Under average. Not bad per se. Just a 5/10.
+Achievements are easy to get, if you care for them.
Cons:
-Total cliché, for the gameplay, for the story, for the characters...
-Little content.
Not recommended.
If you got it in a bundle, like me, you surely have many more interesting games. Should be at the bottom of your stack of games to play.
If you don't have it, skip it unless you are bored and hungry for HOGs, and it's cheap.

A game that takes place in a world where mankind greed for goop has turned them into orks, Your goal as humanity's last line of defense is to fight back with armor and guns, Lots of guns.

After doing a quick tutorial of learning the controls which feels really smooth and very easy to learn.  Alternating between 2 types of dashes, how to pull yourself into vortex with shift, and customizing your weapons. You can either play the game with a controller or a kb+M and pref kb+m is better atm. I logged onto the multiplayer found my friends and started the journey with our guns vs a sea of orks.
The gameplay is a run and gun shooter with co-op capabilities of up to  4 players. The single player could  be pretty tough without friends so make sure ya bring a partner for this one. The goal of the game at the moment is to reach the boss and kill him to obtain  randomized loot drops. From the look of things this game will be turning out really well as stuff is being added since it is early alpha, right now you are offered randomly generated levels and yes, the levels of the area randomly goes up and down also. There are 3 types of things you can modify on a gun at the moment as you find them.  Frames, engines, and the barrel.
The game 2 of us maybe 2 times but the game played smoothly for the others, besides that there isn't too much problems except that we had a blast with it I posted a playthrough video below for you guys along with what is in the game at the moment. + 4 Player co-op multiplayer
+ Multiple paths, anyone can travel bottom, top, middle, and rooftops
+ Destructable armor pieces as you take damage
+ Cool concept with the line showing where your party is, if someone lagged behind you can port them for lagging
+ Devs that keeps in contact with the commnuity is a plus in my book and deserves support.

- Can't wait for more bosses
- More rare drops from orks that will make us take our time killing every orc top down.
- Locations other than the town
- More armors and the customization
- More orc varieties
- The destructables!

Dieselstormers: A Tale of Two Orks
For every misguided youth of the last century who grew up on a healthy diet of Nintendo and Sega, run and gun platformers like the ubiquitous Contra were a staple of multiplayer gaming.  Long before the days of online first person shooters with dozens of players from around the globe, technologically primitive children like ourselves would gather around our ginormous radiation emitting square televisions, fighting each other for a chance to wield the controller next.  Everybody’s household on a weekend was sort of like Lord of Flies, except we had to blow into cartridges before the mayhem could begin.
, the latest effort from Black Forest Studios, is reminiscent of those old school multiplayer shooters of the past, but without the broken controllers (and friendships).  Despite having just entered Early Access on Steam,
is already quite polished for an alpha.  Stylistically, the game stands out with a uniquely detailed art style and beautiful, colorful backgrounds.  Weapons hit the various goblin enemies with a satisfying thud, and the controls are well executed with both keyboard and mouse and gamepad.  Though a full featured single player campaign is already included, the real meat of the game is in the cooperative multiplayer experience, supporting up to four players at a time.
At the start of
, the player is taken to a main area which houses both their main crafting inventory and the mission selection portal.  The first weapon given is a weak, ineffectual pistol, but with the completion of each successful mission another gun part and crafting piece is unlocked.  Missions are short, generally taking around 5-10 minutes to complete.  Multiplayer progress carries over to single player, so players are free to jump between modes as they choose.
Intriguingly, in multiplayer, your character remains alive at “death”, though with diminished powers and barely the ability to push enemies back.  Upon a player finding a health pick up, the deceased will be revived.  What’s most interesting is that death is not necessarily the end if both players die, as long as some sort of health can be found.
Of course, it must be remembered the game is early access and is still a bit buggy at the moment.  During our multiplayer sessions, we had a few crashes and a bit of slowdown, but considering that this is an early alpha, the game shows great promise.  Despite the minor issues we encountered, we found
to be quite enjoyable.
For the adventurous, the developers allow work in progress levels to be toggled in the options menu, what they call “construction site mode”.  As the developers jokingly proclaim on the options page, “unfinished content can look like an ork’s backside and play like its underpants.  You have been warned.”  It’s nice to see a developer with a sense of humor, and of course
plays quite well, even in its early state.  Of course, it’s not Black Forest Games’ first foray into the platformer genre, having developed the recent Giana Sisters titles.  Expect
to only improve as time goes on.
succeeds in bringing back that old school platformer vibe, and is the kind of game you can play over and over again with your friends, whether it be in bite sized sessions or for hours on end.  Pick up one copy, or grab four for some intense side scrolling co-op action.  It is available for Early Access purchase on
.

I didn't have much prior knowledge of the game on purchase, so I generally went with the notion it's a stealth arcade killer. Party Hard is basically a mixed twist of features, both good and bad. There is also a story, of sorts, which throws a few surprises your way which have no impact on the gameplay, other than to provide a shaky narrative to connect different mass murders with each other. Overall, it's a fun diversion for a few hours, but despite the replayability factors, it's not polished, memorable or a game I'd expect myself returning to at a later date.
THE POSITIVE:
+ The game can be challenging despite it's simple appearance and gameplay.
+ The game will definitely keep you on your toes on your initial playthrough due to the amount of unexpected random events and occurences.
+ Easy to understand core mechanics and get into the game after the initial tutorial level.
+ Despite the seemingly simple premise of letting yourself loose upon an unsuspecting crowd, the game does take some tact and planning to complete most of the levels, barring the fortunate accident in which all the random resources scattered about the map provide enough coverage to wipe out all the party-goers.
+ Level Editor for player made content, providing more bang for the buck.
+ Apparently Twitch compatibility, but I am not an user so I can't really say much about that.
The Negative:
- Basically, the AI is a dunce. As some have already mentioned, corpse pickups don't respond to player mayhem in any way and you can literally toss people off roofs or chuck them into barbeques or rotating steel fans without anyone so much as batting an eye. The parties will keep on going despite the player leaving a trail of bodies in their wake, and sometime the only response the player's actions elicit from the locals is 'Can't someone clean this up, this is killing my party buzz?'
- The techno soundtrack might not be everybody's cup of tea. I personally found myself toning down the music since it got to be a nuisance in prolonged maps.
- The player characters all run like they had lead weights on. This is to counteract the law enforcement game of tag the player faces if they happen to be caught redhanded in their wanton carnage. Basically, fleeing from the police is impossible, other than abusing the pathfinding by putting as many turns between yourself and the boys in blue as possible or taking one of the shortcuts in the maps, which brings me to the next item...
- The shortcuts, for some miraculous reason are always expended if you're being chased by law enforcement officers while you take them. A Mario expy will pop out and hammer them out of commission, depriving you their use for the rest of the mission. Granted, this is more a nuisance rather than a real shot in the leg- if you're already doing horribly, you're liable to restart anyway.
- At the time of playing, I encountered several bugs ranging from broken features to cosmetic glithes to a random slow-down.

For me one of the best strategy game of the year. Many fresh gameplay ideas along with a great audio/visual presentation and a smooth running game engine.
Dozents of different units in 7 tiers (Tribesmen, Militia, Convicts, Nobles, Trained, Imperial Guards and Picked), many tactical options (attack, charge, harass, outflang, ambush, defend, reserve, withdraw), upgradeable armor, naval units...ect
I had many epic fights since february and seriously once you played a huge battle in OE, you will not return to the classic 1-Unit per Hex mechanics.
The campaign gameplay is full of random events (locust swarms, bad omen, earthquakes, floods...ect) every single one can break your empire in pieces, if you not prepared.
You will need a good balance between economy/progress and unrest to be successful. Btw OE have two civilian classes the Nobles and the Peasants, both have separate unrest pools.
Edicts can help you in this or that way, but have also a negative (permanent) effect. And many many other nice features.
The negative aspects about Oriental Empires (pre Early Access release) are:
- a very slow and sometimes a little bit boring beginning ( ~ 50 turns)
- the AI needs some improvements
- later in the game you have to deal with very long marching distances for your slow armies
- diplomacy need more improvements / options
- balancing in many areas of the game.
Finally, it´s still a EA game, but unlike many other EA games it´s almost done and it´s very good playable. No CTD in 100+ h playtime and only some minore bugs.
Oriental Empires needs some AI improvments and better balance, but I´m sure the devs will fix it very soon.They definitely know what they do.

Difficulty is not hard or absurd, but unfair. Game mechanics imply that, when you destroy certain enemies, their bullets dissapear, this resulting on you being saved from death. But this only happens if you evade AND destroy them, which results on you being forced to the edge of the screen very often and dying when trying to return to a shooting position.
This mechanic also results on being forced to destroy the enemies as soon as they enter the screen. Most of the time you only see the explosions they left behind which is somehow sad.
Game speed is too high. The backgrounds make it worse, as they have various scroll levels, which make them very rich but very confusing to fight over.
And finally: bullet patters. There seem to be some interesting patterns but, as soon as you evade, a secondary pattern -designed to make you die- shows. You evade big balls, yay, and inmediatly a quick shot is aimed at you at a very high speed. There are bullets so fast in this game that most of the time you won't know what killed you. And this is absurd: you should die to learn, but you cannot learn if you don't see what killed you.
As a result, you continuously have to make use of continues when you run out of lives. This happens so often that makes your will to fight disappear: you simply cease to care.
Claiming to be inspired on the 90s should not lead to some "loose your coin" mechanics.
Maybe if the game could run at half speed and some bullet patters got reworked, it could have been better.

There's good and there's bad in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Borderlands 2 set a high bar, and while the Pre-Sequel didn't feel like it met that, it's still not a bad game. The characters, the story, and the humor weren't as strong as Borderlands 2. Don't expect it to be. What you can expect is an enjoyable first person shooter, good to play through solo, and even better with a few friends.
Despite the shortcomings in story, Pre-Sequel didn't dissapoint in gameplay. Boost jumps and slams were an amazing addition to the game, lasers were awesome, and the classes didn't feel like they'd been recycled from Borderlands 2. Pre-Sequel sticks with the thousands of gun variations, and Diablo style loot system of it's predecessor, but changes up a few things with the addition of Oz (O2) kits, which enable breathing, boost jumps, and slams on Pandora's moon Elpis, where the game is largely set.
The story itself still filled in the gaps between the original Borderlands and Borderlands 2, but, as mentioned above, didn't do a spectacular job of it, it was still enjoyable enough to keep me interested in my subsequent playthroughs. However, there were a few improvements, such as giving the character more of a voice, a feature not present in Borderlands 2.
Ultimately, the Pre-Sequel isn't a bad game. It's not the successor everyone hoped for, but it's probably worth a purchase for a veteran of the Borderlands series.

beautiful game. simple, clean, intuitive.
gentle learning curve, easy to pick up.

no random generation of puzzles means basically no replayability - unlike minesweeper, where there are many permutations the game can generate for you, buying this game is like buying a little sudoku puzzle book. you have a finite number of puzzles to solve, and once you're done, YOU'RE DONE. you may want to replay once if you've made a mistake and want to go back for the perfectionist achievement, but that's the full extent of the replayability factor.

is a fast-paced bullet hell space shooter in a 16-bit style.
The graphics are spot-on, looking exactly like something that would have come out for the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive or the Turbo Grafix 16/PC Engine. The sound effects are great, except for the shooting sound effect of the player's ship, which is essentially just a click, but it's usually so buried under other sounds that it doesn't really matter.
The music sounds fantastic and really fits in with the fast-paced and chaotic gameplay, but it was kind of disappointing in that it didn't really fit with the whole 16-bit aesthetic, so instead of sounding like a midi from a Sound Blaster or anything that would have come out of a 16-bit system, it sounds like modern electronic music (which it is).
On a keyboard, the game controls quite nicely, using the standard emulator presets of Shift, Z, and X as the action buttons and the arrow keys for movement. The use of Shift as one of the action keys feels awkward at times, but it's nothing a quick rebind can't fix.
Using a controller, the joystick controls to move the ship feel quite jerky, with the ship only moving in eight directions, while the joystick, of course, moves in all 360 degrees. The action buttons don't work on first time startup, and must be manually bound using the options menu.
The plot in this game is negligible. It is the standard "aliens are attacking! Save us!" Of course, plot isn't the main draw for this game.
The gameplay is fast-paced and simple. The goal, of course, is to shoot all of the bad guys. To do this, the player has a choice between multiple ships, each of which plays differently. The main difference between the ships is their shot patterns, which, depending on the ship chosen, can drastically change the way the game is played.
The player is given three weapons: the basic shot, a bomb that clears the screen of enemies' shots and gives the player invincibility for a short time, and a "focus shot" which is the basic shot, but slightly more powerful.
The fast-paced nature of the game makes it quite difficult to dodge enemy projectiles, which seem to be everywhere. This challenge is what makes the game, really, since the enemies are really quite easy to defeat simply by holding down the shoot button.
There is a subtle strategy to using the bombs, since the player is only given three at the beginning of the level and there is no way to replenish them.
The game allows for infinite continues, which is wonderful, because it is ridiculously difficult at times.
The game is essentially an arcade game, and always has the incentive of trying to get a higher score (or not use continues).
is a bullet hell shooter, that, while it has its flaws, is thoroughly enjoying and does what it sets out to do.

Classic in every sense of the word but be warned, there is some dust on this gem. The story is easily one of the top stories ever presented in a video game format. The graphics haven't aged gracefully and neither has the game AI. I'll say it now though, they could make this game an nes port of doom where all you do is pick locks, hack computers, and shoot stick figures with a red X over their head so you know they're bad and it would still be one of the greatest games of all time. The story is that good.
With that out of the way, lets look at the rest of the pros. There's an augment system that you can kinda customize based on how you play. For every body part you get two choices, some of them intresting some of them the right one and the "lol who would pick that" one. Speaking of body parts, you don't have a direct health guage in this game. Instead, you have condition of torso, head, and both arms and legs.
Much like other games this is implemented in, having a damaged part hampers its function. A damaged leg results in slower movement  or crawling if both are hurt with a damaged arm or arms equating to worse accuracy. However, full damage to the head or torso will result in death. Luckily when you're drowning because you ran out of oxygen underwater, you can drink soda to keep your lung health up or just say screw it and smoke cigarettes under water and go out like a real man.
Hilariously racist voice acting. Moving on.
There's a skill list you level with experience points. Just about everything gives you experience such as finding a different/hidden path, completing objectives with a various range of exp rewards depending on how you achieved them, completing an objective without being detected, etc. As you gain levels in each of your skills (which you determine by dumping points into them) you'll see fairly noticeable gains though not all of them are really useful.
There's an inventory management system that luckily stores all the ammo separately but its still a pretty tight fit if you plan on carrying more than a few guns.
Overall, a true classic that should be played through atleast once for the story.

Stellaris made me feel like i was a part of an epic space opera. I love the exploring part of 4X games and this game nails it. The anomaly systems and finding new life was such a thrill every time and my first time playing lasted for 13 hours. It brought some sweet memories of getting civilization and just sitting all night on my computer playing it. The feel and atmosphere are spor on and it your internal and foreign politics are so exciting and cool.
However Stellaris has problems. The combat system is either a hit or a miss. You have no strategy inside combat and fights are determined by your unit composition or fleet size. I dont mind this, but i get why people have a distaste for it.
The dimplomacy system and sector managment also needs work. Most effective way to play the game is to make wars. Forming a federation and trying to unite the galaxy is really tedious and there is really no good rewards for doing so.
Sector AI is just terrible. It has severely lacking options in what you can allow it to do and most of the time you are scratching your head at what the AI is doing. Good example of this is when my sector governor decided to enslave all population in my sector even at the risk of a revolution. I had to make slavery illegal just to avoid a goddamn civil war, since there was no way to tell the governor to not enslave my core population.
If these problems are fixed i see the game being one of my favorite 4X games of all time. Aside these issues the game is insanely fun and your first time playing through is going to be some of the most fun you are going to have in a 4X game.

There's good and there's bad in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Borderlands 2 set a high bar, and while the Pre-Sequel didn't feel like it met that, it's still not a bad game. The characters, the story, and the humor weren't as strong as Borderlands 2. Don't expect it to be. What you can expect is an enjoyable first person shooter, good to play through solo, and even better with a few friends.
Despite the shortcomings in story, Pre-Sequel didn't dissapoint in gameplay. Boost jumps and slams were an amazing addition to the game, lasers were awesome, and the classes didn't feel like they'd been recycled from Borderlands 2. Pre-Sequel sticks with the thousands of gun variations, and Diablo style loot system of it's predecessor, but changes up a few things with the addition of Oz (O2) kits, which enable breathing, boost jumps, and slams on Pandora's moon Elpis, where the game is largely set.
The story itself still filled in the gaps between the original Borderlands and Borderlands 2, but, as mentioned above, didn't do a spectacular job of it, it was still enjoyable enough to keep me interested in my subsequent playthroughs. However, there were a few improvements, such as giving the character more of a voice, a feature not present in Borderlands 2.
Ultimately, the Pre-Sequel isn't a bad game. It's not the successor everyone hoped for, but it's probably worth a purchase for a veteran of the Borderlands series.

Even now there are many game-breaking bugs that can ruin hours of playing in a matter of minutes, mostly relating to end-game crisis' that have events that fail to trigger causing you to remain in an endless loop of annoyance. Looking at the future plans of this game it will undoubtedly improve given time as many of Paradox's other titles. This is one of your classic "violent cyberpunk" sports games from the golden era of gaming.
Speedball is suppsed to be a combination of handball and ice hockey, except way futuristic, in space sometimes, and 100 times more violent.
The sound is where this remake really shines. Sound deisgn here is just awesome.
The game features fast-paced gameplay coupled with violent player-to-player collisions resulting in tons of unique gameplay situations to experience. Gaining points doesn't only consist of goal-scoring, but also knocking out the other team's players (each has health bars tha drain upon being hit). As well as hitting certain pinball-type pedastals and such to gain points, and warp-zone and slides to get the ball out of your zone. Tons of ways to gain the advantage against a team that might score often against you.
I constantly score goals that looked so well-played, I can't help but watching the slow-motion replays that play right after your players celebrate.
You have the ability to customize your players, scout to trade for new talent, or go to the gym and train your current team if you're pleased with your current setup. Also, before each game with an opponent you have the choice to compare teams with them to see how you might fare. You can compare your team's defense, midfielders, and forward attackers to your opponent.
Generally, most players will jump into career mode and create their own team (choosing a base team's logo, but creating a new name for your team) which is very fun to do, and feels very engaging and interactive in-between games.
The game features a career mode spanning 10 seasons (I believe) so it makes for a lot of fun trying to win championship cups throughout your career. This game makes you feel like both the brutal, violent players, and the aggressive yet witty coach, managing your team as you go, making trades, and training current players. You can even make certain players swap position if they have stats suited more toward defending than attacking.
9/10
Overall probably the best of the "violent future sport" games ever created.
If you've played and enjoyed games such as Cyberball, Smash TV, Gauntlet and American Gladiators for NES, this is far better, albeit totally different in gameplay.

Classic in every sense of the word but be warned, there is some dust on this gem. The story is easily one of the top stories ever presented in a video game format. The graphics haven't aged gracefully and neither has the game AI. I'll say it now though, they could make this game an nes port of doom where all you do is pick locks, hack computers, and shoot stick figures with a red X over their head so you know they're bad and it would still be one of the greatest games of all time. The story is that good.
With that out of the way, lets look at the rest of the pros. There's an augment system that you can kinda customize based on how you play. For every body part you get two choices, some of them intresting some of them the right one and the "lol who would pick that" one. Speaking of body parts, you don't have a direct health guage in this game. Instead, you have condition of torso, head, and both arms and legs.
Much like other games this is implemented in, having a damaged part hampers its function. A damaged leg results in slower movement  or crawling if both are hurt with a damaged arm or arms equating to worse accuracy. However, full damage to the head or torso will result in death. Luckily when you're drowning because you ran out of oxygen underwater, you can drink soda to keep your lung health up or just say screw it and smoke cigarettes under water and go out like a real man.
Hilariously racist voice acting. Moving on.
There's a skill list you level with experience points. Just about everything gives you experience such as finding a different/hidden path, completing objectives with a various range of exp rewards depending on how you achieved them, completing an objective without being detected, etc. As you gain levels in each of your skills (which you determine by dumping points into them) you'll see fairly noticeable gains though not all of them are really useful.
There's an inventory management system that luckily stores all the ammo separately but its still a pretty tight fit if you plan on carrying more than a few guns.
Overall, a true classic that should be played through atleast once for the story.

I got Hexcells Plus as part of a bundle, and after playing the first few levels I immediately purchased Hexcells so that I could play them in order. I didn't expect to enjoy these games as much as I did. The games are a mix of Minesweeper and Sodoku, plus a few extra twists.
This game ran very well on my netbook at 1024x600 resolution (CPU: 1GHz dual-core AMD C-50), so I think that virtually any computer will be able to hande this game. If you are contemplating buying this game then you might as well get the Hexcells Bundle with both games (especially if you are proficient at logic puzzles). The difficulty curve in the second game starts exactly where the first game ended.
All the levels can be completed without having to resort to guessing, although sometimes you wont believe this. But even when you are unable to determine (for example) which two cells contain the mine, knowing that it is either one or the other may give you enough of a clue to clear a third cell. It is very satisfying when you eventually figure out the puzzle.
The only real con that I found to this game was that despite the harder levels taking some time to complete, there is a great sense of wanting to play just one more level when you do manage to finish it. This can be lead to some very late nights!
Finally, a tip. If you are used to playing Minesweeper, you might like to swap the left & right mouse button actions in the configuration screen so that the right mouse button flags a cell as a blue cell (or a mine in Minesweeper parlance). I kept making mistakes all the time until I did this.

A very short hidden object game with low puzzle variety and an incredibly lame story. Not recommended.
You play as Madam Detective, an apparently nameless yet famous detective. You’re hired to investigate the mysterious disappearance of the crew and cargo of a ship. Almost immediately you are set upon by ghosts and a hooded guy running around with a big hook. If that sounds like the plot of a really bad horror movie… well, it is. The story never rises above bad and the presentation doesn’t improve it. There is very little interaction with other characters; rather most of the story is told through notes and papers with incredibly ugly fonts that don’t match the world at all. I appreciate that they want to make it easy to read, but that can be done without making it incredibly ugly.
Still, the story is not the worst part. The mini-games are few and far between. The HOGs are of the “find 12 items that are completely unrelated to the story and one that you’ll need” variety. At the beginning they have some items being hidden, but even that is abandoned after a few HOG sections. This means that despite the game being very short (I finished it on expert mode with all achievements in 2.5 hours), it still manages to get boring and repetitive. Without a compelling story or interesting gameplay it gets very difficult to recommend this game, even at the low price I got it (1.5 Euro).

Star Vikings is actually a bit like Plant vs. Zombies - but you play the Zombies not the plants. It is a reversed tower defense game, where you have to destroy the towers (slugs) to get through. You have a variety of "heroes" in your arsenal, the tank, able to withstand a lot of damage, the viking, able to throw lightning on the slugs, "angels" able to cast shields (and healing), ...
Each hero can wear a hat, giving him some bonuses, like extra damage, extra energy, more hitpoints, ...
It is a worthwile casual game and quite nice to play.
On the downside:
- Some daily quests simply don't work (and some are somewhat stupid/annoying)
- Some achievements are somewhat bugged. No idea how to get the Leaderboard achievement (I guess, the Friends/Leaderboard feature was simply not implemented yet).
- You need to do a lot of grinding to get the more difficult achievements
- The interface is somewhat optimized for tablets. Not a big deal, but I guess, it would be perfect to play it on a tablet on not with a mouse.
Still, the bugs are mostly minor, I recommend this game to casual players, looking for a reversed tower defense game. Btw.: The game works flawless on Linux (with Mesa drivers).

The Binding of Isaac is an Isometric-viewed Bullet-Hell sort of game in which you escape the clutches of your mother who's gone mad, believing she hears God telling her to kill her son.  Isaac quickly jumps into the basement in which many horrors await in a disturbingly gruesome world.  Isaac's mission is to stop his mother from killing him.  Survival- that's all he wants.  Equipped with only his tears, Isaac must fend off both monsters and personal evils.
First off, there are several characters you can play as, each of which give you a special benefit to the beginning of your run (Isaac has an extra bomb while everyone else has special items as well as a different skin), and gives a definite replay value.  Unlocking them takes quite a bit of time to do so- so expect to be playing as a character several times before you can ensure victory.  There is also a list of challenges to attempt that may make the game easier, or down-right deadly (if you aren't skilled with the attacks), and completing them win unlock other collectable items as you journey through the depths.
The movement is smooth and you feel like you're in control.  Isaac's walking animation is good but (personally) feels lacking.  It looks nice for the art-style, but seems slightly off (again, personally).  Nevertheless, it gives you plenty of room for slipping away from quick spiders and blood-bullets.
Your weapons (for the most part) are simply your own tears.  Isaac shoots his tears- in which he has plenty of- at the opposing beings to damage and inevitably, destroy them.  As one journeys, Isaac will likely obtain power-ups and bonuses that'll up your damage and attack speed or even completely change your attack all together- shooting explosive bile in an arch, or zapping lasers with a mechanical eye.  Each new upgrade gives physical changes to your 'arrows' and, using that knowledge, can really help the new players get a feel for the strength of each shot.
Speaking of design, the Isaac chosen on the main menu is far from the one who completes the game.  Each upgrade, while giving the in-game help, changes his physical appearance- adding slashes to his body, a fetus to his head, and mom's panties around his legs.  The upgrades stack-up, creating horribly disgusting monstrosities and thousands of possible outcomes.  While each change does look well made, some don't stack as well as they should and appear out-of-place or overlapping with previous upgrades.  Nevertheless, it still gives a gruesome character.
The enemies range from cliché- flies and spiders- to bizarre- piles of meat and headless corpses- and each has its own attacking style.  The design for most of the lackeys is really good, giving a disturbing appearance for each monster.  The bosses are vile- which is perfect for the game.  You fight mutated monsters, most of which with human features, the four horsemen, and even the deadly sins such as Lust and Greed.  Again, each boss and pre-boss fight has a unique spin on what the enemy can do and how you can defeat it, giving even more depth to this intense game.
Keys, Bombs, and Coins are scattered around in the randomly-generated world and often appear once every monster is destroyed in the new area.  It is difficult- if not impossible- to beat the game without a consistent supply of these items, so it is imperative for survival that the player takes item consumption carefully.  However, those aren’t the only items found in The Binding Of Isaac- Pills and Tarot Cards are also found among the halls of monsters.  Each game gives each pill a different use- for example, one game may have the pill give Isaac ‘Full Health’, but the next will give him a ‘Bad Trip’.  Picking up pills and using them will show you what the pill does the next time you pick it up- until you die and the pills are reset.  The Tarot Cards are always the same, either summoning helpful items, teleporting Isaac somewhere else, or even summoning Mom’s Foot.  Isaac must use all of these items to their full potential in order to survive the depths of this Hell.
Overall, the best way to describe this game is ‘Difficult’.  It’s a Bullet-Hell and definitely shows in the over-load of projectiles, wandering enemies, and exploding bombs.  Surviving takes skill, persistence, and luck.  Each map is randomly-generated and can overwhelm even the most skilled players.  However, as hard as this game can be, it is fair in its assaults.  You can dodge most attacks and there are plenty of hearts that spawn in certain maps, so survival is very much so possible- it just takes a lot to obtain it.
The story is pretty short.  Mother hears God telling her to kill Isaac.  Isaac jumps into the basement.  Isaac faces horrors underground.  Not much else until you get to the end.  There isn't much to the story, but it doesn't really need too much more for a story.
If you enjoy a fair challenge, The Binding Of Isaac is perfect for you.  Smooth movements and a mess-up attitude, this game has a lot of character and really shows.  Hard, and definitely a work-out, but overall, an absolute journey into this grotesque world.

I will say right now that I love Borderlands 2. I spent about between 400-500 hours into it, and I only have 1 character that is level 72 op8. I have another level 72, but not op8. Even though Borderlands 2 has a lot of dlc, you felt like it was somewhat worth it because of how much it upped Borderlands 2. I was excited for this game because I loved Borderlands 2. To be honest, this game took everything that Borderlands 2 did right, and screwed it up! It also took them 6 months after release to fix some of the problems with this game, and even then, this game still has things wrong with it. First, I will talk about the positives:
Positives:
-There are a lot of guns to find
-Can be humorous at times
-Has the best story out of all the Borderlands games (I will talk more about this in the negatives)
-The new gravity and oxygen mechanics are good
-The new lasers and the cryo element
-No class feels SIGNIFICANTLY better or worse than others (CaxtOnUGH)
-More character unique dialogue
Mixed:
-The grinder. This is a cool way to use up weapons you don't need, but it is mixed because a lot of the legendaries depend on the use of the grinder
-Bugs. This game is not buggy enough to define it as something like Batman Arkham Knight for the PC or a huge portion of Bethesda's games, but the game did crash on me quite a few times, and some quests or other things would not work or trigger properly.
Negatives:
-Endgame has been significantly dumbed down! Although this was somewhat fixed, there is no excuse for how it was at release. For six months, about 90% of the bosses did not respawn, and the legendary loot was incredibly rare, so you would have to keep Alt-F4ing out of the game to reload to get your legendary.
-No "real" raid bosses. Although the game tells you that there is a "raid boss" quest after you beat the game and there is, it is nothing special at all. It is just an amped up version of the final boss.
-A lot of legendaries are borrowed and reused from Borderlands 2, just renamed and a lot of legendaries rely on the grinder.
-DLC for this game is a pathetic joke. With Borderlands 2, the season pass was $30, and what did you get? You got the Mechromancer, and 4 story add-ons with new gear, new loot, and new areas. The season pass in this game is $30. What do you get? Do you get any of the kind of dlc that Borderlands 2 had to offer? No. You get 2 characters, a fighting arena that sucked♥♥♥♥♥ and one campaign add-on! Borderlands 2 DLC >>>>>>>>>>>>>> Borderlands TPS DLC

The beauty of this game is that it's completely logical. There is no element of guessing and no ambiguity. You always have all the information there to solve the puzzle, if only you can notice it. That makes it very satisfying to solve and when you make a mistake, you're the only one to blame, which motivates you to replay levels where you made a mistake. The only very minor irritant is that it's easy to make a mistake by twitching at the wrong moment or just using the wrong mouse button if you get distracted. There's no way to say, "No! That's not what I meant to do!" It's very short: only 36 levels, but I'd rather have 36 levels of good puzzles than 100 of a bad one. Totally recommended

The song was so catchy and over the top that even after beating this game, I still catch myself singing, "Staaarr viikings!!!" then laughing a bit as I remember the silliness that is Star Vikings.
I don't mean silly in any kind of derisive or mean way, but Star Vikings could be a satirical take on an 80's cartoon. My point is, that you aren't meant to take the overall aesthetic seriously, instead when you peel back the layers of this title, you are going to be presented with a clever and challenging puzzle game.
Star Vikings is a weird mash up of Plants Vs Zombies meets XCOM with a big helping of puzzle elements. Well, okay less XCOM, because every shot actually hits when you are standing right in front of the enemy. You get the idea. I know that sounds kinda weird but stick with me. I am going to go over the game mechanics first and then touch upon the more obvious traits of the game.
Starting with the PVZ aspects, the game takes some ideas from the mobile game department and presents to you an overworld map with about fifty levels total. Each planet has different enemy units, modifiers, story based objectives/random objectives, shops, and recruitment stations. Once you select a map you are actually brought into the game itself where your units appear on the left side of the screen. The basic gist of it is kill everything in your way while moving right down five lanes and completing objectives. Objectives can be things like: progress five screens worth of enemies, kill sixty enemies, or open five treasure chests. It all depends on the level and it really does a great job of keeping things fresh.
Just like Chess or PVZ, there are six classes total. Each is dynamically different in the method they deal with enemies, what they bring to a fight or how they move. The six classes are Shooter, Tank, Sneaky, Hunter, Valkyrie, and finally Berserker. This allows you essentially tackle puzzles in hundreds of different ways. Collecting five treasure chests will be completely different with a Berserker then it would be with a Shooter, as an example. It's this gameplay that makes Star Vikings very strategic and makes you think ahead. One wrong step and you will lose a unit. Thankfully, unlike XCOM the deaths are not permanent.(Hint hint Rogue snail, Ironman mode)
Enemies are also constantly changing their method of attack and the game is always upping the ante by introducing new threats. As an example is the addition of traps, or mimics.
Now the way the game reminds me of XCOM, is that not every one of the six classes are always going to be the same. You can recruit new vikings with all sorts of different innate buffs. These guys come with a heftier recruitment fee. I should mention gold and fuel is earned through completion of levels. I personally had a Striker and a Shooter with the ability to avoid death 50% of the time, this was vastly useful, but very expensive. The recruits/innate buffs are all randomized based on a timer that switches out what is available .
On top of that there are MORE customization of your units, as each class has a skill tree that changes how the class might attack, or buff fellow allies. Just like XCOM, as your units level, you pick one of two abilities and this really gives you the opportunity to craft a team and strategy of your own design. It's really awesome watching your Vikings become their own person that looks nothing like their base class. This gives the game extreme replayability and longevity for those of you that like to find the best min/max for class builds and team builds.
I am not done yet though, there are also hats that come with other innate bonuses which add to your characters stats and modifiers. But wait, there's more, you can purchase/find items that you can use in battle to give your Vikings an edge.
I don't know about you, but that doesn't sound like just a silly game about Vikings does it? It sounds freaking awesome. and it is. I was pleasantly surprised by the complexity and level of customization with my units. The puzzle aspects of the game continuously shine because of this, as there are a million ways to deal with a situation. It's like Chess but if your Pawn could suddenly do a backflip and throw an acid grenade, or your Queen could pull out an uzi.
There are some obvious strategies that do make the game rather easy, but I won't divulge those here. I mention that because by the end of the game I had my perfect five Vikings and nothing could stand in our way. To keep that from happening to often the game adds modifiers to certain stages. Normal stages are easy to plow through, but you begin to find levels with a fog modifier, plus five health, and plus two damage, suddenly all your best laid plans are getting put on hold.
What I am trying to basically sum up for you is don't judge this book by its cover. Star Vikings has its silly side true, but there is a deep game here.
The other areas of the game are going to be a hit and miss scenario from player to player. Funny is subjective and as Edmund Kean put it, "Dying is easy, comedy is hard." The game gave me a chuckle a couple of times and when a Viking bares his buttocks to his enemies, that is going to make me laugh. Are all the jokes funny? No. The animation style is very 80's cartoon and that isn't a bad thing. The battle animations are more of the PVZ variety with explosions, zaps, and other cartoon like effects. Again this isn't at all a negative for me but it is going to be up to you if you enjoy this style.
There is a minor story here about a Viking called Thork and his quest for a holy relic that he thinks is a table wedge, but I think that is best savored in game.
In other areas the game is exceptionally well made. This comes from the team behind Chroma Squad, Relic Hunter Zero, so the attention to design, UI, and controls are top notch. Not once did the game crash on me nor did I have any issues whatsoever. The controls are extremely simple and this game is very child friendly. You could use this game to introduce young kids to puzzle, logic and strategy games. The music, as mentioned before, is really quite catchy. Sound effects all have their proper amount of gravitas behind them.
The one thing I did get caught off by was that this game is extremely mobile friendly but isn't, as far I am aware, on any mobile devices. I would've loved to play this on a pad device while sitting on my iron throne. The game is extremely addictive and I really hope that a mobile version is in the works. There is a leaderboard in the game but it mostly is for Trials of Valhalla, a level where the modifiers are constantly rising. I didn't play it all that much. I am not super competitive, but it is there.
For the low price of $10 you get about eight hours of gameplay out of the main story. There are plenty of side secret levels and things to experiment with, giving replay value and obviously the levels are procedural. There are Steam achievements but no Steam cards. The game is criminally under rated and think that this title was lost in the avalanche of Steam games. It's not changing the wheel for gaming and it is probably not super innovative, but it does things in its own unique way enough to warrant your attention.
So if you are looking for an adorable puzzle/strategy RPG to take up your time, give Star Vikings a chance and it might make you smile.

Unfortunately, I'm not recommending Artifex Mundi's "Left in the Dark: No One on Board."  There's no single, overriding reason.  Just a combination of many issues.  First, even for a casual adventure Hidden Object Game (HOG), the voice acting (especially the male voices) are bad.  Second, the HOGs are a bit tough to do.  Not for any puzzle-based reason.  But, because the graphics are very muddy.  The HOGs look sort of like paintings and figuring out what's what is hard.  Third, even the sounds aren't that good.  Some of the birds sound like flutes instead of birds.  And finally, the game is just too short.  It took me exactly three hours to finish the game with 100% Achievements.  That wasn't even long enough to get all the Trading Cards.  I had to let the game idle for an additional 20 minutes after I was done to get my final card drop.  This is especially bad for a game with a list price of almost $10.  So, on the whole, I'd say pass on this game.  If you find it for a dollar or two, you could give it a whirl.  But, even so, I'd be leery.

So everyone really, really likes NieR: Automata. The only negative reviews I see on Steam are because of the problems with the PC port or just people giving up after a couple of hours for whatever reason. I played this game through to the end, all 5 important endings (ABCDE), so I've given this game its fair shake. I still don't like it and I can't really understand why others do like it. I understand the themes it was going for and admittedly those themes are interesting. However, I think the game fell flat in its execution.
First off I could not care less about any of the characters. None of the tear jerking moments caused any emotion in me. Now, you might think I'm completely heartless or a psychopath, but that's not the case. I just felt like the characters and their relationships were never really fleshed out. I still feel like I don't know a whole lot about 2B, 9S and A2 (apart from 9S liking 2B). Most of the cast don't have any real personal motivation for what they do in the story (again with the exception of 9S). It is, at best, vaguely hinted at in the main story. Maybe a lot of this is hidden in away in text entries, but I don't spend hours reading that stuff. But, if important things like character motivations are hidden away in text form, then that's just bad storytelling, in my opinion. Add on top of all this death has no real consequences for reasons explained in the story, and any semblance of my personal investment in the characters or what happens to them just disappears compeletely.
Second off, I absolutely HATED my second playthrough. Barely anything changed content-wise, which leads to a 6-hour slog through a portion of story I've played already. The game drip feeds you some tiny droplets of story, but it wasn't anywhere near enough to keep me interested. ALso, 9S's hacking minigame got extremely stale after doing it for the umpteenth time. The gameplay overall is fairly shallow. The spectacle fighting has less going on than, say, God of War or Bayonetta with less moves than either of them. I enjoyed it during my first playthrough, but after those 10ish hours, I'd had enough. The bullet hell gameplay is much worse and just straight up boring to me. If you hold down the square & R1 button on a PS3 controller and move around a bit, you'll usually be fine.
Also, side quests are Dragon Age: Inquisition levels of bad: fetch quests galore. I stopped doing them after the fifth one had me walking 10 minutes to go collect 5 more bear's asses with barely any story and no voice over to make up for it.
Finally, I felt the overall story was poorly patched together with important plot points being glossed over and hardly explained. I asked myself multiple times why or how a particular event was happening and could not come up with a satisfying answer. Again, I didn't spend too much time reading the text entries. I'm sure many people will tell me I didn't get it and they may well be right. I'm definitely eager to watch some deeper analysis videos on this game. I might come to appreciate the game more in time.
PS: I should add the caveat that I haven't played many JRPGs and no Yoko Taro games before this one. The ones I did play, I didn't really enjoy. If you are a fan of that particular genre or of Yoko Taro, this may well be right up your alley.
EDIT: some people had some questions/criticism in the comments, I'll try to adress those here:
Death really doesn't have significant consequences until the final part of the game (and even then it doesn't really, seeing as they get put back together). The first two times they die (2B and 9S together and 9S alone), their most relevant data gets uploaded back to the bunker and they continue on without missing a beat. Sure, they miss some small bits of memories along the way, but no one really seems to care. In those two situations, the people dying aren't too upset about what's happening to them, and rightly so. I think that says enough about why dying doesn't really matter.
Regarding my time played: as stated in the review, I skipped most side quests. The reason for that, that I genuinely didn't enjoy the first ones I came across. They left a lasting, bad impression on me. The objectives themselves came down to running to a particular area and killing/collecting something or talking to someone. This was extremely boring to me in the beginning, considering I didn't have fast travel unlocked yet. It felt like busy work for too little reward. This really put me off any further side quests, especially when combined with the fact that most side quests in the previous NieR game where utterly forgettable. I played through the main quest only pretty much, because I was interested in the story. The side quests contain a chunk of story, for sure, but I didn't think the hassle was worth it. I also found the gameplay fairly mediocre and thus wasn't compelled to go exploring or further upgrade my weapons.
Regarding the "further analysis" comment: I think you misunderstood what I was trying to convey there. I'm not planning on doing any further analysis myself, but rather watching youtube videos of people with far more time and skill than myself (for example: Joseph Anderson, SuperBunnyHop, etc.)
Regarding not understanding the characters' motivations and whatnot.
First off, A2 isn't fleshed out in the slightest. They vaguely explain to you she's an older model and some audio during a flashback hints at what happens. That's pretty much all you get for a fairly important character.
2B is a little more fleshed out, in the sense that we find out her main role is basically executing 9S when he finds out the secrets of Yorha and she's pretty beat up about it because she likes 9S. That's all the personality she gets.
9S is the most fleshed out, considering he talks the most. He's a scanner model who really likes 2B, but he's too smart for his own good. When everything starts falling apart and 2B dies, he goes on a bit of a rampage brings down the tower. Unfortunately, I didn't like this character. Rather, I found him annoying and childlike, which is odd for a recon android that participates in military operations.
So to me, I've got 2 poorly fleshed out characters that I can't really get invested in and one properly fleshed out character who I didn't like.

One of the best games i have played in several years.
Why?
The combat feels fun and fluid with a ton of possible move sets in the game. The game also change angles and go into "shoot em up" mode which helps the game not get stale. The characters are likable and interesting with development over the course of the game. You will end up knowing that the game's world is ruthless and unforgiving but still hope that everything ends happily for even the side characters. The game's concepts are thought-provoking as it touches upon quite a few dilemmas about life and meaning.
The music is one of the best soundtracks I have heard for a long time. One of the only times I ever got goosebumps whilst hearing music in my life. The Boss fights could benefit from being more difficult but they are still fun. Overall I loved the game
However...
I am aware of many people having issues with the game (I only crashed about 4 times) which really sucks as this could be one of the best games in several years if more people could actually play it. All I can say is that anyone who buys this game should use the "Fix automata" mod to try to help stability and performance (as well as the full screen bug)
My personal score is a 10/10 but as this is a recommendation to others I have to factor the issues that people are having and give the game...

The beauty of this game is that it's completely logical. There is no element of guessing and no ambiguity. You always have all the information there to solve the puzzle, if only you can notice it. That makes it very satisfying to solve and when you make a mistake, you're the only one to blame, which motivates you to replay levels where you made a mistake. The only very minor irritant is that it's easy to make a mistake by twitching at the wrong moment or just using the wrong mouse button if you get distracted. There's no way to say, "No! That's not what I meant to do!" It's very short: only 36 levels, but I'd rather have 36 levels of good puzzles than 100 of a bad one. Totally recommended

This game is quite fun but has it's downsides.
Like all Paradox titles at release it was a great grand strategy game, but you clearly felt something lacking; an unpolished gem so to speak.
Even now there are many game-breaking bugs that can ruin hours of playing in a matter of minutes, mostly relating to end-game crisis' that have events that fail to trigger causing you to remain in an endless loop of annoyance. (Robot AI uprising has the ability to never trigger it's end sequence if you're unlucky, same with the Scourge)
The game offers many different type of empires, but it does nothing to change your playstyle; You will murder your way through the galaxy because there is no other way to beat the game.
Setting up the game has changed for the better since the last update (1.3) as you can now use more options to get the type of game you wish to play. It's still not perfect, but it adds a lot of flavour to your options.
The plant-type DLC isn't worth the €10,- as it's just graphics for species and new ship types. Get it on sale.
The Leviathan story pack is still buggy at times which is a shame really as it adds a lot of new story-telling. This one I'll recommend getting even if it's not on discount, it was worth the €10,-. to aid the developers.
Looking at the future plans of this game it will undoubtedly improve given time as many of Paradox's other titles. The team seems personally invested in bettering the game and they listen to their fans. I wil recommend getting this game but be justly warned: You will invest a lot of time and money in this game as DLC's are Paradox's thing so you'll keep paying and replaying and then wondering why your wife divorced you, who those teenagers in your house are as you swear your wife (whom you can't find) gave birth to your children just yesterday, and what is that ungodly smell? Oh God, is...is that me? Am I that smell? How long has it been since I took a break and bathed myself? Time to peace out people, cya on the other side of the galaxy.
ps: You can totally play as space-Hitler though so that's cool.

Highly recommend this game. The levels are designed in such a way that you never have to guess; what makes it better is that there are usually multiple avenues towards solving each given level. If you're finding it too difficult to solve one area of (solvable, but tricky) hexes, it's often the case that you can make progress in a separate area before returning with a little more information.
I would have liked to see some more content, but it was cool how the game kept with the hexagon theme. 6 worlds with 6 levels each. (Though admittedly, a few of the levels were filler / instructional, and didn't pose as much of a challenge.) I wonder if an optional timed mode would be a good idea. On the one hand, it would be nice to come back to the levels in a few months and see how fast I solve them second time around, but on the other hand, the pressure might take away from the uncluttered minimalist feel of the game.
Overall, thorougly enjoyed Hexcells & Hexcells Plus and would definitely recommend as a stimulating challenge.

Let me start out by saying that this game really brings the best of both the randomly-generated craze and the retro platformer craze to the table with perfect indie aesthetic. The term Roguelike get's liberally used nowadays, and that is a bit sad. This game is far from a rogue game. Yes, it has randomly generated levels every run. Yes it does include a permadeath system. And yes, it does have an old school style, but that doesn't make it a Roguelike.
This game is a 2D-Platformer with simple RPG and Survival elements. And it pulls it off rather well. I really enjoy the style it's presented in, the particle effects are basic, but stunning. I cannot state in short how many comparisons I can derive from two personal favorites of mine (Spelunky & Terraria), and that is a very good thing. The thing that Smash Games' Magicite forges as it's own though is that it's not only a challenge to complete each level, but once you do, you get a very brief respite before being tossed into the fray again.
I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for retro platforming with a few new school effects.
Immense Pro's:
+ Light Roguelike & RPG Influences
+ Vast Amounts of Replayablility
+ Wonderful Soundtrack
+ Gorgeous Art Style
+ Unique Playthroughs (Unlockable Classes, Companions, & Equipment)
Slight Con's (Take these lightly as the game isn't completed yet!):
- Limited Inventory System
- No Mouse-Lock
- Steep Difficulty Curve for Some Players
- Overpriced? (Buy on sale definitely)
- Slow Opening (Take's a couple play's to really dig up the content and fun)

Like some, I skipped directly to Witcher 3 when it went on sale, but not for long.  I was so impressed by Witcher 3, I felt it necessary to explore and finish the prequel, Witcher 2: Assasins of Kings.
I tasked myself to play and finish Witcher 2: Asssasins Of Kings.  Much like a Temerian youth might adorn the lily sword n' shield for King Foltest, I felt it my duty to learn and experience and learn about a piece of Geralt of Rivia's adventure.  I blew the dust off my digital copy and went to work. To my surprise an incredible journey unfolded, with memorable characters, and a compelling story.
The gameplay wasn't half bad, either.
Your journey begins by the side and aide of King Foltest, known for his prow for battle, and his generosity of coin - a Witcher's match made in heaven.  To protect and aide the bombastic King Foltest?  What could go wrong in these troubling times?  It would not take long for Geralt to find out the life of a King - no matter how great or terrible - is beset by danger on all sides.
Positive Bullets
Neutral Bullets
Negative Bullets
Closing thoughts:  I've enjoyed all the Witchers' thus far and a particularly Witcher 2.  If I were to give you my favorite in the series up to this point, it would be Witcher 2, but only because the Witcher 3 primed me for it. If I had not played Witcher 3 I would not have bothered with Witcher 2.  The magnificent irony!   After 30 hours of playing Witcher 2, I am complete and satisfied.  But after 100 hours of Witcher 3, I'm nowhere near satisfied or complete.  I'm almost overwhelmed by choice.  To be a Cat or a Bear?   To wield a controller or to use a KB & M.  It's maddening!  But I'm OK with that; I'm OK with games all having their own peculiar charm and draw.  I hope AAA is not limited to "open world" or "time" or "quantity."  I think most of us worry the open world format is ripe for laziness and sheer volume stripping our experience of the depth demonstrated in games like Witcher 2 and 3.
Naturally, CD Projekt Red, seems to have Yennefer's Raven's listening and following the trend and subsequent outrAgEs of the day:
"@PrettyBadTweets Worry not. When thinking CP2077, think nothing less than TW3 — huge single player, open world, story-driven RPG. No hidden catch, you get what you pay for — no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, just honest gaming like with Wild Hunt. We leave greed to others."
We'll hold you to it, CD Projekt Red!  Light a compelling linear path within the wild, open world and keep on keeping on!

This, in my opinion, is probably one of the bigger let-downs in the Call of Duty franchise. I still recommend it though as it is worth playing at least once so you can get the story and move on to Black Ops 2.

I can understand a few here and there but playing the game more than once is a real drag.
There is a known bug in which non-playable character textures won't show up when hit with a flashlight. This means that in two locations in the game when you are using a flashlight you will shine it on a character and see a black silhouette only. It is not only unsightly and inexcusable that it was never fixed but it is infuriating when those black silhouettes are shooting at you and you can't really see them all too well.
The Vietnam levels, for some reason, just seemed more frustrating to me than anything. I wanted to like the game, I really did but I found myself hoping to get to the next level already more often than not rather than enjoying it.
In conclusion, I still recommend it as being worth getting and playing at least once. Also, if you liked the zombies mode from World at War then you will definitely enjoy the zombie levels in this one.

In this stand-alone adventure - hopefully stays that way - you play as the one and only, "Madam Detective". Seriously? No one even took the trouble of giving a proper name to the protagonist? Oh, well. Madam Detective is asked to investigate the mystery of a lost cargo ship. It is explained to us that the ship never reached its destination, found in the open sea without a crew and its cargo, sometime after its departure. Oh, also we have the ghost of a young girl who tries to sabotage us half way through the game, and aid us during the other half.
My first complaint is about the story's presentation. If you pay attention to the story and the obvious lack of function in procedure for the investigation of the ship, you know the identity of the murderer within the first 15 minutes that you play the game. The rest is spared to understand reasons, that's all. The bonus chapter that we expect in every Artifex Mundi game to shed some light into the background of affairs doesn't exist in this game, sorry.
Puzzles are annoyingly basic. Hidden object scenes are so easy that it becomes boring after a while, and there is no alternating gameplay. There is an obscene amount of backtracking compared to other games. The setting and the art work is pretty, but not spectacular. I've seen better in
or
. You keep listening to the same 30 second music in the background again and again until you decide to mute it.
I know it is not commonly expected for a HOG to bear decent story or event decent gameplay, but Artifex Mundi is supposed to be a decent contradiction to that idea. If this game would come from any other HOG developer I'd smile and write a brief recommendation. Not for Artifex Mundi. Oh wait, this isn't developped by Artifex Mundi! They are only the producer! Now the actual mystery of the game is explained! But why they've attached their name to this game? That is another mystery.
