What the heck is Speedball? No, it’s not a special drug that the kids are doing but it probably has the same effect on your adrenal system. Speedball is a sport designed for cyborgs, played in a not so distant future. Combine football, rugby, and MMA and you have a pretty decent idea of what this brutal sport entails. Matches are quick, taking only a couple minutes, so it isn’t just a clever name. Destroying the other team’s players is just as important as scoring goals and as barbaric as it sounds, Speedball is a surprisingly deep game.
I have always been a sucker for ‘alternative’ sports. Give me Mutant League Hockey over NHL,  Frozen Endzone instead of Madden, and Base Wars before MLB. If I’m going to play a vanilla sport I’m going to do it in real life, reserving futuristic robot sports for the video game medium. Speedball 2 HD is a remake of the Bitmap Brothers’ most successful game, Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe. It’s been over 20 years since the last decent Speedball game and this is the most accurate representation of the sport/game you are going to find. Vivid Games has done the series justice and thank god Mastertronic had the balls to publish the damn thing.
Speedball is astonishingly simple thanks to a refined control scheme, and two basic rules: The first is to put the biscuit in the basket and the second is to devastate the other team with sick tackles. This is all made very easy by having only one button for all actions, and I highly suggest you have a controller while playing as this will make things much easier. When you have ball possession, pressing the action button will throw the ball in that direction and holding the action button will lob the ball in the air. Pressing the action button without the ball initiates a tackle and your player will slide in the direction he is facing, mauling any opposing player in the way. I’m going to level with you, this ain’t no graceful ballet and Speedball games can quickly devolve into all out brawls since points are rewarded for injuring players on the other team. Once a player is injured by having all their health depleted, they are carted off by medical bots and replaced by a substitute. It’s not my favorite tactic, but beating the other team down so you have a player advantage is acceptable in Speedball, and a great way to win games.
Aside from mashing up the other team and scoring goals, there are a number of variables on the field that can change the game. The permanent structures such as bumpers will not only change the course of the ball, but will award bonus points if a team manages to score after the bumper is hit. Bumpers can be used for both offensive and defensive purposes, conjuring up some interesting plays. If you thought it was fun dunking in NBA Street after launching the ball off the backboard...Speedball 2 HD makes that look like child’s play. Ramps on the sides of the field will accelerate the ball and give a 50 percent bonus to points scored on that run, however this is cancelled when the opponent puts it through the ramp. This makes controlling the sidelines paramount to success as it can effectively half the amount of points you need to score during a game. This is especially important when you’re up against a stronger, faster, better team and you don’t have Michael Jordan or Bill Murray on your roster. Other structures on the field include stars on the side that can be used for extra points, as well as portals that will teleport the ball to the other side of the field. Take note playmaking wizards. Finally, random powerups will be littered across the throughout the game that can temporarily boost a player, or harm the opposing team.
There are several modes in Speedball 2 HD including quick play, tournament, and a career mode. Career mode puts you in the role of a GM of a team, which you can name and choose a logo, but that is about it when it comes to customization. As you win games, you get cash that can be used to train your players and increase their stats. I found after a couple seasons my winnings had allowed my team to surpass everyone in the galaxy stat-wise so games became terribly easy and I was blowing out teams by 100 points every game. That being said, the AI isn’t great and Speedball 2 HD is best played on a couch with a friend. Multiplayer is unfortunately limited to local only so you are going to have to convince people to come to your house.
Speedball 2 HD is a great remake, and as I mentioned previously the best version of the game you are going to find. It’s not bustling with features but it has some depth to it. The career mode will keep you busy enough to get your money’s worth and a decent sense of progression across multiple seasons. No online multiplayer is a shame, but if you can manage to get a group of friends over for a small tournament it will be a great game to have. It’s fast, and easy to learn and a hard hitting little gem that satiate your need for a Murderball game.

I was a huge fan of the classic Amiga original, so when i first heard about this i was immediately enthralled. A couple of days later a friend of mine had bought it and told me that it had some niggles that meant it wasn't as good as the Amiga version, but still a good game. Since it's only £5.50 (i'd payed £25 for the Amiga original in 1991!) i figured what the hell, i'll give it a go.
I have to say he was right, it does have some niggles that mean it's not as good as the original Amiga version, but it is still a good game and very enjoyable. Fans of the original will be pleased to hear it plays near identically, with the transfer market, gym and the all important match play itself all faithfully reproduced. Graphically i don't think it compares to the Amiga version though and while many of the sounds have been ported over from the original, some additional sound in the form of in-game music feels out of place. Thankfully said music can be turned off.
In the match play, the ball feels rather heavy and slow, so doesn't travel very far when thrown. But where the match play compares particularly unfavourably to the Amiga original is with injuries. In the original these were somewhat rare, as even the weakest players were still somewhat strong, but here you will find injuries to opposing players are rather easy to dish out and you'll average at least 3 per game. If you get more, they can't bring on a substitute and so with one or more players short they become a bit too easy to beat. That's not to say the computer teams are a walkover, they certainly aren't, and once they have a sniff of a goal they've as good as scored. So the computer is at least competative, which is a good thing since multiplayer consists of LAN play only, there is no online multiplayer at all. Hopefully this will be addressed in the future as this game is just crying out for that feature.
My final niggle is the resolution, with 1920x1200 being the maximum supported, so if you playing at a resolution higher than that (as i am) you'll have to make do. With 1920x1080 and 1920x1200 now being pretty much mainstream resolutions for gamers, this game really should support at least up to 2560x1600.
However, those are the only issues i've encountered with this game. Everything else is very good and make the game extremely enjoyable, particularly for those of us who played and loved the classic Amiga game. Highly recommended.

The machines are very detailed and come with a procedure which is more than just pressing a button - it makes it feel really real but does take some practice. Also, you can build houses! Since the game is still in Early Access, it will will expand on that, but the creativity and possibilities in it are looking to be totally amazing!

Coopting the great poet, Dylan Thomas's words, Deus Ex is a game that refuses to go gentle into that good night.
Deus Ex is a simple game, yet it has a certain soul to it. For many, it's that venerable old book that you ccan curl up with after a long day at the office, always there: a calm, steadiness that doesn't ask anything of you.
So what is it? simply, a First-person, cyberpunk action RPG. Now, these concepts have been done before, and certainly since. (System Shock / Deus Ex Human Revolution) Of course, you're probably asking then, "Just what does this game that causes it alone to stand apart for so many?"
Execution. A classic should be able to hold up to scrutiny after the shiny baubles have faded. The story is well written with solid world building, for one. A few aspects are cleche, to be sure, but what respected works are free from such trappings?
Deus Ex keeps the player engaged and watching their back the entire time. The world of 2052 is a harsh, unforgiving place, and the game shows that. Not just through in game literature, but the landscapes: the use of night time levels, shadowy agencies and civil unrest. All made to keep you on edge.
So how about the gameplay? Deus Ex is played from the first person similar in control scheme to modern FPSes and RPGs alike, so the transition should be an easy one. The shooting mechanics are present, but are as emphesized as the other skills: hacking, stealth, and lockpicking, to name a few.
So why have so many skills? Deus Ex realizes the dream that many modern games attempt: to give the player  many ways to complete an objective.  ...or not. It's up to the player. Will you enter a terrorist hostage situation with your automatic rifle at your side as you bust through the front door? Will you infiltrate the sewer and disable the security grid? Perhaps you'll meet a contact in a back alley and negotiate for some valuable intel for a dubious favor? You can do any of those, and more in Deus Ex.
The game doesn't insult your intellegence and it rewards you for playing smart.
Deus Ex is as close to a mandatory game for any PC gamer as there can be. You'll notice how the industry irrevocably changed as a result of this game, and in some ways, I would say, never again surpassed what Deus Ex achieved over a decade and a half ago.

Navigation: Spherical 2D where the viewpoint of the player is fixed to a vertical axis that is limited in it's vertical range of motion by 180° in each horizontal direction that the player is facing (90° up and down). The players motion is perceived as the distance that the world travels from the playe'rs pov relatively to how far the player itself travels in the world. This type of spherical 2D navigation represents the reference standard for any strategic and/or fast-paced first-/third-person shooters.
Presentation: Being an engine-port from the 1998's fps-ambassador, the source-version brought a set of graphical and minor gameplay-enhancements, such as improved lighting, better water-textures and ragdol physics.
Other than that it's just a heap of dumb fun.

I have played Borderlands enough that I have become intimately familiar wih its various strengths and weaknesses as as series, and Pre-Sequel as a lot of both. An interquel that reuses the engine and assets of Borderlands 2, Pre-Sequel nonetheless manages to reinvent the series tried-and-true, shoot, loot, rinse and repeat gameplay primarily by the introduction of low gravity- moving around on Elpis and the Helios spacestation is infinitely easier then being stuck on Pandora. It brings to mind the low-gravity mutator of Unreal Tournament. Combat additions of cryo-element weapons and lasers are also welcome. I had a lot of fun as Athena the Gladiator, whose elemental tree gives her a hefty punch and whose Aspis denies a huge percentage of incoming damage, giving her incredible durability that the entirety of the Borderlands 2 cast lacked- most egregiously Salvador, who in the course of playing I spent an inordinate amount of time as with my face in the dirt waiting to be revived. I had a chance to sample the other characters, including Doppleganger Jack and Aurelia but most notably Wilhelm the Enforcer, whose autonomous drones are a big help in combat. Since intially writing this review I have also played through the game as Wilhelm and Nisha, and both are notable in the scope of the series for survivability and sheer damage output, respectively. The incredible one-two punch of freezing an enemy and following up with Wilhem's cyber-fist must be experienced to be believed. The game is well-written for what it is, though if you are bothered by an excess of memes and references then it will rub you in much the same uncomfortable way that BL2 did. The combat in pre-sequel, I would say, the most refined in the series, and actually feels reasonably balanced, but the level design leaves much to be desired- the mazelike decks of Helios station in particular left me dazed and vexed, and had I not had my friends to guide me I would surely have needed to look at a guide to find my way around. The moon also has its share of navigational difficulties, with twisting, identical-looking crags and instant-death lava pits, and the vehicle physics are far inferior to that of 2. For the geographically challenged player like myself, Pre-Sequel can be very annoying, but once you can actually find the battle, you'll have a lot of fun. The DLCs, few as they are, are solid- the holodome providing some of the most dynamic arena battles of the franchise, and Claptastic Voyage offering excellent music and asthetics, as well as a very epic final boss and game changing "glitched" guns, as well as being the point where I finally stopped hating Claptrap. Pre-Sequel is a solid continuation for the series and also I think, a good entrypoint to the franchise for newcomers. I'm expecting more improvements in future entries. It's a shame this was 2K Australia's last project, as the team was arguably better at making Borderlands then the series creators.

After the release of Half-Life 2 and then the Orange Box, Valve had already remade and ported Counter-Strike, Half-Life, and Day of Defeat to the Source engine, and also made the unreleased "Team Fortress: Source". These remakes varied in quality, with Counter-Strike getting a full overhaul and Half-Life getting a simple port with barely any changes. It was around this time that Half-Life Deathmatch: Source was released. Like Half-Life: Source, it was a simple port from the GoldSrc engine that introduced very little changes.
In 2013, Valve introduced Steampipe, which would simpify downloading their games and not have them take up as much space. However, the update caused numerous bugs and glitches across all of their games, notably Half-Life: Source and -you guessed it- Half-Life Deathmatch: Source. As of writing, Valve has barely fixed any of these glitches.
Now, where do I begin?
Again, Half-Life Deathmatch: Source suffers from countless bugs and game breaking mechanics. Like Half-LIfe: Source, it shoves so many special effects into assets and maps created in
. The chrome effect that you could see on the revolver in the original Half-Life is slapped onto every weapon and every silver texture in the game. The lighting is okay by itself, but it's ruined by the overpowered bloom. I've seen better bloom in the Cinematic Mod for Half-Life 2! And there is so much more visualwise.
The hitboxes feel weird, and it seems that Valve fixed only the player hitbox so the game is somewhat fair. The MP5 grenade is a one hit kill and you'll bet that me and other players spam these like crazy. Just everything feels like it was stuck into the game, no adjustments, no tweaking,  left the way it is.
Here is the final nail in the coffin for me: sometimes textures don't even show up on the map, and you'll be standing on an
This isn't Valve quality. This is the quality of a fan that just got into Source modding, and released this under Early Access as Pre-Alpha. But this game isn't the scams you'll find sitting under the Greenlight, this is a game released by Valve onto their own platform. And that's pretty disgraceful.
However, at it's core, it's still Half-Life Deathmatch, and it can be fun. So if you own the Orange Box and you're looking for something new, give this a try.
Otherwise, do not buy this game.

Advance notice: there will be spoilers herein.  I'll hold off until I'm safely into "read more" territory.
I've played through normal mode twice now, as Claptrap and Doppelganger Jack.  Having 500+ hours logged on Borderlands 2, I watched TPS for a while to grab it soon as the price dropped.  I grabbed it for about what you'd expect to spend on a decent expansion pack, expecting that it'd play pretty much like a decent expansion pack for Borderlands 2.  And if you want the short version of this review, it pretty much did.  If you liked Borderlands 2 you'll probably like Borderlands the Pre-Sequel because in just about every way that matters it's the same game.  The best comparison I can make for it is to the Captain Scarlett expansion for Borderlands 2, both in good terms and not so good.
Yes, there are some differences.  Aside from ice replacing slag in the elemental table, which is a bit of a tactical shift, they're minor.  Having a whole new class of guns in the Borderlands universe which is already swimming in them really is a lot less noticeable than you would think.  It does seem that lasers are on the overpowered side in Normal mode, and I wouldn't be surprised if that's intentional, but other than that they're not much different than Maliwan sub guns from BL2.  Since Borderlands relies heavily on having a decent gun or couple of guns to make the game hum along, it is kind of nice to expand the field of possibilities a bit.  Oz kits just replace relics and while the gravity slam is nice to have as an option, its usefulness doesn't go far beyond being surrounded by kraggons or torks.  Air supply is not a huge issue (especially if you play Claptrap) and really the main practical use of double jumping is to try to execute some of the annoying jumping puzzles that crept their way into this game.  Really, Gearbox?  Jumping puzzles?
If you're familiar with Borderlands 2, this game leaves you feeling a bit like something's missing that you can't quite put your finger on.  And no, it's not threshers (who only make a cameo here, thankfully).  I thought for a while it was just burnout on the Borderlands universe but after playing some BL2 again the other day the magic is still there.  The translation of the Psychos, Marauders, Nomads, and Goliaths of Pandora to the Scavs and Lunatics of Elpis may have been little more than a skin and voice change, but it lost something in the process that's apparently more important to the ambience than you might think.
Also, the Aussie accents don't make up for the comparatively sparse and not-really-funny things the NPCs say.  Just sayin'.
Mechanically, I have a few minor grumbles.  The vehicles suck.  Seriously.  I never liked the skiff you were given to drive around Oasis with and while the reskin for the Stingray looks pretty badass it's still almost the exact same lemon underneath.  Also, TPS is much too quick with the respawns.  You can run headlong into repops on your way out of moderately small areas after just doing your quest business, not even poking around or exploring over much.  This was an annoyance in the first Borderlands that seemed corrected in BL2 so I hate to see it go backwards.  On a more positive note, side quests tend to appear earlier than they did in BL2.  Instead of finishing the story mission and getting the option to go back to the area you just finished for a milk run, you can see most quest givers on the map as soon as you arrive and can detour to them before you go on with your primary objective, saving yourself a fair bit of backtracking.
I'm neutral on the jump pads.  They walked right up to the line of overusing them in my opinion but didn't quite cross it.
Speaking of crossing lines, possible SPOILERS past this point.
If there's anywhere TPS outright falls down it's in the supporting characters.  BL2 gave us a brilliant cast of background personalities topped off with one of the very best archvillains since Megatron.  In BLTPS, it's hard to pick out any character unique to this game that isn't just...really annoying.  It's possible, but hard.  Our archvillain Colonel Zarpedon is as colorless as she is relentless, far from the constant foil Handsome Jack was in BL2.  And don't get me started on Pickle.  Tiny Tina was genius in BL2, Pickle was an obvious attempt to recreate her that shoulda been strapped to a badonkadonk.
Which leads us to the story in general.  Are we far enough in from the spoiler warning yet?  Ok.  If you liked the story of Borderlands 2 and don't want to see it messed with, then do not play this game.  Of course if you liked BL2 then you're probably way more interested in hanging out some more with Jack than you are in preserving the story, but you've been warned.  The way most of the game plays out, you can start to understand what would drive Jack to go from the hero on Elpis to the way he was on Pandora, then a thing or two happen that almost seem like the writers suddenly remembered they needed Jack to do something bad and/or crazy to get his descent into barking madness back on track.  It really doesn't work, and only results in the game feeling badly written in those spots.  The out-there "here's an evil thing for Jack to do" moments seem like last-minute afterthoughts bolted into the plotline and sticking out awkwardly, and don't keep you from reaching the ultimate conclusion that Jack was right all along, and Lilith is the real bad guy in the Borderlands universe.
Told you not to play if you didn't want the story turned on its head.
So to summarize, as a game, it doesn't measure up to BL2.  In fairness, that's a tough act to follow.  It's still a good game in its own right and viewed as an expansion to BL2 rather than a standalone game it's fantastic.  I know I've been kind of negative here but if you're already familiar with BL2, then telling you it's like an addon for BL2 should cover all the positives.  And if you're not...start with BL2.

You are a mage that can cast spells using the various elements.  The elements can stack together to enhance your spells, and some combinations can be learned to cause special abilities, such as slow time, increase movement speed, revive a fallen teammate, summon a tornado, etc.  You can cast your magicks onto your weapon to give your weapon increased damage, cast in a circle around you to affect all characters nearby, or simply cast in front of you.
Each element has something that will counter it, so not all combinations are possible.  Further, if you try to use one of these when you have an opposites status effect applied (like trying to use lightning when wet), you'll cause damage to yourself!  As an added bonus, all of your spells can also hurt your other party members, so you need to be careful not to kill your friends.
I absolutely enjoyed this game.  The enemies are varied throughout each chapter and each has their own weaknesses you need to discover.  The game keeps you on your toes while allowing you to constantly learn new ways to summon magicks.  The only negative I can say about this game is that it has a terribly steep learning curve.  I played co-op with someone who had played once before and it took me several chapters before I finally understood how all the magicks worked together and could actually contribute effectively to the combat.  I enjoyed these early chapters just as much as the later chapters despite not really knowing what I was doing.
Another negative about this game (that can be completely ignored) is that the gamepad controls are absolutely terrible.  Literally any other control setup would have been better than the set gamepad controls.  I prefer gamepad, but I had to play with keyboard and mouse.

Party Hard is an 80's slasher film turned into a stealth murder simulator. The "Party Hard" name, the neon aesthetic, the mask-wearing slasher with a strange theme to his murders - everything fits so well that you'd almost expect to find this on the shelves of a run-down video rental shop in a dog-eared VHS box with rad over-the-top box art.
The core gameplay is stealth in a top down enviroment. You set off traps such as gumball machine bombs, giant speaker fires, electric dance floors, shark attacks, spooked zeebras, exterminator fumigations and use your quick knife to slash your way through the party. Witnesses will call the cops, who will one shot you in melee range, so run until they say something like "I'm too old for this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and give up. If you hide the bodies (dumpsters, shredding vent fans, throwing them off the roof of the roof party) you may go unnoticed through entire levels. There are unlockable characters, achievements and mayhem all set to a cool dance music soundtrack.
Pros:
+ Top-down Stealth Gameplay is rare and done well here
+ 80's aesthetic
+ Dance music soundtrack sounds great
+ Choice and strategy in clearing levels
+ Unique perspective character
+ Some challenging situations
+ Unlockable characters change the gameplay
Cons:
- Story is barely there
- Cinematics between levels are primitive
- Voice acting isn't top tier
- Short-ish
- Not a lot of depth to mechanics, there are area effect traps and basic melee and that's it
- Experienced a couple freezing NPCs and other bugs requiring level restarts
- Some achievements require tedious, skilless, ridiculous grinding. Such as starting the game 100 times (I used a batch file from the forums to automate it) and dying 100 times (I had only died 20 or so times the entire game).
Party Hard was 100%'ed for this review.

Party Hard is an incredibly mediocre game.
It has a funny, neat idea but is somewhat poorly executed. The stealth system in the game ranges from good to completely random.  I played through and still have no idea why the police would be alerted to me. The basic idea is to kill people who are isolated and then give yourself some distance so that when the bodies are found you are not in the area. This is O'Kay but 50% of the time I will be across the map doing absolutely nothing and they will still pin me as the killer. When this happens you're basically dead because your character moves so slow unless you plan ahead and give yourself distance from the police it's impossible to escape. Basically the way it works is the police chase timer starts off low and then goes up either time they are alerted to you. This leads to a frustrating and slightly boring playthrough. The traps are cool and make things a little more interesting.
Do I recommend it? Not really. TL;DR: Good idea, poor execution.

I did this game, and Witcher 1, this year after purchasing Witcher 3 in a sale. If I was to compare it to the Witcher 1, I would say the first game was the better. But since these games play very differently, it isn't a fair comparison.
The Witcher 2 is chaotic in its story. It is much harder to follow what is really going on compared to Witcher 1 in this regard. Everything is left as a grey area in terms of choice. Only one choice in this game seemed to matter; Roche or Iorveth. Everything else is just filler. Even picking what to happen in crunch moments always seemed like needless choice. Do you kill this person or let them live? What do you gain from killing them, what will happen if they live? Both these questions are answered with 'Nothing much'. Even your end game choices ultimately make you feel as though you're just a passenger watching events unfold, rather than making much impact on them.
The combat isn't much fun. I turned down the difficulty to 'Easy' just so I could enjoy the game, as the 'Normal' difficulty was putting me off playing the game as the combat was far too difficult in some sections. In particular a part in Chapter I when you are stripped of your equipment and have to escape a makeshift prison. My resolution was to craft some bombs in my cell (thankfully they didn't strip me of my Alchemy gear) and throw the bombs at the enemy until they died. Not a fun experience, and one which I reloaded the game 20 times over just to complete. An easy difficulty at this point in the game may have not put me off it so much.
Overall, I will recommend. If only for you to understand some of the story of Witcher 3 going into it. Is it a worthy sequel to Witcher 1, No. Is it required playing for The Witcher 3, yes.

Destiny of Ancient Kingdoms is quite unique compared to some of the other MMO'S I've played over the past few years. Well first of all, I've never played a South African MMO before, and second of all i don't think I've ever played an MMO that allows you to become king of your own kingdom.  I haven't exactly experienced this feature first hand, but i think it would make the way in which the community interacts with one another quite entertaining.
One of the nice things about this game is that there is PVP almost everywhere. I love fighting other players so it's awesome to play a game where you don't have to wait for other players to join arenas or dungeons to experience the PVP.
Another nice aspect of Destiny of Ancient Kingdoms is that the character level progression in the game is not completely dependent on completing quests. There are lots of daily activities that seem to provide enough experience and gold to progress through the game without completing all the boring quests.
One of the other elements of the game that i found to be quite nice was the relaxing soundtrack. I have already spent a few hours just relaxing while mindlessly destroying monsters and completing quests.
Destiny of Ancient Kingdoms is based on a more classic style of MMORPG, so the graphics aren't mindbogglingly beautiful and pristine, but i really don't think that's what the developers had in mind when creating this project. Keep in mind that South Africa is a 3rd world country, so the internet connection and basic hardware that people can afford is quite low compared to the rest of the world. (i should know, i am South African)
One of the things that i wish the developer could have done a little better is the combat system. The classic MMO style game-play is really retro, but it would have been better if the developers made the combat a little more unconventional or unique.
I honestly think that a few people have been unnecessarily harsh when writing reviews about the game. I can guarantee that they haven't really played the game long enough to talk smack about it.
I read a complaint from a player that barely played an hour that said that their auto-potion/auto-fight wasn't quite working. I tested the game's auto-fight function and  i discovered that If you try dragging the required items to the corresponding blocks and tick the correct boxes, then the auto fight function and auto potion features will work perfectly.
There was another complaint that said that there is too much PVP in this game. I would like to ask those people what else did they expect. This is an MMORPG that's based in an ancient time when the world was in a constant state of war between the three kingdoms. If you want to bake cakes or pop bubbles then please do the rest of us battle hardened MMO players a favor and play something a little more lighthearted.
I think that people should do a little bit more background research before making bad reviews. Just because you don't know how something works doesn't mean that the function doesn't work at all. If anybody bothered to read the game data page at data.doak.online then they would probably find the solutions to their problems instead of bashing something that they don't understand.
Overall, i would definitely give this game two thumbs up. Destiny of Ancient Kingdoms is perfect for anyone who has never played an MMO before because the controls are quite simple and experienced MMO players will find that the classic MMO style is quite reminiscent of the MMO's that most people started playing back in the day.
Pros
Free to play
Dynamic PVP system
simple controls
Auto-fight
Auto-navigation
Play to win
Earn free pre-paid points to invite friends
Relaxing soundtrack
Cons
Based on classic style of MMO (outdated graphics)
Minimal character customization
Generic MMO combat system (would have been nice if they were more creative)

I absolutely reccomend Magicite. It is one of the most addicting side-scroller games I've ever played, and it's not limited to mario style obstacle courses. Magicite combines everything we love about Minecraft, Terraria, and side-scrollers like Mario (Don't be fooled, though, Magicite is extremely rogue-like) and puts into one super-fantastic package that will be sure to satisfy those with a thirst for a creative rogue side-scrolling adventure, with a touch of magic, lore, and classic survival. I personally was apprehensive to buying Magicite due to the perma-death and high difficulty of obstacles and monsters, but to be honest, I've truly enjoyed replaying the game over and over and getting better and more skilled, learning the AI of the enemies and adjusting my attack tactics to theirs. In my opinon, this game is a work of art. It truly depicts something beautiful, something I've never seen captured in any game before. It is tough to learn at first, and you will die, but unlike Spelunky, I found it easy to avoid rage-quittting. We've all had the experience of almost slamming the mouse down, getting far more frustrated than we should over the fact that we OBVIOUSLY jumped over the spikes and it's the GAME'S fault. But, in all truth, Magicite has never brought me to that point. You're SUPPOSED to die, SUPPOSED to make mistakes, and Magicite is about learning how to navigate such a vicious and unforgiving enviroment. Part of the reason I like this game is the fact that they don't spend five minutes explaining skills and such. Part of the reason I don't like the game is the same fact. It will be near IMPOSSIBLE to play Magicite without looking up tutorials, and I highly suggest watching YouTube let's plays or some gameplay, because it will show you the basics of the game and help you decide if you want to buy it, or if you've already bought it, how to craft certain items, etc.
So all in all, Magicite deserves, at least in my opinion, much more credit than it currently has. I look forward to updates and news from the developer, I enjoy the controls and ways of crafting in the game, but the game is not perfect. There are plenty of things I could complain about, but that gets hard when you really look at the art that has been presented before you. Magicite is unique, incredible, and is an experience many will love in the gaming community. This is no guarantee you will like it, if you're a casual gamer looking to just have some fun, you may hate it. However, I would like you all to try something different. To play something you've never played before. To be back in that childhood imagination of traversing a dangerous cave in an underground world. This is what makes me love the game the most. It brings me back to those joyful memories, and it can for you, too. This is the game. This is Magicite.

Resource management is the devil. I've believed that for a long time, because it's a ball and chain wrapped around RTSs that basically dictates "he who micromanages faster, wins."
What sets the Total War series apart is that all preparation for battle is done in the turn based stage. If you get caught off-guard or overwhelmed, it's based on your shortcomings as a strategic and tactical player, not who can mine vespene gas faster.
That being said, Medieval II is still probably the strongest out of all the Total War titles. There is a huge pool of traits that give your generals character (whereas Empire had like, what, 10?), very diverse countries and units, and probably the most satisfying of the Total War battlescapes.
Of course, this also comes with the things Total War is notorious for: suicidal AI (i have one province and your army outnumbers mine 20:1, I DECLARE WAR) and backstabbing-for-no-reason AI (I'm going to break the alliance we signed one turn ago).
Still, best in the series. Highly highly recommend.

This review is written in Bahasa. English version is written below.
Magicka adalah game aksi dengan mekanisme sihir elemen yang cukup asyik dengan tampilan gameplay yang mirip DotA. Tugasmu dalam game ini cukup simpel, yaitu hancurkan monster-monster dengan kekuatan sihirmu, kalahkan boss, dan selesaikan setiap stage yang ada. Yang paling menarik dari game ini adalah mekanisme
-nya, di mana kamu dapat menggabung-gabungkan 8 elemen sihir yang ada untuk menciptakan sihir yang kuat sesuai situasi dan selera--simpel sekaligus kompleks. Ditambah mekanisme MP/mana tak terbatas, kamu bisa merasakan menjadi penyihir yang kuat.
Cerita Magicka--yang sedari awal sudah konyol, banyak dibumbui parodi ikon
seperti Star Wars, 300, Castlevania, The Hobbit plus bahasa lucu (English+Swedish+gibberish) sehingga menjadikannya semakin konyol lagi.
Sangat menyenangkan untuk dimainkan sendiri ataupun multiplayer (biar bisa saling bunuh antar teman). Oh ya, ingat-ingatlah mantra sakti 'QFASA' dan kalau suntuk jangan lupa 'dunka dunka'. Happy gaming!
Magicka is an action game with interesting elemental magic mechanism, with gameplay which looks similar to DotA. The objective is fairly simple: defeat your enemies with your mighty magick power, defeat the boss and clear the stage. The most interesting thing about this game is its magic casting mechanism where you can combine the 8 magick elements to produce many kinds of spell best suited to the situation and your personal taste. With unlimited MP/mana, you can truly experience what it feels like to be mighty wizard in fantasy RPG setting (with comedic touch).
The story--which is already funny, is made even funnier with pop culture icon parodies such as Star Wars, 300, Castlevania, The Hobbit, etc. The Simlish-like language (or maybe English+Swedish+Gibberish) is also very funny.
It's a very fun game to play alone or with friends (so you can kill each other 'accidentally'). Also, never forget QFASA and try to do some 'dunka dunka' whenever you get stressed. Happy gaming!

Where to start, where to start...
The insanely intricate magic system that offers a crazy amount of different spell combinations? The quirky humour that is cram-packed with references to popular culture and everything geek? The endearing colourful graphics that turn every second of looking at this game into pure joy? Or maybe the never-ending challenges, be it through several great DLCs or the long list of fun achievements? Because yes, this game, unlike so many, offers achievements that are actually that, real achievements that are either painfully challenging or simply extremely fun to get.
Yet of course, while Magicka offers all that, it only truly unfolds its full potential when played with others. Personally I enjoy co-op most (accidental, yet sometimes not so unintentional, killing of your friends guaranteed thanks to friendly fire), but versus mode as well offers a good deal of entertainment.
There is literally no excuse not to get and enjoy Magicka if you like video games and most certainly a bunch of good laughs.

This game SUUUUCCCKKKSSS. You play on a boring blue grid background where you place uninteresting little squares on a few different possible squares to kill squares and circles that come. No pathing for a TD game. There is very few things a TD game has to do right, and by having uninteresting enemies, bland similar towers, and a boring environment, there isn’t much to keep this interesting. The menu and UI are terrible and don’t seem to have a working or logical main menu. You can’t easily exit the game from the main screen, probably because too many people try to do it after playing this game.  There is no story either. Then there is the terrible tacked on micromanagement aspect which takes away any possible enjoyment. Not only do you have to have to gather resources and use them to build towers, but even THEN they still won’t work. You have to spend each level turning power off certain towers that aren’t in use by clicking and mouse scrolling on them (not a very intuitive control scheme) and then click back on the tower you want to use and mouse wheel scroll up. This means you are constantly going between like 6-10 towers turning power on and off. When it happens they come from both sides, which is often, you then basically are screwed, as you can only have half effectiveness on each, then when they get through to the next towers you have to turn 2 different towers off, then turn the next two on, with the exact right amount of power, which you don’t know what that is and how effective it will be. See how that could be annoying to do continuously. There is no time to build and enjoy, you are just turning power on and off for basically 90% of the game. Management aspect doesn’t work in this TD, and just makes playing a chore. Add that terrible mechanic to the rest of the “meh” game, and you have a “stinker” as DP would say. 3.5/10.

On my list of top ten games I've played, this definitely ranks on number four behind Radiata Stories and Final Fantasy X, and Warcraft 3, which for me is very high praise considering my wde array of games I've played to completion. At first, I thought this game wasn't going to be great, since I had never heard of Yoko Taro nor his works, so this came very much out of the blue for me. I paid it very little attention, and I'll admit, most of that was for 2B's butt, until about a week from launch, when one of my friends got it for the PS4. Out of humor, I watched him play the first portion of the game, and wasn't entirely amazed; it had the look of everything I'd come to hate in games: an overblown romance, very little substance beyond the combat, and an open world.
A few days before launch day, I drunkenly, and probably spurred on by the friend who got it on PS4, got a copy for it. Not really wanting to pay full 60 for it, but having already done so, I planned on doing the two hour demo and just refunding it.
The alarm I set for just under two hours buzzed and I turned it off. I was so enthralled with this game that I don't even remember doing so. Within an hour and fourty five minutes, I was already hooked into this pretty little game. Everything melded together so well - story, combat, art, voice acting (I played English, and the line delivery was fantastic for all characters, save a few specific lines, though the Japanese were their usual quality of fantastic as well,) and the atmosphere. So, I'll cover them in the order I've listed, for simplicity.
Unfortunately, for all the right reasons, I can't go too deep into the story, so let's make this the skim milk of reviews. The story is absolutely fantastic in every respect. It's deeper than what you expect in the first two playthroughs, but shallow enough to not need to go back to the previous games to get into it. It's truly fantastic, especially with some of the late game scenes, which can bring every emotion forward.
Oh, yeah, I almost forgot.
That was important because I almost put it down after the second, but decided on continuing. Moving on,
2B, A2, and 9S, all the characters you play, have very distinct fighting styles. 2B and A2 share the same moveset, but they differ in how quick they are. 2B is agile in every way, able to strike quicker, and A2 is weightier and feel far more impactful (I have been told this is complete false, but to me the two seem entirely different while sharing the same moveset. So bugger off.)
9S, though, has a unique combat style. While lacking in a heavy attack like A2 and 2B, he has hacking, which is borderline overpowered and, overall for me, out of place in how well it works. It takes you to a top down bullet-hell twin stick where the objective is to shoot the enemy's ball(s). If you fail, you lose maybe 10% of your health (Never tested this in the hardest difficulty to see if it kills you,) while if you win, you deal AT LEAST 25% of the enemy's health.
The difficulties range from Easy (game literally plays itself), normal (fairly easy,) hard (more of a normal difficulty than Normal,) and the hair pulling out one shot mode. I personally recommend it on Hard after you realize what your playstyle is. Also, a minor nitpick is that I wish there were more varied enemies outside of bossfights. You see the same 10 or so types everywhere, and it gets dull after a while when you learn their percise behavior.
This game is bloody beautiful. It takes the whole idea of "what if Humans got driven from Earth for a few thousand years, yet somehow the buildings still stand?" to a new level. The city you're in is never specified, it's simply City Ruins, though it is within the northern hemisphere and, I personally think Greenland based on a cutscene. But you'd never know it, because the four biomes - City Ruins, Forest, Desert and Underground are all within spiting distance of eachother.
The weapons in this game are weaponporn. Pure and simple. If you like the old gritty weapons, they got that for you. Beautiful weabo swords? They got that too. Want sexy kawai girls? We got that apleanty. Want a cute little femboy? We got one of those in stock yesterday!
Put simply, this game never got to be a sore on the eyes, since each place was so drastically different from the last that, even after almost 50 hours, nothing ever looked more than familiar, and if you look in all the nooks and crannies, it gets even better, since there's some gorgeous views hidden away.
Always a most controversial topic among nerds is to dub or sub. Well, I can say that for me, and a lot of others, the English dub is spot on in -almost- every situation. There are a few lines that are very much out there, and some where the VAs were obviously not having a good day, since the tone convayed was a bit... Diluted. But to be fair, for every bad line, it had at least two or more good to great ones to make up for it. 9S, especially near the end of the game, portrays a lot of that.
This game is about androids on a world familiar to us without us. You will explore it with the eyes of someone who knows it, while behind the eyes of someone who doesn't entirely. It feels lonely. It feels dark. But it has light moments as well, and the occasional comic relief.
The atmosphere of living where people once did, without seeing any signs of violence not left in the current year, is deeply disturbing at some points. The machines also make this point far more abundant. In Yoko Taro's style, it's truly unsettlingly creepy on some of its basest levels, and it's that that brings the whole game together for the better.

I'm not much for tower defense games, but one made by the creator of Hexcells, with a pretty interesting visual style? Yeah, might as well check it out.
And it's neat. It hasn't convinced me to check out more tower defense games and I don't have the motivation to 100% it, but I did enjoy it. The game's fairly unique in the genre from what I can tell, you have to manage power on towers and they fire to the beat of the music, left to right. It's a lot to manage but never too much. I never failed a normal node, but perfecting them is another thing entirely. And that's the true goal of the game; perfection. Preventing even a single virus from slipping through the cracks. At first, a lot of these seemed tough, but the more you play the game, the more you learn how to deal with things. I got enough perfects to at least beat the game, though I'm not really driven to go for 100% perfection, but that's more because the genre isn't my favorite, no real fault of the game. I think that if you don't learn as you play this game, you'll get stuck and it'll be too hard, yeah, and that's where the negative reviews come from. It's better than people are giving it credit for, but maybe that's because I came into this with no expectations.
The music isn't that great by itself but the sequencer-like aspect of the towers does make it enjoyable and evolving. I still quite like the visual style, even if it's pretty simple. And the framing device of fighting viruses in a computer system is pretty neat as well. Not my favorite game ever or anything but I'm glad I played it, though I wouldn't want to play it more than I already have.

I got this game gifted to me by a generous friend, and was very excited to try it because of the music, artstyle, and effects. I was extremely pleased with my experience.
If you like tower-defence games, managing multiple tasks rapidly (this is very, very important), electronic music, and fancy effects, then you will really like this game.
The aesthetics are very nice - the colors and backgrounds are alive with vivid color. The music is one of the most important elements in this game, and the tracklist is composed of very good electronic music. I strongly suggest you take a look at the trailer provided to get a feel for the music, or even search for the soundtrack on YouTube - the genre may not be to your liking. That being said, I absolutely love electronic dance music (EDM) and most subgenres related to it, so be aware of my personal bias in this regard. Note, the tracklist is more groovy, chillout electronic than the intense type typically played in clubs and on the radio - so don't expect buildups and drops.
I found the music to be wonderfully fit for creating a fun atmosphere despite that many times contrasts with how much task-switching you have to do during gameplay. As the beat progresses, a light flashes left-to-right across the level/background. If you have activated turrets, they will flash when the light passes over it, and the more turrets you have activated, the deeper/fuller/louder the music sounds. You will notice that the music will dull down whenever you have no powered turrets. The dynamic music (interacting with your turret placement) is done very well and has no effect on gameplay besides aesthetics.
The controls are simple - everything is done with the mouse - however, managing your actions/tasks is the most difficult part of the game. There is a very quick and helpful tutorial that begins right you start a new game, and the opening sequence is great. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your familiarity with tower-defence games, but be warned - the game involves a lot of task-switching, so quick reflexes are essential if you want to avoid getting overwhelmed.
Gameplay involves you defending your core against waves of enemy viruses coming from different paths (numbered 1-x). There is a tracker that shows you what creeps are incoming, however, there is no real way of knowing what each virus does until you encounter them (no tooltips, no virus encyclopaedia, etc) and see for yourself. There are a variety of towers to use, each with different strengths. For example, there is a quick-firing beam that removes enemy shields, a slowing program, and an anti-worm (these are yellow non-circular viruses) program. Whenever you place a program there is a cooldown timer before you can place that specific program again. To counter this, a (quite expensive) cooldown reset ability can be purchased (refreshes all towers; must be bought each time you want to use it). There is also a free "manual aim" tower that can be placed, and I strongly suggest you place these whenever they are available to maximize your combat potential. To use the "manual aim" programs, you must click on them, then click and hold anywhere within their attack area. After a certain number of attacks (indicated by a bar underneath the tower), the program will disappear.
As you play, resource pickups will periodically drop from the top of the screen to a random part of the level - you need to click these to obtain the resources. Enemies will also sometimes drop smaller pickups, which are used to either upgrade your programs (up to a level of 2) or buy special items from your core. For example, you can buy a mine for 1 upgrade point, which allows you to place one-shot proximity mines; for 2 upgrade points, you can unlock a power generator program that supplies you with one power.
You start each level with a set number of power points needed to activate your programs. Whenever you build a new program/tower, it comes powered with 1 bar. You can use the mouse wheel to divert power to and away from your programs, and this is something that gets crazy as you progress deeper into the game. For example, you may have one tower with max power near the beginning of an enemy path, but once the creeps all make it past your program, you quickly cycle all the power out of that tower and divert it to your other programs further down the pathway. You must make these decisions in real-time, and it can get chaotic when a large amount of enemies are bearing down on your core.
There are gated checkpoints in the game that require you to beat a certain number of levels before you can proceed further. There is an icon given to you whenever you complete a level, as well as a second icon for achieving 100% (no damage to your core). I love tower-defence games and play a lot of them, so I give you all a warning: this is one of the most infuriating games to try to 100% (not necessarily a bad thing). It just takes one creep making it past you to ruin your run. Worse so are the bonus levels.
Aside from the main levels are bonus levels - which are scenarios that require you to use certain strategies. For example, one bonus level that took me ages involves you using the "manual aim" towers to soften up waves of enemies so your towers can finish them off. The catch? You have to make sure you attack each enemy the correct amount because you are given no resources to build more towers. There is another bonus level that taught me how to take advantage of programs and power (sometimes it is better to just buy a cheap program to get the extra power point) - you start off only able to build power stations, and the only available spots are at the bottom of the screen. To beat this stage, you must
Overall, the game is a great staple of the genre, and anyone interested in electronic music, TD games, and being challenged should definitely give this a try.
Highly recommend!

As far as Tower Defense games go,
is a work of art. It combines some of the best and simplistic elements and crafts them together to form one excellent and strategic game that is very fun to play in bursts.
has the basic Tower Defense gameplay, defending against hordes of oncoming enemies (or "Viruses" in this case) each with different strengths and weaknesses. It's main feature that gives it it's individuality aside from it's futuristic digital theme is probably the power consumption mechanic. Without any units of power, your defenses can't function. For each defensive object ("Towers" or "Anti-Viruses" or whatever you want to call them) you have deployed on the grid, you are supplied with one additional unit of power on top of the amount you are provided with by default (this varies from level to level), each defense can use up to 5 units of power, 1 being the minimum amount required to be funcitonal, 2 units through to 5 units supplies the defense with a strength and / or range boost. It sounds a little bit complicated, but it's very easy to learn after a few minutes of play.
Managing power in
can be very difficult and requires a lot of micro-managing, particularly because more often than not you'll need to sacrifice one of your operational defenses in order to activate another one on the other side of the grid. This game actually requires you to think rather than blindly placing defenses all over the place, especially in the bonus levels, just another thing that makes
great.
One of the other things pushes the right buttons for me is the theme and art-style in
, as you can tell from the screenshots and trailer it has cyber and futuristic features which is already a selling point to me, but on top of that it also includes some rthym elements, meaning that the background music ties in well with the gameplay. Already a definite must-have for my collection.
It's simple and minimalistic menu interface and level selection themes are also really well made, the game is just very easy on the eyes and pleasant to look at.
The interface is very simple and user friendly, thus easy to understand and can be picked-up very quickly, things like the radar will be crucial to your efforts when you begin playing and have learned the strengths and weakneses of each enemy.
The game is however not without some flaws, it has a "Gate" system which requires you to complete levels to acquire credits (at least, that's what I call them) in order to pass through to the next stages, while I don't have a problem with this mechanic, it will likely feel grindy and tedious after a while as the basic level completion credits are not enough to pass through all of the gates, you have to acquire more credits by defeating those levels again without the core taking any damage at all from incoming enemies, much easier said than done on a number of levels. This isn't a problem for those of you that like a challenge, but it can slow down progressing through the game a fair bit as all it takes is one virus to slip through to the core to force you to restart the level once again.
So all in all, considering the fact that this is a game that I acquired in a cheap bundle, it's a bloody good one. If you're into Tower Defense or Strategy games, add this one to your collection, it's a very affordable and fun game to play for when you're in that "I have nothing to play" mood. Honestly, I just wish there were some more levels to play as for me it ended too soon.

That was fun. 115 hours of it in fact. I'm not sure all of it was the same amount of fun, but I was only starting to get bored by the very, very end. I played as Venice and after playing Rome 2 - I found the user interface and some of the peripheral spy/merchant/assassin/RPGish character progression type stuff, and also diplomacy, was a bit less polished than Rome 2, but the actual balance during battles is much better. The main problem with the battles is that they have to be pretty evenly matched for them to be fun - and that happens quite rarely since victory is really determined on the grand-strategic map based on how many units you built before the battle. I felt sieges (as opposed to actual assaults) weren't very well implemented, which is a shame since that's what half the game consists of - starving the enemy out takes too long and is rendered pointless by artillery that is too good against gates and useless against units. The obligatory medieval cow-launcher is pointless and by the time you get it you can probably have cannons instead. City development is also too slow and it's a pain micro-managing which cities can replenish casualties in your units.
During a "long campaign", you'll probably get about five or six really interesting battles - the ones where two huge lines of infantry crash into each other and you manage to flank them with cavalry and cause a rout, and it ends up with a nail-biting finish as five or six exhausted survivors from each army are left in the middle of a pile of lifeless armoured bodies trying to finish each other off - or where you ambush an enemy king without his army and he's trying to run off the edge of the map with two surviving bodyguards with your cavalry in pursuit. Artillery is fun too - it might only land a successful hit once in a battle, but there's few things in gaming that feel as good as blowing up the enemy general and half his guards with a jammy cannonball before they have even started marching.

Deus Ex may have aged well in some parts and not-so-well in others over the years, but it still makes a big impression. It takes elements of role-playing, action, adventure, and intense decision-making, then mixes them all together in a concoction that goes down just right. Deus Ex has paved the way in its specific genre for other games of its nature to take cues from it, and for good reason. Deus Ex isn't without its charming little flaws, but in spite of them, it achieves at remaining one of the funnest games I've played in a long time.
1) The role-playing. I'm a big role-playing geek, so this usually wins out on games for me that include it. There are some situations where you have to make some plot-altering choices, something that a fan of BioWare RPGs can attest to enjoying. While this isn't a game crafted by BioWare, and its depth of choice doesn't reflect that of RPGs similar to it, it does allow you to see a few different outcomes to choices you make. Based on what you do, you could either get a major character killed, or save them just in time. You can choose to oppose someone you know, or agree with them, and suffer consequences either way. I always approve of any RPG that shows you that your actions and decisions resulted in something, and that they do matter. It's important not only for immersion, but to really feel like you're in the game; that you belong to its story.
2) That music. Not only does it fit in with the dystopian setting of the game, it can at times be hauntingly gorgeous. Each section of the game has its own sound track, and I loved every one of them. Some have an upbeat techno tune, and others have a slow and languid synth tempo, and both kinds just rock. Its quality may reek of the early 2000s, but I can forgive this, because the songs somehow make me dance in my seat.
3) The option between stealth and guns a-blazing. While at the start, you're pretty squishy and will go down faster than a sack of bricks, you can eventually aug yourself to perfection to handle close-range fighting. You can also choose stealth and hiding options, and it is possible to go through an entire level without fighting a single enemy. I picked stealth. More suspenseful.
4) The weapon upgrading and modding. There are a ton of weapons in this game. More than I can count, honestly. I just always used a sniper rifle, because that was the funnest for me. You can increase clip size, range, give a gun a scope, etc. By the time I ended the game, my sniper rifle was ridiculously powerful. I killed mechs with it. It took a while... but I did it.
5) Augmentations. Augments improve certain aspects of slots on JC's body, such as the cranium or torso, and each augment gains you a certain trait, such as health regeneration, cloaking, and increase in accuracy. There were a bunch to choose from,
6) The characters. Even the corny ones, I learned to love right away. I especially loved JC's brother, Paul. And of course, JC himself.
7) The storytelling. While the plot confused the hell out of me (and I'll get to that later), there were times where I felt genuinely scared for the characters involved in the story. There was a point where I reloaded a game a few hours back to fix a mistake I made with a character that I was heartbroken about afterward. I actually said out loud once, &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥just got real in this game!" The plot had ways of giving you little surprises, and it was a lot of fun to discover them.
8) The fact that you never see daylight. I have no idea if this is because of JC's uber-eyes, or because the scenery is filtered through his sunglasses at all times, or that this future takes place in a time when the sun has burned out, but it is always nighttime...
. And I
. Needless to say, it was odd, but I love darkness, so it sat well with me.
9) The action. The enemy AI is kind of braindead at times, but when action starts, it's pretty exciting. There were times I had ten guys chasing me down a staircase while I frantically looked for a vent to hide in, squealing all the way down. Then I'd pop them off one by one while they strolled away, and they'd come back looking for me, screaming "what the hell?!" Hilarious fun.
10) The computers you had to log into. I don't know why I liked this. I just did. I almost never used the password. I just hacked them because it made me feel cool-- like some kind of hacker extraordinaire. Especially when I cracked into ATMs.
11) JC is a fun and lovable protagonist. You feel like a bit of a badass when playing him.
12) Shooting down pigeons in mid-flight.
Gotcha, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
13) The choice between "lethal" and "non-lethal" takedowns. This is especially nice for people who love morality role-playing, and love to play as a non-lethal character who doesn't murder anyone. You can either tranq people or shoot 'em dead. It's your choice. Tranq darts are pretty hard to come by, though. That's the main drawback.
1) The voice acting. My ears especially bled at those horrible fake Asian accents, mostly because I couldn't tell whether or not they were real or just some Western people pretending to be Asian. I don't know if that makes me a racist... but damn, it was funny to hear. JC's voice was just ridiculous. I love him all the same, but he should really clear his throat, or maybe suck on a lozenge.
2) The graphics. Even for as early as 2000, there were games out there that looked better than this. Look at Silent Hill 2. That came out a year later (on the PS2), and it was beautiful. The facial animations can sometimes make you squirm with how ugly they can be at times. This flaw can be mended with a few mods that have become available to improve the textures. It's not a huge leap in quality, but it's definitely cleaner and crisper. If you plan to play this game,
3) How stupid the NPCs can be. This works kind of as a "liked" part of the game, too, because it always made me bust out laughing. If you shoot an enemy close to a non-hostile NPC, that friendly NPC will suddenly go sprinting around in a panicked circle, or sometimes back and forth in one straight line. They will do this for several minutes, regardless of how close you're standing to them. It's great for a laugh, but pretty damn silly.
4) Wasting tools and lockpicks on empty rooms or pointless alarms. Ugh.
5) The plot confused me. This could be my fault, because I would take like, five month breaks between playing through the game, so I'd always feel like I was missing something. I got the basic gist of it when the end rolled around, but I remember scratching my head a lot throughout the whole thing.
There is no "biggest disappointment" for me. So I'll conclude with this: If you like role-playing, action, decision-making, science-fiction and big, confusing missions that go on forever, this game is perfect for you. It inspired many other games just like it, and it's a great place to get started in the sci-fi game genre.

Hexcells is a puzzle game that feels like a sort of combination between minesweeper and picross.  Puzzles are pre-made, can all be solved without guessing and combine the hint systems of minesweeper and picross, along with the hexagon twist.  The concept works very well and I found the game quite enjoyable, but it is unfortunately quite short.  There are 6 groups of puzzles, 30 in total, that gradually introduce new concepts and become more difficult.  I was able to finish all of them without any mistakes in just over an hour, though I'm generally faster than most with these type of games.
It's a fun puzzle game and you can't really go wrong with the price.  I've been told Hexcells Plus is much more difficult so it should be a great continuation for those who can solve these puzzles quickly.

After the heady heights of Borderlands 2, this was very disappointing. Pretty to look at, and the zero gravity is fun, but there's a lot which felt wrong.
The change in studio is both obvious and jarring - the humour prevalent throughout the first two games is sadly lacking in Presequel. It feels like there is a great deal of filler content - a lot of fetch quests and needless running from A to B. The rate and order at which you acquire quests also necessitates a great deal of going back and forth to old zones you have already cleared. Very irritating.
Some annoying bugs - perma-slowed if a teammate hits you with a cryo rocket from a vehicle, some completely random CTD, numerous invisible walls leading to insta-death and plenty of places for you to get stuck in the geometry.
On the plus side, the final boss is actually probably the strongest in the series so far, so that is a plus. And there were some cool moments that related to the earlier games. But it is a shame that this does not come near to touching BL2.

Fifteen years and some forty save files later I'm STILL finding new things almost every time I open this game. It's amazing that Deus Ex managed to pack enough worthwhile content to make every playthrough feel unique, and not just in the game's scenarios themselves, but how you handle them. Every single weapon and aug has potential to do great things depending on how you build your character, with the exception of extremely situational, one use items like the P2000, or gimmicky augs like the Spybot.
Deus Ex is a game that's hard to compare to others, because of how neatly the package is tied together. It's the way the atmospheric elements like music or even something as simple as lighting combine with the meandering you'll end up doing in the game's hub-worlds, and the hubs are where Deus Ex becomes a completely different expirience. Sure it's fun to play one of the good ol' linear levels with fairly straightforward objectives, but the sprawling, open areas are where the game goes from an explosive action flick to a gritty neo-noir with hours worth of sidequests and aimless exploring. For me, this is what makes Deus Ex so great. It plays off of the best characteristics or all the pieces that put it together.
The soundtrack can easily switch from a fast-paced electronic beat to a faint ambiance to fit each level specifically. which perfectly coincides with combat. In one level you'll be mowing down every NSF soldier you see with a Sawed-Off, and the next you'll be methodically weaving between buildings, hiding from cameras and deciding to silently take down that group of enemies or avoid them all together. The game reinforces this shift between styles with the limited amount of items you can find. Instead of holding you back from entering an area in the game meant for later, it'll slightly nudge you away by guarding it with really tough enemies, or locking the door with a numpad that takes 4 tools to open. It's the small elements that were taken account with the level design in mind, especially with the hubs that elevate the game so much.
While the story starts to sound like the focus group were a bunch of tinfoil-hatted conspiracy theorists, it's all explained so well and in great detail that makes it seem more "realistic". There's constantly data being thrown at you that it can be hard to absorb, but it creates a scale that really isn't realized until you pay more attention to it. Reading datacubes on tables or emails on a computer will give more insight into what's going on around you, and more importantly the people involved. Characters you liked early on might become more despicable, or vice-versa depending on how much you know about them from those optional little bits of character development that are placed throughout the game.
Hell, this review is just another paper thrown into a file cabinet, but it's more of a personal love letter to the expirience I've had with Deus Ex over the course of my life. It seems every 3 or so years after I haven't played it in a while I'll reinstall it and sink another 50 hours into, and those little things I find that I didn't notice when I was a kid 10 years ago will put a huge smile on my face. It's by no means a perfect game, and it's not the first game to mix different genres in a very similar way (see System Shock), but it's a game that has to be expirienced first hand to know just how great it is.

Before I continue, I should mention that I first played this game after having finished Human Revolution.  So, with that out of the way... this is it.  This is the game that started the series.  The graphics are terrible by today's standards, and the skill system could use a little more polish.  These are minor flaws in what is otherwise a game that can still give every other Deus Ex game a run for its money.  For its time, this game was flawlessly executed, and it's still a blast to play if you can get past the graphics.  There are so many different ways to play, so many different reactions in the game that change based on how you choose to act or how well you perform, that playing again can feel completely new.  If you built pure stealth one run, you can build pure heavy weapons the next run and have a whole new experience.  This game hits all the right notes, even today, and you haven't truly experienced the Deus Ex universe until you've played it.

My hours in this game say all that need to be said in all honesty. Buy it. I never review games, this one won me over in every possible way.
Epic, astounding, beautiful and easily game of the year - though for me, game of all time. Formerly that title went to Final Fantasy 7 for both being a childhood favorite and astounding game in itself; but this one swiped that impossible to claim title without question after the 16 hour mark turned into the 20+ hour mark turned into the 30+ hour mark turned into the-----
It just never ends. I started out on Hard difficulty and replayed the first tutorial mission at LEAST seven times in sheer frustration, it was the peak of dark souls-esk evil whereas normal would have been your more accessable challenge, and Easy mode for those who simply want to dive into the story so there is literally potential for anyone to enjoy this.
But upon the victory of that tutorial mission on Hard, I kept trudging through growing stronger, facing ever tougher enemies and failing, even going so far as to fail in succession and lose all of my plug-in chips (upgrades) more than once, but accepting my failures and breaking past them time and again to see what came next without lowering the difficulty. Now, after -- I believe 45 hours I finally have completed 5 total 'Endings' + over 80% of the sidequests, found about the same % of enemies and a ton of secret locations and such---
Only to start a brand spanking new game+ with so many questions I intend to snuff out as my level 65 and right out the gate I discovered something I missed in the tutorial area ... in my countless times there I simply never thought of it! But instead of further mindless rambling, let me simply say: when the credits roll, always continue onto the 'new game+' and be astounded by what you witness, time and time again. Me? I'll probably be turning up the setting to Very Hard and suffer, so much, for my curiosity on this new run through. But.. first I need to get in touch with those.. Sentinel is a tower defense game with a musical twist. Being a great fan of rhythm games, I was excited to discover it, and found the experience rather pleasant.
This is my first tower defense game. It is not quite challenging, with most levels easy to pass on a few tries. Each level has a distinct feature of some sort, which is often reflected in the name (look for hints!). The bonus levels play on a single idea and are fun to pass. The game encourages you to complete the levels without losses for extra points, which are required to unlock further stages.
As for the music, it contributes rather nicely to the overall experience. It does not affect the mechanics except on a few occasions, but it does add a pleasant sense of flow that is also backed with the visuals. The enemies appear and the towers fire in beat, and each event has its distinct sound. On earlier stages I played around with tower positions to create different musical patterns, but later in the game I had to concentrate mostly on beating the levels.
All in all, Sentinel is a very enjoyable experience. I would place it somewhere between a game and a piece of visual art. If you appreciate rhythm as a part of gameplay, definitely give it a try.

Destiny of Ancient Kingdoms is a F2P MMO from South Africa.
It plays and feels very much like one of these many, many F2P-chinese MMOs. Everything a "bad" chinese MMO would have is there:
- bad translation in many places, generic and bad-looking graphics (that still look quite nice at times - the aesthetic is there, but the textures...not that great)
-old and clunky hotbar-combat
-typical Cash Shop
You create a character from 6 generic classes and very limited customization and then get dropped into the world, doing generic quests and killing generic monsters with generic skills.
It is nothing special, but something with a nice soundtrack that you can spend a few relaxing hours in, mindlessly clubbing monsters and completing quests. After playing it for a few hours however and completing the first dungeon, I decided to change my positive to a negative review. The reason for that - there is no staying power in the game. When you played the first 20 levels, you played the entire game - kill monsters, rinse, repeat. There are far better MMOs out there that do what this game does far better. Still, it can't hurt to try it out - the developers are nice and active and there is some odd charm found in the game. You won't be playing it for long though.

The audio component is unique, and why I initially bought the game, but serves little purpose once the novelty wears off and becomes a bit annoying quickly. Beyond that it's a basic tower defense game, which I like, but an extremely basic one. Normally I'd give it points for that, sometimes you just want a simple game to kill time with, but overall I'd say this game is not that game.

This is every review for this game says but imagine Minesweeper but FUN instead of frustrating.
Between the Soundtrack, the clean minimalistic look, the more forgiving mechanics and the more interesting puzzles this really is the casual 5 minute brain-scratcher you'd fire up without a second thought.
Each puzzle is hand-made (for lack of a better word) and comes with a guarantee that you can solve it logically, start to finish, no guessing or blowing up when trying to uncover the field required (And seriously, don't ever guess, you're shooting yourself in the foot).
The addition of adding column-information as well as the regular tiles, later in the game, adds loads of new possibilities and requires a new way of thinking, reminiscent of solving a Sudoku puzzle.
The only downside of these puzzles is, that because they're hand-made, they're not infinitely generated, but instead treated as 29 levels in 6 "worlds" giving this limited replayability.
Depending on how long each puzzle takes you, you'll get a couple of hours of gameplay out of this, maybe a few more if you want to go for perfect to correct mis-clicks and mistakes. You can replay the levels of course, but I'm not sure how long it'll take you before you can solve the puzzles by memory rather than by logic.
Because of this, I'd recommend buying this with Hexcells Plus included, which will give you an additional 36 puzzles.
