NieR:Automata is one of the best games I got to experience. This is one of the few games that has a story with a powerful meaning, a story I won't forget. Each playthrough reveals more to the vague plot and shows more about the protagonists. The game was able to make me care about the characters which really made the story. I never experienced an ending to a story like this, it's something that can only be experienced for oneself as I can't explain it. Who knew dodging and shooting balls during the credit scene could be emotional.
Pros:
- A story that will never be forgotten.
- Combat never gets old. A good player is able to do amazing things (perfect dodges, counter attacking, pod skills, using weapon sets to the fullest) all in perfect motion.
- The soundtrack is amazing, it really sets the mood during the game.
- Likeable characters, I cared about what would happen to them.
- Plug-in chips allow for various playstyles.
- Each weapon has its own story that can tell a lot.
- Small details to fully understand the story and meaning.
- I was able to play on max with 50-60 fps with an i5-4690 and gtx 1060, never crashed.
Cons:
- Graphics aren't the best for today's standards. It really wasn't the selling point to begin with, but some people do care about it.
- At one point of the game, the map had to load in every now and then.
- Left me thinking about life.
NieR:Automata is one of those special games that comes out once in awhile. The story itself was worth it and everything else just makes it all that better. Get this game if possible, it should be experienced not watched.

I have mixed feelings about Sentinel...
As a TD game, you have to micromanage a lot of little things very quickly and keep checking the upcoming waves to know how to deal with each one properly, however, unlike most TD games, the strategy doesn't come from placement or upgrading, but rather energy. In Sentinel, you have a set amount of energy (and adding a tower to the field increases that amount by 1) which you can divide among your towers, to a max of 5 energy at any one tower. You can later reduce energy in one tower to give it to another, to focus your attack on a different lane. This is the main mechanic of the game and takes serious micromanagement skills. During each round, random extra money might fall from the top of the screen for you to collect, and dead enemies might drop special icons that allow you to upgrade or buy different towers, and while the game itself isn't terribly fast-paced, all of this happening at once makes for a real challenge keeping up with it all.
Outside of the TD, there's a stage-select map, which I actually quite like, apart from the gates you have to "hack". Every so often you'll come to a locked node that you can't get past without spending a certain number of "credits". Each stage gives you 1 credit for completion and 1 for getting through it perfectly (and bonus stages give just 1, since you have to do it perfectly or fail). As you get to the later gates, you realize very quickly that you'll have to go back to some levels and get a perfect on them if you want to continue. I find this a little frustrating, as in my (admittedly limited) experience with TD games, I've never had to do a round perfectly to move on to the next.
That's about all the bad I can think of for this game, though, and there's plenty of good to mention. First and foremost, it's just fun! The music suits the game very well, going from calm and relaxed to active and upbeat as you change stages, and it's always very unintrusive, letting you focus on the gameplay. Although it does take skill to use properly, I like the energy mechanic as an idea, being able to focus more on one part of the field at first, then spread out your power later, or turn off a useless tower that round to make a more needed tower a bit stronger.
The bonus stages really make you think about every little detail of the game, from which towers to place where, when to have them on or off, how much energy they need, when to sell them, when maxing out their strength isn't a good idea... the list goes on and on, and each one is very cleverly constructed to make you aware of some aspect you may not have known before, making it a very cool way to teach the player without sitting through a tutorial. One example that really jumps out at me is a bonus stage near the beginning, where you have to collect the early enemy drops to upgrade your towers, and then sell them because the upgraded ones are worth more, and that gives you the money to set enough mines to take out the remaining enemies which can't be destroyed by the towers. If you do it perfectly, you will end up with zero money, so there is no room for error, and you definitely have to know what you're doing to get the job done.
For me, $3 is absolutely a bargain. I'm getting a fresh twist on a cool genre, and I'm learning to think in terms of what makes the most effective strategy, not just which gun does the most damage. So far I've played a little less than 3 hours, and I'm maybe halfway through all of the levels, which means I can expect another 4-5 (after going back to do everything perfectly) for my money, which is considerably more fun per dollar than, say, going to see a two hour movie for $10.
It's not perfect, and it's really frustrating sometimes, but it's enjoyable unique, and that's what I look for in a game. For the price, I have to say yes, I do recommend this game.

The Witcher 2 is horrible. Not just horrible but fkn horrible. Aside from graphics and story, NOTHING in this game is good at all.
The inventory is awful. The interface of this game is designed by idiots. Very clunky, slow, and no clarity. The highlight is indistinguishable. When you select something, the text of the item you select is just a little larger than the rest when you highlight. The cursor is slow to move. Worse, if you press a certain key, another slot light up very clearly, as if you were selecting it. Isn’t it supposed to light up the thing you select? Even at 30 hours in, you can still make mistakes when you trade or drop items. All because the lit up part of the menu is NOT what you select. You end up selling or dropping unique, obtainable-only-once items. The radial menu in this game is not a radial menu. It’s just a menu. Most radial menus in other games require you to tilt only the analogue stick towards the desired direction and the item/magic is select. In this game, you have to tilt it up, or left, or right, or down to select a category. Once you get inside the category, you tilt up or down again to move the cursor up or down to select the item. Imagine doing that in real-time battle. What’s the point of making the damn thing radial menu?
The map is stupid, especially the maps of the cities. It doesn’t show paths but cartoonish drawing of the area. There are arches, bridges, ridges, and lines. The buildings are almost artistic, but none of them useful. Many of those don’t correspond with the accessible paths that you can walk. Unreliable in dungeons and in the wilds. You have to guess and remember the paths.
The game has low spawn rate. Enemies give little experience. You cannot level up fast. The only solid way to level up is doing missions, and even when you do all of them, you’re still seriously under-leveled.
The main character’s ability at the beginning is awful. The awesome Geralt of Rivia has to spend the majority of the game trying to get from♥♥♥♥♥♥to useable. The basic, unaltered character can’t even freaking block.
The controls are unresponsive. While it is an improvement over the first game, it does not do what it is meant to do. If you play keyboard, there are over 10 keys to remember. In the heat of the fight, which is terribly difficult even on normal, lifting your fingers from directional keys to press something else far away is a death sentence. That is, if you remember them at all. You want to change weapons? The game will not respond unless you stand still or running. You stand up almost straight and you want to switch? Nope. The game ignores you. You have 0.001s of casting animation left? Nope. Screw you. In a fight, sometimes you need to try 3-4 times before you can change ONCE. If the animation is interrupted, it is cancelled. The animation lasts 2-3 seconds in a fight with a boss that can kill you in 3 hits in 3 seconds.
The bosses are horrific. Cheap as trash. This is not Doom or Dark Souls or Monster Hunter where your always know it’s your mistake if you get killed. This game is random, and odds are stacked against you in every way. You dodge everything; you land every hit; but whether the enemies take damage is randomized. To win doesn’t require skills. Just luck against numbers. The battle areas are confined, but bosses have large AOE that takes away half of your life and covers almost a half of the area, ON NORMAL. One optional boss has three enemies crammed into one tiny room. Two of them can close the gap towards you in five steps and kills you in three hits. The boss itself shoots projectiles that take down a third, maybe even a half of your life. Oh, and Geralt of Rivia cannot walk over a fkn brick. He has as to go around it. A gargoyle can corner you between two bricks. The actual fight takes only about 3 minutes. The total number of retries take over 6 hours. You lose not because you screw up. You always feel “the game cheat me” sort of loss.
Some might say it is challenging. As a fan of difficult games, I strongly disagree. This game is not challenging. It is cheap, sort of the-game-cheat-me trash cheap, not difficult. The difficulty is the culmination of collective horrible designs.
Save your mental health and ignore this game. Watch people play on YouTube if you want the story.

An interesting take on the standard Tower Defense game. Your defense goes by the beat of the music, and the music changes according to your defenses, and how much power you divert between defenses. Very interesting and fun concept.
For example, you don't really have any music playing without defense, or power running through it, but depending on the defense tower set, and how much power you have, the more interesting the music picks up. Keep in tune and in beat with the music to optimize your defenses. A good musical ear helps with planning (make good music) and timing your attacks/defenses (but don't be foolish with where you focus, power-wise), along with a good knowledge of strategy and patience for micromanaging (It's tower defense, it comes naturally). With good enough skill in micromanagment, a good tune might come out of the blue.

The only 4X game that ever got me hooked. I have played quite a few of them, and this one, for me (warning: the following may be shocking) it is better even than MOO. Still, MOO defined the genre, and Stellaris owes much to that game, as do all in the genre.
In Stellaris, there is simply so much to do! Not just the usual 4 X's, there is also adventure to be had. You cannot know what you are going to encounter in the next system, and with the 1.3 patch (and even more with the Leviathan DLC) the Galaxy gets even richer. The visuals are good enough to suck youin, and the game, although it remains a Paradox Grand Strategy game and has a learning curve, is not as hard as getting into as other PDS grand strategy.
That being said, is it all good? No, there are some things that can get better. Nonetheless, Paradox is a very active developer, and content is added all the time, as well as balance fixes. They are not afraid to shake things up and change how the game functions. But the changes are, as far as I can see, all for the better.
They have promised great stuff for the future, although the first thing I would hope they add, is good espionage, which is imho the only thing lacking at the moment (although it remains a great game without).
You like 4X, you generally like scifi, and/or you like a game that you can play and win in a really different way each time? Try Stellaris.

Deus Ex is a classic FPS/RPG from the year 2000, but it manages to offer more player choice and better level design than most games today. The story also manages to stay compelling and creates a sense of tension as you uncover a massive international conspiracy.
tl;dr for gameplay: loads of choice and neat weapons plus the signature augmentation system, offers a lot of replayability even if the gunplay and melee are weak by modern standards
Deus Ex plays like traditional stealth games from the late 90s with RPG and FPS elements. It has some odd controls that may take some getting used to for those of you more used to modern games, but keys are fully rebindable. Deus Ex offers a massive range of weapons and tools to help you through levels, from tranquilizer crossbows and 10mm pistols to sawed-off shotguns, snipers and an energy sword.
If you wish, you can finish the game without killing any enemies and silently strike from the shadows with your trusty baton or riot prod, or you may choose to assault your enemies with shotguns and rocket launchers. Deus Ex is all about choice.
The signature feature of Deus Ex is the Augmentation system. Throughout the game, you find canisters that, when installed with a medical bot, give you a choice of a new power. This may be an invisibility cloak, health regeneration, stronger melee attacks, ballistic protection, etc. These drain bioelectric power, which may be refilled with biocells or a repair bot. You can also find augmentation upgrade canisters that let you upgrade your existing augs (less energy consumption, new perks, etc).
Health is also an important system, as each body part has its own health bar. For example, if you lose all health on your legs, you lose your legs and crawl around until you heal them with a medkit or Regen aug. Lose all health in your chest or head, however, and you will die.
Deus Ex also has a skilled system. Each major gameplay function has a skill associated with it that has four ranks (Untrained, Trained, Advanced, and Master). Each rank increases your proficiency in that area. You automatically start with Trained Pistol skill from the outset. Upgrading your skill in a weapon skill (Low-Tech, Pistols, Rifles, Heavy) increases your damage and accuracy with that weapon type with each rank you take and in the case of Heavy lets you move faster with said weapon equipped. Upgrading your Electronics or Lockpick skills decreases the number of multitools or lockpicks required to hack defense systems (cameras, laser grids) or open doors. Computer skill controls how much time you have to hack a computer terminal and access emails, security controls, etc. The list goes on and on.
Weapon mods exist in Deus Ex, too. Silencers obviously make weapons quieter and more effective for stealth purposes, laser sights negate the need to line up a shot for max accuracy, scopes let you fire accurately from a distance, recoil and accuracy mods affect those traits respectively, clip mods add ammo to your magazine, etc. etc. etc. Beware of adding a scope and a laser sight to a weapon, however, because having a scope installed negates the laser sight's accuracy bonus for whatever reason. This does not apply to sniper rifles, however.
Almost every weapon has multiple ammo types. For example, the minicrossbow has lethal darts, tranquilizers, and flare darts. The assault rifle has an underbarrel grenade launcher, the shotguns have buckshot rounds for organic targets and Sabot rounds for armor-piercing (security bots, etc), and so on.
As far as actual combat goes, the gunplay and melee gameplay are very weak and unsatisfying overall thanks to iffy hitboxes and unsatisfying animations, but that's more of a limitation of the time the game was made at. Again, the combat is defined by augmentations and creative combinations.
Overall, the gameplay holds up to modern standards in terms of creativity with items and the unique augmentation system, but the gunplay and melee combat is weak thanks to it being a very old game. Loads of choice and replayability offered by the augmentation system, weapons, and skills.

For a fifteen-year-old game, Deus Ex has an amazing globetrotting story revolving around conspiracies in a world ravaged by a plague. Deus Ex contains many exotic locations and memorable characters to assist you (or fight you) along the way. I would rather not spoil too much of the story or locations, but I will say that your choices do matter and some will come into play later in the game than you would expect. I don't know what else to say about it without spoiling, but it's a crazy story with plenty of twists and turns along the way.
I feel like Ion Storm got the 2050s cyberpunk aesthetic right. It mixes the current world at the time with their vision of the future. Plenty of neon lights, futuristic weapon designs and armor, hologram communications, etc. Even though this game is 15 years old, it manages to be immersive with its very natural-feeling level design. The excellent visual mods New Vision and HDTP also do wonders and I would highly recommend them.
But back to the level design; it's quite amazing how much work went into the levels. Each hub area or level is tailored for any playstyle you could have. They made it feasible to complete the game with perfect stealth and no kills, melee only, full-on combat, or just hacking security systems to mow down enemies with turrets at your disposal. This adds even more to the replayability, knowing that the game will never force you into any particular playstyle.
As someone who played Deus Ex for the first time this year and just finished it, I feel that Deus Ex is a masterpiece. It gets everything right where it counts, and its only real weakness in my opinion is the dated combat. The level design and player freedom combined with the story more than make up for it, though. I strongly believe today, as I write this, that Deus Ex is the best game ever made, hands down. I love Ocarina of Time, Half-Life 2, all the usual suspects, but this is really a special game that every RPG/stealth/FPS fan owes it to themself to play. I got it in the 2014 autumn sale for $1.74 USD, and it's absolutely incredible value. Even at the current full price of $6.99 it's well worth it.
I'd rate Deus Ex a 10/10. Masterful, timeless game. The only thing that could make this game better would be a from the ground up remake with modern visuals, mechanics, etc. You owe it to yourself to play this game if you're even slightly interested in Deus Ex.

I absolutely adore this game.  The basic idea is Picross/Nonograms + Minesweeper on a Hex grid.  If you like either of the forementioned games, please do yourself a favor and pick this up.  The learning curve is wonderfully laid out and it seems as though most of the game is slowly moving you towards the final few puzzles where it puts everything you've learned to work.
The ambient music and minimalist design makes this game soothing to play, even when it is taxing on your mind.  The controls are simple and flawless, just using the left and right mouse click as in the classic Minesweeper game.  It is rare for an experience so simple to be this enjoyable.  I can't wait to play Hexcells Plus to see if they add either more to the already great puzzle system they have put into place, or if it is just more of the endgame style puzzles to be wonderfully entertained by.  Again, if you like Picross and Minesweeper, even things like Sudoku or other logic games, do yourself a favor and toss the few bucks it is asking.  You'll get a few hours of fun out of it and definitely not be disappointed.

Well upon finishing this movie, i came to a conclusion.
This movie is a summery of what I beleive would happen to you when you die.
From every event that takes place some what recently before your death it is recorded by your brain and made into a mix of understanding and non-understanding, like thinking what life and death actually is.
From Ian seeing things that make him question his existance at that very moment to something interupting, making him think about what can or could be. Going from one situation to another as quick as surfing tv.
Lots of events that occur repeat, but not in the same order. like dreaming, thinking about a plane to jumping out of one to thinking about buying a plane to paying for sky diving lessons, it's a mix and bundle of the same things over and over, but not quite.
The movie goes very deep ( if you're following along with it) into mental health and what one can, might or does experience in a state of poor mental health, or even so, death. I certainly can say I have found my self feeling, or thinking like this while very sick. It's that feeling of being pulled out. being a spectator of that whom cannot understand ones self meaning but yet goes on with it's routine, aching at every day, things being but not being, understanding is to understand what not understanding is. that I believe is what life is. just doing to move on, being to be what is to be but what cannot be until the right time.
A final point, if you expirience something, whether in a dream or some sort if vision or thought. did it happen? your mind has felt it and taken it, as if it had happened. nerves twitched, thought and feeling laid out. so what's to say it didn't happen? the experience is there, and from then on always will be.
If you had not gathered, this movie is about what a man named Ian experienced, and kept on experiencing, and was being manipulated by it.
This movie is truely how life or death should be thought of, I give a full recomendation to watch it, aslong as you can break down key points and ideas, sort them out and make an analogy you should love this movie.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

It isn't all that bad. Think of it as the love child of picross and mine sweeper, except that child grew up to be a bit simple and shallow. So, I decided to wait until I had completed every bit of this game to write this review and I should say:
This game is easily one of the best game I have ever played and enters the category of
- Soundtrack:
The music in this game is AMAZING, one of its strongest points. It works so well with the story and bosses fights that makes you have goosebumps from how epic this makes you feel. Also  exploration have some nice and peaceful musics that keeps you really immersed.
- Story:
I wish some characters had more development on their personality. But overall, it is very nice and on some points really makes you think about life and existence. It has 5 main endings, 26 on total. All of them based on the choices you make during the game.
- Gameplay:
There's a variety gameplay elements and the combat is very responsive and fun. Also you have a lot of options to build with the plug-ins, weapons and pods you can find.
- Difficulty:
I like how difficulty works in this game. Yeah, theres some weird difficulty spike between normal and hard, but if you have never played this game before, you should play on normal until you are familiar with the controls, then you can change to hard. On hard you can be one shotted if you aren't careful, but it's cool that you have some sense of danger instead of just face rolling through everything on normal. Very hard are for hardcore people and pretty much anything can one shoot you, so you have that option too if you feel like it.
- Graphics:
It's alright, it fits the theme of the game.
- PC Port:
Until this day, the port still have problems with fullscreen resolutions and performance, but it can be somewhat fixed by some 3rd party mods and it's totally playable. Hopefully improve their next ports in the future.

It's a simple, tower-defense game, nothing game-changing. But it's still fun, challenging, and forgiving at the same time.
Here's a quick look I did of the game. Feel free to skip around to get a general idea of the game and what you'll be getting into. Or you can simply read my summary below.
I'll start off by saying it's got a good atmosphere to go along with what it is. The basic premise is that you're an anti-virus program defending off viruses, and the visuals and music that accompany it fit their their roles well to put you into that world.
The basic gameplay is simple. You have lanes of creeps that mindlessly run into your core. The bare bones of all TD games. However, the game isn't as simple as plopping down a tower and forgetting about it. You have to allocate a limited pool of power to to each tower, and the more you give it, the stronger it is. So you're always frantically shifting your defenses around as the waves progress. That means you aren't staring at the screen and letting the game play itself, which is always a good thing. You also have to click little cubes and diamonds for ressources to upgrade and build your stuff, so you always have to be on the lookout for those. The game even grants you a free limited-time tower to help clean up some of the creeps that make it through, which is also nice. Nobody likes banging your head against the keyboard as the final creep runs into the core with only a sliver of health, ruining your perfect run.
The music is also good, if repetitive, but that's kind of what techno is all about. I also really enjoy the fact that the music changes as you add power to different towers, and that when the tower themselves fire, they also add to the beat. It's almost as if you're remixing the song yourself.
But now let's talk about some of the negatives. While the game does give you a good tutorial to get you started, it doesn't do a good job explaining the newer things you get later on down the line. It's all about trail and error. You also have no idea how much of a difference you're making when you upgrade a tower or give it power. You get a visual cue that the range has increased, but not about how much extra power you're giving it. A percentage or something would be nice to have. Also, the game kept on sending in new enemies at me that I had no idea how to deal with properly. The first being a big cube that only slows down when you constantly hit it with something. But the only thing that constantly fires is the free tower that's on a long cooldown. You also have to control it manually, so you can't allocate resources or build new things until you've finished dealing with the threat. Then the game snowballs into something you can't recover from, so you have to start over.
Then there's the problem of not knowing how effective a certain tower is against a certain enemy type. I got a tower that was supposed to be effective against shielded enemies, but when they came, even at full power it wasn't that great. And when you start throwing other normal minions into the mix, you're never sure what tower you should prioritze over another as they enemies bum-rush you from all directions. And not only that, it's extremely frustrating when the tower that's effective against certain types chooses to fire at another enemy, and the one it's supposed to kill struts by unscathed. There needs to be some sort of target priority.
But yeah, all of that is only a problem if you're OCD like me and want a perfect score. There's plenty of lives you can leak before you get a game over and have to retry.
So in summary, this is a solid TD game at $3. The game offers good content, a variety of enemy types, keeps you engaged constantly in what's going on, interesting setting and music (if you like techno), and is genreally just a good time waster. Get it now, or even wait for a sale when this game won't cost more than a dollar. You'll get some enjoyment out of it.

But when I got over the fact that I'm apparently easy/story mode material and just couldn't be bothered with all the dying (myself as opposed to others) I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Yes, the characters sometimes look a bit stiff, but it's an overall rather pretty game, the story is great, the cutscenes are well-done and typically not so many or long as to become annoying. There's also good replay value as you can make serveral choices that impact the story, and I for one will have to try Iorveth's path some day. And if you're looking for something more challenging than story mode, I'm guessing you'll find something in all the other more difficult modes.

Third person and radical attitude in adult cartoon style carnage.
FPS casuals will appericate this swift action game, which features adequetly timed modes of team deathmatch, cature the flag and control points while there are some other modes as well, the main focus is loudouts unique weapon style approach. Letting plays craft their guns to their hearts content
Players have access to various styles of weapons, Bullets, Lasers or Rockets. Whatever you pick, from there you can modify bits and pieces of the weapon to fire differently, some addons will increase your stats in areas but as a balance decrease in other areas. Example: A larger mag addon for your rifle provides more ammo in the clip, but will take longer to reload, thus leaving you vunverable if you are in the middle of combat.
there's a good amount of options you can pick from, players can switch between faster shooting, faster reloads, behavior of ammo, etc. You can name your weapons to whatever you wish and save them to a character of your choice.
Gameplay consists of well structured levels of heavy detailed comic book style surroundings, humourous, rude and shocking behaviour from the cast in game and an easy to understand HUD. Controls strangely are very minimal and combat is frustrating at times. You can't crouch or prone, so you'll rely on your third person shoulder for ambushes around corners and combat introduces the kyting and classic bunny hopping techniques again which has been removed from most shooter games recently. Years ago this was considered to be an elitist move but these days even the most green of players can quickly learn this and provide even the most experinced player a rage fueling defeat.
Post game will show your player leveling up and also your weapons and addons you use, You also collect and in game currency which is used to spend on upgrades and addons. While your personal player upgades at a decent rate. Your weapon addons are proven to be much more time consuming It will take many hours just to reach level 2 with even one weapon addon.

Deus Ex is a cyperpunk RPG with FPS elements and an incredible tale of chaos and conspiracy, exciting from beggining to end.
Gameplay:
Deus Ex was one of the first games to capture a true nonlinear expirience.
Each level is large and vast with multiple pathways and hidden secrets, rewarding you for exploration.
There is a massive amount of freedom for play style, would you like to be a Pacifist or Killer? Do you want to go guns blazing or make a stealthy infiltration, or would you like to use the power of technology to do the job for you?
At any given moment, you can kill an NPC, whenever you would like, and these choices are not meaningless, they will have an impact on the overall story. Like for example, if you kill the target in the beggining of the game, Paul Denton (JC's brother) will call JC Denton a "jackass" and will lose trust with you, as well as you losing an op bonus (extra cash) from your boss Manderley.
This is no game that holds your hand, the game has what tools you need to play with your style, and bea a level, you just have to find those tools yourself, creating a learning curve for the player.
Some mechanics may be considered "clunky by today's standards. For example, there is no aim down sights, it is instead replaced by a lock on mode that may not be 100% accurate all of the time. Also, the skills swimming and environmental training skills are useless, and you shouldn't make the mistake of choosing either of these in the beggining. But none of this matters now at least, most of the issues can be fixed by mods like the Shiftor Mod, or even graphical mods to improve the visuals.
Story:
Deus ex starts you off on Liberty Island in 2052 where you learn some of the elements that make up Deus ex's world. One of these would be the sense of danger; terrorist attacks were very common in this time, like for example, the head of the Statue of Liberty was blown off in a terrorist attack by a group named the French Sillouette, and there is also a disease spreading known as the Grey Death.
There is also a strong element of conspiracy, once you hit mission 4, you are hit with a massive plot twist followed by the possibility that everything you know is wrong.
You play as the character JC Denton, who has a personal character, but is ultimately defined by your choices. JC is one of the first nano-augmented human beings with machine parts known as augmentations built into his body, but still has his human personality making his character intersting.
There is also his brother Paul Denton, who plays a large role in the game's plot twist in mission 4. Paul was the first ever nano-augmented human being and is identical to JC, taking on a pacifist role encouraging him to use non-lethal tactics.
There are also side characters like Anne Navarre and Gunter Herman, who are mechs, and are viscous and brutal.
Other than that, there are not to many characters I can talk about without spoiling the game.
Visuals:
Visuals in Deus Ex weren't the best for its time, and people would often make fun of its graphical flaws today, but Deus Ex manages to make you forget about visuals through its tremendous atmosphere with the mixture of the feeling of conspiracy and curiosity, the intersting takes on popular cities in the future, and the amazing soundtrack.
Music:
Deus Ex's soundtrack is one of the best Science Fiction game soundtracks ever made, creating atmosphere in almost every level.
The best of the soundtrack includes the title song, the infamous UNATCO theme, the Hell's Kitchen theme, the Hong Kong theme, and many others.
Overall:
Deus Ex remains my favorite game of all time 15 years later, and when someone mentions Deus Ex, I do indeed reinstall it, for it is an incredible atmospheric nonlinear cyberpunk RPG that still to this day hasn't been equaled to, and is worth every penny you spend on it.
Overall Expirience Score: 10/10 - A Legendary Expirience

I'd give this game an A, almost an A+.  It was almost the perfect adventure game.
While they could easily have gone for cutesy, they didn't.  The result is charming and haunting.  It has anthropomorphized mice, squirrels, and other little creatures of the woods living in the town of Mousewood.  The whole story is a charming fairytale.  Yet, it rises above the corniness and cuteness that that usually implies.  This is no Disney movie.  It has points in the story that are sad and points that couldn't help but make me want to reach through the screen and smack the villain, because they were just the right level of creepy to make this story a class act.  There are also some really creepy characters with masks who infiltrate Mousewood who really gave me the willies.  The whole charming setup with talking mice and squirrels makes a great backdrop for the creepy villains.
The story keeps you guessing, too.  There are times when you ask yourself, "just what IS going on..."  It all gets explained eventually, but all the strangeness
The gameplay and problem solving well done.  It's mostly using items on objects or with other items and having conversations with other characters, but you also learn four spells that you have to use to solve problems.  One really nice feature is that, almost at the beginning, you get a magic coin that lets you see invisible things as well as anything that could help you in your adventure.  One things it does is show you everything you can click on.  That's really nice, because it means that you don't have don't miss solutions to problems or items just because you didn't happen to wave your mouse over a few cursors.  I think every adventure game should have something like that, because I really hate it when I have to get an online hint in an adventure game and finally find out that I just didn't know I could click on something.
Also, they keep a journal for you and you have a spell that allows you to have your magic teacher, the magician rabbit the Marquis de Hoto, remind you what you're supposed to be doing.  That's really nice in case you leave the game for awhile, pick it up weeks later, and then forget what you were doing.
One undocumented feature that I'll pass on is that the right mouse button will skip through dialog.  If someone's saying something that you've heard a dozen times before because you're stuck on a problem, for example, you can just click the right mouse button to skip each line and fast-forward through it.  Another undocumented feature that's really handy is that, while your character normally walks around in the environment and, therefore, physically walks to a new location, double clicking on an exit will cause your character to just appear in the next location without having to wait for the character to physically walk there, which is fun the first few times, but can get tedious when you're stuck.
There were only one or two places where I needed hints.  Most of the problems were very logical and of intermediate level.  The game starts out with extremely easy problems, just to teach you the game play, moves on to easy to medium ones, and then plateaus at about an intermediate difficulty level.  I think it would make a wonderful introduction to adventure games for those who have never played before because it's such a class act, has such a great story, and is just so beautiful all the way through.  It leads slowly enough into the problems and is easy enough early on that I think newcomers to the adventure genre will pick it up easily early on and be challenged later.

I usually don't write reviews, but I felt like i owe it to the people behind it to make one. This movie was really set apart for me by the surreal aspect that was produced masterfully throughout the movie. The cuts between animated scenes and reality, along with a retro soundtrack, really made this movie pop. I am a fan of artistic movies, so those sorts of aspects appeal to me personally. Beyond that, the acting was fairly good, I don't expect anything masterful from indie developers in that regard. In its whole, the movie reminded me of something the Coen brothers might make while on acid. I applaud Devolver and Imagos for making a strange, and memorable film. It isn't for everyone, and it consists largely of dialogue. If these aspects turn you off to the movie, then don't bother. However if you are interested in a strange, fairly thoughtful film, I would recommend Motivational Growth.

I'm loving this one.  Pure logic puzzles.
To oversimplify, the game is like 6-sided Minesweeper without the random elements, with elements of Sudoku entering the later levels.  Every puzzle can be solved without guessing.  There's a clear difficulty progression through the levels.  Low stress too, since if you get one wrong, the board doesn't blow up - you just increment an error counter.
The ONLY thing wrong is the lack of a random level generator.  Once you beat the included levels, you're done.  But looking at the value (time/money), it's still a great deal.  (And the follow-on game, Hexcells Plus, is also cheap and just as excellent, with slightly higher difficulty.)
Very highly recommended.

Another addition to the Call of Duty (COD) franchise, Black Ops delivers a tale of agents from the American army who don’t exist. Whatever actions they take are solely their own, and aren’t even recognized by the U.S. military. This game includes a strong single-player campaign, a memorable multiplayer, and the ever-challenging (Nazi) Zombies mode.
What I liked about this game:
The single-player campaign wasn’t too bad at all. In fact, it had some of the most memorable moments of the franchise. However, to be fair, each COD campaign HAS their one moment of an emotional scene or two. The different levels were fun to play, and each mission was challenging on certain degrees (I immediately play Veteran Mode on every COD game I play). There were even a couple of easter eggs and in-game cameos worth noting too. The story leaves one thinking who the real villains of the story are.
The ‘main menu’ is also fully interactive. Sitting in a chair restrained by a mysterious agent in the upper window, the player is able to choose the settings (while listening to the guy in the room berating the player with ‘numbers’ and ‘confirming the kill’ haha). After escaping the chair, one can move the player to a computer in the corner and access in-game information. Not only that, one can play a secret top-down zombie shooter which is just as fun as (Nazi) Zombies! The information one can hack from the computer will allow players to access concept art, transcripts, and hidden lore. There’s even another hidden game for those who enjoy using their imagination and typing.
(Nazi) Zombies mode (in my opinion) is the best mode in the game. With the DLCs adding up to fighting zombies on the MOON, one can’t help what these developers were thinking creating this sub-game. Playing with friends is a must to reach higher rounds (counter stops at 99, but the mode continues), but playing solo is just as fun to get used to the layout of each level. The in-game characters are hilariously fun to listen too, and the story/lore for the mode is surprisingly well-developed.
What I don’t like about this game:
For those who love COD for the multiplayer, I respect that. I will not bash one for playing it in this review. Since Modern Warfare, most of the gaming community should understand how COD multiplayer works by now. I bought the DLCs for the zombie maps, but the maps that came for multiplayer are nice too. The golf course DLC map, in my opinion, is the most unfair map for new players or those who don’t use sniper rifles considering… it’s a golf course with barely any cover. This game still has a strong online community, however, one may face quite the challenge if one starts fresh. It can take a while to climb up the ranks. [Aside: I can care less for the multiplayer. I just use the M60 with Big Ammo and hold the trigger down until it clicks. I still make sick kills with it on high ranked players]
Overall:
Even if it’s another COD game to some people, it’s still fun to pick up fresh from the used game store, or even return to it for old time’s sake. I recommend it, and the DLCs (provided they turn up on Steam sales) are worth the buy.

NieR: Automata is incredible at being a video game. Yoko Taro, the director, has combined his mad genius with the elegant combat stylings of Platinum to create an experience that truly explores what it means to be human.
Notably, humans aren't even around.
Instead, NieR first appears to be a game of dichotomies. There are segments of high action, segments of low action. You play adaptive androids, you fight mindless machines. An army of good, an army of evil. The duty of loyalty, the risk of curiosity.
It is by ruthlessly breaking these concepts that Yoko Taro and his team manage to make you feel genuine emotion for these constructs. I dare not spoil any of this adventure, so suffice it to say that even what appears to be a silly fetch quest will surprise you or make you reexamine how you looked at a character.
That is not to say that it doesn't have silly fetch quests, however. While any medium uses highs and lows to accent its points, jumping the difficulty every story mission means you are practically forced to wander the game's open world to be strong enough to progress. As meaningful as the game's content is, a quest to kill four giant robots is still just a quest to kill four giant robots, no matter the discussions and ramifications that come from it. This game is not a spectacle fighter or arena brawler -- my one word of caution before purchasing is to ask yourself whether you can handle either playing Easy mode or exploring the world maybe a bit more than you'd like before progressing to the next story segment.
And that's everything off-putting I have to say about this game -- this beautiful experience. The use of music, voice, color, cinematography, queer ladies, and twinstick shooting segments coalesce into what can only be described as utterly magnificent.
I have never played a game that so thoroughly made me think beyond "are these actions correct?" We have plenty of games that profess grey morality and make you choose aribitrary solutions. Again, NieR breaks the "do bad" and "do good" dichotomy. 2B, our mechanical heroine, must make her own choices and assumptions just like the player. Sometimes you will be struck by the childishness of a crying robot in overalls. Other times, by the frankness of an antagonist who freely speaks their plans. Or, perhaps, you will simply be struck by the buzzsaw arm of a sentient oil rig.
NieR: Automata is a masterpiece.

Borderlands 2 set a high bar for the series; it combined raunchy humor, infinite variable and fun weapons, multiple unique classes with three seperate specializations each, a lovable villain, fun and interesting characters, and a straightforward but complex story. Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, unfortunately, did not live up to its predecessor. Much of the raunchy humor that made 2 and the 1's DLC so memorable is missing, the playable characters are bland (though still fun to play as), a forgettable villain, boring NPCs, and less of a story than slightly guided wandering.
However, much of the gameplay that makes the series so memorable is still there, and the game provides a backstory to the main villain and one of the side villains of Borderlands 2. It's still fun, the oxygen mechanic is interesting and useful, and the new laser weapon type can mimic every other weapon type, with its biggest advantages being the obscenely large amount of ammo and the extra damage when in oxygen. The Cryo element is also a welcome addition, as it is the first elemental type dedicated to something other than doing more damage.
Final Score: 7/10. Feel free to try it, but don't expect it to be as good as the last one.

A hybrid of Paradox's famous grand strategy game and a traditional 4X strategy game, Stellaris is a game for all who desire galactic dominion (whether military, diplomatic, or otherwise).  Stellaris has a considerable range of options for creating your own species (played by you, run by AI, or even shared with others), each of which has decided impacts on the strengths you will bring to the game without pidgeonholing you into a single path to victory.
Paradox did the strategy genre a great service by introducing a non-linear, non-static tech tree.  Instead, each time you complete a technology (in one of three very broad themes: physics, society, and engineering), you "draw" 3 (or more, depending on your government type and other technologies) possible technologies you can research, much like a card game.  The options you do not select have a chance to reappear again, although many factors keep it from being truly random (e.g. colony ship options are very likely to reappear soon, if you do not pick the tech from the start).  The game, including the new mini-expansion Leviathans, has several other systems (End Crises and Fallen Empries) that keep the mid and late game more interesting than the lull it can be in many other strategy games.
Multiplayer can be a blast, where you and your friends may have radically different playstyles, but can still band together in a powerful Federation, each become regional hegemonies, or just brawl to see who is the last human player standing.  Options to seed other players close together or evenly distributed among the rest of the galaxy let you really decide how much interaction you want to have with other players in the early game.
If you haven't played a Paradox game before, you'll be in for the promise of the game being continually updated and upgraded (even if you don't buy expansions) for years to come, much like their other products: Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis

Is it Borderlands? Yes. Does it have the same brand of humor? Yes. Is the iteration on the theme interesting? Yes.
But it's not as good as its predecessors.
The game seems more expansive than the two that came before, but bigger doesn't necessarily mean better. The best way I can describe it is that the "Borderlands" games set on Pandora seemed to have a better flow from area to area, both in the large and small senses. You felt like you were going from interesting thing to interesting thing, even within a single locale. There was sort of a natural "pathing" that took place. "The Pre-Sequel" doesn't quite pull this off, which leads to a feeling of sprawl without as much to keep your attention.
Also, I had this odd feeling that it was harder to find loot that was interesting. Sure, not every weapon is going to be legendary, but this game seemed inordinately stingy. In my playthrough, the engine seemed to have a strange love of handing out pistols over every other possibility. Also, the Luneshine weapons seemed underpowered compared to the expenditures necessary to get them.
The low-grav and boost jumping elements are a neat idea, but a lack of fine polish seemed to get in the way. Jumping to higher levels proved a lot more finicky than it should be, especially because the threshold between making an upward jump to a platform and not making it was a little too sharp. Also, generally speaking, in no other "Borderlands" game have I ended up "hanging" on world geometry so much.
The experience does seem to improve in the latter half, and like I said: It IS "Borderlands." In a sense, that exposes the flaws. The previous two titles were basically perfect, and this one stumbles a bit as it tries to get into new territory. Mistakes are to be expected when doing something creative, so I can't complain too much - and I still had plenty of fun.

This is a masterpiece of a game from a quality standpoint. It's definitely a labor of love, and appears to be the brainchild of at least one or more people on the team that made it. There are so many little touches in the game that seem to point to this being a game they were very enthusastic about creating. It's triple A, no doubt about it. Amazing art, great voice acting, decent sound design, and most of the puzzles are reasonable and straightforward. The starting premise and setting are decent concepts as well.
However, I found myself bored throughout most of the experience. The game's story seems to be the root of the problem. It starts decently enough with a call to adventure. The protagonist has the dream of becoming a magician, and sets out to play around in the woods near his house. It's a long story, but he basically gets pulled into another world by some sort of extradimensional being that promises he'll be able to wield magic like a true magician.
The problem is two-fold, and lies mainly in the story-telling.
First, you're never really given much reason to care about the plot or the protagonist. There is no clear antagonist or goal. "Become a magician" is extremely vague, and even when you finally start down the path, collecting spells as you go, it feels very underwhelming in the grand scheme of things. It's just another item in your inventory to unlock some path you couldn't take before. I found myself somewhat bored throughout most of the experience because the game just couldn't give me a reason to get engaged. Everything I was doing felt kind of arbitrary and objective-less. Even worse, the main "antagonist", if you can even call him that, isn't revealed until the last 30 minutes, and you're given no reason to really fear or hate him. He's just a villian for villian's sake.
Second, the game's story starts to slowly become more and more incomprehensible as it goes on. I wouldn't say it is the worst I've ever seen. Far from it. However, it slowly starts to degrade into incoherence after the first act. The puzzles seem to follow suit as well, becoming less and less recognizable as puzzles, but instead confounding leaps in logic. To make matters worse, the entire game takes place in one expansive hub that changes based on day and night.
When I got to the last 30 minutes, I was beginning to question if I was even playing the same game anymore. I almost felt as if I had skipped an hour of the game, or perhaps this was the sequel(or prequel) to some other game I didn't know about. The finale dumped a metric ton of plot on me that was never really setup prior to that moment, and after the fact left me utterly confused as to why these revelations were at all important. I'm reminded of the dream sequences after you kill Kellogg in Fallout 4. Why are we characterizing a villian we just beat? We should have done that BEFORE we fight him, to give us more reasons to get hyped for fighting him. Even the end credit stinger made no sense.
I can't help but think that this story would have been better as a series of books, an animated show, or an animated movie. The point and click format doesn't seem to work here.
There is too much quality here to discredit it on plot alone. Perhaps, for the right target audience, this is a golden point and click opportunity. For me, it was mostly a boring slog that ended in utter confusion.

Here are a few items that I found of interest in
:
Roleplaying - As protagonist JC Denton, players traverse various stages with given objectives while gaining experience points to enhance aspects of their character’s statistics. The upgrade system is impeccable, and allows the player to proceed in situations in nearly any way possible, which allows for multiple forms of play and progression. Another element of great importance is how choices-both in and out of dialogues-affect an abundance of things within the game. For example, your starting equipment choices and statistics will influence how you manipulate the world and its peoples, allowing you to uncover a multitude of secrets.
A touch of realism is portrayed in
as well since getting paid actually feels like getting paid. For example, Director Manderly will explain your monetary and experience gains after each mission within a conversational flow, which accentuates a seamless transition between operations and downtime.
Stealth System - It is difficult to entirely describe the sensation that is this title’s stealth gameplay presents. Character augments, statistical upgrades, and player skill all contribute to the experience, yet this game seemingly knows how to also look past these and simply demonstrate a stealth ‘feel’ in comparison to relying on only the said features. Like nearly every other game created in the genre, the player can maneuver while hidden through territories by utilizing the crouch command-activated with the Control key-and by passing silently in the shadows, preferring muffled or melee eliminations over brutal assault. Several useable items such as the stun rod and tranquilizer rounds for the crossbow emphasize the purpose of stealth, but are not so overpowered that it makes the approach simple; player timing and cunning are key to success while dodging enemy forces in
.
Player and Non-Player Dialogue - As described previously, many of the actions that JC Denton can perform may be mentioned by non-player characters throughout the game; some of these exchanges can occur randomly-such as in the incident mentioned within the spoiler text-, but mostly appear within conversation with others. There is also a great dialogue selection when speaking with civilians or UNATCO personnel ranging from calm and inquisitive to brash threatening.
Level Design - Though similar themes may be present through individual missions, each level retains its own unique feel and layout that abstains from any two levels being blindly alike.
utilizes a multiple-layer design in many of its missions, with street-, basement-, and roof-accessible venues that contribute to the open-ended gameplay; this may not seem like a huge feature, but with so many stealth action games forcing players to endure ‘straight’ level mechanics while claiming its style to be open-world, this ideal is magnificent. Strewn throughout each level are also intricately-placed traps and alarms that Gary Gygax himself would be proud of.
TL:DR -
is undoubtedly a legend in the gaming world, and continues to shine in its current age. This title near-flawlessly executes a stealth gameplay experience that all fanatics of the genre must play. There is so much more I would like to say about
but nothing anyone could say can truly bring justice to how innovative this game was and still is. I highly recommend this title to individuals who enjoy stealth action, roleplaying, and cyberpunk themes. Thanks for reading.

"Witcher 2" is a 3rd person RPG that's exciting, interesting and beautiful-- but also tormented by broken in-game mechanisms. If you're stuck during the _tutorial_, don't fret, it's actually super common. It's NOT your fault. And the whole game is like this, including (but not limited to) an inventory from which items disappear, crafting recipes that attach themselves to the wrong item, and rooms with enough sconces on the walls that our hero becomes paralyzed for wanting to activate everything everywhere rather than walk. Yikes!
Yes, in most ways, even the Enhanced Edition of "Witcher 2" is an irritating, glitchy disaster ... And yet, it is also compelling storytelling, well acted, magnificently visualized, and delightfully smart fun. It does not overstay its welcome, taking only 3 increasingly-consise Chapters to complete-- with just a tiny bit of the annoying 'run back-and-forth' that absolutely ruined the original Witcher.
"Witcher 2"s story is epic, full of intreigue, told with sweeping interactive cinematics, and it gives us choices that result in big consequences:  including two COMPLETELY different Second Chapters! On top of it all, taking down the bosses in battle can be as rewarding as any feeling in any RPG. This may be the most replayable game ever made.

It is thanks to Markiplier that I actually took notice and interest in this game. It would seem as though that the trend for games is the 8-bit style of character design; some indie games specifically.
With the game "Magicite" however, despite this design it does not disappoint. There is a continuous effervescent glow throughout the background and the enemies with which you fight. The music itself is rather fitting with the rest of the world which is both relaxing and has the potential of becoming sort of hypnotic if you happen to not be paying close-enough attention to what you're doing [ADHD for the lose]. The characters themselves which you get to play are both adorable and are formidable foes against the various monsters you hack and slash with; but it is not a hack-and-slash game as it is with the Diablo series...
The down-sides:
There aren't really any "levels" per-se; you are sort of plopped into the world. If you're a first time gamer or just simply a novice as I am; there's not really a tutorial, there aren't any sort of difficulty ranges you can work with [beginner, normal, hard, die-inside-it's-so-difficult]; there's just you being thrown into the world.
While yes, that does make you feel like you need to fight for your life and gives your character a sense of purpose [based upon the back-story that the creator has made rather clear and very cool]. If you're going up against a boar (boars are♥♥♥♥♥holes in this game if you're a beginner) like any natural boar you're going to get charged at; and the gaming gods help you if you don't know which button the "jump" is.
I did notice, took note and did my best to follow through with the [while very sincerely appreciated] guide to what you're supposed to do; it would have been nice to have some sort of walk-through within the game itself. The gaming guide is pretty long and the writer did in fact take the time to even put a disclaimer that basically says: "Your eyes are going to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with ALL THE WORDS. FOR DAYS." Which was smart of the writer to put on. Pixel Cheese is their name? Not sure, but no snark at all when I say: I am genuinely grateful for the time you took to write out this review. But what about some pictures for more of a better reference? While that does sound very immature; it also helps those who are more visually inclined and can help the gamer apply what you took the time to write in exchange for better game experience. Plus for the sake of efficiency the visual reference or perhaps a video you can insert into the tutorial would be beneficial as opposed to reading through all the words, and then finding the right video on Youtube of a "let's play" to see which situation said video is on can help you with precisely what you need. Texting a friend is always an option if that friend has played it before - however you do run the risk of getting your balls busted for it. Or in my case my ovaries busted.
The controls are kind of finicky when you fight monsters. The "WAD-etc" controls are a bit to get used to; but the seasoned PC gamer will have no trouble. As for the n00bs such as myself... Trust me as you read this; it will take some getting used to, but you will get the hang of it.
Despite the minor pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥details I'd give this game a 9.5 out of 10 in its simplicity, its music, the adorable-looking green monsters that you get to bash with a wooden ax, and over-all despite the 8-bit design it's rather polished. Color me impressed.

NieR: Automata is incredible at being a video game. Yoko Taro, the director, has combined his mad genius with the elegant combat stylings of Platinum to create an experience that truly explores what it means to be human.
Notably, humans aren't even around.
Instead, NieR first appears to be a game of dichotomies. There are segments of high action, segments of low action. You play adaptive androids, you fight mindless machines. An army of good, an army of evil. The duty of loyalty, the risk of curiosity.
It is by ruthlessly breaking these concepts that Yoko Taro and his team manage to make you feel genuine emotion for these constructs. I dare not spoil any of this adventure, so suffice it to say that even what appears to be a silly fetch quest will surprise you or make you reexamine how you looked at a character.
That is not to say that it doesn't have silly fetch quests, however. While any medium uses highs and lows to accent its points, jumping the difficulty every story mission means you are practically forced to wander the game's open world to be strong enough to progress. As meaningful as the game's content is, a quest to kill four giant robots is still just a quest to kill four giant robots, no matter the discussions and ramifications that come from it. This game is not a spectacle fighter or arena brawler -- my one word of caution before purchasing is to ask yourself whether you can handle either playing Easy mode or exploring the world maybe a bit more than you'd like before progressing to the next story segment.
And that's everything off-putting I have to say about this game -- this beautiful experience. The use of music, voice, color, cinematography, queer ladies, and twinstick shooting segments coalesce into what can only be described as utterly magnificent.
I have never played a game that so thoroughly made me think beyond "are these actions correct?" We have plenty of games that profess grey morality and make you choose aribitrary solutions. Again, NieR breaks the "do bad" and "do good" dichotomy. 2B, our mechanical heroine, must make her own choices and assumptions just like the player. Sometimes you will be struck by the childishness of a crying robot in overalls. Other times, by the frankness of an antagonist who freely speaks their plans. Or, perhaps, you will simply be struck by the buzzsaw arm of a sentient oil rig.
NieR: Automata is a masterpiece.

Borderlands 2 set a high bar for the series; it combined raunchy humor, infinite variable and fun weapons, multiple unique classes with three seperate specializations each, a lovable villain, fun and interesting characters, and a straightforward but complex story. Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, unfortunately, did not live up to its predecessor. Much of the raunchy humor that made 2 and the 1's DLC so memorable is missing, the playable characters are bland (though still fun to play as), a forgettable villain, boring NPCs, and less of a story than slightly guided wandering.
However, much of the gameplay that makes the series so memorable is still there, and the game provides a backstory to the main villain and one of the side villains of Borderlands 2. It's still fun, the oxygen mechanic is interesting and useful, and the new laser weapon type can mimic every other weapon type, with its biggest advantages being the obscenely large amount of ammo and the extra damage when in oxygen. The Cryo element is also a welcome addition, as it is the first elemental type dedicated to something other than doing more damage.
Final Score: 7/10. Feel free to try it, but don't expect it to be as good as the last one.

A hybrid of Paradox's famous grand strategy game and a traditional 4X strategy game, Stellaris is a game for all who desire galactic dominion (whether military, diplomatic, or otherwise).  Stellaris has a considerable range of options for creating your own species (played by you, run by AI, or even shared with others), each of which has decided impacts on the strengths you will bring to the game without pidgeonholing you into a single path to victory.
Paradox did the strategy genre a great service by introducing a non-linear, non-static tech tree.  Instead, each time you complete a technology (in one of three very broad themes: physics, society, and engineering), you "draw" 3 (or more, depending on your government type and other technologies) possible technologies you can research, much like a card game.  The options you do not select have a chance to reappear again, although many factors keep it from being truly random (e.g. colony ship options are very likely to reappear soon, if you do not pick the tech from the start).  The game, including the new mini-expansion Leviathans, has several other systems (End Crises and Fallen Empries) that keep the mid and late game more interesting than the lull it can be in many other strategy games.
Multiplayer can be a blast, where you and your friends may have radically different playstyles, but can still band together in a powerful Federation, each become regional hegemonies, or just brawl to see who is the last human player standing.  Options to seed other players close together or evenly distributed among the rest of the galaxy let you really decide how much interaction you want to have with other players in the early game.
If you haven't played a Paradox game before, you'll be in for the promise of the game being continually updated and upgraded (even if you don't buy expansions) for years to come, much like their other products: Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis

Is it Borderlands? Yes. Does it have the same brand of humor? Yes. Is the iteration on the theme interesting? Yes.
But it's not as good as its predecessors.
The game seems more expansive than the two that came before, but bigger doesn't necessarily mean better. The best way I can describe it is that the "Borderlands" games set on Pandora seemed to have a better flow from area to area, both in the large and small senses. You felt like you were going from interesting thing to interesting thing, even within a single locale. There was sort of a natural "pathing" that took place. "The Pre-Sequel" doesn't quite pull this off, which leads to a feeling of sprawl without as much to keep your attention.
Also, I had this odd feeling that it was harder to find loot that was interesting. Sure, not every weapon is going to be legendary, but this game seemed inordinately stingy. In my playthrough, the engine seemed to have a strange love of handing out pistols over every other possibility. Also, the Luneshine weapons seemed underpowered compared to the expenditures necessary to get them.
The low-grav and boost jumping elements are a neat idea, but a lack of fine polish seemed to get in the way. Jumping to higher levels proved a lot more finicky than it should be, especially because the threshold between making an upward jump to a platform and not making it was a little too sharp. Also, generally speaking, in no other "Borderlands" game have I ended up "hanging" on world geometry so much.
The experience does seem to improve in the latter half, and like I said: It IS "Borderlands." In a sense, that exposes the flaws. The previous two titles were basically perfect, and this one stumbles a bit as it tries to get into new territory. Mistakes are to be expected when doing something creative, so I can't complain too much - and I still had plenty of fun.

10/10. This game is simply amazing.

Not to mention the hunger bar looms over you, making you feel like life is even more important. Death is permanent, so you had better make each step count and choose your battles wisely.

This game tries to combine Half-Life, Omikron, old X-Com games, and Metal Gear Solid together, surprisingly doing an alright job of it.
If you are able to get through the bugs, glitches, and quirky mechanics that occasionally present themselves in this game, than Dues Ex will provide more hours of fun than any other PC game released during the year 2000.
Pro's:
- Good use of unlocks/upgrades to add more gameplay hours at a cheap programming cost
- Physics are not nearly as good as Hitman: Codename 47, but it was one of the pioneering games of physics for it's age
- Typical, easy to understand conspiracy story. (I consider this a good thing because I'd rather be learning  game mechanics than who is betraying who)
- Usually 2 or 3 ways to beat a quest/level. Stealth, Combat, or using Technology.
- Skills and augmentations (cybernetic upgrades) are a cool idea
- Limb, Torso, or Head specific damage and must applie med kit to the injured body part (hence x-com reference)
- Graphics are on par for the PC games of that year, nothing exceptional though
- Has some really unique and innovated paths for some levels
- Introduces hacking and bypassing security
- Long, compared to something like half-life
Con's:
- Augmentation system was very poorly implemented. Keys are horrible (can't rebind), don't know what to upgrade till endgame but thats okay, because it takes forever to upgrade anyway.
- Skills take forever to upgrade
- Suffers typical generic game killer cliches (accidently quick saving in a spot you can't get out, having a boss fight you spend all your items trying to win and  you are supposed to lose, not having a clue where the objective is and given no hints in your quest log, reusing models for different characters, and sometimes frustrating mechanics)
- Platforming is nowhere near the quality of half life, it's quite unacceptable for this year actually
- Swimming is glitchy without fluid movement, makes me wonder why they added so much of it
- I feel like half of the game is spent crawling in a vent
- Weapon damage makes me wonder sometimes, like the shotgun does the same as a dark gun at point blank.
Overall, the game is worth it for getting into the serries. It's simple, easy to follow, almost kind of cheezy at times, but its good fun and some very unique gameplay concepts that work well with the game, as long as you can get through the occassional frustrating aspects.

While it may be true that the game was terrible before, I applaud the devs for continously updating and improving it despite the criticism. Some of the developers actually play this game from time to time and interact with the community, which I found neat.
The gameplay isn't that groundbreaking but the classes give the game some variety; as limited as it is, if you cooperate with your friends and compliment each other using the given class abilities, it often works in a satisfying way for the entire team. This, in turn, keeps the game balanced and fun most of the time. However, they do need to improve the PvP games as those who have a higher level tend to stomp on the lower ranks due to their perks.
Single-player isn't so bad, but this is where the game starts to show how simple it is; I think this is sort of fitting since the game is meant to be a cooperative multiplayer game. Single-player difficulty tends to fluctuate but it really depends on how well you can adapt to situations using your class. Don't expect on the A.I team mates to help you or make a difference; for the most part, they're stupid and only manage to distract the dinos away from you so that you can temporarily recover. At times you can get immersed just by being alone during the outpost intermissions and exploring the map (which are beautifully made by the way), especially in Conquest mode maps. Overall, a good practice mode at  best.
Weapons and gunplay are confusing since several of the weapons' stats, for some reason, don't accurately potray the values displayed on the shop menu. This is the issue I found in the Laser Rifle; the damage is apparently set to 3,400 but when you actually get to use it; it does only half the damage of the rocket launcher which you can get for the same price and do more DPS with. That and all of the weapons except for the Ion Trek Blade (Which is a melee weapon) have Accuracy ranks set to "B". Meaning that they all should have the same accuracy when you use them, but they're all marginally different.
Graphics are good but they aren't extraordinary. Small warning though: to people who get motion sickness, disable all instances of motion blur! This game makes heavy use of it to the point where every character model, including the dinosaurs, get blurred when they move. This does depend on the setting though and I didn't bother to check the other ones. Graphics remind me of a mix between Far Cry and Borderlands. They do need to revamp or rework the animation of the player models, I think most of us wouldn't be bothered with the third-person camera setting since the animations are so annoying that they tend to distract you; that and the camera angle is terrible too. Nothing that a quick update would fix, which I hope would come soon.
I would give this one a 7.5/10. For a dollar though, you could have great hours of fun with your friends, so I'll up that rating to an 8/10. It's practically a steal for all the content it has. Needs more players though.

Hexcells is a great puzzle game. While the game borrows elements from picross and Minesweeper, I find Hexcells to be an improvement on both. Unlike Minesweeper, every puzzle is completely solvable based on the available clues - no frustrating leaps of faith required. The game becomes more rewarding with each new puzzle as new strategies are needed and solutions go from obvious to head-scratchers. The final sets require a variety of styles of deductive reasoning to solve the cleverly designed puzzles without errors.
The puzzles themselves are fantastic and engaging, but the ambiance is what should make this a must-buy for fans of any genre. Each click helps weave together a living soundtrack that connects you with each puzzle. The aesthetics put you into the perfect "flow" mentality and add immensely to the overall experience. If you're a puzzle fan, don't hesitate to pick this up, and don't be surprised when you return to send a few copies to your friends and family.
