So, new Borderlands, played it for a while, decided to right a review months later. Here we go!
So what's new? New characters, new moon physics, new element, new gun type.
Unlike the old copy paste redux the characters were from  BL1 to BL2, the new crew are fresh, despite being preexisting characters in the series (Fragtrap takes all the copy paste for his own crazy ability, Vault_Hunter.exe).
The physics are what you would expect, though the oxygen mechanic does add a sense of urgency for (most) characters dawdling on the moon.
New gun type (fire ur lazors!!) Adds a neat little change, with the varying laser types catering to different wants and play styles, and the Ice Element is also a neat addition, one that definitely is felt when used and used against.
The story provides some nice back story on the events between the first two games, gives an idea of how characters became who they are and answers some "what happened to them?" Questions.
My only major gripes are that the base areas get to feel samey as you often frequent the same locations multiple times (but that's nothing new), and as much as it pains me to say it, 2K Australia made a good game, but a lot of the humor is very much so Australian based, so many jokes and references that aren't blatantly laid out or popularly known can be lost on some of the international audience.
Overall, a few small other gripes and the above two keep it from being absolutely great, but, if you love Borderlands and want more Borderlands, here's some Borderlands in space.

Shrooms is definitely an alpha, but a unique one with fun and potential! Give it a buy if you're hopeful, or maybe hold off and see where it goes for a while if you're unsure.
+Gameplay: Unique and interesting, barebones but good survival elements.
+Graphics: Exotic level design, variable player model.
+Audio: Sparse, but functional, good ambience.
-Couldn't go above 25FPS on any setting.
-Interface slightly clunky.
-Forest seems to be a deathtrap.
+/-Slightly finicky targeting issues.
Hello and welcome to this review of Shrooms, a game where you...eat shrooms! Wait, wait, that's not all there is to this, you eat shrooms to alter your body which changes the way you interact with the world! There are critters, monsters, basic crafting, and survival elements brought into the mix!
There's only so much to Shrooms right now, but what's there is good! So for every shroom you eat, it alters a part of you from the head, arms, legs, or your torso. This gives them different effects or passives such as but not limited to: invisibility, damage absorption, damage reflection, a high damage punch, longer underwater time, etc. This will allow you to interact with the world and its inhabitants in different ways. A refreshing and fun game concept!
The general gameplay will have you running around collecting ingredients so that you can make tools so that you can more efficiently gather ingredients (or better ones) so that you can fight, keep warm, or stock up on bow ammo. Basically, you're doing what you have to to survive and eating mushrooms to help along the way!
The graphics, while good, could use some improvement, especially given the FPS I get.
The environment design is exotic and unique, with a lot of glowing lights and unique land and rock formations, pretty water, and vegetation.
The UI is a bit large, but in terms of design seeks to be minimal, and currently could use a facelift. Getting around it is easy enough once you get used to it, though, with simple hotkeys, and everything spelled out conveniently in non-distracting places.
There isn't much there, but the ambience is nice, and the sounds your character makes sufficies with no crack or pop in the recording. For what they are, they're actually believable, too, which is nice.
All in all, in its current state, Shrooms is fairly barebones, but imaginative and unique, and it deserves credit for that. Unique player models for the mutations is a nice touch, which indicates not only time spent but love given. It's easy to envision this game becoming something great, however, and time will tell if the developers get it there!

The card game is annoyingly shallow and slow, but fortunately completely ignorable, except for an achievement that requires you to play too many card games.
The magic spells are disappointing and seem under-used. Most of the game is about overcoming dozens of obstacles to acquire magic spells, and then each spell only has limited effect and gets used in just one or two puzzles.
Still, I'd happily play a sequel if it ever happens.

This game tries to combine Half-Life, Omikron, old X-Com games, and Metal Gear Solid together, surprisingly doing an alright job of it.
If you are able to get through the bugs, glitches, and quirky mechanics that occasionally present themselves in this game, than Dues Ex will provide more hours of fun than any other PC game released during the year 2000.
Pro's:
- Good use of unlocks/upgrades to add more gameplay hours at a cheap programming cost
- Physics are not nearly as good as Hitman: Codename 47, but it was one of the pioneering games of physics for it's age
- Typical, easy to understand conspiracy story. (I consider this a good thing because I'd rather be learning  game mechanics than who is betraying who)
- Usually 2 or 3 ways to beat a quest/level. Stealth, Combat, or using Technology.
- Skills and augmentations (cybernetic upgrades) are a cool idea
- Limb, Torso, or Head specific damage and must applie med kit to the injured body part (hence x-com reference)
- Graphics are on par for the PC games of that year, nothing exceptional though
- Has some really unique and innovated paths for some levels
- Introduces hacking and bypassing security
- Long, compared to something like half-life
Con's:
- Augmentation system was very poorly implemented. Keys are horrible (can't rebind), don't know what to upgrade till endgame but thats okay, because it takes forever to upgrade anyway.
- Skills take forever to upgrade
- Suffers typical generic game killer cliches (accidently quick saving in a spot you can't get out, having a boss fight you spend all your items trying to win and  you are supposed to lose, not having a clue where the objective is and given no hints in your quest log, reusing models for different characters, and sometimes frustrating mechanics)
- Platforming is nowhere near the quality of half life, it's quite unacceptable for this year actually
- Swimming is glitchy without fluid movement, makes me wonder why they added so much of it
- I feel like half of the game is spent crawling in a vent
- Weapon damage makes me wonder sometimes, like the shotgun does the same as a dark gun at point blank.
Overall, the game is worth it for getting into the serries. It's simple, easy to follow, almost kind of cheezy at times, but its good fun and some very unique gameplay concepts that work well with the game, as long as you can get through the occassional frustrating aspects.

The successor to the classic Rome: Total War, Medieval II: Total War is a fun game that introduces new concepts and deals with a period of time from shortly after the Norman Conquest of England to the Age of Discovery. Among other events that will be affecting you in this time period are the Mongols showing up, gunpowder being introduced, the Black Death arriving and killing most of your population (don't worry it does the same to everybody), the Timurids following their Mongol ancestors, and then the beginning of the Age of Discovery. Castles and Cities develop in two separate ways, and produce different units.
If playing a Catholic nation, you have to deal with the Pope. He can make or break your nation, so keep an eye on your approval rating with him. After a victory, most of the factions are then unlocked. They are also unlocked individually if you happen to be the one to land the killing blow.
Side note: If you do unlock all the nations, three are the Moors, Egypt, and the Turks. Do take care of your volume at that time, because when you click a unit, move them, or attack with them, they do have a slight vocalization. Which at times could make people nervous (about killing infidels and the like). Some who hear you play may also get a bit nervous when you play the Holy Roman Empire (or the First Reich).

Not only can you create a weapon from scratch that suits you best, but you can then slightly tweak it to ensure it perfectly suits your playstyle. Want to sacrifice some accuracy while aimed in favour of accuracy for the hip? There's a stock for that. Prefer to see your enemies through walls over using a scope? There's a sight for that. The list goes on.
The majour flaw, however, is that with such indepth customization, there will ALWAYS be some combination that is over powered, or just plain annoying to deal with. My personal pet peeve is people creating generic, point and click high damage sniper rifles akin to those seen in modern shooters. Others will be greatly frustrated by people creating beam weapons which bounce damage to the nearest target, basically elimating the need to aim accuratly. You might even stumble across people who have leveled up and customized their rocket launcher to a point that it instantly kills you. Good fun.
So, if you have a lot of patience and yet a thirst for adreneline, you will adore this game. If you don't, you may find yourself rage quiting rather soon. Either way, it's free! Give it a go, darn it!

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a sequel to the original Witcher game. This one can be described as a "Console Port" and i reccomend a controller for gameplay (I did not use one and it was fine however). The game can be described as a Third Person RPG medieval fantasy with open combat. You play as Geralt a witcher...... yea I dont wanna spoil anything.
COMBAT COMPARISION TO THE FIRST GAME
I would like to compare Assassins of Kings to the original Witcher especially for first timer Witcher buyers who have heard of bad reviews for the first witcher. The combat is vastly improved from the "quick-time" combat system in the original to a more free form movement and attack system which is comparable to Dark Souls or similar TPS's I'm glad that the developer moved away from this tiring rhythm based clickfest to a more clean,fluid and deserving style which really pulled me away from all the great elements in the original Witcher's story and crafting gameplay.
Graphics - 6/10
I didnt run into any major graphical glitches such as black or grey glitched meshes and the graphics arent to outdated  or at least they wont be too distracting from the gameplay and story elements, no arguements in the style choice too the characters faces are geared more to realism then a cartoon style. For negatives, there seems to be an annoying haze over the whole game, im sure its part of the atmosphere of the world , but it just seems so unfiting to have a bright haze in a world which is all but bright, even nights seemed to have a "cheery " feel about them. perhaps if the bloom wasnt so high this would be tolerable but im just nit-picking right now and its up to personal preference. Shadows were aslo overdone imo I changed the brightness but some areas just seemed to dark even though torches were right there maybe its because there was no ambient occulsion or ray-tracing idk. This made me wish there was a feature to bring out a torch especially when you are crawling around a dark forrest.
Gameplay/Level Design -6/10
Combat is quite fluid once you get used to it. It is pretty much similar to many hack n slash games such as god of war however it relies more on blocking,dodging and signs(magic). Initally There is a good amount of balance in all skills, since you cannot rely on a singular OP skill to deal with every enemy some enemies are almost impossible to damage unless you cast a spell, and there are ample situations where blocking and dodging will have to be used to get into favourable positons. There are no completely redundant signs however generally Igni and Aard are the best in any situation.Skill trees branch off to sword use, magic and alchemy some of the skills are completely useless but  most found in each tree have a purpose(somewhat) sword use is the strongest out of them all by far (imo).
Geralt uses silver swords for supernatural beings and steel for regular beings this dynamic means that you will sometimes have to switch between the two swords which really spices up enemy encounters.
Alchemy is a nice touch to gameplay but not a necessity which is good for players who do not have the time to invest in it.You can coat your blades to do extra damage to specific enemies or drink potions to improve your in game stats , herbs and plants are found throughout the world basic RPG stuff. However there is one gripe, once you reach a certain part of the game you become so strong that you can literally spam one skill to kill any enemy which is strange since I played on hard mode.
Level design is quite annoying  in some situations where you are just spammed enemies in a corner to be baraged by hit after hit, just to die by constant staggering. It is espcially annoying since you can only hit 1-2 targets at a time unless you unlock a special skill. There arent many puzzle elements but the ones they included were quite entertaining and creative enough to not be regarded as mere "distractions"
Story/Soundtrack 7/10
Initally the story was a little generic I mean the war's where to highlighted and the "supernatural beings" were kind of disregarded in this release however once I started to become more invested in the story with the absolutely beatufiful comic-style flash backs ( I mean seriously these are just excellent) I started to have a real interest in the lore and gave myself to the story with the cliff-hangers suprises and disapointments that will be cleared up in the final game(I hope). I trust you It seems a bit slow at the start but I believe it is mostly world building for those who skipped the first game once you start to play into the game more it starts to really pick up.
The soundtrack was fitting but didnt really strike me as amazing or awe-inspiring its your typical medival-fantasy mix of real instuments with little audio adjustments.
TL;DR 19/30
Great game overall it took me around 30 hours to complete and was completely worth it. The game overall is quite well rounded and i have to occured any glitches or issues and it doesnt look like absolute trash compared to other games released around the same time period. Combat is vastly improved from the original game and can be compared to Dark Souls.
If you have not played the any witcher game and are considering purchasing The Witcher 3 make sure you pick up this one as a prelude for $2.50 when it goes on sale it is really worth the experience and sets you up with anticipation for The Witcher 3. It may seem slow at the start but give it a chance and you may become invested in the series like I  am!

A hybrid of Paradox's famous grand strategy game and a traditional 4X strategy game, Stellaris is a game for all who desire galactic dominion (whether military, diplomatic, or otherwise).  Stellaris has a considerable range of options for creating your own species (played by you, run by AI, or even shared with others), each of which has decided impacts on the strengths you will bring to the game without pidgeonholing you into a single path to victory.
Paradox did the strategy genre a great service by introducing a non-linear, non-static tech tree.  Instead, each time you complete a technology (in one of three very broad themes: physics, society, and engineering), you "draw" 3 (or more, depending on your government type and other technologies) possible technologies you can research, much like a card game.  The options you do not select have a chance to reappear again, although many factors keep it from being truly random (e.g. colony ship options are very likely to reappear soon, if you do not pick the tech from the start).  The game, including the new mini-expansion Leviathans, has several other systems (End Crises and Fallen Empries) that keep the mid and late game more interesting than the lull it can be in many other strategy games.
Multiplayer can be a blast, where you and your friends may have radically different playstyles, but can still band together in a powerful Federation, each become regional hegemonies, or just brawl to see who is the last human player standing.  Options to seed other players close together or evenly distributed among the rest of the galaxy let you really decide how much interaction you want to have with other players in the early game.
If you haven't played a Paradox game before, you'll be in for the promise of the game being continually updated and upgraded (even if you don't buy expansions) for years to come, much like their other products: Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis

Taro Yoko... a name that I will never forget and someone who's products I will always at least consider.
In merely roughly 30 hours I witnessed the uhmm, interactive credits (trying to spoil as little as I can). Right now I am going through the whole game for the second time, with full knowledge about the story and the world... this is one of the very few games that I will complete for 100% and I will enjoy every single bit of it.
So a few things you might've already heard or know from the first Nier game (haven't played it so can't compare it, but plenty of people that I know did). This game has multiple endings, from which plenty are for amusement but some aren't. Some users might experience issues with fullscreen mode and the game is locked at 60fps, whilest cutscenes are at 30. I am very used to keyboard and mouse controls, but if you aren't I do suggest a controller.
And that's it about the negative aspects from the game. They aren't exactly.. bad and most users won't mind them, neither did I actually. I will try to keep my review as much spoiler free as I can. The information you will find in here is pretty much common knowledge if you've googled this game at least once or looked through the community.
This game has a lot to offer. And each aspect is actually something that you will embrace... sooner or later.
Let's start out with the story of primarily 2B and 9S. Two androids that have to work together on a forsaken planet full of enemies and strangely enough plenty of nature. The story around those two is worked out extremely well as you will see and experience it from all perspectives. This causes the list of characters that you will get fond of to expand.
Whilest you are progressing through the story you will find some sub-quests to do. There aren't many compared to your average RPG, making this a lot more bearable and 100% worthy. Each sub-quest has it's own story. You don't need to finish it in order to understand the whole plot, but finishing them gives you a bit more information about the bigger picture. Making it required yet not. They don't take long to complete either, roughly said, most are just collecting resources. But it is worked out nicely.
There is a minimal upgrading system for weapons and skills in game. It isn't complex, works pretty well and will definitely enhance your experience. For example your characters makes use of chips. Each chip has its own perks. You can equip an x amount of those and upgrading a chip makes it stronger but reduces the amount of other chips you can equip.
The replayability in this game is really good. The first time you finish it, don't stop. You will be missing out on a lot. That is the one and only spoiler I will hand to you. You will be awarded with so much knowledge about the plot. You will look at things from another perspective, making things more interesting.
The story in this title is so rich that you almost think it can't get any better, but it does. The amazing soundtracks are one of a kind. I yet have to encounter a game that has a soundtrack so fitting to the game that I would enjoy it less by playing my own playlist on spotify. There are plenty of tracks that I just listened to, just standing at a not so crowded place in game to just enjoy the superb music. I've certainly wasted 1 hour doing this by now lmao. There is probably a total of 6 hours of music. And trust me, you will enjoy every minute of it. The genre really fits well with the environment, the scene and ofcourse the story.
So that brings us to the combat variations! There are plenty in game, a lot more than I expected to encounter and each of them is worked out extremely well. In the first 2 hours you will encounter all styles and it might be difficult in the beginning to get used to them in this combination, but you will appreciate the variaty. The classic hack and slash as shown in the trailers works a lot better than you'd guess. I'd say plenty of AAA titles could take an example from the combat system in here. Only Doom has a combat system as fluent as this. And I say this while having my fair share of combat games.
While at this point the review might be a bit hazy as I don't want to spoil the content as it is pretty easily spoiled am I willing to answer questions from people that are in doubt. It is worth buying and if you want the 100% it will take roughly 50 hours to do so. It will be enjoyable hours, otherwise if this game isn't your kind of thing you will notice it within the refund period of 2 hours.
If you are considering to buy it, buy it.
If you have doubts about the graphics, buy it.
If you need some relaxing music, buy it.
If you want to experience some great combat, but it.
If you want a story rich game, buy it.
If you want a complete game, buy it.
If you dislike the game, buy it, you will love it eventually anyway.
TL;DR:
- SOME people have issues with the fullscreen mode and windowed mode as well as the fps cap being at 60 and cutscenes at 30.
In order to make up for this you get:
+ A complete game
+ RPG elements
+ Great combat system
+ Amazing soundtracks
+ Story rich game
+ Replayability like no other
+ Probably some wisdom for life itself once you make it far enough

Harry Potter defeated his formidable antagonist, Lord Voldemort, and saved the world at the age of seventeen. Jeremiah Hazelnut defeated his formidable antagonist, Zaroff, and saved the world at the age of twelve.
Well, now I know why no letter-carrying owls nor magicians looking for apprentices had ever visited my house.
Okay, let’s be serious. Overall, The Night of the Rabbit is a very charming game that I have certainly had fun playing. It may seem to be a mundane game that teems with trite ideas at first glance: On a fine summer day, a little boy named Jeremiah Hazelnut, who desperately wishes to be a magician, is offered a chance by a mystical creature to make his dream come true. So he sets off on an adventure in another world to learn magic. Along his way, he encounters and befriends many other intriguing creatures. As he helps them resolve their problems and run their errands, his affection for this fascinating world and its residents grows. This affection, together with the discovery later on that his own world is, too, falling apart from the threat posed by the evil illusionist, Zaroff, turns into a will to challenge evil and make things right. In the end, he successfully saves the world and is eventually able to return home to his loving parents and a hearty dinner.
Yes, this game doesn't have an amazing plot, but it is the way the story is told that makes it enjoyable.
The start of the story is rather fairy-tale-like, giving rise to a somewhat childish tone – Similar to how in every fairy tale, no prince has ever asked why he has to save a princess, and no child has ever wondered why he must go on an adventure, you are not given any explanation as to why you should do what the game expects you to do. Let me elaborate. In the beginning of The Night of the Rabbit, Jerry receives a flying letter, so Jerry, without asking why, follows the instructions on the letter and summons a magical bunny. Then the bunny, who claims to be a magician, tells Jerry that there are so many things he needs to learn if he wants to be a magician, without explaining why Jerry has been chosen and why he is willing to help Jerry become a magician, and that they better hurry up. Then Jerry, without asking any questions, says “Ok” and together, they travel to another world. I know this may deter some players from continuing it. But trust me, after you get through this part, the story will only become more captivating. Plus, I was rather surprised to find out that these questions were answered in the end. A thumbs up to the developers for being scrupulous about this. :)
Now, let’s move on to the puzzles. Oh I really loved them. They are challenging but super fun to solve. Since there is a direct reference to Grim Fandango in The Night of the Rabbit and I had recently completed Grim Fandango, please allow me to make comparisons between these two. Generally, the puzzles in The Night of the Rabbit are a lot more player-friendly and logical to me compared to those in Grim Fandango. (Don't get me wrong, I love Grim Fandango.) Yes, some of the puzzles are obtuse, but most of them are good. I don’t want to sound like a know-it-all, but if you are stuck, checking your journal and giving yourself some time to stare at your inventory may help. Some puzzles may not be as hard as you think. Thinking out of the box is key.
However, the not-so-good aspects of this game are evident too. As much as possible, this game attempts to encompass a wide range of themes, such as friendship, courage, hope, love, and acceptance. But as I felt that the developers could have expanded their points further, I was generally unimpressed, at times even annoyed when their points sounded too pretentious.
Speaking of being pretentious, I still haven’t figured out why this game is called The Night of the Rabbit, and what Marquis means by that “Nothing is impossible” at the very end of the game. It feels like an awkward reference to what he has said in the beginning, but it’s so unnatural to say that under that circumstance.
Moreover, the ending of this game felt rushed, and it was clear that the developers weren’t planning their story so carefully anymore. Throughout the 11 hours I’ve spent on this game, I only genuinely enjoyed the first nine hours of it.
Besides all that, this game is still a lovely one that tells a story of bright imaginations, and is definitely worth a look if you are a fan of fairy tales and puzzle games.

One of the last decent games of the franchise
is nothing more than the linear shooter you've come to expect from the genre and series.
It doesn't revolutionize anything gameplay wise so you might be thinking why is this any different than any of the other CoD games I've played? Well its main selling point for me was the very riveting storyline and narrative the game has to offer. This is in my opinion the epitome of good stories featured in the CoD series.
The game will take you across several years of its timeline, featuring the war in Vietman, to the Cuban Missile crisis and even some late WW2 elements. The characters are there, over the top as you'd expect, with dialogue and voice acting fresh out of your American summer blockbuster (if you're a sucker for those look no further for your needs) but in truth it is really quite fitting and fun for the spirit of the game. There's twists and turns in the story as your delve deep into the depravity of war and the mind of the main character Mason, a CIA special operations agent who served during the Cold War . There's a lot to be said about the twist of the story, some might call it cheap and predictable but for me back when I played in 2010, I was pleasantly surprised and satisfied.
There's a nice atmosphere in the game overall and the transition between the different playable arcs and environments is excellently done.
Gameplay wise... well it's Call of Duty. It's as linear as it gets, it's aim down the sights until enemies die, it's the awkward vehicular combat (if you've played any of the battlefield series you know what I'm talking about), it's the 'shooting gallery' from a minigun/machine gun, it's the weird gadgets you'll use for a mission and then never see again. It's nothing new, it's nothing challenging but it's fun for a couple of hours. There's plenty of guns to use (side note, the sound design is pretty mediocre for most of the weapons) and there's plenty of enemies to kill and the level design is adequately done and some of the environments are part of a less explored theme in the FPS genre.
I know it's a 7 year old game but if you're a die hard fan of the CoD series like I am, you'd be remiss if you somehow haven't experienced Black Ops. Furthermore the game features a killer soundtrack and it is guaranteed to keep your blood pumping through the action sequences.
Before the downfall of the series began, before the over-saturation of the franchise, Black Ops stands like a beacon on how good Call of Duty used to be. These days might be long gone, but it's always nice to return to this after many years and see if it actually holds up to other titles. Naturally as years pass by this will steadily become less relevant but for a 7 year old game, it's actually not terrible visually wise. A great addition for your Call of Duty collection.

I've had this game outside of Steam for quite a while now:
For years, games come out one after another in a specific genre with the sole intention of being better than the last in many fields, or being unique in a multitude of ways. The genre of "RPG" or "shooter" is one that is often explored to the very end of it's capabilities - the introduction of new technology in games like Fallout 4 and The Witcher 3 are games that were and are very easily promised Game of the Year time and time again. But through the embers of blazing releases and trailers, there is a game that pioneered a variety of things in undue time.
And a measly review wouldn't do it justice.
Deus Ex is most likely one of the best games I've ever played. It's old, unoptimized, and sluggish nature is something I can very easily ignore and regard as setbacks of the age it was released in. Though it's time deteoriorated the mechanics and features, it also gave it an advantage - it shook the medium, and the seismic shock can still be felt to this day. The story is something that draws you in and immerses you into a world of conspiracy. The music is a lovely additive, and you can feel every synth, piano key, and guitar riff even for the time it was composed. The set pieces are convincing, well-made, and lovingly crafted with attention given all the way down to the back bowels of a New York City borough. Deus Ex is a marvel of engineering for the year 1999, and it's accomplishments can be appreciated in the present time.

First things first, this game works fine for me in Windows 10.
With an odd mixture of German and English text, this game seems like a half-hearted attempt to reach a larger audience than it would otherwise have.  The tutorial is minimal, but I did pick the gist of the game quickly enough I suppose.   The graphics look fairly dated and generic, but are serviceble enough I suppose.
The game play was the weakest part for me.  Basically the player is tasked with picking up vehicles with various thought-balloon "wants' and then dropping them at the appropiate venue.  Varous venues can be built, but several require the currency of "Bonuses" as well as in game money.  This one got very boring and repetitous for me very quickly.
Oddly, that doesn't mean it's easy.   One has to periodically restock one's venues, which is fair enough.  The problem is that I even dragging and dropping as quickly as I could, I found the restock fee negated any profit I was turning.   So I can add the word "fustrating" to the list of things that describe this game.
I got it during a 40% sale, for the price $1.79.  I don't have high hopes for games that run that cheap, so I guess I can say it's a fair value, if drag and drop games appeal to you.  For my part though, I wish I had given this one a pass.

Very fun game that's all about creating chaos. The premise is simple: you're a psychopath on an insane cross-country killing spree. You have to kill everyone at each party you attend without being arrested or dying yourself. You can stab people, or kill them in groups with various amusing traps. The core gameplay is super fun, though the game can occasionally get frustrating when you get stuck on some of the harder levels. And the difficulty is inconsistent, with a few levels feeling almost impossible at times. Still, as your skills grow, you'll appreciate some of the subtle strategies more and more. After beating the regular campaign, you can play another half dozen bonus levels that are wacky variations on the regular levels, and you can also unlock four additional characters, each of which have their own restrictions and extra powers that significantly change the nature of the game. It took me about ten hours to beat all the regular levels, but I feel like there's probably another 20-30hrs for completionists who want to beat every party with every character. Some of the combinations are incredibly challenging. So yeah, if you're looking for something a little different, where you're the unapologetic bad guy, check this out.

When I had a Commodore-64 there was a cheap knock-off of the "Friday the 13th" franchise.  I know that I probably used "Fast Hack'em" to get a copy.  ANd I wouldn't have paid for it.  But d*mn it was fun!
This game reminded me of my high-school days.  It's one of the few retro games that I think actually captured the spirit of the 1980s.
This game is surprising deep in the amount of strategy required to succeed.  Sure, you can just go on a rampage and start killing everything in sight.  But to do so successfully, without being caught -- therein is the rub.
Like many games, I could do without the plot.  I don't particularly care about why this guy is killing a sh*t-ton of people.  Though I do think it's pretty funny that basically he starts his killing spree because his neighbors won't stop partying and keep the noise down so he can get some sleep.
There is a ton of humor in the game -- it's funny sometimes to watch how the protagonist (who I guess is more anti-hero than protagonist) how he manages to kill people.  And perhaps the most satisfying elements is that you can take a hatchet to many of those hard-core gamers who live in their mothers' basement.
More than enough laughs here.  Hit the Lamborghini so that it runs over everyone standing at the entrance to the club.  Make sure that nobody see you duck out the window with that corpse.
And who truly know that dumpsters could hide so many bodies?  Nevermind, I don't want to know if you already had an estimation of that...
$13 is about right for this game.  There is a lot of content, a ton of replay value, And enough intrigue and strategy to make the idle moments of a Sunday afternoon pass with a high degree of content and satisfation.
As everything I write and review -- I am a casual gamer.  I have a life, a family, a career, and I work hard to pay off soul-crushing student loan debt.  I evaluate games based on whether I would purchase them again because they help me espace the real work.
Buy this game.  Yes, yes, yes, yes.  Buy it.  You're missing out on some fun if you don't.

I played Human Revolution so many years after the first Deus Ex that it wasn't clear to me why I had such a better experience with this game than with the newer one. To find out, I tried replaying this, but it was just too old-looking, too ugly, too clunky for me to bother. Enter Revision, aimed at exactly what I wanted to do: replay the first game, in such a state that I might be able to actually enjoy it.
The mod pushes the original game's engine to its limits and beyond. But even with that in mind, don't go in thinking Revision will look like a game from 2010. It's more like what we remember games from 2002 to look like, and this game, unmodded, looks like what we think we remember games from 1991 to look like. But suffice to say, although it does look old, it is a smooth and enjoyable experience. You're not playing Revision in order to get wowed by next-gen graphics, you're doing it in order to enjoy the original Deus Ex using a modern computer. And the mod delivers a really great experience, preserving the important elements from the original year 2000 edition, and upgrading what needed it. Awesome. This game gets a 10/10. And I don't hand out 10s easily, at all. But it deserved it back in 2000 when it was released, and still deserves it today, given that Human Revolution was no match for it.
Now back to the comparison between the original (well, the Revision Mod, but it's the original anyway) and Human Revolution: this is better than HR, and here's why. Over the course of the first mission in this game, my guy had obtained: a pistol, an electric prod, a mini crossbow, all of which are given to you at the start, depending how you choose what they give you, as well as, 4 gas grenades, a sniper rifle, a flamethrower, a crowbar, a combat knife, a baton, 3, yes, THREE weapon upgrades: a laser, a scope, and a mag expansion, and then the non-weapons: 2 sets of night vision goggles, a hazmat suit, a rebreather, and I might forget a toy or 3. Oh, and an augment to add to your character.
Compare that to the MISERY that the 2011 game imposes upon you, where you have practically nothing (I forget the details) and weapons and upgrades are hard to come by, not mentioning that you have NO ROOM in your inventory to carry anything extra.
BUT THAT'S NOT ALL
The first Deus Ex allows you to use your augments a LOT during the game. As such, you eventually turn into a kind of super-human being of disproportionate abilties, only the missions get progressively more impossible, REQUIRING you to use your augments and numerous toys in order to accomplish them. The 2011 game gimps you. The energy bars are SO RARE that you rarely get to use your superpowers.
So between the lack of invetory space, toys, and energy bars, the 2011 Deux Ex: Human Revolution is far from as enjoyable as this game, which lets you do so much more.
My hope is that Mankind Divided brings us back to this formula. I don't mind having to expand the carrying capacity, but I mind being so gimped that I can only carry a pistol and a tranq gun, and then 2-3 knick-knacks, for the first 5 hours. I don't mind upgrading my energy cells and recharge capacity, but I mind not being able to use my augs because there are 2 energy bars per level, allowing me 20 seconds of augmented abilities per 3 hours of play.
I understand those things make it EASY to "balance" the game difficulty, but I also know it makes the game a hell of a lot less fun to play. We want toys and we want to be able to use them!!!
This game? AWESOME. The Revision mod? AWESOME. It lets you see all that there is to hope for in Mankind Divided, and it's a heck of a good time.

Don't waste your time and just go straight to Witcher 3. You would think being a 6 year old game, that it would actually run decent on a 3 year old computer, but this ♥♥♥♥♥ is a system hog even on the lowest settings. I tried to make it work with a mod to tweak the settings to even lower, but it is just not worth it.
Once you get the game to run smoothly: The story is excellent. However there is alot of running from point A to B, backtracking from point B to A, talk to person x, y, z etc. At its core the gameplay is a simple hack and slash with a few unique spells, some dodging and rolling. The spell combinations along with enhancements can make things interesting, however they end up feeling tedious.
The tedium of the gameplay comes from how obtuse the controls and interface are. You can only drink potions and apply enhacements out of combat when you meditate. The game goes for a minimalist interface, showing you almost nothing except your health and currently equiped spell. Everything else is hidden away under the quick menu. Also the game has no way of viewing all the controls, so you spend the first few hours fumbling away until you are forced to open your browser to google the actual controls.
But even then, lo and behold the FULL controls aren't even listed online. For example the game never tells you that you can loot everything by pressing space, as opposed to having to click on each item individually. The "tutorial" is also an absolute joke, whoes idea of showing the player the ropes is shoving a bunch of textboxes in their face and having them press each button a few times. Maybe it would have been better if the tutorial and help boxes were voiced and better explained.
But then if you get past the control scheme and hope to start playing the game in earnest, sure there's a great story, but this doesn't diminish the tedium of going back and forth from points A to B, Or quests or bosses that have stupid gimmicks that force you to play in a very specific way/order to pass it. For example the game has a purely stealth section very early in the game, but the help box that tells you how to do a ♥♥♥♥ing stealth kill fades in 2 seconds, and the hitbox for it to register as a stealth hit is ♥♥♥♥ing tiny.
In another instance a boss seems to be literally whipping your♥♥♥♥♥ Until you watch a youtube video and it tells you to watch out for when it raises its gigantic tentacles so you can properly dodge it, and that the boss literally cannot touch you if you back away to the edge of the arena... The game could have given these tips to you during the fight through the accompanying NPC in the fight, but all the NPC does is repeatedly shout at you to cast the trap sign. Great! I would do that if I knew how to survive.
At the end of the day you hack and slash your way to victory once you've figured out each quest/bosses gimmick and enjoy some well earned story. Finally! But honestly if story is the only saving point of this game, then I would be much better of simply watching a playthrough of it, or better yet, playing the much improved and better sequel Witcher 3.

So depending on what resolution and hardware you are running you may need to turn some setting down to compinsate. The game also includes an arena section accessable from the main game menu and is a great way to try out new to help get you used to the control scheme or even help you to dial in your controller settings. Now if you look at this game and go "Oh, look! A space Team Fortress 2!" You wouldn't be too far off, yet you would be so, so, absolutely far from the truth. There are certain aspects of this game to me that define it. This game is 3rd person although from the steam page you don't get that feel... I don't like 3rd person shooters... at all. But this one I decided ti give a chance and where it let me down I was rewarded in MANY other catagories. The controls are great except rolling is a little finnicky to get the hang of (you need to kind of hit control with the middle of your finger, unless you're not sprinting whilst rolling which almost never happens). This game's art style is similar to TF2, its feel is like TF2, however, gameplay wise, this game is very unique. Rolling, sprinting, jumping, aiming, shooting and gore... lots and lots of gore. But if you don't like that it CAN be turned off in the options.
But the real winner here is the guns, yes that's right, the GUNS. This takes CoD's gun making system and make it look like child's play. Weapon types, stocks, barrels, scopes, magazines and even the bullets themselves have a billion options as to how they behave and if they're special bullets. This game is great too in saying that in casual there is no ammo, so you can shoot away to your hearts content until you die rather than stressing about running out of ammo. You can name individual guns and customise your loadouts (and yes, name them too). This game also has a very friendly community as I've seen so far, so don't be afraid. At the time of writing the team speak id bugged, there are a few problems with ALT+TAB'ing but they are so easy to forgive when you play this game.

So, I decided to wait until I had completed every bit of this game to write this review and I should say:
This game is easily one of the best game I have ever played and enters the category of
- Soundtrack:
The music in this game is AMAZING, one of its strongest points. It works so well with the story and bosses fights that makes you have goosebumps from how epic this makes you feel. Also  exploration have some nice and peaceful musics that keeps you really immersed.
- Story:
I wish some characters had more development on their personality. But overall, it is very nice and on some points really makes you think about life and existence. It has 5 main endings, 26 on total. All of them based on the choices you make during the game.
- Gameplay:
There's a variety gameplay elements and the combat is very responsive and fun. Also you have a lot of options to build with the plug-ins, weapons and pods you can find.
- Difficulty:
I like how difficulty works in this game. Yeah, theres some weird difficulty spike between normal and hard, but if you have never played this game before, you should play on normal until you are familiar with the controls, then you can change to hard. On hard you can be one shotted if you aren't careful, but it's cool that you have some sense of danger instead of just face rolling through everything on normal. Very hard are for hardcore people and pretty much anything can one shoot you, so you have that option too if you feel like it.
- Graphics:
It's alright, it fits the theme of the game.
- PC Port:
Until this day, the port still have problems with fullscreen resolutions and performance, but it can be somewhat fixed by some 3rd party mods and it's totally playable. Hopefully improve their next ports in the future.

Beat the game on Hardened in ~7 hours.  Didn't do any achievement hunting, and didn't notice any collectible intelligence tapes until I was about 2/3rds through the game.  4 missions in, I very nearly stopped playing because I wasn't having any fun. I would only recommend this game 1) if it was a deep discount and 2)you really want to be a completionist for the Call of Duty series.
(I had just finished Modern Warfare 3 and immediately started playing Black Ops.)
Treyarch simply isn't as good as Infinity Ward when it comes to this series.  Their writing and level design are ok, but if you put them into close comparison with IW (again, I literally finished MW3, uninstalled it, installed Black Ops, and started playing it) there are huge gaps.  AI is a great example - with IW, the AI serve to guide your character along, fill in plot points, and generally not get in the way of you having fun.  In Black Ops, the AI basically stands around and say the same 4 or 5 lines over and over (such as Enemy Down. That's a confirmed kill.  You're getting shot up, get to cover.)  What a waste of Ed Harris, Gary Oldman, Ice Cube, and Sam Worthington.
AI is monumentally stupid as well - they are completely dependent on your character and will just stand around occasionally shooting until you get far enough ahead that they run up after.  Meanwhile, enemy AI will run right past them and kill you while your squad does nothing.  Enemy AI is almost singularly focused on you.  There was one level "Khe Sanh" where marines would be scripted to literally stand in a line at the top of a ridge even though there was a barrier 5 feet to the right.  If you stand near these marines, the enemy from all over the battlefield would take shots at only you, and when they charged right up the hill shooting at you, the marines would stand there.  This behavior was standard - enemies could frequently run right past your squad to melee or shoot you.
Level objectives are often unclear - they don't appear on screen and what exactly you need to do isn't always told to you.  The Khe Sanh level is a good example.  You are being overrun by infinite enemies and there are two napalm barrels you need to puncture and knock over for some reason.  There is nothing to tell you that you need to do this (the AI mentiones they haven't been buried yet, but that's it), though sometimes the AI will yell "We need to improvise, Mason!".  There are no objective markers on the barrels, no "target" floating over them like other levels.  They aren't glowing, and shooting them does nothing (but apparently your knife will punch right through the steel).  You have to get right next to them before the prompt appears for interaction which has your character stab them with your knife and them kick them down the hill.
Level design is sparse compared to the IW entries in the COD series.  Lots of small alcoves and staircases that end in closed doors which were purely there to give them a place to spawn enemies to pour out of, but also invisible barriers in tall grass and knee high rocks that you can't scale...hallmarks of level design that doesn't organically guide the player through the game.  In comparison to MW3 where you found that they filled levels with a lot more detail.  There, you can move through a burned out apartment building that actually looks like an apartment building.  Black Ops is very much an On Rails game.
The game has many aspects that you'll find familiar in the COD series - controlling a gunship, riding and shooting in vehicles, regenerating health, invisible checkpoints you need to cross to get enemies to stop spawning, planting explosives, and so on.  Some weapons have different types of ammo you can switch between, or different firing modes.  For some reason, they have a crossbow as one of your military-issued weapons.  No idea why except maybe they thought it was cool?  Personally, I'd rather have a scoped dragunov.  You can't say the purpose is to have a silent distance weapon, since you are literally told to use the explosive bolts when you first get it.  Again, give me an M16 with an m203 "Thumper" under the barrel instead.
The story of this game was interesting, but Treyarch was much more interested in the sci-fi delivery of it than actually telling it.  The premise is that you're being interrogated and are reliving all the missions as memories.  This is a jarring break when you're in the middle of evacuating a base in the middle of enemies and the screen goes to black and you hear the voiceover chime in "That's how you escaped, but what happened to...." and you find yourself pulled out of the action.  This is basically makes it a poor version of Assassin's Creed but without any attachment to the character.  The President literally tells you that are "The Best. Anywhere."  But I never felt like that in the game's story.  I was an idiot surrounded by bigger idiots.

I played Human Revolution so many years after the first Deus Ex that it wasn't clear to me why I had such a better experience with this game than with the newer one. To find out, I tried replaying this, but it was just too old-looking, too ugly, too clunky for me to bother. Enter Revision, aimed at exactly what I wanted to do: replay the first game, in such a state that I might be able to actually enjoy it.
The mod pushes the original game's engine to its limits and beyond. But even with that in mind, don't go in thinking Revision will look like a game from 2010. It's more like what we remember games from 2002 to look like, and this game, unmodded, looks like what we think we remember games from 1991 to look like. But suffice to say, although it does look old, it is a smooth and enjoyable experience. You're not playing Revision in order to get wowed by next-gen graphics, you're doing it in order to enjoy the original Deus Ex using a modern computer. And the mod delivers a really great experience, preserving the important elements from the original year 2000 edition, and upgrading what needed it. Awesome. This game gets a 10/10. And I don't hand out 10s easily, at all. But it deserved it back in 2000 when it was released, and still deserves it today, given that Human Revolution was no match for it.
Now back to the comparison between the original (well, the Revision Mod, but it's the original anyway) and Human Revolution: this is better than HR, and here's why. Over the course of the first mission in this game, my guy had obtained: a pistol, an electric prod, a mini crossbow, all of which are given to you at the start, depending how you choose what they give you, as well as, 4 gas grenades, a sniper rifle, a flamethrower, a crowbar, a combat knife, a baton, 3, yes, THREE weapon upgrades: a laser, a scope, and a mag expansion, and then the non-weapons: 2 sets of night vision goggles, a hazmat suit, a rebreather, and I might forget a toy or 3. Oh, and an augment to add to your character.
Compare that to the MISERY that the 2011 game imposes upon you, where you have practically nothing (I forget the details) and weapons and upgrades are hard to come by, not mentioning that you have NO ROOM in your inventory to carry anything extra.
BUT THAT'S NOT ALL
The first Deus Ex allows you to use your augments a LOT during the game. As such, you eventually turn into a kind of super-human being of disproportionate abilties, only the missions get progressively more impossible, REQUIRING you to use your augments and numerous toys in order to accomplish them. The 2011 game gimps you. The energy bars are SO RARE that you rarely get to use your superpowers.
So between the lack of invetory space, toys, and energy bars, the 2011 Deux Ex: Human Revolution is far from as enjoyable as this game, which lets you do so much more.
My hope is that Mankind Divided brings us back to this formula. I don't mind having to expand the carrying capacity, but I mind being so gimped that I can only carry a pistol and a tranq gun, and then 2-3 knick-knacks, for the first 5 hours. I don't mind upgrading my energy cells and recharge capacity, but I mind not being able to use my augs because there are 2 energy bars per level, allowing me 20 seconds of augmented abilities per 3 hours of play.
I understand those things make it EASY to "balance" the game difficulty, but I also know it makes the game a hell of a lot less fun to play. We want toys and we want to be able to use them!!!
This game? AWESOME. The Revision mod? AWESOME. It lets you see all that there is to hope for in Mankind Divided, and it's a heck of a good time.

While the game looks and sounds very nice, in the end, it just isn't fun. There's enormous potential here, but it isn't utilized the way it could be.
Traps are one-use-per-level, and rarely take out enough people to be considered effective. By the time you've used up all of your available traps, there's still 20-30 people left to kill. This means you have to wait for each of them to move to a secluded spot so you can kill them.
Additionally, being seen next to a dead body means the police will be called on you. In many cases, you have nowhere to run, and even your (extremely limited) sprint isn't fast enough to escape. If a cop grabs you, you instantly lose and have to restart the level from the beginning. For me, this meant spending an hour on one level, waiting for people to wander from the group so I could kill them, only for someone to see me and force me to start from the very beginning.
The game has a ton of potential, but it just isn't executed well at all. If there was a way to lure people towards traps or to more easily escape the police, the game would be much, much better. As it is now, it just turns into a long, tedious grind.

I'm gonna be honest: I haven't played the original "Don't Starve" and I also received this game as a gift from family. As such, you may want to take my words with a grain of salt. That being said, there seems to be little difference between the two games (at least from what I can gather), so most of what I say should apply to the original as well.
"Don't Starve Together" is exactly what it sounds like: It's "Don't Starve" with multiplayer. Even so, if you insist on going alone, there's absolutely nothing stopping you from starting up a game and setting the maximum player count to 1.
As in every survival game, the goal of the game is, you guessed it, to avoid dying of starvation... or dying in general. You have three stats to contend with: Hunger, Health, and Sanity. Hunger is pretty much a staple of survival games. You know the drill, eat food or you'll die of hunger. Health should also be a familiar. Try to take on a monster unprepared, and you'll be dead quicker than you can say, "I'm sorry, Wilson!" Sanity, however, is unique. As you play the game, certain things take a toll on your mental health, such as battling monsters or being in the dark. As your characters goes more and more nuts, strange things start to happen. You start imagining monsters, you hear creepy ambience, glowing eyes stare at you in the dark, etc. If you let your character go COMPLETELY off the deep end, those monsters that were just incorporeal, transparent silhouettes become much more real and will attack your hysterical character. Of course, there are ways for you to regain your levelheadedness, such as through sleep, picking flowers, certain foods, etc.
This game has some rather unique bits to it. For one thing, it actually has a season system. As you play the game, the seasons will start to change, and with each seasonal change comes new survival challenges. You have to stave off the cold in the winter and avoid roasting to death in the summer, for example. Along with those seasons comes changes in the daylight cycle. Nights become the shortest in the summer and longest in the winter, much like in real life.
Perhaps the biggest selling factor of this game is its art style. Take a look at some gameplay footage or screenshots. Does  the art style not remind you of a certain animator? Between the hand-drawn art style, the grotesque and bizzare monster designs, and the exaggerated character features, this game just screams Tim Burton!
One final note is that this game has a pretty excellent modding community on the Steam Workshop. With new characters, custom items, and fan-made utilities, there's something for almost anyone! Don't want mods? Not a problem! The vanilla game is still just as much fun!
My verdict? 94/100. I would definitely recommend this game! The only reason you should NOT get it is if you already have "Don't Starve" and couldn't care less about multiplayer.

The plot is almost perfect, Geralt is caught and is accused of killing King Foltest, and from here starts his journey together with other characters to clean up his name and to save Temeria. Plots, action and unexpected twists. Old-fashioned but still pleasant graphics, certain settings can still amaze. The combat system that I found fun, is very similar to the one of The Witcher 3. Classic of the RPGs, the choices that the game makes us do are reflected on the plot to follow, and often are very difficult, making us fond or hate even more to Geralt and the characters involved.
Some things that I found uncomfortable are perhaps the lack of mobility of Geralt in the movements, in the sense that if you want to get off a wall or a small hill you can not. You have to go around, unless it's a default point by the developers. Fast transport is missing, but honestly it is not even necessary in this chapter of The Witcher, take a few steps more never hurts and the routes are always short-lived, even if sometimes they are a bit repetitive. As for the longevity, while in The Witcher 3 losing much of the secondary I arrived at 50h, in The Witcher 2 leaving almost all secondary to finish the story as soon as possible I arrived at 20h. I remember you guys that I did not play almost any secondary, so it will certainly be more long-lived.
The price would be more than justified even if it costs 50 euros, while it normally costs 20 (which already in my opinion is like stealing).
If you wait for discounts instead, the price usually comes down to 3 euros, which is the deal of your life.

I have started a new game of The Witcher 2 on three separate occasions. Each time, I had difficulty getting interested in the setting. I completed the first Witcher game years ago, and liked it originally, but despised the sheer volume of backtracking in it. It felt akin to playing an MMO. This sequel fares far better when it comes to backtracking and distance between locations, in my opinion, wasting a lot less of my time, though the issue does still remain to some extent.
The Witcher 2, however, doesn't really get under my skin in that regard, though. While the combat is significantly harder than it was in the first game, in my opinion, and despite me being a wuss who doesn't like a lot of difficulty much of the time, I actually prefer the changes to this game's combat when compared to the original game. I feel like I have more agency as a player while rolling around and choosing my attacks against specific targets. It also feels kinda rewarding for me when I take out of tough arrangement of enemies.
My qualms with The Witcher 2 lie mostly with simple dissatisfaction with the lore/setting. This is entirely subjective, of course, but I did not really like where I was, what I was doing, etc. The place, the people, the monsters...none of it appealed to me. I recommend what I like, and I have been staring at this game on my installed games list for months, not touching it despite this being my third attempt at completing the game. I got just barely into the second act (I finished the prologue and Act I), and could not force myself to push on for much longer. The monsters lack personality or intelligence, all seeming to be dumb and ugly, without any qualities that made me interested in them, amused by them, or liking them. The people, aside from Geralt's friends, didn't interest me or seem all that likable. The area I was in during the first act was just a place...pretty, I suppose, but nothing that made me interested in it.
I would have wagered that my preference for modern and sci-fi settings over fantasy might be to blame, but Game of Thrones has my complete attention and fascination when I watch it. I love the characters, the locations, the lore...but in The Witcher 2, nothing grabs me. When all else fails, only gameplay is left to try and keep me playing. It's certainly a decently made game when it comes to gameplay, but I did not find The Witcher 2's gameplay to be enticing enough to make me choose playing it over dozens of other games I would rather play that have gameplay I enjoyed more or superior characters/story/settings, etc. It is for this reason that I think my third attempted playthrough of The Witcher 2 will be my last. People claim The Witcher 3 is phenomenal, but if the lore and people are anything like in 2, I cannot see myself having a pleasant time with it. Also, missing out on story from 2 seems like it would make playing 3 offputting.

Borderlands: TPS has taken a lot of flak for a variety of reasons, including game length, lack of DLC, sometimes-awkward humor, impressions that some game areas were rushed, and other complaints along those lines.  Certainly there's truth to a lot of that, but the game is quite solid overall, and I've had a great time with it (played through the main storyline with three characters so far).
Mechanically, I think the combat in TPS is better than that in B2, mostly just because of a wider variety of weapons thanks to the lasers, and the added low-gravity boosting and butt-slam techniques.  When I hop back into B2, I've found I miss those quite a bit.  I've been finding the player characters a blast to use as well, with some fun skill trees to explore.  Humor's subjective, of course, but to me the jokes land far more often than they miss, and I'm quite fond of the pervasive Australian influence.
Complaints about the amount of story content are difficult to shrug off when compared to B1 and B2, which were both longer and featured far more story DLC, so your hours-per-dollar ratio is going to be lower than with the other two.  However, TPS really only suffers in comparison - there's plenty of story to be had here, and even though it seems likely we'll only ever get the Claptastic Voyage story DLC, there's a lot to keep you amused.
It's certainly a shame that we don't seem likely to get more story DLCs, though.  Likewise, some areas do certainly feel like they were rushed.  Vorago Solitude feels particularly empty, for one.  The TPS narrative is a little underwhelming as well, partially because it's acting as a bridge between two already-established plots, and partially just 'cause the Vault Hunters seem to have less agency this time around than usual.  (Not that you ever did anything but accept other people's missions in B1 and B2, but I felt more like a spectator this time around.)
Still, I can't imagine that anyone who enjoyed B2 wouldn't also enjoy TPS, so long as they're not mentally expecting something "bigger" than B2.  B2 is almost certainly the better game overall, due to the sheer amount of content and relative tightness of the plot, but TPS has been keeping me well amused for some time now, and I'm already looking forward to diving in as another character.

Where do I begin with this game? This game is good in various aspects... and honestly, terrible in others. The main aspect of the game is supposed to be "
". Well, you can certainly build what you want within reason, but if you're just starting out, don't expect more than a standard rocket launcher and/or assault rifle, and maybe craft yourself a healing beam weapon to aid your allies. More often than not, you're only going to be using one weapon offensively anyhow while the other is a more 'show-y' weapon. And I mean, that's good—you want a game that gives you variety, and this game gives you the means to create whatever you want... but the 'play your way' part gets sort of left behind when there's really only a few ways that some game modes can be played. In a game with near-infinite construction capabilities, it's just a sad fact that some weapon combinations are just going to perform much better than others. Why get fancy with a long-range Pyro beam gun and a laser-guided ricocheting Tesla rocket launcher with six rockets in a clip... when I can just go standard with a custom-made sniper rifle and a silenced fully-automatic machine gun and just play the game really well?
And speaking of game modes... if you're going to play,
. So far, there are four... what one could call 'finished' game modes:
•
, in which one person is the 'collector' and the other three players try to defeat the other team's collector in order to slow their progress (
);
•
, which is a King of the Hill / control point-centric game mode;
•
which, if you've played Call of Duty, is like the 'Kill Confirmed' game mode in simplest terms; and
•
, which is a more traditional version of Capture the Flag only the flag is a hammer and you can crush people with the flag and it has an absurdly high range.
While these are good game modes, playing with ignorant players—of which there are many, I won't mince words—can easily mean your downfall.
For starters, in Extraction, it does the team no good to be constantly healing the collector when he's off in the middle of nowhere picking up hunks of glowing blue ore, nor does it do anyone any good to let the enemy collector go about his business because you're in a race to see who can collect and extract the most 'Blutonium', as the game mode implies; in Blitz, everyone just runs off on their own without any objective... as with any King of the Hill-type game, it takes teamwork to capture a point, and it goes faster with more people; with Death Snatch, most players don't think to pick up the glowing things that drop from enemies on death (
); and with Jackhammer, the range of the hammer is completely inconsistent as you can try swinging at someone directly in front of you and they have a chance of surviving what should be a one-hit kill, but you can be anywhere from twenty to fifty feet away from the enemy and the hammer's shockwave will seek you out and make sure you suffer the most excruciating death imaginable.
That said, I can't fault the game in any way so far except maybe being too brief or non-descriptive; it's the players that really make or break the game, and this early in the game's infancy, the players just don't know what's going on... but hopefully that will change in time, presumably for the better.

This game has a great balance of whimsical, charming and adventurous, to dark, mischievous, and  meditative. The art is very pleasant to look at and there are many elements and details drawn into the scene so you never get bored with what you are looking at!

The dialogue between you and the characters are never too long, you can easily end them if you want to, but I found what they had to say very interesting that most of the time i'll be clicking on each speech option to see how the characters will reply!
Some of the puzzles were a bit obscure and frustrating (meaning I clicked around for over 15 minutes wondering if I missed something and I will have to look up a hint online) but 80% of it is just challenging enough (able to progress to the next part of the story in less than 15 minutes)
Overall this is an awesome point-and-click game, and I highly recommend it!

Party hard is a puzzle game whereby you must kill everyone at a party that takes place on a single screen (40-60 people on average) without being seen.  You accomplish this by your knife and evironmental interactions.  You also must hide the bodies so nobody gets wise of what you are doing.  The levels are also partially randomly generated and the behavior of the people at the party always differs.
The game LOOKS a lot like "Hotline Miami", but dont make the assumption it is the same type of game. This is a much more slow-paced game where you have to decide who to take out next. Picking the right victims and the best times and using all the resources available to you is key.
The game is really quite fun and well made. My only real gripes are some of the voice acting, dialogue in the cut-scenes, and while the music is catchy, it can get old, especially when the levels are 25 minutes long.  Other than that, the game is really great.
It is also getting workshop support for unlimited content, which is really cool. Would very much recommend.

This game is really fun, but not for everyone. Even though I do think the appearence is very nice and do not care about the
preferred 30fps you play it with, there is a slight problem: There is no real stress or adrenaline-powering motion within 90% of the game. Let me explain it a bit further.
Most songs are pretty long, which isn't a real problem itself, but how the game works is that you try to hit as few 'bullets' as possible. The player is really free to move however he wants to, because he is not asked to move to a specific point most of the time, but to the emptiness to hide from everything that is flying across the screen. Even though this may sound promising, in reality it makes it really dificult to know where the *** you have to go for the first hours you play the game.
Secondly, the only moment you feel happy is when you're able to get 100% out of a level, while hitting things doesn't mean you die, it only means a little number goes down. I do really think the game would be better if you somehow could die and the level started again, while it makes the ending of the song more of an surprise and makes you more active trying to dodge all bullets.
The game looks like a very intens game, but when played, feels like the slowest thing you have ever done with a mouse, even though everything rushes past you.
But this is all just my opinion, I have a few friends who don't think this is a real problem and LOVE it. So, even though I do think playing this game for a long time isn't really what it's made for, it sure is fun at the beginning.
Sorry if my opinion isn't really build up well, first time doing this :p

Loadout is one of few F2P games that doesn't force you to buy items to get an advantage. There is plenty of free guns you can use that make you just as good as the other guy. Character customization is limited to free players, but that is understandable.
The game itself feels like a mix of Brink and TF2. (before you say anything, this is a good thing). The action is very fast paced, with creative maps and great visuals. All of the weapons each have their pros and cons, which balances them out greatly, so no one really has a huge advantage over the other. Loadout is all about loadouts, obviously, which allow you to have grenades and two weapons. The taunts in Loadout are also hilarious, and never get old. The gore in loadout is also quite funny and creative. (for example, you can be running around with no face...only your eyes and brain, which mixed with the cartoony visuals makes it very funny.)
So, to wrap things up, Loadout is a very fun multiplayer arena shooter, and I highly advise that you download it now! There is plenty of content for F2P players, and the 4v4 combat is very fun.

Borderlands: TPS has taken a lot of flak for a variety of reasons, including game length, lack of DLC, sometimes-awkward humor, impressions that some game areas were rushed, and other complaints along those lines.  Certainly there's truth to a lot of that, but the game is quite solid overall, and I've had a great time with it (played through the main storyline with three characters so far).
Mechanically, I think the combat in TPS is better than that in B2, mostly just because of a wider variety of weapons thanks to the lasers, and the added low-gravity boosting and butt-slam techniques.  When I hop back into B2, I've found I miss those quite a bit.  I've been finding the player characters a blast to use as well, with some fun skill trees to explore.  Humor's subjective, of course, but to me the jokes land far more often than they miss, and I'm quite fond of the pervasive Australian influence.
Complaints about the amount of story content are difficult to shrug off when compared to B1 and B2, which were both longer and featured far more story DLC, so your hours-per-dollar ratio is going to be lower than with the other two.  However, TPS really only suffers in comparison - there's plenty of story to be had here, and even though it seems likely we'll only ever get the Claptastic Voyage story DLC, there's a lot to keep you amused.
It's certainly a shame that we don't seem likely to get more story DLCs, though.  Likewise, some areas do certainly feel like they were rushed.  Vorago Solitude feels particularly empty, for one.  The TPS narrative is a little underwhelming as well, partially because it's acting as a bridge between two already-established plots, and partially just 'cause the Vault Hunters seem to have less agency this time around than usual.  (Not that you ever did anything but accept other people's missions in B1 and B2, but I felt more like a spectator this time around.)
Still, I can't imagine that anyone who enjoyed B2 wouldn't also enjoy TPS, so long as they're not mentally expecting something "bigger" than B2.  B2 is almost certainly the better game overall, due to the sheer amount of content and relative tightness of the plot, but TPS has been keeping me well amused for some time now, and I'm already looking forward to diving in as another character.

This is quite frankly one of the best games I've ever played. A responsive active battle system, on top of a beautiful world for you to explore, with deep characters and a multi-layer storyline, topped with a great soundtrack.
Keep in mind that "playing again once you beat it the first time", in this game, is not about "replayability". It's part of the story. If you thought you knew what the game was about after finishing it once, you're in for a ride. You've not finished this game at all until you play it to at least three of the endings (all of which happen in sequence).
The plot thickens. The characters get more human. You get to know each the characters better (even the enemies), understand what happened from their point of view, and get to the bottom of what is actually happening behind the scenes.
I highly recommend you play this with a joystick (I myself play with a DS4). Oh, and if you're wondering, you can play it with the audio in Japanese, and English subtitles.

This game starts off in a very casual fashion, it illustrates a world of a boyhood adventure and instantly throws the magic. The puzzles are nothing compared to Professor Layton, but none the less most are quite engaging. In addition to that the plot plays a strong part in these puzzles and if you haven't been paying attention you will miss out on critical elements of the solution. There are a few moments in this game where I found myself completely lost for any kind of direction, perhaps because I played it in small sessions. Regardsless, a guide might well be called for and I think the developers anticipated the player's access to the internet, so they could tell a story rather than make a mechanically perfect game. The plot itself is lovely and quite imaginative, it really manages to spark the inner twelve-year-old. That said due to the game's short duration and proportionally long build-up to the climax at the very end most if not all the characters recieve an amount of depth that is just short of truely satisfying. I find the level of detail revealed during the final reveal to be a bit lacking, fleshing out the characters with just a few more sentences would have completed the spark of childhood fantasy. Instead the characters fall a bit flat where they really shouldn't, the same goes for the names. I perfectly understand if not all names are all that imaginative, but the density of imaginative names is just the tiniest bit off, especially considering that all the shops have properly fleshed-out names. Blue juice really ought to have had a proper brand name, even if the colloquialism would be blue juice.
In short if you want a boyhood adventure game this ought to suit you very well, don't hesitate to use a guide where it is called for and enjoy.

Edit after finishing:
I wrote the review above after playing for a few hours.  Having finished the game, I want to add "Will kick you in the nerves of the ballz of your patience."
This is the best 10 hour game I've ever played that took 30 hours to complete.  So, it is a flawed gem.  Had the devs not padded the gameplay by making you play the same sections over and over and over again, with no new bosses, environments, or perspectives, I wouldn't judge it so harshly.
So why would you play something so aggravating?  Because it has a great story.  It is not as compelling as FFVII, but it comes close, and all of the characters here (2B, 9S, A2) are captivating.  Having finished the game, I miss my time with them, and they were well worth getting to know.  But boy was it a slog.  If you are content waiting 30 hours to get a story that can be told in 5, go ahead and play it.  If you need your stories told more efficiently, then I recommend playing What Remains of Edith Finch instead.
