Imagine TF2, except with 10x more bugs, crashing, and waiting to begin a match. Then throw in a gallon of in-game purchases, and I mean Candy Crush-amount. Finally, lock 3/4 of the playable roster for those who play for free, and demand $20 to unlock them, and any future characters, OR you can spend hundreds of hours grinding gold from matches that will constantly either crash, not load, or freeze the game altogether, and you will have a summed up experience of playing Paladins. It may be in beta, but it's been almost a bloody year, they should have patched at least s o m e of these gamebreaking bugs months ago.
If grinding your life away to unlock the entire game's roster sounds like paradise, expensive in-game purchases [spending $1 just for a single character costume-expensive], and waiting minutes [yeah, MINUTES] to start a match, then this is the game for you.
The game, although wonderful for a F2P game, as similar as it is to TF2 even, the only thing that ruins what makes it comparable is the amount of patching needed on some bugs. The skins, although overpriced, I can overlook, it's just the bugs that just barely get my disapproval. Once the developers take care of some of the more... important bugs, then I'll be able to solidify my recommendation.
[and P.S., this isn't due to my system. My system runs games w/ much larger minimum requirements just fine, but Paladins, you're going to get the experience of a Windows 98 desktop.]

One of the most important games to come out in a long time. Though it is far from perfect, it's irreplaceable in my eyes.
The existential themes of Automata have been attempted by countless works of art. This game joins the ranks of very few that are intellectually honest about the subject - despite the uncharacteristically cheery ending.
Regardless, the display of genuine grattitude and the final request it asks of you is enough to make a lasting memory for most. Regardless of how you feel about the philosophical ruminations throughout, that particular monent cannot be called pretentious in the slightest. If all else fails, this is its most redeeming moment.
The hand waving canned inspiration the plot delivers at the end isn't where the true anti-nihilistic message lies, it's this final attempt at genuinely connecting people in some small way. It's an appeal to emotion and feels quite meager in retrospect but its an act I entirely respect and view as rather important. This is especially true when thinking about Japanese culture. It's not a coincidence that so many JRPGs and anime works are based around things like making lasting friendships.
The Platinum combat mechanics are made well enough but the game becomes sluggish at times due to its vague level aesthetics (a deliberate choice that fits with the underlying themes mind you) and stunted pacing. This, along with its lazy PC port makes for a game that under any other pretense wouldn't be worth anyones time except the most crazed fans of the mechanical genre. This is a true Yoko Taro game. It's about an idea first, foremost, and above all else.
Who would have thought a (almost but not quite) existential horror game could have come to us in the form a Platinum RPG about scantily clad gothic lolita androids?

Expanded review: As a striking and enthralling gothic horror card game with visual novel elements, Lamia's Game Room is completely unique in its field. Produced by an independent studio, this game only suffers from a few noticeable flaws. The actual game is very solid, and feels satisfying to win or bluff the AI opponents. However, after you realize that you can immediately win or lose a round based on each player's hands, the game suddenly becomes more frustrating. I personally enjoyed this game a lot, and with a better translation, I would wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone interested in a disturbing but intriguing simplistic card game. Currently, the English translation is so poor that it's mostly laughable, with major game elements containing blatant errors such as "frist" for "first." The main story of the game remains understandable to an English audience, but it's hard to get over the Engrish at first. 7/10.

Deus Ex is both my favorite game and arguably the greatest PC game of all time. It appears frequently at or near the top of best ever lists by both journalists and the gaming public. It was ranked #1 of the top 100 PC games of all time by PC Gamer, PC gaming's most widely respected publication.
These accolades are no surprise when one sees how brilliantly the game succeeds on so many levels. The story is a masterfully crafted, globe-hopping cyberpunk adventure through which the player's character navigates a dystopian future world on a mission to unravel a Gordian Knot of conspiracies, secrets and lies. Both the player's character and the world he inhabits are shaped by nanotechnology, the former for better, the latter for worse. The player assumes the role of JC Denton, an agent of UNATCO, an international anti-terrorism organization. The terror he combats is largely attributable to the Gray Death, a nanomechanical virus that has ravaged the planet. Denton, however, is immune to the virus thanks to nano-augmentation, a cutting-edge technology available only to elite government agents. Nano-augmentation endows Denton with an array of superhuman powers such as infrared vision and invisibility. Augmentations may be customized to suit a particular playing style, for example stealth artists may opt for the footstep-silencing lower body augmentation while aggressive circle-strafing gunners can choose increased speed. The game's augmentations perfectly complement the open-ended design that is its greatest feature of all. Every level features secret areas for circumventing enemies, gathering intel or finding resources. These avenues might be accessible only with certain abilities, for example a fence might be surmountable only to players with the speed-boosting aug that allows them to leap it or the strength-boosting aug that allows them to stack enough heavy crates to climb it. Every mission can be approached in multiple ways using stealth, force, diplomacy or a combination of the three. The story itself actually adapts to the ramifications of the player's approach to the missions. The game is so open-ended, in fact, that there are only two required neutralizations. It can played as a straight-up run-and-gun shooter, a sneak-through-the-shadows stealth adventure or anywhere in between. Further complementing the open-ended gameplay is the RPG-style stat system in which players can develop proficiency in certain weapons or skills such as hacking, lockpicking, or even swimming. This level of freedom was unprecedented in shooters at the time of the game's release. Before, such games would tell the player  "Go here, do this." Deus Ex, through the very end, asks: "What do you want to do?"
Deus Ex is superb in other areas as well: There is a great arsenal of weapons both lethal and non-lethal, familiar and futuristic. A favorite of many is the nano-edged sword, which when combined with footstep silencing aug, is immensely fun to assassinate enemies with. The weaponry is so well-integrated with the augmentation and skill systems that by the end of the game the player feels like a techno-deity. Although the story veers rather outlandish at times, the game never stops encouraging players to think skeptically. The graphics, from an artistic standpoint, convey the game world's bleakness very effectively. The game is set entirely during dusk and nighttime; blues, blacks and grays feature predominantly in its palette. The soundtrack never feels incongruous with its setting and the theme music is one of the most memorable in gaming history.
Deus Ex is not a technically perfect game. Its graphics were somewhat dated at the time of release, the foreign accents are hilariously bad and the boss fights are a drag (though all but two are optional). These flaws do not detract, however, from what a monumental achievement this game is. Deus Ex may not be the most technically polished game of all time, but it is among the most influential. Doom and Wolfenstein 3D established the first-person shooter as a genre, but Deus Ex elevated it to an art form. This was accomplished through its ingenious fusion of role-playing elements with familiar shooter conventions, giving birth to a new genre: the action RPG. The action-RPG has become one of today's most popular genres; echoes of Deus Ex can be seen everywhere, from the decision-trees of the Mass Effect trilogy to the plasmids of BioShock.
Any game as influential as Deus Ex must be considered a classic, but to call this game a classic is almost an understatement. The defining aspect of video games as a medium is interactivity, and interactivity is maximized when the player is granted as much freedom to shape their role within a game as possible. Deus Ex fostered this freedom to the utmost degree. Deus Ex was not only the instantiation of a new genre, it was and remains to this day, the highest instantiation of what a game can be.

Here is Digital Crafter's first game,
as an enhanced version of old maid card game, with a horror theme and a quite mediocre bluffing system. Well, there is not much else to say about this game, but I'll try to present a decent portrayal anyway.
The game has the hint of a story, drowning under really bad translation, a scanty vocabulary and various spelling mistakes. Apparently, our protagonist - and some other people are abducted by Lamia into a "game room" and are forced to play "old maid" - yup, you've heard right, that is one unimaginative villain. We have no idea why the hell we are there to begin with, or who are the people that we play the game with since Lamia conveniently erased our memory. We only wish to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of there, go back to our friends and family, presto. All people we play the game with seemed to possess certain vices, and are presented as A+ jerks for some unknown reason too. Losers of each chapter are punished with some gruesome ways, being taken away by Lamia's "pets". So we keep playing to stay alive, and hope on the scarce possibility that we can eventually get out.
Our protagonist is forced to play this quite so ordinary card game again and again with not so ordinary stakes. In each chapter, you are presented with 2 new characters. With their AI, you go for an old maid game run of 6 rounds. Each player has 2 soul fragments. When you lose a game, you lose one. When you lose both, you lose that chapter permanently and have to retry the same chapter again. So you gotta win 4 times without losing 2 time within a chapter. During the gameplay, you are presented with a questionable bluffing system, allowing you to choose a gesture or a facial expression to mislead your opponent and make them choose another card from your hand. Same goes for you: when you are about to pick a card from their hand, their gestures and mimics change, hinting about the card you are about to choose. Yet, those gestures are not always reliable. Their “tells” do change or do not react as they should all the time. Thus, the game ends up relying on pure luck most of the time.
With some patience, and the aid of Lady Luck,
presents you 2 hours of game time, only to be forgotten forever in your library. For each chapter completed you'll be rewarded with an achievement, and there is also a bonus chapter at the end, allowing you to go for a final run and learn some more - if it would allow you with it's unbearably broken English - of the backstory. For a dollar game, it is not bad. But it is nothing good either. Without these horrendous translation mistakes committed upon elementary school vocabulary, it would be an acceptable 1 dollar game. Considering the developer didn't even spare the time to check the translation, or at least run it by a native speaker, I really cannot recommend this game.
Get yourself a pack of cards, invite some friends and play old maid during the night, only with candle light around. Oh, and laugh wildly or gulp with terror whenever the old maid exchanges hands. You'll be enacting the same concept properly and having more fun compared to playing this game. I guarantee it.

Party Hard is easily the most baffled I've been by a game's positive reception since Sir You Are Being Hunted. Though this is by no means as bad as SYABH. It's just not very good. It fundamentally misunderstands both the stealth genre and Hotline Miami giving you a hodgepodge that doesn't really do justice to either. There's so many basic design mistakes that playing this ends up being a frustrating experience rather than an elating one. And it's a shame because the concept is absolutely brilliant.
There's the components of a good game here, and it's very pretty, but levels are too long for the ease of failure, mechanics are poorly explained, there's no indication of how far an NPC can see which prevents effective stealth, it's buggy - I've had the AI glitch out on 2/6 runs, and there's not enough different mechanics leaving very little variation in how parties play. The game feels like someone took a game jam prototype and expanded the number of levels to full game length without thinking through what needed to be added in order to accommodate that much content.
It would take so little for this to become an enthusiastic recommendation, but Party Hard is unrefined to the point where it overshadows all merits that the game has. There's no reason to pick this up, I'm hesitant to even give a 'get this when it's in a bundle' recommendation.

PROS:
1. You can pretty much do everything in terms of survival, for example you can make campfires to keep warm, chop down trees, make clothing like earmuffs, set traps, ride animals, build your own safe haven, find little odd items and creatures a long the way and much more!
2. At times you feel anxious like your life depends on it if you don't survive which I find is very realistic! *The perks of playing a survival game*
3. Me being a Harry Potter fan, they have the mandrake from the chambers of secrets which i thought was so adorable! Although they constantly wine and don't leave you alone and of course I don't have the heart to kill the poor little things.

Soundodger is by far the best rythm game i've ever played, and by many means.
First, the variety is really important and it is what makes the game so sweet to play. From classical music (Austin Wintory) and electronic ambiances (Louis Gorenfeld, Anoctave, and even the creator Bean himself !), with also 8-bit (Bill Kiley) and dubstep (Ghost Kollective, Mike Forst), the game shows numerous music styles, which is so rare in games nowadays.
You've also got the minimalistic design that fits so well, for example the vast choice of colours that gives the player a different view of the music he's playing. 140 and Super Hexagon are cool references for Soundodger+, there is even a level on a Chipzel's song (the composer of Super Hexagon). Disasterpeace, the composer from the game FEZ (which i cannot recommend playing enough) is also in the game, with a more rock-ish music.
The editor is very intuitive and unique, with infinite possibilities, though the autogen-mode would need some improvements (soundodger memes intensify). Many level creators are very talented, so you have a whole lot of levels waiting for you from the community !
I will conclude this review by saying that Soundodger+ really gave me a new way to see music. If you're a fan of any sort of style, you will most likely love this game, by the approach it gives you on songs you're familiar to, or discover. It expends your culture and makes you understand that there is quality anywhere in music, not in just ONE single genre. The price is nice, the soundtrack's amazing and constantly evolving with the community levels, and the gameplay really changes from other rythms games like Melody Escape or Geometry Dash, because it really feels like you're dancing with the songs as you move through them.

In Magicka, you're a wizard. You've got eight elements that you can stack up, mix, multiply, and unleash. You can cast them at goblins, cast them at anything next to you, cast them at your specially blunted sword, cast them at your own face.
Singleplayer mode is a light comic fantasy, narrated by your dodgy mentor, Vlad. The black-clad Romanian wizard keeps pointing out that he's not a vampire, and making bad puns about sinking his teeth into things. It's a mix of satire and pop culture references that'll have you smirking dangerously throughout.

Lots of care has gone into the way the elements combine and contort in your spells. Combinations shape the form (Missile? Beam? Cone? Wall?) and function (Healing? Burning? Shielding? Exploding? Freezing? Drenching? Zapping?) of each glorious experiment. There's enough variety for every wizard to have his or her own favourite attack style. Mine is a steamy lightning beam that scalds you before dealing bonus lightning damage from the water element in steam.
Concocting these spells is a little confusing at first, as you're commanding eight elements across eight keys, but you're rarely faced with enemies that can't be killed by particular elements. Button mashing will get you far, and a mistake might just surprise you.

The environments are top-down, linear jaunts through bright and breezy fantasy tropes: forests full of goblins, orcish trenches, swamps, mines, the land of the dead. Wander off the beaten path, and you can find powerful equipment and new magic spell recipes that reach beyond the scope of your regular elemental concoctions - spells such as Revive and Teleport.
Singleplayer will soon wear thin, sadly. It's not that you can't beat it with the right spells and an awful lot of goes – it's that if you make a mistake and burst like a sticky water balloon, you get chucked back to the last checkpoint you reached. In once case, that involves fighting three big groups of face-pounding orcs and one-hit-smash-to-deathing ogres, in a row, before you hit another checkpoint. If you quit before you complete that level (perhaps out of, ooh, say, frustration), you'll have to start it all over again when you boot up the game again. Ultimately, you'll hit this annoying boss or that overpowered yeti thing or this boring underworld level and you'll just give up on singleplayer. Then you'll turn to multiplayer.

And multiplayer is good, when it works. If you've got a few networked computers and three eager friends with Magicka on their Steam accounts, you can enjoy the splendour of four death lasers combining neatly into a super-beam that bursts ogres in seconds. You can have tactics and gambits and laugh as they end with one wizard left, deciding if he wants your gear before he resurrects you.
The bulk of us, however, will be butting our heads against the brick wall of online multiplayer. At the time of writing, developers Arrowhead have been releasing patches every 24 hours, and they're gradually improving on the terrible connectivity issues. Despite their efforts, you no sooner host a game than Steam Chat dies, Skype calls drop, and flatmates start inspecting the router for flashing lights. For a game so reliant on multiplayer to be fun, there are lots of missed opportunities. There's no chapter select function, no joining mid-session for latecomers or disconnected players, no voice chat, no dedicated servers, and tons of lengthy, wordy cutscenes that only the host can skip.

Get it working, and it's great. For £8, you'll get your money's worth before everyone forgets about it. But it could have been game of the year material! Silly wizards.

This is a card game with a sinister story that needs a complete rewrite.
In Lamia's game room you play a young man who has been trapped in a room with others, the only hope of escaping being behind winning in a card game.
While the art is nice, the atmosphere creepy and the premise interesting -- as well as the card game not being based purely on luck -- the game falls short thanks to one of the most horrible writing and translation jobs I've ever seen. The VN style story bits are full of unnecessary "..." and exposition/thoughts written out as dialogue. The English translation is weak at best and full of typos. The most glaring is the "cancle" = cancel option in the card game scenes.
This would be a very interesting casual VN/card game hybrid if only you didn't have to wade through a sea of bad writing.

This is a nice looking game, with a decent atmosphere spoiled by an extremely bad english translation, given the gameplay in between the story sections is fairly simplistic, basically being old maid with a very limited bluffing/tells system, that is fairly crippling.
With the story being only barely comprehensible, the entire weight of whether to play this or not falls onto the card game, which isn't really up to it, seeming more a vehicle to stretch the story out presumably in the original language. In early rounds the tells are fairly clear and consistent, so even if you get unlucky and lose the first time, by the second game you should be able to bluff each of your two opponents enough to tip the scales.
Later opponents however clearly have much more complicated patterns to how and what they react to and how they bluff that you can't reasonably work out, so about all you have is randomly clicking one of your three bluff options any time you have the Lamia (Old Maid) card in the hope you pick the right one, apart from that you just need to keep playing until you get lucky enough times.
Overall this isn't a great game, if the translation was there the storyline might have been enough to make it worth playing as a whole, but the card game it is based on just isn't a good fit for a computer game by it's nature.

The premise of this game is interesting: the protagonist is locked in a room with other people, and they must play a card game (Old Maid, basically) to determine who "lives" in each round.  It's an interesting idea, but the execution is bad and ruins the experience.
Here are my main complaints with the game:
- The English translation is not done well and needs serious editing for typos, grammatical errors, and formatting.
- The font used for the in-game dialogue is painful to read in the UI (looks like Arial?).
- The UI of the game is clunky, slow, and not particularly intuitive in its back buttons.
- The gameplay becomes extremely repetetive as the new characters introduced bring very little story-wise and the majority of the game is the protagonist playing Old Maid.  Each "level" you have to play a minimum of 4 rounds of the same game, and the only variance in gameplay between levels is trying to judge characters' reactions to which card you pick.
- The art is not consistent in quality or style.
- Options are extremely limited, lacking standard visual novel controls like text speed.
- Once you start a level, there's no way to exit out to some overall menu; you have to quit out of the entire game or complete the level to be prompted to continue or exit to main menu.

Lamia's Game Room is a card game with a somewhat dark atmosphere. Technically it runs fine (no crashes), but the misspellings and grammatical errors can become annoying.
The player attempts to escape the eponymous creature by battling two opponents in each chapter to progress to the next. The game is basically Old Maid with a modified card design: the paired cards are the seven deadly sins with the "Old Maid" being the Lamia. When a card is selected but not yet taken, the holder may have certain expressions that can clue the player in to whether the card is the Lamia or otherwise. In practice I found this system to be unreliable; the bluffs are often inaccurate and only get worse with each subsequent chapter. This can make the end games tedious as the player's low win rate will require more than a few retries to progress.
However the game is still worth a recommend as the ending shows some potential story expansions. There is also the possibility that more game types could be added in a sequel. Overall the game is worth its price and the achievements are easy to get (one for completing each chapter) as long as the substandard writing is overlooked.

Skip to the bottom for TL;DR
On paper and indeed in the desciption- this seems like a cheesey, but entertaining premise for a game.
Your character is a bitter and tired individual looking to take out his rage and frustration on those keeping him awake while simultaneously not getting killed/arrested- an idea that seems very cathartic and was enough to make me want to give the game a spin.
The tutorial is a brief mission comprising of 4 or 5 individuals laid out in a way to THEORETICALLY teach you all you'll need to know throughout the game, but it only teaches you how to stab people and introduces you to the fact that environmental interactivity will be a thing in this game.
The next mission proceeds to inject you into a party of FORTY SEVEN people. Not only does that up the ante significantly, but this is our first introduction to more/different contextual environment kill options that we don't know the ramifications of screwing with.
I.e; if I poison this food do people die on the spot? Do they walk around choking? Will they not know they're poisoned until they suddenly drop dead?
Simultaneously; how will people react to finding dead bodies? The only level I've played thus far is laid out in a way that I can't determine this.
If the police are called on me; how do I get away? Can I resist arrest?
If I use this phone, who do I call? (I got two different results- some weird bulky guy and an exterminator team with no way of distinguishing which would show up)
I've noticed from having to restart various levels that some rooms/areas in certain levels are randomized and the things within them are as well meaning that you can't bank on a certain item being in the same place if you fail at any point (this isn't necessarily bad, but it's a bit unexpected that I wasn't prepared for)
In my mind this is Party Hard's biggest failing: it gives us way too much way too soon and doesn't explain enough before letting us go crazy at bigger parties.
Calling the police, fire department, weird Russian guy, etc will cause them to suddenly rush into a level, run over eight people standing out front, rush into the party to do whatever it is they're there to do, run back to their cars, book it, and run over four more.
While it does make my job easier it creates a solid disconnect from the story of some detective guy recounting the investigation of the "Party Hard Killings" (or "Killer", can't remember off the top of my head) when his coworkers are responsible for near as many deaths in the course of my rampage.
On a final note; human life has little-to-no meaning to anyone in this game. Five dead people on the dancefloor? PANIC! CALL THE COPS! PANIC A LITTLE LONGER! Oh the bodies are in bags now? Back to dancing right on top of them!
There's no reward for being extremely cautious besides not having the cops called directly on you while simultaneously there's no risk for just leaving a body where it falls because if someone does call the police about it the cop that comes to investigate will just bag it before taking off again and leaving it there.
All this combined just ends up with Party Hard not being fun.
It attempts to make us believe there's a level of depth that just ultimately doesn't exist because once we've sabotaged the stove, burnt down the bedroom, knocked two trees through the windows, stabbed some guy at his computer, shoved a guy into a fire, poisoned six people, stabbed three in the bathrooms, and shoved four more into freezers, garbage bins, and manholes- there's still twenty more people to be killed and I'm fresh out of novelty/environmental/contextual kills. So at that point it boils down to stalking the rest of the partygoers one-by-one as they split off from the main group over the next ten minutes before decapitating the DJ and dancing my way to the next level.
Bottom line: Party Hard just isn't fun because it quickly becomes tedious and there's just too much going on too soon. Combined with too many options that don't do enough damage to the partygoer numbers and aren't explained well enough to understand immediately or sometimes even after repeated use.
TL;DR- Party Hard is a less interesting, more confusing, and less fun stealth/Hitman game.

I just LOVE this game. Id describe it as a goofy combination of Minecraft and Terraria with darker undertones. It's unique style of combat, loveably ridiculous characters, and immense diversity of content ensures many hours of fun... Not to mention that the developers are continually updating the game with new content and even special events. Whether you are new to the game and struggling to survive the Winter when your friend accidentally lights your base on fire or you are highly advanced and working out intense strategies with your pals to defeat yet another boss, this game will never never ceases to entertain, amuse, and occasionally enrage you. It is different than most other games I the genre because it is actually difficult and unforgiving, which makes it more rewarding when you finally manage to make it through the Winter... only to find the Spring even worse. It's science and magic elements make the game both more strategic and more hilarious. The only two problems with this game are that the constant updates somewhat cut down on the game's originally simplistic playstyle and that several of the characters have been given overhauls to try to make them more multiplayer-friendly, which have instead made them more difficult and less fun to play, while making them less valuable to the team. Fortunately, only a couple characters have this problem (Willow and Woodie). Overall, this game more than makes up for its negatives by being incredible fun, challenging, diverse, and strategic. And, of course, being multiplayer is the best part. I would recommend this game any day! Thanks you, Klei, for an amazing experience (with friends).

You can hardly contain yourself as you cut the first slice of the cake.
You raise the first bite of the cake to your mouth.
Its everything you hoped it would be...and more
The texture, the consistency, the deep chocolate flavor with just a hint of caramel...
If there is a god, surely he has ordained this cake into existance solely for this 1 moment of otherworldly bliss

but now you just cant do it...

You've literally bitten off more than you can chew.

You cant just throw it away. That would be a disservice to all pastries everywhere
You take a moment to think, and you decide to eat a salad.
With the taste of cake no longer in your recent memory, you decide to take another shot at the cake.
Again, the cake delivers on providing a mindboggling taste sensation.
But again, you just cant bring yourself to eat anymore.
"♥♥♥♥ing christ this is a big cake" you think to yourself.
OH CRUEL AND MERCILESS GOD, WHY MUST YOU TORMENT ME SO?
YOU'VE GIVEN ME ALL I'VE WANTED, AND YET YOU TAUNT ME WITH THESE FEELINGS OF HATRED!!!
The cake has ruined you
It's far too much for your pathetic mind to comprehend
All that is left of you is the hollow shell of a defeated and broken man
But still there is cake

Long story short. Witcher 2 tries to achieve something original, but unfortunately fails. Every good idea it has is either poorly implemented, countered by a design flaw or your progress is halted by poorly thought out events. It's a mediocre game. The only thing that is up to scratch are the music and sound effects. Everything else you've already seen, wouldn't care to see or will ruin your time. It has some moments that seem important to the overall story of Geralt and the series, which is a shame, because the story of the game itself is trotting rather slow and a lot of the details are rather obscure. The story has a bad tendency of giving you a collection of information that doesn't really fit well as a whole, only to have one of the characters conviniently tell you what is going on in short and sporadic bursts during conversation. It heavily utilizes info dumps. It is trying to be complicated and mature, have a solution to every problem, portray an epic journey a la Fellowship of the Ring, come up with a lot of complex issues, but in the end it comes across as a mess...
Without a doubt, though, the abundant backtracking is this game most horrendous sin. It's just like death from a thousand paper cuts. MMOmisms don't belong in a single player game. For ♥♥♥♥'s sake...if it didn't have that, it would be recommendable, in spite of everything said so far.
Edit: A small update. One very good thing I came across in Witcher 2 are the moments when it is not taking itself so seriously. There are parts in the game where characters will shortly parade with the situation they are in, almost as if to mock themsleves. Immagine my reaction when I was contemplating how Tolkienesque the world and events of W2 look, when, no sooner, the characters themselves started joking about finding one of the rings of power. At that point Geralt quipped that before he knows it, he will be striding up the side of a volcano. Much appreciated!
Unfortunately these are far too few. Too much time spent with the game's horrid mechanics after that.
Edit 2: Combat.
In the first Witcher you were able to charge in, swords blazing and use AoE technique and it was getting the job done. Instead, when you swing your sword, you will be treated to a very theatrical display as Geralt is spinning around like a balerine with a rotating top syndrome, mostly hitting one enemy. Every offensive action you do has a dead window both before and after said action, during which you will be unable to roll away/move/escape/parry. Remember this if you want to play this game. It is not something that is annoying, more like something that extends the time you spend in combat. You will also need to learn to watch out for any non-passable terrain, as even the smallest pebble/root/box/ect. will stop your movement. Geralt will be running and rolling on the ground but remain on one and the same spot. Again, it is not a big game breaker, but definitely a thing to watch out for. Whether fighting enemies in the open or in closed quarters, it does not matter in the end, as they are equally stupid and generally reluctant to charge outside of boss battles. Generally, combat is nothing spectacular in Witcher 2, but it also does not stand significantly in your way. I suppose it was meant to be more tactical, but you can literally spam your craftable consumables, some of which--AoE granades, and those are the quickest way to move through any non-boss encounter. Execution sequences are done one on one without the rest of the mobs interfering, which is nice. Boss battles are more varied, with quick time events and tricks up their sleeves. You will need to pay close attention to your screen, though, as the quick-time event indicator is tiny.
Edit 3:Grasphics.
The game looks possitively good. Much better than Skyrim for sure(every occassion I get to bash on Bethesda is welcomed). It has got optimization issues, unfortunately, and it even crashed on me already. Nothing game-breaking, though. Other titles with better looking graphics produce more fps than Witcher 2. Texture quality is good for its time but has aged. Geralt and all of his armour sets and swords look very detailed and realistic and this time around he is even able to show emotion with facial expressions, as limited as they come. There is a huge and constant asset reuse as the models for the NPCs are limited. Triss' face, for instance, is every other human female's face. The architecture you encounter is very athmospheric and genuine. It is also much more varied than the previous title. You will see some very nice medieval places. If you pump up everything to max the game will glare too much and you may want to keep a few settings lower because it ends up not looking that good for the gas it requires from your machine. The game has got a lot of colour but looks best when you deal with darker environments, as the light reveals low res textures and an unpleasant grainy effect, which I cannot switch off. There are a few spots with creepy mist on an uneven ground, with plants here and there, among giants trees. That particular setting looks fantastic when not in daylight. That said, it may become repetitive as you will need to back-track quite a few times.

is one of the underrated and unfortunate titles of cinematic puzzle-platformer genre. Due to visual and mechanical similarities it is hard to not to compare it to
's indie hit
. However, Monochroma offers more complex mechanics, musics and visuals that some of them were clearly inspired film noir movies as well as Schindler's List.
Injured young brother mechanic offers different gameplay styles by letting player consider different movement speed and jump height. However, not being able to leave the young brother in the dark and not being able to go far away from him makes the mechanic a bit dull. It would be more thrilling and creative to provide a relative time limit of leaving him in the dark and/or alone which would create many possibilities. Current form creates invisible walls that I'm not fond of.
Level variety is as satisfying as it can get; the game starts in rural environments; second chapter takes place in urban places; third chapter is located in manufacturing facilities and the final chapter let's protagonist to wander around classical furniture. Visual variety provided in second and at the end of third chapter is quite impressive.
HOWEVER... As the game uses an early version of Unity engine which should be from Unity 4.x branch given the release date, controls in particular are not well optimized. Launch version of the game suffered from that problem which resulted low review scores; later on some of controls problems were fixed but it was already late. Honestly, controls are still not precise enough which is a shame. Let me give you a hint;
, otherwise it is easy to misland. It looks like developers didn't have time to make some jumps more forgiving in order to compensate unoptimized controls.
Ending of the game is probably the weakest part of entire experience; it feels rushed, unpolished and annoying.
That is probably the only portion of the game that frustrated me to the core... I wish the studio had more time to make the final scene better.
As far as I know, during the development of the game, political turmoil in the country caused street riots some of them took place near the office of
in 2013; in fact employees were affected by tear gas in one point. That might explain clunky controls and tiresome ending due to production environment and time constrains but later updates left some of the issues mentioned unfixed.
If you loved Limbo and looking for even more, Monochroma is a great title for you. But if you have concerns about controls, just wait for a sale, then grab it. Lastly,
composed original music of the title that can also be listened in
.

Lamia's Game Room is a quirky take of the classic old maid card game with a dark, gothic atmosphere reminiscent of the Danganronpa series. In this death game, you are given 2 souls, which will decrease as you lose a game by being stuck with the maid card- in this case, the "Lamia" card. The match will end when 2 other opponents lose all of their souls.
Although the game presents a simple and intriguing premise in the beginning, it falls short as there is actually not much covered as the game progresses. There should be at least more interactions with other characters to make them more interesting. Plot issues aside, the major design flaw of this game is its heavy dependence on luck. Sure, the first few levels are actually fun as it lets you try to outsmart your opponents, but the last two levels lets the AI to cheat, rendering the bluffing options useless. Heck, I was even lucky to beat the last two levels with only 3 losses each. There are several issues that need to be taken care of, don't let that hinder you to play and support this $1 game. The game itself is actually fun when played on short sessions.
+ Nice atmosphere
+ Fittting ambience music
+ Beautiful art
+ Fun when played on short sessions
+ Low price
+ Steam Trading Cards and Achievements
- Extremely short (Only 2 hours in length)
- Heavy dependence on luck (Particularly the final and the God-forbid Extra level)
- Storyline doesn't cover much
- Awful translation. The English Language obviously wasn't proof-read, presenting you with the first of its many typos just a mere few seconds into the game.

The original Deus Ex blows all its sequels out of the water. It was one of the first -- and remains one of the best -- FPS-RPG hybrids. Most traditional FPS games tug players from one obvious objective to the next. At the same time, traditional RPGs are often so sprawling that you can easily forget about the "main story" while you spent 50+ hours doing sidequests. Deus Ex seamlessly blends the best of both genres.
VERSATILE GAMEPLAY
You have all the action of a shooter, but the customization and item variety of an RPG. You can blast enemies away with rocket launchers, or you can do silent, non-lethal takedowns with a mini-crossbow. You can run-and-gun. You can sneak around and find alternate routes to your objective. You can hack into computer terminals and reprogram enemy turrets.  Players are allowed to develop their own style -- and all this versatility lends the game considerable replay value.
IDEAL BALANCE BETWEEN FREE-ROAM AND LINEAR MISSIONS
You generally have a clear objective in each section of the game. However, there are numerous ways to complete these objectives. This keeps the story focused, but it also gives players the freedom to accomplish assignments as they see fit. Choices you make throughout the game will have consequences later on. The mostly-linear plot gives the story a constant sense of urgency, but the freedom within each level always makes it feel like you're ultimately in control of the narrative.
A CLASSIC STORY
The original Deus Ex is famous for its complex, well-paced conspiracy tale. The plot takes a whole bunch of twists and turns. It's complex without being needlessly confusing (*cough* Metal Gear *cough*). Talking about it will spoil the fun, but rest assured that it's one of the more satisfying stories in both the RPG and FPS genres. It'll stay with you -- and it has clearly influenced the industry.
Recommended? Heck yes. Throw money at Valve right now.

This is probably the most fun I've had in an early access game so far to date. As of the time of this writing, the game is still in Early Access, but there is a seemingly endless land for you to (attempt) to fight through as far as you possibly can, all the while gathering raw materials and crafting them (simple 1 & 1 combinations; think Resident Evil) into tools, weapons, armor, potions and more.
This is a roguelike, so if you get frustrated by dying a lot (and you will) and losing all of your progress in the blink of an eye (which will happen), this game may not be for you. Those who do enjoy roguelikes need no further explanation :) When starting, you create your character and have many unlockable hats, races and their variants to choose from. Don't worry, the hats actually do give your character unique abilities :P On top of this, the game also makes use of a "trait system" that gives each player two randomized traits (which you can re-roll) that do things like raise ATK, but lower DEF, cut down trees faster, brew stronger potions, increase DEX, etc.
If you make it to the end of an area, you will see 3 doors of varying color (which indicate the area type), each taking you to the next area's village where you can sell treasure, buy weapons, smelt ores, refine pelts and hides into leather for armor, and generally terrorize the locals and their chickens. Once you're geared up, you'll leave the village and repeat the process of trying to get to the end once again, only with harder enemies ;)
Enough about the baseline details though...let's talk about actual gameplay! Generally speaking, you have the movement skills of a friggin' ninja; you can dash side to side, double jump, and even dash midair (several times if you have the stamina)! Mastering movement is one of the first keys to survival in Magicite; if you can't be hit, then you can't be killed (as easily). Other than your ninja-like abilities, every 5th level (I believe is the increment...don't quote me) you can choose a new skill from 3 paths to unlock and use to further aide in your adventure. These can be anything from a giant sword that shoots underneath you and propels you into the air (allowing for a triple jump, or even a quadruple jump if you have a special item), a fireball that you can shoot arrows at to make flaming arrows, berserker rage, to a protective aura that reduces all damage taken for everyone in your party.
At risk of spoiling more potential fun and shenanigans in figuring the various aspects of the game out just by playing (like me and my friends did), I'm going to end here. Pick up the game! Seriously, this is one of the most fun Early Access games out there, you will not be disappointed!

Visuals are nice, the music is passable. Voice acting is downright annoying and the dialog just goes on and on and on and on.... I like long dialogue in games (and adventure games are all about story and dialogue) but this one is just an incoherent, illogical, mind-numbing. non-sensical mess.
You'll hear the same repeated lines over and over and try to complete utterly illogical, pointless puzzles to advance the game. You'll then grind and grind some more, pixel-hunting for the one object that you must click or the one object that you must use with something to continue. And the ending... the ending takes the cake - I've never seen such a letdown in an adventure game; the ending was bad even in the context of this game, which is saying a lot, because the game is already awful.
Some reviews mentioned that this is a children's game but that's not correct: no child in their right mind would suffer through this mess of a game. They may get wooed by the nice visuals but 5 minutes into the game they'd give up in utter boredom. Only an adult who paid money for this would try to finish this game, trying to see if there's some sort of sense to it and trying to see if there's something to be gained for the money paid.
There's nothing, as is the case with most Daedalic games. I should've learned this from their earlier games but from now on I'll avoid anything this incompetent bunch dumps on the markets and I advise you, reader, to do the same. You'll save your money and you'll use your time for better things.

The Night of the Rabbit Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Becoming a magician and learning the craft of magic is the greatest dream of 12 year old Jeremiah Hazelnut. During the last two days of his summer vacation this dream finally seems to come true. Out of thin air, an elegantly dressed rabbit that goes by the name the Marquis de Hoto appears, carrying Jerry with him into an enchanted realm...
The Night of the Rabbit, regardless of what it’s called and the few other minor complaints I had, is a triumph. It’s Daedalic once and for all proving that they are indeed capable of producing an adventure that can stand tall with the classics of the genre. Night of the Rabbit faithfully follows the tried and true traditions of the adventure game genre while leveraging modern technologies in a very well-produced game. Appropriate for the entire family and providing a compelling, well-written story, this one is worth a look. The Night of the Rabbit still contains all of those classic "ah ha!" moments when you, at long last, cease to be dumbfounded, and the novelty of the magic spells surprisingly doesn't wear off, continuing to be implemented cleverly throughout the long experience. With a lot of patience, you could find yourself having a bloody good time. Overall an excellent title! Lose yourself in a tale of magic and wonder, where anything is possible and where nothing is quite as it seems: All in all, Night of the Rabbit is an extremely enjoyable game, one certainly that most adventure game enthusiasts will have a fun time with.
A great way back into the point and click genre - but be prepared to invest a little time.

That there are absolutely no context clues is a death sentence for an adventure game. Enough has been said about its other aspects, but this in particular makes it look like Daedalic has forgotten how to write one. I've played many of their other titles and so far liked every one of them, but this one is just frustrating.
Example - you have three things that each do the same thing according to their description. Item 1 and item 2 simply give a "I should hold on to that" when trying to use them in the exact right spot, item 3 miraculously works. Example - you need to combine something with a liquid. Attempting to use the several containers you have with several liquids gives exactly the same response as combining them with rocks. "Use mug on water" - "my mug is not a weapon", really? Example - an item can be in different states, you need one of them in a specific location. Use the right item at the right time in the wrong state, the character simply and literally says "No...".
Sorry, but that's just thoroughly unenjoyable. I've been playing adventure games for decades and this is the first one I've come across where exclusively the correct combination of items (or sometimes a future but still unavaliable combination) shows any interaction at all. And that from the people who made something like Edna Breaks Out where almost any conceivable action at all has a unique line of dialogue.
If only the characters, the story, the humor, the puzzles were able to save it, but as others pointed out, that's far from being the case. At least the artwork is nice.

INGREDIENTS

Chocolate Buttercream Frosting Recipe
INGREDIENTS AND INSTRUCTIONS FOR FROSTING:
1½ cups butter (3 sticks), softened
1 cup unsweetened cocoa
5 cups confectioner’s sugar
½ cup milk
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
½ teaspoon espresso powder
INSTRUCTIONS:
Add cocoa to a large bowl or bowl of stand mixer. Whisk through to remove any lumps.
Cream together butter and cocoa powder until well-combined.
Add sugar and milk to cocoa mixture by adding 1 cup of sugar followed by about a tablespoon of milk. After each
addition has been combined, turn mixer onto a high speed for about a minute. Repeat until all sugar and milk have been
added.
Add vanilla extract and espresso powder and combine well.
If frosting appears too dry, add more milk, a tablespoon at a time until it reaches the right consistency. If it appears to
wet and does not hold its form, add more confectioner’s sugar, a tablespoon at a time until it reaches the right consistency.
Now back to the cake
CAKE INSTRUCTIONS:
Preheat oven to 350º F. Prepare two 9-inch cake pans by spraying with baking spray or buttering and lightly flouring.
For the cake:
Add flour, sugar, cocoa, baking powder, baking soda, salt and espresso powder to a large bowl or the bowl of a stand
mixer. Whisk through to combine or, using your paddle attachment, stir through flour mixture until combined well.
Add milk, vegetable oil, eggs, and vanilla to flour mixture and mix together on medium speed until well combined.
Reduce speed and carefully add boiling water to the cake batter. Beat on high speed for about 1 minute to add air to the
batter.
Distribute cake batter evenly between the two prepared cake pans. Bake for 30-35 minutes, until a toothpick or cake
tester inserted in the center comes out clean.
Remove from the oven and allow to cool for about 10 minutes, remove from the pan and cool completely.
Frost cake with Chocolate Buttercream Frosting.

is a point & click adventure game. Classic gameplay for the genre is you solve problems by collecting items and using them on objects in the game world or combining them in your inventory first.
doesn't add any real puzzles to that. There is one cards minigame, though.
After the first bit of gameplay you'll learn a 'skill' that enables you to highlight all objects you can interact with by pressing a button. This is always useful in point & click games. However, there are a number of optional items to collect for some achievements and these do not get highlighted. So if you want all the achievements, you're still in for some pixel hunting.
Jerry is a 12-year-old who wants to be a magician. One day, a man-sized rabbit appears to him and takes him to another world called Mousewood, where he will train Jerry to use magic spells. Mousewood is inhabited by all kinds of man-sized talking animals.
You're probably thinking this story sounds extremely generic. And you would be right, of course. Most fairy tales and other stories for children involve magic and/or talking animals.
So that's what you need to know about the story of
: it's a story for children and an unoriginal (even a bit boring) one to boot.
The only other element that's worth mentioning here is that Mousewood is being attacked by feral crows. This may sound familiar if you played
, also made by Daedalic Entertainment, where the exact same element was a large part of the story. For a studio that only developed about a dozen games, this may come across as lazy or at least repetitive.
's graphics are cartoonish but they look sharp, colourful and full of life.
The music is not particularly memorable, but it does sound nice and varied.
The protagonist's child voice actor does a decent job for his age, but you always hear a voice actor reading lines and you'll never hear a character with personality, so there's little feeling of immersion.
Most of the other voice acting sounds like it was meant for the dubbing of an animated film for young children: the voice actors force their voice and try to sound very weighty in every line they speak, which makes it all sound very fake and a bit ridiculous even.
The humour is tailored for children, too. Ok, I get that I find myself in a world inhabited by animals that talk and all that, but the humour could still have been a bit more original than childish wordplay like a book called 'Harry Otter and the Chamber of Egrets', a message signed 'Anonymouse', and so on.

This game would have been pretty damn good if not for the terrible controls. The level designs were good, graphics were great, and sound was decent - but the bad taste from the controls overshadowed most of that. Aside from controls, there were a few issues with collision detection where I got stuck and needed to kill myself. A few areas also felt unpolished such as the poor animation when a particular type of enemy kills you... he just walks into you (often literally due to collision detection issues) and you drop dead.
It's amazing that, despite how few player buttons/actions are available in the gameplay, they still managed to screw up the controls for basically all of them. It really makes you wonder if any unbiased user(s) ever tested this game prior to release. Most of the challenges in the game were a result of awkward controls that never seem to do what you want until you eventually learn to account for them like a crooked sight on a rifle. It's one of those games where you're trying to quickly drop down a few platforms and your character keeps accidentally getting stuck hanging on the ledge or climbing back up to the top again. If you're hanging on a ladder or rope, one accidental slide of the joystick at a downward angle can make your character fall to his death. Your character has poor jump control so sometimes I'd just slightly tap the joystick to move forward to drop to a platform below and he would leap over it to his death. I could go on and on about the awkwardness, but I did get used to it after 30min to an hour.
Since I like games similar to this style of gameplay (Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares, etc), I stuck with it and eventually it became less noticable. The "gimmick" to this particular game is that you have a brother you're carrying around with you the whole time so you have to make sure he escapes safely with you too. I'm reluctant to give this a positive review but I did have some fun with it. If you really love this style of gameplay, it may be worth playing despite the flaws but I'd wait for a sale.

Badly Designed and Disappointing
I really thought Party Hard would be a funny, over-the-top game with lots of creative traps and quirky AI.  Instead, every level feels like a slog and that's partially because the player character is always the SLOWEST, most PLODDING sprite on screen.  Your standard speed is slower than anyone else, and your "sprint" lasts only moments and just puts you on par with the most standard of NPC's.  This is probably the worst element of the game, because it means even moving across the screen is a tedious exercise, never mind trying to accomplish anything.  If someone actually decides to run, you're out of luck because without a massive head start you can't catch up or out-run anyone.  This in itself is a terrible design decision but even without that you still move like molasses in a deep freeze.
What about the game play?  Well one would think playing the psycho trying to kill a bunch of mindless morons would make for at least a half-way entertaining game but not in this case.  The NPC's don't even have slasher-film-victim levels of personalities.  They react to dead bodies and pools of blood, but not someone throwing a live person off a building or into a bloody fan trap.  They don't notice a dwindling number of guests, they don't care if you carry unconcious ones around, and they don't seem to mind when people get run over by the cops.  The only thing they react to is your dancing (and not in a meaningful way), dead bodies, you stabbing someone and explosions.  There's a mechanic to allow other people to take the blame but it's not consistent enough to be useful.  The special NPC's all fail to be meaningful as well.  The bouncers always try to chase you down for no reason if they spot you, but that's all they do.  The cops give up the chase either ridiculously easily or not at all due to the game's mechanics (you usually get one escape grace) but you still need a ludicrous lead because your character's inability to move faster than a crawl at the best of times.  Then there's the mechanic and paramedics who you simply can't do much about because they're clearly game mechanics and not subject to any rules and thus just leech more fun out of the game.
There's just not enough traps or enough variety to make doing anything have any feeling of satisfaction.  Due to the fact that EVERYONE out-runs you it means that eliminating the stragglers is just a chore.  So there's no joy in using the traps, no entertainment in eliminations, it's just a slog and a grind because you have to treat every situation with caution because if one NPC makes it to the phone you'll have to have to gimp from the cops and hope you had enough of a lead to start with or it's back to the start of the level all over again.
And then there's the fact that the game doesn't teach you the mechanics properly.  There are newspapers with tips -- most of which are after they would have been useful.  Worse, there's no real rating after completing the game so you have no idea if you blundered through or aced it, and the fact that you CAN blunder through easily means you can get by without learning any real mechanics.  It's entirely possible to just murder a pack of idiots because they all run for the phone you're right in front of, but it's also possible that one idiot will decide to actually be smart and run for the other phone... which means you're screwed because you can't catch up to them unless they're unconcious.  So the game punishes you when it shouldn't with your crap movement speed and yet doesn't punish you enough for screwing up so you can learn.
The final nail in the coffin is the 'story', because you'd think the plot of "You're just a grumpy guy who wants to get some sleep and people keep having loud parties" would be funny, right?  Make the protagonist sympathetic despite being a murderous psychopath, right?  Nope.  It... seems to take itself straight.  There's not enough wit for it to be satire, and not enough humour to be a parody.  Everything from the voice acting to the dialogue to the unfolding story feels bad-bad instead of hilarious-bad.  I kept playing, waiting for it to get better but instead it got worse.

Lamia's Game Room is a casual card game done by Digital Crafter. Lamia's Game Room is a mystery card game that plays [for me] similar to Old Maid, with a visual novel type story tied to it. It's a bit short, it took me about 4-5 hours to beat and get all of the achievements. At the time I played, spelling and grammatical errors plauged the entire game.
The game is all about fooling your opponent by playing your cards and when you can, expressions right. You got a "Lamia" card you need to get your opponent to take and hold onto, so they "lose." I focued more on the gameplay then the story, though I didn't feel it very interesting.The levels starting out were rather simple, easy to catch on and get into the rhythm. Towards the end, the characters you're playing against get a lot better and their factial give aways are no longer always accurate.
I recommend this on I enjoyed the gameplay and goth-style art, though this game is NOT for everyone.

This game is like a box of your favorite cereal: you might have accidentally left it open in the cabinet and forgot about it for  a couple of weeks, but after you pour another bowl of it, it still tastes great.
I say that because this game is outdated, cripplingly so in certain regards.  The enemy guard AI has a field of view that can be equated to holding two paper towel rolls up to your eyes.  If they spot you, you can trolley out of sight, and they won't come investigate.  The AI doesn't noticeably improve as you progress further into the game (it's especially jarring because the guards you come across look like menacing and dangerous, but it's like they forgot their prescription glasses at home), and instead the game relies on subsidizing the amount of cheese tactics you can perform (by the end of the game, some of the enemies can only be taken out by a soft spot on their back using the cattle prod).  The controls are beyond archaic, and I don't think they even made sense back when they were conceived in 1999 (you use the + button on the number pad to quicksave).  The resolution does not appear to surpass 480p without getting yourself one of the many mods this game has to make it playable in the days of DirectX12.  The general quality of the game (from a presentation perspective) is so bad it's legendary.
How's the actual meat of the game?  Well, the story is serviceable.  It's beautifuly timeless due to its themes of how far are we willing to give the government control over our lives to protect us from terrorism, and whether or not the government might get carried away in abusing their power.  This game was released before 9/11 and world paranoid about terrorism, but not so early before that society was wildly different.  There really isn't a lot of character development; a character starts and ends the game acting similarly (you could argue the protagonist, JC Denton, gets development, but he could act wildly depending on your actions).  With that said, the people you meet along the journey become good guys or bad guys solely depending on your opinion of them (for example, is Paul Denton justified in wanting to treat being a UNATCO agent like a day on the police force, or is he just being a blind hippy by not wanting to kill some ♥♥♥♥ing ragheads (or this game's French equivalent, the NSF).
Gameplay wise, the primitive AI doesn't really lend itself to any tense gameplay you might see in other stealth games like the Arkham games, Metal Gear Solid, or successors like Dishonored.  The stealth approach is just as valid as the loud approach, and it's not impossible to adjust depending on your supply reserves (save your cattle prods, kids).  You get skill points by doing objectives.  They improve your general skills (though they're not impossible to use without the said skills).  Don't put skill points in Swimming.  This game carves out its niche with its use of the nano augmentations.  As you progress through the story, you'll get the choice to augment yourself by choosing one of the two options you're given (e.g. you can choose to augment your feet to move quicker, or to move quietly).
The game really shines through with its level designs.  If you dedicate the time to explore the levels, you start to realize that there is no one way to approach a situation, and there are areas you could easily miss which houses a ton of augment upgrades, supplies, or even some weapon modifications.  You might want to invade a park through the front door, being caught immediately and blasted down, or you could survey the park, and find a back door that's loosely guarded, and housing your true objective much sooner.  Which objective is best?  Well, you get to your target either way, and that's all that matters.  The first path to the objective might not be the best route for you if you want to want to pick people off, but somebody who wants to toss a tear gas grenade in and then take down the group would already be stroking their boner at the opportunity.
This is why I recommend Deus Ex.  Nonlinear stealth is tough to pull of meaningfully (looking at you Metal Gear Solid V).  This game blends together talking with civilians to learn how to get your best edge, to watching your step so that you don't get caught by the bad guys.  You can try to bypass an electronic grid by using a multitool, or by just looking for a route to bypass the grid.  It's a game where the only reason your choice matters is for what you had to do to do it.
Final Words: "A bomb's a bad choice for close-range combat."

Soundodger+ is a rhythm-bullet hell game in which bullets spawn from enemies on the outside of a rotating circle in time with the music. You must dodge them on the inside of the circle. The main game includes 20 basic levels, 18 advanced levels, and 5 heart levels. Each of the advanced levels is an upgraded version of one of the basic levels with harder bullet patterns. Levels are unlocked in sequence by getting enough score on all the previous levels. Each advanced level also contains a heart bullet, which if collected acts as a free hit. Heart levels are unlocked by finishing the required number of advanced levels with your heart intact, and consist of two upgraded basic songs and three all-new songs. The game also comes with 12 DLC levels for free, which do not contribute to the main game. Finally, the game includes a level editor and auto-generation feature so that you can play levels from your own songs.
Pros:
+The soundtrack is incredible. I listen to nearly all of the songs in it on a daily basis. They aren't just regular game-soundtrack songs, they're SONGS, from genres all across the spectrum. Dubstep, downbeat, chiptune, and classical are all there.
+The main levels are very fun with a fairly consistent difficulty curve.
+This game has several very talented creators who make great user levels and have been for a while, so there's no shortage of content.
+The level editor itself is intuitive and fairly easy to use, although it has a few bugs and can lag.
+There is a community for this game, and it isn't literal trash. It's actually pleasant to be in.
Cons:
-It has a few game-breaking bugs, but if you're just playing the main game you're very unlikely to come across any of them.
-The auto-generation feature doesn't make good levels, or even levels that sync up with the chosen song very well. Use it only if you want to hear a level from a specific song and don't want to bother making it yourself.
-The difficulty markers are vague at best, and often non-indicative of the difficulty of the actual level. They are rarely very far off, though -- there are no 3-difficulty levels that should be marked 5-difficulty.
Tips for playing:
=In the audio settings, there is an option for "smooth listening." Turning it on means the level no longer speeds up when you get hit, although score is calculated the same. Turn this on, it's better.
=The 60fps mode works and works well, but may mess up some levels with lots of rewind. I recommend not using it because you don't want to get used to it and then turn it off to fully experience the levels it doesn't like.
=Your first level you make in the level editor will, invariably, be not very good. Don't be disheartened.
Overall, the cons are very minor gripes and the pros vastly outweigh them. If you like rhythm games or bullet hell games, buy this game.

Stellaris is not perfect, but still a fun game with lasting appeal. Creating your very own civilization with custom traits and government style allows the player to rule the galaxy in his/her style. The art style and music are truly wonderful. The addition of Leviathan DLC provides further enjoyment in mid/late game. The combat is mediocre, but the game forces the player to set goals and objectives for wars prior to the declaration. This mechanism prohibits boring unending wars from occurring, which frequently results in later stages of many other grand strategy games. Where the game is lacking, however, is diplomacy. Diplomatic options are available, but I seldom felt I could negotiate with or manipulate A.I. players.
Despite its flaws, I thoroughly enjoyed Stellaris, and will continue to do so for a long time. I’ve also felt that the developers are actively listening to the community feedback and improving the game bit by bit. If you enjoy games like Civilization, Anno, or the campaign portion of Total War, I recommend Stellaris.

Hey Sean! Before rolling out future patches, you may want some good feedback from someone who plays this genre for a living with my fiance. We've instantly taken a liking to Magicite and compiled a list of possible improvements or add-ons, this is all opinion, so dont mind shooting down anything here, Its fine by me.
• For starters, do NOT adjust the difficulty, I know a lot of people are a bit fidgety about the perma-death and the difficulty, But the difficult as is right now is perfectly set, We've spent hours on it and right now we get pretty far in with no issues. (Around Tier2/3 Biomes it gets a bit more strategic)
• Improved Camp-fire hit box: By this I mean that it has improved range when trying to cook, though it works fairly well, there has been a instance or two where even though Im on the fire and clicking on it, I instead consume the raw meat rather than cook it. Just a very minor annoyance.
• (BUG) When youre facing against a corner on any map, and toss a item, it goes through the wall , into the void of nothingness, and is not able to be repicked up. (Can try to get screenshots soon)
• Viking hat: I really like the melee system and combat system, the skills and slow/fast weapon speeds really make for awesome team play, however, being as melee class players have more of a high risk = / = reward factor when fighting more dangerous mobs, I dont see the 10% benefit of the viking hat coming into play. I would find it more reasonable if the % ratio for the viking sword was between 15-20%.
• HP gained on level-up ALSO restored: When you level up its a great feeling, the randomized stats is a good feature and increased health is great, but whats NOT so great is that the hp gain doesn't also get restored. For example: I have 5/5 Hp, and I level up gaining a maximum of 5/8 Hp, the 3 HP needs to be healed, rather than already being restored. Now this doesnt mean I want all my health restored with every level up, but we found that it'd be better if health restored what it increased by at the very least.
• Possible Healer Npc (Costs gold) included in town ~?
• Possible increase in rarity stats on crafted gear? When crafting, we love getting higher tier items with bonus stats, but we feel the rate of crafting a item with bonus stats is fairly low. A increase in the rates would be nice.
----------------------------------------------------------
Other than that we have no complaints! The game works flawlessly and is providing hours upon hours of entertainment, keep expanding and adding more content!

M2TW is a fun cheap game, that will cause you to stay up much to late telling yourself "just one more turn". The game runs well on nearly any PC and its unbelivably well-priced for how entertaining and detailed it is. Now, I am sure someone could argue that there are better RTS games out currently, but considering the release date of this game and its price it is definitely worth the buy. The Pre-Sequel is an enjoyable game that you might get 10's of hours out of without DLC, and 100+ potential hours with all DLC. Without DLC, the game has many aspects that will give you hours of enjoyment and replayability, disregarding the story. If you DO have DLC, mainly the Claptastic Voyage Campaign DLC and the +10 level cap one, your playtime is bound to increase. Beginning with the base game, the gameplay is very enjoyable, however the story and some missions depreciate the game.
The story is interesting the first few times through; the first time you play watching Jack transform into Handsome Jack is fun, and the next few times you play through you might enjoy finding ECHO's and uncovering more backstory. After that however, the missions become annoyingly repetitive and laborious to do. However, even though the missions are chores after a few playthroughs, the amazing characters and movement mechanics provide near infinite entertainment. Not being too specific, but all 4 base characters have diverse and fun skill trees (except for Claptrap, who has a very unpredictable and obnoxious skill tree. But who cares, no one picks Claptrap :D), and the boost jumping and butt slams are good enough mechanics to be a staple in the Borderlands series from now on. I'm still playing through the game with each character because they each offer different and fun playstyles. Now, the game with DLC obviously still has the aspects mentioned above, but the DLC simply adds more enjoyment and replayability.
The Claptastic Voyage was the last DLC 2k Australia released for The Pre-Sequel, and that DLC ensured they went off with a bang. If you only wanted one DLC for TPS, buy the Claptastic Voyage. It is a decently-lengthed campaign and has funny and interesting dialogue, cool level designs, new enemies, new gun variants, and multiple references to previous Borderland games. Although this DLC is the star of the show, [I've heard that] the two add on characters have funny dialogue, and powerful skills, and the Holodome DLC has an uninspired Holodome with reused enemies, but it also contains +10 to the level cap, which is always nice.
The Pre-Sequel, while admittedly not offering as much replayability as the previous("next") game in the series, this game has unique gameplay mechanics, fun and diverse characters, and a couple good DLC's. If you own and still play Borderlands 2 or even Borderlands 1 a lot, then I advise you to heavily consider whether or not you would get your money's worth out of The Pre-Sequel. If you are simply wanting more Borderlands experience, then this game offers unique enjoyment, which is only multiplied by buying DLC.

Positives:
Beautiful hand-drawn art style.
Wide variety of Interesting characters.
Nice combination of humour, seriousness, and emotional moments.
Well-worked, non-linear puzzles.
Often difficult and quite absurd puzzle solutions. I list this as a positive as I enjoy these, as long as they don't go too bizarre, which I didn't feel any in this game did. The first point-and-click game I really got into was the first Discworld game, which probably accounts for my enjoyment of absurd puzzles. This could be a negative for some people.
Enjoyable Go Fish-like card-based mini-game.
Bonus hidden-item collectables throughout the game, unlocking extras such as audio stories based in the game's universe.
Charming voice acting. The child who voices the main character does a brilliant job of making it the main character believable as a young boy struggling with being out of his depth but also excited about the adventure he's been set on.
Negatives:
Editing of the sound files is sloppy at times. Seems to be most noticeable when looking at inventory items.
There were some themes introduced in the game which ended up not going anywhere. For example, towards the middle of the game a fairly strong anti-urban-sprawl theme comes in, but then is never really addressed or averted throughout the rest of the game.
Similarly with some of the abilities you learn throughout the game - some you learn so late in the game that you don't really then get much use out of them before the game ends. I felt more puzzles could have utilised these abilities.
As mentioned in the positives, some of the puzzles are quite difficult/absurd, which may be frustrating for some players.
Overall I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys point-and-click adventures, and in particular, comedic, fantasy-based ones. The story is wonderfully developed and the characters all add their own unique flavour into making a very charming, immersive game world to explore.
