Summary: It may be more compatible with Windows 7/8/8.1 than HL1 normally is, but aside from compatibility and better lighting, there's not much to make this game worth your money.
First off, nothing has changed from HL1's multiplayer mode.  The maps may be running on Source, but there's still no props or anything-- it's still all just the map geometry.  More than that, you have to deal with the regular HL1 models without the HD pack, unless you feel the need to go through HL1 with Photoshop and do it yourself via modding (which will most likely not work on some servers).
Here's the real reason you want to stay away: 1) the GoldSrc HL1 has more players (source is pretty much empty, HL1 has a few players), and 2) this game is an EXTRA price.  That's right.  It's not like "oh, they just separated it because it's a big file" as Red Orchestra 2 and the CoD games do it.  No, you have to BUY the singleplayer for HL:Source (a broken mess) for $10, then HL Deathmatch Source is a standalone for you to slap down more money for.  Why not just buy HL1, with Deathmatch mode included?
Aside from what's above, what's advertised in HL Source isn't really that great.  The ragdoll physics are present, yes... however, they're bugged.  VERY bugged.  They lock up as soon as you die and you fall sideways in a stupid pose, whether you're posed to run in place on the ground, you're failing at parkour by getting your arm phased into a guardrail, or you're doing a handstand... sideways.  Other than ragdoll physics, the lighting looks better and the skybox is now 3D rather than a few jpg's of a New Mexico backdrop, but other than that this game has no real improvements.
Final verdict: It's a waste of money.  Just buy the old HL1, which will include this mode AND the singleplayer for $10 total.  It will also have HD models and the old death-animations rather than the failed ragdolls you see here.  It also has more players and better servers (both vanilla and modservers as opposed to a few vanilla).
It's not worth your cash, just add the original Half-Life (not HL Source) to your cart and move along.
EDIT: Take a look at these next gen ragdoll physics!

One of the most well-developed and well-written Visual Novel-esc games I've played in a long time.
It does have a few themes that might turn some off (Gender Bending, People with Animal Ears and Tails, a Slimegirl) but it by no means feels like it's overly-pandering towards that demographic. It takes itself quite maturely, which is refreshing to see when it comes to games in these genera.
It is by no means soely a 'choose A or B' game; There are surprisingly enjoyable Detective segments that require actual thought, not just random clicking around, and Trivia games that, while not essential to the story, do at least make you more inclined to actually pay attention to the ingame universe as a whole.
Its characters are a riot to watch; I had more than a few belly-laughs throughout. The story never takes itself too seriously, and overall is just a fun ride to sit through.
If you aren't exactally enthralled by the gender-bending trope or the idea of having 25% of the cast have animal ears, this probably isn't your thing. But if you're just looking for an enjoyable visual novel with a relatively unique perspective on the genera, I highly reccomend you checking this out.

The game is a classical simluator, if you have played classical Ace Combat and HAWX, this game does even better in regards to gameplay.

The only reason I am not skipping some much-needed-sleep hours and playing this game is:
Controls; while the game has a very good control system that allows for great expereince on jpysticks, doulshocks and hotas (BEST, tried it with my Saitek X52), it is not keyboard+mouse freindly, and here is why:
the game allows for mapping, and mapping reognises the mouse axis and allows you to use it, however, it does not work well because the input is threshold based; so this means when you try to pitch the aircraft, you will have to move the mouse for a couple of meters to do a half loop!
This issue is quite common in many flight sims, an example of a better system is the one with HAWX, where you only need to move the mouse a little bit, the game registers the input and keeps it until you move the mouse back to its original place.
In General, if you like flight sims, played Ace Combat, Il2, HAWX, or any other semi-arcade, or full simulators. You will definantly love VT. And it is even better to expereice with a gaming pad (HOTAS, or joysticks).
Word for the developers. Good job, but Please look into improving the keyboard+mouse controls to allow to use the mouse to do better roles and pitches. It will make this game a 10/10

Firstly, I'd recommend it for fans of hack & slash gameplay. However, it has several issues with the PC port. It's got a hard time with widescreen monitors. The resolution scaling is totally off! Setting it to fullscreen actually shrinks the game's screen and distorts the text, as if stretching a lower resolution. I needed a MOD to get it to run in proper fullscreen. Using that mod, I don't have a mouse cursor in the game... at all. Using the windowed mode doesn't let me adjust the size of the window, so I can only see about 1/3 of the game. The keybindings can be awkward since this game was designed for the PS4. There is no dodge button, nor can you bind it to a key. If I equip the taunt module for 2B and 9S, I can't use it using a keyboard. The "flight" sections of the game are awkward with a mouse and keyboard. If you play for long periods, it will begin to stutter more often, at least for my rig. I've had about 7 crashes so far. Most, if not all, crashes were due to using the steam overlay or alt-tabbing. Other than that, it runs mostly well. Though, with an i7 4790k, 16Gb of DDR3 RAM, about 4 TB of storage, and a GTX 980ti, I really should not be dropping FPS with this game's graphical fidelity.
Onto subjective things: The melee combat, music, and story are all well done! The "flight" sections of the game are basically galaga sections or similar types of games. Combining that with the epic music and an epic setting TOTALLY destroyed my immersion. It's like putting nerf guns into the fight scenes of serious war movies. I would have liked them to do what games like Black Ops 3 did with their flight sections. They were simplified because the main focus is obviously infantry combat, but it did not destroy my immersion. I wasn't going to expect Ace Combat, nor should anyone. The big slow-moving jpeg bubbles of damage definitely didn't help with the immersion either. Sure, fire enough and it'll get very difficult to avoid being hit, but geez how did humanity lose to an army that uses bubble-blowers as their primary ranged weapon? Not to mention they can be destroyed by shooting them with bullets or smacking them with melee weapons. The machines are derpy-looking except for the bosses (thankfully). I do appreciate the effort that went into the story as well as the easter-egg types of endings and nostalgia-like gameplay segments, like with the hacking minigame (except for the "flight" sections). It makes sense why 9S is a young boy. (It's a stereotype) The graphics are... pretty bad. I wasn't going to expect Crysis or Battlefield, but geeeeeez they make half-life 2 look like a graphical masterpiece in 2017. The animations are thankfully well done, except for lip-syncing.
It may sound like I expect too much from games, but this is a $60 release. It has to compare to other $60 games. It comes up short in too many areas to justify recommending it at its current price. This is a $50 game at maximum! $45 would be good. It's like selling a beat-up used car with a good sound system at the same price as a brand new car of the same model. If The Witcher 3's devs could do it, so could these devs. Now THAT is a game deserving of the $60 price!

What an under appreciated gem this turned out to be. Monochroma is a short, highly stylized puzzle platformer and feels like what would happen if you mixed equal parts of Limbo with Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons. It's definitely a flawed gem and comes with a small share of annoyances and problems, but gameplay is mostly solid and enjoyable and the beautiful interactive scenery is a real joy and makes this very worth seeking out.
The thing that brings Monochroma above the level of just an average platformer is undeniably the art style. The background layers and assets marry each other fantastically and it makes for an incredibly visually appealing world. More than that though, the first level sets the tone and more than just introducing the gameplay mechanics in a subtle and fluid way, it visually prefaces the overall story and starts the first transition. The story tone defined by the visuals, and cinematic elements all compliment the game as an experience rather than just gameplay, and it never feels forced.
The story is subtle and more of a shadowy overlay throughout, until the end where it starts to ramp up, and gets interesting. It's quite strange and I don't feel like the story is as good as it could've been, but it does add a little personality and interest that might not have been there had it just been a game about two brothers going somewhere.
* The close checkpoints help to detract from some of the issues with the puzzle segments
* A great level selection menu screen makes revisiting areas hassle free.
Monochroma has all the hallmarks of an ambitious project without the budget to back it up and while those are often the games I love most, they're also some of the most frustrating because of the lack of polish and technical problems, and this game suffers from plenty of both. Fortunately they're subtle enough and the other aspects are strong enough that overall it redeems itself, at least in my experience, but mileage may well vary on different systems and for different players.
The controls and animations are often clunky and more often than not you'll find yourself repeating the same step, jump or movement because something didn't line up properly. This isn't much of a problem, but the saturation of tiny fidgety annoyances from start to finish starts to scrape after a while and really takes away from the whole experience.
These issues are compounded by some frustrating repeated trial-and-error like sections where you're simply iterating the same steps til you get it right. It's often unclear what you should be trying to accomplish or where you should be headed, and the game does a poor job of communicating these things. Again, just a general lack of polish that some time and attention could've and should've taken care of.
There are also a ton of small bugs that come down to just a lack of polish, time or dedication that you'd expect for a game like this, especially when it feels like it's had developers love poured over it from start to finish. I found multiple instances where I was unable to progress, or got stuck in a place that shouldn't have been possible.
* Loading screens are infrequent but very slow, especially for quite a small game. Reload times after death are also tedious and slow which is particularly annoying when death is very frequent.
Monochroma is available on Steam for £14.99/19.99€/$19.99 at the time of this review, and while it's striking and very much worth exploring, I feel it's overpriced, especially considering the 4-5 hour average playtime. For comparison, it's around 30% more expensive than Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons and twice the price of LIMBO, which I think most would argue are fuller, longer games. My recommendation for most people then, is to stick it on your wishlist and wait for this one to hit at least -50% on sale.
The DLC includes the soundtrack, a comic book, a development design book and some extras which are all quite nice to get more of a feel for the game, but at half the price of the game for what is essentially some PDF and wav files, I have to say it's ridiculously overpriced and should be avoided by most.
* There's a free demo available on the Steam store page.

I love this game. But it's weird, inventive, infuriating, and fun.
It's also a great way to test the strength of your friendships or romantic relationships. Because there
friendly fire, and you
kill your partner with a mis-aimed lightning bolt, and you
accidentally do it five more times in the same battle despite apologizing profusely each time in chat. Don't feel too bad--you'll also probably kill yourself by accident a whole bunch of times too, so it'll all come full circle.
The combat mechanic maps different elements to keys, creating a huge number of potential unique combos depending on the order, type, and number of each key you manage to mash out. You'll probably settle on a couple of go-to favorites as you learn the combos, but enemies have different elemental weaknesses, which requires you to switch it up from time to time.
You can play the campaign solo--it gets crazy tough at times, but it's doable and it's very satisfying to beat. But it's built for co-op, which is where it shines. I played it with a good friend and we had a blast despite the many, many, many accidental deaths (mostly caused by me and my stray lightning bolts). All in all, this game is a riot.

But after a buggy release, with a short, umpolished campaign and with the prices raising, everything went downhill. As I write this review, no word has been released by the creator or the studio in
No updates, not even a message from the devs. The game in its current state is playable, but far from polished. It still need some MAJOR changes in order to worth its final price. And the fact that those amazing ideas and plans unveiled by the creator himself (in the ModB forums are several articles written about new aircraft, jamming systems, among other ideas) will likely never happen just make me depressed. I, who helped fund this game since its alpha state, feel cheated, because a bunch of people believed in a guy who seemed passionate about his work, who left a incomplete game and just vanished without a word.
This game is the reason why I'll never support an indie game ever again.

This game's title is appropriately descriptive, Soundodger, because if sound was manifested as colorful, rotating cones, then dodging sound is the thing you do, but I often like to think of it as Danmaku Danmaku Revolution instead.
If you're familiar with bullet hell (danmaku) games, then the core concept of this rhythmic interaction is already understood. You play as a small circle, and it's your job to avoid a collision with the colorful array of cones and spheres thrown at you.
In typical bullet hell fashion, the lethal shapes you're set to avoid are often fired in pleasing patterns. Danmakus are like Dark Souls in that respect. They seem hard as hell, but once you know the patterns, it's merely a matter of conforming to the design to achieve success.
There are two (and a half) things, however, that I feel that make this game noteworthy when compared to already established bullet hells like Touhou. The first, and primary, is this is rhythm-based. No doubt, Touhou has some great music, but in Soundodger+, the curtain of fire you're meant to transverse is generated in a pattern synchronous with the music. If you're playing a DnB song, four-on-the-floor might as well describe the attack frequency. If you're doing a dub step track, when the song scratches out a rewind, you'll find the on-screen clutter suddenly reversing in sync - but it's still coming after you!
The second point that makes this title is its circular nature. Bullet hells are prefered to the usual SHMUPS because of the elaborate geometric designs of death exuding from the big guy of the stage. In Soudodger+, though, the stages are neither vertical- or horizontal-scrolling; they don't even scroll at all. Your whole arena is a circle with circles outside shooting at you in time with the music. Even though I'm unable to adequately describe it, having a static, circular arena lends a particularly unique feel to the genre. Because of its circular nature, instead of strafing through the colorful streams of bullets of typical danmakus, playing Soudodger+ feels like one designed with a Spirograph which I think adds a unique, if not terribly significant, difference to the staling genre.
The parenthetical "half" I mentioned previously is a more obvious characteristic of the game, and that's its general visual appeal. The design is minimalistic, and the colors are bright and bold (and I don't have to play as a loli). Apropos, while graphics of games are hardly paramount, I feel compelled to mention the game's 60 fps setting. The game looked just fine - great, even - with however many fps it was running by default, but when I turned on 60 fps mode... The difference was immediate and obvious.
I only discussed the previous points first because this title is a game after all, but being a rhythm game, the quality of its soundtrack is inextricable from its quality as a game. To put it in an unimaginative adjective, it's awesome.  Broadly speaking, the OST is electronica (I guess?), but I see it as chiptunes crossed with drum and bass while listening to dubstep (but the tolerable kind; not the dial-up modem kind). It features songs from artists like Disasterpeace (Fez, BIt.Trip 2, It Follows), and a bunch of others I doubt you've heard of; I haven't. But that's inconsequential because, familiar or not, the tracks are wonderful. Of course there are a few I don't like (I Do, What I Want) or seem out of place (Lost Age), but that's unavoidable in music-based games. If it says anything, I've purchased the OST, and I've listened to it embarassingly more than I've played the game.
This game seems to me fairly niche, so I'd think that by now you'd know whether or not it's for you, but if you're still uncertain, Soundodger can be found as a game on Adult Swim's website if you care to check it out. I only gave it a few minutes try since I already had Soundodger+, but it seems to me to be just the same. Think of it as a demo, I guess.
TL;DR Soundodger+ is an interesting rhythm-based twist on the small but well-defined bullet hell genre. Both the gameplay and the soundtrack complement each other nicely, but both are still strong on their own.

I received a review copy of this game and was very excited to play it because I had seen many gameplay videos showcasing an element I love – crazy, mindless mass murdering. I was extremely pleased with my gameplay experience.
If you enjoy mindless violence, creative executions, serial killing, and retro pixel graphics, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good – the amount of detail in the character models and everything in the game world is very high. The sound effects are good, and the music for each level is great; however, in certain levels the part where the track loops is quite obvious. The music helps to project a very retro-like atmosphere and feel. The story is decent, however, I personally find the voice-acting to be a bit sub-par (although there definitely is a certain charm behind each voice).
Controls are simple and easy to familiarize yourself with, however, I strongly recommend using a controller to play. There isn’t really a tutorial, and in-game tips are provided via newspapers that you can read. This aspect could have been handled better, however, because the newspaper tips are randomized. An important thing to note is that “restarting” a level is a literal restart – everything in the level restarts from the beginning. The game has a very heavy RNG (random-number generator) element, however, restarting prevents the RNG from coming in. For example, if a stun bomb is located in a nearby item case, restarting will always cause a stun bomb to be located within (while dying/getting busted and restarting will randomize everything again). The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your patience (you will need a lot) and planning skill. Do not be surprised if you have to replay a level hundreds of times – I had quite the rage-fest when I had 50/51 people murdered and got arrested by police before I completed the level (this happened a handful of times to me already). The most challenging element of the game is probably accounting for the RNG that affects everything.
Gameplay consists of you killing everyone in a level so that you can go back to sleep. Your standard killing technique is a knife attack, however, the environment always offers a variety of other methods. For example, in some levels you can push people off the side of the rooftop, electrify a dance floor, or push someone into a ventilation fan. Disposing of dead bodies (via rooftops, garbage dumpsters, etc) is critical because people will panic from seeing corpses and will run around (breaking any route patterns) and/or call police.
If police are called in, an officer will arrive and body bag any corpses – an arrest attempt will occur if you have been spotted by a civilian. You can run away from police, but you have a very limited sprint bar – and police have faster walking speed than you. Preparing traps can kill police, however, they can still be set off by you or other civilians. Some levels have travel points (doors, slides, etc) that you can use to quickly dodge police, however, doing so when you are being chased will cause a Mario-like person to arrive and barricade certain points (use these as a last resort). Sometimes, police can arrest the wrong person, keeping things entertaining.
Maintaining stealth makes the game a lot easier, and a great starting tactic is to dispose of any sleeping people first – you can carry them and throw them off roofs, for example. Interestingly, carrying people does not alert anyone, nor does throwing them off roofs (or into other environmental hazards) in front of others. There is a button/key that shows you all the environmental objects you can interact with – and another useful thing it grants is an indicator on any people that can “see” you. This is great for gauging who will react if you kill someone.
You can make a single call per level, and this will summon a random NPC to the scene. Sometimes I’ve had a Jason-Chainsaw-like person arrive, who proceeded to kill a few people before being arrested. I’ve also had a pizza man arrive – dropping a pizza that attracts a lot of civilians. NPCs can also randomly arrive to the area, and I’ve had a party of civilians show up – much to my dismay because that meant more people to kill.
There are item cases in many of the levels, and sometimes a black market dealer will come and offer you a free item. Items include a stun grenade, dynamite, and (my favorite) a smoke grenade. When using the smoke grenade, you are granted invisibility in a small radius – my favorite tactic is to smoke a dense area and kill as many civilians as possible before the smoke dissipates.
To keep things interesting, there are unlockable characters. I have unlocked the Jason-like character, and selecting him starts me off with a powerful chainsaw.
After playing for a few hours, I realized a very, very efficient way to kill a lot of civilians is to camp near a telephone (or a chokepoint leading to one) and to just kill everyone that tries to pass by/call police. This is not as effective when you have not cleared certain areas of a level – like one that has a second phone. Doing this can allow you to chain massive score combos. Achievement hunters will have an exciting time trying to 100% this game.
Overall, the gameplay is lots of fun and very entertaining – especially with the variety of RNG events. Levels can be frustrating when you are so close to completion, but get busted for whatever reason, however, once you actually overcome these you will be happy for your achievement. The RNG elements and unlockable characters add great replayability. Anyone interested in mindless massacres should definitely give this game a try.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,

+ Absolutely tons of customization options; with such variety, few people can really boast that they have played the same game twice
+ Narrative is both mature and showcases an impressive amount of depth
+ Augmentations, also, offer great freedom in character tailoring; some are arguably more useful than others, but overall the sense of freedom inherent in this mechanic does well to complement the same freedom found throughout the rest of the game
+ Modular damage; limbs and body parts experience damage separately, and this translates competently to gameplay (eg. taking too much damage in a leg will result in poor movement)
+ The player is offered spectacular freedom in how level objectives and advancement are to be handled
+ Level design is applaudable; everything flows well from one area to another, and layouts are generally sensible
+ Soundtrack is absolutely fantastic; sets the mood, doesn't necessarily distract, and stays with you when the game is off
+ Dialogue and writing is absolutely superb; this is easily one of the better aspects of the game, and it presents well even today
- Speed/compatibility issue; this may not affect everyone, but there is an issue with compatibility on modern machines which causes overall gamespeed to increase drastically (there is a workaround, but it's something of a hassle to fix)
- Visuals and animations really show their age; these don't hold up well today, but it's not bad enough to detract from the overall experience
- Voice-acting, though it can be quite good, is a mostly underwhelming effort; some voice actors go as far as to be terrible

For those of us who remember the N64, Goldeneye 007 was up there with Ocarina of Time, and Super Mario 64 as one of the most popular games of the system. Deus Ex reminds me in many ways of Goldeneye.
The gameplay is unmatched. Every level presents new scenery and new challenges. Just like in Goldeneye, you have various objectives that must be completed. And to complete the objectives, you have to deal with enemies as well as many other hazards, There are multiple ways to get to the objectives; do you clear the resistance or do you use your tools to get through the securely locked doors?
This game features level ups in the form of augmentations and skill points. Skill points are gained by finding secrets and clearing objectives and can be used to better your skills, while augmentations are enhancements that can enable you to do things like healing, causing enemies to blow themselves up with rockets, or seeing through walls! You find these in canisters; found throughout certain areas.
It's a fun game and for all you diehard Goldeneye fans (and even if you aren't), you'll love this game. Quite frankly, I don't know why anyone wouldn't. So go and get it.

Alright time for an updated first impressions of Magicite. Remember again that this is an early access review and thus I am reviewing the game in its unfinished state. At the same time the game is being sold as an Early Access game and thus it is more then fair to judge whether or not that feature is worth it.
The basic concept of the game is that you are an adventurer stuck in a dungeon using nothing but his/her wits, brawn, and later on 3 magical/skillful/strong skills to survive as well as a wide assortment of craftable weapons, potions, and gear. Enemies require skill to deal with and the game rewards patience and isn't afraid to punish you if you decide you are fed up.
On the surface this is a very interesting concept for the game and its simplicity is by far its greatest asset, in spite of disliking the game immediately I found that I really couldn't put it down and found myself enjoying it otherwise. This can be rewarded to its harsh environment, heavy skill focused gameplay, and overall simplicity once you get the hang of things.
The downside is that the game is almost too simple. Melee weapons come in very short range swords and extremely slow huge axes (ohh the game has a noob trap in the form of Axes not being effective in combat while still taking durability damage). Arrows will run out of ammo fast, and the magic system while strategic is very underwhelming. Which is sort of the keyword, everything in this game is very underwhelming. Attacking gives the same overhead strike (That doesn't actually hit overhead) and enemies can take several strikes to defeat, making many enemies just a slog to defeat. The Skill system is a lottery as you can end up with rather useless skills or life saving ones (the mage in particular has a few that are essentially and a few that are outright useless).
The stage layouts are by far the game's weakest area as they are dull and uninspired. They are just endless hallways with platforms, populated with a few traps and enemies. Some areas certainly look interesting, but you will find out at first glance that all the stages are essentially the same, just with a few elements switched around.
Crafting is both the game's strong point and weak point. It doesn't leave a good first impression after a while if you chose to go without a guide... and not having some of the essentially recipes can make things difficult or impossible if you don't find them out. Then once you get the hang of it, it starts being fun... but that fun is ultimately capped off.
To confound this the optimal playing strategy is to minimise risk and maximise reward, which makes sense. Yet the game doesn't amply reward risk. Add in that the game is really a fight to perserve your resources as much as possible (The game is part survival game), and you start to understand that risks tend to eat more resources then they reward while low risk areas often reward you quite a bit, for example the forest gives out the most healing items.
Multiplayer suffers from the fact that playing with other players makes the game harder. This is because enemies get stronger, take more hits, while not giving anymore resources and being more capable of dealing more damage. In fact if you and your partner do not know how to make cooked meat this mode is infact outright impossible. The optimal strategy ends up being having one party member clear up an area ahead because that is ultimately safer, essentially making multiplayer a single player experience. The game certainly has hints that multiplayer could be very fun, but this is an early access review and I cannot review a game on what it could be in the future.
In the end I just found myself completely untempted to play the game, and the fun just sort of at a dull level. Sure the game is only 5 bucks, but so are a lot of really fun games.
As of the 21st of May 2014... I give this game a 5/10

This game was a breath of fresh air after playing other Daedelic games- particularly in terms of the likability of the characters (a highly subjective opinion of course), the user friendly features and the logic of a good protion of its puzzles. There were still a number of puzzles that missed the mark on this count and may cause some frustration. Personally, the world was a charming one and I didn't mind going through it multiple times while trying to figure out what the solution was. Mini games and optional side quests also helped enhance the experience and take attention away from the potential points of frustration (not totally but sufficiently so for me). Did I mention that I really enjoyed the voice acting? I could listen to the woodsprite all day and night.
I appreciated the mystery and 'grandeur' of the storyline and script (which can in some cases be seen as taking itself too seriously- but a healthy dose of suspension of belief will cure that) with its fairy tale atmosphere.
The inclusion of the Japanese mythological creature was somewhat dissonant and the voice acting and script for those elements felt forced and a little jarring. They felt similar to caricatures that were pummeled into the script for the sake of including them particularly when considered side by side with the other characters.
Another concern was that layers of stories, the build up of certain mystery around characters, and hints to potentially moving elements were dealt with almost all at onceat the end of the game in a cutscene. Certain story items were practically mentioned like an afterthought and discarded while too many layers and elements were crammed together. That felt a little unsatisfying in the face of the great story telling up until the finale.
All this being said, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and its story, and would play it again. Thank you very much for the great experience!

So before I begin, let it be known I am a huge fan of the first Superhot.
TL:DR:  Fans of the first game will feel right at home.  The basic premise of the game is time only moves when you do, allowing the player to plan out moves/shots in a FPS environment.  It's done very well and is quite fun.  The sequel adds different playable "minds," special abilities, stores, and tons of new environments/weapons.  Even in early access, it feels worth the $12.
First Impression Video:
Mind Control Delete follows the premise of the first game.  Graphics, game play, strategy, and general aesthetics will all feel familiar.  Despite the allure of simply more game to actually play, this sequel adds a few new game mechanics to keep action interesting and game play fresh.
The biggest difference I've noticed so far is the existence of "perks," which give you special abilities (such as extra health).  There also seems to be many more items laying around levels to kill enemies with.  I've noticed toy planes, skulls, floppy disks, etc.
I haven't gotten to play around with the new minds feature yet, so I'll update the review once I've had some time to mess around with it.
Levels seem to vary a bit even upon replaying, which I'm assuming is what the Dev meant by "rogue-like."  Failing missions will have you replay sections that are not always the same as your first failure.  Simply memorizing level layout and enemy spawns is not the way to win here.  I think it works well, keeping the game fresh as you continue on.
Even though it's in early access, it feels like a full game.  Even if the Dev wasn't actively implementing new features, I would have been happy to just have new levels to play with.  I'm really looking forward to see what the Superhot team is planning for this, and the idea of new experiences with each run of the game excites me.
If you dislike early access games and are undecided about purchasing, then perhaps wait a few months to see where this goes, but fans of the series who just want to play some more Superhot, go ahead and grab it now.

Magicite is an addicitng game of crafting, strategy, and survival. In it, you star as a lowly peon (or other unlockible race) as you fight monsters underground in order to make your way to the surface world. There's a lot of craftible weapons, armor, and potions, as well as special abilities and hats with various effects (any TF2 player will know just how important it is to have hats in a game). The various biomes you traverse include grassland, veldt, tundra, lava, cave, and dungeon, and they are all randomly gererated, with their own sets of enemies. This adds a lot of strategy to the game, as no two areas will ever look alike or have the same enemy placement. Resource management will also be a big factor during gameplay.
The creator, Sean Young, is very dedicated to the game and has put a lot of work into it to make it the game it is today. I got this game a couple months ago [March 2014] back when it was still in ver 0.7.3., and a lot has changed since then. However, the in-game bestiary, quest generation system, and PvP battle arena that were mentioned on the game's kickstarter page have yet to be added, but that may change as time goes on. The game is now on ver 0.8 and just got a lot of new content added.
Honestly, as fun as single player is, the real fun is experiencing this game with a friend. It is a lot of fun to plan out long-term goals and strategies with them and work towards meeting those goals. When your plans go off exactly as you planned and you both display excellent coordination, it's hard not to be excited about it.
Overall, the game just keeps getting better with each update and it is still being worked on, so I would say that there is no reason to not get this game. Whether you play it alone or with a friend, you are bound to enjoy this game and also get extremely frustrated when your charater dies (I forgot to mention until now that this game uses a permadeath system), so if your character dies one you will need to start from the beginning again. It really isn't that big of a deal, but if you are someone who dislikes permadeath I would not recommend this game to you. For those who stick with it though, you will really enjoy everything this game has to offer.

An excellent game, it surpasses its predecessors. That said it marks a fundamental change – Empire and onwards are significantly different.
Crank the graphics up to max and it still looks good. The sound variation gets somewhat dull though.
As is par for the series, there are some issues: the AI has pathfinding problems, especially inside cities/castles. You’ll see units running back and forth over the same spot, refusing to move onto walls, or refusing to come down from walls, or getting stuck in between – if you need to move units and walls are involved, plan for the movement to take a long time to complete.
Siege/archers will ignore orders, even with fire at will off.
Units have a strong preference to chase routing units, may have to order them several times if you want them to stop.
The difficulties can cause odd behaviour – on very hard combat difficulty, the auto resolve will almost never favour you, even when you have 10-1 or better numbers. On the campaign, very hard causes the AI to go mad on you – some nations will attack you out of the blue, others will ignore you entirely.
The late game, due to the map spacing and timeline developments can be a bit of a letdown.
Editing the ini files to change things such as rebel frequency is recommended – it’s a shame there’s no easier way to do so. The vanilla concentrated mod is a fantastic way to keep the core of the game the same, but address some of these issues.
Overall, these are reasonably minor compared to the full gameplay and I would highly recommend this game and the series as a whole.

Summary: Pretty, easy to play, overly convoluted story. Better than average but not great.
Long version: MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD.
This could have been a fantastic game. It could have been sitting in the top charts for the point-and-click adventure genre. There are so many promising ideas in this game, and most of them end up being overkill, overly convoluted, or badly executed.
I will preface also by saying that absolutely the BIGGEST issue with this game is the delay in the dialogue pacing. There's a pause between each "action" that a character does, and a character can't speak and also move or go through any non-speaking animation at the same time. This is made considerably worse by the fact that some characters, like the titular Rabbit, punctuate every other line of dialogue with expressions or gestures. So the rabbit's long speeches turn into, line, pause, line, pause, gesture, pause, line, pause, revert to non-gesture pose, pause, line ..... it gets SO ANNOYING and absolutely destroyes any replay value because you do NOT want to sit through those cutscenes a second time.
And it's even worse because the game is REALLY well voice-acted and some of the exchanges are actually really interesting. There's a lot of stuff being said that's supposed to make you go "huh" and then go "ohhhhhh" later on, but you end up aggresively clicking through the dialogue because it's so freaking SLOW.
Moving on to the game itself.
Let's start with interface and mechanics. The simplicity of the interface was pretty good. The inventory system is easy and the controls are intuitive. I loved the tutorial and how it actually kind of fits into the story. But as you go on, it starts getting needlessly complicated. I liked how the holed coin was both an actual useful inventory item and functioned as a hot-spot locator, but then there's also an advice spell that also ends up being actually needed? That's overkill. Then you get items that you're going to use often, so they get their own inventory "slots" for quick access, but other items that you're ALSO going to be pulling up all the time (like the frog clicker) that DON'T get quick access. Sometims combining items auto-closes the inventory window and sometimes it doesn't. The sum total is that it feels really well-designed but then badly executed by multiple game designers who weren't talking to each other.
The gameplay itself is middling, as P&C adventure goes. Some of the puzzles are obvious, some of them make the logical part of your brain give up and go on vacation while you click everything on everything. There are enough clever moments to earn a few brownie points. The collectibles are appropriately frustrating, sometimes dropping into "urge to kill" zones (I STILL can't find all the ************** stickers). Oh, and making us play "go fish" 20 times for an achievement? And then turns out one character vanished before I remembered to try to play "go fish" with him so now I have to start a new game to get than achievement? Yeah, **** you, achievements.
The cards factor into the other issue that I have with this game, which is the plethora of story elements that are all really interesting on their own but never culminate into a satisfying conclusion. There are SO MANY elements of this game that could have been a game all to themselves, or at least a bigger part of this game.
Half the cards are just given to you, but there's a strong emphasis on the cards as a major story theme and representative of the various spells/characters/arcs. Wouldn't it have been more interesting, rewarding, and made more sense to someone trying to collect them all, if the cards were each found somewhere appropriate to the card? Not to mention that the cards as a physical item are never used outside of getting some achievements. What a waste of a theme and a mechanic.
OKAY NOW THERE WILL BE MAJOR SPOILERS. MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD.
So many sub-plots could have been their own game. Just fending off the crows, or dealing with the crows who went "crazy" due to human landfill, could have been it's own (admittedly more preachy) game. The game was so seriously suggesting the idea that everything was fake (including Jerry's "home" and "mom") that I can't help but suspect a more Whispered World-style plot reveal was once on the storyboard. Come on, red-and-white checkered dressed mom making blackberry pie? All the allusions that went back to Jerry's room, his dislike of the city, his absent father? The whole absent father thing got wrapped up so quickly and deus-ex it might as well not have happened. And the story was BEGGING for Jerry to be revealed either as Zaroff or the Old Magician when he gets older. In fact I was actually deeply disappointed by the fact that Jerry WASN'T Zaroff somehow, because it would have been such a better frame for the whole mentor-apprentice story.
Pro tip: if you need a ten minute cutscene at the end of your game to explain the plot, you failed at storytelling.
The lizard quartet themelves could have been enough antagonist for a story, they were certainly set up like one. The master-apprentice cycle and the revealing of true selves planting seeds of darkness could have been its own story. The whole thing could have been set in Mousewood and didn't need "other worlds" and portals, but then portals got jammed in; it was like Mousewood was supposed to just be the first world but tons of time was spent on it, but someone remembered that traveling between worlds was supposed to be a theme, so they hurriedly stuck some two-screen "other worlds" in without considering universe consistancy. Is Mouseworld a seperate WORLD from ours? Because that's a bit demeaning when we also travel to "Ireland-world" and "Japan-world." And then we travel to "somewhere in the arctic-world"? What? Why?
Why is the Marquis cold? Because he was just a memory or because of what he became? Why? What did he become? What did he do to the moths? What the heck is up with the moth queen bit at the end there? There was supposed to be something dramatic about the fact that the Marquis had eyes like the moths but then that was never explained. We didn't actually fix the crow problem! Why is Mousewood both in the middle of the woods and also there's a tunnel that leads underground to a clearly above-ground house next to a train station IF THE ANSWER IS "MAGIC" THEN AT LEAST SAY SO.
And the ending! Bringing everything around full circle to that foggy loop place in the beginning was great. Fantastic. But then that mood was spoiled by Zaroff's show dragging on after it. And then a magic duel that was basically "guess which nail goes with which spell" was so anticlimactic.
If you're wondering why the writing of this review is getting less coherent, it's a reflection of how much the story just loses all attempts at coherency, and not in a good way.
Now if you'll excuse me I have to boot this up again and go play another dozen games of ******* Go Fish to get the achievement because I'm OCD like that.

In the interests of not only full disclosure but avoiding the tendency to give out unwitting spoilers, I will say that I have NOT finished this game. I have, however seen enough to get a grip on the story and the way the game plays. I got this game for review exclusively for The Hidden Levels. The Publisher/Developer provided a review key. My opinions are, as always, my own.
I'm recommending this, not because it's flawless (it isn't), or that I know the dev (I don't), or even because I think the anime girls are cute (I do). It's a well-assembled game that the Dev obviously cares about, and that's a Good Thing. It gets points for not doing the standard thing with the gameplay, having the cute animu style, and for a somewhat different take on the gender-bending thing.
Now, about those flaws: The early part of the story, in which they establish the character of Max and the way he operates
being turned into a busty blonde, can get more than a little confusing. Max and Brad are part of a tiny department of the local police force whose role doesn't seem to make a while lot of sense. There are already divisions of most police forces that do the things that this one "elite" force does-- why that sort of overlap?
A couple of hours in, and I still don't have a solid answer to that. In a Crapsack World, one would expect that major drug operations would be undertaken by Vice, and murders by Homicide.
Several other bits of story stand out in similar ways, all of which are dropped nearly immediately or handwaved away as Normal, or at least not out of the ordinary. Some things, like transformatives, are in fact common enough that there are methods available to reverse them-- albeit rather expensive ones.
The investigation game after that is rather interesting, and here's one of the places where the game shines-- you will want to use those neurons to solve the cases Max has to deal with during the bulk of the game. You CAN brute-force your way through, but a lighter hand and some logic will serve you in better stead.
The other thing that I really did like were the little animated cutscenes. They could have been rendered a bit better, I think, but they make for a nice touch to punctuate high points in the game.
Much as I was down on the story, there are several high points: Max's reaction to being transformed was hilarious, while seeming mostly natural-- He didn't like what happened to him, but appears to get over it... Eventually. Captain Nekorai, on the other hand, has been modified a-purpose with cat ears and a tail-- which he adores. He swears the story is about him, when in fact he's the occasional walk-on cameo and boss for the gang.
I still want to know what exactly he does with that disco ball...
A nice, kind, and beautiful fairy tale adventure. Recommended!

Note: I've played approximately twelve hours or more on this game, but that was on a separate computer so I'm assuming it didn't keep track of it.
I became interested in this game to do rpgminx's playthrough of it. After watching her, I knew I had to get my hands on it myself. Buying this is a decision I do not regret. I have not played (nor watched gameplays of) many genderbender games, but this one has lured me in and set the bar for any others I might play in the future.
I played all the yuri love interest routes, being a lesbian, and each one I loved for different reasons. Ember's was sweet and somewhat amusing, due to Max's naivety. Holly's was surprisingly romantic, and her personality actually reminds me of myself (whether that is a good thing or not, though. . .). Victoria's was flat out amusing, but also affectionate when it came to the art. Speaking of. . .
The art is lovely. The animations surprised me when I was watching rpgminx's playthrough, and it made me want to play it all the more because that is not something you see in a typical visual novel, or so my experience of them says, anyways.
I like how Max's situation with his/her flipped gender is dealt with.
(and I say that for a reason, at least in the beginning) is very upset and resistant to being turned into a girl. It's not immediate acceptance, and it's actually his primary concern - he wants to turn back into a man. Even when he starts becoming more of a
, Max stills talks about returning to his original gender, although I believe she's actually embraced her new form (or at least I hope) and is now content with her body.
The characters are actually pretty far from bland, even the background characters. I have a fondness for all of them, even if that fondness mostly shows up in the form of irritation for a certain panda. . . They're pretty unique and can amuse you. Sometimes the situation can build and I'll be struck by how tense the scenario actually is.
The investigation scenes can actually require some thought, but they're not ridiculously complex or anything like that. Trivia is something I wasn't expecting, but I enjoy those parts too.
The only thing I would say that actually detracts from the game is the grammar - there are a few mispellings, typos, and what seems to be absent words, but in all honesty these are pretty far apart and don't interrupt the flow too much or confuse you, so it's easily ignored.
If I had to rate it, it's an actual 10/10 despite that little issue. I had a lot of fun with this and I'm looking forward to more as soon as more comes out.

TLDR: This game is amazing. Not a 10/10, but an 9/10 with a Must Play attached.
Firstly i'd like to mention that i haven't played any of the prequels such as Nier: Gestalt or Drakengard 3. I had no idea what was expecting me going into this game and just bought it because i had some money to spare. I was worth every penny.
Gameplay: 9/10
+ pretty much standard action gameplay (somewhat like witcher 2/3)
+ variation through different types of weapons and ranged combat
+ the skills you equip have actual impact on what your character is capable of (counters are only available with the right
skill-chip)
- the Keyboard+Mouse controll-scheme
have a dedicated evade button but rather uses doubletapping
the directional keys to dodge attacks (I played it with KB+M anyways because i can't stand playing with controllers)
- for newcomers it can be pretty tough the first time and takes some getting used to
Graphics: 9/10
+ lighting is phenomenal and conveys the athmosphere perfectly
+ animations of the chracters are gorgeous
- textures are fairly low quality
- cutscenes slow down to 30fps
Story: 10/10
+ without spoiling anything: Just Godly.
(sidenote: will take ~50 hrs to complete so bear that in mind when you think you might be done with the game)
+
All in all, as said above the game is a Must Play. The story alone makes it worth every penny of the price. The Gameplay is a little rough on the edges with KB+M but enjoyable, though I recommend playing with a controller if you're comfortable like that.

Three years after I first played Deus Ex: Human Revolution and enjoyed it immensely, it was finally time for its big brother. I tried the original Deus Ex a few years ago, but I just couldn't get passed its outdated visuals (including New Vision) and especially its awful animations. Which I think is probably typical for the Deus Ex series, since Human Revolution also wasn't a looker to begin with. But I suppose I kinda matured in terms of gaming in the last two years, because when I started Deus Ex again a few months ago, the visuals didn't bother me.
But enough about me. Besides the convincing dystopia future with its own share of society problems dripping with atmosphere, I needed some time to adjust to the gameplay. Because it has been quite some time that a game didn't spoon-fed me how to play the game or which way to go with a huge pointer on-screen. Overwhelming at first, but the level of player freedom makes you comfortable very quickly. You get a relatively big area each level where you can go where ever you please, do whatever you want in a manner you find appropriate. The excellent level designs makes sure of that. Later on, based on the augmentations you choose, you get even more options that suit your play style. No wrongs or rights.
+ Excellent level design, a lot of player freedom, all roads lead to Rome.
+ Not a single moment of holding hands, just good ol' fashioned exploration and finding the way on your own.
+ Dystopia cyberpunk future and its problems are represented very well and convincing.
+ A great story to boot that rarely to never loses its grip.
+ A lot of choices and consequences that can make your life later on easier or harder.
+ Great atmosphere and an even better soundtrack.
- Ugly face animations, probably even for 2000 standards.
- Mediocre/static voice acting, except Bob Page whom I thought sounded excellent.
- Stupid AI, though understandable considering it's 15 years old now.
I still prefer Human Revolution (first love and all that), but now I can understand where most of its brilliance comes from. If the next Deus Ex, Mankind Divided, can combine the strengths from both Deus Ex 1 and Human Revolution, and somehow iron out their respective little flaws, Mankind Divided will be a very, very unforgettable experience. The hype is real.

**MOTION SICKNESS WARNING**
Let's just get that right away out front.  I usually do not suffer from motion sickness in video games.  But the stark contrast of dark colors rotating rapidly, back and forth, on a white background was enough to make even my eyes and stomach cry mercy after little more than half an hour of play.  If you do suffer from motion sickness easily, than this is simply not the game for you.
However, if you aren't subject to that, or play the game in small doses, then this is a pretty fun musical avoidance game.  Not unique, but well put together.  The music choices are solid.  It's easier with a mouse, but there's option to use a controller as well if you have one.  There's plenty of songs to unlock, and simply playing through a song once unlocks "Zen mode" where you can basically just have the song play through and not worry about being hit.
One other part that can be annoying for some: The game likes to mess with timing.  The things you're trying to dodge can slow down, or speed up, or even reverse, depending on the music.  This does make things more challenging.  It's somewhat frustrating, because an integral part of dodging is  being able to time things.  On the other hand, it does make for a bit more uniqueness in the game, and makes it just a little more challenging in those moments.
Pick the game up when it's on sale, but grab the soundtrack too - though it only has about half the songs.

An excellent game, it surpasses its predecessors. That said it marks a fundamental change – Empire and onwards are significantly different.
Crank the graphics up to max and it still looks good. The sound variation gets somewhat dull though.
As is par for the series, there are some issues: the AI has pathfinding problems, especially inside cities/castles. You’ll see units running back and forth over the same spot, refusing to move onto walls, or refusing to come down from walls, or getting stuck in between – if you need to move units and walls are involved, plan for the movement to take a long time to complete.
Siege/archers will ignore orders, even with fire at will off.
Units have a strong preference to chase routing units, may have to order them several times if you want them to stop.
The difficulties can cause odd behaviour – on very hard combat difficulty, the auto resolve will almost never favour you, even when you have 10-1 or better numbers. On the campaign, very hard causes the AI to go mad on you – some nations will attack you out of the blue, others will ignore you entirely.
The late game, due to the map spacing and timeline developments can be a bit of a letdown.
Editing the ini files to change things such as rebel frequency is recommended – it’s a shame there’s no easier way to do so. The vanilla concentrated mod is a fantastic way to keep the core of the game the same, but address some of these issues.
Overall, these are reasonably minor compared to the full gameplay and I would highly recommend this game and the series as a whole.

What is there to say about Loadout? Other than it's more graphic than 80% of Adult Swim cartoons, it's hilarious, intuitive, and addicting as hell! Now, where to begin...
| Concept |
Stop me if you've heard this one before: a competitive team-based shooter with stylized graphics and rediculous, non-stop action and humor. Sound familiar? Yes, lots of people like to draw comparisons to Team Fortress 2, and in a way, I don't necessarily blame them; the game draws a great energetic vibe of pulse-pounding adrenaline mixed with off-color comedy, much to the comparison. Though I feel the gameplay actually compliments more to the comparison of Unreal Tournament than anything else. While Unreal was in first person, Loadout tends to draw the same kind of wavelength Unreal had back in its prime. Classic FPS gamers, this game is definitely one to look at.
| Gameplay |
I don't know where to start. There's a whole lot of content to cover, and so little ability to keep it brief. Let's start with the main selling point: whatever weapon you want to make, MAKE IT. You want to make a machine gun that fires syringes to heal  your teammates? Done. You want to make an energy shotgun that fires endlessly-rebounding death and destruction? Go for it. Want a Rocket Launcher that shoots remote-detonated sticky bombs? Sure thing. How about a sniper rifle that unloads 10,000 volts of pure brainmelt into your target's skull? Got you covered. Want it? Make it!
Basically, any setup you can think of, the game can allow you the parts and creativity to make it. Any weapon chassis can be outfitted to any job of any type, whether it be razing, to tazing, to blazing. Weapons are customized by a pre-set amount of parts and payloads you can add into your weapon. Infintesimal amounts of customization allows that no two weapons are alike, and that's just for one weapon. There's 4 different types with different styles of gameplay, and lots you can customize: the rocket launcher alone has 5 different customizing options for just the rocket itself!
And then there's the gunplay! Matches, long or short, are fast-paced, action-oriented, and sure to leave you in a couple stitches your first few go-arounds. For those weak at heart, this game is INCREDIBLY gory. You can charge head-long into battle with naught but your naughty bits still attatched. You can still play even reduced to a brain and a couple eyeballs! This can be changed in the options, but...why would you want to!?
Teamwork is rewarded incredibly well in this game. It PAYS to be a team player, and you'll learn quickly that charging in head-long into battle with your naughty bits is probably not the best idea unless you bring a big gun and a hella lotta backup. Your teammates are your friends, and, like it or not, it's work together or die together.
As for game modes, Loadout does the standard staple game archtypes, but with its own little devious twists. There's a few to cover, so before we do, let's check off the styles of play one by one.
| Casual/Competitive Play |
Don't let the name fool you, this selection is FAR from casual! There's basically two types of Casual Play matchmaking. The first is Cooperative Play, where you and 3 other friends, enemies, or frenemies come together to take on Loadout's rediculous AI. A word of warning: the AI is NOT to mess about with. it knows what it's doing, and you should too. You'll want a team and loadout you can rely on before you jump in, or prepare Uranus, they're going to have their way with you. You'll learn your teammates are a godsend in this mode.
On the flipside, there's Casual Play with other warm-blooded human beings over the webernet! No near-psychic AI's screwing newbies over a barrel, just other normal joes like yourself that are equally capable of messing up horrifically and in sometimes comical ways. In this mode, you're teamed in a 4v4 match against other random people to shoot over a standard internet web connection. This leaves more room for error, as your opponents aren't going to know how to win the whole game completely textbook (you know, unless they're one of those incredibly amazing people who play near-religiously.) Whatever screwups you can manage, so can your opponent: falling off bridges, fragging yourself, accidently dodge-rolling into an endless abyss which will make you swear for 20 minutes about adding guardrails, it can all happen, and you're not going to suffer terribly for it. There is the increased chance of humiliation, of course, which comes with playing against people who can (and will) laugh at you for the longest period of time, but tradeoffs come with everything.
And then there's Competitive PvP. People argue that this is the blood of the game, where players show off their rediculous weapons and crazy game-winning tactics to prove their superiority over a random internet game. Teamwork is key in this mode, even moreso than against the AI's, as this is considered the big leagues: you're against seasoned players, with incredibly powerful weapons. Tread lightly.
| Game Types |
Each match you play in Loadout is catagorized into several different game types. This including:
Death Snatch: Think Kill Confirmed, but a whole lot more frantic and fun. Basically, you kill opponent players for their Blutonium Vials, which, when acquired, increases your score. Scores can be denied, and assisted, so long as you go for any and all vials you see. In this type, there's power in numbers; it helps to stay with your team, and bring some healing weapons, as going off by yourself in this type generally end up with you being ganked by the enemy team...repeatedly.
Blitz: A certain point appears on the map at random from one of several designated areas, which you must, you guessed it, defend or take back from the enemy team. Some argue staying as a group works, some argue divide and conquer works; there's many a strategy involved in Blitz, which makes it utterly frenetic.
Jackhammer: All Hammertime jokes will be nuked.
That said, Jackhammer is Capture the flag, but with a very intesting spin: instead of it being the average, generic flag, you're stealing a huge♥♥♥♥♥hammer from the enemy team. As is implied from that statement, this makes the "flag" bearer able to fight back, unlike the average CTF game. The Hammer grant you a special attack that does INSTANT kill damage within a large radius! Each successful kill with it increases the hammer score by 100 points for if you successfully score it! However, this comes with a catch: did I mention the hammer only gets 5 charges? Make them count!
Extraction: Arguably the most fast-paced type, the name implies the job. One player on your team acts as a Collector, who grabs chunks of Blutonium on the map, and brings them to a processing machine to score. The objective of the game is to score more Blutonium than your opponent by protecting your collector at all costs, and hunting down and denying the enemy's collector. By the way, quick tip for the weary: that Blutonium you run past? Yeah, them and projectiles don't mix. Players can shoot Blutonium sprawled across the map and turn them into volatile explosions of pain! Even the collector can use the chunks they're holding as a makeshift grenade! Plan tactics accordingly.
And finally, we have Annihilation. This one's reserved to the Competitive Play mode, and, I'm ashamed to say, I don't know much about it. I've really stayed away from the Competitive Play mode, as all the more competant players hang out there. Play at your own risk.
In all, Loadout is an incredibly addicting and action-packed joyride through gore and mayhem! Whatever your playstyle, you'll find that this game delivers. It's quirky, tongue-in-cheek humor mixed with intense, graphic gameplay, where teamwork and cooperation will bring you victory! Create. Compete. KILL!
Loadout gets a full recommendation to any die-hard TPS-lover.

Paladins is the first person, class-based, gem-powered shooter from Hi-Rez studios. Sporting four distinct roles with multiple memorable heroes from which to choose, Paladins releases new heroes and content faster and more reliably than any of its competitors (or other Early Access games.)
The graphics in this game aren't bad persay, but are rather bland. Other than the characters, which are quite good looking, the textures in the world will tend to be rather saturated. However, the game runs exceptionally well and stable. In addition, the effects and animations used for the heroes both in first and third person are quite stellar.
The balance of this game has been rather hit or miss, but has been relatively well situated right now. In general, each team needs one support, two tanks, and a remaining combination of flankers and offense. With this composition, the rest of the balance in a match comes down to how well you know your hero. Most matchups between two heroes can be won by either hero, only depending on who is better. This encourages mastering a small selection of characters (I personally recommend one from each class, as well as one more from your favorite class.)
The setup of each class is a primary and secondary fire, two abilities, and an ultimate. All of the abilities of the classes are important to their kit, powerful in combat, and help fill their role. All flankers have a form of escape and engage in one ability, all tanks have a way to soak up damage, et cetera. You can expect just about every class to mesh well into a team, which greatly encourages basing your hero choice (as you cannot change once the game starts) on what the rest of your team will pick.
The game features standard gamemodes like its competitors (KoTH, TDM, and PL) that are fought by two teams of five. You'll definitely feel the effect of having a team of five, where teamfight's individual player performance is definitely weighed heavily to capture the objective. Where this game stands out from other similar games of the genre is that Paladins has a three part card system, where out of game you create loadouts with a combination of different cards at different levels as well as an ingame system where you choose a legendary card that has a great effect on your character, then choose different loadout options to get smaller generic benefits to assist in your current situation in the fight.
Out of game, the progression is based on unlocking heroes and cards. The cards (both legendary and standard loadout cards) will have great effect on your performance ingame, creating genuine reason to continue leveling up and progressing. Default loadouts are available for every character, and are not bad, but rather just the uninteresting default. I hesitate to even call this a grind as very few matches I've played felt the same. Once you unlock enough cards, you can create a loadout benefitting a certain play style for a character as well as unlock a legendary card to further increase your customized loadout's effectiveness.
Note: Legendary cards are not bound to loadouts, and are much more expensive and cannot be unlocked in the same standard way.
Servers are only officially run, and are stable. They go down for game updates frequently enough but this shouldn't be a huge problem. The only other thing to take note of here is that this does mean you can't do much besides part up with friends to queue up.
There isn't a story I've been able to find besides character backgrounds. These can be interesting, but are definitely not important to the game. I do wish there was more of a background story to this game, but it doesn't detract a whole lot from how this game plays.
The maps in this game are generally really well designed. Besides a few strangely placed invisible walls, the maps are well balanced and look good enough. There's enough detail to at least make you understand the map, and the balance between team's sides even on asymmetrical maps is quite well done.
The business model of this map is a hard thing to talk about. It is a free game that has a founder's pack you can purchase to unlock the heroes and some exclusive cosmetics. Heroes can be unlocked with a bit of grind (took me about six hours to unlock each hero.) While this in and of itself would be fair, they made it possible to purchase cards easier through chests (that can be purchased with gems, the usually paid currency,) and skip the grind. In addition to making thme purchasable, they INCREASED the price of the cards (and made the new legendary cards they added at the same time extremely overpriced.) Despite these flaws, they have decreased the prices and made it more reasonable. The last thing of note here is that there are cosmetics you can unlock, but as of right now most heroes only have recolors available. The few model changes that ARE available do look good, but do not exist for every character (this is subject to change in the future.)
Overall, this game is really well done and adds a true sense of out-of-game progression that does not create imbalance between new and old players. If you're looking for a free class-based shooter with real progression, this is where you should look.

I have really enjoyed Stellaris for a long time.  Despite their overpriced DLC's the game has been great and provided me many hours of entertainment.  I would give this a thumbs up, except for the fact of the upcoming changes to this game.
Currently, the game has three traveling methods:
1.  Warp drive, which is the easiest to do as you can travel almost anywhere, but also the slowest.
2.  Wormholes, which requires players to set up wormhole stations in systems to allow ships to have almost instantaneous travel to every system in the distance of the wormhole stations.  It's less free than warp drives due to restricted movement and the wormhole station network can be destroyed, but it is very fast.
3.  Hyperlanes, which are essentially pre-determined roads in between systems.  They are the fastest method of travel but also the most restrictive as you could have systems within another race's territory that you cannot go through to get to your target system.
These three methods provided replayability due to different methods of travel.  Well, it's about to die off.
With the next major patch, the devs are going to do one of the stupidest things they possibly could do:  kill off warp drives and wormholes to pigeonhole everyone into hyperlanes.  They are taking away what this game is well-known for, diversity and player choices, and shoving them out the nearest airlock.  It's not only lazy, but it is also completely detached from the wants of their playerbase.  It will completely split the community in half between people who continue on with updates and people who stay with the current update that actually offers more player choice.  This is the reason I'm giving this a negative review as this extremely stupid change could kill Stellaris in total.
I guess the moral of the story is, NO ONE should buy any Paradox Grand Strategy games until they're fully finished with no more DLC's and patches because the devs will destory their game with stupid decisions.  I know that if this change goes through I will follow that advice from now one.

Monochroma is a very interesting platformer. Without any story told, you will pickup your little brother and help him go through all the obstacles you are facing and escape from bad people.
Pro:
-Graphics: The graphics are REALLY good. I love the black'n white with hint of red style. Feels reqlly unique (despite this is not the first platformer who offer this, check out Limbo an excellent platformer).
-Sound: The music is really good, feels like 1950's musics, with a bit a jazz, it is a good experience for your ears.
-Puzzles: Puzzles feels rewarding when solved, almost all of them are well designed, there some that could use a visual hint or two (like the double lift, I was looking at the wrong solution for quite a long time, had to look up for the solution as I couldn't see it but just the one I was trying which at some point seemed possible). I tink sometimes visual hints to go backward could have been good.
-Story: Despite being without any background, this is a success I think. You understand things one bit at a time, the background is the narrator. The story told here is not very big, it rely mostly on helping your brother. You get attached to that task.
Cons:
-Controls: Controls are sluggish at time. It is not that important except when you need to do timed jump, and at that time the game gets frustrating. The tutorial was not clear enough about the jumping system, as I was succeeding all my jump, I didn't give any thought at first, and then you are in a chase scene and you need to do thing fast and it is not well responding, then you start yelling at your jump. Specially on the achievement Conscience to save a robot from crushing under a press. Looked up a playthrough online, and the layout of the button was different from mine (perhaps a different build than the final one), You have to do some timed jumps and be very reactive, I was trying really hard for at least 15min, then doing more or less the same thing as before, the jump activated as wished and I was able to complete it.
I should'nt stop you from completing the game but a bit of polishing on the control would have been good.
-Bugs: I found some bugs, mostly collision, when that happens you are a bit in a bind as you have to restart the whole checkpoint, despite them being well spread it's still a bummer.
To conlude:
I finished the game in about 4h (a bit more with the achievement of the robot), found 9 out of 16 secrets (I will probably look up for info in order to get them all).
Will you, like me, help your brother? I do hope so.
I do recommend this game to people who like platformers (specially if you liked Limbo, this one should be in your taste).

The Metacritic rating for this game is quite harsh, especially considering the game is exactly what it wants to be. The aim of the game is simply to navigate your way around several different party environments, gradually killing off all of the guests whilst avoiding being arrested. The concept of the game is quite macabre, the fact that your character is  murdering hundreds just for some peace and quiet, along with the narrative cutscenes in between levels that give you an insight into slasher movie culture. In practice the game is actually incredibly difficult, stealth is of paramount importance, because if people notice you, you have limited methods of escape to evade the police who are much faster than you on foot. I thought the different traps set up around the level to help you off a few of the guests were pretty funny, although a little more variety would have been nice. For example almost every level makes use of a car/punch bowl, but at least the traps are semi randomized, I noticed upon repeating some missions over and over that the position of them changed, and sometimes there were traps added/omitted from the level. The addition of several 'Heroes' as the game calls them is refreshing, but offers little in terms of real variety. The soundtrack, repetitive and electronic fits the game perfectly, and doesn't get annoying even after I have had to replay the same level several times over. The art style is the same as is very popular in indie culture, pixelated, yet charming and colorful. Level design is varied enough not to get stale, and there are a lot of different character models. The addition of achievements and trading cards is always nice. I would love to see a future update that added multiplayer, even if it was only two player co-op, because the I feel the teamwork dynamic would work well here.

Three years after I first played Deus Ex: Human Revolution and enjoyed it immensely, it was finally time for its big brother. I tried the original Deus Ex a few years ago, but I just couldn't get passed its outdated visuals (including New Vision) and especially its awful animations. Which I think is probably typical for the Deus Ex series, since Human Revolution also wasn't a looker to begin with. But I suppose I kinda matured in terms of gaming in the last two years, because when I started Deus Ex again a few months ago, the visuals didn't bother me.
But enough about me. Besides the convincing dystopia future with its own share of society problems dripping with atmosphere, I needed some time to adjust to the gameplay. Because it has been quite some time that a game didn't spoon-fed me how to play the game or which way to go with a huge pointer on-screen. Overwhelming at first, but the level of player freedom makes you comfortable very quickly. You get a relatively big area each level where you can go where ever you please, do whatever you want in a manner you find appropriate. The excellent level designs makes sure of that. Later on, based on the augmentations you choose, you get even more options that suit your play style. No wrongs or rights.
+ Excellent level design, a lot of player freedom, all roads lead to Rome.
+ Not a single moment of holding hands, just good ol' fashioned exploration and finding the way on your own.
+ Dystopia cyberpunk future and its problems are represented very well and convincing.
+ A great story to boot that rarely to never loses its grip.
+ A lot of choices and consequences that can make your life later on easier or harder.
+ Great atmosphere and an even better soundtrack.
- Ugly face animations, probably even for 2000 standards.
- Mediocre/static voice acting, except Bob Page whom I thought sounded excellent.
- Stupid AI, though understandable considering it's 15 years old now.
I still prefer Human Revolution (first love and all that), but now I can understand where most of its brilliance comes from. If the next Deus Ex, Mankind Divided, can combine the strengths from both Deus Ex 1 and Human Revolution, and somehow iron out their respective little flaws, Mankind Divided will be a very, very unforgettable experience. The hype is real.
