The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
This game was awesome. I loved it entirely. The premise, the pixelized graphics (which I usually could care less about), the music, the gameplay. I was hooked from the beginning. I saw it and picked it up thinking, huh great story. Guy wants sleep, it's 3am and there is a party next door. So, you handle it exactly how you always wanted to handle it...efficiently. I died about 15 times in my first 30 minutes of playing until I started seeing the pattern and picking up exactly how to go about the room. Then, it all clicked. Even when a new level would start. Was this game training me to be a proper sociopath? Was I going to be capable of infiltrating large parties, and even public places, to chaos mayhem after all this? Is that voice actor finally going to just say "I'm Batman" already? Even knowing when to strike and avoid all eyes, then slowly stroll by the cops like nothing when they'd inevitably arrive to check things out become an art and a game to me. This...this is Party Hard. It's making me a better person, really. Won't you join me? It's a solid 4/5 and worth $10 easily. I feel like I stole it (small crime, relatively speaking) by getting it 50% off.
Happy Gaming!!!

Assuming the role of a spree killer, but far from being a cathartic exercise in mindless ultraviolence, Party Hard is about careful and methodical premeditated murder.
It plays a lot like a hybrid puzzle/stealth game in that sense, with a few procedurally generated elements in each level making it nigh impossible to complete a level by simply learning a pattern, but forcing you to figure out your course of action on-the-go as events and traps are randomly selected from what appears to be a rather large pool.
Usable items are another random occurence within each level that, along with the potential spawning of a trader, might give you even more options to dispatch unlucky partygoers.
Later in the game, you are also introduced to different playable characters, which might not seem that different at a first glance, but after a bit of learning will show weaknesses and strengths that you will have to play with in order to beat each level, thus adding a nice bit of variety to the already rather strong gameplay.
I do, however, have a few personal qualms with this game:
- the art style, although brilliant in its simplicity, is not the best when it comes to differentiating places you can or cannot walk over, and it did happen that I lost track of my own character in the more crowded parties
- the visibility system, while acceptable and usually not a real issue, can at times be a tad basic and misleading
Other than these, I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who wants to indulge in a bit of the old ultraviolence, while at the same time being given a challenging brain tease that requires you to keep thinking on your toes.
Before I start, I will mention that the game has been patched with seven extra levels for FREE!
As for replay value itself, the character unlocking is really the strong point of the game, each one providing a new playstyle for every level, with pros and cons for each, some more difficult than others.
If I had to say one more thing about this game, it's that it is a great example of beauty in simplicity.

Ahh, Soundodger+! A breath of fresh air from all the triple A madness that goes on around the passing holidays. If you've ever played any arcade shooter, you already played soundodger. It's far from perfect and further from being original, but you will definitely forget about that once the music kicks in! You're a little circle that dodges the particles made by the music itself.
You dodge the sounds of music eminated by the likes of Austin Wintory, Mike Forst, and Disasterpeace! If you don't, the music will become mixed up and will transport ahead of your mistake, while keeping track of your percentages. You can also enter into a bullet-time like mode, but be warned; if you do it will affect your overall percentage! You can go a whole song in this mode, but you'll never complete with a 100% because of this.
It isn't without it's faults either, unfortunately! My main problem is it's repetitive nature, of course every game like this is going to be repetitive, but this is different. Like after a while (20 minutes I'd say) you're going to be bored with it. Not to mention the tracklist starts over when you hit the new levels! The game does have a level editor, which you can import songs and track it yourself, but the problem here is it's tedium. You'll be sitting at your desk, face smooshed into the screen, trying to get that one bullet into the perfect spot.
In reality, if you have time to kill, this game is right up your ally! It has a great soundtrack composed of some of the most talented personnel, ever. This game is meant to fill the gaps between shower and bed time or coffee and work!
Is it worth your money? I think so!

It is adorably filled with tons of imaginative little ideas, easygoing humour and clever references to other classic adventures. Scenes are generally pretty and well rendered, albeit often with uniform levels of detail.
I found myself enjoyably humming the game's music regularly in between playing sessions. The majority of puzzles rely on conventional logic, challenging in their own rights but never a strain to solve (only a few items are obtained or used somewhat arbitrarily).
Individual components are mostly soundly executed but their overall sum unfortunately does not translate into a very exceptional experience. The game does not intentionally sabotage its appeal in any drastic way; its only real recurrent negative quirks are dull writing and repetitive dialogues.
Despite its promises of magic and adventure, the game remains uniformly average with few moments of awe delivered at a slow pace.
Typical inventory puzzles have you play errand boy for perfectly incapable townsfolk who would likely forever remain in limbo if you hadn't shown up to fix everything for them. Its uncharacteristic leading young man is neither especially charismatic nor particularly witty, making these tasks rather mundane. Secondary characters are a mixed bag of highly intriguing and static types.
The plot becomes more compelling, perhaps a little too late, after an interminable initial exposition. Once you finally get to the real magical bits, you will find the world portals lead to small underdeveloped and self-contained areas where each spell you learn has a handful of highly specific uses.
A more interesting game mechanic lets you switch between night and day, which significantly alters areas you can visit.
Increasingly mysterious story threads with no immediately obvious connections are satisfyingly and nicely tied together in a properly lengthy conclusion, served as an elaborate cutscene that explains everything in detail. Reaching the end feels good.
A surprisingly twisted final segment lets you briefly revisit the other small worlds in a re-imagined version. This original part breaks positively from the regular pacing of the game.
There are a few missteps, such as when your magical adventure temporarily turns into a moralizing threat of ecological disaster that is not even central to the main plot.
Technical glitches sometimes make the game skip dialogues or break down the UI, in some cases forcing a restart. Save often.
A journal keeps track of current objectives and even occasionally offers subtle cues towards their solution but its information is poorly organised. An ineffective in-game hint system disguised as your first spell simply repeats key dialogues you've previously heard without providing additional direction.
Annoyingly, there is no way to pause the game during dialogues.
There are a surprising amount of optional collectibles for a game of this genre: dewdrops, cards, stickers and audio books. Most of them are entirely useless outside fulfilling a compulsive need for completion, except for the dewdrops, which expose a minor plot detail ahead of the ultimate reveal, and audio books that add a lot of folklore to the game's world if you have the patience to sit and listen.
The optional Quartet memory game is very basic and not very challenging. Completing your card set does not improve your available strategies and playing it becomes rapidly boring.
Overall I found The Night of the Rabbit simply too banal to recommend to everyone. It is by no means a bad game, in fact it is moderately enjoyable, but with better pacing and a fully revised dialogue system it would have been vastly improved. Perhaps you will enjoy it better than I did but make sure you get it during one of Daedalic's insanely advantageous sales.
Otherwise I would instead recommend the more fulfilling and better executed
by the same developer.

I played this on CD to the point that the disk stopped working. I don't have an hour total, but I can assure you I spent a good two or three years putting about as much time into this as I did my full time job.
Probably the last really well thought out Total War game, and one of the least buggy. There is no stupidly awkward city management system (Empire), most of the factions are reasonably well balanced (with the exception of the Italian States, who are crushingly overpowered in a player's hands - still better than pretty well all the other total war games out there), and things move at a pace that doesn't feel to relaxed or too rushed (shogun, napolean).
It's not a masterpiece by any means, but now that I revisit them, I don't think any of the Total War games really are. It is a pretty fun game though, and certainly worth getting if you've are looking to get into the series.
Edit: When I say "the least buggy", I'm just refering to the Steam versions. Rome:TW on CD, from like a decade ago, remains stable as a ♥♥♥♥ing rock resting on the surface of a giant steel cube with the gravitational pull of a black hole. There is also a 6 billion ton weight sitting on top of the rock. I've been told the Steam version doesn't work that well, but haven't had to try it despite having lost my Rome CD recently, because Rome is from an era where devs depended on human decency and CD codes as DRM.

Arcade air combat games are very much my cup of tea. Want to take an F-15 or a MiG up with minimal fuss and hardly any learning curve? These games are all about that.
Vector Thrust is overall a really good arcade air combat game that mimics the feel of Ace Combat and HAWX, and, in my opinion, even outdoes the disappointing Ace Combat: Assault Horizons. The cell-shaded graphics look and feel great, the narrative isn't bad, and the gameplay is fast and exciting.
The game offers a good array of beautiful aircraft, each with their own characteristics. Stealth and detection are represented in a fairly simple way - taking a stealthier aircraft confers some benefit but it doesn't seem decisive.
It's not all good - some of the missions seem exceedingly difficult, and I'm personally stuck on one that doesn't seem to be particularly beatable. I'm told that this was the result of a patch that increased the effectiveness of a common missile, but I'm not certain. Some of the missions aren't laid out very clearly and mid-mission changes often have little to no explanation. While that's certainly realistic, it can make parts of the game a bit frustrating.
Some of the missions appear to have no briefing or pre-mission narrative, which feels a bit jarring. It makes the game feel unfinished.
However, for the game's faults, it remains a budget Ace Combat clone that generally plays well and is worth the money. I'd suggest getting this over Assault Horizon any day, but overall I felt HAWX was a better game.
If you're looking for something to hold you over until AC7, Vector Thrust isn't a bad choice.

Cannot advance the main story, but after a dozen or so tries to even get past the first mission, I've lost all interest in whatever story was trying to be told here.
Other gamemodes play better, and the game runs smooth enough, but even with all settings on ultra it becomes very hard to see anything that's going on aside from how beautiful your plane looks. This is a game involving transformations, primarily focusing on guy to girl.  Though animal ears and tails are pretty prevalent too.  If you dont care for that kind of stuff you should probably just move on, because though there is more than that to this game it is the central theme.
The main character is a Police Officer working in an elite unit tasked with taking down a new drug, MinX.  Through a bit of stupidity, the character gets turned into a girl.  This is a world were people can buy drugs to alter their appearance so it's not considered a big deal.
You have the standard romance options with the people you work with.   You also have some detective type puzzles to work through, which i rather enjoyed.  Other than that there's alot of dialog to go through and it feels very well written.  I rather got to enjoy the characters in the story.  The game world itself is an extension of another game, "Gender Bender DNA Twister Extreme".  As a result the game worlds lore actually has some depth to it, though its mostly only hinted at here.  I'm not sure but i think this game picks up a year or two after the last one ended, and in a different city.  You will see some return characters though.
Simply put, this game is better than its predecessor.  Or at least i think so, sure you don't get to jump around characters like before and see their different angles of the story.  But, this game seems like it will ultimately be larger and already has more variety of actions, namely the detective style puzzles and i'm hoping they do more with the mini game on your phone.  Regardless, if you liked the previous game get this.  If you thought it was lacking a bit, get this.  If you hated it, don't get this.  And if you have no idea about the other game ask yourself two questions.  Do i want to play a date sim style game?  Can i tolerate transformations that include gender change?
The only thing i didn't really care for was the serious lack of variation on the characters picture's.  I'm hoping its nothing more than a mark of being early access.  Admittedly it was funny when the characters made a comment about this in regards to a criminal but i'd rather have more variation than a sly 4th wall gag.

Monochroma review by Dionysis Spinos (as presented on

Black & White games! What is not to love in them! The atmosphere they create, the sense of mystery and old 50’s films. And these are only some of the virtues today’s game has to offer. Its name? Monochroma. The story takes places in an alternate version of the 1950’s where there is a huge company selling robots to the people in a fantastic city. You are playing the big one of two brothers. On the night that your brother gets injured and you are seeking help around, caught in a storm, you find yourself in a warehouse and reveal an awful secret about that company. The younger brother is afraid of the dark therefore the player can only put him down under the light to be able to jump higher and move faster but you can’t leave him behind like in real life! The really strong element of this game are the amazing visual and music. The black and white is in perfect balance with the red color and creates a really unique environment the player can move and unfold the great story of this two kids!  Of course, you can’t have such type of game without 50’s music. The soundtrack in this game is really amazing that enhances the overall experience a lot. Moreover, I loved the realism in the locations where each Act takes place. They blend perfectly with the story and the silent narration helps the player think and imagine the dialogs and how everything will evolve next just like in the 50’s movies we all love! (Too bad they couldn’t add red color to them). Furthermore, it is really worth mentioning the fact that there are also puzzles in this game. The puzzles are really well created in a way so they will fit in the story and it is really fun to be honest to solve them, so you can continue to unfold the story of the game. On the other hand, there are some negative aspects too that should be mentioned. Even though the game features puzzles unfortunately they are of moderate difficulty. Moreover, even though the game is a platformer and a good one I may add, most of the time you will find yourself walking. So more platforming aspects are recommended.
Finally, even though the game has some negative aspects, the positive are the ones that rise in the surface. The game has some stunning visuals and gameplay that I will totally recommend to everyone who loves games like Monochroma. Monochroma promises and delivers hours of fun in a ’50s atmosphere we rarely see in detail in titles like this. Must try game and a unique experience that will satisfy even the most demanding gamer!
Verdict 8/10
+ Stunning Visuals
This game makes you love your brother and family in general
Unique gameplay and mechanics
Realism in locations and a silent narration that sets a unique atmosphere
-Puzzles of moderate difficulty
A little platforming features and more walking in the game

The gameplay doesn't match the aesthetic.
I didn't manage to pitch into the Kickstarter as I found out about it too late but the art-style, reminding me of Limbo, floored me and I picked the game up instantly. Sadly I should have just watched a playthrough of the game rather than lay down the $20 I paid for it (I'm thankful I didn't back it either), and you probably should too.
The gameplay is simple, you run around, jump, swing from ropes, push crates and interact with switches. Every 2D platformer trope in the book, except none of it is done well. Your top speed while running is somewhat slow and when you jump or land you come to a pause which really breaks up you pacing so it only makes your speed worse. Swinging from ropes is the worst as it takes way too long to build up momentum to make it across gaps and if you lower yourself to the bottom of the rope (for the most momentum) you're probably just gonna go too far and drop off and die. The controls just feel really, really stiff, it feels like you're desperately trying to get the boy places and do things because of just how "off" the controls feel. Also the "controller" support in this game is abysmal: the game was made for the keyboard while the controller was definitely an after thought, you can't rebind any of the controls on the keyboard either if you want to opt into using those so enjoy the arrow keys for movement, Space for Jump and Alt/Crtl to interact. You also can't interact with any of the menus with a controller or even the mouse, the controller also doesn't feature the "interact" command anywhere, so you HAVE to use the keyboard in combination for the controller. Also, at the very beginning your brother/friend hurts himself and you have to carry him on your back a lot which is a really tired mechanic and never fun. He can't interact with anything (from what I've seen) and he's just a burden to make the "puzzles" challenging by figuring out how you're support to get across obstacles with him.
The game has the intrigue of similar titles, the story is all told through actions and the art-style set forth and there's secret flowers for you to find if you're so inclined. I'm 40~ minutes into it and while I'm usually a sucker for art games I don't know if I can bare to play through the rest of the game because of the controls and and gameplay. If you're expecting something to the calibur of Limbo, this isn't it, I'd only recommend this if you could find it for $5 on a Steam sale.

Assuming the role of a spree killer, but far from being a cathartic exercise in mindless ultraviolence, Party Hard is about careful and methodical premeditated murder.
It plays a lot like a hybrid puzzle/stealth game in that sense, with a few procedurally generated elements in each level making it nigh impossible to complete a level by simply learning a pattern, but forcing you to figure out your course of action on-the-go as events and traps are randomly selected from what appears to be a rather large pool.
Usable items are another random occurence within each level that, along with the potential spawning of a trader, might give you even more options to dispatch unlucky partygoers.
Later in the game, you are also introduced to different playable characters, which might not seem that different at a first glance, but after a bit of learning will show weaknesses and strengths that you will have to play with in order to beat each level, thus adding a nice bit of variety to the already rather strong gameplay.
I do, however, have a few personal qualms with this game:
- the art style, although brilliant in its simplicity, is not the best when it comes to differentiating places you can or cannot walk over, and it did happen that I lost track of my own character in the more crowded parties
- the visibility system, while acceptable and usually not a real issue, can at times be a tad basic and misleading
Other than these, I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who wants to indulge in a bit of the old ultraviolence, while at the same time being given a challenging brain tease that requires you to keep thinking on your toes.
Before I start, I will mention that the game has been patched with seven extra levels for FREE!
As for replay value itself, the character unlocking is really the strong point of the game, each one providing a new playstyle for every level, with pros and cons for each, some more difficult than others.
If I had to say one more thing about this game, it's that it is a great example of beauty in simplicity.

As a big RPG Maker fan, and a person suffering from depression from over 10 years, I had high hopes for this game.
However, the developers managed to break two concepts at the same time. They broke the RPG system, and the Anti-Depression campaign.
There are only two outcomes from playing this game. Either you are depressed and don't really care, or you're not but after playing this, you'll become depressed!
We take a role in the life of Nathan, a chef-soldier who had a regular life, but events changed him to a different person. Players are invited to observe these changes in his mood, behavior and habits.
The developers also had metaphors to exemplificate the life changes and enemies, as well as our battles.
In terms of design, the game is very simplistic, not because the engine, but due to the lack of skills from the person or individuals who design the maps and areas. Some areas are just too big, basic and barely with anything interesting. Definitely lazy and with poor choices for environments. I'm also not counting the bugged areas, nothing is perfect and it's a common thing with RPG Maker games.
is extremely short, 3 hours of gameplay, maybe more if you're new to RPG mechanics. Not only the design is basic, but the gameplay is a way too much simplified. A "
" but without anything related to it in terms of game basics.
Not only the creators never played Final fantasy, as they probably never played any RPG before. In
you cannot farm for XP, and therefore the feeling of taking enemies at your own abilities is inconsistent. There is no economic system, although there is a store available with prices. There's no opportunity to upgrade or gain new weapons. There's only one side-quest and works as an exploit to get free potions.
We know nothing about the World, the NPC's barely say anything decent, and to make any sense, we must hold on to a group of fighters that joins the player.
A series of events, fights and items can barely be called an RPG... If this is a game of options, challenge and side effects, maybe RPG Maker wasn't the best option. Maybe this would work much better with a Visual Novel engine, or a Point & Click one.
There are no depression references at all. The metaphors cannot justify everything and hope for the best. Plus, the interview occurring throughout the game is really basic and generic. If it is real, I couldn't feel any relation.
Overall, this game is absolutely not an RPG. It's a strange mix of ideas and concepts that looked amazing on paper, but are miserable in an RPG Maker game.
This has been the worst RPG Maker game I ever played, and if you are looking for a push up in your life, you'll not find it here.
is boring, repetitive, shows no respect for your time, and in the end you'll learn nothing from it. Doesn't matter if only friends can help you, this game won't help you find any!

I did appreciate that many of the townsfolk said all the typically unhelpful things that real people say to depressed people. "Have you tried smiling more?"
Halfway through, the game breaks the fourth wall in a way that made me very uncomfortable and forced me to question why I was even playing the game, or any games, and it actually worsened my depression at that point, so thanks a lot for that.
tl;dr If you want to play a GOOD game about depression, play The Cat Lady.

This is an amazing game, even if it can be difficult. The story is simple and clear, and very close to the heart. I suffer from only mild depression, and I have still felt the emptyness inside. It is always a good thing to find people who recognize that depression is not sadness, but a lack of any emotion, sadness included. I am definetly going to share this game with my cousin, who also suffers from depression and often more strongly then I do. However, DO NOT play this game if you are currently suffering from an attack. This game does break the fourth wall, and if you are already feeling empty inside this may hit exactly the wrong buttons. This was a good day, and it still hit me very hard. However, if it is a good day, do play this game. If you do not suffer from depression, you may find it enlightining, and if you, like me, my cousin, and so many others, do have depression, then this game is a reminder that you may need badly that this is one monster you cannot fight alone, and that true friends will stick by you and hear you out. It may also be helpful for those of you who have a depressed friend or family member, and help you to at least know a little bit of what they are going through and what they need.
Whether you suffer from depression, share your life with someone who does, or have never even thought about what it can do to a person, you need to play this game. It may not change your life, but hopefully it can open your eyes.

Medieval II: Total War is the best total war game I've played, though I've only played the more recent ones. Still, there are countless hours of fun in here, and if you like strategy games there's absolutely no reason not to pick this up.
Still, there are problems with the game. It's pretty old, and while I have few complaints about the graphics (kinda unfair to rag on those), I did have some problems making it run on Windows 8.1 - so keep that in mind. There are also quite a few things that could improved; the campaign goals are a bit ridiculous, though that doesn't mean that it's all that hard to beat the campaign. The AI - while it has moments of brilliance - is pretty bad in general: on the battlefield it'll often charge forward with little thought (though this seems to happen less late game, for some reason), and on the campaign map in can be incredibly stubborn (unless you have an enourmous advantage), attack you for no discernable reason (sometimes accepting peace the turn after with no battles fought) and in general it's just incredibly hit and miss. The ship battles are also basically non-existent, and there's an annoying lack of control, but who ever liked ship battles anyway, so that's a minor point.
The unit variety is also somewhat lacking, though it isn't all that bad - the selection is okay, but your armies will often look alike, and you'll find yourself just building the same army again and again. Of course as you grow larger, you'll encounter enemies with completely different units, but it happens fairly late in the campaign. It's sad because the game actually includes quite a few more units, but they're only "unlocked" very late game where you're already totally dominating. Talking about selection, you have a choice of annoyingly few factions when first starting the campaign - you have to beat it to unlock minor factions.
I have more minor complaints, but the good news is that mostly everything can be fixed with the huge number of mods made for this game.
Overall, I'd love a MD III: TW - where they don't ♥♥♥♥ up as they did with Rome II - where they incorporate the good stuff they made for the new games (tech tree, mini settlements), but drop the stuff like mo-cap and whatnot. I could talk for awhile about what shouldn't be included, but anyhow: I wholeheartedly recommend this game, and you should buy it even if it isn't on sale. It's probably the game I've had the most fun with. It's easy to get into, and it's entertaining throughtout - I have a few nitpicks, but yeah, there's nothing majorly wrong with this game in my opinion. Music's great as well.

The Night of the Rabbit is a game that has earned a special place in my heart for its beautiful art, endearing characters and a very nice story. You can't help but feel that this game was made with a lot of love.

And that happens more often then I would like.
Everything else about the game, though? Good or better. Well thought out storyline, charming vistas, excelent voice-acting, a likeable if not particularly brilliant protagonist, wonderful soundtrack, solid gameplay, etc. It all fits very well with the overall 'children's story book' idea of the game.
To sum it up: if you can take the puzzles more as an excuse to enjoy all those good aspects than as the beginning-and-end of the game itself, I would tell you to grab The Night of the Rabbit right away. You won't regret it (unless you do).

What can I say? I thoroughly enjoyed this game; it exceeded all my expectations, and then some. (This is especially right after having played A New Beginning, a game which I probably wouldn't wish on anyone.)
Pros:
- Very captivating storyline; the game is mysterious throughout, and succeeds at maintaining suspense
- Voice acting (English) is truly exceptional, especially for a game which doesn't have English as its native language
- Art style, cutscenes, and music are all utterly beautiful and very fitting; reminded me very much of those cartoons I used to watch as a kid of talking animals in enchanted forrests
- Main character is likeable, which makes the game all the more a joy to play
- Fairly interesting mini-game (Quartets)
- Unlike most other point-and-click games, this one has several different types of objects to collect along the way (e.g. dewdrops, stickers, cards, stories) which make you pay more attention to the environment; personally, this made me appreciate the art better
- Generally solid gameplay, very decent amount of content
Cons:
- For most of the game, there will be concurrent side-missions or objectives available for you to do (e.g.
) which you will only be able to actually solve towards the later part of the game; the fact that these objectives can still be activated by the character early on in the game makes it a bit confusing for the player, because it is unclear what should or can be done first, especially since the main plot is still linear
- Rather strange mini-game in the finale
Overall, this is a very beautiful and captivating game which I would recommend to anyone. It even comes with audiobook stories which, if you'll excuse me, I shall go listen to now.

6 hours of gameplay so far and it's still in development? Wow, I sure feel that I got what I paid for!
So after running the game from beginning to the current end, I have to say that I am not disappointed at all!
The plot (scroll down to my review below to avoid spoilers)
The plot is apparently set in the near-future, where it's been popular with transformation-gas and half human-half animal surgeries and stuff. The technology is quite similar to current, with taser-weapons as regular non-lethal weaponry, normal TVs, cars on wheels and trains still on tracks etc. The gender-transformation is apparently still in its early days with a few biproducts (like lactose-intolerance being a biproduct of cat-ears). Our protagonist however, is a young police officer with about three years of experience. He and his partner, Brad, are part of a department that deals with drugs and stuff and they are currently trying to deal with a new sort of drug called MinX. During their first dispatch, our protagonist ends up having a "tiny" bit of an accident and ends up as a woman. Now, for all of you that came here just for that par, I can promise you that he's not the only one that ends up having to deal with a female body... *giggle*
Now, here's my veiw on other features in the series:
Music/sound
I like the music and sound effects, but I miss being able to hear voices and possible have a on/off function of this. What I think would be great is if one could choose between having the characters speak or not. I like the game, but it's a shame when I have to read things 2-3 times because I can't seem to register what I read (this often happens when I'm feeling a bit tired, and that I do often). I also think this could help making the game differ more from other visual novels.
Animation
This part I feel should be separated in two parts: the animated scenes and the regular scenes.
I have to say that I love the scene from the trailer. However I have been playing for 6 hours and only at the current end did I get to enjoy a new, short animation that looked quite similar to the last one. To be honest I feel a bit disappointed. I would very much love to see action or comedy-packed scenes receive even just a short scene now and then. Especially special scenes containing unique situations or characters. It would give the game more interesting content that adds to the regular content.
For the regular content I want to make one thing clear; NEVER use a picture of the character that doesn't fit in with the action. It's important with variation to ensure that it doesn't look cheap and poorly made. So if a character is bloody, it is bloody, and if a character got ther gender swapped and they have a belt to their pants, they won't try to hold them in place with one hand all the way to their boss's office and then all the way home. Besides,  a womans waist is wider than a mans, and hence it doesn't add up that the protagonist lose his pants (and not the underwear?) when turned into a woman. But enough of that pricky stuff. Overall aside from these few things, the content is good-looking and most of the time it fits well into the situation.
Texting
I've found some, but very few errors to the texting. So far I guess I have only found places where words are missing, so I just add them in my mind when reading the sentence a second time. It would be nice to see these minor errors corrected, but it's not something that would need to be prioritized at this stage. It may actually be a good thing, as the reader has to stop and read one more time to get the whole picture. It creates a pause and a difference, and it certainly gets the reader's attention back a little. As long as it's only happening 4-5 times in like 6 hours of content, it's not something to get all worked up about.
interaction with the game
I simply love how one can affect the game with multiple choices and this should definitely have a continued focus throughout the development. Even though it's a story-based game it should give the player the possibility to interact and affect the game, and even though I haven't really got to test this out much, I have to say that it's still a bit funny. In my case I'm a justice-person so I have an issue with accusing the wrong suspect and stuff like that, in fear of getting both the hard-working protagonist and an innocent in trouble... But I did get an opportunity to run away from a certain cute-girl loving maniac that eventually stunned/tazed the protagonist and dragged her to a swimsuit shop... it was quite funny actually...
And that's it for my review! Personally I don't think I'm the right person to set a "grade" on stuff, but in my case I would say 8/10. As the game is not finished yet, my estimate is only for the content so far, not for the finished product.

Short version: Abandoned early-access game
Long version:
I'm going to start this off by saying I really wanted to reccomend this game. After so many years without a new Ace Combat game (and no, Assault Horizon was not an Ace Combat game; it just had the label slapped on), I was excited when this came out of early access.
Starting off with the good: this game has a massive selection of aircraft, both real and fictional. Like, it's huge. The gameplay is also good: combat flows well and the controls feel like they should. It also has a single campaign which has a pretty standard arc of "no-name pilot nobody's heard of turning the tide of a conflict to become a famous ace"
This game has a ton of promise, and a lot of potential. It was in early access for a long time, and there was nearly constant feedback by the devs showing their progress. There was very steady progress, but eventually the publishers forced the devs to release early. Despite this, the devs acknowledged that it wasn't complete, and promised continual updates until it was done.
The last update was in summer 2016, described as a "quick update," and no dev has posted on the discussion board since then either. If you really want this one, I wouldn't pay the full $25 for it: it's just not finished. Definitely wait for a sale. Besides, with the upcoming announcement of Ace Combat 7, it's better to hold onto your pursestrings and wait for that.

This might be more of a comparsion between Monochroma and Limbo than just a regular review. The artstyle and surroundings in the pictures of Monochroma was what drew me to buy this game since they reminded me of Limbo, one of my all-time favorites. With that said, if you have not played or heard of Limbo this review might be somewhat undescriptive.
In Monochroma you are the older brother of two, who has to protect the younger brother who is injured and pretty much lifeless by carrying him on your back through the game. So basically the entire game is one long escort mission. You can drop your brother off at certain points which allows you to jump higher and so forth, this is a core mechanic of the game and it's puzzles. The gameplay and puzzles are quite good although sometimes they can be quite unclear of their objective. I had to resort to a guide online several times throughout this game. I don't know if that is a sign of a somewhat poorly designed game or of me being stupid. I should point out that throughout my intial playthrough of Limbo I never had to resort to a guide. Another criticism I have is the controls. (I played this with a Xbox 360 controller.) I'd say that the jump button has a little delay and is not nearly as responsive as in, surprise, Limbo. You might get used to it, I don't think I did cause it made me irritated pretty much through the whole game. I think the controls in general could be better and more responsive. Also the game can be occasionally buggy.
It might sound like I dislike this game since I've only brought up criticism but there are good parts as well. The music is pretty nice although the "death jingle" is ironically happy. My biggest praise for this game would be for it's beautiful graphics and the settings. I usually don't care that much for graphics and such but in this game they are just right. The atmosphere in the many different settings and surroundings is great and fits just right. The plot is pretty basic yet interesting with tidbits being
during the loading-screen.
All in all, I would recommend you to buy Monochroma if you already have played Limbo and are looking for more of the
. If you have not played Limbo, go buy that and play it. I'd say that Monochroma is more of a poor man's Limbo since it is not nearly as well polished as Limbo if you ask me.
TL;DR: Buy this game if you have some spare cash and enjoyed Limbo.

Monochroma is a puzzle platformer with cinematic visualization.
The main story centers around two brothers; an older, skinnier
brother who carries around his pudgy younger brother in an attempt
to escape a city.  While I appreciate the games nod to silent black
and white films in their atmosphere, the lack of any
narration or dialogue, and the spare usage of any music made this
game boring and somewhat monotonous. I found the brother to be more
of a bother instead of becoming emotionally invested in his character,
as he didn't offer anything useful to the experience.
The majority of the game is spent walking, and I'd have liked to see
more puzzles and platforming as what was used was implemented very
well into the game. Many of the platforming elements centered
around strategic timing, leaning heavily on trial and error strategies
and making this more geared towards those new to the genre.  In my
video review, I cite specific examples of this try- die- try again
philosophy.
While the character movement can feel a bit clunky, the developers
did an excellent job of balancing this out by working around this
shortcoming in integrating the puzzles into the game. The puzzles are
creative but basic, and fit well into the game.
Overall I wasn't able to complete this game due to boredom from the
lack of music and weak story, and the simplicity of the puzzles coupled
with the long gaps between any puzzles or action. The games doesn't
respect your time, and it gets old relatively fast.  For the current
asking price, I cannot recommend this game.

Deus Ex has to be one of greatest games of the 2000s. Deus Ex was a fantastic games from developers who were not that good at the time. It's a genre defining classic. Well okay, the graphics might not be the greatest, the gun play is really bad, and the AI really acts like blind maniacs. But the idea and concept of the game was truly uncomparible to any other game at the time. One of the greatest aspect of the game is the writing. Pretty alright voice actors and you can choose what kind of sentence you want to say to a person and that can affect the game. If you do something to character, like walk into the womens bathroom, they will remember that and will mention it and even my boss told me about it. The controls are extremely clunky for todays standards and there are also a crazy amount of keys. Not very user friendly for todays standards. If these controls came out in a game in this day and age, it would spark up some controversy with some.
The health was also like no other. You have health bars for your head, torso, left and right leg, and left and right arm. This can really affect your gameplay if you've damaged a part in your body. If you damaged you leg, you would start limping. Augmentations are also really interesting. You can get a augmentation for turing invisible! I wished that seriously every game had that ability. While I was playing, but you can't swap out these augmentations for other ones, so you have to be careful with what you are sure you are getting. Now lets talk about the soundtrack. The soundtrack is very well composed and the person who made the soundtrack also made songs for the Unreal series. Look, this game isn't for everyone. Some people will like this and some people not. When first playing the game, I found it one of the most confusing games that I've ever played and I didn't really enjoy it. Would I recommend this game today? Yes, if you arn't too bothered by the graphics. As for the sequel, NO! Never play it. It's as if the developers didn't know this game was going to be this great and they tried too hard to do the same thing again. I can't wait for Deus Ex: Mankind Devided. 10/10

While playing this game i got more and more into wondering, why it has so many bad reviews.
So here is what i think about it:
First off, as someone who deals with depression since primary school and is now in their early thirties, i know quite well what we are talking about here.
And let me tell you, this game sucked me in. I could really see me and stations of my own journey depicted in the story. Some of the things that were said and especially parts of the interviews were actual thoughts that i had/things that i said myself in some points of my life. As this game is so real it is unarguable painful for people with similar experiences. And on some points the game is even brutal.
So i would definitly recommend, to take the start screen warning seriously.
This is not a game to ease your fears or enable you to dream away. This game will stick its imaginary finger right into your wounds and tear them open. Which makes sense to me as in my experience it often is necessary to look at things for them to get better.
However, i think it is still a good game and it can help people suffering from depression. And it may also do a good job in making other people experience what it feels like to be depressed? Can't really say, because that is not my point of view. Others may answer that.
Lets go on with the inevitable pro's and con's:
Pro:
-decent artwork, nothing unique but still nice
-really good story, packed with rich symbolism
-really good dialogues, read all of them without getting bored
-nice, not annoying soundtrack
-game mechanics and controls are pretty standard and work
-had it running on my ubuntu machine using wine (playonlinux) without experiencing any flaws or bugs
-free!
Con
-no native linux port
-can be pretty triggering especially for people who are suicidal (don't play if you're suicidal right now!)
-although i understand that it's a crucial part of story and symbolism the "cape fights" can be pretty annoying and tedious for many players and may repell them from finishing the game (play on! :))

Soundoger+ is an interesting take on the Musical-game market, mashing it with bullet-hell type gameplay to make a fun and quirky little game. A minimalistic stage design combined with bright and contrasting colours allows the player to see every bullet and distinugish it from your "ship" with ease. I found the game suprisingly hard at first , compared to other similar games such as Beat Hazard, but soon got addicted to the challenging gameplay and lovely contrasting colours,and as the stage fires waves of bullets upon you, based upon the tempo, bpm and other characteristics of the song, you have to try and dodge them, and with each hit taken it fastforwards the song. However, on left click you have a 'time-slow' button that allows the player to slow the song down while retaining full movement, but at the cost of not having a multiplier bonus carry through the slow, in order to make the game a bit easier. I found the game suprisingly hard at first , compared to other similar games such as Beat Hazard, but soon got addicted to the challenging gameplay and lovely contrasting colours.
Pros;
Fun, addictive gameplay
Ability to play own music
Clear gameplay.
Cons;
File-selecter takes you out of game, would be nice an in-game one so you can see the colours provided for the stage.

I can see what the developers wanted to do and I like the effort the encoder(s) put in the world. Even with a whole bag of creative common sprites at their disposal a lot of game developers don't add the images to all the sprites, so I can appreciate that they add multiple expressions for the protagonist and a fitting image to the dialogue of even the most irrelevant characters. And for what's it worth, I liked the story for as long as I played.
I cannot recommend the game however for it's practical unplayable design. I've seen some reviews about this game being too hard but that's not really an issue. You can make it through the bandits and defeat the demon with the items you've been given, and I can even imagine getting through the next levels without putting on the cape if you're motivated enough.
What's the problem then?
While doing that intentionally is interesting, the developers made the pace of the game way too slow because the original engine already suffers from this issue on it's own. And you can't expect of the players that they'll spend several minutes with each random encounter because they have to defeat them one strike at a time. If you could grind to make the other characters relevant again or if you could speed through the fights by either disabling the cutscenes or holding a button for fast-pace like I've seen in some games, I would be inclined to take back my critism. But right now, the game part of the game just becomes too stale and tedious for the story to be worth it as it is.
Possible ways to solve this and improve the game:
-Skip through button during fights: Hold a button for fast paced game, rapidly going through the attack scenes and auto-selecting targets. This won't work with proper fights because advanced mechanics like guard and using skills and items won't work, so it's just for the no-brainer fights. (For reference: a game with this mechanic is 'Hero and Daughter')
-Make it possible for the player to turn off attack scenes in options, only seeing damage without the flames and other grandeur.
-Or at the very least also buff up the protagonist's accuracy so he'll never miss. Even more annoying than a no-stakes fight is a fight with several turns that are completely pointless because the opponent hopped out of the way.

This bullet hell game can be fun and intense, if you're into these kinds of games. This game's main purpose is for you to dodge a barrage of bullets in a circular field that fire rhythmically with the music. The songs included are already pretty fun to listen and play to, and the game lets you add in songs of your choice and create your own map, or simply auto-generate a game for them (which isn't as fun as actually creating the bullet patterns yourself).
The game is incredibly straightforward, however, as there is only one mode of play. With the absence of variety, this game can get boring quickly, or if bullet hell games just aren't as fun to you. Personally, I stick around for the music and the sole purpose of seeing how many retries it'll take me to get a 100% before I rage quit.
As for recommending this game, I probably would not. It is a fun game, but it doesn't last, especially for its price. Perhaps, adding a few more game modes or more music (besides user-created ones, which tend to be over-the-top hard just to impress) would make this game worth buying.

People complaining about this game being tedious never discovered the undocumented key feature. If you double click on an exit, you will immediately take it, without having to watch your character cross the room with agonizing slowness. This makes movement far more palatable.
Anyway, on to the review.
When you were 10, did you love magic? Did you read books like Redwall that immerse you in a world of talking animals and adventure? I was that kid, so let me tell you, this game pushed all of my buttons. The story has it all: mystery, magic, and stakes that start small and escalate until they're terrifyingly high, especially when you consider the age of the protagonist.
This is an adventure game that really feels like an adventure, and the story has stayed with me. I really hope they do a sequel, because they left lots of room for one.
The art is all hand-painted, and it looks like an old animated movie. The Secret of NIMH is a good comparison. I think it's gorgeous. My one complaint is that the animation is not particularly smooth.
The music is great, as is the voice acting. Jerry himself is a little flat, but most other characters sound awesome. The puzzels can be tough but are generally fair. I only got frustrated enough to use a guide a few times. Since this is a deadalic game, expect some humor, but also expect things to get pretty heavy.
If you're on the fence, grab it cheap when it's on sale. It often is. Use the wishlist feature to get notified. If you like adventure games set in fantasy worlds, you won't regret it.

Wonderful game! The music is fantastic and I really enjoy the pixel art as well, particularly in cutscenes.
Party Hard follows a series of murders carried out by a man whose neighbors had a crazy party one night. All he wanted was some sleep. Once he popped, he couldn't stop, and the murders continued at parties all over the US, gaining him attention from the police and fans. There is a story, pieces of which are revealed after each level's completion. Each level includes traps which can be set off to kill (make horses buck and kill passersby, make outhouses mysteriously tip over onto a sleeping victim, rig speakers to explode, etc). There are also devices you can use to kill, like stun bombs, smoke grenades, big ol' swords, and more.
New levels and characters have been added since the game's release. Plenty of cool achievements to try for, maps (including Vegas and Halloween party maps, among other intereting venues) to enjoy, and party-goers to kill.
The creator is very nice and can communicte with you via Twitter. He retweeted a few of my achievements.

But that just adds to the challenge, otherwise it was a very relaxing game. And for a point-and-click, it has such an amazing amount of content as opposed to a number of other point-and-clicks I've played in the past.
Definitely a recommended game if you're a fan of point-and-click games!

Spelunky, Terraria, Rogue Legacy, and to a lesser degree Risk of Rain
The Good:
- The overall sense of wonder and exploration as the player progresses in the game keeps it exciting and engaging
- The crafting system is deep and relatively intuitive, which helps with the overall feeling of discovery that the game continually conveys
- Experience point generation leads to leveling up the player’s skills in different manners that can complement a player’s style of gameplay
- Current skill trees are strength, intelligence, and dexterity
- Procedurally generated biomes that feature random enemies, resources, and loot drops
- Weapon and tool crafting has the potential to attach bonuses to the stats, which can greatly improve a player’s chance of survival
- Character creation has different benefits with each character that the player unlocks through game progression
- The game is quite difficult, but as is the manner of this genre, it adds to the sense of accomplishment when the player beats a previous record or level
- Multiplayer is a blast and can really encourage proper teamwork and planning due to the difficulty level of the game in general
- The developer(s?) Sean Young is constantly responding to feedback within the steam forums and also implements many of the ideas brought up by the community
- Updates and patches to the game are common and consistent, which keeps the experience fresh and exciting
- Hats!
The Bad:
- As expected there a quite a number of bugs in this version, which mostly reside in the user interface
- As explained above, many bugs are known and are being addressed in future releases
- While multiplayer is a blast, the process to start a network game with others is not very intuitive and may leave some non-techie gamers fustrated
- When first starting out with the game, the crafting system and difficulty can seem overwhelming and may scare off players that don’t bother to hang with it. This could be remedied with a comprehensive in-game tutorial that explains the basics of the early gameplay.
- Having a timer for each level can be a bummer as this is a crafting-heavy experience. Since crafting doesn’t have a craft-book or interfaced crafting system, early players will be spending a lot of time Alt-Tabbing between the game and the wiki figuring out what resources build different items. That time will cost them dearly as the “scourge” will inevitably destroy them before they reach the end of the level.
-A streamlined crafting method would potentially address the feeling of a “cheap kill” and encourage the player to move swiftly through each level to avoid the scourge
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
Sure. The game is pixelated and does not contain excessive gore. There are blood sprites, but again the retro look diminishes their effect.
Did I make time to complete it?
The version I played did not have a final boss, so the levels repeated endless or appeared to do so. I did, however, spend a lot of time playing the game with friends and found the experience very enjoyable!
Redlight or Greenlight?
This game is currently at a greenlight.
Magicite will appeal to any gamer who enjoys a challenge. The sense of exploration and achievement really encourages that feeling of wanting to play one more game when your last one ends. As a fan of the PDL genre, I highly recommend our readers pick this one up.

I have 214.9 hours on record as of this review. In reality, if we include the time using the No-Steam Executable made by Egosoft themselves, it's well over 1000 hours.
Albion Prelude takes Terran Conflict, already a solid open-world game, and throws away most of the narrative in favor of giving the player ultimate control. Do you want to spend your entire career mining? Do it. Do you want to be a cargo hauler? Do it. Do you want to be a pirate hunter? Do it. Do you want to be an industrialist manufacturing goods for the entire galaxy? Do it. Do you want to build a fleet of battleships and lay waste to the civilizations of the galaxy? Do it.
Do you want to do all of these things, simultaneously? DO IT.
X3 is guided by its astounding freeform nature, which is to say there's not much guidance at all. It's not just a game about you, in some ship you incrementally make better and better, or maybe upgrade/change hulls. Instead, it is encouraged, and virtually required, that you have other AI-controlled ships in your fleet. These can be cargo ships; fighters; cruisers; battleships; carriers -- whatever you need to accomplish your goal(s), you can have available.
Unfortunately, the sheer scale of the gameplay, and lack of a specific endgame (or any) goal, means that it can be a few hours, if not days, until you've gotten used to the minutiae. You have to manage a property menu that can grow larger and larger, showing all of your ships and stations, giving trade commands to your traders, ordering a squadron of warships to jump to you to assist, etc.
FORTUNATELY, there are a LOT of community-derived mods that can fix some of the quality-of-life issues, merging or improving commands and functionalities to ease this process. I won't even go over them here, because to do so would require more time than I care to spend; but basically, you have mods ranging from adding a centralized defense network that will automatically dispatch a predetermined fleet to a sector under attack, to ones that vastly improve the carrier interfaces, to ones that can turn your traders into fully-autonomous agents that are basically equivalent to the AI of the game (but putting money into your account).
The most interesting part of the game is the closed economy. Weapons and equipment are manufactured using materials gathered from around the universe (Ores, components, etc.), and destruction of a factory producing Weapon XYZ will reduce the number of XYZs available for your purchase. Meanwhile, though, you can make your own XYZ factory, and then the AI will intelligently send traders to buy up your product to stock the various shipyards and equipment docks around the galaxy, netting you a tidy profit.
There are some issues with the intelligence of the central AI tracking all of this, offset between TC and AP, and improved considerably by the larger mods. Still, options. Options are great. And with this game, you get all the options.

Magicka is an hack and slash game developed by Arrowhead Game Studios that puts the player in a comedic fantasy world as a wizard in training who is tasked to save the land of Midgård from the darkest menace.
Each player can choose a specific robe for him/herself that provides specific bonus and malus accordingly (for instance, a heavy armor gives the wizard more health but can decrease the amount of healing recived, and a more nimble armor will make the character faster, but also extremely fragile). The main beef of Magicka is navigating the various levels and defeat the hordes of enemies coming at you (and the occasional boss) by using a great variety of spells. In order to equip a certain spell, you must first conjure it by mixing up different elements and then use it. There are primary elements and secondary elements and, given their sheer number and in how many ways they can interact with each other, a lot of spell with different effects to wield: some are mainly use to damage foes, while others can create protective barriers or even resurrect a character. Spells can also interact with each other, for better or worse, and different enemies may be more or less susceptible to them. Each wizard also comes into the game with a weapon depending on the robe chosen, althought spells are definitely your main source of damage for the whole run.
It's worth mentioning that Magicka was mainly developed as a co-op game, therefore playing the story mode solo borders on impossible and you should invite at the very least two friends to help you out. The game also allows for PvP matches of some sort and features a dedicate server lists to join other players in their adventures or battles.
The main problem with Magicka is that, once the first two hours of novelty expire, the game reveals itself as kinda boring and repetitive. This is due to two factors:
1) While a great deal is made about conjuring different spells as the different situations and enemies require, most players are encouraged to stick to a fixed number of spells (two or three) and spam them against any opposition, which tends to work wonders most of the time. Generally speaking, changing the active spell in the midst of battle is more risky than anything and there are severall spells that deal an incredible amount of damage to foes regardless of their individual resistances (boulder and arcane beam come to mind)
2) The always active friendly fire, while a source of several funny moments the first few times you'll kill your own team mates, willingly or not, becomes more and more aggravating as the game progresses and enemies waves become so wide and special enemies pop out that much more frequently that even a small misfire killing another member of your party can lead to a quick death and a fast trip to the last checkpoint
It also doesn't help that Magicka's already rather thin main plot premise carries itself around only by neverending shout-outs and references to popular videogames, films and fantasy books and pretty much nothing else, meaning that it's very easy to lose interest and entertainment value in the game after a while.
Magicka is a game that can only be suggested to player who have a small group of friends to play the game with untile they'll get bored of it and call it a day. A little fun until it outlives itself

X3: Albion Prelude is a great update for X3: Terran Conflict.  It has better trading options, stuff to do, and most importantly BUG fixes! I highly reccomend this game if you like long drawn out scenerios that, for the most part, are commited by the player. The story is actually kind of cool and takes you on a very long journey that can last as long as you can tolerate. Albiet not very rewarding, as the story line will typically only reward you with some ships, a tiny bit of cash, or something thats damned near useless. But when you do finish the main story line it is very rewarding. :) im not going to tell you why either. :P  Google it.
X3: Albion Prelude is a game that you can play for months and still be able to see a way to expand your empire.  Resource allocation and fleet division are a huge part of all of the X Series which is its trademark. X3: Albion Prelude also expands greatly upon this compared to its predecesors and gives more visability to its complexity but often not descriptive enough. A lot of this is a guessing game until you understand the combat and trading system, how its applied to you and the X Universe, as well as the function of commands and automation of your empire, which can be very challenging at times and frustating.
The level of detail for the trading system has been expanded as well, adding stock markets, which is very helpful when you start building your trading emipire, allowing you to see supply and demand and figure out what may be most profitable. Spread sheets in space. :)
The size of the X universe is quite expansive which makes for many trading options and territoral delemas if you mess up with ceratin factions, which, can make the game more engaging and difficult. There are few dead zones for you to "claim" as your own and allow you to control the market just a little bit more in those regions of space. Proper application of supply and demand is key to becoming a successful buisiness mogul.
The game itself runs smoothly on laptops even with an older graphics card, which is very inportant during fleet battles which can be massive!
Now on to the dark side of this game.
I will admit that this game can be extremely frustrating due to the existing bugs, such as randomy exploding because auto pilot (or yourself) bumped into something (or random missile explosion) and kills you and have to load a save from an hour ago, not to mention the loss of time and resources if you dont. It can be very difficult to make money to replace/repair things that took you forever to get and got destroyed because of the clunky AI or just random crap.  as well as stations being built litterally in other stations clipping box, or in some cases a trading stations with rotating parts destroying passer-bys which, once again, have to reload a save. Even if you cheat its still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
The X Series has always had serious issues with bugs, however X3: Albion Prelude has fixed many of them, it is still something worth noting.
On that note, the AI.
Understanding exactly how the AI follows its commands can be confusing or just flat out broken. Well at least it seems that way at times. It takes a lot of experimentation to know what needs to be installed in a ship for it to follow a command string and the explanations can be very vauge, until you find out that its not the tech in the ship but instead its the pilot of the ships skill level. Which is NEVER explained in any way shape or form. This can be impossible to grasp if you are unaware that these pilots need to train themselves in order to properly do market trading.
Whilst on the topic of fittings and inventory managment. It can be very confusing to remember what can and cannot be installed on a ship or even whats in its inventory without going through even more windows that can be very time consuming, even with simple tasks, such as, transfering goods, buying the right weapons or missiles, the right shields or just getting the information on these things.
Now onto the UI.
The UI is a serious pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(I mean its devastating) during fleet battles and you can loose every thing because of the menus and application of commands. So make sure you set up their orders properly before going into any engagement, or anything for that matter. I personally think they REALLY need to overhaul the UI and set it up like the UI in EVE Online to allow more stream line ship, trading and inventory managment, and allow you to have multiple windows open (or even be able to move them around would help) and have easier access to informations and views of complex situations, which happen often. This would make hasty fleet commands actually practical, and that they are not.
Going back to the reward system.
Causing destruction to your enemies, whether it be for the story line or for your own love of chaos is extremely costly and is not worth the time, unless your capturing ships, you are loosing money on each missile fired or each of your ships destroyed. After a battle, if you dont have repair beams or a specified repair ship, the repairs from the battle can cost almost as much as the ships value. This only makes sense in the way, like you have to replace the engine in your car because it got a couple plasma rounds to its head gaskets. ( Note: your astronaught has a repair beam on him as well. )
Last notation, there is no tutorial other than flight school in the beginning of the game. So, i recommend Google the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything before commiting to something.
Anyways.
End rant. :)
Even with all of these downsides I still highly reccomend this game to players who enjoy resources management, risk assesment and a slow game progression which become exponential as you gain wealth and understanding of its dynamics. The pride you feel when you can afford your first M6 (A large but maneuverable machine of death and chaos) or your first TL (a station hauler) all the way to your first factory is very rewarding. Watching as you start with a puny POS ship, then build into a fleet, then into a serious market influence, then into an empire is like watching a child grow into a bad♥♥♥♥♥machine of profit and destruction. :P
Overall I give this game a 8/10 and will be playing for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amount of time.

The game is ok, it isn't great and I wouldn't personally recommend it but it is not terrible.
Pros:
*The world is well thought out and the story makes sense(mostly). As you play the game you will get to learn more and more about the world and everything falls into place
*While it has it's flaws, the combat system is fun for the majority of the game. There are times when the game disables one or more of your basic abilities (sometimes all of them) though which detract from overall gameplay
*There is a lot of developer humor in the game with a lot of easter eggs, you are free to make unconventional choices and see what happens as a result
Cons
*The game is rather short. The game is very linear and doesn't contain a lot of playtime. With about 30 hours of gameplay I've unlocked every main ending and all misc "endings" except for one.
*There doesn't seem to be any endgame content. The game is purely story driven and once you've cleared the game in all possible ways, you start over against level 1 mobs as if nothing ever happened.
*When the game tries to get emotional, it often gets cringy. I understand the whole "androids developing human emotions" bit, but when it is well established that the androids reboot from backups, it makes some death scenes pointless. To further this point, the main characters both kill themselves as early as the tutorial.
*You often find yourself running around holding one button. The POD firing button is just a free source of damage and the fact that you basically spend the entire game holding it down makes for mindless combat especially since the number of mobs you usually fight at once makes melee significantly more risky.
All things considered it is a good game, it is merely not what it's hyped up to be and probably not worth the $60 price tag. I expect more than a weekend of play time from a game I drop that much money on. If you find this game on sale then I'd get it, otherwise you might as well wait.

With Mankind Divided, I am going to review one of the greatest franchises of all time (which had a few mistakes along the way), Deus Ex.
Deus Ex is a cyberpunk First-Person RPG developed by Warren Spector, who worked on Ultima and System Shock 1. I first found it on sale this year and everyone was calling this game one of the best games ever made! So I bought the whole franchise and Deus Ex quickly understood why people like it so much! The story, the setting, the open ended gameplay, the characters, the augmentations! These are all reasons why you should buy this game now!!!! But let me elaborate on this.
Deus Ex is set in the year 2052, in a time devastated by plague and terrorism. You are JC Denton, a nano-augmented agent at UNATCO (United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition). The game starts off where JC and other UNATCO agents are looking for a terrorists group who are stealing the vaccine for the Grey Death (the plague). However, you start to realise it’s deeper than that and you are thrown into a middle of one huge conspiracy involving the Illuminati, Majestic 12 and many more.
The game is filled with philosophical questions and design choices. Warren Spector said that Deus Ex, at its heart, was about
. The design of the game was all about “how you think the world should be like” (again, I am quoting Spector). There are 3 different endings in total, and each of them are completely different! And the game has certain moments where you can determine the fate of so many characters.
One of the reasons the game is so famous, apart from the story and gameplay, is the fact that it predicted the 9/11 disaster.
Deus Ex is a game which has a lot of player choice throughout the level. There isn’t one way to approach a level. You could sneak past everyone or kill everyone in the room. Do you want to play lethally? Or do you want to kill no one. You could possible get through the entire game without any enemy seeing you! The levels make for multiple choice allowing for multiple playthroughs. Thief might have been the first to do this, but Deus Ex perfected it!
I haven’t even talked about levelling up. Deus Ex is a role-playing game, and like most RPGs, there is a levelling up system! Instead of most RPG’s like Skyrim where you level up and get to put your points into special perks, you get points and level up each ability. You could be untrained, trained advanced or a master at whatever you do (just don’t pick swimming). When you start a new progress, you get 5000 points to put into:
Adding points will make your skills even better. For instance you put points into lock picking instead of rifles, you will use less lock picks, however, your sniper rifle is inaccurate and when you look down the scope it flies around the screen like crazy. You can find these points by finding new areas and proceeding through the story. Personally this is a great levelling up system (with the exception of swimming, if you chose that, you haven’t played Deus Ex) and I prefer it over level up to the next level and add perks!
Now, let’s talk about the star of the show, AUGMENTATIONS!!! You find augmentations around the map, and it kind of is a chore to find each and every one of them! However, it feels like a reward for searching them. You have different slots for augmentation in the Head, Torso, Legs, Eyes, Arms and the subdermal areas. Some areas have more slots than others. Augmentation canisters have two different augmentations in them, allowing for you to choose which one you want and what builds you want to go for. It’s again about choice and how you want to play. You can further upgrade most augments by finding upgrade canisters.
Each augment changes gameplay on the field. For instance, you can summon in a spy drone which gets close to robot and takes them out with an EMP blast. You can use cloaking abilities to sneak past humans or the Radar Transparency ability allowing to hide from machines and security devices. You do have to activate each ability with the F3-F12 keys. Personally, there are some abilities that shouldn’t be activated, but I can see why they did it. Each ability uses bioenergy, which can be topped up. These biocells and energy restorers are rare, so be careful.
The health systems is one of the most inventive that I have seen in a video game. You can
(for all you Zero Punctuation fans out there)! This means if you have one leg blown off, you will be slower. If both, you are always in crouch mode. If you lose an arm, you are less accurate, lose both arms, you can’t use anything except a medical bot. However if your torso or head goes black on the HUD, you die. This made Deus Ex better than most other shooters! And it still is my favourite health system. You can heal each the head, torso, the arms and legs individually, which is awesome
Deus Ex has some flaws. First of all rebind your keys!!! There are some awkward key bindings like Left bracket to scope, colon to reload etc. And the game’s graphics aren’t that great, even for the year 2000. And do I need to mention putting points into swimming??? The voice acting in this game is bad, I mean Bob Page, Everett, Savage, Jock and Paul are the only actors that aren’t that bad (but it’s nowhere as bad as Invisible War or The Fall)
Just check out this if you want to see how bad it is

It's a unique game with some really neat little easter eggs to find on each map.
I really enjoy people's reactions to certain things, they are funny and generally quite crass. Dancing for extended periods of time let me konw just how these folks feel about this guy. That's all the motivation I needed to set up a speaker bomb, and watch their bodies burn on the dance floor. My preferred method is to set up a "kill room" and keep piling the bodies in it as they become discovered less frequently that way.
I'm concerned about the judgement of these party goers... I'm thinking that after the 2nd or 3rd murder, I'd consider leaving the party for the night, or at least going to a diner for some eggs. If I were a band hired to play a party and our guitarist was killed and thrown in a trash can, I think we'd pack it up and call it a night.
The only thing I felt was lacking in the game a bit is the voice acting, especially during the cutscenes. I'm not sure if it's the voices, the dialouge, or a mix of both, but it just seems off. That really is the only downside I found, the game is challenging and fun. I would suggest this for adults with a darker sense of humor, those nostalgic for the leisure suit larry days, or who would like a strategy game far outside the conventional box.
