I'm a big fan of the classic rhythm games - stepmania, osu! and the like. The games that get you immersed in the music and entwined with the beat. I could never get into audiosurf because the obstacles were on the beat, which meant you had to move out of time with the music - for me this breaks the definition of rhythm game.
And I love bullet hell; played Perfect Cherry Blossom to death (which incidentally, had great music). So how does Soundodger+ stack up?
Well, the bullet hell falls short at times. In a traditional shooter you have to focus on (a) dodging and (b) being in the right position to shoot your enemy(s). Here there's no shooting, just dodging -- which I have no problem with in theory, but in practice I found some levels had large periods of time where no bullets would come my way. I had a safe spot and with no other pressure to reposition I just sat still - which didn't make for very engaging gameplay. Other levels were better, including homing missiles to keep me on my toes.
How about the rhythm? Well, there's two things that
the rhythm of whatever song is playing. The first is the slow motion ability which you invoke via the left mouse button. This slows down the music aswell of course, and for me the effect simply doesn't work. The second occurs whenever you get hit - everything speeds up for a short time which has a hugely jarring effect on the music. I'm not suggesting death should be fun, but in a rhythm game the music
, and if you kill my enjoyment of the music you kill my enjoyment of the game. Fortunately you can simply avoid activating slow motion, and there's an option ("Easy listening") to disable the speedup when you get hit. So while I don't think these are worthwhile features, I don't hold them against the game as a whole.
Soundodger does a pretty good job of matching the song's energy, both in pre-made levels and the auto-generated mode (when you plug your own music in). But it suffers from the same issue I had with audiosurf - it doesn't encourage me to move
the beat, or draw me into the music. Yes the level is generated from the music, but the gameplay
that emerges is on a totally different beat. As such I can't recommend it as a rhythm game.

I bought Party HARD for Halloween and thoroughly enjoyed it, but it's definitely not for everyone.
The Good:
The premise and gameplay of Party HARD is chock full of dark humor.  Remember Mortal Kombat back when it was satisfied with being silly (punching people two stories, people exploding and having dozens of hearts and stomachs fall out, dropping arcade machines on people, etc.) instead of serious?  It's like that.
While it uses pixel art, it's not because the developers can't draw and won't hire someone that can, as is often the case.  It's actually good.  Each party is uniquely themed, and there is a lot of variety in how partygoers look.
The music is memorable, and I liked it.  I think the voice acting was pretty good for it to have been done by one person.
Most of the time the AI behavior is surprisingly good, and amusing.  Individuals choose between fight or flight based on the number of partygoers around them, and their behavior.  Paniced characters will often wrongly accuse others, usually the one nearest the body when they spot it (as it should be).  Large numbers of frightened partiers will often move together like a herd.
The Bad:
The funny setup is squandered on a serious generic slasher flick plot.  The cinema scenes clash badly with the gameplay.  They should have gone with something more fitting, like the poor guy moving after killing his noisy neighbors, only to keep having the same thing happen time and time again.
Another thing that clashes with the humor is the surprisingly high difficulty.  I find laughing and feeling frustrated to be mutually exclusive.
For the most part, the levels are badly designed.  It's easy to blame this on procedural generation, but procedural generation can generate well designed levels (e.g. the original
).  It's just harder to program.
The real culprits behind the bad level design:
While it makes sense for some parties to be packed, not
of them should be.  Anyone familiar with stealth games should understand why this is a problem, but it interacts with several
problems to make things much worse.  By itself, the excessive number of enemies on each level primarily inflates play time, without adding any enjoyment to the game.
You can't save in the middle of a level.  Due to the glut of enemies on each level, if you do get caught, you may have lost a half hour or more of progress.  This is the primary cause of the excessive difficulty.
With so many eyes on you there better be lots of places to hide, pick of stragglers, and dispose of bodies…  Well, there aren't.
The ninja was a great idea for a character with a very different play style.  Unfortunately, due to there being eyes everywhere, placed arbitrarily at the start of the level, and little or no cover, he is almost impossible to play.  It's not unusual to be spotted as soon as the level starts.
Your character is poorly equipped to deal with the overpopulation problem.  You can dance (and risk getting beaten almost to death) or use freshly killed bodies to scatter partiers, but this is repetitive, and provides poor control over victim movement.
You might expect an unabashed murder simulator to provide you with many items you can use to dispatch victims in creative ways.  Prepare to be disappointed.  On most levels you're going to be stuck with the variation on a knife (knife, sword, or chainsaw) your character starts with.  On some levels you may find a knife with a slightly longer reach (i.e. a sword) if you don't already start with one.  The lack of ranged attacks feels especially strange.  The only remaining items that can be used for killing are (time) bombs and poison.  The rest (extra clothes, running sneakers, smoke grenade, and stun bomb) just make your job slightly easier.  Everything except the sword is limited use, and there is usually only one item per level, which makes some items, like the extra clothes, almost worthless.  The ninja can slowly regenerate smoke bombs, at least.
There is considerably more variety in ‘traps’.  I use the term traps loosely, because I lack a good word for “object or feature that can become dangerous in the right circumstances”.  Each level will start with quite a few.  Sadly, there still aren't enough to keep the game feeling fresh.  About midway through the game you will have seen all the traps there are.  It doesn't help that most traps are single-use (forcing you to rely on your much more boring knife most of the time), and many have the same effect (namely exploding after a short delay).  The traps could have been made so much more interesting by allowing you to place or move some of them, and set up chain reactions.
Continuing with the theme of lack of variety, its a good thing I enjoyed the music, since there's so little of it.  The same tracks get used for party after party.
I mentioned that
the AI behavior is good.  Well, the rest of the time it is
bad.  The worst problem is when a body is found and someone calls the cops, you are frequently known to be the murderer
, and the police automatically know where you are and are impossible to hide from.  The police also move faster than you, so are usually impossible to get away from.  Less serious problems include silly behavior like the drug dealer calling the cops, and the firemen, handyman, and medics not caring about you killing people in front of them.
Despite having the graphics and sound options PC users expect, there is no way to remap the keys.
There are bugs unlocking the characters (specifically The Butcher) and achievements (most of them).  They seem to only work if you perform the task in the expected way (see Youtube videos), instead of merely meeting the requirement.

I bought the Daedalic Adventure Bundle on sale for $5 and was starting to regret it - I didn't like Edna & Harvey or The Whispered World at all. But Night of the Rabbit is fantastic. Although it looks childlike, there are certain scary/disturbing elements throughout the game that would make me not recommend it for younger kids.
Pros:
- Artwork. I just love the art style and each scene is full of things to look at. The final cut scene is especially great.
- Voicework. Jerry's voice is great, as are most of the other voices. I do wish they had added more variation, as it's very obvious sometimes when one voice actor is voicing other characters.
- Length. I'm used to playing free P&C games, so this is the longest P&C I've ever played (ignore my gameplay stats...I fell asleep to this game a lot). And you don't have to worry about waiting for a sequel to find out what happens (although I totally am). The story here works as a standalone.
- Replayability. There are "side missions" to do that are not necessary to the main story. I didn't find all the dew drops or stickers, so I wouldn't mind playing again.
Cons:
- Puzzles. Sometimes nonsensical. Sometimes you can't do a certain action because it's not the right time yet. I did have to check a walkthrough 5 times.
- Mr. Churchmouse. It's kind of irritating clicking through his dialogue because he has these long pauses when he talks to his son.
- Humbert. Just really annoying. Too annoying.

I cannot recommend this game because I found it much more frustating than anything else.
There are some quite good things about this game:
* the art style is quite reminiscent of Limbo, largely murky greyscale (not much use of sharp contrasting black and white) with and the ocassional splash of red which makes it a bit less dull.  The game is a 2d platformer but the background and foreground that you can't interact with are used well to conjure the world and tell the story
* the menu allows you to revisit bits of the game that you've already completed, so if you've missed collecting secrets or want to replay a bit you liked then you can do that without needing to replay through from the beginning.
* check points are spaced fairly closely together, so when you die you usually don't lose too much progress.
But mostly I'm afraid that I found it a frustrating experience, without much fun.
* No attempt to develop connection to brother
The main gimmick of this game is that your brother has broken his leg, and cannot walk so you must carry him everywhere, and because he is afraid of the dark you can only put him down in (very infrequent) spotlights.  Because do not spend much time with your brother before he breaks his leg you don't develop much connection to him.  He makes you jump less high and he basically just feels like a burden, because he does nothing for you, and doesn't interact with you very much.
The story would have much more impact if your brother had more depth, if he had a personality and you could develop a connection to him, instead of just feeling like he's a burden.
* Long reload times and not infrequent deaths
Each time you die it takes about 5 seconds to reload. That is quite frustrating in and of itself, but it is also quite easy to die, some of the jumping puzzles require a fair amount of precision, and some of the puzzles require a bit of experimentation to see how things work, so unless you are pyschic you won't work out how to solve it without dying at least once.
* Bugs - not many
The game is a little buggy, a few times I have passed through walls and floors that I shouldn't have been able to, but it doesn't happen so often that this is a big problem.  Dying takes you back to the latest checkpoint which isn't far away, and solves any problem that the bug would have caused.
* Slow and unfun controls
Platformers often have characters who are very nimble and are fun to control, and much of the fun comes from the sense of agility that the game gives you. In this game your character is a bit slow, and while you are carrying your brother you can jump less high.
In Limbo, and to some extent this game, the unfun controls to some extent serves to make you feel less powerful than you normally do in platformers.  In Limbo that feeling of powerfulness and lack of fun emphasises what the game is about.  Here it also makes you feel not very powerful, but less so than Limbo because you can still make a jump equal to your height even when carrying your brother.  So while there are design reasons for these limits on your abilities the effect makes you feel weak, but not really that much, and is still not fun.
* Punishing puzzles
Almost all of the puzzles are not very difficult, and can be solved mostly through trial and error, but some are rather fussy about their timing and it often feels like the fault of the controls that you fail.
In a lot of platformers you have a range of abilities and solving puzzles involves combining them in an interesting way.  Here you can only run and jump, which limits the range of puzzles/challenges to timing/precision based puzzles (which the slow controls don't really lend themselves to), and interacting with objects.
As I said above the puzzles often require experimentation, which is okay in and of itself, but you will die quite a few times because of this and the slow pace, unfun controls and long reload times make the puzzle solving feel more chorish than fun.  Often you quickly workout the key idea of the puzzle, but sorting out the details involves dying a few times, and repeating the bits you've already done.
* No camera control
It is quite helpful in platforming games to look up or down, so you can tell where you need to go next, but here you have no control.  So sometimes you make leaps downward to explore and maybe find a secret, but you just die.
* Short - I completed the game in 7 hours
I do not think that this is a big deal: Short experiences can be much more rewarding than some longer experiences.  But some people do think this important, so I feel it should be mentioned.
This game is by no means terrible, and if you can forgive unfun controls for pretty art and an okay story then it might be worth getting this game.  But even then I think there are games out there that do that better.

I should start by saying that this is a review purely of the technical issues that currently plague this game, not the content of the game itself. I don't feel that I've been able to get far enough into the game to thoroughly review its story or gameplay, so I'll leave that to other reviewers. To clarify, this review probably doesn't apply to you if:
1. Your PC well exceeds the recommended specs listed on the store page, and
2. You own some sort of two-stick controller which you are able to use on your PC
The sole reason that this review is a "Do Not Recommend" is as a warning to potential buyers to research VERY carefully before making this purchase. There are MANY issues that players are having right now, including myself, which make the game effectively unplayable.
First, do not even consider purchasing this game unless your GPU is sufficiently powerful to run the game at a solid 60 FPS on the settings you choose, with NO dips whatsoever. For some absurd reason, the game compensates for a framerate below the 60 FPS cap by actually slowing down the game, so that the same amount of time passes between frames regardless of how long it takes to render them. This means that, if you can't put out a solid 60 FPS, your game will literally be running in slow-motion. If you are on a laptop, or if you are on a desktop that hasn't had its GPU upgraded in the past few years, you will NOT be able to run this game playably in its current state.
Second, do not even attempt to play this game with keyboard and mouse; it is effectively impossible, and certain sequences will be beyond frustrating to complete with the game's insanely broken K&M controls. The game naively treats your mouse as an analogue stick, meaning that as soon as you stop moving it, your aim snaps back to the direction your character is facing. This means that you essentially have to use only WASD to aim, and the mouse is literally useless - a control scheme which is so mindbogglingly stupid that I have a hard time believing anyone at SquareENIX or Platinum Games ever tried playing this game with K&M controls, despite the game claiming to support it.
That said, I don't want to make it appear that I am "trashing" this game. From everything that I've seen, it seems like an absolutely lovely game, and I am sorely disappointed that I am unable to play it in an enjoyable way. If you own a console that this game is offered on, or have a sufficiently beastly PC and own a peripheral controller, give it a shot. I did enjoy the brief portion of it that I was able to barely stumble through, and reviews of the game's story have been absolutely sparkling. Just be aware that this game was clearly never intended for PC, and almost zero effort was put into porting it in a playable way. If you're okay with that, and you have the right setup to be able to play it, then by all means, do.

Amazing game. Tons of content, you discover something new in every run. Even after 150h + (and even more hours in the solo version) I feel like I haven't seen half of the stuff that's in the game. This is due to an unbelievable amount of Mobs, Craftables, Biomes, Food Items and even special mechanics. Also there is a system by which there are "set pieces" the world-generator can choose to place in the world upon generating it, many of which are quite rare (and also there are A LOT of them), so you will only see them after multiple times playing. (Nothing essential is locked by this, but rather you just find small new biomes or structures which you've never seen before.)
And the game is still getting new updates and even more content.
Pros:
- Addictive Gameplay
- Tons of content (e.g. lots of bosses, mobs, enemies, objects, craftables, foods, biomes etc.)
- A proper randomization which makes every run feel new and fresh in some way
- Still getting updates
- Good variety of characters that give the game even more replayability
- Seasonal events
- Very humorous (e.g. quotes and naming puns etc.)
- No loot crates, but an engaging skin system (which you get randomly by playing the game)
- Challenging but satisfying
- Workshop support and great amount of mods
- Every characters name starts with a 'W'
Cons:
- Can be very challenging for new players as it's very unforgiving
- Might not be very accessible for people who don't have tons of time to figure everything out for themselves (Wikis can help get you started)
- Rare desynchronization issue with "the caves" level (has happened two or three times in my 150h and required a restart of the game)
- Addictive gameplay
Also it has workshop support, so you can spice it up in many different ways with the huge selection of mods available.

If you enjoyed Borderlands 2, you're going to enjoy the Presequel. It isn't as large a game as the previous entry in the series, but it still has enough content to merit a 4/5 rating from anyone who enjoys RPG/FPS games with a sense of humor and tons of action. Like the previous two games in the Borderlands series, it is most fun when played with friends (up to four players), but is also great when played solo. Many hardcore fans of Borderlands 2 pan this game for being "Too small" or "Lacking post-game content,' and while I agree with the second point, It should be known that the Presequel was never meant to be Borderlands 3, it's just an awesome game meant to satisfy old fans and attract new ones. It's sort of like a stand-alone expansion for BL2, the kind that takes the core aspects of a large game, adds a few twists, and alters the setting/characters/plot for one last ride, bigger and badder than before. All four base classes, plus the two DLC classes, are super fun to play as, the classic Borderlands humor is still here in it's fullest, the gameplay is fun as ever, and there is almost as much sweet loot to hunt for and bosses to take it from.
To adress the genuine cons, though:
-There truly isn't nearly as much post-game content, especially given the saddening lack of DLC expansions.
-On that note, the Season Pass is perhaps 1/4 as useful as those of the last two games, offering only one big DLC campaign rather than the four given by the old passes. Claptastic Voyage is fun, and they did clearly try to put as much in it as possible, but it's still telling that only one big DLC, two classes, and a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Holodome are given.
-When the entire setting of a game is divided between Icy, Magma-filled Moon(With a hub town and shipwreck level) and a Space-station, the scenery gets old fairly  quickly. If you want to do lots of sidequests, get ready for lots of backtracking. But hey, nothing new there. BL2 was the same.
Gr8 Game tho.

first of all, I've never been a big fan of Indie games nor puzzles. But the whole character of the game is so intriguing that I am fascinated by it. It is a dark and tense game, you feel the tension all over the place. A good thing about it is that, the game does not rush you at any time, as it happens in many games(i hate that) yet it is not slow in any way and achieves to be somewhat dynamic and entertaining. If you are a clumsy gamer when it comes to the controls, you gotta be careful, I am a bit clumsy and had to repeat things for several times at times, so that could be a downer if you are both clumsy and impatient at the same time. As I said before I am not a big fan of puzzles, and that is because most of the time they are impossible or too easy, and not very well constructed, now this is what makes Monochroma special; the puzzles are constructed in a very intelligent way, not only that you enjoy while figuring them out, but also you get to feel smart after you solve them=D. And an A+ for the music, not only it suits the game perfectly, but also independently from that it is real good, actually I am listening to it on Spotify. Kudos to Gevende for the amazing soundtrack!
What got to me the most, are some details as you can not leave your little brother anywhere you want, you have to leave him at some place where it is sufficiently illuminated because, as a little kid, he obviously is scared of dark, that's gotta be the cutest thing I've ever seen in a videogame, and it is especially beautiful, when it is in such a tense, cold and hostile environment that the game is set in. The last thing, before going back to keep playing some more, while in the immense majority of the videogames, you have to compete no matter what, be reckless, merciless and etc. a game set in a (not so far from the potential reality of a) distopia, in this game, you have to take care of your little brother and be compassionate of him; this is a breath of fresh air! Amazing job! It is not so often that I feel almost proud of being a fan of something. But I think I get can pride in being a fan of this amazing videogame! Monochroma is definitely a must-play game! get it, play it, enjoy it!

I didn't give this game much time because I realized pretty early it had its problems.
Pros:
- Decent graphics in certain aspects
- The environment has a decent amount of things to interact with, at least in the starting village
- It seemed to have some sort of development on the game's world and lore
- The starting village was very promising in some ways
Cons:
- Volume is way too loud, I realized this the second I loaded up the game
- The graphics, while decent in some areas, are inconsistent
- Expanding on the graphics, there's a lot of assets used from the base RPG Maker assets, and I can't differentiate what might have been made by the developer(s) and what was free to use assets they borrowed (consistency in graphics would improve this)
- Moving on to gameplay, the starting plot develops way too quickly, and you barely get to grasp who your character is and what kind of person they are before you get tossed three more characters your way and you have no clue who they are or what their significance is
- The maps could use some improvement; while the directions on what I had to do and where I had to go were clear, the maps made it a bit confusing on what exactly the path was. Specifically, there's two doors inside the building you have to go in, and neither are easily visible, which is something that should just not happen in a game like this
- The "combat curve" as I've seen it called is terrible; the first encounter you have is against four bandits who actually stand a real chance, and as I've experienced in developed RPGs, fighting easy stuff like Slime and Rats makes total sense when it familiarizes the player with the combat, how to maximize your damage effectivity and figure out weaknesses/resistances, and get an understanding of the rewards you should expect for your level
- Going off the last point, the second encounter was what seemed like a boss encounter, which is a huge downside. How to make this sort of thing feel more natural is by extending the difference from starting point A, the village, and mission point B, the bandit building, and putting hostile mobs in between, as to get a feel for the combat
I could ramble a bit more, but this game just isn't anything particularly amazing. It seems like a game that the developers were passionate at first about making, before realizing/remembering how much work a game like this can actually be, and quickly the patience they had dissapated. I cite the fact that the room where the first two encounters were had absolutely no real detail added to them.

I bought Party HARD for Halloween and thoroughly enjoyed it, but it's definitely not for everyone.
The Good:
The premise and gameplay of Party HARD is chock full of dark humor.  Remember Mortal Kombat back when it was satisfied with being silly (punching people two stories, people exploding and having dozens of hearts and stomachs fall out, dropping arcade machines on people, etc.) instead of serious?  It's like that.
While it uses pixel art, it's not because the developers can't draw and won't hire someone that can, as is often the case.  It's actually good.  Each party is uniquely themed, and there is a lot of variety in how partygoers look.
The music is memorable, and I liked it.  I think the voice acting was pretty good for it to have been done by one person.
Most of the time the AI behavior is surprisingly good, and amusing.  Individuals choose between fight or flight based on the number of partygoers around them, and their behavior.  Paniced characters will often wrongly accuse others, usually the one nearest the body when they spot it (as it should be).  Large numbers of frightened partiers will often move together like a herd.
The Bad:
The funny setup is squandered on a serious generic slasher flick plot.  The cinema scenes clash badly with the gameplay.  They should have gone with something more fitting, like the poor guy moving after killing his noisy neighbors, only to keep having the same thing happen time and time again.
Another thing that clashes with the humor is the surprisingly high difficulty.  I find laughing and feeling frustrated to be mutually exclusive.
For the most part, the levels are badly designed.  It's easy to blame this on procedural generation, but procedural generation can generate well designed levels (e.g. the original
).  It's just harder to program.
The real culprits behind the bad level design:
While it makes sense for some parties to be packed, not
of them should be.  Anyone familiar with stealth games should understand why this is a problem, but it interacts with several
problems to make things much worse.  By itself, the excessive number of enemies on each level primarily inflates play time, without adding any enjoyment to the game.
You can't save in the middle of a level.  Due to the glut of enemies on each level, if you do get caught, you may have lost a half hour or more of progress.  This is the primary cause of the excessive difficulty.
With so many eyes on you there better be lots of places to hide, pick of stragglers, and dispose of bodies…  Well, there aren't.
The ninja was a great idea for a character with a very different play style.  Unfortunately, due to there being eyes everywhere, placed arbitrarily at the start of the level, and little or no cover, he is almost impossible to play.  It's not unusual to be spotted as soon as the level starts.
Your character is poorly equipped to deal with the overpopulation problem.  You can dance (and risk getting beaten almost to death) or use freshly killed bodies to scatter partiers, but this is repetitive, and provides poor control over victim movement.
You might expect an unabashed murder simulator to provide you with many items you can use to dispatch victims in creative ways.  Prepare to be disappointed.  On most levels you're going to be stuck with the variation on a knife (knife, sword, or chainsaw) your character starts with.  On some levels you may find a knife with a slightly longer reach (i.e. a sword) if you don't already start with one.  The lack of ranged attacks feels especially strange.  The only remaining items that can be used for killing are (time) bombs and poison.  The rest (extra clothes, running sneakers, smoke grenade, and stun bomb) just make your job slightly easier.  Everything except the sword is limited use, and there is usually only one item per level, which makes some items, like the extra clothes, almost worthless.  The ninja can slowly regenerate smoke bombs, at least.
There is considerably more variety in ‘traps’.  I use the term traps loosely, because I lack a good word for “object or feature that can become dangerous in the right circumstances”.  Each level will start with quite a few.  Sadly, there still aren't enough to keep the game feeling fresh.  About midway through the game you will have seen all the traps there are.  It doesn't help that most traps are single-use (forcing you to rely on your much more boring knife most of the time), and many have the same effect (namely exploding after a short delay).  The traps could have been made so much more interesting by allowing you to place or move some of them, and set up chain reactions.
Continuing with the theme of lack of variety, its a good thing I enjoyed the music, since there's so little of it.  The same tracks get used for party after party.
I mentioned that
the AI behavior is good.  Well, the rest of the time it is
bad.  The worst problem is when a body is found and someone calls the cops, you are frequently known to be the murderer
, and the police automatically know where you are and are impossible to hide from.  The police also move faster than you, so are usually impossible to get away from.  Less serious problems include silly behavior like the drug dealer calling the cops, and the firemen, handyman, and medics not caring about you killing people in front of them.
Despite having the graphics and sound options PC users expect, there is no way to remap the keys.
There are bugs unlocking the characters (specifically The Butcher) and achievements (most of them).  They seem to only work if you perform the task in the expected way (see Youtube videos), instead of merely meeting the requirement.

Call of Duty Black Ops is when the series starts turning its focus and intentions in a very different direction. While Black Ops is the 7th Call of Duty game it is the 5th chronologically, which why I chose play it after World At War instead of jumping to Modern Warfare. Now I know that canon wise it really doesn’t matter, but I just like to see how the technology evolves in terms of guns and warfare.
In Call of Duty: Black Ops gone are the days of a Call of Duty game feeling like an actual war video game. Granted you are partaking in the Vietnam war, but it feels less authentic than the other Call of Duty’s in a different way. You don’t “Hold the Line” or “Hold out for reinforcements” You don’t partake in actual war strategy. Now the other Call of Duty games weren't’ strategic war shooters, but while the strategies were preselected for you, I felt that it was interesting to partake in them. Making sure you popped smoke grenades or that you drove your tank close to the enemies because your tank was not powerful from long range. Now does that make Call of Duty Black Ops a bad game? No, absolutely not, but it does make it quite a different experience than well pretty much any Call of Duty before Modern Warfare 2. And it’s an experience that is action-filled and thrilling to partake in. It’s set-pieces are well designed and from an artistic view beautifully rendered. Call of Duty’s artists are definitely a talented bunch. Whether it be Infinity Ward, Treyarch, or Sledgehammer you can never really complain that they aren’t good-looking games.
So how does the game hold up an action-movie like experience? Surprisingly well it turns out. Call of Duty picks up it’s influence from Half-Life or even Uncharted in the sense that you are always pretty much in control of the action, even in the bombastic set pieces. While these set pieces aren’t particularly difficult they are fun to play. Most of Black Ops’ campaign is fun to play while never really having a dull moment or heavy repetition, besides the fact that you are shooting all the time. I guess about the only negative thing I could level at the campaign is that it’s frustratingly short and ends a bit too quickly. I finished it’s campaign in about 4 and a half hours. Pretty much the same length of almost every COD campaign after the first Modern Warfare.
Thematically COD is as strong as ever. The graphics while using the same engine are still improved. The environments and effects still hold up even in 2017, while it’s obviously no match for its contemporaries it’s still a good looking game. The soundtrack in the game is pretty good, while having some songs that, while are always used in the Vietnam setting, are great to listen to all the same. The voice cast is pretty darn impressive and seems to be the most extensively Hollywood COD ever. I mean you have Ed Harris, Sam Worthington, Ice Cube, and even Gary Oldman. I don’t think I’ve seen this much recognizable stars in a COD game before. The great thing is that they are good to great. Ice Cube and Ed Harris are easily the weakest, but through no fault of their own as they are only playing their type. Gary Oldman as always just disappears behind a role even in a video game. He’s easily the strongest. The most surprising however is Sam Worthington who definitely gives it his all in his performance. While he mostly is just sitting in a chair the whole time, anytime he has to show a bit of emotion he does it really well. I could feel his confusion, frustration, and pain of his character.
Black Ops is definitely different from the World War 2 based shooters and follows after it’s modern brethren, but it’s still an entertaining action romp through the 60’s with all the bells and whistles  one expects in a COD campaign by now. Recommended if on sale.

Sounddoger+ is a Bullet Hell game in which you have to avoid "sound" as it comes at you in various forms such as spikes, balls and other shapes. The primary game has you playing through a succession of songs in which the higher your percentage score is, the more songs you unlock. That's essentially all there is to the game's progression outside of a few advanced levels that are unlocked by collecting hearts as you go. This doesn't leave much motivation to play for an already quite simple/boring experience. No matter how much you play, all you'll ever do is move your mouse to avoid obstacles. This isn't a horrible thing and the game can be a fun distraction in short bursts, but I wouldn't recommend spending much money on it. It's obviously very polished and well designed, but a monotonous experience is still monotonous no matter how well it's presented.
It is important to mention that there is a 'level creator' in which you can use your own sound files to create levels. This wasn't too worthwhile to me in this particular game, but others might appreciate it more. You may want to give this game a try if you get it in a bundle or a deep discount, but I definitely wouldn't recommend spending $8 on it.

Wow, I cannot believe I didn't come across this game sooner, and it surprises me even more that there are so many negative reviews (I have to assume most of them are from people who played the Early Access version). I found Vector Thrust in passing on Steam a few times but never paid much attention, especially after seeing the “Mixed” review summary. I picked it up when it went on sale just to give it a try, and I'm sorry now that I didn't get it sooner.
As someone who loves the Arcade Air Combat genre, but abandoned consoles after the PS2, I've been looking for a decent PC game in this category for probably the last 10 years. There have been a few attempts (including that abomination that was the "Ace Combat: AH" PC port), but nothing really ever met the mark... until I found this.
Vector thrust has everything you could want when it comes to arcade-style air combat: Lots of planes to choose from, lots of targets to shoot, and LOTS of ammo to shoot with. The interface is familiar to those who have played other games in the genre, and the controls are fully customizable, including support for a wide variety of controller and joystick options (though the keyboard controls are actually surprisingly good for a PC flight game too). On top of all that, the developers have gone out of their way to make the game extremely moddable, and even include an in-game editor for making custom missions. While the game does have Steam Workshop support, there is far more content available from other sites like ModDB that add to the experience of the game.
Now, all that said, it isn't perfect, there are a few gripes I have with the game; I'm not a huge fan of the Cell Shading art style, though honestly I stop noticing it after the first few minutes. A few of the missions have some minor bugs, that may cause you to have to replay them occasionally, and sometimes the mission objectives are not particularly clear (like when you are told to fly to a waypoint, but then fail the mission for flying out of the area when you go a bit too far). The graphics are lackluster (especially ground textures) for a modern PC game, and whoever decided on the "actually zero-visibility" for the desert mission needs to be smacked (you literally cannot see anything outside the plane, at any altitude, for the entire mission, it’s REALLY boring). The dialog is long and drawn out far more than needed (especially the briefings and debriefings), and the storyline is confusing (lacking any sort of context for the events that occur, or the factions involved), uninteresting, and, as longtime fans of Ace Combat may notice, a direct copy off of the plot of Ace Combat Zero (minus back-story and plus a few twists). My final, most frustrating complaint though, is that the game has probably over 100 aircraft built-in that you can unlock for "challenges", but only about 10 of them appear to be actually useable in the campaign or skirmishes (unless I'm just bad and missing some trigger to unlock more after I played through the whole thing).
But even with all its shortfalls, Vector Thrust has gotten me back into a genre that I haven't played in years, and I'm thoroughly enjoying playing through it. I hope the developers continue to give the game a little love where it needed, and I wish there was still a more active community (I suspect they made the mistake of over-advertising the Early Access version, and turned people off with all the, now mostly fixed, bugs), because Vector Thrust has a lot of potential, and the community content that actually IS out there is great!... I just wish I could get a few people to join my (or anyone’s) multiplayer server every now and then.
Overall, I would recommend this to anyone interested in Arcade Air Combat games, and emphatically recommend to anyone who has enjoyed other games in the genre before!

There are many reviews already published here on Steam that praise the game so I will keep this review short.
Stellaris is, without a doubt, the easiest (grand) strategy game from Paradox to date. It is a good thing because other games such as Europa Universalis IV, Hearts of Iron IV or Crusader Kings 2 can be a bit too difficult for new players. It is not to say that this game is easy when you are playing it on harder difficulties. Sure, it can be a bit wonky and sometimes AI acts a bit strange but overall Stellaris is still being polished and, knowing Paradox, will continue to be in years to come.
As with other major strategy games from Paradox, you are allowed to create and install mods. From a simple cosmetic mod to major total conversions and various fixes, balances - if vanilla game does not suit you and you are able to create or find a mod that changes this one, frustrating little mechanic... than it is as simple as pressing this subsribe button. Very easy and very helpful.
I am sure that many other reviews say what I have just said. It is worth repeating however as it is my belief that Stellaris is worth its price. Sure, when you have played it long enough you start to notice a lot of repeated events (planet discoveries etc.) and your performance of the game is getting worse with each passing decade but that is the nature of those games. If you can forgive those small nuisances than you are going to really enjoy Stellaris.

I have to admit, I wasn't exactly sure what I was in for when I first started this game by Nowhere Studios. The game literally starts immediately and you are thrusted into the role of a young boy wearing a red scarf, and the majority of the world in different shades of whites, blacks, and greys. Now of course there will be some red that will poke out from time to time but the majority of this game will give you the feeling of one of those futuristic and yet old noir feeling movies. You will soon find that your little brother is in this bleak world as well, and you are going to have to protect him if you are both going to survive what is ahead of you.
Graphically I have to admit that I LOVED the look. There's something to be said about not trying to make the game extremely complex. Sure there was always this feeling of depth to the areas that you are moving around, even though you will always be running from left to right, right to left, up to down, down to up, and so on. The subtle use of red throughout the game makes certain things pop. Sure most of the time the reds don't mean anything to the character, but the balance of colors, and the lack of many of the usual colors in the game drew me into the feeling of a shady world filled with unease. A world where not all is what it seemed, and a world that even though there might be pictures of happy people there was something fundamentally wrong going on that was just out of view. Now there are several different areas to this game, and I have to say that all of them make you feel like you are actually progressing through a city. It definitely does not have that rinse a repeat feeling that some games have, where they simply change a couple of assets and try to sell it off as something new and different.
The music in the game was another thing that was was subtle but definitely fit right into the game. It made me think of an old crime story. You know where you have that lonely saxophone in the background, where you know that there's some dame, or person in danger.
The controls took a bit to get used to and was probably one of the weakest parts of the game. The just didn't feel precise enough. There are times where you have to make a jump, grab a ledge, or some other feat just right to continue through the game, and it was just a smidge off, just enough where frustration could creep in, especially if after doing the exact same type of movement in the game, you got different outcomes.
Alright so lets get into the game. The thing that impressed me the most about this game is that they had challenging puzzles throughout the game. There were puzzles where you had to move platforms, you had to clear the way of something, you had to time a swing just perfectly, you had to climb, you had to sneak, you had to push and pull, and more. The thing that makes this game different from a lot of games that love to put obstacles in front of you was that there wasn't this ever growing curve of difficulty. Now I'm not saying that there weren't puzzles that were difficult, but there was something about the way that they laid the puzzles out in the game where I never knew what to expect. To me that is an even better layout. Now I'm faced with maybe underestimating the next obstacle, or maybe I end up over thinking it. There was this hidden balance where no matter the difficulty if you kept an open mind you were going to be able to complete the puzzle/obstacle.
Now I know that I mentioned the not tight enough controls, but there was one other thing that bugged me to death about this game, the load screens. It is beyond odd when you are playing the game and you are advancing through an area and then all of a sudden, BOOM, load screen. Now not only does this happen, but because it is so abrupt I feel like the developers made the decision to put in a "Press Any Key to Continue" mechanism in there so that the player doesn't just get thrown right back into the game.
Alright so all is out on the table, I would love to tell you about the story, but I'm not really sure what it was, I know that I'm trying to protect my brother, and I know that I'm running through a city. I'm not sure why I'm doing it, though I know that I have to be careful around certain corners because there are those who will chase me down if they see me. I also know that there doesn't seem to be anyone but those around the corner that seem to be around. I know that this game is supposed to try to pull at your heart-strings a bit when it comes to your brother, and I have to say you are going to see a big payoff on that piece, though I'm not telling you when in the game (that would be cheating).
Ok so lets get to it. If you are looking for a game that definitely is not your average game, that uses an art style, a bleak world, and actions that will draw you into a story filled with obstacles, this is the game for you. It is only violent when you mess up in the game, so if you are looking for blood, guts, and glory, this is not the game for you. This was a pleasure to play, and overlooking the two shortcomings of this game, I have to say that I would play another game much like this one, so with that I have to give this game an 8.8 out of 10.

This game has exceeded all of my expectations. I went in expecting one sort of thing and came out with so much more. Each character you can't help but fall for despite some of their flaws and the performance by the VOs are phenomenal. Yoko Taro and SE gave us a game worthy of an award. Every time you beat the game it gets better and better. Don't let the words of others discourage you when they say there are too many endings. These endings are worth the time to get because each route you take isn't the same as the last. I won't get too into detail by what I mean by that so as to avoid spoilers but playing this game more than once is absolutely necessary to get the emotionally compromising and mind-blowing experience it truly has.
Another thing I would like to point out is that some say the game isn't difficult and because of that it starts to get boring. At first yeah it is a little on the easy side but the further you go into the story there will be a spike in difficulty. So you really have to work for those other endings.
Now that I got that off of my chest; on to the cons. The port is wonky. Even though you can switch the game to full screen it doesn't actually stay on full screen. For the first few days of me having it since release I was able to but now it automatically reverts back to windowed mode. It doesn't really bother me personally but I can understand why it would bother others. Yes the game caps at 60 fps and it caps at 30 during cutscenes. It's clearly noticeable and can be a bit annoying. Especially when you're trying to enjoy whatever it is that's taking place and there's a slight lag. Is it so bad that it isn't enjoyable? No it's not. When you're used to playing games without caps it's noticeable at first but the more you play the game the least likely it will bother you. At this point I'm pretty over it.
So in the end, is the game worth it despite the cons listed? Yes. Absolutely, yes. I promise you that what you have seen so far is nothing compared to what the game is really all about. The more you delve into the game the more you'll unfold the story and the meaning deep within.

X3: Albion Prelude remains to this day a stellar paragon of development follow-through. Despite a publishing infrastructure that pushed this out into the world only "mostly" finished, for years afterwards this has been lovingly maintained and updated and honed and fine-tuned. The community surrounding it is a treasure trove of supplementary data to inform your gameplay and generally extremely pleasant. And the game itself, well, if you make it at least some way along the somewhat steep learning curve and the many options for free sandbox style play where you can choose and keep varying your occupations as a fighter, pirate, trader, empire builder, fleet manager and armada captain in a huge game universe that keeps evolving, then you will quickly realise just how many hundreds or thousands of hours of quality solo gaming time there is to be had here. Years in, it still looks gorgeous, the sound and music still do not grate on your nerves, and the atmosphere is still one to thouroughly immerse oneself in again and again. Luckily, I have mostly played with an offline (no-Steam) patch provided upon community request by the developer, so I must never admit to myself the thousands of hours I have enjoyed playing this! One of my all-time favourite games and still worth checking out today, especially the expanded, revamped version, X3: Albion Prelude, and to be preferred over X: Rebirth, its bold but ultimately disappointing sequel! Keep playing X3: Terran Conflict and/or X3: Albion Prelude until X4 Foundations comes out and has had a few years to mature!

Ive been a long time fan of the Ace Combat franchise and in addition to to Ace Combats 4, 5, Zero, and 6, I have also played other flight arcade/simulator games such as Over G Fighters, Lock On Modern Air Combat, and the IL2 series. It was my fond memories of the Ace Combat franchise that lead me to this game.
I want to start off by mentioning this, while the game is marketed as a spiritual successor ( I would say that its more along the lines of paying homage to the series specifically AC4, AC5, and AC Zero), its not exactly like the franchise. So if you are looking for a PC version of the Strangereal Ace Combats and expecting this to have alot of the game mechanics and poignant storyline of the AC franchise then you will be sorely disappointed.
With that being stated, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this game. For starters from my understanding of the news I have been hearing, the person who created this game is ether working with a small staff or by himself so the updates for the game maybe slugglish when compared to other games in a similar genre. Nevertheless some of the content is well worth the wait. Secondly, one of the primary traits of this game is the ability to modify it as well as build missions. So if there is a certain factor you dont like, chances are you can change it. If you want a more Ace Combat feel then you can make it that way. The modding community is small but can provide you with most anything you are probably looking for.
So onto the gameplay, the gameplay is kinda what you would expect for an arcade flight game, planes carrying 100+ missiles, non realistic maneuvers etc. Nevertheless there are some things that you will find moreso in flight sims rather than Ace Combat such as the ability to despense chaff and flares.
Graphics wise, the majority of the detail went into the planes that you fly so the planes look pretty good for the style of illustration the creator used. Currently of the large selections of planes you can fly, only the F-16 has an actual cockpit but its not functioning, yet. Nevertheless like I mentioned before, the game is still recieving updates though.
Story wise, you can tell that the game's universe was heavily influenced by the Strangereal universe in the Ace Combat series. The cutscenes in the current campaign thats availible took queues from specifically Ace Combat 4 by using stills rather than video. This is where in my opinion was the biggest let down simply because the cutscenes only have one still that would give you a picture of the beginning of the scene but you hear an entire scene unfolding.
Overall would I recommend? Yes because in spite of all of the negative things I have just mentioned, this game has alot of potential. Between the mods, the mission builder and the future updates, the game can potentially become a decent, enjoyable game. Sadly the game will never be able to break out of the shadow of Ace Combat because Ace Combat is really the only game to really compare and or relate to this game (in spite of not liking that comparison, I was a hypocrite and compared it to the Ace Combat series constantly). Overall I would recommend waiting a while for the games bugs to be worked out and more content to be added. Also as much as I love the game, paying $25 dollars for a game that is still progressing slowly may be a bit too much. However I justified it as a donation to a guy who is most likely working with a small crew or no crew at all to keep working on this game.

I had high, possibly loftly like  hopes for this game as did many others who have ever played this game and saw the potential for greatness that this game has. Borderlands has always been a very good franchise, as far as delivering an enjoyable first experience and end-game content goes, it always leaves a mark however, after the first few playthroughs the storyline does get very tedious as you're forced to repeat even the more mundane parts of the story which is rather quite bland and a small grind to finish the first and second time around, but with the addition of talking player characters, each playthrough can vary a little in your characters response, which always makes it refreshing.
Borderlands 1 introduced Raid Bosses in the form of Crawmerax and Raid Bosses have since been expanded apon in the other series and even made more challenging and more rewarding than the previous games, however the raid boss which takes place at the end is very much enjoyable as it's possible to complete without a full party (it just takes longer)
It's no secret that in both Borderlands 1 and 2, the enemies are bullet sponges which makes playing the game rather irritating at the end-game, however in the Pre-Sequel I'm glad to say that the enemies have all been moderately improved so each enemy will only take a few seconds to drop, instead of spending several to kill a single enemy from the prior games.
Storyline wise, it's definitely interesting to see how the villian of Borderlands 2 is born which is quite refreshing and there are a few rather entertaining moments within the game, but also there are some moments which make me feel rather quite sorry for the people who 'cross' Jack, and again, it's still an improvement on the previous titles. The side-quests are also entertaining and contain a few rather funny moments and verbal exchanges.
We all know that Borderlands boasts the biggest collection of guns, this much is true but I think the original was superior in terms of what enemy dropped which weapon, as in the original, an enemy using an SMG, when killed - Would drop that exact SMG, but in Borderlands 2 and the Pre-Sequel, they've since stuck to a more randomly generated weapon, which is a fraction more disappointing and annoying.
Legendary weapons in Borderlands are always something awesome and to write home about, however in the Pre-Sequel they do seem to nerf the list of Legendaries to a mere handful, however instead of spending hours apon hours to find a legendary, you're introduced to a Grinder which can produce Legendary weapons for you, should you invest time in gathering a special currency and learning a recipe or two.
I'll admit I was a little unsure how the Oz Kits would play, as I originally thought they would limit your ability to explore, however, thankfully you're able to 'double-jump', not vertically, but horizontally which makes for better exploration and getting to places more efficiently than if you were to run, ofcourse if you run out of oxygen you start to lose health but it's worth it and I rather enjoyed the Oz Kits as a whole.
In Borderlands you can typically expect 4 character types: 1) A sniper. 2) A support class. 3) A Gunzerker. 4) A Melee-centric class. In the original, the Support class was Roland, the Soldier, In 2 it was Maya, the Siren, in the Pre-Sequel it was Wilhelm, the 'Gunzerker', each of the aforementioned were all very playable characters, but Maya was definitely the best one, as I haven't fully 'experienced' Wilhelm I can't say whether he succeeds, but his playstyle simply did not fit me and so I wasn't able to try.
If you're a fan of the franchise (And for some reason haven't bought, or played it yet) you should.

I decided recently to jump back into the X3 series, but this time with a twist. I chose to download a couple of minor mods, plus one major mod. This being the "Star Wars Reborn" mod. As a Star Wars fan I decided that I would give it a try, and I was astonished with it. I played as an "Alliance Peacekeeper" which is the bog standard Argon start, just as the Rebel Alliance. I started off imeaditly with an X-Wing, and was happy that i could open and close the X-foils. I was excited to see Star Wars ships, and earn a couple along the way. I had heart-pounding battles, which X3 brings, and great thills at destroying fighter squadrons.
If you are on the fence about this game i suggest you get it, and if you are a Star Wars fan I suggest you get the "Star Wars Rebon" mod after going thtough a campaign once, or immeadiatly, if you are lloking for a space sim with Star Wars ships. The only thing you need to understand before getting this game is to have patience, you can not become the top trader or commander of the bigggest fleet in 1 hour, 10 hours for a matter of fact, but along the way you will find great joy, sadness and relief. You will eventually miss out on those times where you piloted a single fighter then be interrupted by explosions on your port side as you enter into a massive duel agiants another capital ship.
There is very little that I can say negativley about this game, I suggest that you get it, it does not cater to a specific player, but many different kinds.

The X3 franchise is an amazing and intense one. With that said it's not for everyone. It's a huge sandbox game that requires you to use your own imagination. With mods I went from a nobody to a sector destroyer, even taking out large faction NPC's. I built huge empires of self sufficient factories and laid claim to many unclaimed territories. Towards the end I became so large that I started taking over huge portions of the universe..
Any game where I can take over the universe is a good one for me.
I recommend this game to everyone who likes space sim games. With mods you can move this game into anything you want it to do. Building, Fighting, Exploring..the options are endless.
Also, my play time is not representative of my actual playtime between this game and X3 as some of it was outside of Steam. I have sunk close to 1000 hours in these games in the last 8+ years. It will always have a special place for me and I can't wait until Egosoft releases X4!
The one thing I want from the start already built into the game is the ability to takeover sectors without mods or respawn points. If the sector is mine they need to use the gate like everyone else. They can meet my ships when jumping in to rethink their options. Egosoft must understand that the eventual end of every game is war. You cannot build an entire empire and continue to look away from the transgressions of others. Resources are everything in space, if you cannot defend them they will not be yours anymore.
Cheers Egosoft! Bring back the ability to fly every ship in X4 and keep the franchise going.

If you collide (and the collision is very generous in the player's favour), the current enemies go zooming off as the music fast forwards, and you lose score. To get yourself out of danger, you can press a key to temporarily slow down music to give breathing space to dodge.
Repeat until the music ends.
It is utterly wonderful. I haven't played a single screen shooter as pure & focused (and without ridiculous neon/bloom) in a long time.

It's an open world and not an opend world style of game. it's somewhere in between.
every NPC interaction will lead you to a different story and a different ending

Soundodger+ is a simple, yet elegant rhythm game that has nothing to do with the host of Daily Byte, and requires you to dodge a small variety of projectiles that shoot relatively to the beat of the music. The mechanics are extremely simple, dodge bullets with your mouse until the song ends. It obviously borrows from shmups, but don't let the term "bullet hell" scare you here: Lives are unlimited and you have a seemingly infinity slow mo (at the detriment of your final score). The less you are hit, the higher your percentage score is. That's practically it, though, the bullets shot from outside of the arena by generators range in angle, size, speed and heat-seeking ability while those said generators rotate around the arena. It comes with a decent handful of tracks, though the most fun and interesting art is to see how the auto-gen mode uses your own MP3 to thrown bullets at you.
There are also so extra user levels and you can create your own levels and bullet outputs to your music with a levle editor.
That's pretty much all to say about Soundodger+. Mouse control is smooth, vector graphics are stylized and look great when you change the settings to 60fps with "pretty" fullscreen settings. Soundodger+ is a carthartic and interesting way to experience your music. The game is worth of buy if this all sounds interesting to you. It isn't expensive, though some players may not find their value if they don't intend to play all the included songs for completion, or expect to get alot of time out of it with their own music.

Soundodger. A music-based bullet hell that scores you based on how perfect you can avoid
.
The main objective, as aforementioned, is to be perfect at avoiding
--bullets that spawn into the playing field and follow a particular rhythm and beat of the track. There are four different bullets: linears, bubbles, homers, and hearts. In game, the hearts unlock a new track that can be played as well if you seek to unlock special achievements.
includes user levels, an editor, and auto-gen mode (creates a randomized level with whatever song selected). By default, there are six premade stages, five that, like the advanced stages, have the heart bullet that can help unlock the same bonus tracks.
I'm finding myself enjoying the editor a lot, using my favorite songs to craft nice and partially fancy levels. And after achieving perfection with the standard songs, unlocking the advanced stages as well as a couple heart stages, I'm in a constant liking of this game. A nice time-killing on a boring day. I have yet to officially unlock all hearts and getting 100% score on more advanced and premade user levels.
Part of me wish there were at least another mode to this game, possibly an alternative, where the game rates how well you can collect specific bullets. Auto-gen, too, isn't very good in creating stages either, but there must be a way they're done. I don't know what more to put here...
Soundodger is a pretty amazing game with all it already has. Plus, this game is accompanied with a worthwhile soundtrack that I fell in love with the more I kept playing those particular stages. Hopefully, I'll share some of my created stages with the public later on...

Monochroma is actually a really good atmospheric puzzle-platformer. As many have mentioned in the reviews here, it evokes memories of Limbo to some extent, which is not a bad thing. Gameplay wise, I am liking the puzzles in here more...in Limbo, the puzzles let the game down after the opening third.
Visuals are really good. I like the touch of red in the otherwise black and white landscape. Music is good too, though for some reason the music doesn't play all the time in the background. The sound effects at times feel rough though, but nothing major.
Now, the game does have issues, particularly with the animations. They really could have been better. Nothing bad now, just noticeable at times the lack of smoothness in animations.
The bigger issue for me personally is the jump button is inexplicably tied to the UP arrow key instead of the SPACEBAR or another key like X or Z or S. And it's hardwired...no way of changing. The reason I have an issue with this in the game is because then basically your right hand does the work all the time, and the SPACEBAR is used by default to carry/drop your brother, something that could easily have been mapped to the E or Q key for example. I play other games where UP is jump (like Giana Sisters) so that in itself is not the issue.
Overall, it is really good, but an hour in I stopped playing due to the poorly thought-out controls. If you are going to be playing with the keyboard and don't find it desirable such that the jump is tied to the UP arrow, then I reckon waiting it out. Animations have some slight issues but nothing major. Most important thing is that puzzles are good, and the atmosphere is amazing.

Maybe my expectations were too high, but I'm disapointed. First of all: It is NOT an "unforgiving survival game". If you run around to collect some berries and mushrooms, and sometimes set a fire or stay in a building then that's it: you survived. Survival is not hard at all, your life is in no danger unless you look for it.
So the main drive of the game are rather exploration, crafting and fighting than struggling for another day to live. The problem is exploration is also way too easy, you can just run across the map without any difficulties. Crafting is ok, but not particularly interesting, and I don't really like the combat system.
The theme is also disappointing. The music is not connected well to the theme. The snowy pines and reindeers are just decoration, because most stories leading to a mutant zombie boss monster. (Maybe they started developing a zombie survival, but changed the theme at the end? :P )

There are many reviews already published here on Steam that praise the game so I will keep this review short.
Stellaris is, without a doubt, the easiest (grand) strategy game from Paradox to date. It is a good thing because other games such as Europa Universalis IV, Hearts of Iron IV or Crusader Kings 2 can be a bit too difficult for new players. It is not to say that this game is easy when you are playing it on harder difficulties. Sure, it can be a bit wonky and sometimes AI acts a bit strange but overall Stellaris is still being polished and, knowing Paradox, will continue to be in years to come.
As with other major strategy games from Paradox, you are allowed to create and install mods. From a simple cosmetic mod to major total conversions and various fixes, balances - if vanilla game does not suit you and you are able to create or find a mod that changes this one, frustrating little mechanic... than it is as simple as pressing this subsribe button. Very easy and very helpful.
I am sure that many other reviews say what I have just said. It is worth repeating however as it is my belief that Stellaris is worth its price. Sure, when you have played it long enough you start to notice a lot of repeated events (planet discoveries etc.) and your performance of the game is getting worse with each passing decade but that is the nature of those games. If you can forgive those small nuisances than you are going to really enjoy Stellaris.

I bought this game mostly on a whim because I had some money lying around in my Steam wallet and because Jim Sterling recommended it. This turned out to be a fantastic decision. Here's a quick rundown of why I can highly recommend this game:
Pro:
- The storyline is fantastic: it comes with several plot twists, is highly nuanced, extremely dark and full of philosophical undertones (-> existentialism and absurdism). As someone who really enjoys that kind of thing (e.g. I also really liked SOMA for this reason) this alone makes the game worth while.
- The soundtrack is incredible and I really hope it finds its way onto Spotify. It's not just that the individual tracks are beautiful and memorable but also that they are used to great effect in the actual game. For example, some of the songs sync up really well with certain boss battles.
- Overall, the game is quite original and is certainly a breath of fresh air in an industry oversaturated with AAA titles full of rehashed concepts.
- The animations are really fluid and the combat (especially the boss fights) looks pretty damn cool.
- While the graphics aren't particularly noteworthy from a technical perspective the game features tons of varied and beautiful environments. At the same time it manages to keep a cohesive aesthetic throughout the entire game.
- Some of the sidequests are really interesting and tie into the main storyline in important ways.
Contra:
- Some of the sidequests have dull / annoying objectives (fetch quests, escort quests etc.) and there is quite a bit of backtracking. The game is clearly aware of this as one of the main characters even complains about it multiple times. That doesn't make it that much better, though.
- There are some technical issues with the game such as the fact that it doesn't run in 1080p fullscreen currently (however, this can be easily fixed using Borderless Gaming). Also, there is a noticeable amount of texture pop-in particularly in the ruined city area. However, I did not encounter any serious glitches or crashes.
- The combat can get a little bit repetitive by the end of the game.
- The game initially recommends the "normal" difficulty but even as someone who doesn't really play singleplayer games for the challenge I found that the game became way to easy towards the end. If you put any effort into optimizing your plugin chips you'll be nearly invincible on normal.
Overall I'd give NieR: Automata a strong 9/10 and even though we're only 3 months into 2017 I'd be quite surprised if a better game comes out this year. Also, if you decide to pick up this game you must keep playing after the first "ending" since otherwise you'll miss most of what makes this game so good.

[Overview]
This game isn't finished, it can get better than it current is. It is currently quite good. I'm a fan of Terraria, which has farrrrrrrr more content than Magicite, but 4 hours into this game, I can easily see myself logging more hours into Magicite than Terraria.
This game has 3 main components which I like: Multiplayer coop games, a simple old school platformer combat system, and permadeath.
There are also some issues which I dislike, namely: obvious implementation problems like bugs and crashes. Some are hilarious, some are annoying, all are unnecessary.
Then there are the other issues which I'm neutral towards: crafting, attribute rolling and unbalanced playstyles.
[Good: Multiplayer]
This game's single player component is already fun. Add to that the ability to cooperate, coordinate and help your friends, and the fun is enhanced. Playing together with someone also means that when the inevitable glitches occur, they are more funny and less frustrating.
[Good: Combat system]
This is the sort of game developer who wants to put you in a world where death is the norm rather than exception. If you want to think of mobs as free resources to collect to enhance your character, you should be playing (working?) in an mmo.
Enemies are challenging. They have terrible pathfinding, which, in an easier game, would be a reason to complain, but here, it has come to become my main reason for survival.
Your mighty character could walk up to an enemy, waving the best sword you've managed to craft, and suddenly lay on the ground waggling like a helpless turtle with it's shell on the ground and it's legs in the air, permanently dead.
And that's just from the noob looking slimes.
[Good: Permadeath]
Speaking of death, this game does not focus upon the accumulation of resources or wealth for its success. The mechanic introduced to drive this direction of focus is simple. When you die, you restart. The journey is not only more fun than the destination; the destination is simply the option to restart the journey with potentially different settings.
If you want to win a game by patiently becoming game-rich enough to blow enemies away, in a flash of particle effects, cutscenes, while wearing costumes/accessories tailored to your beloved and carefully named character, then this game is not for you. Because your progress is routinely wiped. You can't stay in a field too long or you get killed. You can't hoard riches because if you don't spend them to stay alive longer, you've just died a rich and foolish death.
Don't be fooled by the character creation screen. Your character is not unique. The tiny boost in stats in some direction of your choosing are nowhere near as important as your ability to press 'jump' or 'attack' at the right moment.
Permadeath is a design choice which takes the gameplay focus away from hoarding, away from character build designing (oh man, I'm still in love with Path of Exile..), and plonks the player (perhaps that's you!) right into where the developer wants you. In a world where you jump, attack, survive, and repeat.
Permadeath is also my favourite portion of this game. Why? Because you look ridiculous dead.
Your character's death waggle is so pathetic that it is almost like a reward in itself for playing this game. "You got this far in Magicite, only to lie on the floor as some noob looking path-findingly-incompetant sprite casually jumps up and down upon your body. Enjoy your death waggle!"
If some games are designed so that the player takes joy in killing, Magicite's permadeath mechanic perhaps does the opposite. Dying isn't upsetting, it's awesome :D
[Bad: Crashes]
The bugs are not acceptable of course. This game crashes. Multiplayer usually works but occasionally players cannot connect properly or one person sees something different to the other on their screens.
This game is fun enough that I'm willing to keep trying to play it through such problems, but really, these problems should not exist if the game is being sold for money. In fact free games don't really need to strive towards being bugged either :P
[Neutral: Crafting]
There is 0 room for creativity in this game. That's ok with me, because it isn't being advertised as such.
Crafting is not a game mechanic to allow the player to design anything beautiful, interesting or useful. Crafting is closer to a quasi plot device, which explains why you suddenly have a sword or hp potion in your hands. Did you chop down 3 trees? Well then it's only natural that you have a wooden sword in your hands.
(Yes, a wooden sword, while smaller than the smallest tree, takes quite a bit of wood to craft. Lucky you are wood spammed in your game, and the focus on ores gains a much higher priority)
As a plot device, I find it cute, yet unnecessary (since enemies could just drop useful items). I like that there's choice, and the player can direct and plan what they wish to focus on. In that sense this game's crafting system offers an advantage compared to a random drop system.
That's as far as it goes.
[Neutral: Attribute rolling]
I find it completely unnessary that attribute rolling is random. Why? Because you can roll as many times as you want. This combination feels like a waste of time.
If the attributes given are to be random, that's fine. Then the player gains the fun of learning to adapt to random conditions each playthrough.
If the attributes given can be simply selected from a list or menu, that's fine too. Then the player gains the fun of deliberately affecting their gameplay settings to control/vary their experience according to their own tastes.
But the combination? You don't get the satisfaction that you've successfully adapted to a random change, because you choose when to stop rolling. You've simply used the menu allowing you to pick whether you start with extra speed, hp, strength, etc. But the menu sucked, and you had to click nonstop and stare at the display until you got what you were planning to choose.
This doesn't hurt the game, but it doesn't make it fun either.
[Neutral: Unbalanced playstyles]
Edit: I removed this comment because I now think the playstyles are not unbalanced.
