Where do I start... X3: Albion Prelude is a really fun game, one might call it "singleplayer-arcade version of EVE Online". But it is very exotic kind of fun, which I cannot comprehend. I'll try to explain it.
The first thing you'll be baffled with is a lack of tutorial. Tutorial at the start of the game just tells you how to control your ship, and that's all. If you like to discover aspects of the game by yourself without any systematized information whatsoever (game wiki is just not enough), then you'll like this part. For me it was boring and frustrating.
Next, you'll have to choose your activities - combat, missions or trade. Let's start with combat. Actually, it's really fun and well-made aspect of the game. I would spend hours in it only if was really often happening. Don't get me wrong, you can always find some problems for yourself, but these fight won't be balanced at all and will result in your death. So the only thing you can battle at the start is a small pirate ships, which will become only rarer with time. It is especially problematic when you're starting as Bankrupt Assassin and need to increase you rating. Not only resonable packs of pirates rare, they give minescule increase in rating with factions. So, if you're bankrupt assassing, you'll be stuck there forever.
Missions are incredibly boring, even plot-related ones. You'll have to either grind kills, move some stuff from A to B, or just follow some ships. Well, that's all I can say - it's uninteresting and boring.
Trading is very similar to EVE Online. You'll have to discover systems, check out their goods, buy some on low price, then sell it on high price... I'm already tired typing that.
Overall, i found the game incredibly frustrating and stupid. You're unable to save game in space, which combined with ridiculous encounters with enemies results in tons of wasted progress and time. So, if you want to waste some of your time, like I did - definitely buy this game.

This game is extremely charming and well worth your time. The art is great. The music is lovely. The voice acting is stellar. The story is compelling and far more substantial than it first appears. Finally, I'm fairly new to point and click adventure games, but I found the game play to be challenging enough to feel rewarding but was generally not so hard (read: idiosyncratic) as to be frustrating.
I would also note that I found the tone of this game to a little disjointed. It starts with pretty, melancholy music on the title screen and an opening cut scene with an enigmatic creepy dude in a misty labyrinth talking in riddles. Then, all of a sudden, we're in Winnie the Pooh meets Brian Jacques' Redwall meets (Disney's) Alice in Wonderland. As the game progresses and the stakes become clearer, some of the plot points dialog, voice acting, and music take a rather creepy turn (relatively speaking; this is a game about a 12 year old boy and some talking animals, not Silent Hill) while Jerry, for the most part, continues to cheerfully march through the game. Normally, I think I would find this to be off-putting or immersion-breaking, but, for some reason, it seems to contribute to Night of the Rabbit's weird charm.

This is the very last of the great space sims. Never again will you be able to Fight, Trade and Explore without having to buy buy buy. You can choose from a vast array of ships from various races, upgrade ships, equip a huge choice of weapons and explore until you find yourself in a tent in the South Pole. You can build complex stations, fly missions, choose who to fight for and what path to take and encounter aliens without encountering the most deadly of enemies, the dreaded IN GAME PURCHASE. DLC on this is free and uses content largely developed by the long standing in game community. Sadly, despite keeping with the same formula as in several previous game titles Egosoft bit the bullet in the follow up, X-Rebirth and the bullet won. Hence this really is the last of a generation. Hopes remain high for the recently announced follow on, but guarded after customers were left sadly disappointed with Rebirth. X3 Albion Prelude was the pinnacle of the space trading sim long before the word "griefer" had been discovered. I look back on this and feel the same Skywalkeresque experience as when I first played Elite on the Commodore 64. True, it doesn't have the same graphical qualities as Elite Dangerous but the gameplay keeps me coming back for more, after all, "Game play" is really what it's all about and not paying your hard earned credits buying virtual ornaments to be displayed in virtual ships so we can live out our virtual lives. Recommended whole heartedly and thanks for the memories Egosoft.

Yup this is a late review but some people might find it handy.
Is this a bad game? No. But it is not nearly as good as Borderlands 2. If this had been the first game in the series it would be getting praise across the board... but it isn't the first game and it's going to be damn hard to live up to BL2. The main problem is the game just feels like a large BL2 DLC. It took me 22h to do a playthrough, which is very respectable until you consider it took me 35h to do a playthrough of BL2.
And that's that TPS' biggest problem... it is a smaller game than BL2 in every respect (even if we ignore DLC) the first 5-6h of the game take place in a few very boring and samey moon levels. Eventually the game brings you to some awesome locations including a space construction site, a testing facility, and a Hyperion city and these levels are great! I just wish there were more of them. Overall this game has far fewer areas than BL2 and far less environment variation too. The maps are smaller as well. The same goes for the side missions. There's just not a lot of them and many feel kind of like missed opportunities.
The story at points feels like it will take an awesome turn and in some ways it is really cool to see the events leading up to the events of BL2, but it feels like 2K was rushed because the story never hits the levels it could have and never goes into the depth we would have loved to have. Before you know it the story is over and it leaves quite a bit of room for more. Old characters return but many never actually appear in game... they say a couple sentences over echo. The game introduces a few new characters but they are mostly forgettable.
I've said a lot of negative things up until now, but this is NOT a bad game. I love that the playable characters actually talk and give their own opinions on events and that characters dialogue changes depending on what character you choose to play. For example, playing as Athena I had Springs (female Scooter) hitting on me and I enjoyed the way Athena reacted.
The shooting is as fun as ever and the introduction of low gravity is a good one in my opinion. Double jumping and slamming enemies adds an awesome new facet to the gunplay and they nailed it, although I feel like O2 could have been a bit scarcer. You will not die if you run out of air. As for guns, there are new energy guns that are fine, but there's no overhaul here as was done between BL1 and BL2. However the Boganella shotgun was awesome and had me laughing all the while i used it (which was most of the game unfortunately).
There are a few new enemies (emphasis on few) that are fun enough, but mostly you fight scavs which are basically bandits. More enemy types would have been cool, and some of the new additions could have been used to more effect.
Overall this game is good. It doesn't really do anything wrong, but I can't help but compare it to BL2 and see all the things it isn't. BL2 had me so hooked I bought all the DLC and pumped over 225h into it and would come back for more in a heartbeat. I will likely do a second playthrough of this game, but I feel no need to go beyond that or purchase any of the mostly lackluster DLC (HINT: if the base game is short, character packs are probably not the best idea for DLC).
Anyway I can recommend this game because it is a well made and fun game. It is worth playing if you pick it up on sale, just be aware that this is not BL3.

I've been a gamer for a long time, having gotten my start playing all of the snes classic RPGs, so when I saw this game and its particular style, I brought it immediately. Being the type of player that enjoyed Lufia 2's ancient dungeon, and Star Ocean 2's Bonus dungeon's, I thought that I would really enjoy some of Disgaea's game mechanics -- in particular randomly generated item worlds, and the ability to level your characters well beyond the typical 99 cap (the cap in this game is literally 199000 levels....yes, you read that right).
Unfortunately, This is the most unnecessarily complicated game I have ever played in my life. There is simply too much going on to make it enjoyable. The game plays more like a single player MMO in terms of sheer grindiness, none of which is remotely necessary to complete the storyline.
Pros:
Fun storyline and reasonable plot
Great voice acting (main character sounds like Goku)
Good music and graphics for the genre
Cons:
This game has everything and the kitchen sink thrown into it, and yet there isn't even that much variety.
You can create as many characters as you want over a broad range of your typical RPG classes (thieves, knights, mages, etc). Each of those classes has multiple tiers that are unlockable through leveling. Each of those characters can be leveled to 199000, by repeatedly going to level 9999 and reincarnating back to level 1 again. Additionally, all characters can train in any of the 5 types of equipment (swords, bows etc), and gain skill levels (up to 255) that unlock new abilities. Those abilities can then be leveled up to 99 each.
If all of the above wasn't enough, you will also level every single item in the game, from your lowly potions to your high level gear. In order to do that, you have to enter into the "item world" which is basically a RNG created world for that specific item. Items come in common (30 floors), rare (60 floors), and legendary (100 floors) qualities. Every 10 floors you have the chance to leave the dungeon. Every 30 floors there is a boss character. Each floor you complete adds a level to the item...though the max level for a legendary is actually 200, which you can get to by burning even more time in item world by going into "mystery gates" which are random encounters.
And if all that wasn't bad enough, items also have "specialists", which are 20 different types of souls that can by slotted into an item to provide additional benefits like raising stats. Sound easy? Nope. You have to level those too....up to level 20000 for a stat related soul. Oh and those souls have to be "subdued" so they can be transferred to other items....a process that consists of killing them in the item world.
But wait! That's not all! In addition to the normal slog of killing things and leveling, most maps have what's known as "Geo Panels", which come with their own sets of effects. For instance, you could stand on a 20% damage panel and lose 20% of your health per turn. Now that doesn't sound so bad, except that you're going to be completing thousands of these floors, and you can't even autopilot. Even when your character is 1000x more powerful than the enemies you're encountering, you still have to pay attention, or else you might find yourself dead regardless.
This whole game is a tireless, neverending slog which is almost entirely devoid of purpose. It's almost as if it was created solely to laugh at completionists/perfectionist players that want to maximise their gaming experience. Anyone who actually does it, after the thousands of hours it would take to achieve, has absolutely no life.

Alot of mixed reviews here but here's my take....
I buy an Early Access game on Steam expecting there to be bugs / stability issues, which this has it's fair share of at the moment (v1.400 3rd April 2016), and there is clearly alot of work still to go in terms of fleshing out the campaign and the economics of buying fighters as you progress. BUT. I accepted happily when I paid 6.74 GBP that this would be the case.
Surely the reason that early access games have become such a success on Steam is that it provides the developers with the incentive to finish the game properly, act on feedback they recieve and ultimately, have a surge of community support when the title is ready for a full release. This should be one of those games.
The graphics engine and UI remind me of XIII in terms of style, whereas the features that the game offers are VERY similar to the Ace Combat series. I've been waiting for this style of arcade flight sim, and I like the way this game is going!
Sure - it's crashing alot. But I keep playing it and getting hooked on each mission, and I think many, many others will to. Once the stability issues are ironed out, I'll consider the small investment I made purchasing this to be an absolute bargain.

Deus ex is a really good game and a tough one. Unlike other games at the time like half life, deus ex is the ultimate first person shooter. It feels like system shock 2 and fallout had a baby, Deus ex is about skill and thinking, this isn't a game where you shoot everything you see on a map which is in my opinion a really good thing and thats what most games do today, for example in cod ghosts the story isn't good because its just a bunch of shooting and crouching at the same time. Here in Deus Ex it switches a lot of things up, its either you're in a area looking for clues or you're assisting your allies to fight against enemies or your just crouching with a knife and backstabing the enemies.
Now there are a few things bad about deus ex, first of all on modern systems its a little messed up. The first time I installed it and started it it crashed and I had to download a more recent .exe to get it to work, another issue is the audio it seems when ever someone is talking they are cut off at some points. Also in the luancher options use open GL because all the others are a ♥♥♥♥ing nuisance to get to work. Second in the gameplay, if you aren't keen on a game that has RPG elements where you earn skill points and spend them on skills then you might as well pass this game and especially if you hate stealth games. And the hit detection is awfull as well as the health the enemy has, in fps games like half life it takes a few seconds to kill the enemy with a shotgun, here I have had to constantly shoot an enemy with a shotgun and half of the time the bullets scatter everywhere, even when a pistol is aiming at the head nine times out of ten will it actually get the head.
Now I'm not saying its a bad game because of the issues I have, some of you might not expereince the issues I have but this is one really good game, I can see why when ever you mention Deus ex some one will reinstall it. The story is excellent and a lot of conflicts will occur in the game, sometimes you'll have an option to kill someone or help someone. Unlike other games where you have just one occurnce that seems critical, in Deus ex you'll have many occurnce's which is a really good thing as it opens more abilities and choices for the player and thats how a game should be. If you think you like a good fps challenge with RPG elements in it and stealth then this is for you and its worth the $3 (on steam summer sale) or the $6 it costs. This game is amazing.

The original Deus Ex is my favorite game of all time. You play as an augmented man named JC Denton. You work for the United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition (UNATCO). As JC continues, he starts to unravel a global conspiracy. Not everything is as it seems.
Regarding Deus Ex's gameplay: The graphics have aged poorly. However, the gameplay and story have somehow managed to get better. With themes like humanism, terrorism, government over reach, and technology's role in the modern world, they are even more relevant than when the game released over a year before 9/11.
One of Deus Ex's strongest points has been smart level design. Each level is large and supports all types of play styles. Want to be stealthly? No problem, there's always an alternate route. Want to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥who kicks down the door with guns ablazing? Go for it. This type of freedom is seldom properly executed today. Back when this game released in 2000, it was a god send!
If you want an intelligent shooter (or stealth game if you choose to play as such) that has something to say about society and humanity than this is absolutely the game for you.

Some spoilers, probably. I cannot be arsed to write a spoilerless review. Or a proper edited review onthat matter, so here are some thoughts:
If you like what you see in the trailer and usually play stuff like this, go ahead. If not, wait for a sale for these kinds of games I would say there aren't enough thnings to do. There is a ton of stuff to do (40ish bours worth of it) but for the stories being presented, I think the villains and characters need a bit more fleshing out so am hoping for some kind of expansion. The plotline should feel long yet the events that transpire happen in a seemingly short period of time. Perhaps this is a little flaneur into absurdism though it seemed to me at least be a bit weak.
A rigid level scaling system suffers from the same problem games like Borderlands 2 suffers from. This game can quite easily be GG'd with a couple damage/offensive healing/XP overleveling and increased droprate chips defeating any kind of challenge presented. If you fall behind on the leveling however, it is pretty unfogiving.
The plugin chip system itself, partly based on loot drops though you can buy them at vendors I felt was a asanine experience and took my focus off the rest of the game which I was more interested in, fortuntaely it doesn't play a vital role in the game.
Combat animations and control are smooth. I would have wanted more adaptive and intelligent enemies, otherwise its a mindless button mashing smackfest beyond the prologue. Having played a bit of Bayonetta, I would have wanted something more from it which I did not get
As for... Immersion...Go play a Fallout game with a ton of mods or something similar. I felt the game was less about that and more about posing questions to the player which in some aspects was trying to be a bit too clever at the expense of emotional investment. I could not care for the existence of the programmes Adam and Eve and the emotional connection they share though I appreciate the child-like quality that Eve posseses as both programmes attempt to learn sentience.
On a fundamental level the question of sentience is a little more complicated than what the game attempts to present  though it is a great piece of entertainment and I do hope the creators improve on the inevitable sequel. Or prequel. Or a DLC that ties up the lose ends to the main characters.

So I bought this in a bundle with the Witcher 1 and 3, mainly because I wanted to play through the first 2 before 3. I wasn't expecting much from either of them except maybe a pretty good story. I will admit I skipped TW1 after a bit over 5 hours of gameplay, as I couldn't stand the mechanics and ell of the game. But I am glad I stuck at it, cause damn this game was good. The mechanics got better as I got used to them, and actually got pretty fun when you started using the signs and stuff in more effective ways mixed with improvements through the character development screen.
But the main thing was the story. It starts of pretty slow, but gains a lot of momentum as it goes through the game. It really starts to pick up at the end of Chapter 1/Start of Chapter 2. You really start to feel for the characters and gain great connections to them, and the decisions are great, especially when you get to see the actual result in the game. Sometimes you regret stuff, but that's all part of making decisions.
Even if your PC can't handle TW3 or you don't want to play it, I would totally reccomend playing this.
Now, time to carry on playing the Witcher 3!!!

I seldom play point n' clicks, but I must say that Daedalic are a force to be reckoned with in the genre. I'd recently played the entire Deponia series and had an absolute blast with it, so afterwards I simply had to seek out their other titles. The Night of the Rabbit was my first choice, and I do not regret it one bit.
This game was a wonderful experience. It has a very whimsical and sometimes touching story with a colorful cast of characters with great voice acting, a gorgeous art style that reminded me of Child of Light and Over the Garden Wall, and a fantastic musical score. For a point n' click it also never went into frustratingly difficult territory in regards to the puzzles and solutions. Also, the Quartets card minigame I found shockingly addictive.
If you're a fan of point n' clicks, it's a no-brainer that you will enjoy this title. Also if you've never played point n' clicks before, I'd say this game would be the perfect introduction.

100% recommend: This is the best Total War in terms of single-player experince; it rivals the original Rome Total War in terms of multiplayer.

The modding potential for this game is great; you get things like Stainless Steel and The Lord of The Rings + more. I'd highly recommend doing more research on mods that are available for this game.

This has many more features than the modern turd that CA are pooping out these days:

The feel of the soldiers is close to perfect: Everyone has weight to them, also Medieval 2 is the slowest paced Total War and is more focused on cavalry and out-flanking.

This game has religion; if you anger the pope as a European faction, you can expect hell. Of course you can call crusades and Jihad's.

All factions are playable apart from the ones that can't feasibly played, like the Mongels and the Aztecs.

There is an RPG like element to the regions, you have to decide what regions are going to be soldier spammers (Castles) and which ones are going to generate money (Cities).

There is a unit pool system which means that you and the AI can't spam one type of unit. This is great because it forces army variation. It also means that you will be more careful with heavy and elite troops, as the unit pool will take longer to fill.

Of course your generals have traits and can go rouge if their loyalty falls too low.

The AI is still dumb, the game gets challengeless late game when you mothball into a giant nation.

This game doesn't run as well as it could on modern hardware, you will get 30+ fps with a relitvly good machine. I have experienced a small amount of crashes.

9/10 would recommend.

A great TW Game, with very good grahics, good campaign map, and many other cool features. Gameplay is easy, and simple, with little experience in other TW games needed, though it does help to have a knowledge of TW games in general when playing *any* Total War game. Diplomacy is greatly improved, giving   the feture of seeing what the proposal's strength is(a HUGE plus, when compared to Empire's rather un-responsive AI Diplo), and the Campaign Map is of excellent quality(obviously not Rome II quality, as i is some years older, but still very good, and very detailed) Battles are great, with a good UI allowing full control of the battlefield, and immersive maps that truly do the game justice. This game has so much untapped potential.
It is currently incomplete, although you can play through the entire campaign and see the ending credits.
The game only ever crashed on me once!
- it is hard to adjust the sound so you can hear the dialog over engine noise etc. There are several sliders, but they are only available from the main menu :(
- The challenge mode boasts tons of unique airplanes with interesting history, but only 95% of the aircraft can be unlocked and many of the 'fun' experimental fighters have really horrible stats when you do play with them.
- The Mirage in the campaign had no special weapons and when I play with it the XP is given to another plane.
- The story is cool enough, but the missions suddenly become very unbalanced when you use realistic missile stats on easy. (I had to cheat to get through 2 of them).
- Mission 1 has two parts, it teleports you halfway but I did not notice, so every time it said "stay with target" I changed course - apparently that ends the mission (it could do with checkpoints!)
- The third camera mode is awesome to look at but impossible to play in. Game could use a replay feature post-mission so you can use awesome camera mode.
- All models are extremely detailed despite the low-res textures on ANGELS etc. Too bad you only ever see it in the editor. Consider making scripted events mid-mission so you get to see close-up footage of the gun-emplacements and tanks at least once in-game.
- Audio Dialog should be normalized - there was one issue of a squad member being VERY loud while the others were almost silent (Good thing it has subtitles!).
- The game lacks dooms-day weaponry. It would be awesome to have at least one aircraft with a laser or swarmer-missiles or scorched-earth-cluster-bomb-of-doom or something.
- Last level is ideal for some underground flight, so open up those hangar doors and put a generator inside.
- Sometimes scripted events cut off dialogs early. Like in mission 11 where I still don't know what Lynx wanted to tell me about the ANGELS.
- There are a lot of abbreviations that never gets explained. Consider adding dialog to explain what CAS, AWACS, RCS etc. is before every NPC starts flingin pilot jargon everywhere.
- The game could do with explanations for special options. E.g. I had no idea what the AOA limiter was until I disabled it and performed a turn so sharp, my aircraft suffered structural damage :D The AOA limiter and the engines_off button could perhaps become usefull if it was not so harmfull. Oh, and I was wondering if disabling the AOA limiter can lead to black-out and red-out. It should.
- The title of the game is vector thrust, but there is no button to enable vector thrust. I suppose it is another 'thing to come' item, but I am disappointed that even VTOL planes do not have any special mode of operation. ... There IS a button for Special Operations "O", but it does not do anything as far as I can tell.
- This game could end up beating both Ace Combat and HAWX, and it is so close - it is just incomplete. I can't wait to see the finished product.
- I read the list of "mutations" in the editor. Now we just need maps that use them, and we'll have even more fun!

I'm so glad they released this for Mac. I remember seeing a let's play of this and thought it looked really fun. Well, it is!

With 800+ hours it's obvious I love X3 and X3AP is my fave of the seires.
X3 is an empire building game more than a space sim, you're objective is to make money and build massive fleets to go rampaging around the galaxy with.
Some tips:
First off grab the bonus pack found under the DLC, along with the turbo boost there's also commercial agent which is one of my fave scripts, it's like adding a mini RPG to the game as your pilots level up and gain new skills.
The auto pillock (auto pilot):
It has issues, after playing the game for a while you get to know when and when not use it, not as bad as it's made out to be just situational (I mostly don't use it).
Game starts:
I recommend the Bankrupt Assassin which is the sandbox start, you have a decent M3 but no money, it will put you staight into the action with M5 pirates chasing you down.
SETA:
SETA starts at a default of 600% go into options and crank it up to 1000% this will make the auto pilot less reliable though I find the better your CPU the more reliable it is. SETA is very handy if you want to use the stock market as you can sit outside the station and speed up time for some easy early game money. The stockmarkets a bit cheesy as it's too easy to make money, plenty of guides online if that's your bag.
Reputation:
Building up reputation with races unlocks higher teir weapons, ships and equipment for that race; though some missions are easier than others. Patrols are best for rep grinds especially if you can pick up station defence missions in the same sector. Military transport missions are also a good early game source of rep and cash, cargo life support is needed (find at pirate bases) and time limits can be tight, I tend to use manual docking until I get a docking computer.
There are missions to avoid such as convoy missions unless you have a decent M6 or better.
There's also racial hatred so killing Boron's in Split sectors will get rep for Split but with loss of rep for the Borons, can be useful when rep isn't high enough for missions.
Boarding:
I love boarding, you can wait and get a missile frigate (50mil) using boarding pods and flail barrage missiles but for a challenge try an M3 and TP combination (recommend Geochen), there's plenty of guides on you tube. It's tough but very rewarding and gets you access to some big ships you could'nt otherwise afford in the early game. This type of boarding is called 'spacewalk' as you dump your marines close to the target and hopefully they make it to the hull alive, salvage insurance (quicksave) invaluable.
Early game targets should be TM and M6 class ships until your marines have levelled up. An M6 that can mount ION Disrupters will make boarding much easier, you get a Centaur as reward doing the Argon story line, it'll come with some marines.
The Hyperion Vanguard, a paranid ship which can't be bought is about the best player ship there is, you'll find it in paranid sectors. If your not ready to board buy an m5 and put it on follow to keep track of it.
Marines:
It's a pain training marines, when buying go for the fighting stat as it can't be trained, they get better at fighting if they survive a boarding mission. Train all in engineering, a couple in mechanical and hacking.
Factories and complexes:
This is where the real money is, setting up a lucrative Bliss place in Teladi territory will fill your coffers in no time but you can't beat well designed complex either for money making or for kitting out your fleet with missiles. Check google for the complex calculator.
OOS:
Out Of Sector plays a big part in X3, basically every sector your not in is OOS and the rules change. OOS combat for instance relies more on shields than weapons so fighters like the Falcon Hauler with 200mj shield fair very well even though they have very little weapon energy.
Docking also becomes instant, telling a freighter to dock and then jumping out the sector and using SETA will speed things up with no risk of your freighter crashing into a station.
Carriers:
Setting up carriers is quite labour intensive, I suggest the Solano M4, good shields and can be bought in bulk (10 at a time) and they can be equiped en mass though Legend Home doesn't provide much in the way of ship equipment.
Setting your fighters into wings and asigning their homebase makes life alot easier.
One of my favorite early game strategies is to head for Yaki space and grab a Chokaro, it holds 3 fighters and good storage space for jump drive energy and missiles for restocking, there also handy for picking up ships that bail.
Plugins:
Plugins, except for the bonus pack, add 'modified' to the game so no achievments but there are some great mods out there. Grab Cycrow's plugin manager and the no-steam.exe.
Check these out:
XRM
Pirate Guild 3

Improved Boarding

Well there, after I saw all the endings I guess it's time to write a review. I recommend this game to people who enjoyed the first Disgaea, Final Fantasy Tactics or any kind of grindy turn-based RPG. The game is a little bit too grindy for my taste, but later games in series make the process more enjoyable (they are yet to be ported though...).
In comparison with the first part of Disgaea series, it looks pretty solid.
Gameplay contains much more features than the first one, which, however, are yet to be polished (in the next games that slowly make their way to PC users). Usage of monsters in your squad is more interesting than before (a pity that the brand-new mechanic starts working only after your first playthrough...)and special abilities make classes truly unique. New specialists are good and amount of skills is great.
However, the gameplay contains some annoying features like (completely luck-based) farming for Treasure Maps to unlock an area with better stuff and, well, basically endgame content. Another one is 'Felony' system, which represent an interesting mechanic and has some entertaining cutscenes, but requires a little but too much effort to provide valuable results (also required to be used to have bad endings).
Plot-wise the game seems slightly inferior to the first game. The plot still contains a nice range of emotions (upbeat/cute/sad), but the scale is more shallow. In my opinion, it references (okay, simply uses) Etna and Laharl, a little bit too agressivly. The main rival, Axel, is rediculed way more than Mid-Boss/Vyers was in the first game and he fails to provide a nice impression, unlike Vyers, even though being mentioned for longer periods time - they needed 'Dark Hero Days' expansion, which allows us to play a story of Axel, to truly show us what a person he is. Endings are abundant, but only the main ending feels complete, while others leave an impression of being cut just after the culmination. The worst ending cuts back and provides some nightmare fuel, something that children of sin deserve <3
Music is still great. That's it, I highly recommend to listen to some heartwarming, cool, encouraging tracks: Cyber Dance, White Tiger, Sparkling (main ending ost), ETONA Rock, some others.
To be honest, I am not a perfectionist/completionist, I don't have enough love for grinding. It slightly spoils the endgame content for me since you just have to earn these sweet 9999 levels, Yosh*tsunas and so on, but I will probably try to complete this one.

What makes a good man? That is what ‘Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel’ asks of you in the last 10 minutes, as the avalanche of betrayals, heartbreak, and madness culminates in the creation of one of the finer video-game villains in the last few years. But, is he really the villain? He certainly believes himself to be the hero of this yarn. I guess, in the end, it is left to the Vault Hunter him or herself to decide upon the matter in a way they them self see fit. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the prequel (and, of course, sequel) to one of the finest shooter games of last generation, and the origin of Handsome Jack.
Getting in to the meat of this look-back on this game, we shall start with game play. If you played Borderlands 2 (or the first Borderlands, for that matter) you already know the gist of how this game works and plays. You shoot enemies, you collect loot, and you kill more enemies. Subsequently, you also get more loot (and so on, and so on…). The Diablo-esque loot system was already refined in BL2, and did not require much in ways of improvement in TPS. The addition of laser-type guns is a fun one, and is a great addition to the stock experience. The beauty of what makes this system work is of course what every player loves-to-hate, RNG. Do you get a purple VLADOF sniper rifle that shoots corrosive bullets, all the while playing Mozart’s ‘Requiem’ in a solemn remembrance for the hundreds you have (and will) kill? Or do you receive a six shooter, which in a true Joker fashion doesn’t even shoot bullets? RNG at its finest.
The general game play, which is pretty much copy-and-paste from BL2, is enhanced by the addition of zero (almost) gravity. Jumping around has never been more delicious, and the fact that you can kill your enemies by butt-slamming on to them is just pure awesomeness. As fun as it is to just jump  up and down, all around, whilst breaking necks and taking names, the addition of platforming proves to be a two-edged sword. Whilst it does give a certain sense of exhilaration, going higher and higher, and exploring the countryside, when you get knocked back by an explosion or a ‘Lunatic’ (TPS’s Psycho) landing right next to you, or (as it happened many times to me) you just accidentally walk off of the edge, yer dead. And it’s back to the last save point for ya! This happened in such a rarity to me in early game that it didn’t prove to be more than an annoyance. But as the game progresses in to the late-game parts, especially in the purple-land-of-go-f***k-yourself, I could swear the developers were playing a practical joke on me.
The moon of Pandora, on which this game unfolds, is called Elpis. And hot-damn! How beautiful it is. As much as I loved BL2, one thing that always annoyed me (which was kind of bad, it being the most important part of it) was the world of Pandora. There just were too many browns, and reds, and just purely dull colors. Elpis, on the other hand, is a lot of…white. White ground, white walls, black sky. But look just over the horizon…and you’ll see some damn awesome backgrounds. The beauty of the space, mixed with all kinds of stuff that comes out of the ground, just makes the view very pleasing to the eye.
But, enough with that chatter. Let us enter the REAL meat of this review (and my favorite part of the whole game): the story, and characters. I personally hold these 4 Vault Hunters (Athena, Nisha, CL4P-TP, and Wilhelm) to be the best VH’s from the past 16. Maybe it’s the fact that we FINALLY get some interaction from them in regards to what happens in the story. Or maybe it’s how awesomely these 4 fit with the story of BL2. (*slight SPOILERS FOR BL2*) If you played BL2, you must remember Wilhelm, the slaughterer of New Haven, and someone, of whom even Angel was afraid of, and Nisha, the iron-fisted ruler and sheriff of Lynchwood, and Handsome Jacks’ girlfriend. They, of course, are one half of the VH quadruplet that saves Elpis. The second half is (oh god…) CL4P-TP (or Claptrap), and Athena. Claptrap you’ll know from the beginning, and entire game, of BL2, who heralds your ability to walk as being “…Handsome Jacks’ downfall!” And Athena actually comes from the first Borderlands, from the DLC ‘General Knoxx’s Secret Armoury’, as well as the EXCELLENT Tell-Tale’s ‘Tales from the Borderlands’ game (which actually happens after TPS).
To complement these excellent VH’s, you have Mad Moxxi (of course), Lilith and Roland, a new character called Janey Spring’s (who actually also appears in ‘Tales...’), and of course, Jack. I do not want to spill anything, but this game made me despise Lilith EVEN MORE than I already did, and made me love and feel sad for Jack (EVEN MORE than I already did).  Let’s just say that Lilith is kind of a (huge) ♥♥♥♥♥, who may have single handedly caused things that happened in BL2 to be as bad as they were. I actually rooted for Jack (duh, he’s one main characters) the entire game, and it this had been a completely ‘choose-your-self’ game, I would not have blinked a single eyelash before joining forces with Jack, and sticking a hot skewer through Lilith’s eye. But, alas, it is a fixed story, and I, playing as Athena, walked away from Jack, saddened that the man who was a Hero, who saved hundreds of people, descended in to madness.
Now, the final thing; the score. I personally loved the game, and I bet anyone who has had even a vested interest in BL2 will love, or like, this game as well. But for someone who is brand new to the franchise, Borderlands 2 is a much better starting point (even so than Borderlands 1). Though I loved the game, the last chapter of the game, which happens as you fight your way to a vault, was one of the most infuriating and skill-demanding levels in any game I have ever played. I, myself, play solo completely, and thus I had no help whatsoever as I faced a wave after wave of some of the most infuriating enemy types and mini-bosses. The level represents, in my honest opinion, a HUGE rise in difficulty. And it will be VERY infuriating. But, once you have finally gotten to the end, you can’t help but smile. ‘The Pre-Sequel’ is a great game, from a now defunct studio, and one that any self-deserving Borderlands fan should experience. 8.5/10

I can not and will not say this game is perfect in any way, shape, or form whatsoever. I'll say it up front, this is a buggy, crash-ridden game with a lot of half-baked content in it. There are a bunch of aircraft in the game you've probably never even heard of, and unlocking them is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥all the way through.
The campaign isn't bad, nothing new or interesting, but not bad. It's like being a regular at a restaurant and ordering something good that you normally get. It doesn't push any bars, but it isn't awful. The only part of it that bugs me is the voice-acting, which needs some work. Everyone sounds disinterested, though the lore of the world itself is pretty interesting from what the campaign tells you.
The gameplay is mostly trial-and-error. Once you learn the controls and spend some time beating the AI that tries so very hard to shoot you down even at lower levels, there's actually some meaning behind the consistent 'heroic'-sounding music that plays 24/7 while you're running down MiGs and bombers with your machine gun. Vector Thrust takes a lot from Ace Combat when it comes to boss encounters, you've got experimental superplanes and flying aerial battleships mixed in with the standard fighter jet fare.
There's also an Editor mode, for those interested in making their own missions. This is what's got me sucked in for the most part. I've spent a fair amount of time on this thing, and still haven't figured out all these fancy commands and functions yet. It's also where I've gotten the most crashes, mostly from trying to make xbox heug scenarios.
Vector Thrust is still a very buggy, buggy mess. I don't personally believe that it should be out of Early Access at the moment, because a lot of people would pick this up and spit on it after about 10 minutes. Unfortunately, I've been sucked in with 50 hours of my life taken from this game way back in Early Access, and honestly have grown quite fond of it despite the flaws. It's not perfect, but it's fun to screw around with if you're a fan of arcade flight sims.
If you're unwilling to spend $25 on a game that still has a long way to go in development, don't go for this. But if you want to appease your inner 'Maverick' and don't mind a game that's still very much a Beta, Vector Thrust is worth a try.

EDIT: THIS IS NOT A PRE-RELEASE REVIEW. Check the date of this review before harassing me.
This game shouldn't have left early access, it feels like it was never finished, and it feels like it never will be.
At least, not anytime soon.
I really wanted to be able to get into this game, but it never happened for various reasons.
When I bought this game, I wasn't expecting a serious flight simulator, I was expecting a game that was going to be similar to Ace Combat's arcade-y feel.
However, I never got that feel. In fact, a lot of the planes feel very awkward and strange, and the story feels completely uninspired, and the music is alright, but it's nothing to write about. I knew the flying mechanics would be different, but the mechanics in this game need a lot more work before they feel like they have enough depth to be a good thing. I personally think there should be more feedback with every action, not just visually, but in the audio, the HUD, in anything. The immersion in the game is also extremely weak, which I personally believe is made worse when players hear the awkward voice acting.
One of the strongest positives about this game ( and perhaps the only one ) is the ability to mod the game and to create your own content.
However, the game is very small, and the modding community is even smaller. That means we will never be able to have intensive modding scenes that other games have, because this game died before it even had life. There are a few mods out there already, but they are nowhere as amazing as they could have been.
This game was developed by like one guy, however, the video game industry is a competitive market. There isn't a moment where we can say 'You get an A for effort.' because in the end, the consumers still need to spend money for the product. I'm hoping that this game somehow gets revived in the future, but it's very unlikely, and I cannot recommend this game unless players are absolutely sure that this is a game that they want to invest in the game as it is.

Overall this is a really entertaining action game where you combine different elements to make spells. It's very zainy and chaotic.
It's also quite hard. If you try to play the campaign by yourself it's almost imposible. The enemies can stun lock you infinite times quite easily and there can be way too many for one person to fight at once. The difficulty does not change based on how many people are playing either.
There's also the fact that you can kill yourself or your allies quite easily, and there are infinite revives. Once you factor all of that, it's very clear this game is designed for multiple players. Why they couldn't adjust the difficulty, I don't know. This is my only complaint.
The rest of the game is awesome. You can pretty much do any kind of magic you can think of. If you're playing with friends, you're sure to have a great time because there will be all kinds of hilarious and chaotic action.
The game in general is also very silly. It breaks the fourth wall quite a lot, has a bunch of funny dialouge and voice acting, and makes a lot of fantasy, sci-fi, and gaming refrences. Not that this is a bad thing, it's what makes the game shine.
So anyway if you want a serious or singleplayer game this is not it, but if you're looking for multiplayer and/or a goofy time this is it.

The sequel to the semi-popular flash game Soundodger on Adult Swim Games, Soundodger+ offers much more in terms of difficulty and replayability.
If you haven't already, check out the original on Adult Swim, here (it has half of the levels, and the same gameplay):
Though it may be easy to jump right to the level editor or auto-gen mode, Soundodger+ is mostly about its single-player experience. There are many edge-of-your-seat moments where focus and concentration are key. This may not be apparent from the first few levels or trailer; the game starts off slow, easing you into the later levels with simplified versions of the patterns; it feels a little too slow moving in, and you need to beat ~10 of these levels before the advanced levels can be played. This is my only real gripe though; the level of polish and love put into the later levels is evident in spades. (Look for advanced levels indicated by a black background.)
The quality of music is also exceptional. If you peruse the Indie section of Steam often, there's a good chance that you'll recognize some of the artists; Disasterpeace, Sonic (also known as Jasper Byrne, who did all of Lone Survivor [music too]), Austin Wintory, Danny Baranowsky, Lifeformed, and Bill Kiley. That's not to say that the others not mentioned are bad; far from it. You may recognize Ghost Kollective, but other names such as Mike Forst, D. WIGHT, Anoctave and Bean proved to be exceptional with the tracks they provided.
Next, the editor. Soundodger+ has plenty of very interesting mechanics; you can slow down and invert time, fill the screen with bullets, and control the movement of the outside "enemies." All of this can be accessed and used in the editor. Though initially appearing dense and convoluted, the editor makes a ton more sense after viewing the available online tutorials, and it can be a blast not only to play finished levels, but also to watch said levels as well. Be warned, Soundodger+ only accepts tracks encoded at 44.1 kHz; I ran into the problem of not being able to use some tracks I wanted to because of this.
Finally, the Auto-Gen mode. I put this at the bottom because it's easily the weakest part of Soundodger+. Levels are typically created on a scale of how loud the music is, similar to Audiosurf. If you don't have loud tracks, you'll end up with a level that's too easy, on the scale of the early campaign levels. The levels generated often don't make sense either; the game creates a pattern only when there's a spike in the noise, causing bullets to fire off at seemingly random times. And again, the Auto-Gen mode only works for songs encoded at 44.1 kHz, same as the editor.
TL;DR: Soundodger+ is highly recommended, especially if you're looking for something in the vein of Bit.Trip, Audiosurf, Sound Shapes or 140. Do not buy for the auto-gen; rather, buy for the single player experience.

Party Hard is a game about starting a murderous rampage because your neighbors had a loud party at 3AM. It sure sounds like a grim premise, but who knew the actual game could be so entertaining?
Just so you get a proper idea of what kind of game this is, here is a list of notable events that happened during my 8 hours (as of this review) with Party Hard:
For the record, this is primarily a stealth game, your main objectives being "kill them all" & "don't get caught", but the game isn't over if you are spotted by a partygoer. You'll just have to run all over the place and hope that your character has the stamina to flee long enough, but evading the cops is doable. FBI on the other hand...now that's a challenge.
And sure, some of the events I described may mention some things that may come off as flaws of the game, but overall I was just having too much fun to care for its imperfections. I just wish it was longer than 6 hours (about 8 hours if you want all the achievements.)
That being said, here are my pros and cons:
+Just enough randomization in the levels on repeat attempts to keep things interesting, without making restarts seem harder than before. Ex. SWAT raid, biker bar brawl, aliens, zombies, etc.
+AI movement patterns are good enough to make you think about how to take out a group of people, while also preventing you from exploiting one cheap way to do so over and over again
+Four unlockable characters (5 total playable) which require different playing strategies, adding replay value in case you want to try replaying levels with their different playstyles
+New mechanics / changes in level design are introduced at a decent rate through the campaign, keeping things fresh. Ex. bouncers, swimming pools, the super short but thoroughly amusing "Party Bus"
+Cheesy but mildly entertaining storyline with some nice looking cutscenes shown each time you complete a level
-Not enough levels in my opinion. A game like this needs more than 12 levels. If a sequel to this is ever made, Steam Workshop support for custom levels would be AMAZING.
-You can get away with some pretty ridiculous things without alerting anybody (horse kills, "natural hazards", food poisoning, throwing people off of rooftops in front of other people's line of sight. Then again, this is a small indie game, so this whole point is probably nitpicking. It's better I at least mention it than leave it unsaid, though.)
If Party Hard looks fun at all to you, get it. You'll most likely enjoy it if the negative points above don't bother you too much. It could be a little bit longer, but this is a full price purchase I don't regret in the slightest.

Soundodger+ é um jogo de perícia cujo objectivo é evitar chocar com as partículas sonoras emitidas pela música que é reproduzida, tarefa que se revela muito mais difícil do que aparenta. A premissa inicial, como deverão estar a pensar, não é extasiante, mas a sua execução é surpreendentemente exemplar, incluindo um editor de níveis muito completo, um gerador automático de partículas para quando queremos escolher uma música da nossa biblioteca e a possibilidade de abrandar o tempo para sobreviver em situações mais sufocantes.
Perante um género em que a música é o motor de todos os processos, fiquei apenas desapontado com a falta de variedade de estilos. Foi obviamente uma decisão consciente já que a música utilizada vai desde a electrónica até à electrónica, independentemente dos subgéneros que engloba dentro desse universo. Apesar de ser uma boa selecção de faixas, gostaria de testar a minha perícia com, por exemplo, música clássica, jazz, rock ou mesmo folk, e sentir que cada género teria a sua própria consequência gráfica e física. Ora, para tipos caretas como eu, o jogo oferece a opção de abrir uma faixa à nossa escolha e jogá-la, o que o valoriza muito. No entanto, o gerador automático de partículas não é eficaz nem interessante o suficiente para executar as nossas faixas, tornando-as muito fáceis e monótonas do ponto de vista da jogabilidade. Em compensação, e para valorizar Soundodger+, o título permite-nos desenvolver os nossos próprios níveis e, aí sim, é possível jogar “As Quatro Estações” de Vivaldi devidamente, mas apenas após uma longa sessão de edição.
Graficamente, o jogo é muito simples mas muito bonito e atraente, constituído por cores vivas e uma aparência muito poligonal. É possível que fiquemos baralhados, zonzos e/ou até deslumbrados com algumas das sequências apresentadas pelos diferentes níveis, os quais, devo dizer, estão maravilhosamente arquitectados.
Mas no fim de contas, Soundodger+ é o jogo mais casual do mundo. O que quero dizer, recorrendo à óbvia hipérbole, é que este é um jogo que pela sua ideia geradora, que não é especialmente iluminada, nunca poderia ser um marco na indústria. No entanto, é um título verdadeiramente bem executado e muito indicado para preencher algumas horas da nossa vida passadas filas de espera, salas de espera e outras situações solitárias ou “tempos mortos” em que não tenhamos sudoku, palavras cruzadas ou literatura disponível.

Long story short. Witcher 2 tries to achieve something original, but unfortunately fails. Every good idea it has is either poorly implemented, countered by a design flaw or your progress is halted by poorly thought out events. It's a mediocre game. The only thing that is up to scratch are the music and sound effects. Everything else you've already seen, wouldn't care to see or will ruin your time. It has some moments that seem important to the overall story of Geralt and the series, which is a shame, because the story of the game itself is trotting rather slow and a lot of the details are rather obscure. The story has a bad tendency of giving you a collection of information that doesn't really fit well as a whole, only to have one of the characters conviniently tell you what is going on in short and sporadic bursts during conversation. It heavily utilizes info dumps. It is trying to be complicated and mature, have a solution to every problem, portray an epic journey a la Fellowship of the Ring, come up with a lot of complex issues, but in the end it comes across as a mess...
Without a doubt, though, the abundant backtracking is this game most horrendous sin. It's just like death from a thousand paper cuts. MMOmisms don't belong in a single player game. For ♥♥♥♥'s sake...if it didn't have that, it would be recommendable, in spite of everything said so far.
Edit: A small update. One very good thing I came across in Witcher 2 are the moments when it is not taking itself so seriously. There are parts in the game where characters will shortly parade with the situation they are in, almost as if to mock themsleves. Immagine my reaction when I was contemplating how Tolkienesque the world and events of W2 look, when, no sooner, the characters themselves started joking about finding one of the rings of power. At that point Geralt quipped that before he knows it, he will be striding up the side of a volcano. Much appreciated!
Unfortunately these are far too few. Too much time spent with the game's horrid mechanics after that.
Edit 2: Combat.
In the first Witcher you were able to charge in, swords blazing and use AoE technique and it was getting the job done. Instead, when you swing your sword, you will be treated to a very theatrical display as Geralt is spinning around like a balerine with a rotating top syndrome, mostly hitting one enemy. Every offensive action you do has a dead window both before and after said action, during which you will be unable to roll away/move/escape/parry. Remember this if you want to play this game. It is not something that is annoying, more like something that extends the time you spend in combat. You will also need to learn to watch out for any non-passable terrain, as even the smallest pebble/root/box/ect. will stop your movement. Geralt will be running and rolling on the ground but remain on one and the same spot. Again, it is not a big game breaker, but definitely a thing to watch out for. Whether fighting enemies in the open or in closed quarters, it does not matter in the end, as they are equally stupid and generally reluctant to charge outside of boss battles. Generally, combat is nothing spectacular in Witcher 2, but it also does not stand significantly in your way. I suppose it was meant to be more tactical, but you can literally spam your craftable consumables, some of which--AoE granades, and those are the quickest way to move through any non-boss encounter. Execution sequences are done one on one without the rest of the mobs interfering, which is nice. Boss battles are more varied, with quick time events and tricks up their sleeves. You will need to pay close attention to your screen, though, as the quick-time event indicator is tiny.
Edit 3:Grasphics.
The game looks possitively good. Much better than Skyrim for sure(every occassion I get to bash on Bethesda is welcomed). It has got optimization issues, unfortunately, and it even crashed on me already. Nothing game-breaking, though. Other titles with better looking graphics produce more fps than Witcher 2. Texture quality is good for its time but has aged. Geralt and all of his armour sets and swords look very detailed and realistic and this time around he is even able to show emotion with facial expressions, as limited as they come. There is a huge and constant asset reuse as the models for the NPCs are limited. Triss' face, for instance, is every other human female's face. The architecture you encounter is very athmospheric and genuine. It is also much more varied than the previous title. You will see some very nice medieval places. If you pump up everything to max the game will glare too much and you may want to keep a few settings lower because it ends up not looking that good for the gas it requires from your machine. The game has got a lot of colour but looks best when you deal with darker environments, as the light reveals low res textures and an unpleasant grainy effect, which I cannot switch off. There are a few spots with creepy mist on an uneven ground, with plants here and there, among giants trees. That particular setting looks fantastic when not in daylight. That said, it may become repetitive as you will need to back-track quite a few times.

My verdict: Most engaging Racing Sim I've played
If you have a wheel or itching for a reason to buy one, get this sim. You'll have fun. Its not about stock cars: there's about 20 other types!! For multiplayer experiences, I can't really comment just yet as that has many other qualities to consider beyond the sim itself. So how does this sim stack up by itself?
First, this sim's force feed back is very good (logitech G920 here) and a real factor into contributing to this being the most immersive experience of any sim I've played: you'll be sweating and busy as you'd be in a real race car. It's not a casual affair. Also if I compare this sim to Dirt Rally, Assetto Corsa, rFactor2, ... this one stands out in that it makes me smile (bit more on that later).
With the physics, everything seems to makes sense.. sliding off on dirtier parts of the track, lift off leading to spins.. bit by bit I found myself learning, adjusting and driving faster. It was a challenge to drive consistenly fast and crash free for 20-30 minutes, and so the feel of achievement is just great when crossing the finish line. Luckily this is not because the game is harsh or anything. That all combined with the competent AI is I think why overall experience of racing in this sim is so good.. and FUN really. I can't help but feel that a certain thing of Brazil is showing through .. a certain something that others just lack...
AI - Good and certainly the most enjoyable I've experienced. The AI is cheecky and may nudge you, it jumps in gaps, it respects racing lines decently but also doesn't drone around in one long line up. Overtaking is very rewarding.
Graphics - Less than for example Asseto Corsa but easily good enough to not break the spell. My GTX970 runs 3440x1440@60Hz pretty smoothly (Maxxed but 14 cars, x2 AA, shadows high, 4xAni).
Sound - Great. Just watch/listen to the videos! Works in 'hearing' the distance to others.
Realism - Not a race driver, but weight transfer, weight, tweaks, grip all seem to be realistic.
Gameplay - Great fun. Find a car and track(s) that gels with you, tweak the AI to be a good challenge and start a 15 minute race. The rolling start works well. Default setups are very workable.
Content - Most complete sim out of the box. Plus many community tracks / mods if you're looking for a track you may want that is not in the game. Wide range of cars and car types, many South American tracks and tracks you won't find in other sims.
GUI - Slightly confusing at start, not perfect but easy to get around once you get used to it.
**9.8/10** Highly Recommended for anyone that is not looking for an arcade 'sims'. Great value.

Verdict: Not for me.
Steam refused to install this game. To get it running I had to consult the internet. I read a thread where someone was berated for trying to play this game without having the previous (unrelated) game installed-- why would you expect that to work?
To my naive senses. this game is exactly the same as the others. The introduction was nonsense (I gather a terrorist cosplayer set off a war? Maybe). Gameplay was tedious and slow. Plot was non-existent. I was glad when it was over.
I'm reminded of a Douglas Adams quote I read long ago and can't quite remember the details for. If I recall correctly, the BBC had created a fan-site/forum for HHGTTG, and then promptly forgotten about it. The forum was used religiously by a small group of people for 10-15 years. When Adams discovered this later he claimed it was like "You left food in your refrigerator so long that it developed sentience, and a little civilization evolved in your icebox. One day you pull open the drawer, and the inhabitants thank you and ask you to please close the drawer again, they liked things just the way they were."
Somebody loves these games dearly. They've evolved their own genre that is the pinnacle of their gaming experience. To the rest of us, it tastes like moldy cheese.

You live in a world, which is ruled by Overlord Zenon, a demon who cursed all inhabitants to become demons and slowly succumb to madness - you play as Adell, the only person not affected by the curse and you are looking to stop his family and all the people he knew from becoming monsters, by slaying Zenon.
In contrast to this grim story, the game doesn't take itself seriously at all. With goofy monsters and characters, you find yourself grinning at the absurd take of theirs on this rather dark setting.
In many ways this game feels like a typical strategy-jrpg, but it brings many new ideas to the mix.
You build up your party by purchasing and by unlocking characters, the many classes that exist all specialize in different types of combat.
The stages of the game are made up of squares which can be occupied by characters. This system is used for the positioning of characters, to manage their range etc., this is quite normal in these kinds of games. What is special in Disgaea, is the addition of different heights on the map, and whilst this adds an interesting new dynamic to the movement and placement of your units, it's often enough quite frustrating, for many times you cannot see certain areas properly.
There are different weapon and attack types and those, in addition to the positioning of your characters are basically what you have to manage throughout the game, to preserve as much health and items as you possibly can and kill hordes of corrupted demons.
Due to the lack of permadeath in this game, most story missions feel quite easy - you can just revive all lost characters inbetween each mission. This takes away that feeling of risk and challenge that these games thrive off, at least in the first few chapters.
In a different mode, which is used to improve your items, you enter the so-called item world. Here, you aren't granted respite after each stage, but you will have to efficiently manage your characters and items to push on as far as you can and gain as much as possible. This mode is the most challenging and feels the most rewarding.
A key element in this game is the grinding, for higher levels and better items, and whilst the idea of grinding sounds stale in general, Disgaea does an amazing job at giving it value and making it feel rewarding, so that it doesn't lose its charm.
+Many interesting units
+Interesting story/Goofy characters
+Strategically challenging combat
+Gameplay that doesn't get stale
-Story missions very easy in the beginning
-Stages often confusing to overlook

Then welcome to Disgaea. It's a treasured console series from the PS2, PSP, PS3, and Vita days. The "Master Race" is indeed a very deprived race... this games over 10 years old and it just came out in 2017 on PC. WTF?
Disgaea 2 PC is a strategy RPG, with countless hours of fun, grinding, hundreds of items, armor, weapons, and about "200" unit classes... supposedly. It's kinda like chess... after a few grams of mushrooms... for geeks.
The combo's, spells, and basic attacks are all amazingly BRUTAL looking. When you see an anime girl throw a penguin up in the air and kick him in the sack, then she squeels in ecstasty... it's at that moment you'll realize this was the best money you ever spent.
It runs on any potato, smart-phone, or laptop smooth as butter... and put away that keyboard and mouse Dood!! This game requires a controller to operate it at full speed and nostalgia. Although if the controller still baffles you after it's invention in the 1970's, you can use a KB/M. NIS did an upstanding job of giving Disgaea the HD treatment. It looks as good as can be expected in 1080p considering the games age.
Don't expect top of the line graphics though! Those boobies are pixelated and you know you love it! The sprite animations are in a league of their own. The music sounds like it came from a PSP (and it did), but it's catchy and well done. The menu system is quick and inuitive. The RPG elements and statisics analyzing will melt your brain. Long story short... if you're looking for your SRPG fix, and you missed Disgaea back on PS2 because you were tea-bagging bad kids in Halo 2, or dungeon crawling in Diablo 2... now's your chance. Strategy RPG's are a dying genre with only Disagea and Fire Emblem still active as franchises.

The X series of games is certainly not for everyone, and if you look for flaws in this arguably best of the bunch, there's plenty to be found. The menus are endlessly convoluted, the default key config begs customization, advanced features are hidden in separate scripts that you have to find first. Sound design is inconsistent, comm portraits look laughably outdated, and sometimes the auto pilot will just decide to kill you by running into a nearby station, potentially taking hours of progress with it.
So why even play this?
The game is just that absorbing and consistently entertaining. You get a real sense of accomplishment after every little milestone - start as some deadbeat down on his luck in a cranky vessel, and work your way up the food chain until you find yourself baseballing away smaller spacecraft with your warship that looks like a giant metal dong.
Everything is forgiven.
See your employees breeze by on your travels as they expand your gargantuan accumulation of cash into even more absurd numbers which you can then blow on even bigger ships, your own illegal drug farms, or go wreck entire sectors just for some sick fun. Sky's the limit, and you're well past that border.
Plus, despite this game being years old, and a polarizing sequel out, the devs are still fixing bugs! Even adding content sometimes! Kudos for these guys.
If you like games with depth and don't mind investing a little effort into your games, and if you have patience, this is
game to get. Or, just play Dwarf Fortress I guess.

What makes a good man? That is what ‘Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel’ asks of you in the last 10 minutes, as the avalanche of betrayals, heartbreak, and madness culminates in the creation of one of the finer video-game villains in the last few years. But, is he really the villain? He certainly believes himself to be the hero of this yarn. I guess, in the end, it is left to the Vault Hunter him or herself to decide upon the matter in a way they them self see fit. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the prequel (and, of course, sequel) to one of the finest shooter games of last generation, and the origin of Handsome Jack.
Getting in to the meat of this look-back on this game, we shall start with game play. If you played Borderlands 2 (or the first Borderlands, for that matter) you already know the gist of how this game works and plays. You shoot enemies, you collect loot, and you kill more enemies. Subsequently, you also get more loot (and so on, and so on…). The Diablo-esque loot system was already refined in BL2, and did not require much in ways of improvement in TPS. The addition of laser-type guns is a fun one, and is a great addition to the stock experience. The beauty of what makes this system work is of course what every player loves-to-hate, RNG. Do you get a purple VLADOF sniper rifle that shoots corrosive bullets, all the while playing Mozart’s ‘Requiem’ in a solemn remembrance for the hundreds you have (and will) kill? Or do you receive a six shooter, which in a true Joker fashion doesn’t even shoot bullets? RNG at its finest.
The general game play, which is pretty much copy-and-paste from BL2, is enhanced by the addition of zero (almost) gravity. Jumping around has never been more delicious, and the fact that you can kill your enemies by butt-slamming on to them is just pure awesomeness. As fun as it is to just jump  up and down, all around, whilst breaking necks and taking names, the addition of platforming proves to be a two-edged sword. Whilst it does give a certain sense of exhilaration, going higher and higher, and exploring the countryside, when you get knocked back by an explosion or a ‘Lunatic’ (TPS’s Psycho) landing right next to you, or (as it happened many times to me) you just accidentally walk off of the edge, yer dead. And it’s back to the last save point for ya! This happened in such a rarity to me in early game that it didn’t prove to be more than an annoyance. But as the game progresses in to the late-game parts, especially in the purple-land-of-go-f***k-yourself, I could swear the developers were playing a practical joke on me.
The moon of Pandora, on which this game unfolds, is called Elpis. And hot-damn! How beautiful it is. As much as I loved BL2, one thing that always annoyed me (which was kind of bad, it being the most important part of it) was the world of Pandora. There just were too many browns, and reds, and just purely dull colors. Elpis, on the other hand, is a lot of…white. White ground, white walls, black sky. But look just over the horizon…and you’ll see some damn awesome backgrounds. The beauty of the space, mixed with all kinds of stuff that comes out of the ground, just makes the view very pleasing to the eye.
But, enough with that chatter. Let us enter the REAL meat of this review (and my favorite part of the whole game): the story, and characters. I personally hold these 4 Vault Hunters (Athena, Nisha, CL4P-TP, and Wilhelm) to be the best VH’s from the past 16. Maybe it’s the fact that we FINALLY get some interaction from them in regards to what happens in the story. Or maybe it’s how awesomely these 4 fit with the story of BL2. (*slight SPOILERS FOR BL2*) If you played BL2, you must remember Wilhelm, the slaughterer of New Haven, and someone, of whom even Angel was afraid of, and Nisha, the iron-fisted ruler and sheriff of Lynchwood, and Handsome Jacks’ girlfriend. They, of course, are one half of the VH quadruplet that saves Elpis. The second half is (oh god…) CL4P-TP (or Claptrap), and Athena. Claptrap you’ll know from the beginning, and entire game, of BL2, who heralds your ability to walk as being “…Handsome Jacks’ downfall!” And Athena actually comes from the first Borderlands, from the DLC ‘General Knoxx’s Secret Armoury’, as well as the EXCELLENT Tell-Tale’s ‘Tales from the Borderlands’ game (which actually happens after TPS).
To complement these excellent VH’s, you have Mad Moxxi (of course), Lilith and Roland, a new character called Janey Spring’s (who actually also appears in ‘Tales...’), and of course, Jack. I do not want to spill anything, but this game made me despise Lilith EVEN MORE than I already did, and made me love and feel sad for Jack (EVEN MORE than I already did).  Let’s just say that Lilith is kind of a (huge) ♥♥♥♥♥, who may have single handedly caused things that happened in BL2 to be as bad as they were. I actually rooted for Jack (duh, he’s one main characters) the entire game, and it this had been a completely ‘choose-your-self’ game, I would not have blinked a single eyelash before joining forces with Jack, and sticking a hot skewer through Lilith’s eye. But, alas, it is a fixed story, and I, playing as Athena, walked away from Jack, saddened that the man who was a Hero, who saved hundreds of people, descended in to madness.
Now, the final thing; the score. I personally loved the game, and I bet anyone who has had even a vested interest in BL2 will love, or like, this game as well. But for someone who is brand new to the franchise, Borderlands 2 is a much better starting point (even so than Borderlands 1). Though I loved the game, the last chapter of the game, which happens as you fight your way to a vault, was one of the most infuriating and skill-demanding levels in any game I have ever played. I, myself, play solo completely, and thus I had no help whatsoever as I faced a wave after wave of some of the most infuriating enemy types and mini-bosses. The level represents, in my honest opinion, a HUGE rise in difficulty. And it will be VERY infuriating. But, once you have finally gotten to the end, you can’t help but smile. ‘The Pre-Sequel’ is a great game, from a now defunct studio, and one that any self-deserving Borderlands fan should experience. 8.5/10

Discaimer: I only have 30 minutes of gameplay logged at this review, but I looked through a lot of the functionality to make sure the game meets all of the expected functions I want from a game. I also did about 20 minutes of skirmish gameplay to see how the general look-and-feel handled.
Pros:
- This isn't a HARDCORE simulator that you need a joystick and pedals and TrackIR and hundreds of other $$$ for.
- This uses modern aircraft rather than WWII aircraft, which at this point is a dead horse beaten for years that I've never had a liking for personally. (Sorry; pet peeve)
- The game lets you jump straight into a generated skirmish game or into a scenario for basic practice and quick fun.
- Mission Editor~! (Haven't personally tried the editor yet, but at least it's included)
- Actually WORKS with mouse+keyboard, AS WELL as with a joystick (the latter of the two I don't have at my current location, so that was an assumption) (This is another pet peave about aircraft games: I know aircraft are flown with a stick, and playing with one is part of the experience, but some of us aircraft fans can't pack a joystick in our only backpack during frequent real-life flights between living areas!)
- Did I mention that this isn't a WWII frenzy? (Again, sorry, pet peeve)
- LOTS of planes, from what I've seen in other reviews (haven't unlocked any myself)
- Very casual and easy-to-access fun and action
- Not a AAA quantity of gameplay variety, but what this game has, it does VERY well!
Cons:
- Cockpit camera doesn't have as much flexibility as external cam does, which gives external cam an advantage
- Not a HARDCORE sim, cause I know a lot of aircraft enthusiasts (like me) are all about that sort of thing
- Not a WWII game (which is fantastic for me, but given the popularity of WWII games, I'm sure a lot of you will be dissapointed)
- Others report bugs, but I've encountered only one and could fix it myself uses help from the Web
- Your game controls are still in effect when you're typing into number value boxes. For example, if BACKSPACE does a menu function, then pressing BACKSPACE while editing a number will do that function, likely interrupting your typing. (I assume this may be fixed in the future.)
Overall:
This isn't a game for everybody. However, if you're not looking for a DCS-like simulator, and if you're sick of nothing but WWII vehicular combat games everywhere, this is probably perfect. Remember that this was made by a lone developer, so don't be looking for AAA perfection.
