Yoko Taro's approach to storytelling is like increasing the temperature of a hot tub by 1 degree at a time. You won't notice the difference until you look down after 30 hours and realize you're in a pool of lava. Only then will you realize you actually prefer lava.
Each Drakengard game starts with a simple and relatable premise: Man and dragon fight evil empire. Father wants to find a cure for his sick daughter. And NieR: Automata, at its surface level, is about androids battling machine-servants of aliens while humanity takes refuge on the moon. If it sounds like your typical JRPG sci-fi story, congratulations: You've fallen into Taro's trap.
To call the events of the game a mindf**k is both accurate and a disservice. It implies a lack of meaning or direction, when in reality you're given everything you need in order to understand the story; it just might not come in the order you like. Not only is the main story an enigma that leaves you hungry for more details, but even the sidequests add important context to the events of the story, as well as having some seriously strong foreshadowing that you'll likely miss until you're thinking in retrospect. And that's the real beauty of a Taro story: it keeps you occupied for weeks after you finish the game as you slowly stumble upon epiphanies, information the game gave you clear as day but that your brain failed to piece together until it was too late. After several of these moments you'll come to not only love the game, but respect the writers as intellectual superiors that played you like a damn fiddle while, somehow, respecting your intelligence at the same time.
If you've played a JRPG in the past, you know that there is often a trifecta of qualities and you have to pick two and only two: graphics, gameplay, and story. If a game has great graphics and gameplay, it usually has a bad story (Bayonetta, DMC, etc.). If it has a fantastic story, it usually either has bad gameplay or bad graphics (Xenoblade). The pattern so far for Drakengard has been good story, decent gameplay, and bad graphics. However, they've teamed up with Platinum Games this time, who's known for great gameplay, good graphics, and bad story. Combined, they've managed to cover each other's flaws beautifully. This game is a treat to look at, the gameplay is fun as hell, and the story is some of Taro's best work yet.
I can't remember the last time I had so few complaints about a game, and I'm an incredibly harsh critic of games (especially ones that I love). Throughout NieR: Automata, I kept thinking "what's the catch?" There has to be a really terrible part coming up soon, right? No game goes this long without any glaring issues. That point never came, though.
If you've never played Drakengard, you'll probably still have a great time with this game. If you've played most of the series up to this point, it's a masterpiece.

Few games are quite as influential or prolific as Ion Storm's Deus Ex. Taking cues from Quake, Thief and System Shock 2, Deus Ex was a genre-bending masterpiece whose influence can be seen far and wide. While the graphics were never groundbreaking for 2000, and the voice actors sound like they were hired off of the street, the gameplay and story are where this game truly shines.
Deus Ex is an RPG/FPS/stealth game hybrid, and there are multiple solutions to every scenario in the game. You wanna be John Rambo and shoot the whole place up? Go right ahead. Or do you prefer to get your Solid Snake on and sneak to your objective? You can do that too. The RPG elements are also really deep, and you're given a lot of flexibility and choice with how you want to customize your character (just don't invest any points into the Swimming skill; it's useless).
Choice also factors into the game's fantastic story. This is one of those games you'll want to replay just to see what happens with every dialogue choice and moral decision. It's a riveting sci-fi tale rife with espionage, suspense and plenty of cyberpunk style. If you like Metal Gear Solid, Ghost In The Shell or Blade Runner, or even if you just like reading Illuminati conspiracies on the internet, then this story will pull you in. There's a reason why this game has made so many "Best of All Time" lists and become the subject of many internet memes- it's just that good. Believe the hype and buy it now.

The rotting horse has been beaten to a pulp with what has already been said, written, and discussed about this game with regards to its oft-touted status as the metaphorical pick axe of truly groundbreaking work. It has the kind of prestige that allows it to appear on "greatest ever" lists with a consistency that would make any old man suffering from constipation jealous. This original iteration of Deus Ex is the stuff of industry legend, and after playing it nearly all the way through, it doesn't take me wearing this thick pair of glasses to see why.
Today, the game manages to mix choice, action, RPG elements, and grand storytelling together in a way that still feels fresh, avoiding the Seinfeld effect masterfully. Many games since its inception have tried to emulate it, but there is something natural about the way the game plays that simply feels right, and it easily held my attention for hours on end, despite clunky controls and ugly graphics. Your most minute choices in the game actually matter, and the world within the game adjusts to how you choose to play. Walk into the women's bathroom? Expect to be berated by your boss. Kill off that innocent NPC? You better believe that someone somewhere is gonna give you $#!+ for it.
Moreover, the game also grants choices in ones progression towards completing any given goal. You can choose to walk openly through a hallway and fight off enemies, or go through the air ducts instead and come out unscathed. Either way is equally effective, and it is these kinds of choices that further cement the organic play through of Deus Ex. I know very well that games have been doing these kinds of things for years, and yet, there is something about the way DE presents it and runs with it that makes it feel, as I stated before, natural.
Some may find challenge with the game's age, but I really do believe that if you stick with it (save often!), you'll find it to be an incredibly rewarding experience.
Greatest ever, indeed.

It's a fun first person shooter that you can get for a mere 99 cents.
It can be played Player vs. Player or 5 player Co-op -- I think Co-op is more fun so that's what my review will focus on.
There are three different classes to choose from each with unique skills and weapons. As you kill enemies you gain class-specific levels which provide more options for your character.
Your basic goal in Co-op is to survive waves of dinosaurs that attack your generator. You'll have a variety of high tech weapons and vehicles to help you out, everything from laser guns to hovercraft to futuristc mechs to flamethrower turrets. There are all kinds of dinos, everything from huge Triceratops that can charge to Raptors that attack in packs.
Why are primitive dinosaurs attacking your high tech forces? Who knows! Who cares! It's fun!!!
Fun stuff that I've seen happen:
I'm driving around in a jeep with two friends. I'm gettings roadkills, my friends are shooting dinos left and right. I try to ram a giant dino, only for the giant dino to toss our jeep up into the air. The jeep is smashed, all three of us die, I get an achievement, "Teammate from Hell: Drive a vehicle full of buddies to their deaths." We all can't stop laughing.
Or, I see a teammate get grabbed by a Rham (flying dino) as I try to come to the rescue I'm swallowed whole by a giant alligator. Another teammate in a tank comes to the rescue. Hilarious!
The game takes itself seriously but the whole premise (high tech infantry versus low tech dinosaurs) is so ludicrous it creates an amusing dichotomy.
The game does have flaws. We had some glitches where a player got stuck inside the terrain (and had to rejoin the game). There's also some collision detection issues (my massive mech can't walk through a tiny tree branch? Really?). But overall there's about 10-20 hours worth of fun gameplay here which is a steal for only 99 cents.
Only one thing in this game is certain: every other spell you cast will always be a revive.

Party Hard is a 2d pixel top down Slasher game, where you use stealth and guile to complete your mission. The music is decent, but a lot of the songs sounded similar.
Gameplay;
There is a sense of progression, as new characters and options open up to you as you  forge through the game. The game is fairly simplistic, and uses a point system. This would have been ideal to have a leader-board, but unfortunately you can only compete with yourself. Your character attempts to navigate a map and kill all of the party-goers
without being seen. You are able to sneak around and hide bodies, but the stealth aspect is hampered by a lack of places for the character to hide, such as in the shadows or in  a closet. Killings are done on a line of sight basis, which can be interesting, as you are able to pin killings on others if they are the first seen by the body. Stealth becomes
more of a puzzle strategy, in figuring out how to kill everyone without getting caught.
Story;
The story is told in a third person manner, listening to a cop talk about the killings. Overall I enjoyed the story, and wanted to find out what was going to happen. The story gives the game a cops and robbers feel, which makes the conquest of completing levels even more sweet.
Summary;
The game is not perfect, it does have its' suspension of disbelief issues, such as the zombies that run around and need to be killed, but the cops don't attack them. It is a  basic hide and seek game, with a line of sight kill mechanic and a puzzle feel, rather than a pure stealth game or slasher. The gameplay was decent, however, and though it could be rather repetitive, I enjoyed it well enough. I can recommend this game, though just barely...

Considering all my experiences with Daedalic Entertainment so far, I tend to hold a middle ground in my judgements. The game is either perfect - like
- or consists of a perfect idea ruined in rushed display - like
. On a 50-50 gamble, I took my chance and I'm happy to declare that
went to snatch itself a place among the perfect ones.
Meet Jeremiah Hazelnut, a young boy who lives in a forest hut with his mother, and it's the last two days of his summer vacation. Young Jerry ventures out to the forest to find himself an adventure before dinner, and ends up meeting a strange rabbit named Marquis de Hoto who offers Jerry the great opportunity to become a wizard's apprentice! Marquis promises Jerry that he'll be home before dinner, and takes him to the village of Mousewood, where he'll be trained in the art of arts: magic! As Jerry proudly declares:
Before getting into gameplay, I'd like to take a moment to talk about the atmosphere of the game. The whole setting is already captivating with beautiful 2D art backgrounds, enchanting soundtrack and loveable characters as if they are taken out of a beloved children's book. Aside the trademark folklore themes of mainland Europe, numerous other mythologies are carefully wrapped up into a well-balanced setting of its own in this wondrous little tale. Character depth and storytelling are marvelous, voice acting is stunning and dialogue interactions vary between conjuring a warm smile on your face and inviting you to sudden striking realizations on human nature. Don't let the cute setting fool you; I took a pause to consider the wisdom behind an unexpected remark made in game more than once.
For the gameplay: it is a bit more than your casual point and click adventure. For the most part of the game, you are presented with a townful of people and places to explore, and also a handful of side stories and/or quests to accomplish aside the main scenario with card rewards. Item combinations are imaginative, yet not obscure at all. With some observation, it is possible to go through the whole game. Through his adventures, Jerry will learn some spells that will enrich the gameplay and present you new options of exploration; like talking to statues, growing plants in mere seconds, changing shape... and even make impossible, possible!
One of my favorite parts in the game is that you are encouraged to collect some mysterious cards in your explorations which you can use to play a card game named Quartets with the town's inhabitants. It is a lovely mini game that takes some attention and an exercise of memory. The game also contains some collectibles for you to look for - like stickers, dew drops and stories told by a mysterious woodspirit. They are not a must, but collecting them reveals some side lore to the game that you may enjoy very much. Every detail is carefully placed to make a whole masterfully. There is a variety of things to do in this game which offers at least 10 hours of gameplay roughly.
As a final word, when I chose to play
, I wasn't expecting this kind of quality in setting, story, narration or gameplay. This is a wonderful and imaginative tale that I'll remember for a long time. Jerry's tale might have ended here, but I wonder if Mousewood or Marquis made their last appearances... I wish not.

Finally figured out that the background art in the main menu is what selects the car class. Hit the little arrow on the side until it says "all cars / all tracks" and then play whatever you like.
I immediately hopped into a Formula Vee and was impressed at the driving experience. You *must* heel-toe downshift or else the clutch will drag and you spin. You *must* be progressive on the brakes or the wheels lock and you spin. I never thought I could have so much fun driving a sim (this is my first "real" driving sim). The sounds and graphics aren't nearly so old as people make them out to be.
I'm playing with a Track IR 5 and Logitech G25 at 3440x1440 ultrawide and absolutely loving it. The next update will enhance the graphics shaders and add some new content as well. The community is super friendly and the devs are very helpful.
If you want to drive the latest unobtainable Ferrari via chase cam at the Nurburgring, look elsewhere. If you want to experience high fidelity sim driving, this is the absolute best bang for your buck.

The children's story of Jerry Hazelnut and the Maquis De Hoto is just "wow"... The creativity is just amazing and it makes for such an enjoyable game... Especially with the hint of the Ninja shadow bunny planeswalker!!! So cool. Definitely a thumbs up.
Note : I had to complete the game with a walkthrough. The hints were really lousy.
PROS
1. Story
So interesting. It's great to see all the little details in the story slowly get unravelled as the game progresses. The blurred overlap between a boy who is dreaming up his own imagination and a real fantasy world is fantastic.
2. Artwork
Fantastic. The details of Mousewood are so intriguing. The level of creativity is something amazing.
3. Secrets
Dewdrops. Need I say more?
4. Card Game
Very cool. It's nice to know that there's another game designed within a game. It's the hallmark of the good game to have mini-games within the main game. E.g. Final Fantasy series. Do note that The Night The Rabbit is a simple game of Go Fish.
5. Credit Ending
Nice to see that there was so much more. I won't spoilt the ending but there's a lot more to do. It's much better than the standard boring credit roll. I must admit that I didn't really pay attention to who's who in the credits though.
CONS
1. Frog Clicker
Very tedious method of travelling. Can't you just blow on the horn to call Plato, the frog.
2. Spells
Not really useful except in specific circumstances. I was hoping for the spells to interact more. E.g. Stone Whispering spell was good as you could use it on all the statues, Green Growth and Fox's Cunning were a little too limited.
3. Items
Way too limited to be used only for specific locations. It would be great to use them on non-quest objects and Jerry would tell you if it was not important.
4. Hints
You need better ones.

A sim racing game about a race series that I never heard of. How well does this game turns out? It's fantastic.
As I said before, I never heard of the Stock Car Extreme (SCE), let alone the Brazilian Stock Car series. But don't let the title fool you - this game gives a plethora of race cars to choose from. I found this game through a sim racing youtuber, which praised this game quite a lot. I'm curious and decided to give it a go, and how! What a wonderful racing simulation game it is. Prior to this, I have only played old - but trusted - sim racing games such as GTR 2, rFactor (old one), Richard Burns Rally, and Race series from Simbin. I can say that this game belongs up there with the sim racing greats. Granted, I never really played any of the more modern sim racing titles such as iRacing, rFactor 2, Assetto Corsa, or Project CARS, but I'm going to get there someday - and this game is the start. Hopefully they wouldn't disappoint me with their much higher price tag!
What I can say from this game is it feels really immersive, at least with the cars I've tried. I currently only have driven the stock cars and several of the formula cars. My trustworthy Logitech Momo Racing still gives a very good force feedback, the sound of the cars are impressive, and the handling of the cars are very good - it's not overly hard to drive, but it is much harder to go fast. It's a bit forgiving, actually, but it's still a heck load of fun. The only down side is probably the graphics - it's definitely not as impressive as the previously stated titles, but I don't really care about the graphics anyway. I'm here for the handling physics, the racing - not for how beautiful the game looks. It's probably just me being biased for not having an impressive computer set up, though.
Overall, this game is a blast - it's my first game here in Steam, and this game also introduced me to the online sim racing community in my country. Absolutely, positively, a highly recommended game for sim racers out there. Whether you just want to try out how it is to be a sim racer, or for the old time sim racer - this game is for you! I can't give it a higher score for what it did with the price. Thumbs up!

English:
After 108 hours I finally 100% completed The Binding of Isaac + Wrath of the Lamb expansion (all 84 achievements).
The amount of hours you can put into it until you don't have nothing else to do is simply incredible given the price you can pay for the pack with the game and expansion (0.99 on a sale).
If you never played the game before expect to finish it completely in 150-200+ hours (depending on your skill in this kind of game).
For new players the game will probably be kinda difficult and even more with the expansion content so i would recommend playing without it installed (under DLC tab in game properties) at least until you have unlocked It Lives or beaten Sheol once.
After that you'll be able to handle most of the new enemies and bosses, and you will appreciate the addition of trinkets and new items.
There are several drawbacks with the expansion. Mostly glitches that it introduces such as enemies glitching through some corners, not properly working Brimstone controls, etc. but with all the new game elements you can easily forget about this.
PS. Gorgeous soundtrack if you don't know it yet.

Bad game developers now adays are looking to cash in on Genre buyers and decided to make their own survival crafting game. It is nothing but an exploitation of what is popular now and
This one is isometric 3rd person with quadrant north south east west camera directions ONLY. The first thing you will notice, is that the pick up button is the same as the attack button. You're friends will be happy with you. The second thing you will notice, is that when you die, all of your upgraded crafting tables are destroyed as well as half of you items. They really thought little to none about the genre and it seems they didn't take the time to put in the well developed essentials that others in the genre have. You can upgrade more storage in time but it will take hours and hours of mining wood and it just doesn't feel like you ever accomplish anything in this game. When I first saw that this game was coming for the PC, I was extremely excited. After putting in over 250 hours in the first game (I had it on the Nintendo DS an told myself i would buy Disgaea2 when I finished it) I never got sick of it. This game is highly addictive, beautiful music, beautiful graphics, and mechanics/control intuition that surpass every tactical RPG I have ever played.
Disgaea 2 expands on the item world, the Dark Assembly, and character selection. Even at the beginning of the game (Currently at 24 hours at the time this was written), I am in love with the pirates invading the item world and new geopanel status effects all the way to the drunkards trying to slap my bribes down. I have always loved the Disgaea mechanics on leveling up the stats, items, characters, and seeing everyone grow into terrors to be reckoned with. If you have Dragon Ball Syndrome, you would love this game. You grow your characters into killing machines while measuring their aptitudes in weapon abillities and stats.
Disgaea 2 PC introduces new downloadable characters to play as well. When I played Disgaea HoD, I never used the story characters except Laharl. I also never used the monsters either because the monsters were not nearly as strong as the humanoids. It was a shame because I often got bored raising monsters in HoD that weren't near as powerful as my humanoids. Disgaea 2 fixes both of these problems. Personal preference, but I love AdelxRozalyn. I also love Majin Hanako, Gig, and Dark Eclair. This extended cast is just more likable to me than those in HoD. The monsters are very well balanced in this game, I find the Monster Tamer to be a fun addition for now. My opinion might change on the Tamer later on, but for now I enjoy using monsters more than ever. Even making some to raise with the Tamer to beef up the stats and set them loose to kill.
The Disgaea series has been my favorite game for years now. I hope the other sequels make it to Steam since I don't own the consoles to play these on.

Bought it, tried it for an hour. It crashed three times in that hour, twice on the same mission. I got three missions in, and was bored or angry the whole way through.
Pros:
It does emulate Ace Combat to some degree, but not in the places that count
Cons:
-Voice acting is bad. Not even like mediocre. I can handle medicore, but this is just bad. I think CASTLE is supposed to be Irish, but the accent is barely there. Everyone sounds either unenthused or forcing their lines. I ended up turning the volume down during their side sequence. It's supposed to be touching and emotional, I think, but it's ruined by the voice acting since the cutscene is just a still.
-On the subject of sound design, it's honestly infuriating. This game will not let your ears have a moment of peace. If a missile gets locked to you prepare to hear the most piercing, annoying beep every .5 seconds until you break the lock. IF you break the lock. Game is very missle spammy, which isn't too big a problem, but with that missile lock sound it's horrible.
-As well, music is very off. I'm getting this slow, rhythmic, 'heroic'-esque music in the middle of a dogfight.
-Flying is slow and dull. It's almost like their design was split between arcade and flight sim, and it ends up being neither. Pick one.
-Dogfighting isn't fun. This is partially due to to how the flying feels, but mostly how locking on works and how terrible missles are. Locking on takes forever, it takes a full two-three seconds when behind a target and flying straight for the lock on to align. It's the same for ground targets. Locking on is a joke. I point my nose at something I clearly want to bomb, and I lock onto something halfway across the map.
I'm being harsh because I just got my third crash, which by the way happened in one of the still cutscenes, which causes you to have to replay the mission you just completed because for some reason the game hadn't registered I had passed it already. I've requested a refund.
I want this game to be good, I want it to be great. I grew up on Ace Combat and other flying games. I can understand it doesn't have to be a perfect clone, nor might the designers want it to be. But it has to be fun, and this isn't. Hopefully i will be able to change my review one day.

A Masterpiece of story telling through narrative, gameplay, and an always evolving plot marred by minor graphical issues created from a less than adequate console port.
Lets start with the short list of cons
-cutscenes are choppy and capped at 30 fps(with i6500/OC'd 1080)
-noticable popin from NPCs and scenery
-bug which caps fullscreen mode at 30fps(this is easily fixed by using "borderless gaming" but 3 weeks after launch its disappointing this has not been patched)
-optimization is average with 4k medium settings running around 40fps(witcher 3 runs same but with high settings)
Hopefully these issues will be patched soon, and the pros..
STORY, 10\10. Nier has one of the most intriguing and perfectly paced story lines Ive every played. Easily comparable with the best games from the Bioshock, Mass Effect, and Metal Gear franchises but with 5 playthroughs (currently on 3rd with 45 hours invested)worth of story that never stops captivating.
GAMEPLAY 9/10. Hack and slash mechanics feel precise and fluid with no lag. Camera operates fine and never causes cheap damage or death. The combo system is fairly simple with ~ 5 combo moves per weapon(light and heavy). Nothing exceptional but still works perfectly. There is also a dark souls'esque death system where if you die you will need to find your previous body to acquire your items. You will need to enable the "network" to enable this but it allows you to have temporary buffs or allies from other fallen players. This gives the game a sense of connection with its players knowing your body will litter other players games.
MUSIC 10\10. Orchestral music with bits of cyberpunk and well done vocals does a fantastic job conveying emotionals of heartbreak, urgency, and tranquility. Again masterpiece.
If your a fan of hack and slashes, RPGs, or especially story rich games this is a must own and feels like a bargain for only $60. Absolutley take a chance and try it, you wont be dissapointed.
One last thing....DO NOT STOP AT THE FIRST ENDING. I cant stress this enough as your only seeing about 1\4 of the story and gameplay

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Possibly the greatest game of all time.
Absolutely unparalleled story and immersion, just the ideas behind this game are so wonderfully fleshed out. The scary part is that it doesn't even feel far fetched, deus ex feels like it could occur in real life, it's just so well crafted. I feel like no other game can quite reach the level of awe that deus ex had, who cares if the graphics are a bit dated, the ideas and story are fantastic and you just want to hear more about it and read all the scattered books and emails throughout the game, thirsty for more of the deus ex world. No other game do I bother reading the tidbits and lore scattered, I'll normally skip or skim them but the deus ex world is just too amazing to miss.
On the topic of actual gameplay its just as great as the story. You can approach any situation in the game through methods such as stealth, guns blazing or a bit of both. There are multiple ways to progress through a level, entire areas to explore that don't even have to be touched to progress. The level design is superb. You can actually beat the game without killing anyone. Probably the only thing that I didn't like about human revolution was the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t boss battles that were unavoidable and sometimes overly difficult, kinda jabbing the pace of the game. In the original the boss battles aren't even necessary or that hard so rejoice!
Gunplay and stealth are, as expected also great, very solid and always kept interesting with the addition of new weapons or upgrades throughout the game. The game never feels stale as it progresses as environments constantly change and new enemies are introduced at an appropriate pace. The only issue I had was that I kept under-utilised my augmentations, as much fun and useful they can be I just felt that the keyboard would get a little clunky and was hard to pay attention to which button was which augmentation during the middle of a fight so I wouldn't end up using them very much and rarely did I ever bother to open the inventory and manually select the augmentations as it would really detract from the battle.
The amount of different skillpaths is another great feature, surely to keep players interested for multiple playthroughs for different game approaches if the story wasn't somehow enough to keep people coming back. You can focus on hacking and computers to turn machines against enemies and being able to access areas without scavenging for codes and logins or you can build a more tanky one man army skillset with a focus on healing, explosives and gunskills.
Would highly recommend

If you've never played this game before, I really don't know what to say, because it is extremely old as of this writing (2015) and for that matter, it was technically quite outdated already when it came out in the year 2000 (which the reviews at the time noted with gusto). People who wouldn't have liked it back then most probably wouldn't like it now.
But if you can get into old games just fine without having played them when they were new(ish), there really is no other game I can recommend as much as this one - assuming that you have an affinity for FPS/RPG hybrids. It still remains my absolute favorite computer game of all time, but I'll spare you the "FGR loves Deus Ex" backstory this time.
When it comes to gameplay mods, there are gems like GMDX that make the gameplay feel more modern and competent. Mods like Deus Ex: New Vision and Deus Ex: HDTP enhance the graphics (to ultra-high resolutions in the case of the former), which might make the game more pleasing to some people. And don't forget Deus Ex: Revision, which enhances the map architecture to the limits of Unreal Engine 1.5.
Yet for me, while playing the game with ultra-res textures and high-res models is extremely fun, it is only when I play the original game with its outdated graphics and exploitable gameplay functions when I feel right at home.

For any Daedalic fan, this is a worthy addition to your library. This is a game that I would not regret buying at full price (I got TNoTR on sale) for it is a quite meaty game. You'll get around 15 hours of gameplay and maybe more if you listen to the audio books ingame. While the game was mostly enjoyable there are some glaring issues such as pacing...
For a huge chunk of the game, there's not much plot progression until toward the end. You're going to be mostly trying to set up a festival in Mousewood and trying to complete your magician's training. Afterwards the plot speeds up and it feels crammed, especially with the additional exposition they add at the end. I don't get the feeling that the game's development was rushed at the end but the final act implies otherwise. With the pacing problem it did make it difficult to play through most of the game because I felt quite bored. I wasn't engaged in the plot until at the end. What really pushed me through was the visuals, audio, and world.
Visually the game is stunning and the audio is complements it greatly. I never got bored of looking at the game's backgrounds or character designs. The voice acting also stands out too, I particulary enjoyed the Marquis' voice actor. And the theme song of the game is very enjoyable to hear. It's one of those songs that can get stuck in your head but you're not bothered by it.
There's also the world the game inhabits which I feel like isn't explored enough in this game. There's good potential, as for many game universes, to expand the lore of this universe with how it goes about it's "Alice in Wonderland-like" idea. And with an interesting character like the Marquis de Hoto, I feel there's worthiness for a sequel especially with how they ended the game.
Overall a solid, competent, point & click adventure from Daedelic that suffers mostly from it's pacing issues and a few plot decisions such as the exposition cram at the end. But it does make up for it from everything else; ranging from visuals to dialogue. A worthy buy for $20.

Well here is my little insight.
PROS:
- The story is awesome.
- The lore of the land, races, characters, etc. is really deep.
- Huge graphical improvement from Witcher 1.
- Characters are really charismatic.
- You can make choices about almost anything giving you true sensation of free will.
CONS
Here is the big downside, you are forced to play a really wonky designed character and battle system:
- Battle animations are truly horrible, I mean I have played real garbage sometimes but THIS, this takes the crown jewel: the attack animations dont match hitboxes properly meaning you will get hit even if your enemy took a swing 2 ft on your left, your enemies do a parry animation to the fronside when you are attacking them from their backside negating all damage and then flipping instantly to hit you.
- On some battles you regain control way too late after a cutscene, that means you are gonna get hit, and die.
- The customization looks great, but it offers you 0 rewards for leveling up your character because everything can kill you from 2 hits (3 hits if you upgraded your armor), while you need to really smash the enemies over and over to make their health drop (normal difficulty). Instead of a powerful witcher I feel like I'm controlling a 80 year old man with arthritis and muscle atrophy.
- You can get hit/killed on different animations where you should not, precisely because you can't control your character: talking, falling to the ground, doing an execution sequence...
- Action Geralt comes with 2 movement sets: wonky slash you can smash on a braindead mode, and wonky heavy swing without range you should definitely not use because you are most likely to get parried and die.
- The enemies sure have learned from witcher 1, now they learned to move as a swarm of 5 or more enemies and just swarm you, just that, making melee combat impossible, you will be dead before you can even get parried, so full melee characters are really in for a good time...
- I need preparations for drinking a potion... W T F... I mean... It's ok if I need time to make them, that was an ok thing from Witcher 1 why force you to drink potions BEFORE you know you need them? You still need to meditate to brew them so WHY do I need to meditate to drink them? Does Geralt need to steel his resolve to uncork a bottle and drink it? Will he need therapy after that? I certainly will...
- The 0 healing on combat is something also driving me crazy, unless you get something (like a potion you CAN'T DRINK while in combat) to get you health regen you will be in for a reaaaal bad time in fights, because you got nothing like regen or healing, no magic, no items, nothing.
- So then is magic the solution to this malady? Nope. The very low base range of magic makes you think: "That is certainly not a fireball, he could just have ignited his fist and punched the enemy in the face". The magic drains your stamina like in witcher 1 but with an awesome stagger animation that will leave Geralt ready for a very nice chakra opening session (dead, DEAD, DeAD, dEaD). Trapping the ground with one of your spells is your biggest chance to actually  achieve something and thats not realiable at all: some enemies just step on it and absolutely nothing happens.
- Targeting is horrid, just horrid. I know it should be designed to help you in combat but it doesn't if there is more than 1 enemy, which I think should be the main purpose of targetting enemies in battle IMO.
- Minigames: I didn't ask for them, why am I forced to play them to actually complete some quests? There is arm wrestling (too easy to be entertaining), boxing (great concept but poorly applied, too easy to entertain) and dices... Oh dear god, the crown of the jewel of minigames, do you like minigames based on RNG? Where is the fun on that? Where do exactly I partake and test my skill if its random luck?
Conclusion:
This had the potential to be a really good game I mean, you got the story, the characters, the beautiful scenarios, all those choices and quests! They are awesome!
But the playability of this game is dreadful, I would give a straight 0 to that section, it drags down some parts of the game to a frustrating level instead of a challenging one because of a really poor coded battle system that you are FORCED to play.
Would I recommend this title? Well, if you ever played Witcher 1 and liked the story, yeah why not give it a shot, but expect some parts of this game being frustrating to play and just a plain nightmare. To every other mortal soul I can just recommend to stay as far as possible from this game.

I hate parties. There, I said it. They make me feel awkward and there always seems to be a forced atmosphere. It’s not that I want to murder everyone when I’m being at a party, though, so when Party Hard came along I was intrigued by the idea to say the least. So, if you’re like me, and want to know if you’ll have a better time playing this game than being at an actual party read on!
Clearly the game is meant to be over-the-top, while still feeling somewhat realistic in terms of environments and kills. Yes, ‘somewhat’, because even though your goal is to kill everyone at the party you can’t go around and stab everyone just in the face and be done with it (well, you can try, but you’ll most likely end up being arrested or beaten up).
The story is being told through flashbacks of the events that (recently) occurred – these are your missions - while cutscenes tell us a bit more about the current situation. This is mostly told through a detective’s perspective (who is being questioned/asked about the killings), but to avoid possible spoilers I won’t go into it any further than this.
The game’s style reminded me a bit of Hotline Miami. It’s not as vibrant, though, and a lot of the people found in the levels won’t even fight back. This doesn’t make it easy, mind you. On the contrary: although it’s not a main objective the goal is to still try and create a big combo in order to score big points. You will have to rely on luck, stealth and skill in order to do this. I’ve managed to create a combo of, I think, 10-12 or so, but that was because a lot of the people were turned into zombies and standing close to one another, since, well, zombies are mindless. Again, it sounds very easy this way, but trust me when I say that I had to retry the level more than once.
The levels are pretty big in size, but they’re limited to just one screen. Despite that there is still more than enough detail in them and you also have plenty of room to move around (freely). Unfortunately, it can be hard to see where you can or can’t walk sometimes because everything is shown in 2D with pixelated graphics and because of that objects sometimes lack the fine(r) detail that normally distinguishes these parts (a bit) better.
Levels include a cruise ship, dance club, biker party and garden party (and many others!) and the AI characters move around freely in all of these levels, doing their own things. This can frequently become annoying, though, because your character doesn’t stand out all that much and if there are a couple of people (walking) near you you might just lose track of it all.
So the goal is to kill all of the people who are currently present at the party. The people are randomly generated so if you play the same level a different time then you will have to kill a different amount of people. Same goes for the available objects in the level. Some of them are static, but some of these are also randomly generated and placed. It adds a bit of replay value but to be honest there’s not much incentive to replay a level once it’s finished, unless you want to improve your high score.
You will be able to kill people by stabbing them or by using the environments to make it seem like an accident. Keep in mind, however, that you must not be caught, because if you’re close to a murder scene then it’s likely you will be pointed out as the murderer. The police will then chase you until you’re caught or until they’re too tired to chase you further. You can then start killing again, just like before. If you’re lucky a different guest will be arrested and this will then also count as a ‘kill’. So sometimes it pays off (but most of the times it doesn’t, because crime doesn’t pay!).
From time to time you will also be able to find items in the levels in the form of a suitcase and once opened these will give you either a smoke bomb, explosive bomb or different clothes (handy if you’re being chased), among a couple of other items.
You can also use a dance move to spread out groups of people (because they somehow don’t like the way you dance; well, it’s their loss) and you also have a sprint button (with limited, but rechargeable stamina bar) and a listen button that shows you all of the available interactive objects around you.
The music is just amazing; there are a lot of catchy, upbeat songs, and best of all, this music would actually fit in a game about parties. Just for the music alone I could easily recommend this game. The sounds effects are mostly basic but, as always, at least get the job done. The voice acting ranges from mediocre to good, but I *think* this might have been done on purpose, since it’s meant as an over-the-top experience.
Visually the game also looks stunning; it uses beautiful retro graphics and a realistic color pattern/scheme. Only problem is, unfortunately, that the graphics don’t have enough detail and because of that it sometimes is hard to see where you can exactly go to. I think ‘cutout’ 2D or just regular 2D graphics would’ve helped the game in this department. It’s not a big deal, but could’ve been easily avoided with a little more care (maybe even by just changing up some of the graphics).

Each level should take you about 5-10 minutes, but it’s unlikely you’ll finish most of the levels on your first try. Since there are 12 levels I estimate it will take an average user about 5-7 hours to complete, including retries, which is more than enough in my opinion. And also considering the price, of course. We don’t want the game to overstay its welcome and thankfully it doesn’t, but this will of course differ per person in the end.

If you ever played Hotline Miami and wanted something similar then Party Hard might just be the thing you’re looking for. It uses similar, pretty, retro graphics, it has amazing audio and the gameplay is just solid. The story might be a bit ridiculous, but if you can look past that then there’s a fun and engaging game to be found here.
Pros:
+ Retro graphics
+ Amazing music
+ Fun, sometimes challenging, gameplay
+ Pulling off a perfect ‘run’ feels very satisfying
Mixed:
+/- Not vital, but it’s sometimes unclear where you’re character starts off
+/- Random objects and amounts of people give the game a bit of replay value, although not much
+/- Environmental kills are fun, but sometimes it’s a bit too limited (read: there aren’t always enough objects in a level to keep it (very) interesting)
Cons:
- At times there are too many people walking around, close to each other, and you can lose track of it all
- Some of the levels feel a bit empty in terms of environmental interactivity, which is disappointing

I'm not actually a very public person, but in order to get one of these shiny Steam Award badges, I actually have to post a review for something...and I feel like if there was ever a game I needed to talk about, this one would be it.
Joking aside, this game has become almost a part of my daily routine at this point.  After dealing with the rigors of work, family issues, health issues, and all that good stuff, I find myself coming back to this game to continue my ever-important career of space...important guy.  That's one of the first things I could touch on, there is no real set -goal- for this game, you aren't corralled into some plot line where you make or break the sanctity of the universe.  Note that my experiences do involve a couple of mods such as XRM, but as they are totally free I feel that it shouldn't take away from some of the points I'll bring up here.
Do you want to build a massive commercial empire, complete with your own factories that produce anything from weapons to foodstuffs?  Go for it.
Do you want to develop a huge armada of warships and ethnically cleanse all other species from the galaxy?  Harsh, but you can do that.
Do you want to just cruise in your little trade freighter making deals both legal and...less than legal?  All while playing your music of choice in the background?  Have at it, lad.
This game never jumps in the way of what you want to do and screams about some overshadowing metaplot that you're supposed to be crux of, leaving you free to make your career into whatever you want it to be.  While some may find the graphics lacking in the current age, I found they placated me nicely.  Plus, let's face it, it's going to be hard enough to process having the massive fleet engagements that take place at the drop of a hat if you drift into the wrong (or right, depending on your viewpoint) sector.  I will agree with critics of the control system though, it does seem rather easy to crash your ship into another, and autopilot isn't always reliable either.  I find myself at the 'Game Over' screen far more often due to bouncing off of a capital ship than I do for it actually doing me in with laser fire.
All in all, the game does have certain control and UI flaws, and there will be times that you may find some of your losses to be unfair due to collisions and the like, but I honestly don't find myself to be enough of an expert to come up with proper solutions to these problems.  Regardless, I didn't find that these detracted from my experience enough to keep me from playing, though I did unsurprisingly need a break if I lost a hard-fought engagement.
If you want to have an expansive universe to explore, combat, or colonize, I can't think of a better game to do it with.  While there are other wonderful excursions into making your mark on a galactic scale, such as Stellaris or Endless Space, not as many actually give you the chance to start off as some wayfaring vagrant in a tiny scout ship.  From there, it's up to you to upgrade your starting ship, find ways to acquire more, and learn to deal with the ever-present threats of pirates, xenophobic swarms of uncompromising aliens, and even a Skynet style set of automatons that want to terraform your face off.   Few games have left me with so many options while retaining a living, breathing galaxy full of factions with their own economy and conflicts.  In a world where we may not feel like we have any control left, at least in the realm of X3, you have a galaxy within which you can forge your own destiny...and confront the consequences of doing so.

X3: Albion Prelude, is a weird game to describe. It isnt weird in the sense of something like LSD Dream simulator, just, hard to explain because of how much the game does.
In Short, X3: Albion Prelude is a 4X game played from the first person perspective. What this gives itself is instead of focusing on stratergy it then ultimatly becomes a sort of, life game. You start off with you being often the weakest in the galaxy, and you have to find ways in order to make money to become more powerful and see more of the game.
Will you be a bounty hunter, drifing in between systems, taking odd jobs that will grant you a huge boon of money and reputation with the faction you are working for, at the risk of your own life, and the risk of huge damage done to your property?
Will you become a trader, finding great deals to buy a ton of resources, only to sell them again much later for much more money?
Or, maybe you dont want to have yourself be roped to certain factions, break off and become a pirate? Shooting down, taking as many ships as you can for glory and profit?
After all, in the galaxy, money is power, and, the more money you have, the quicker you can gain more, building stations across the universe to supply the traders with goods, whilst they pay you to make those resources, eventually allowing you to build even more, and build your fleet, to protect your investments from others.
Eventually, if you are willing to put  time and effort, you can have massive fleets, which could have THOUSANDS of the tiny ship you started off in within it, and then a few hundred capital ships such as the Panther Raider, or Colossus to store them in, protecting them from threats such as the Terrans and the Xenon from fighting in it.
Whilst Terran conflict has a lot of the same, Albion prelude is an expansion pack to an allready great game, and it is well worth buying, Just don't pick up Rebirth, it isnt worth your time. And if I had to pick a game for someone to get into the X series with, I would recommend this due to the Argon Peacekeeper start, which gets you right into plot missions at the start of the game, letting you ease into the game in some of the more powerful ships, and following a plotline, which at the end, the player has enough resources to quickly set up a small empire and continue from there, or try another start, and work up to that plot quest, compared to the rather unforgiving starts of some of the other games.

Disgaea is sort of like Final Fantasy in that it's a series of titles with their own stories and tales in each iteration. The difference being that Disgaea has character's that make cameos and/or play roles in the other titles (at least, thus far). Additionally, Disgaea keeps the same battle system and follows the incremental upgrade pathway for a series, whereby each following title improves on the last.
So nothing comes as a surprise here: Disgaea 2 follows the same conventions as Disgaea 1:
-Story mode is progressed through a Menu whereby each episode consists of 4 battle maps (varies, but typically 4) and upon completing the final one, a new episode is unlocked
-Everything you need to access (item dungeons, shops, etc) are all accessed from the hubworld; there is no open world exploration (or even linear world exploration) like most JRPG's
-New characters are unlocked/gained through regular progression in the story as well as character creation with mana attained from battles.
-No grinding is necessary to complete the story mode
Just as in 1 I love the streamlined manner in which story mode works. There's no long JRPG quest here; you just go straight into the battles with a short cutscene always proceeding it. There's no forgetting where to go next if you stop playing for a week or having to go grab items in several towns and dungeons to continue onwards with the story. The story itself is also a relatively light-hearted romp with a usually comedic tone.
The item world makes a comeback; the randomly generated maps whereby progression is done by getting to the exit. Included now are random encounters that occur without notice; enemies drop by the maps and you can either face them for good loot or just proceed to the next level of the map. They appear sparsely so facing them is always recommended, the problem is that as it's random the random encountered enemies might be leagues beyond your own level, making the whole ordeal moot. Given that these encounters rarely occur and some of the enemies carry items required to open optional maps in the story mode, some consistency would've been appreciated in their levels relative to the player's. There are also "mystery rooms" in the item world, which are alternate exits that take you to a dark room which either consists of merchants hawking rare wares, fights that will increase the items level, or treasure chests with items in them. Always recommended to go into the rooms unless you're not hurting for money, items, or planning on ditching the item after getting the specialists.
The Dark Assembly receives a rather large change; not only are the different bills you can pass more varied, but character unlocking is now done through the assembly itself. Whereas before unlocking new classes to create required meeting certain pre-requisites, now they've added the additional step of having to pass a bill allowing access to the class once the pre-requisite is met. Bills, as before, are passed through an assembly whereby you spend accumulated mana from battles to pass bills of varying costs; bills have an approval rate and if they fail you can eliminate senators unfavorable to your bill in a battle or just give up on the bill and attempt passing it later (spent mana is not recouped).
The assembly itself requires less fighting than in the previous title. As senators will hate you more and more the more you fight them, it's not recommended to do so unless you're going to go level 1000 as many of these senators levels are in the hundreds. This penalty for fighting is a bit of a shame, as tossing no votes on top of higher levelled yes votes presented an enjoyable level of strategy; granted this is still possible but having hatred of your actions persist on the playthrough is a bit cumbersome and annoying when you just can't fight your way through a bill. Rather, gaining favor with senators and parties is the way to go now, which is certainly duller (and easier). It's not that an option was taken away, it's that it's not optimal now.
As for the fighting system: same old same old. Veterans will feel at home and it's as if nothing changed. The few differences are minimal: classes now have passive abilities unique to them that differentiate the classes more than just what weapon affinities they have. The series still requires a bit more differentiation between the classes to provide an impetus for creation past merely wanting to have every class in the game.
So past me giving out on a few points, is this an improvement over Disgaea 1? On a base level there is more here; so yes. But as the largest difference is the story and characterization, I'd have to say it's lower on the totem poll in that regard. Laharl, Etna, and Flonne made a good trio that often clashed. Here you have Rozalin and Adell which have an interesting dynamic as they are technically enemies working together, and for the manner in which the developers went about their relationship they deserve a thumbs up. Otherwise there's less laughter here; Tink is rather memorable as is Axel, but characters like Hanako and Taro are just there. The story was alright and had more "substance" than the "I wanna be the strongest!" plotline of Disgaea 1, but I still prefer the first games title as it still had multiple plotpoints occuring at once whereas here it's just Adell and Rozalin with the same goal of meeting Zenon. The fact that Etna steals the spotlight here even though she's not the MAIN character (albeit an important one) gives substance to the claim that the main cast from 1 was more memorable.
Sounds like I'm giving out about it, but the item world is still fun as hell, the grind is addictive *even though it isn't necessary*, which is almost paradoxical for anything with "RPG" in the title. You'll still waste inordinates amount of time going to the item world to level up equipment (every level traverssed increases item stats), and you'll be going to the item world to subdue specialists in the items themselves-which give a variety of effects and can be transferred to better items once subdued. I still spent more time doing things other than the story for no reason other than being addicted to moving specialists and strengthening equipment.
Final verdict? Good title albeit not as good in plot or characters *overall*. But on the game itself and the mechanics, more of the same and if you enjoyed it previously you'll enjoy it again. Just be sure not to play it directly after the first game.

Let's start with a simple fact: this game is not perfect. It's not even amazing, nor great. It is buggy like hell, tedious with its menu interface, annoying when it crashes and, in all honesty, shallow with content.
But where Vector Thrust shines will be enough for people who are just looking for one thing - simple, plain, fast-paced dogfight action. The game is a perfect example of a title that you can play for an hour or so a day, on a break from duties or between other games.
And to be honest, it has all the features it needs - the flight experience in Vector Thrust is just fantastic. The plane acts like you imagine it would, has the proper weight and feel to it. Guns and missiles are done really well and splashing a sidewinder into enemy's face is really damn satisfying.
There's a nice variety of fighters - even if most of them are reskins, or slightly different meshes, they all pilot differently and can carry a huge array of various load. And if that's not enough, then one of the game's strongest sides is the modding community - there's quite a lot of skins and there are even entire fighters (Morgan! <3) that you can download. So far I had no problems with mods too.
All in all, I can't recommend VT to everyone, all the negative reviews here are a proof why. But if you turn a blind eye to the early-accessy feel to the game and give a little trust to the developer, who constantly, though slowly, adds new stuff, then you get a great relax-issuing title, with one thing that it does amazingly well. If you're a fan of fighter combat and don't mind the fact that the campaigns barely work, you might just get a few really good hours with skirmish or multiplayer. Especially if you find it on a Steam sale (recently VT was 40% off, that's a good deal).
Also, a tip: learn to use the goddamn AOA Limiter. The game doesn't point that feature at all, unfortunately, but it's only when you turn it off and let the G-Forces flow through the plane that you feel like a real goddamn ace, swinging in aerobatics toe to toe with foes.

Alright, since I enjoyed the game so much I feel like I have to write a proper review so here we go. Let me start by saying that I don't enjoy anime that much and from what I've seen in the trailers it looked like the game had some anime style behind it. After all it's a Japanese game so I was not really sure if I would enjoy playing the game at all. Additionaly I never played the previous game or the Drakengard games which are suppose to be intertwined with the NieR franchise if I'm not mistaken. So I had no idea what to expect from this one but since it got so much praise I was curious still so I decide to try it out anyway. So after about 3 playthroughs and 50 hours spend on NieR:Automata I can certainly say that it was worth it.
What people have to keep in mind is the game is designed to be replayed multiple times. Of course you can be done after your first playthrough but then you would miss a huge portion of the story. The first two playthroughs narrate the same story but from different perspectives. The third one is actually pretty clever because the game makes a sequel to itself. In the first one you play as 2B a battle android that is part of the YoRHa Project designed to protect the remnants of mankind which was nearly wiped out but managed to flee to the moon. The story that is told us when we play 2B is failry simple but once you're done and start you second run things start to unfold drastically and the game becomes so much more interesting. On your second run you play as 9S, the latest infiltrator android model who is designated to gather intelligence behind enemy lines. Suddenly all the things you've learned as 2B appear not to be that simple anymore. Not only does the story become exciting but the enemies, setting and even the bosses do too. I could name dozens examples or so but that would spoil the game. The third playthrough was pobably my most favourite because like previously said, the game essentially plays as a sequel to itself. This time you play as A2, an older android model and a deserter. Things get even more complicated and you get couple of story twists which blow your mind.
The game is a hack'n'slash RPG. The combat system is not as advanced as the one in the Devil May Cry games where you can pull insane combos but is more similar to the one in Metal Gear Rising, straight forward and simple but very enjoyable. You have 4 weapon categories: small swords, large swords, spears and combat bracers. You have two slots if you play as 2B or A2 and depending on the combination and order the weapons are equipped you get different results each time. 9S lacks in this category since he has only one slot for only one weapon. His combos are dull but it is suppose to be balanced out with his "hack" ability which is a bullet hell minigame. Unfortunately the hacking gets boring quickly. Then there is a small crafting system. You can upgrade all your weapons and your Pod, with materials that drop from enemies or are scattered troughout the world. It's basic but still. My favourite part of the game was probably the chip system which allows you to customize your character quite a bit. You get lots of different chips as loot from enemies and as a reward for quests. Each chip has a different attribute and a value, the better the attribute the higher the value. However you can only equip so many until the combined value of chips doesn't reach the characters threshold. You can be jack of all trades or have insane melee damage with time slow on counter attacks. You can even remove parts of the HUD since these are chips too to make more room for other chips.
It's an open world game, the world however is not that big which is great in my book. Things are pact more tight, hehe, and there is always a quests somewhere nearby. You don't have to run 15 minutes to get things done and I really enjoyed it that way. The world offers a lot of variety in its locations too so there is not much to complain about. The music is fantastic. The only thing that really botheres me is the mediocre port which could be fixed of course but the developers take way too much time to do so.

I wanted to love this game.  Really, I did.  As an avid fan of the second gen Ace Combat games (4, 5, Zero, and then 6 on XB360), this looked like it would fill the void left after my PS2 and XB360 went off to meet the great HDTV in the sky.
Unfortunately, I couldn't play the game.  Despite numerous troubleshooting steps posted in the forums, including reverting back to an older version the dev had uploaded as a beta branch, the game just would not start for me.  As it turns out, the crashes on startup were directly related to my controller being connected to my PC.  It was an NVidia Shield controller which requires no special drivers and should function as a standard Xbox controller.
I did what any good gamer would do; made a few posts on the forums in the relevant topics, uploaded the requested logs and system specs, and waited.  And waited.  And waited.  I heard nothing.
I realize that TimeSymmetry is just a one-man outfit (or close to it), and there are rumors swirling around the forums about Iceburg forcing him to release from EA early, and that he's released some patches since official release, so it was with a heavy heart that after 1.5 weeks and under 20 minutes played, I submitted a refund request from Steam.
I wanted to love Vector Thrust, and I will check back from time to time, but in its present state I can't in good conscience recommend it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

As many of you who are reading this review must be doing, I read the top negative reviews before buying the game. And to be honest, right now, this game is abselutely not worth it. In fact, it is the very first game that I requested a refund. Here's a few reasons why, as well as some good points. Yes I did only play about 20 minutes, but yes, that was more than enough.
Cons:
-THE biggest issue: took me 3 hours to get this to actually work. The only fix that worked? Switching back to the last build (as proposed by the devs, using a beta option they created). Problem with this is that even this fix needs manual fixing.
-No tutorial. Want to know the controls? Go read.
-No access to options in-game, need to go back to main screen. Launched the campaign expecting the first mission to teach you how to play? Nope! And no, game doesn't even allow you to know in-game what controls to use.
-Unintuitive keyboard controls. I though GTA had bad flight controls. Mouse for view, arrows for up-down pitch and roll left or right, WASD for thrust, brake, left-right turn. Don't have 3 hands? Too bad. This could have been improved by using the numpad instead of arrows. Also, chaff, flares, etc are bound by default to 6-7-8, while cameras are 1-2-3. I think that defenses are more important than a good angle of vision, but maybe that's just me.
-Boring fights. I tried to play the first mission, and it pretty much resumes to: fly to target, fly to enemy, keep on rolling with enemy and wait for missile lock. Launch. Repeat. All you do is do loops again and again. That is not realistic, because any real pilot doing that would loose consciousness.
-Equipment information seems wrong: the first rockets you get are described as "unguided", yet they still lock and follow targets...
Pros:
-Combat system is good, but the poor controls and poor AI just doing loops pretty much negates this.
-Lots of play modes, including (but not limited to) campaign, multiplayer, skirmishes.
-Graphics. Although even on max graphics the planes still look a little low-res (see the game screenshots above for examples), one thing that actually amazed me is that they added the visual effect of passing the speed of sound. That I haven't seen often.
-Sounds. I tried the two planes that are available initially, and both had they own engine sounds, weapon sounds, etc.
So, as you can see, and as many others have said, the bases are there and good, but the finishing touch was scrapped.

Magicite is one of those rare gems which makes you want to play for just that little bit longer. It's fiendishly difficult at times, but it's so much fun to play that you'll be eager to get back into it to beat your previous attempts. With each level offering a random assortment of enemies and resources every play is unique, and as you progress you'll aquire better armor and weaponry to battle the creatures you will face. It's a thrilling ride all the way.
That's not to say it doesn't have it's flaws however. The crafting system employed is similar to early days Minecraft in that the recipes are not necessarily intuitive and often you'll need a wiki page open to view them. Also, with your inventory inevitably filling up with the various items you'll find you might find that simply find a spare slot to create the most basic of tools becomes a challenge itself.
Even some the earliest enemies can take a lot of damage before they go down and it will take a few runs before you know what monster you can safely fight and when you should run away. The bosses are incredibly strong and can appear as randomly as normal targets, making some opening levels exceptionally difficult.
These minor points aside though, it's a fantastic amount of fun to play and well worth the kickstarter funding. If you like Spelunky or Terraria, you should definitely give this game a try. It's well worth your time and money.

Magicka is, hands down, one of the best "cooperative" multi-player experiences out there. The quotation marks are, of course, ironic - cooperation in this game is likely to be an often impossible endeavour. It is notably easy for players to blow each other's heads, be it on purpose or accidentally, due to the fragility of the characters and the experimental nature of the game's spell casting system. Massive battles where magic runs amok often result in a huge death toll, which is only partially mitigated by the invaluable ability to revive deceased wizards.
As daunting as it might seem, players usually get the hang of it after a few minutes of playing and some sort of collaboration occurs, not without a few casualties every now and then. In the end, the game manages to be fun and extremely addictive, as well as short enough not to be repetitive. Most DLCs, though, do not live up to the high standards of the main game. But that's another story and shall be told another time.

The Night of the Rabbit is a really charming game. The art (both audio and visual) were absolutely beautiful and played off of one another very well to help create a mood and atmosphere relative to the plot. The characters were lovable and relatable, and the plot was mostly well done in its creation. The mini game, Quartets, was another fun way to pass the time if you didn't particularly feel like going on with the main game itselfl.
Unfortunately, that's about all that's positive to say about The Night of the Rabbit. I've enjoyed point-and-click puzzle-based games for nearly ten years, but the puzzles in this game were nearly impossible to figure out on your own. I ended up looking up close to half of the game just trying to progress. A lot of the stuff I did get were from the very vague clues that I was actually able to understand, or just from randomly clicking on things in the hopes that it would either work or give a clue clear enough that I would be able to figure out the missing elements. While the daytime/nighttime game mechanic was really, really cool, it also made for more complexity. Some actions are only able to be performed at night, and some of those weren't even made possible until a puzzle during the day was solved. It created a bit of an issue for me, trying to solve two puzzles at once in two completely separate areas. In addition, the ending of the story was incredibly anticlimatic. I don't want to spoil anything for those who still want to buy the game, but after all the puzzles that I had seen and after all of the involvement in the story, I expected something a bit more satisfying. It felt a bit like being cheated; the end had potential but fell very, very flat.
In the end, I don't think I'd recommend the game, or at least not at its full price. I was lucky enough to catch it while it was on sale, but for all the unsatisfaction of the ending and the frustration of having to look up a walkthrough every twenty minutes, I'm not sure it's worth the full $20.

It took about five lines of dialog for me to get the feeling that the game might be aimed at an age group maybe 20 years younger than myself. But then, I can't imagine anyone in that age range having the sheer amount of patience that this game requires you to have in order to complete it.

There simply aren't enough games with dinosaurs & even fewer of these that are actually worth playing! For me, Orion: Prelude (O:P) is that rare exception. Although not much in way of a story in the game (no single player after all), there is quite a tale on how Orion came to be the game it is today...
The short version is, that O:P is an evolution of previous Orion titles, Dino Horde & Dino Beatdown originally dating back to a successful 2011 Kickstarter campaign. Although recieving early criticism (that would normally kill a game ..dead.. disappearing into obscurity), the game continued to evolve with constant updates (big & small) over the years from the developers. Spiral stuck with it! This dedication & gradual refinement of the game has resulted in an excellent first-person co-op experience, with a well rounded collection of modes, weapons, enviromental effects, vehicles & more to enjoy.
PvP isn't forgotten; it's also selectable. PvP feels more alike to a retro deathmatches, than a modern PvP (in a good way!), but I mainly enjoy the co-op modes. In co-op, you essentially have to defend your power core against waves of bloodthursty dinosaurs. Dinosaur kills will reward you credits, which you can use to buy perks & weapon upgrades, in-turn helping you survive the later, harder waves. Some waves also have you securing objectives. Co-op doesn't feel ultra competitive, most of the time you don't watch your credits/kills, rather finding yourself just having fun surviving & helping your teammates! I've found the community to generally be helpful & friendly in-game too.
One of the real stand-out features in O:P has to be the enviromental effects randomly cycling on the alien world. From the day/night cycles to the extreme variety of climates & types of weather. Adds so much to the atmosphere. Couple this with excellent lighting effects through what seems to be a thicker atmosphere and the results can sometimes be spectacular! Even overwhelming! You definitely get that feeling when your final wave gets a night cycle with heavy rain .. you know you are gonna see an epic close quarter battle!
Along with the awesome effects, there are 3 distinct classes to mix-up the gameplay. Each has unique strengths & each you can progress/level-up in online play to unlock starting weapons, power-ups & perks. Initial learning curve isn't steep, so once you get the hang of the basic flow it becomes very easy to sink multiple hours killing dinos! O:P rarely feels like a grind; even at lower levels (without a lot of perks) you competently kill dinos & gain good XP. Plenty of dinos to go around too :)
If you can't find a friend to play with, there is also bot-support added in O:P to fill the ranks. This can be helpful to get playing quickly if server populations are low (which regrettably does happen).
The trilogy of classes are well balanced (no need for any other classes), as is the gameplay in general. Difficulty is super scalable. Weapons are mainly shared between classes so quickly become familiar, and vehicles are easy to use & offer a good range of practical & destructive uses. Repetitive? Sure, to a degree, it is the same thing over & over and despite there being a lot of 'accessories' to the spice up the character classes & tactics, modes etc, there are not a huge number of maps for each mode. I expect this will change soon with Steam Workshop support being added.
The A.I. generally employed by the dinosaurs is a fairly basic 'rush' tactic, which can feel pretty predictable (there are a few surprises though), but I find the larger dino numbers to counteract this limitation to a degree anyway. There are also the occasional technical glitches like querky physics (flying Stegosaurus anyone?) or clipping inside a dinosaur. Nothing game-breaking that I have experienced, but sure does make for some funny moments! Just like my many failed attempts at some of the more creative 'Ride a Dino for 10secs' & 'Slap T-Rex 100 times' achievements :)
O:P reminds me a bit of those classic, simple shooters like a Serious Sam or Left 4 Dead, but with a bit of high-tech sci-fi flavor. This future-tech feel across the game contradicts the jurassic era dinosaurs & remote wilderness landscapes nicely! O:P is not as complex mechanically or technically when compared to a top end AAA FPS, but its simplicity is also its underlying strength. It is great value ($1!), has strong replayability and the focused, balanced gameplay (some bonus ..ahem.. querks) offers a truely fun & intense, dino killin' co-operative survival experience!

Playability: A difficult game that does take some time to master. You will find that survivability is key, and to always try to get upgrades that change your physical appearance, because YOU WILL NEED THEM. Expect multiple deaths, and constant cornering. 4
Entertainment: The story itself is kind of humorous and does have its moments especially during loading screens. Bosses are like normal enemies and can be really tough if not tougher than them, nut with trial and error anyone can proceed through the game. The game offers many different challenges, complete with stats and collectibles. 4.4
Replay Value: High
Overall: The Binding of Issac is an insanely tough dungeon crawler plastered with a ton of powerups. The enemies may not suite someone with a weak stomach as they come off a bit grotesque. The story is funny, but anyone can assume the stereotypical ending. After you master the game in some aspect it get a bit easier and offers a ton of replay value. 7.3/10
