12 hours in the game and alll I have to say its one of the most underated multiplayer survivals out there.
-PROS
Its leveling system is is relatively in depth and isnt very tedious to level up. Unless your playing on the harder difficulty which means you'll lose all progression if you die. But it makes it more exciting and has you play the game in a different way you would normally in other survival games. Of course theres another difficulty which if you die you dont lose any progression.
The map is ungodly huge but not overwhelming. Its really fun to explore and find new buildings and animal locations.
The combat is simple yet rewarding and somewhat requires you to think about what fights you should be taking. Along with how you progress in crafting better items and weapons to fight the enemies in the game, (wolves, bears, etc).
You can grow crops, food, and have a whole bunker to yourself which later when you find other safe houses they all have a subway system that connects them to one another allowing you to fast travel around the map.
The weather effects in the game are nice and makes its risky to go out and explore until you get better equiped with a risk/reward type a feel to it.
-CONS
Early access bugs. Like sometimes items dissappear or you fall through the map type things. (very rare in my experience).
Wish the story was longer. I felt sad when I finsihed to quests, I wanted to keep learning about why we were there and keep fighting bosses. XD
For around 20$ its a solid game that I think if you're looking for something to play with a friend or two, or even alone its more than worth it.

Having a blast playing this game after 10 years since I went throught the PS2 version. Fortunatelly this version has some improvements since Dark Hero Days in some ways.
The story is nothing new but is pretty decent; difficulty wise the main story is very easy if you go offtrack and go to the Item World, which can happen a lot if you like to be overlevel. The postgame is very grindy, but fortunately less tedious in some ways from most of the usual RPGs since the levels are randomly generated.
Pros:
+ Improved UI. The item's icons and menus looks pretty good.
+ No need to buy the DLCs since the game automaticaly gives you the events to unlock the DLC characters. This is the only reason why I won't say the game is overpriced (even more I got it in a sale).
+It's a strategy RPG. If you love to grind, craft you perfect items and characters this game is for you.
+ The grinding is less tedious since Item World generates all the levels. You can get some pretty and nasty surprises from enemies holding that item that you want and Pirates ambushing you!
+The OST is awesome AND you can change it for Item World anytime. Even the DLC's characters got their songs added to the PC version.
+Aside from the real final superboss, you can beat most of the endgame stuff with almost every character. It's good  since you're not forced to abuse Magic Knight / Lahalh / etc to beat most of postgame bosses. But the same can't be said from the final superboss (if they kept his difficulty as the PSP version)
Cons
- The grinding has a LOT of resets in the Item World for you to pray for RNG to give you Good/Great Luck on the Mistery Gate (only applies for perfecting Items for the fina superboss). I had Mao showing up 4 times without an Old Man appearing on the Mistery Gate one afternoon! Also grinding Lovers and Felonies can consume a long time.
- The game is 99% a port. I would love to see the same game with HD characters.
- Dark Eclair's portrait looks awful AND I didn't unlock her OST in the Item World even after obtaining her and buying songs from the Item World's Succubus. Maybe you need to get all the DLC characters and the devs screwed up on the unlocking musics for the IW?
If you like SRPGs and grinding, this game is for you. If you don't like to grind, stay away from this game unless you only want to do the main game. It's one of the few games when it was released that you could inflict millions of damage and the game needed to use short lenght for the damage! If you like absurd levels of damage and going up to LV OVER 9000! This game IS for you!

Borderlands 2 and Borderlands Pre Sequel in my evaluation could be top rated A+ games.
The graphics are tremendous, and the gameplay and control movements are very stable.
Outstanding contol technique for driving vehicles with steering by mouse (instead of the awkward arrow-keys as some games do). The storylines are very entertaining and the adventures will keep a player up all night playing.
However, there are some major gaming frustrations (for me), that turn the game into a B-grade game, I refer to these a game pissers, and list these below;
Game pissers!
...as player “Levels-Up”, so do the enemies level-up ...however players weapons held remain at last level!
...vending machines always dispel lower-level items than at the players current level!
...items found -or- purchased genrally always below players current level!
...mega-boss ‘drops’ are random and extreme rare finding anything leveled!
...FORGET about equipping with anything but a hail of rapid firing weapons,
as powerful slow-firing) single-shots are useless with enemies and hoards running upon player!
...Once player finds and obtains a 'favorite' weapon which is effective in damage, soon the player is leveled-up, along with the enemies, making all those favorite weapons basically useless, with no means of leveling the weapons up to meet the leveled-up enemies.
*Very Frustrating gameplay with ‘bosses’ always overpowering player to the ridiculous degree!!
(evidently some think it’s “cool” to always being underpowered and out-manned)! ...But I find it being so impossible to sufficently damage the 'boss' it's more comforting to just delete the game!
For me, if there was some 'cheat', such as god-mode or invisibility so as I could just make it through the game,  would be much more appreciated than deleting the entire game out of frustrations!
Also, by not having 'quick-saves' and repeatedy getting 'killed' and restarting way back from a programed saved-game makes for a frustrating gameplay.
I understand Borderlands encourages 'team-player' so as to gang-up on the difficult bosses...however I often do not have the capability to play-online and so must play in single-player mode...which too often pits me against some horrific 'boss' fight along with ever numerous minions 're-appearing' making the fire fight frustrating.
There have been times whereas I can completely leave the scene by fast-traveling to a old area and farm points for leveling-up to the previous 'boss' fights levels and be somewhat sucessful, however that gets old real fast (needing to evade out of the area and gain points for leveling up so as to continue the adventure!
Basically there is no "hiding" from enemies by 'crouching' as ememies will continually be rushing the attack and more enemies responding all the while only having lower-leveled weapons which do minimal damage. Enemies poor-grade weapons always over-power players higher-leveld weapons it seems.
Why even have a 'level' system, after all, a level-one weapon is just as effective against a level-one enemy as a level 50 weapon is against a level-50 enemy... making the system redundant.

Nier: Automata is a philosophical meta game that distracts you with flashy fights and genre bending game mechanics
(It's at least Third person shooter, shoot'em'up, rpg, hack and slash, platformer and spectacle fighter)
The story is fine but the characters are so fleshed out that I can't believe it.

Although you can reach "happy ending" in the game it still also embraces the fact that purpose, hope etc. are subjective and some people might find reality dark and hopeless, meaningless. Although everyone can find peace in the end if they want to.

Maybe it's just my strange fascination for RPG-type games with really low numbers (it emphasizes the fact that every point of health is very important), but I got drawn into this game pretty quickly. Usually I'm not a fan of "rouge-likes", but this game is one of the better of the genre; you build up gear at a good pace, your chance of survival increases dramatically all the time, and after you've snowballed into almost an almost unstoppable menace, it doesn't feel too upsetting when it almost inevitably ends in your tragic death nevertheless.
The combat and platforming are very smooth, and the delay before each of your swings makes each well-timed hit feel really satisfying. The crafting system is quick, simple, interesting, and rewarding to anyone who manages to get their hands on some good materials.
The random stat and ability rolls can get a bit annoying, seeing as there are few enough possible stat combinations that it's usually only a matter of time before you get your ideal stats and decent abilities. But overall, it's still quite satisfying when you end up with a perfect combo of stats and traits right away.
Although beginnings may be rocky (my first few runs lasted literally seconds), a little bit of practice goes a long way towards sustained runs.

Overall, I would reccomend this game cautiously. Despite the previous sentence, there are a few big things with the writing that are going to cause me to give this a negative review.
-The game WILL ACTUALLY LECTURE YOU on issues like friendzoning and why if you think this you are a dark, terrible misogynist. To see this, in the Light Reactor quest in the beginning of the game return the Light Reactor to Janie Springs. Torgue will come in with the friendzoning claim, and then he later interjects how he has seen the light and is a much better person now.
-There are many homosexual queer characters (Which is great! More representation is better! All for that!), however the game will rub it in your face constantly that they are queer, as if this is their defining trait. We get it, they like the same gender as they are, stop pushing it in my face constantly.
-Game is comparatively shorter, only being 11 Chapters which will take you about 15 hours to beat (including 95% of sidequests)
-You will constantly have to find oxygen, as about 80% of the game is outside where there is no atmosphere (speaking of, how are they outside without any suits to protect against the cold? No real explanation for that).
There are also a few really awesome things I like about this Borderlands that should be included in all future games.
-When doing quests, your character will actually hold a conversation with the quest giver (giving you more immersion as well as giving insight into the character's personality), and for me, this gives me a reason to play all the characters to hear what they all will say!
-When doing a second playthrough (True Vault Hunter Mode or Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode), the game actually changes the dialog. The first playthrough is framed as Athena telling a Story to Lillith and company, and the Second playthrough is framed as Brick and Tiny Tina wanting to hear the story again, but more awesome. It makes a second playthrough feel much fresher.
-The plot is pretty interesting, as it details Handsome Jack's descent from "Hero of Elpis" to "CEO Psychopath" in BL2.
So with all this in mind, buy if you want. It's not a bad game by any means, but not really a great one either.

Relatively short but fun game with you as a man 'who just wants some quiet'. Your mission is simply to kill everyone at a party, or rather at party after party. Just that - without being spotted and caught by the cops or the bouncers. You can stab people, poison them or use the environment and traps to maim them. Assassins of Kings is the best title in a phenomenal series and a must buy
The story revolves around a witcher (monster hunter) named geralt as he is framed for a king's murder and tries to hunt down the real culprit.  The main story is a massive, well written tell that features great elements of player choice and style on a a level I've never seen on a video game before as the entire 2nd act is completely different based on the choices you make.  Outside of the main story, even the side quests are often deep and compelling with the player forced make heavy choices and decide how they want to shape the world.
The gameplay is a difficult mix of swords, spells and potions that is not necessarily easy and has a massive skill cap.  Once you get the feel for it, it's massive fun though and the challenge always feels rewarding.  Plus, with the rpg skill trees to focus on, it allows the player to change thier focus and fundamentally affect thier play style.  The enemies also provide a noice variety as a main focus of this game is the monsters. Despite being well designed and creative, they all have thier own strength and weaknesses making knowledge a uniquely featured component that I've never seen donen to this level.
The game is massive and will take you a healthy ammount of time to finish, as well as fantastic title to replay through trying out new things and looking for new outcomes in quests and the main story.
The artistic strength was in the beautiful environments, good music, and a well acted voice cast.
The only two factors that should stop someone playing this game is A) the length and B) the content.  It's a bit raunchy in all aspects and definatly not for children.  If you're good with all that though, don't even think about skipping the best title in the Witcher series.

Loadout is a weird game. Seriously: it combines exceptionally detailed physical trauma, the worst twinge of sexual humor a-la Saint's Row, and pop culture references into a third-person arena shooter that seems to really like TF2's art style. And it still manages to pack a ridiculously detailed weapon customization system after all that. While it sounds like the perfect pick-up-and-play shooter, spending time with it quickly dissipates the initial appeal, however.
The first thing you get tired of is the rampant, middle-school level sexual humor. The player characters (a Rambo impersonator, a Mr. T impersonator, and an overweight trailer-trash woman named Helga) can be customized with items and taunts to purely flaunt their genitalia or repeat the same obscene gesture over and over.
After some time in the game you'll quickly learn that while building your guns piece by piece is tremendously fun, you're going to be shoehorned into specific variants simply because they're the best in their class. Unfortunately, all things equal, Beams and Rockets will beat out Pulse and Bullets the majority of the time. Similarly, while Tesla is great fun, Pyro trumps it except with certain gun builds due to higher damage plus after burn. Sniper mods can make instagib laser cannons, while that cool recoilless rebounding-tesla bullet Gatling gun you made seems to do no damage or hit targets further than arms reach. Health payloads seem to heal you for almost nothing, while Juice payloads feel like a wasted gun.
The game is, unfortunately for those who have tastes similar to mine, an arena shooter. This means it is exceptionally fast, and relies on a matchmaking service to pit two four-man teams against each other. If anything, this game SCEAMS for some form of server support. Somewhat larger maps with a higher player count would likely make the game much more fun to play and actually have that boot and play feeling. Plus, it'd be a great way of trying new gun builds against human opponents without worrying about the credit grind.
Yes, that's right. There is a credit grind. Luckily, the developer has done well by the unlock system. Mostly. Gun parts are unlocked permanently through the use of "Blutes," the in-game currency you're awarded at the end of each match. Each gun type - Bullet, Launcher, Beam and Pulse - have its own tech trees. While parts are duplicated across the gun tech trees, you need to unlock each individually; buying the suppressor barrel for Bullet cores will not unlock it for the other three core types. However, the rather slow Blute farm rate - roughly 500 per game if you're MVP on the winning team - tempts you to buy boosts from the real-world currency shop.
Here's the rub. Cosmetics, gun and load out slots, and boosts can only be bought with real dollars. While this is a good thing compared to how other games follow the F2P-P2W shop setup, those who have money to spend on boosts will inevitably earn faster and have the "better" gun build sooner. This can definitely suck the enjoyment out of the game for a new player still adjusting to the speed of the game. Even worse, for 3800 Blutes, you can permanently have a shield which adds another health bar to your character.
Tech unlock prices are questionably set. Tesla and Pyro grenades are very cheap compared to their support counterparts. However, the respective payloads are exactly the opposite.
At least gun customization is fulfilling, even if you feel forced into what could be labelled as a "meta build" when actually playing. The parts available are awesome and sometimes downright wacky: imagine a handheld fully automatic hex barrel tesla-flak firing mortar that has an x-ray scope you can see enemies' skeletons through walls with. The disgustingly detailed ways player characters die is also hilarious despite the morbidity of it. Surviving headshots might leave you running around with just a brain and eyestalks. You might suffer an explosive wound that leaves a gaping hole in your torso with which you can assess the remaining number of organs you have. And the play modes are varied and enjoyable - wait till your first time nabbing the enemy hammer.
Loadout is at a crossroads right now. On one hand it can stay awesome and get new weapon parts and some rebalances and stay free of the P2W mentality. On the other, it can tread down the same road Tribes: Ascend has and become a great idea marred by a terrible microtransaction system and a clearly imbalanced meta. Time will tell; for now, I can recommend this as a truly fun F2P game, despite its minor frustrations.
Edit: It feels like the game has become a novelty concept that has fallen into the common trap of F2P. The humor wears thin, and the gameplay isn't solid enough to carry the game forward, in my opinion. Worth having some fun with, but don't expect any real compelling drive to play.

This is my first experience within Yoko Taro's creative mind and I am in love with it.
The themes are strong (even though most of them only truly appear in the last third of the story, after A and B endings). I'm pretty sure I will think about some of the questions asked for the years to come. The story left me with a bittersweet taste, which is pretty appropriate within the context.
The gameplay is decently fun, don't expect DMC or Bayonetta level of mechanics but you should find enough customization within the system (through weapons, pods and chips choices), enough stylish animations and variety in the gameplay to find something that suits you. It should be noted that about half of the side quests are either pretty boring or just plain bad (lots of goings of comings), don't power through it if you don't want to, you can 100% the game after the final ending thanks to a mode unlock.
The art direction is breathtaking. NieR is not the best looking game of this generation - far from it - but it fights its technical weakness with a deep dive in an apocalyptic dreamland. I find myself teared apart between the feeling of loneliness/desolation and the awe of this weird beautiful and fully living world that seems so familiar yet so alien.
Last but not least the OST... let's just say it's hands down the best game soundtrack I have ever listened. Poetic, tragic, sometimes really catchy, it finds itself perfectly in sync with what happens on the screen.
I never was a fan of JRPG, beat'em all or shoot'em up, yet this game found the perfect balance for me. With its unique perspective on the game as a media, NieR:Automata conquered my heart.

Alright, since I enjoyed the game so much I feel like I have to write a proper review so here we go. Let me start by saying that I don't enjoy anime that much and from what I've seen in the trailers it looked like the game had some anime style behind it. After all it's a Japanese game so I was not really sure if I would enjoy playing the game at all. Additionaly I never played the previous game or the Drakengard games which are suppose to be intertwined with the NieR franchise if I'm not mistaken. So I had no idea what to expect from this one but since it got so much praise I was curious still so I decide to try it out anyway. So after about 3 playthroughs and 50 hours spend on NieR:Automata I can certainly say that it was worth it.
What people have to keep in mind is the game is designed to be replayed multiple times. Of course you can be done after your first playthrough but then you would miss a huge portion of the story. The first two playthroughs narrate the same story but from different perspectives. The third one is actually pretty clever because the game makes a sequel to itself. In the first one you play as 2B a battle android that is part of the YoRHa Project designed to protect the remnants of mankind which was nearly wiped out but managed to flee to the moon. The story that is told us when we play 2B is failry simple but once you're done and start you second run things start to unfold drastically and the game becomes so much more interesting. On your second run you play as 9S, the latest infiltrator android model who is designated to gather intelligence behind enemy lines. Suddenly all the things you've learned as 2B appear not to be that simple anymore. Not only does the story become exciting but the enemies, setting and even the bosses do too. I could name dozens examples or so but that would spoil the game. The third playthrough was pobably my most favourite because like previously said, the game essentially plays as a sequel to itself. This time you play as A2, an older android model and a deserter. Things get even more complicated and you get couple of story twists which blow your mind.
The game is a hack'n'slash RPG. The combat system is not as advanced as the one in the Devil May Cry games where you can pull insane combos but is more similar to the one in Metal Gear Rising, straight forward and simple but very enjoyable. You have 4 weapon categories: small swords, large swords, spears and combat bracers. You have two slots if you play as 2B or A2 and depending on the combination and order the weapons are equipped you get different results each time. 9S lacks in this category since he has only one slot for only one weapon. His combos are dull but it is suppose to be balanced out with his "hack" ability which is a bullet hell minigame. Unfortunately the hacking gets boring quickly. Then there is a small crafting system. You can upgrade all your weapons and your Pod, with materials that drop from enemies or are scattered troughout the world. It's basic but still. My favourite part of the game was probably the chip system which allows you to customize your character quite a bit. You get lots of different chips as loot from enemies and as a reward for quests. Each chip has a different attribute and a value, the better the attribute the higher the value. However you can only equip so many until the combined value of chips doesn't reach the characters threshold. You can be jack of all trades or have insane melee damage with time slow on counter attacks. You can even remove parts of the HUD since these are chips too to make more room for other chips.
It's an open world game, the world however is not that big which is great in my book. Things are pact more tight, hehe, and there is always a quests somewhere nearby. You don't have to run 15 minutes to get things done and I really enjoyed it that way. The world offers a lot of variety in its locations too so there is not much to complain about. The music is fantastic. The only thing that really botheres me is the mediocre port which could be fixed of course but the developers take way too much time to do so.

I'd honestly like to recommend this game, but the current state makes it hard to accept its status as full retail and the overall price. While it has its redeemable elements, the issues outweigh the cost for the game at the current moment. Unless there's something like a considerable discount  (50% and above) the price isn't right.
First off, if you're here wanting an Ace Combat experience, the game is not what you're looking for. Boot up Ace Combat Infinity or hook up an emulator and dust off your PS2 disks instead. Vector Thrust has a lot of promise but at the moment there are many issues that need to be addressed before it happens.
Vector Thrust is an indie air combat simulator game with a cel-shaded art direction developed by the TimeSymmetry team, published under Iceberg Interactive. The game features arcade shooter elements such as large amounts of ammunition and fictional aircraft as well as setting, quick-action and skirmish modes, several challenge stages, standalone battle scenarios and a story-driven campaign. There are dozens of aircraft families to chose from, with several variants for each, with aircraft both famous and less-widely-known. The game features original musical score by José Pavli.
● Interesting proposal of a constructed world and timeline, in similar fashion to the known Ace Combat series.
● Active modding community with many additional aircraft, paint schemes, NPC voices, weapon, scenery, and extra content
● Good graphical detail on aircraft exteriors as well as weapons.
● Cel-shaded artstyle that gives a colorful, unique appearance to the game.*
○ Underwhelming amount of content for a full release, with many placeholder and seemingly rushed material, as well as incomplete or missing individual aircraft, challenge and aircraft family descriptions.
○ Disorganized content that yields misreferenced audio and dialogue, mismatching speech and text along occasional typos.
○ Slow campaign story pacing, with little emotional response to character interaction.*
○ Scenery seems simple and uninteresting at best, and downright barren at worst.
○ Removal-- and subsequent lack of restoration of HUD customization from older versions.
○ Steep AI difficulty curve from unresponsive to highly challenging during gameplay.
○ Friendly AI ground units during campaign seem to be mainly unresponsive to enemy presence.
○ Occasional crashes during gameplay.
○ Sound effects are toned down from how they actually sound in reality, along a distinct lack of sound in some occasions (sounds after a certain distance are inaudible, secondary aircraft explosions lack sound, etc).
○ Anti-air artillery and guns are exceedingly lethal (ranging from straight bullet death rays with zero spread to one-shell-kills) for a game that tries leaning to an arcade style, and missile guidance seems to be overly inaccurate.*
○ Voice acting can be described as "campy" in some lines, while it seems to be toned down in others.*
*: In my personal view and/or opinion.
Now, I will admit that I didn't buy this game expecting a perfect Ace Combat Infinity replacer on the PC, with all its features and complete, polished game mechanics, but Vector Thrust fails to accomplish a few things that I needed to have the patience to personally dig up info around (missing descriptions for aircraft like the XF10F, find proper replacement sounds for explosions and gunfire, add and reposition special weapons on aircraft that lacked secondary weapons while there were obvious hardpoints to support those, etc.) which wouldn't be needed to be done otherwise, which eventually got wiped as files were revalidated and updated into newer files, which, while I had hoped would have even more accurate info than what I had found out and filled in, sadly were the previous state of the files before I made any changes.
I'll give the TS team credit, the game has come a long way from the start as far as I see, but despite the slow update frequency I would rather have it that way than leave early access in the current state-- which just feels forced. Many things like aforementioned typos and dialogue lines being cut short or misreferenced, or even missing, it all makes me feel like the game still needed more development and content before being branded as full retail version.
This doesn't mean I gave up on the game, and all things considered, it is a decent game on itself with good potential, but for its current price Vector Thrust is not a reasonable deal at all, which is the main issue and a huge turn-off for anyone interested. I'm hoping that the devs don't take this review wrong as being only me lashing out disappointment, because in fact, those are just issues I'd rather see addressed sooner than later, since I hope to see this game attain a proper status as spiritual successor to Ace Combat. Right now however, it's not.

I want to tell you a story. It has spoilers, so consider yourself warned.
My JC Denton was a good agent. In the field, he was an intelligent, efficient snipe-happy hacker, with a pistol for emergencies. (Side note: Silenced sniper rifle + laser-sight pistol, both at Advanced skill level =OP.)
However, when he infiltrated the building Paul Denton told him to to show him that UNATCO was corrupt, my JC mixed up his objectives and went to the roof, where the satellite dish he was supposed to change if Paul was correct was located, instead of the basement, where the proof was. This was a bit of a dilemma.
Then my JC Denton had an epiphany.
He realized that he would work for whichever side allowed him to shoot, loot, and hack as much as possible. So right then and there, my JC hacked the satellite dish and looted what was inside, betraying his country for some immediate cheap thrills. Don't get me wrong, he wasn't psychotic; my JC was just extremely vindictive, self-righteous, and challenge-seeking, and he had a lot of guns.
He then went through the rest of the game, shooting and looting and hacking all over the place, and when the time came, he took the only sensible option and merged with Helios.

It looks awful, there aren't enough character options for the action-oriented player, the voice acting is atrocious, and some enemies have way too much health (lookin' at you, greasels). However, any game with this amount of player choice and understanding of the player (one time, when lost and trying to leave a cathedral, I walked up to a French chef and JC promptly asked how the hell to get out of there) deserves whatever recommendations it can get.
Seriously though, f*ck all the transgenics.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
I didn't think this kind of game would be my cup-of-tea, but "wow" what a refreshing and entertaining game. In Party Hard, you play as someone who is really tired of the neighbors having loud parties. Instead of calling the police, you decide it’s a better idea to kill everyone – using your faithful knife and the environment. The tactical strategy follows a series of killings at parties through-ought the USA.
The developers used to work mostly on casual, family-friendly games - until they participated in a game jam, creating the first prototype for Party Hard. TinyBuild backed up the original developers – Pinokl Games – to create a full version that’s coming to Steam on August 25th.
Party Hard has semi-procedural environments and focus on unique ways of killing people. In the greatest traditions of sneaking games, your main goal is not to get caught, while silently picking off unsuspecting victims one by one. Dancing and blending in during a suspicious situation is key.  - Highly Recommended!

It makes me sad to not recommend this game because it has so much potential. My main reason for not recommending it is that the autopilot is completely broken to the point where it is mostly worthless.
Autopilot cannot safely fly "fast" ships: it will crash them into star gates, other ships, and asteroids. Autopilot also cannot be used to gather the many pieces of the asteroid you are mining in a slow freighter as it will crash into asteroids, obliterating your ship. Unless you have the famous 3rd party "Bounce" mod installed (which marks your game as "modified"), your wingmen will collide into each other and explode. It's just ridiculous.
It is shocking to me that Egosoft has not only left the problem unfixed, but haven't even given the players the ability to mitigate this game-ruining defect. For instance, one user asked in forums if we could be given an option to simply turn off collision damage for our ship and Egosoft responded: "No, I'm afraid not."
It is not fun for me to manually pilot my ship through space or asteroid fields. It is also not fun to slowly float around, picking up the many chunks of the asteroid I have just exploded with my mining laser. Thus, I sadly cannot recommend this game.

It's one thing to have a hugely high learning curve.  That can actually be a positive thing; it generally means a complex and layered game, requiring thought and strategy.  But to marry this with some of the worse tutorials in gaming history, along with no documentation is mind boggling.  Fortunately, this game is popular and the fan base does provide much needed hints and guides, which without this game would be unplayable.
But the issues with this game go much farther.  After over 200 hours into it I am forced to ask this terrible question: Is this game full of bugs or intention AI cheats?  Consider.....
- My ships constantly ram asteroids and my stations.  NPC ships never do; not while trading or attacking.  Are they not using the same flight algorithms?
- Docking at stations:  I have 5 trader ships, all set with orders to deliver required goods to my hab complex.  But they refuse to dock.  Some will enter the vacinity of the hab and then refuse to move while others will ram my station destroying themselves.  Meanwhile, despite my setting my hab to  refuse trade with other races, their ships come and go as they please.  Again, it seems like the game has different NPC and player ship docking scripts.
- In combat.  I no longer carry missiles.  I was dying from missile attacks a lot.  Eventually I decided to watch one of my missiles in actions.  It was a silkworm and it ignored my targeted foe and came back and destroyed me.  In my experience, this misfire never happens to NPC ships.  Again, why the different behavior between player assets and computer.
- The addon package gives players the opportunity to blacklist sectors and stations for trade.  Doesn't work.  My assets still preferentially travel into Omnicron Lyre, in the hope of a quick death at the hands Terran's continual raids there.  I have found nothing that stops this behavior other than not exploring those sectors.
- SETA (Time Acceleration) is interrupted by almost every possible keyboard, mouse or game interruption.  It is frustrating and completely unnecessary.  But there is one thing that doesn't stop the game acceleration - notification that one of your ships is under attack.  This means that by time you stop the SETA, whatever asset was under attack is gone, with no hope of intervention from the player.  Why such an anti-playable implementation?
-  Station placement.  After placing and connecting two stations together, I often find myself unable to connect a third station to hab complex, even though I place the new station exactly between the previous two.  This requires many, many save and reloads until the game randomly (as far as I can tell) lets me connect the new station to my hab complex.
- The game promotes itself as having an in-game economy, but that is a lie.  All I have to do to massive increase an enemy's manufacturing ability is drop a bunch of Laser Towers in a sector they are attacking.  They immediately get a boost to production permitting them to quickly annihilate my defensive buildings.  Once my twenty  or so Laser Towers are destroyed, their raids return to fewer and smaller ships - meaning the best defense is absolutely no defense!
- Enemy ships instantly build and travel.  I'm in Omnicrom Lyre and I've destroyed all enemy forces there.  All I have to do to replenish them is travel out of system and then immediately return: my foe will be back in full force, despite their shipyards being many sectors away.  For me to rebuild a fleet of that size, fit with weapons and shields, and then to fly to the sector of combat, would require at least an  hour, assuming I had the huge mountain of resources already available.
- Mission difficult assignment.  This is the biggest joke of the game.  One mission will describe itself as being 'Hard' and send you to fight a couple scout class ships.  The next will be labeled 'Very Easy' and you'll find yourself  in a fight several  frigates and 6-8 escort fighter.
Great ideas with this game.  Part of me still loves it despite its warts.  It is a thinking man's game, very complex and requires many, many hours to master.  It is an incredibly nice change of pace from all the button mashers that dominate the game market.  And maybe I am wrong and all my complaints are the result of buggy code and poor game design but the preferential treatment NPC assets get over players make this a hard to believe hypothesis.
Still, if  you don't mind spending days on end figuring out how to meta-game around the bugs/cheats then this game is recommended.

I am so very, very glad that Disgaea was ported to the PC.
Super short - if you miss a good SRPG like Final Fantasy Tactics, this is in the same neighborhood. It's a slighlty different game, but nothing has scratched that itch like this, since - to include FFT-A (!).
This game is amazing, if you're at all a fan of gearing up, tweaking, and grinding in an RPG. It doesn't have the perpetual "oh no, didn't get lucky for that 1 in 1,000,000 roll" of the ARPG Diablo style games, and it doesn't have a "you must grind 1,000 levels over years" of a KRPG. With any RPG sensibilities, you most likely can clear the main game without ever grinding - natural leveling should cover things. If you *want* to keep going, you can - there are layers upon layers of additional challenges you can further advance your characters through, with commeasurate "hidden", "side" or "post-game" bosses/challenges to match up your advancement with.
Some don't like the story, and it isn't exactly going to win any awards, but I thought it was fine enough - and better than most JRPG stories (no fate of the world hanging in the balance, but still serious movers and shakers).
Love, love, love. And, the best part is... it looks like I can keep playing until I feel done. Awesome. Definitely not everyone's cup of tea, and if you're a completionist... better set aside the next year of your life.
And how many RPGs dare you to break "the rules" of the game? "Ah, I'm going to lift my characters and throw them over here and extend their movement and get bonus points on this or that..."

The first sim i bought for the pc was Race the WTCC game. which was about 4 or 5 years ago. I wasnt massively into sim racing then, it was just something i'd occasionally do, and i bought a cheap wheel and pedal set. Main reason i bought Race07 was coz i was into the BTCC and the WTCC in Race were the same cars (not exactly the same, but similar performance though some cars were in the BTCC that were the same such as the BMW 320 si).
A few years later i bought ETS2 and decided i wanted to play that properly with a proper good wheel so bought a G27, which was great. Not long before i bought this wheel i bought my second racing sim, Assetto Corsa but i was hardly playing it, mainly due to the steering rotation limit on the cheap wheel i had and i still wasnt into sim racing that much. It was the G27 that really got me into it then as i thought i'd try Race07 and AC with the new wheel and boy did i love it, the FFB and everything, felt great. So ever since i've been mostly just playing racing sims and went on to buy others such as GTR2, Raceroom Racing Experience, and iRacing which is subscription based.
One day i saw Stock Car Extreme, and by the sound of the name i thought it was some arcadey type play around game not worth a second look...but it was recommended to me in steam, so i gave it a look and saw so many positive reviews and i watched the videos and liked what i saw, couldnt believe it was a proper sim going by the name of it. So i ended up getting it and i can honestly say that despite the amount of different sims i have, i play this the most by far, in just offline racing as it is great. The physics, the FFB are spot on, despite the old graphics i've been loving it and i'm playing it the most despite paying a subscription for iRacing, along with the content on Raceroom.
Now i said that touring cars such as the WTCC as what i like the most so i should really be playing Raceroom the most as that simulates them and has the official cars from 2013 (and now 2014) but theres just something about Stock Car Extreme that i love so much with just the physics and FFB and it has such a great range of different series including multiple types of karts and different eras of F1.
I so highly recommend this game and hope everyone makes a contribution to Reiza studios' recent crowdfunding campaign. They deserve it with making such a great sim and adding so much content for free which for games like iRacing and Raceroom would cost you, per car and track, so buy this game you wont be disappointed and make a contribution so Reiza can push it beyond extreme whilst they work on their new sim, which i'm drooling over the thought of!
10/10
The only negative which is a downer for me is the championship scoring isnt implemented correctly and seems to be bugged, but Reiza have said they'll rectify this, even though it has been a while now but hopefully soon they'll have a permanent fix for it.

I'vr played this game for  hundreds of hours but just recently bought a Steam key for it.  This is hands down one of the best driving simulations on Steam.  It's moddable, easy to play, and has great cars and series that come with the sim.  The controls, handling, design, and artwork are fantastic. The force feedback is spot on and Reiza is one of the best developers in the business.  They have never charged for DLC for this game and have given several cars and tracks free as part of updates.   Short of not being able to create custom championships, there's not much missing nor are there many bugs.  This is the game that Assetto Corsa and Project Cars wish they could grow up to be.  The AI is the best on Steam and the single player portions of the game are fun and very time consuming.  I normally play with a Logitech DFGT, but before I bought it, I played this game forever with an XBOX Controller.  It works just as well as the wheel.  This is well worth a purchase.  As a matter of fact, buy this game now and leave Project Cars and Assetto Corsa on your wishlist for a whlie longer.  If you tire of the in game content, there's a downloadable mod or track for just about any series or track thats out there.  An amazing experience.

Honestly, I'm not too sure what to think about Vector Thrust right now, and it would require more experementation to figure out what the key issues is, if you come expecting this to be a direct Ace Combat clone, you will run into a few problems since the game doesnt play like a direct Ace Combat clone. I don't think it helps that your starting planes are so low tier that you won't have a real clue on how the flying feels like until you go through challanges to unlock each plane seperately, and there are a lot of aircraft to unlock, perhaps too much at a glance. Plus, there are some challanges that are either just pure broken or harder than it should be, that doesnt really help things.
I think whats throwing so many people off is that its not a direct Ace Combat clone, because of that. You end up playing this in the Ace Combat mindset and it ends up backfiring. This might have something to do with the flight model, or the planes. Or just the game in general. I'm not too sure.
Let me do a proper review in the future, i'd really need to put more time into it but as of right now. I really can't recommend buying this right now, especially with the asking price being nearly £20, in the state that its in right now.
Sorry, TimeSymmetry. I really didnt want to give you a negative review right now, seeing how you've been working on this since mid 2011, and what you have done is great. People say Disgaea is grindy, but what does that actually mean?
First off, I would say it's not grindy at all... if all you care about is beating the story (which is a good 30-40 hours of gameplay). The campaign is fun and well worth anyone's time. If you choose, you can overlevel your characters to have an easier time (it is really not necessary), but that can also suck the tension and fun out of the gameplay.
If, however, you want to play the post game content (which is upwards of 100 hours of gameplay time), this is where you have to grind your♥♥♥♥♥off. Let me give you an example.
The true final boss of the game essentially requires you to have several perfect items equipped. To get a perfect item, you need to collect bonus levels while leveling up an item. The "mystery" (aka RNG) portal that gives bonus levels CAN (but doesn't always) spawn every 3 floors. Even if the portal does spawn, it  LIKELY DOES NOT contain the bonus levels you need.
It means that every 3 floors, you RESET THE GAME if you don't find your portal. If you find a portal, YOU RESET your game if it isn't one that gives bonus levels. To get a perfect item, you'll end up quitting and reloading the game upwards of 200 times. By the time you've beaten the true final boss of the game, you've reset thousands of times and there is simply *no way around that.*
If you want to beat the post-game, you'll get really acquainted with this series of events: Menu, down down down down, quit game, yes, continue game, yes, talk to item worlder, enter item world, yes, check for portal, see that there in no portal, menu, down down down down, quit game, and repeat. You'll be doing that for hours. After a while your fingers hurt solely from resetting so much.
Does that sound like fun?
The true final boss of the game also requires you to have maxed out stats through leveling. Which means you'll be playing one map (Cave of Ordeals 4) over and over and over and over and over to level up, store somewhere between 6000-9999 levels, reincarnate to level 1, and do it again.
Does that sound like fun?
Just know what you're getting into. Personally, I don't mind leveling in the manner I just described. It's definitely not ideal, but you do get to watch your numbers go up, and in true "role-play" fashion, it does feel like your character is actually training.  I *DO*, however, mind being forced to reset the game so often in order to actually complete it. It's poor design. What happened is that people basically broke the ps2 version of the game by forcing perfect items through resets, and to compensate they released a boss that requires perfect items in the PSP version of the game. This version.
Disgaea 1 did not require resets very often (just fringe cases of rarity matching and removing specialists). Having 100%'d both D1 and D2 here on steam, I can say that I enjoyed the post game a lot more in the first installment.
I'm giving this game a lukewarm positive review because the story was fun the whole way through, and the post game has some decent content until you need to start perfecting stuff. I've read Disgaea 3 and upwards contain less of this "reset hell," so here's hoping.

It's very frustrating that I can't recommend this game, because I quite wanted to like it. There are several things I DO like about it, but, imo, they do not adequately compensate for this game's shortcomings.
The art and music of this game are wonderful, and I do not use that word lightly. The art style is one that draws your eye to every superb little detail. The music too is well-crafted, perfectly suiting the atmosphere of the game. The characters, with the sad exception of the irritating and monotonous protagonist Jerry, are delightful, delivering funny and engaging dialogue with tremendous voice acting.
However, the most important part of any game that has puzzles is that the puzzles are fun and challenging, without being overly difficult or convoluted; this game's puzzles fail on all these points. The puzzles depend on you clicking on everything in the game world, to make sure you have all the necessary items. Then, if you cannot deduce the often absurdly specific solution to a problem, you have to resort to trying every possible solution. Compounding this problem is Jerry, repeating himself every time you get something wrong, and it gets annoying VERY quickly. All in all, the needless complexity and ridiculousness of the puzzles means that they are an unpleasant distraction from an otherwise very enjoyable game.
I feel, with this game's strengths and weaknesses, that this game would have suited the visual novel medium better, so the characters, music and art could have more room to express themselves.
If you are a veteran point-and-click player who's used to these sort of poorly designed puzzles, then by all means pick the game up. Otherwise, I would suggest that the best way to experience The Night of the Rabbit would be to watch a playthrough on YouTube.

The second Witcher game is pretty good. The story is a little disconnected from the first due to "time missing" between them, but that hs to do with the story and never seemed to be something the developers forgot about. Graphically it is fair. Once you turn off all of the empty garbage they included like DOF, bloom, and motion blur, there is a nice looking game underneath. Positives would be overall a good game, a good story, and combat that is fair. Negatives would be the combat due to a sluggish combat system (hittin a button over and over again, waiting for the character to do what you want them to), and a game-breaking bug known to many that causes the game to just stop working when you try to save or when it auto-saves.
This save issue caused me to have to go back and forth from 1080 with all settings maxed out (except for the DOF and blurring stuff I dislike), to a 720p resolution with everything off JUST to get the game to run. FYI 7700k 1080ti and SSD built system. It's not me... Once the auto-save finally worked I could exit the game, turn the graphics back up to 1080p and even 4k and play with 60+ fps.
The area with the worst problem is the middle part of the game where you have to go back and forth between something, and it is poorly optimized so every time you move between this area the game auto-saves and crashes. Want to know more or are having the same problem? Search for it online and you will find thread after thread talking about the save issues.
Overall worth the money if you have not played this game. It is a little dated now, but much cheaper, you get the full package, and can play it on a midrange system with everything maxed at 1080p probably. I turned sharpening on by changing the user ini file and it also made many things look much better. Just my personal taste, but FYI some options not available in the advanced settings ARE available to change using the ini file. You can read more about it online if you want to turn off crap or make the game look nicer.

So, I'm going to try and make this as short as possible. This game, is devastating. It crushes you. It beats you so hard, you'll feel like someone just ripped out your spine.

You see, this game will most likely completely take you apart, but still. In the end, you WILL realize, if you don't want that sadness in your own life, then you have to enjoy it as much as possible.
Tomoyo After is all about loss. It shows you how cruel life can be, but it also shows you that there are people that bring some light into the darkness. Yes, people like Tomoya. Always trying, always giving there best, just so others can be happy.
But even so, what Tomoyo After is trying to say here is, you shouldn't let yourself get downed by tragedies. You always have to keep going. You have to move on, so you can expierence other happy and fun things in life. Even when it's hard, you have to keep fighting, to achive your own happiness. The happiness that can never be stolen away from you!
I know, this review didn't tell you too much about Tomoyo Afters actual content, but what exactly do you expect from a Key/Visual Arts production that is labled as a Visual Novel? Anyways, I tried to explain the way I feel about this game and why, to me, it's the most beautiful piece of art ever created.
Peace out. Im going to hug all the Dangos in my collection now, so I may be able to gather the strength, that is necessary to leave my room after playing Tomoyo After.

*- This game picks up almost immediately after the end of Tomoyo's Route in the original game CLANNAD, so if you haven't played that Route, you will be completely lost in terms of the overall context of the game, its main characters, and the various references and callbacks obviously won't make sense to you.
Also, I don't have a review for CLANNAD at the time of writing this, but I would highly recommend it; it is a quality VN with great music and varied and well written characters, and is definitely one of the better VNs on Steam.
I'm also going to avoid mentioning really any characters names or specific plot threads from either game, as discovering those things and coming up with your own impressions is the main fun of these types of games. -*
As you might expect, I can only recommend checking out this game if you enjoyed the world of CLANNAD in general or really liked Tomoyo's character and want to continue her story.
That being said, my first annoyance with the game is that the recurring characters (Tomoya and Tomoyo) don't entirely act the same way as they did in CLANNAD. The beginning of the game shows this most glaringly. I think I mainly found it hard to believe since almost barely any time has passed since the end of the original route, so in theory the characters should be much more familiar than they are. Tomoya is a lot more forward and kinda pervy in the beginning, and Tomoyo is much more girly and has mostly lost her tomboy-ish charm. She also basically ingnores Tomoya for a good portion of the game when a certain character is introduced, which is odd considering the game seems like it wants to setup the continuation of their romance and life together. I got over it pretty quickly, but I had just finished Tomoyo's Route for the first time the previous day before starting this game, so it was a little offputting.
Which brings me to my other big problem with the game, (and I feel like CLANNAD and Air seem to have this problem as well) which is that a lot of the depressing and bad things that happen to the characters kind of fell like they are there simply because they CAN happen, rather than whether or not the SHOULD happen. I'm not saying that everything needs to always be tied up in a nice bow by the time the credits roll, but overall it feels like the the final overall tension in the plot is somewhat forced rather than organic.
Example: The tension in the original Tomoyo Route in CLANNAD makes perfect sense given what you know about Tomoya and Tomoyo by that point, so all the drama and strife that complicates their relationship and how they respond to it makes perfect sense and is totally believeable (In fact, Tomoyo's original Route is probably the most realistic/believeable one in CLANNAD).
Those are my main issues, other than that, it is actually a really fun ride just watching Tomoya's everyday life. The side characters are decent and fun to talk to, if not lacking a little depth. The final arc of the True Ending was actually quite touching and very enjoyable, but again, I felt the actual final moments of the game with a bit half-baked and forced. In most of the endings it seemed like they were going for a "bittersweet" vibe, but really ended up feeling a bit abrupt and unsatisfying. Specifcally, the final CG "cutscene" quickly runs through a lot of really important threads that could have maybe just been expanded on in 2-3 normal VN gameplay moments to make a little less rushed.
The best thing I can say about it is that the True Ending will surely make you feeling something about it, whether that's good or bad. The overall normal day to day characters interactions are really good, but lacks some side character depth when compared to the original game.

I really wish I could give this game a positive score, ideally this is an ace combat style game for PC with a touch of realism added on top of it, but this doesn’t seem the case, so let’s see all the issues that in my opinion the game has.
First of all the missiles: missiles in vector trust are next to useless, all of them seem to point to an imaginary target behind the enemy aircraft instead of at the aircraft itself, for the so called rear quarter missiles, or in front of the enemy aircraft for modern all-aspect missiles.
While it’s true that I haven’t tested every single missile in the game, which has a vast arsenal of weaponry, just seeing the R-73 not behaving like it should in a game that is supposedly something a bit more than plain arcade is not a pleasant sight. On top of this the game locking system is clunky, cycling all the targets in the area instead of giving priority to the ones near your aiming point is a severe drawback in close dogfights or against large amounts of ground forces, as it makes AA targeting rather difficult.
Overall you are better off using the guns on your planes rather than missiles; these are both more accurate and more damaging.
Secondly, the planes: Vector Thrust offers a vast array of planes and this would be a good thing if there weren’t some odd decisions in their lineup, a lot of them are either made up versions or obscure prototypes. It would be good if planes like the Mig-25 and 31, Tornado, Eurofighter, Harrier and F-18 weren’t missing from the game. Instead we get stuff like the Lampyridae, a prototype German stealth fighter that didn’t get past the mockup phase, XF-10, a prototype from the 50ies, and a plethora of fictional version for almost all aircraft in the game.
All of this coupled with the total lack of a cockpit view (there is only third person, virtual cockpit and cinematic mode) makes the vast plane array a weak point rather than a strong point: it would have been much better to focus on few famous planes, with full cockpit, rather than dispersing the focus on one off prototypes.
Thirdly, the challenges: on paper the idea sounds great; each plane in game has a challenge that you need to complete to use the plane in quick action, skirmish and multiplayer mode, furthermore planes are divided in families and you need to unlock the planes one by one in each family. For example completing the F-16A challenge is required to unlock the F-16C challenge, this is again a good idea that could give a good sense of progression as the player slowly gets better and better planes.
The execution though is sub-par as challenges are repetitive and more often than not they are unrewarding: one of them requires you to gather at least 20 floating stars while two F-16 will happily sit on your tail firing everything they have, the reward for that is a Jaguar A, unless you are a real Jaguar fan this is not worth the hassle.
Not every plane has its challenge so, unless you mess around with the game files or buy them with in-game points gathered after every challenge, you can forget getting the F-22 or Su-47.
Lastly there is the rather important fact that this game is supposedly complete, while from my understanding Time Symmetry is largely a one man development team and there are updates coming our way including more planes and challenges (and eventually cockpits). Currently the game is in a broken state and it’s not worth the money.

This is one of the best games I've ever played.
It's an action/RPG first person game with a lot of different ways to play. You can go inside a building through the front door, or you can find a back entrance. You can hack computers, digital locks, and security consoles, but you can also get the password somewhere. You can pick locks, but you can get the key from somebody. You can kill your enemies, but you can just avoid encountering them at all.
The level designs are just brilliant. They're big, but not huge. You can easily memorize them, so it's easy not to get lost. Some of the levels are visited more than once and it feels different everytime, yet you still remember the places.
The graphics aren't amazing and they may look outdated, but they fit the atmosphere perfectly. The music is great and every location has its own soundtrack that fits to what you're currently doing.
The story is great and a little bit complex with conspiracies here and there, but there's not much to tell without spoiling it. This game is set in 2052 and it takes place in a chaotic world filled with terrorists, drugs, diseases, and augmented humans. There's a lot of memorable characters in this game, and every single one of them has their own personality. You can kill some of the important characters but instead of failing the mission, it will change the story and you will have to face the consequences.
In short, it's a great classic game with a great story and music that combines RPG, FPS, action, and stealth elements with a lot of different playstyles to choose.

I bought this game long before it ever came to early access. I was looking for a decent Ace Combat clone for the PC. This is not it.
Flying feels almost innertialess, and as long as the plane remains upright, The plane doesn't have the tremors of a normal plane that has wind acting on it, and instead stays perfectly steady. Neither combat or flying feel particularly fun. The developer decided what Ace Combat lacked was realism and sought to make the fifty or so missles your aircraft carries perform more like real missiles. However, the end result is that they perform more like rockets and even a slight incline will cause the missiles to miss.
Not only is it not fun to fly or fight in this game, the game takes place over almost featureless terrain. The first mission features a crater in an otherwise perfectly flat desert. The dialogue in the mission give the impression that the crater was created by a bomb; however, why someone would use a nuke or superweapon to attack a featureless desert is beyond me.
Lastly, the voice acting is bad: genuinely bad. The quality varies wildly between actors as does the clarity and volume level. The music is better, if unmemorable, but seems to be poorly used and paced.
I know it was a small development team, and likely the work of passion of a small team of programmers, but the game seeks to emulate a style of story that requires comptentences that this team simply did not have. I cannot, in good concience, recommend that you buy this game.

Awesome little game from the makers of Smite.
The comparison with Overwatch are getting old, also because to be honest, only people who didn't play Paladins but for a couple hours could utter such nonsense.
I own both games, and it hurts to admit I find Paladins to be considerably more fun than its pay to play counterpart.
Every character is deeply customizable through a card system, each of which boosts various aspects of one specific ability of the champion they belong to. To make things even more different, prior of chosing a deck before the match starts, you also can choose a legendary card, which turns the champ's focus towards a specific gameplay rather than another.
Another peculiar aspect of Paladins is the in-game item shop.
Your opponents are trying to be clever and got a 3 tanks push force? Have your damage champs pick the Wrecker item and see them crumble as a house of cards. Not really THAT effective, but it helps a lot in making the point of an all tank team moot. 16 items to choose from, 1 for each category, if you're good enough to get the necessary credits to buy them that is.
Game keeps getting update after update, more and more champions and maps. As I write this review, Lian the noble rifleman(woman?) has been released, Janos the astronomist support is coming next patch and two more heroes called Owl and Demon are on their way.
A specific mode makes the players face off on test maps to make the necessary changes before release and so on and so forth.
What did we get from Overwatch? Freaking 3 heroes in almost a year and no other extra content. For the pricetag it wears, I'd expect as much activity as Paladins' demonstrates.
Community. Maybe I have been lucky and I still am, but I didn't find an ounce of OW toxicity in Paladins' community than I keep meeting in the Blizzard's title. I have no issues admitting than I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at having tossed money at Blizzard for this, but what's done is done.
Gotta love those who yell "UNBALANCED!" then go play OW. Those are really the best.
TL:DR - Good game, continuously updated, frequent new content, customizable champions' playstyles and not overpriced unlocks for what regards the champs. Some skins are quite pricey but not necessary.
Skip OW if you're lucky enough to not have bought it yet, and come have fun on a game that's competitive but tries to be casual.

The short version: If you're a BL fan and you haven't played this yet, then get it when it's on sale and it'll be OK.  Don't pay much for the DLC, and it's not the end of the world if you don't get them, unless you really needed to play as "Jack" or the Huntress, which are both OK.
Series Ratings:
Borderlands: 8.5/10
Borderlands 2: 9.5/10
Borderlands - The Pre-Sequel: 7/10 (at best)
It's more Borderlands fun and if you're a big BL fan, then sure, get it cheap and have some fun.  But this definately feels like it was created and coded by the B-team, if not C-team.
It's just not as fun and well written.  The coding is pretty sub-standard for the series, there's a ton of minor glitches that you run into.  None of them are major, but they're just all over the place.  Whether it's items or enemys falling through surfaces, events that don't trigger properly (but will eventually, so don't panic if it happens), or one of my big game pet peeves, getting caught on textures while running around.  I mean, it happens a lot in several areas, but for example there's one spot on the Helios space station where I always get stuck running down a hallway.  Then I have to jump over the texture to go forward.  Just a lot of minor lack of polish that says to me that having that dev team disband was no great loss.
One issue with the story is that it's pretty much being told from the perspective of one character, Athena.  I briefly played as another character to see if I'd like it, and everything seemed the same to me.  So unless something changes that I just hadn't gotten to, it's kind of jarring to be playing as someone other than Athena and then keep getting these interuptions with Athena and Lilith. (though those are more common early in the game, so maybe doesn't seem as bad the longer you play).  I'm also not crazy about any of the character power sets.  As it was, I ended up using Athena just to stick with the story.
There was a nice story twist near the end on Helios that I liked, but I won't say more to spoil it.
Running around in vacuum is a double-edged sword.  It adds some new game eliments which are interesting, but also some slightly annoying ones, like when you open a chest and everything gets blown out.  Now on the one hand, that's kinda cool and funny.  But then it's not funny when the ammo you wanted goes flying up and falls down somewhere you can't reach.

It's actually a surprisingly fun game.  It's addicting to play, and very difficult to master.  However, in a lot of ways I feel it falls flat--to the point where I really just wish it was NOT a rogue-like.  The crafting system is positively atrocious.  Combining one item with another in a sequence in order to make something.  It could easily be overcomplicated and become very tedious when starting new runs.
The monsters themselves are also an issue.  Some monsters are fun and challenging and rewarding to defeat, whilst others are just ridiculously annoying.  I can't stand going around a corner only to be killed by something I couldn't even see to begin with!
The camera system can be a very useful thing, as it allows you to easily pan the screen (to a degree).  Though it doesn't seem to get disabled when the window isn't active, so if you quickly alt tab to do something don't expect to be able to see something coming at you since your screen will likely be far away from your actual character.
I want to like this game--and more than anything I want to recommend it--but it's just far to frustrating right now and this isn't mitigated enough by playing with friends for it to matter.  I really hope the developer just trashes the current crafting implementation and reworks it entirely, as it's just not fun or intuitive.  Especially at that price.  There are just other games that would appeal more for the same amount, or cheaper.  I'm interested to see where the developer takes this, but I just cannot recommend it as is.
Note that this is currently only a review of the Early Access (I believe 0.7), so obviously these are subject to change.  It's just a matter of if they will or not.
Thank you.
Edit: After full release, I still cannot recommend.

A decent space flying game with a lot of variety in the gameplay... but also a very broken game.
X3: AP is about flying and doing whatever you like. "Whatever" in this particular case can mean a lot of things, such as fighting or trading or completing missions or playing with stock exchange, building your own fleet and base, exploring new territories... and most of these things are fun. When they work.
The flying is pretty good, and the gameworld consists of many small areas (which is pretty weird for a space game, I think), many of the mare quite similar, but the environments are impressive nonetheless. There is about 270 areas to explore, and flying to see new places is a joy in itself.
Combat is alright, but it could be better. It's not bad though, just very average. Fortunately, building your own fleet and base give a lot of satisfaction and are worth your time.
There are both main quest missions and generated random missions. While I can say that I quite like the randomized missions, which are varied and even interesting (for a generated ones), the main quests are simply... broken. Sometimes I could not complete a main quest because one of the missions bugged out. The story isn't really that interesting in the first place though, so you might as well forget about the storyline.
Trading is alright, just like combat, and it's a totally viable option too. If you don't want to fight, then trading is a good way to spend your time in this game, enjoyable when combined with exploration, and it's also the easiest way to generate a lot of money. Avoid stock exchange though, it's broken and developers never cared enough to fix it.
AI is dumb as bricks... or even worse. Autopilot crashes you into other ships (or "buildings") a lot, and if you are near gates, then sometimes a ship spans at your position and you explode. This is quite frustrating. Enemies are easy to out-maneouver.
The sounds in this game... are bad. You should accept the fact that apparently there is air in space and you hear sounds of everything around you, while explosions look very... Earthy. Sounds disappoint, but music is great and differentiates a lot between various areas. Some of the tracks are great to listen to even outside of the game.
X3: Albion Prelude is even larger than previous X games. It has more territories and more ships. It's a decent game well worth a purchase, and probably the best to play in the series, especially if you have never played any X game before. I recommend it to those who like space action games (some people wrongly describe it as "space simulator", do not get mistaken, there is no simulation in this game) and sandbox games where they just play around without any specific goal, and I recommend it to those who have never tried any space game before as X3: AP is a good way to check out if you like the genre. Overall, a good game, but quite bugged.

If you've got a couple months you don't need for anything, buy X3:AP.  I've been playing off and on for a few years (plus time spent with X3: Reunion, which was probably around 500 hours), and I'm still discovering new features.  I've also now fallen down the rabbet hole of mods and add-ons, which just make it even more complex.
The basic game is relatively simple:  fly around space, shoot pirates, and trade.  But there are a bunch of other races, and it may turn out that you want to befriend some of the pirates instead of shooting them, and what is going on with the Terrans?
There's really one downside to this game:  it's hard to get into.  Many games have a learning curve:  that's not unusual.  I have heard it said of this game that "it has a learning brick wall, topped with broken bottles."
Yeah, that's about right.  Do not buy this game expecting to jump in and get everything.  Don't expect to do well early on.  There are a lot of mistakes to be made, and you're going to make a lot of them... I think just about everyone who plays it has.
Despite that, the graphics are excellent, it's old enough that it runs OK on lower spec hardware (although if you turn up all the graphics options it can push a modern low end gaming machine), it's complex enough to stay interesting, and there's a huge community making and publishing modifications for it.  Oh, and as you reach milestones, you'll unlock harder and harder starting positions.  Like a Paranid who has no money, no goods, a death mark on his head, and three days to live... and the cure is going to cost 25 million.
All in all, I think it's a fantastic game.  It's well worth the money, and well worth the time spent learning to play.

tldr:
- A rather mediocre top-down rogue action game with dark humor. I keep returning to it when I have a minute and I don't feel like doing anything complex or time consuming. too long part:
You're playing as Isaac - a little kid whose mom is nuts and wants to kill him, so he descends through a trap door in his room to fight his way through creepy places with creepy monsters in them.
- Simple but hard to master controls. Depends on anyones taste.
- The game has its own economy and a SH*TLOAD of upgrades, active skills and consumables to be discovered. Each upgrade and skill is very interesting and fun to mess around with. While it's tempting to google what does what, it's way better fun to just pick something up and see what it does.
- Levels are randomized and there is a lot of various monsters and bosses to spice things up. You won't play the game the same way twice. From this point of view the game offers infinite replayability, but...
- The fact that everything is so heavily randomized prevents you from forming any sort of your own strategy. You just dive in and keep going until you win or die. Over time, this reduces the cool variety to the point where you're doing the same thing over and over again and it's only a liiiiiiiittle bit different because of some dice roll.
- There is not much persistence to keep you returning for more. There are few unlockable characters and mandatory achievements but upgrades and skills are limited for each run where you find them. While it's nice to know that the game doesn't have you on a leash trying to unlock everything, it doesn't really motivate you to achieve anything when you start from zero every single time.

First, before you read this, go buy either the reiza bundle or game stockcar extreme, and start installing it while you read this, you'll thank me.
At first sight, the title might not seems so appealing, if you are like me and nascar ain't your thing, then likely, like me, you have never checked really what was game stockcar.
I've been driving in rF2 since 2012, and I had heard game stockcar mentioned a few times.  And often, people were talking about it with convictions.   I had enough with rF2 and then AC came out, spent some time with it, realized it wasn't really my cup of tea, so I'm back to rF2.  The gMotor engine sims are just the best.
It is only recently that I realized that game stockcar extreme is actually brazil's stockcar, which are more like touring cars than nascars.
So I bought the bundle.  And boy... I should have gotten this long before.
You have to know that game stockcar is using an heavily modded rFactor 1 engine.  And pushes it so far, that you'd almost think they are using the rFactor 2 engine.
For a long time, I believed ISI/Simbin were the best at making tracks, regarding accuracy, details, texturing, blending,  repetitions, etc.. they are certainly above Kunos... and I'm not talking about how they look in game, AC have a better graphic engine.
But after trying out GSCE, it's clear that Reiza is at the top.  I have yet to try out all tracks, but so far, might have tried 7-8, and they all look fantastic.  Tarmac textures are the best I've ever seen.  And this goes for pretty much everything.
The tracks themselves are super nice.  I would move to Brazil any day to be able to race these tracks as much as I would like to.  I'm a huge nordschleife fan, and I've raced this track for 3 years straight, and the tracks in there are very nice.  Why did I mentioned the nordschleife, not because GSCE have such a track, but I mean, the nordschleife is a nice flowing tracks, and most of those in GSCE are like this.  Very few tracks with tight hairpins, and lots of tracks with nice fast bends, plenty of challenging S, and all kind of long curves.
The track surface (road definition) is probably the best I've seen as well.  The tracks feels very alive.
The AI is what you would expect from a gmotor engine based game, excellent.  I have to train quite a bit on a given track in order to beat the AI at the default 95%.  They are certainly very challenging.
FFB is awesome, and it's hard to say which I like best between rFactor 2 and GSCE.  That's much to say, since it's using an older engine.
If you buy the bundle and get the formula truck, then you can race racing semis on the same track selections.
If you like real simulators, then you are missing on much if you are passing on this.
