tl,dr: SCE has tons of great content and compelling gameplay and is worth your time and money.
When I first saw Stock Car Extreme on Steam, I thought it seemed like something that wouldn’t interest me. “Stock Cars” mostly means NASCAR in the US, and I don’t like that kind of racing. And “Extreme”? Huh?
It turns out the “Stock Car” comes from the Stock Car Brasil series which is similar to DTM. The “Extreme” is from Reiza’s (the developers) connection to “Cockpit Extreme Racing” which is a line of sim-racing cockpit products. I have forgiven the somewhat puzzling name.
After reading some reviews and watching some YouTube videos, I tried the demo found on Reiza’s website (actually based on the 2012 version) and it clicked with me right away, so I uninstalled it and bought the game.
SCE packs impressive content right there in the box. As of right now, there are 62 tracks included with the game. Most of these are located in South America or are historic versions of tracks from around the world. I think that is very cool. These are excellent circuits that are new to me, but aren’t contrived “fantasy” circuits. (Reiza knows how to make them look absolutely beautiful, too.)
For me personally, not seeing Spa, for example, is a little refreshing. I do really like that track, but seems that almost every racing game these days has the same core set of famous tracks while there is so much else to see. SCE supports tons of existing mods as well as SCE-specific mods, so you’re sure to find just about any track or car you like anyway.
Even though SCE is named after the Stock Car Brasil series, it offers many other classes of cars ranging from 1976 F1 cars to the Metalmoro prototype to Karts to 2014 F1 cars and more. Each class feels so different from the next that you are offered a very broad range of driving experiences.
Scroll up and look at the list of DLC. Hint: it isn’t there. Reiza is continually updating the game and providing new content for free. New tracks and cars just show up in the game updates. For free.
SCE has fantastic gameplay. Most sims these days have convincing vehicle physics and SCE is right up there with the best of them.
• The engine, tires, and road sounds are all well done and sound great. Some of the metal-on-metal scraping sounds aren’t great, but everything else is really good.
• The AI behave realistically and they make realistic mistakes, just like anyone. With the default and most appropriate aggression setting, they won’t crash into you like a dumb human, but will pass you when it’s proper to do so.
• The force feedback effects are very good, but can be inadvertently ruined a little by the user if the controller settings are wrong outside of the game. There is a guide on the official Race Department forum for setting up your wheel. Once you have it set up properly, though, the FFB effects are as good as you’ll find anywhere.
• There is a 24-hour cycle present in the game, so if you start an evening race (which looks fantastic), you may end up finishing in the dark.
• The game modes are the usual simulation kinds of modes: there is Single Race, Testing, Championship, and of course Multiplayer. There are no “challenge” style events or modes. Just the kind of racing you might have in the real world.
The in-game options let you tweak all the things you’d expect, but if you dive into the various config files, you can really tweak everything to exactly what you want. For example, I have my track map going the full height of the monitor, but only within the leftmost 20% of the screen. I also have the sectors of the track on the map display in different colors.
There are many in-game options you can change while in the garage, without having to go back to the main menu like some other titles.
SCE will likely work on whatever computer you happen to have. Because it utilizes the original rFactor engine (though you wouldn’t guess by looking), it is really light on system requirements. It’s almost guaranteed that anyone can get high framerates in SCE. It looks very good, but of course it doesn’t look as sugary-sweet-beautiful as Assetto Corsa or Project Cars, but sim racing is about more than just pretty pictures, isn’t it?
One drawback I could scratch up is that the interface in the menus looks dated and stretched by default. There is an easy to install mod (literally just replacing a folder) that makes the front-end much nicer and easier to navigate.
Also, it really works best with a wheel. You don’t need an expensive force-feedback setup, but a wheel (even non-FFB) will give you a better experience than a gamepad. When I first got SCE, I tried my Xbox360 controller and a Saitek P990 and never really got the settings dialled in very well like you might have in a Codemasters game.
The gamepads were just a little too twitchy, so I dug my 16-year-old Microsoft Sidewinder Wheel (non-FFB, 200-degree-rotation) out of the garage, and it was so good. I played SCE with that wheel for a couple of weeks before the game compelled me to buy my G27.
Stock Car Extreme is definitely worth buying whether you’re only interested in trying simulation racing or if you already have a collection of sim titles.

It's actually a surprisingly fun game.  It's addicting to play, and very difficult to master.  However, in a lot of ways I feel it falls flat--to the point where I really just wish it was NOT a rogue-like.  The crafting system is positively atrocious.  Combining one item with another in a sequence in order to make something.  It could easily be overcomplicated and become very tedious when starting new runs.
The monsters themselves are also an issue.  Some monsters are fun and challenging and rewarding to defeat, whilst others are just ridiculously annoying.  I can't stand going around a corner only to be killed by something I couldn't even see to begin with!
The camera system can be a very useful thing, as it allows you to easily pan the screen (to a degree).  Though it doesn't seem to get disabled when the window isn't active, so if you quickly alt tab to do something don't expect to be able to see something coming at you since your screen will likely be far away from your actual character.
I want to like this game--and more than anything I want to recommend it--but it's just far to frustrating right now and this isn't mitigated enough by playing with friends for it to matter.  I really hope the developer just trashes the current crafting implementation and reworks it entirely, as it's just not fun or intuitive.  Especially at that price.  There are just other games that would appeal more for the same amount, or cheaper.  I'm interested to see where the developer takes this, but I just cannot recommend it as is.
Note that this is currently only a review of the Early Access (I believe 0.7), so obviously these are subject to change.  It's just a matter of if they will or not.
Thank you.
Edit: After full release, I still cannot recommend.

Awesome little game from the makers of Smite.
The comparison with Overwatch are getting old, also because to be honest, only people who didn't play Paladins but for a couple hours could utter such nonsense.
I own both games, and it hurts to admit I find Paladins to be considerably more fun than its pay to play counterpart.
Every character is deeply customizable through a card system, each of which boosts various aspects of one specific ability of the champion they belong to. To make things even more different, prior of chosing a deck before the match starts, you also can choose a legendary card, which turns the champ's focus towards a specific gameplay rather than another.
Another peculiar aspect of Paladins is the in-game item shop.
Your opponents are trying to be clever and got a 3 tanks push force? Have your damage champs pick the Wrecker item and see them crumble as a house of cards. Not really THAT effective, but it helps a lot in making the point of an all tank team moot. 16 items to choose from, 1 for each category, if you're good enough to get the necessary credits to buy them that is.
Game keeps getting update after update, more and more champions and maps. As I write this review, Lian the noble rifleman(woman?) has been released, Janos the astronomist support is coming next patch and two more heroes called Owl and Demon are on their way.
A specific mode makes the players face off on test maps to make the necessary changes before release and so on and so forth.
What did we get from Overwatch? Freaking 3 heroes in almost a year and no other extra content. For the pricetag it wears, I'd expect as much activity as Paladins' demonstrates.
Community. Maybe I have been lucky and I still am, but I didn't find an ounce of OW toxicity in Paladins' community than I keep meeting in the Blizzard's title. I have no issues admitting than I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at having tossed money at Blizzard for this, but what's done is done.
Gotta love those who yell "UNBALANCED!" then go play OW. Those are really the best.
TL:DR - Good game, continuously updated, frequent new content, customizable champions' playstyles and not overpriced unlocks for what regards the champs. Some skins are quite pricey but not necessary.
Skip OW if you're lucky enough to not have bought it yet, and come have fun on a game that's competitive but tries to be casual.

The short version: If you're a BL fan and you haven't played this yet, then get it when it's on sale and it'll be OK.  Don't pay much for the DLC, and it's not the end of the world if you don't get them, unless you really needed to play as "Jack" or the Huntress, which are both OK.
Series Ratings:
Borderlands: 8.5/10
Borderlands 2: 9.5/10
Borderlands - The Pre-Sequel: 7/10 (at best)
It's more Borderlands fun and if you're a big BL fan, then sure, get it cheap and have some fun.  But this definately feels like it was created and coded by the B-team, if not C-team.
It's just not as fun and well written.  The coding is pretty sub-standard for the series, there's a ton of minor glitches that you run into.  None of them are major, but they're just all over the place.  Whether it's items or enemys falling through surfaces, events that don't trigger properly (but will eventually, so don't panic if it happens), or one of my big game pet peeves, getting caught on textures while running around.  I mean, it happens a lot in several areas, but for example there's one spot on the Helios space station where I always get stuck running down a hallway.  Then I have to jump over the texture to go forward.  Just a lot of minor lack of polish that says to me that having that dev team disband was no great loss.
One issue with the story is that it's pretty much being told from the perspective of one character, Athena.  I briefly played as another character to see if I'd like it, and everything seemed the same to me.  So unless something changes that I just hadn't gotten to, it's kind of jarring to be playing as someone other than Athena and then keep getting these interuptions with Athena and Lilith. (though those are more common early in the game, so maybe doesn't seem as bad the longer you play).  I'm also not crazy about any of the character power sets.  As it was, I ended up using Athena just to stick with the story.
There was a nice story twist near the end on Helios that I liked, but I won't say more to spoil it.
Running around in vacuum is a double-edged sword.  It adds some new game eliments which are interesting, but also some slightly annoying ones, like when you open a chest and everything gets blown out.  Now on the one hand, that's kinda cool and funny.  But then it's not funny when the ammo you wanted goes flying up and falls down somewhere you can't reach.
All in all, I liked it enough to put alose to 50 hours in, so I guess it can't be all that bad, right?

The single player is surprisingly deep and  harrowing. It's at it's heart is a brutal tale about vengeance and the savagery of warfare against the backdrop of Cold War politics and top secret plans by the government to use traumatised soldiers as pawns. You are taken on a trip around the world during hotspots during that period i.e. Cuba, Vietnam and Eastern Europe to stop the development of a super weapon with its roots at the end of world war 2.
The gunplay is immensely satisfying, a whole host of weapons from the age are available in both their original and heavily modified forms.
Graphics are very crisp, the environments ranging from inner city environments to jungle and laboratories. There are some great smoke, heat and bloom effects running throughout especially during the Vietnam missions.
Characters are rich, memorable and very well acted by some A list celebs.
All in all a great call of duty - a memorable and haunting deep single player with a rich multiplayer aspect.

This is the point-and-click game I've been waiting for.
I played Deponia and loved the gameplay and art style... unfortunately, I absolutely hated the plot and characters. Every time the sequels went on sale, I sat there staring and trying to debate if really fun gameplay was worth the insufferable main character and lack of actually engaging plot. Never could convince myself to. So I decided to try out this game instead, hoping for something better.
combined creative puzzles, an intriguing world, lovable characters, and a moving plot to far exceed my expectations. It was definitely worth the $5 I payed for it. I'd even go so far as to say it'd be worth the original $20, if I were the sort to ever buy games that aren't on sale.
Also, I am now in love with a large, anthropopmorphic rabbit.
+ The plot is fantastic. It starts out as merely intriguing, leaving just enough mystery to keep you going. But as it goes on, the story gets more complex and meaningful--the pacing is just perfect to keep the tension and questions balanced until it culminates in a beautiful, but open ending.
+ The characters are adorable, funny, and you'll probably end up more invested in them then you previously thought. Now, they are fairly simple characters (excluding the Marquis, who deserves an entire game devoted to his adventures), but I think this fits what I'm going to talk about next.
+ It's got a lovely fairy-tale feel to it, so things that may seem overly simplistic actually work as part of its charm. But the plot and complexity of the magical world drive it beyond what most fairy-tales are made of, so the sense you get is less "simple" and more "nostalgic."
+ Gorgeous art style, fantastic music.
+ The world is endlessly intriguing, and it opens up bit-by-bit. Though you go back and forth between many areas, you unlock more bits and pieces of the map at a pace that keeps things fresh and interesting.
+ Lots of creative puzzles. You also use many items more than once, which I think is more interesting and refreshing that gathering a bunch of one use items that mysteriously vanish once you use them.
+ It has a few really clever gameplay elements that make the game more than "combine this item with that item" or "try using this stick on everything until you find something that works."
+ The Marquis. Just... the Marquis.
- The animation could be a bit smoother, and there's a reliance on stock poses rather than unique reactions to events. However, it doesn't overly detract from the style.
- Some of the puzzles don't make that much sense or are far from obvious. But I could say that about every point-and-click game I've ever played. Sometimes I'd think I was supposed to do one thing, but then it would turn out that I actually had to do the opposite. I think if the Advice Seeker spell was more specific (it was, for the most part, entirely useless in telling me anything I didn't already know), this could have been avoided.
- Really could benefit from something like a quest log. There are so many different requests to keep track of, and the journal doesn't give much detail or organize them well.
- Voice volume seemed to fluctuate and sometimes the music was much louder than the voices--and turning music down to almost nothing in the audio settings didn't help.
In the grand scheme of things, my problems with it are very small and nitpicky. Long and short of it is, it's a great game, pick it up during the sale. You won't regret it.

Deus Ex is one of the best accidents I have ever tripped over.  I received this title as software bundle when I bought a video card, back in my early days of building rigs.  I had no idea what it was, but my roommate at the time said he had heard good things.  Boy was I in for a treat.
Deus Ex is (yep, still is) the pinnacle of you picking whatever way you want to achieve your objective.  On top of that, you get conflicting objectives, forcing you to choose your path; thus shaping the game into one of three outcomes.  Sometimes it’s easy to get lost exploring the alternate routes you didn’t take on the way to an objective; it’s that engrossing.
You are given a wide variety of skills, powers (cybernetic augmentations), tools, and weapons to go about your business; more choices to shape your gameplay.  As you play through you’ll get “skill points” (just another unit of RPG exp), and pick up “augmentation canisters” to establish your superhuman abilities.  You can even get upgrade modules for the weapons (silencers, lasers, etc.).
To tie it altogether is a polished cyberpunk atmosphere with a well-written narrative.  The graphics limitations of the time are compensated for by legit voice acting, and AI behavior that’s impressive for the time it was released.
A testament to this title is how the fan community has produced patches to maximize its performance on modern systems.  It makes playing it all over again that much more fun…over a decade later.  It is far better than its sequel (garbage), and still better than its flashy (but still good) prequel.
Now, for the paltry price offered, why on earth would you not pick this up?

RELEASE REVIEW:
+ Ace Combat feel with a unique cell-shaded look. Dev's dedication to the Ace Combat formula shows in spades in the game mechanics.
+ Solid flight mechanics with a touch of HAWX-like departure from forward flight to exceed safe angle-of-attack limits to aim one's weapons to the side, or behind you, at cost of airframe stress damage.
+ large aircraft repertoire, which includes favorites such as the F-14 Tomcat, F-22 Raptor, etc with varying statistical differences between them, from air-to-air capability, to electronics sophistication, to airframe strength, to maneuverability, etc.
+ larger weapons selection between each airframe, angled to the craft's strengths. An A-10 wont be carrying advanced A2A missiles, but neither will an F-22 carry the same ground-attack payload, nor the GAU-8 Avenger cannnon.
- Campaign is VERY rough, and difficulty is sorely imbalanced against you.
- Sound and V/O work is also very rough, oftentimes the volume between each spoken line is VASTLY different, causing near-ear-grating transitions. Constant engine sound is also of the same poor quality, as well as the menu selection.
- Odd game balancing across several aircraft and weapon systems, and a clear "power gap" between aircraft and weapons between early campaign aircraft forced to fight superior numbers of later aircraft, with better missiles vs weaker airframes, and the weakness of missile tracking.
TL;DR
Fans of Ace Combat will find a solid (if extremely rough) successor to the Ace Combat formula in this game. The roughness of the campaign and V/O work however is a large deal-breaker however and as such has led me to the same recommendation I have in my Early Access Review, seen below. It is a wait-and-see. An updated review will be posted once several of the issues mentioned have had some work done on them, and I would not be surprised if my overall recommendation changes to suit.
ORIGINAL EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
I wholeheartedly recommend this game for fans of Ace Combat and similar games, but not at this time, due to the unfinished and unpolished nature it is in at the moment. If and when it is in a more complete state, my recommendation will henceforth be changed posthaste, and a more complete review will follow.

At first glance this game looks like an Ace Combat clone. Well, in some aspects yes, however it's not entirely that. Vector Thrust borrows elements of the classic arcade style flight simulator, however keeps all the difficulty of realistic air combat. You have various different subsystems that you can enable or disable in your aircraft using the keyboard and while controlling all of your primary weapon and engine systems with your joypad or flight stick. Enemies aren't dumb as rocks waiting to get killed by incoming missiles and will use flares just like you to evade incoming projectiles, and they will organize themselves and cover each other as proper wingmen should, covering their allies as you engage them and even doing their best to distract you from your main objective. Its a bit refreshing to fight against a properly and equally matched AI.
When playing this game, I was shot down on my second mission playing on normal difficulty. On any other game I probably would have thrown my arms up in rage and said "screw this, this is stupid!" but instead I smiled and nodded, accepting my defeat and coming to realize that this game doesn't treat you like the hotshot ace you think you are in Ace Combat. Aside from the game being in beta and using starter aircraft, the game didn't hold back, which in reality is "normal" behavior in a combat situation. I went off ahead of the squad and lost all my wingmen because I didn't properly cover them or cooperate with them, and as a result toward the end I was out performed and outnumbered ultimately leading to my failure, which is NORMAL in a combat situation, especially if you're in an aircraft unfit for long term dogfights like the starter aircraft.
Normally when I want to truly enjoy an arcade sim like Ace Combat I crank up the difficulty to hard, which is rare for me to do in many other games because they often fall back on cheap gimmics like enemies that simply have more health than you and pinpoint accuracy, or enemies that are too aggressive and bullrush players into submission. Ace Combat would subvert this, but when I wanted to feel the thrill of having an equaly matched opponent and actually earn that "ace" status I'd turn it up to 11. Ace Combat however, excluding Assault Horizone, was a very story driven franchise, (which I loved before it turned into "Call of Duty: Jets"), So it did very little to get in the way of progression, giving you just the right amount of challenge without making it too difficult to where you'd be stuck and frustrated with the game. Vector Thrust however treats each mission like an everyday sortie, and going it alone will only get you killed like the hotshot you are.
This game has the potential to be something great and I hope they continue with what their doing. Realistic combat in an Arcade style simulator isn't all that bad. "Operation Flashpoint: Red River" is a decent example of that fusion of Call of Duty mixed with Arma style gameplay. I definitely recommend this to anyone into old school flight sims, but also what the "pickup and play" style of arcade flight sims.

Right, firstly I have to say something before I go into the review. There are things about this game that I really enjoy, and both my girlfriend and I have had a lot of fun playing it.
However I have to be honest in reviewing it, and in being honest I have to say that I cannot recommend this game.
Why?
It is basically broken as a game.
No, I haven't experienced any game breaking bugs, but instead, the core game mechanic is entirely flawed because it is simply pot luck in the later levels.
By the subway level you are faced with a party of 44-46 people, with 2 bodyguards who will attack you on sight without provocation, and then after any number of kills, 2 secret agents will show up. These guys break the game. They are faster than you, nearly impossible to kill and will also attack without provocation.
However, if by some miracle you beat them, or they don't show up, the game decides that that isn't good enough and will just have a random party guest attack you without warning. No anger bar, nothing. Just simply kick you to the ground and you are dead.
I have no problem with a game being difficult, providing it is fair and can be beaten with skill and practise. But this game is hard because it is poorly finished. Don't add unwinnable levels just to make a game hard, it doesn't make it better, it just makes me not want to ever load it up again.
Its not the worst game on steam by a mile, but honestly not worth your time unless the game is fixed or altered.

Party Hard is a game where our character, finding himself unable to sleep due to loud parties, comes to the only logical conclusion: Kill everyone at the party, and then do the same to parties all over the US.
For this, you have several tools at your disposal. Throughout the level there will be several traps you can use. Many of them are randomly spawned in set locations, so you might have different opportunities and ways of approaching the level each time you play.Placement of the victims in the level is also randomly set to an extent, as are some events (sometimes a robbery can take place, a drug deal, etc, etc) You will be able to poison food and drinks, tinker with electric devics, rig speakers to explode, start the engine of cars so it runs over, people, etc. You will also find tools like stun bombs, bombs, new clothes and smoke bombs on a briefcase that it's somewhere on the level, or given to you by a strange man in a trenchcoat.
The game in concept feels somewhat like a mix of Hotline Miami and Hitman, coupled with a soundtrack that wouldn't be out of place in the former. While good, the soundtrack really needs some more inclusions, since you will restart the levels several times and many of the tracks are shared between levels, so it can eventually become somewhat annoying and make you mute the music.
You are encouraged to keep it stealthy, as otherwise the witnesses will call the police and pin you as the murderer, which will run after you and most likely catch you, as sadly in this game your own movement is too slow, and the sprint ability is both way too short and takes too long to "refill", so you will need to be smart to where and from you into (if you manage to evade the police office for enough time, he will give up). You can use the shortcuts scattered through the level to have easy escape card, but you are punished for using those shortcuts while being chased by the police. A Mario-lookalike will spawn, and close whatever shortcut you used, and you will be unable to use it until the level ends, so you can't really use it as an easy way out without consequences, you need to use it smartly.You can also activate many of the level traps and lead the officer onto them. You can hide bodies so people don't call the police, and you can grab blackout-drunk people, put them somewhere hidden and kill them there and dispose of the body. As well, you will need to pick out slowly people who stumble into less populated areas(bathrooms, bedrooms), as if you try to stab people in heavily populated areas, your♥♥♥♥♥♥will be quickly kicked by the party-goers. Slowly picking out people, playing it smart and activating traps at the correct time is essential, and when everything fits perfectly it was a very nice flow to it.
However, there's definitely some issues with the game. One being that your success will be somewhat limited by the randomness of the spawns. Be unlucky, and you will be looking into a level with very few traps or victims that barely ever go near it. This will make your progression awfully slow, and you will spend a awful lot of minutes waiting for people to go to places where nobody can see you. Coupled with this, the game has a combo system that encourages you to kill as many people as possible in quick succession, but this is very rarely accomplishable within the level design and your own character limitation. Your character moves awfully slow, and you will barely be able to kill a couple of people before everyone runs away or kicks your♥♥♥♥♥ The only way to really get a good combo going is having the luck of a stun grenade or smoke bomb spawning and then you will be able to exploit it in heavily populated areas. Your success is more times tied to luck than it is to skill. You will be repeating levels many times, which will eventually make you bored of the soundtrack, which while is good, gets quickly old after quite a few repeats between levels that themselves will be restarted many times.
By completing various objectives, you will unlock new characters. A Police officer than can send another officer to arrest someone, and that can move dead bodies without suspicion( as long as he isn't seen killing them before). A girl that can kick people to knock them out before killing them( which makes a few levels way too easy, as you can just knock out anyone and drag them to a hidden place) as well as a few others I won't spoil, each one with different abilities and limitations (though some levels do not play all that well with them)
I really like the game and the concept, and I would love to see it being improved in a sequel, with more tight level design and expanded social stealth gameplay. It's not quite a "gem" yet, but it could easily be with some improvements. Let me able to sneak into a party if I find the right attire, access to closed-off areas with a VIP pass, poison drinks just as one of the employees grabs them and distributes them between party-goers, or having other ways of attracting people to places other than the pizza item(that spawns way too rarely in this game).
7/10
+Great soundtrack
+Feels great and has a nice flow to into when everything is in the right place
+Satisfying stealth
-Repetitive
-Soundtrack is not big enough and eventually annoys you after too many repeats
-The outcome of the levels feels way too tied into having the luck to have good item and trap spawns in the right places
-Character movement is way,wayyy too slow.

With any suspense now ruined, let's continue with the review.  X3AP is a game that has a 12 year legacy behind it, itself nominally the expansion to X3:Reunion released in 2005.  It's "Yet Another Elite Clone" (the 1984 grandaddy that defined the Space Sim we all know and love today), part of a series that had done at the time what no other Space Sim could:  it faithfully expanded upon the core gameplay and scope of space sims.
Before Elite: Dangerous, the X series was considered the spiritual successor to Elite, and X3AP stands as the final product from years of refinement.  X3AP is far from a perfect game; its quirky with flat race and character design, simple narrative and mission systems, and plays better as a sandbox "universe" than it does as the story-driven experience it toys with.  The UI is functional but clunky and opaque without practice.  Its learning curve is more of a mountain, however the game's designed to be picked up piecemeal without forcing all of the meta and control systems down your throat at start.  It crashes, somewhat often, and many of the useful time-saving features (like in-space save) have to be earned.  Music can be glitchy; I've had it improperly download the music files on clean installs before and have found out recently these files might be the cause of some of my crashes.  Auto-pilot will end up killing you more often than missiles if you use it, and combat's fun but somewhat simplistic.
Sounds like a solid 6-7 "meh" of a game, right?  Except that it isn't.  At the time X3 came out, it was a visually stunning game that pushed the benchmarks of PCs and user expectations.  Its dynamic world system created actual working trade where destroying a transport could affect the economy of a sector, either raising prices for the needed items or causing its weapons or munitions production to stop.  GoD (The Global Decison Engine... I know, we call it GoD anyways) would remove factories that were no longer in use and add new ones as required creating a unique playthrough every time.  It also creates military patrols for the different races in order to protect areas that come under attack and pirates to disrupt trade.  There's even times when "war" happens, with two race militaries facing off in large skirmishes within sectors (this is different from AP's War Sectors, although it's pretty rare to see).  And the universe is always running, even for the sectors you aren't in, the game calculates the lives of near a hundred sectors filled with ships and factories.  Profit and death continues, regardless of what you do.
Add to this a vibrant world where there's no "tier" system of ships, and all races offer competitive fleets to choose from that follow unique fleet doctrine (eg, Split field fast and aggressive ships, Teladi defensive and slow) while also giving players a chance to OWN their own fleets and factories and command their own battleships.  It's expansive,  it's literally a game greater than the sum of its parts.  And AP has only honed this by adding new features (namely the war zones, some ship upgrades, and the stock market), some re-balancing and overall improving the experience to make it a solid 2011 game.  It's a game with few peers if any (I haven't played Eve).
If it sounds too complicated or in depth for you, I don't blame you.  It can take more than 40 hours of playtime to hit "mid-game" of a playthrough.  There's a great modding community which can expand on the game's playability endlessly.  The game's script engine is readily accessible if you want to try adding in new features.
If you think you're up to the challenge, I highly recommend this game to you, if only until the release of the 2016 "next gen" Space sims.
If you're reading this and No Man's Sky, Star Citizen, and Limit Theory are already released?  I'd recommend watching their LPs and getting those games first (assuming they're good).  Afterwards, get this.  X3AP is a milestone in the Space Sim genre.  And it might still remain the best example of a first-person fleet-strategy-action-economy-simulation game we'll get for a long time.  It's worth the money, at least until Egosoft releases its proper successor.

Having raced this simulator for months (since before the steam release), I can say with certainty it's one of the best, and constantly evolving, simulators currently in the market.  Here's a few bullet points:
- Varied racing categories, from small compact cars to beefy V8s and several generations of F1, and even multiple kart categories
- Car handling is realistic (this is, first and foremost, a simulator), while also being great fun. It's not uncommon to want to go "one more lap", and completely lose track of time. Mind you, I'm playing on a Thrustmaster T500RS steering wheel and pedal set, which gets me great force feedback.
- Tracks are also plentiful, varied and well-made, plus it's not hard to find extra content (both tracks and vehicles) online. The out-of-the-box tracks are hard to beat for their quality, tho.
- The graphics are functional and performance is great. While the game cannot compete on eye-candy with games based on newer engines, it's still being polished and upgraded (in fact, a graphical shader update is just around the corner).
- While we're talking about updates, the team making the game is one of the most dedicated dev teams in activity, always listening to fan feedback and constantly adding more and more (and free!) content to the game.
So, yea, great game, great dev team, great price. Highly recommended!

Singleplayer in this game is pretty much perfected. Myself, i have not experienced any bugs in singleplayer mode whatsoever. The game has decent survival mechanics, with a quest system that explains the situation of the survivor, albeit a bit cheesy, but endurable. Difficulty in the game is well balanced, i find the game to be fine in terms of gameplay, and the constant monitoring of your vitals is just like in any hardcore survival game.
Multiplayer, however, is a different story. The game being very client sided, causes players to experience various bugs otherwise hidden in singleplayer mode or in a solo multiplayer world. Bugs range from minor bugs that cause more of a nuisance such as being unable to host servers after saving and exiting a previous world, to more game breaking bugs, such as invisible loot, disappearing chests, and most importantly - client sided issues, other players may cause different items to spawn - invisible trees to completely invisible animals, such as wolves, who would attack you as if you are blind. The only way to fix it is to restart the server, which would cause the aforementioned hosting bugs.
But all in all, the game is still in devolopment, especially multiplayer. There are many ways to fix bugs found in mutliplayer, and im sure the devolopers are planning something big to fix most of the issues in multiplayer. Aside from the bugs, this game is a great multiplayer hardcore survival game, combining survival and crafting with adventure: a perfect mixture.

Randomly generated good times full of disgust, horror, and a few really good chuckles. If you like raunchy comedy, and you like video games The Binding of Isaac has got what you want. In this game you play foremost as Isaac. A poor child who has been shut away from all worldly pleasures and is about to be sacrificed. All thanks to Isaac's mother who hears voices. Voices of what she believes is God telling her to do these things. Which is an obvious reference to the story of Isaac from the Bible in the 22nd Chapter of Genesis (Hey now you know). In the game you retreat from your bloodthirsty mother into the basement (the entrance to which is located convieniently in Isaac's room). There you will fight against the demons that haunt the house using little but your own tears (no really his weapon is crying) and your ablility to dodge moderatley fast enemys and projectiles. Learn the secrets, make a deal with the devil (or two), collect the power-ups, and confront your mother for your very life.
Pros:
+One of the most strangely addicting games I've ever played
+Replay value is immense
+Funny (for the right audience) and packed full of references to pop-culture and internet memes
+Doesn't take a powerful computer to run it (most laptops should be able to handle it even)
+Totally affordable at $5. (Personally I got it on sale with the dlc for under a dollar)
+Soundtrack is notably well done. A lot of love went into the score of this game
Cons:
-It's got a fairly steep learning curve
-Luck can be a defining factor
-Sometimes it can become unreasonably offensive to the more sensitive audience (I personally like the humor but I know people who I would not show this game to)
All in all I'd give it a solid 85/100

If you're a fan of games like Ace Combat, HAWX, or even some of Airforce Delta games, then Vector Thrust might be what you're looking for. I say might because of several glaring issues with the beta version of the game as it currently stands (12 April, 2015). I early accessed this game well over a year ago after spotting it on moddb. At the time I had just shedded off my last console, and was no longer able to play one of my favorite arcade flight sims Ace Combat 6. Becase Vector Thrust obviously targets those who love arcade flight sims in the vein of Ace Combat, it's worth noting that Timesymmetry's current offering meets some-but-not-all of the benchmarks set by the franchise's 10+ years of success.
Vector Thrust definitely strikes the "Strange but real" tone set by the AC fanchise by constructing a fictional world where global superpowers fight geopolitical battles not with large land armies or diplomacy but with hyper-powerful air forces. That impression is essential to a game like this because it sets the stage for moment you the player realize your own heroism in the heat of battle. It's all riding on you the ace pilot, and Timesymmetry has definitely set their sights on keeping with that tradition througout the game's story missions.
Fans of the genre will probably drool when they read the developer's roadmap for all of the playable aircraft to eventually be added. If you're unsatisfied with it currently you can always download custom planes and drop them right in the game's directory--it's standard for PC games but it is refreshing to see an arcade flight sim clearly decendent from a console gaming tradition embracing this powerful and compelling feature.
The gameplay is getting better with every update it seems. Enemy fighters are hard to shoot down as they should be, but you very seldom feel cheated out of a missile shot once you get a handle on the game's lock-on and fire mechanic. With Ace Combat most of the aircraft were fairly even in terms of weapon range and damage, and the advantage was conferred more on the player that could more skillfully weave their fighter in and out of a hairball using guns and missiles. That principle applies here but more in accordance with aircraft performance stats and weapon load outs. Timesymmetry has made sure that newer aircraft outperform older ones in more respects than just maneuverability and speed. It makes for a fun skirmish when you span 15 enemy MiG-21s and an F-15 J Kai+ for yourself, sometimes the results might surprise you.
Challenges need work, and feel very asymmetric in terms of difficulty and time required to complete many of the objectives. It's a matter of balancing primarily, and the farther along TS gets in development, as well as the more player feedback they get, the more refined the gameplay modes will become (hopefully).
The game desperately needs work in the controls. I've played it with an Xbox controller and it plays fine, not too  unlike it's relatives in the genre. However the lack of smoothed mouse-aiming is a huge turn off to many players, and is something that I think the devs should focus a great deal of time perfecting. It's a PC game after all, so ensuring that you can just as easily boot up and play with a KB/M combo as you can with a controller is an essential feature. Currently, the game lets you map pitch and turn to the mouse, but it's sluggish, inconsistent, and not helpful wheny you're trying to dogfight. Your mouse is essentially locked to the plane, as the camera would be to the head of the player in an FPS, this not ideal though. What they should implement is a control scheme using the mouse that borrows from War Thunder, where you can aim freely in front of the aircraft, and the plane responds based on where you place your mouse pointer, not based on how your mouse movement corresponds to the control surface movement (if that makes sense?). \
I think adding some features like this will help distinguish it against the background of its parent genre. Vector Thrust is an Ace Combat clone with some cool unique features added into the formula. It could easily take on an identity of its own if the controls are more friendly to casual playing, and once the campaigns are finished and playable. I'm eager to see where this game goes.

Spent 20 minutes writing up a well-reasoned review, and Windows Update decided to wipe it.  Sigh.  Anyway.
This game is great, and extra cathartic for anyone who's ever lived in a college town.  The number of times I've lost sleep to idiots with nothing to do but be loud all night....  This game is a wonderful balance of planning, opportunism, and luck.
The level randomization is just enough to keep restarting from becoming frustrating, and the different, clever level layouts make you excited to see what's coming next.  Respawn is suitably quick and easy.  The unique traps in each level are always fun to discover and play with.  The random and somewhat unpredictable behavior of the NPCs makes for fun variation within each scenario.
I only encountered one small bug in my first playthrough (I suddenly couldn't interact with objects; the contextual cues wouldn't appear), but a quick level restart fixed it and it didn't happen again.  The story is trite and predictable, but it mostly stays out of the way with short cutscenes between levels.
My biggest gripe: I wish it was longer.  And that's an okay gripe to have, because it means I was having fun and didn't want to stop.  I'm sad that I don't have any more levels to discover.  Twelve levels (eleven if you don't count the bus) made for about eight hours of gameplay for me (I'd call myself an "average" gamer; not brilliant, not terrible), which I mainlined on a day off.  The replay potential is high, but I want more!  I've got my fingers crossed that once we're through the bugfixing phase, more levels will be forthcoming.

The opening of The Pre-Sequel begins some time after Borderlands 2 and Episode 3 of Tales from the Borderlands, on the flying city of Sanctuary, where the three former Vault Hunters Lilith, Brick, and Mordecai interrogate Athena after having captured her earlier. Athena then recounts her story, starting after the death of General Knoxx, when she received an offer to go find the Vault from a Hyperion programmer named Jack. She then joins fellow Vault Hunters: Nisha, Wilhelm, and Claptrap, on a spaceship headed for the Hyperion moon base, Helios. On the way, they are ambushed by the Lost Legion, an army of Dahl soldiers led by Colonel Tungsteena Zarpedon, and crash-land onto the moon base. After meeting up with Jack, they attempt to use Helios's defense system, but realizes there is a jamming signal coming from Elpis, Pandora's moon. They attempt to escape, but they are stopped by Zarpedon, and a mysterious alien-like warrior. Jack then sends the Vault Hunters to Elpis on a moonshot rocket.
After landing on Elpis, the Vault Hunters are helped by Janey Springs, a junk dealer, who guides them to the spaceport known as Concordia. Here, the Hunters, under Jack's orders, request help from Moxxi to find the jamming signal. After raiding a former Dahl station, they find out that the signal was put up by the Meriff, the person in charge of Concordia, as well as Jack's former underling. While this is happening, Zarpedon also activates Helios' weapon system, the Eye which fires powerful lasers on the surface of Elpis. The Meriff is later killed by Jack at his office due to a failed attempt to kill Jack from behind. With Concordia secured, Jack and Moxxi guide the Vault Hunters to the next step in retaking Helios. They then proceed to infiltrate a Lost Legion base, run by two Dahl officers, The Bosun and The Skipper, in search of an artificial intelligence, which Jack plans to use to build a robot army. After defeating Bosun, it is revealed that the Skipper, who renames herself Felicity, is the A.I. they were looking for. Next, the Vault Hunters travel to a robot production facility, where Jack enlists the help of a scientist named Gladstone to build his robot army. Gladstone suggests using his prototype robot, named the Constructor, which has the ability to construct an infinite amount of robots. At first, Felicity agrees to help them by becoming the A.I. for the Constructor, but upon witnessing the violence she has to go through,she begins to hesitate. After being forced into the Constructor bot, she takes control of it and battles the Vault Hunters. Felicity is defeated, and her personality is deleted from the Constructor bot.
Having now achieved his robot army, Jack and the Vault Hunters travel to Helios, while enlisting the help of Moxxi and two former Vault Hunters, Roland and Lilith (who were on Elpis for a vacation). They defeat Zarpedon and the Lost Legion, and proceed to reboot the Eye of Helios. It is revealed that the Eye is actually the eye of the Destroyer, the beast that was released from Pandora's Vault by the first Borderlands vault hunters team. The Vault Hunters then begin to inject slag into the Eye, under Moxxi's directions. When attempting to reboot, Moxxi reveals her true motives for helping Jack: to destroy the Eye and prevent Jack from gaining ultimate power. Jack and the Vault Hunters then travel back to Elpis, where they find its Vault having already been opened, as mentioned by Zarpedon during her last moment. The Hunters then battle several of the Vault's guardians, and defeat its ultimate weapon, the Deva-like Empyrean Sentinel.
With the Sentinel defeated, Jack enters the Vault and greets the Vault Hunters, but finds no item of value, other than a mysterious symbol floating midair. As he attempts to interact with it, the symbol then shows Jack a vision of the Warrior awakening. However, the vision is interrupted by Lilith, who phasewalks in front of him and punches through the Vault symbol, burning it onto Jack's face. She then disappears, leaving Jack behind with the Vault Hunters. Jack, having gone insane from the vision as well as Lilith's attack, swears vengeance on her, and all the "bandits" on Pandora. Realizing that the hero who once saved her on Helios is no more, Athena leaves Jack's employ.
Having finished listening to Athena's story, Lilith then orders the Crimson Raiders to execute her, against Brick and Mordecai's protests. However, as they open fire on her, Athena is saved by the alien warrior who appeared on Helios with Zarpedon that day, which reveals itself to be one of the legendary Eridians. The Eridian then warns the Vault Hunters of an imminent war, and that they would need "all the Vault Hunters they can get".
During the credits, several scenes showing what became of the Vault Hunters after helping Jack play. Wilhelm is transformed further into a machine, Athena discards the money given to her by Jack, Nisha and Jack establish their reign on Pandora, and Claptrap is dismantled and left for dead by Jack. In a post-credit scene, Jack is seen strangling his CEO, Tassiter, in his office, and announces to a woman on an intercom that he has replaced Tassiter as the new head of Hyperion, and tells her to now call him by his new name, Handsome Jack.

As a huge fan of Hotline Miami, i was both excited and sceptical going into this. Turned out the two games only thing both games really have in common is the theme "mass murder". You are a dude who just wants to sleep, but your neighbors are having a party and are way too loud. It's up to our anti-hero with mask and knife to not only go to the neighbours next door, but go on a complete rampage all across the US to stop 11 obnoxious loud parties. That's basically how the story goes.
The gameplay itself was pretty interesting to me. The goal of each stage is to murder every single person at the party. Doing so proves a little bit more difficult then expected, the places are crowded with people, most of the time close together, and lots of times these people don't hestitate to call the cops to investigate or worse, get you arrested. So what do you really do to kill everyone? Our beloved mass murderer isn't the fittest guy, being exhausted after a 2-3 second sprint, just enough to get out the scene or escape the cops (atleast for a short while, as the cops get more persistent). Besides sprinting, the main character is capable of killing, obviously, picking up sleeping person or corpses or setting up various traps around the stage.
The game encourages using the traps, as there are many different on each stage, each with different effects, may it be poisoning food, gumball machines which explode or a horse which kicks your victims to valhalla. But also multiple items are avaiable in the game, such as Smoke grenades, bombs or Spare clothes to escape the cops.
Stealth is a very important part of Party Hard aswell. You must be quick, efficient and not to  be seen while stabbing a person. Hiding bodies in trashcans or other various places is also an option to not get found out about your rampage.
The level design can be a bit frustrating at parts (especially that damn Miami Party), but overall i liked it. There are multiple 'variations' for each map, meaning that some traps are in other locations, switched with others completely, etc. Every time you start the map new (or get busted/die) you get a different variaton. I enjoyed this system quite well, as all the maps and every playthrough felt familiar, but still different. Also the music in this game is just great.
Only thing i could complain about is the price tag and the lenght. The game may be a bit difficult but can still be finished rather quickly, depending on your skill. Also the voice acting in the cutscense wasn't really my cup of tea.
Otherwise i can recommend this game  alot. In the end it was pretty different to Hotline Miami. It's a way more calm killing spree, but that's what i really liked about it. I just hope there will be a second Party Hard aswell, as i think there are still much possibilities for this gameplay.

Party Hard is a slightly randomized strategy / stealth game where you have to kill everyone in a level, without getting caught.
The game has a beautiful and richly detailed pixel art style and is accompanied by a thumping dance soundtrack, perfectly fitting the levels (which are all parties).
Randomization means that while a level will always be the same in layout, the placement of party-ers and other elements can change. One time you may see a drug deal or robbery take place, another time you load it the same room will simply be empty or filled with a beer keg instead.
The various pick-ups which can spawn, or be delivered by a helper character, will also be random. This makes each playthrough unique.
Getting caught by the police means restarting the entire level (with new randomization), so you don't just have to rehash the exact same level.
There is also optional integration with Twitch chat for streamers, where your viewers can trigger some of the random events. These range from relatively normal like extra party goers, to a zombie invasion or a Sharknado. Seriously.
Fortunately these elements can also occur at random in a singleplayer game without Twitch involvement.
The game is almost punishingly tough at times and at others laughably easy, even on the same level, thanks to the randomization, but that's part of its charm.
Beating the game unlocks extra characters who have their own characteristics, for the completionists.
There's also a story tying the levels together, but that's just your cliché slasher film affair. It doesn't add much but doesn't distract either -- at least it's told in beautiful pixel art comic style.
Worth picking up if it meets your price point. As I'm writing this review I'm 5 hours in, not beating the game yet, and I pid about 6.50 for my copy. At a Euro per hour, it's a good deal for me, since I enjoyed every second of it.

As with all X universe games there is a fairly steep learning curve.   Ok that's a lie, it isn't a learning curve it is a learning cliff.  You get basic flight school then you're "good to go".  As with most X games it is true in a sense, you are technically combat ready (if you ignore your ship's readiness) not much more to dog fighting than what you're taught in flight school (and honestly difficulty takes a while to ramp up).  However an argument can be made that some of the most fulfilling moments of any true X game don't take place in ship to ship combat.  Building your own navy and busting enemy sectors is fun in it's own right and (at least when i do it) my ship to ship combat isn't all that common, i'm generally in my carrier corrdinating the battle effort.  The trading game (especially in AP) is another vast area of fun (and generally where I get what i need to build my navy).  Building factory complexes and setting up trade routes and manipulating the market is where I spend much of my time.
Sadly this is where the learning cliff is your tutorial mentions none of this.  One thing X2 did well was they had instanced tutorials that, while not explaining everything, gave you an idea of how to do the other stuff.  AP could really do with a bit more training especially with the stock exchange and trading game since it is a big part of it.  The market is dynamic, there are mins and max sure but your involvement (or lack there of) can really produce an impact.  A pirate base springs up in a civilized sector, they're going to need weapons and shields so demand is going to increase while supply decreases.  You build a missile factory, supply is going to increase and if done in the wrong area you may shoot yourself in the foot.  These are things that happen in the previous X games however with the stock market it adds a whole new dimension to the trading game in that you can buy stock in damn near everything from common resources up to weapons, and in various companies.  Having a baseline understanding of the trading mechanics is almost a must.  I'm not asking for spoilers but some idea of what is going on may be useful.  That being said, for myself, finding out the stuff through trial and error was also somewhat fun, my main file's home sector will never be hurting for wasp missiles now, though my wallet will forever feel the sting lol.
In short, AP does what its predecessors have done for years, adds a few little goodies, and integrates them beautifully.  It suffers from some of their struggles that they never changed (learning cliff, menus within menus within menus where someone who is new may get lost without explaination) but that may be part of its charm that it isn't a game that you just are given the information you need to make it big, you gotta get it for yourself.  All in all the game is very much worth the buy.

Party Hard is a game about killing all the party goers so you can go back to sleep ;)
You basically wander around a pixellated party and try to cause as much damage without anyone noticing what you're doing and calling for the police. Poisoning the drinks, breaking the oven, knocking down trees, setting fire to the loudspeakers or outright stabbing people. But you can't just go on a rampage in the middle of the dance floor because you'll be quickly overwhelmed by the party goers. You have to be smart about it, try to utilise the enviroment to cause a panic or pick off lonely targets snuggling in some bedroom. Hell, once people start dropping from that poison you poured in the drinks maybe theyll blame some random unlucky dude and the police will take care of him for you.
There's a lot to do and you'll need to think fast because people are constantly on the move and one wrong move can lead to an arrest or getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the bouncers.
It takes around 10-15 minutes to beat a level but you're practically guaranteed to be restarting each one a few times until you get the feel for it (or just manage not to screw up).
The game keeps things fresh by randomising some elements of each party like the traps or certain rooms. To top it off there are random events happening now and again where a bunch of bikers may crash your party to kick someones♥♥♥♥♥ Another time the feds might get a wind of you and start patrolling the party, or a dancing bear might show up to bust some moves on the dance floor.
There are two problems with it though. For one - the tutorial is really kinda useless. The game drops some strategy hints around parties in the form of newspapers you can stop to read, but it lacks any sort of introduction on how to do well. You either have to discover stuff on your own or watch a youtube video of someone playing to realise for example that the 'listen' button allows you to judge if anyone will hear you stabbing a person. There are a few simple gameplay elements that are not really explaind very well but are very important if you want to do well and not end up frustrated.
The other thing is that the game is kinda short. There are around 13 (or so) levels and I finished them all in around 6 hours. The groundwork is there and I could see the game having double the amount of levels and giving the player more incentive to replay them with the other characters.
I still recommend it, its great fun, maybe wait for a sale though.

I recently discovered the 'NieR' series on a hunt for music/OSTs that were akin to 'Shadow of the Colussus'. A lone comment in a reddit thread lead me to the first 'NieR' album and was pleasantly surprised to learn that NieR: Automata had literally just launched. Compelled by the music of that first album, I decided to purchase the game and give it a whirl.
Initially I was concerned that I would need to play 'Drakengard' or the original 'NieR' in order to fully appreciate the game, as I had not. The game stands alone perfectly, like a different house in the same neighborhood (thousands of years in the future).
I won't spoil the plot for you (So I won't remark on characters, etc.), but please note that game's story plays out a bit different than most. Instead of a -very- long story, it's a tad bit shorter if you think of it in a linear fashion. However, the story is structured in such a way that you revisit the same story from a completely different angle in a truly varied way, and it feels quite different (thus far). It's NOT the typical: change Yes to No and Ending A becomes Ending B. It's nothing like that, you'll definitely want to keep playing.
Good: Combat is fun, the customization is an interesting spin, the music is SUPERB. Controller combat wasn't bad, I thought I was going to hate it, but it works well. Try all the weapons, try all the abilities. This game isn't about min/max. The scenery is bleak feeling, but gorgeous.
Bad: Fullscreen looks atrocious, but the windowed setting looks great. There isn't an auto-save, so be warned! I was hoping for a little more varied enemies, but it's not too bad.
Things I wish I knew first: Use your POD target/lock on to allow for certain combos. All weapons are fun in their own way, it's worth trying them all and upgrading them all as you can. Don't worry about 'maxing' them on the first play through.
Last thoughts: For purchasing on a whim, based on the music, I'm more than pleasantly surprised how fun it is. This game is fantastic. 9/10

Stellaris is an excellent 4x Strategy game whose exploration in the early game is one of the best of the genre.  This is a game that you purchase now with the idea that with every expansion the game will get better.  Much like Crusader Kings 2, or Europa Universalis IV.  Right now, after several patches and one small expansion, I can say that the game feels more "complete" than it did when it first launched.  There is always something going on that grabs your attention.  You spend most of the early game exploring with science ships, finding planets to colonize and finding anomolies to research.  This is by far the best the game has to offer.  The early moments of the game are perfection.  However, once you get into the mid game, you start to notice some of the things that Stellaris is lacking.  For one, diplomact options are very weak.  If you are coming from EUIV, be prepared to be shocked by how little options there are.  This leads to another issue.  There are only 3 victory conditions, and two out of three really require you to expand militarily.  The third a federation option is a bit more interesting but if you are looking for a peaceful means to win the game it is very limited.  I can't help to think that Paradox should look to the Civilization series to flesh out other means to get victory in the game.  I'd think a cultural victory would be awesome, if the idea of cultue in a civilization since exisited, it doesn't.  Also, the leaders in the game feel like a partial idea.  It feels like leaders should be more akin to what you find in Crusader Kings 2, but they are just stats at this point.  Basically, I was hoping for a Crusader Kings 2 and EU4 mash up, but in space, but it is much more bare bones than that.  The late game can be very brutal.  There are late game events that effect the entire galaxy, but more often than naught when the galaxy is threatened by something that will call all life in the universe, the AI generally ignores this threat.  So you end up being the only person fighting the end game crisis with any kind of seriousness.  Perhaps if diplomacy was more fleshed out this would be less of an issue.
So up to this point it might seem I have done nothing but crap on the game.  It does have it's fair share if issues, but it is because a lot of the game is so good that where it is lacking, it makes the bad stand out more.  I would say at this point if you are thinking of Stellaris, on a sale price it is worth while a pick up.  Just keep in mind that like most Paradox game, expansions will flesh out the game, but also increase the overall cost to get that better version.

Tomoyo After is the continuation of one route from the highly esteemed VN Clannad. Naturally, this story references events from the first game. Also included is an optional parody SRPG minigame.
VNs live and die by the storyline so I'll discuss this first. Key is infamous for their (nukige) heart-wrenching stories and they certainly don't skimp on the drama here. The focus for most of the game lies upon newly introduced characters, giving everyone at least one arc.
There are a handful of decisions that seem out of character for the protagonist, but he does come to realize his mistakes and reflect upon them. The actual choices given to the player are minimal and generally have obvious outcomes. A couple choices work counter-intuitively though, so don't fret over keeping a guide open to prevent yourself from getting an abrupt bad end.
Every arc connects to one another in a fluid narrative with one exception. The final arc marks a massive shift and while the transition is rough the content is well worth experiencing. Just be sure to have read the original Clannad before diving in.
A remarkable improvement from the portrait art in the prequel, even the gallery images are smartly drawn. Recycled assets are sprinkled among the newly drawn backgrounds.
Not as impacting as its predecessor, but what can possibly compare to it? The same artists worked on music in both games, so expect more somber, foreboding melodies to rain down upon you.
The story meanders a bit since the focus is split between so many different characters. It's easier to empathize with the protagonist--since the final arc so sharply focuses on him, it makes the ending that much stronger.

Randomly generated good times full of disgust, horror, and a few really good chuckles. If you like raunchy comedy, and you like video games The Binding of Isaac has got what you want. In this game you play foremost as Isaac. A poor child who has been shut away from all worldly pleasures and is about to be sacrificed. All thanks to Isaac's mother who hears voices. Voices of what she believes is God telling her to do these things. Which is an obvious reference to the story of Isaac from the Bible in the 22nd Chapter of Genesis (Hey now you know). In the game you retreat from your bloodthirsty mother into the basement (the entrance to which is located convieniently in Isaac's room). There you will fight against the demons that haunt the house using little but your own tears (no really his weapon is crying) and your ablility to dodge moderatley fast enemys and projectiles. Learn the secrets, make a deal with the devil (or two), collect the power-ups, and confront your mother for your very life.
Pros:
+One of the most strangely addicting games I've ever played
+Replay value is immense
+Funny (for the right audience) and packed full of references to pop-culture and internet memes
+Doesn't take a powerful computer to run it (most laptops should be able to handle it even)
+Totally affordable at $5. (Personally I got it on sale with the dlc for under a dollar)
+Soundtrack is notably well done. A lot of love went into the score of this game
Cons:
-It's got a fairly steep learning curve
-Luck can be a defining factor
-Sometimes it can become unreasonably offensive to the more sensitive audience (I personally like the humor but I know people who I would not show this game to)
All in all I'd give it a solid 85/100

Okay...spoiler alert, first off. (Spoilers will be noted throughout the review.)
+BEAUTIFUL music. All of the music fit wonderfully with each and every scene.
+Lovable characters. Every little creature in Mousewood (save one or two) caught my attention and made me love them almost immediately. They're freaking adorable.
+Voice acting. The voice acting was great. A little bit awkward in a couple places, but fun nonetheless.
+The graphics are lovely. They usually have a good deal of color to them and can set a scene very well.
+The mini-game, Quartets. This, I can say without a doubt, was a fun little game. I loved it. The point of the game is to...well, it's like go-fish, only instead of getting a pair of two cards, the goal is to get all four cards of a suit and make a quartet. Whoever has the most quartets by the end wins, and you can play with ALMOST everyone in Mousewood. I genuinely enjoyed the mini game.
+/- Story. Story was...meh. The story was very...grindy up until the middle where The plot finally came into play. The only thing that kept me interested that long was my love for a couple of the characters. Even towards the end of the story (SPOILER), it got so bland and many of the questions posed in the game were not answered properly. There was so much more that could have been done with it. (Jerry's dad? Anyone know that guy? Who is he again?)
-Puzzles. Puzzles puzzles, those freaking puzzles! I cannot even begin to explain my frustration with those puzzles. Several times I rage quit because they just made no sense to me at all. I put the game down for a week or so on several occasions, and then came back, only to have to resort to a walkthrough, Honestly, the puzzles are what spawned my dislike of this game. It's all either trial and error (and error and error and error) or go find a walkthrough. Most of the puzzles make little to no sense at all, and the hints given to you are obscure. You're given a spell called "Advice Seeker" and more often than not it doesn't give you any suitable hints on what to do to actually progress in the story. So for a good long while I was wandering around, wondering what on earth I'm supposed to be doing. When I found out "hey, this guy needs some ____!" and actually got him some _____ he wouldn't take it. Why? Because he's picky.
-Dialogue (when using items and such). BECAUSE there's so much trial and error to this game, there's going to be a lot of your character telling you that's not how this item should be used. But...could they at least do it in a less annoying way? The reason I hated the trial and error because Jerry's response (over and over again) was always (the same thing every time you used a certain item) something along the lines of "Mmm...I don't think so." or "That doesn't go there!" or "That doesn't need any special spice." (yes. yes that's a thing.) It gets tedious. And annoying. Very quickly.
+/-The Audiobooks. Throughout the game, you will come across a fascinating character. In fact, you meet him in the very first scene. The Wood Sprite. He's a great guy. He loves telling stories. Later in the game, he'll give you stories which are saved in your bonus collection as audio books! Ain't he swell? Yeah, well...that's all fine and dandy, but the audio books are (I don't know what else I expected them to be) quite long for my taste. Especially when I'm trying to rage through puzzles. The books are somewhere between 8 and 15 minutes long (though I've only listened to two) and a bit monotonous. I actually dozed off a bit during the first one. (However, I was in a dimly lit room at the time.) So...they're cute, but long. And they take a bit away from the immersion (if you ever manage to gain any) in the story.

+/-The ending (obvious SPOILER here). Gods. I don't know what to say about that freaking ending. It was just so...anticlimatic that if it wasn't for the explanation of the past of my favorite character in the game (Marquis de Hoto/the rabbit) and why he was having his troubles throughout the story, I would have downright put the ending into the negative section of this review. The last puzzles were fairly simple compared to the rest of the game which made me rage a bit, given how...boring the results of the puzzles actually were. The actions of Jerry (the main character) during the last few scenes were not even remotely impressive. You would think if you spent all that time learning about the inhabitants of Mousewood and all those spells you would at least be able to use them in a SLIGHTLY impressive manner. But no. Not Jerry. The final battle was downright upsetting, as well. It was...one hundred percent different from anything else done in the rest of the game. Okay, maybe not one hundred. Maybe like ninety-five percent. Everything about the ending was just...bland and altogether anticlimatic and IT LEAVES SO MUCH UNTOLD. SO. MUCH.
All in all...no, I would not recommend this game, at least not at full price. Maybe at like...75% off, but not full price. It left me so disappointed. The only thing that raised my opinion of it at the very end was the Marquis. No, I would NOT play a sequel to this if one ever came out, not unless they severely dumb down the puzzles. Or at least make them reasonable.

Deus Ex is very dated. Polygons everywhere. After all, it was made like fifteen years ago. However, once I moved past the poor hit-detection and occasionally awkward combat, I realized it's a fantastic game. Depending on your play style (and skill level) it can be either an action or stealth game, and for me, usually ended up being both.
I started the game, having just recently played Dishonored, trying to be entirely non-lethal. I used stealth as best as I could, and tranquilizer darts and the stun gun when I was discovered. But what started out as me saying "Why should I kill these people?" turned to "Why SHOULDN'T I kill these people?" right around the halfway mark. Once you start having to deal with multiple soldiers, robots, and cameras scanning the room at once, the difficulty of being stealthy goes WAY up. This increase in difficulty also coincided with my acquiring of a really powerful melee weapon, so I just decided to kill a lot of people.
That's not to say it wouldn't be possible to do it without killing anyone. After leaving trails of blood in my wake, I would often go back (for loot) and realize "OH....there's a ventilation shaft I could have used to sneak past these guys," and then move on happily with my slaughtering. On any future playthroughs, though, having the knowledge of the level designs I do now, I would probably do a stealth run. For real this time.
Why should you buy the game, though? I got it because the whole Deus Ex series was on sale for like 7 bucks, and spring break had just started. You might not be so lucky. You might be working full time, or be trying REALLY HARD to graduate. If so, it's probably not for you. You need to focus a lot attention to the game's story to fully appreciate what's going on. The whole thing has that old-school feeling of being something greater than it is. But if you have time on your hands (or an impressive memory for seemingly inconsequential details), and are a fan of older games like this, I'd say go for it. If anything, it'll serve as a long intro for Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which I am now SUPER pumped for!!!!

I think the Night of the Rabbit holds the all characteristics that a wonderful point-and-click adventure games needs.
Great artistic style and music.
The art is amazing, especially the design of the different settings. The use of color and shading really brings out the atmosphere. This is also true for the music, really adds the touch to each of the places you will encounter through the game. Character design is also wonderful, and the character voice truly displays the character personalities.
Classic puzzle solving.
Very classic mechanism. Talking to NPC and bring items to them. The item collecting, combining and utilizing are all the components I enjoy about this type of adventure game. Although I will say some of the puzzles and item combinations are not as intuitive as it could be. Some item usage are rather a stretch. There is a help mechanism in the game the player can utilize, but I have to say it is rather useless. The help mechanism only continuously repeats the general goal of the section of the game you are on, it does not provide small clues to the smaller parts of the puzzle. The journal is more helpful in every way, although it does not provide hints, but it does keep track what you have to do. But this is a puzzle solving game, it would take away all the fun if the puzzle was too simple.
Interesting story.
The story isn't just about a boy with a dream, it has a lot more just than that. But it is hard to speak about how I like the story without spoiling a big part of it, so I guess I won't be talking too much about it. There are a lot that lies behind Jeremy's adventure. The people of Mousewood, the story of the Treewalkers, all the environment and the people of the other worlds. I feel like there are a lot more the game could have emphasized on, but the game was too short to cover everyone's story. I do hope there will be a sequel or maybe DLC to bring out the others' story.
The in game small game, item and achievement collections are great touches to the game itself. Adds a lot more to the game itself. Overall, this is a great point-and-click adventure game, and I would be totally excited for more stories.
