SPOILER FREE REVIEW~~ STEAM KEY RECEIVED FROM KAZAMATSURI FORUM CONTEST
Tomoyo After ~It's a Wonderful Life had lofty shoes to fill. As the title suggests, it's Tomoyo's After Story. Comparisons and contrasts will inevitably be drawn with the parent visual novel's penultimate chapter. Regardless, Tomoyo After holds up remarkably well. It may not reach the heights of After Story, but it is about as close as you could feasibly get.
Tomoyo After takes place soon after the ending of Tomoyo's story in Clannad. Having resolved to spend their lives together, Tomoya works a modest job at a plant that collects broken parts and re-purposes them for better use (a subtle parallel to how Tomoya himself hopes to make better of his withered husk of a life up until now). Tomoyo visits him every day after school in his apartment. After a disappointing prologue that does little but objectify Tomoyo, the plot kicks off when Tomoyo's younger brother, Takafumi, drops some startling news on their couple; Tomoyo's father had a daughter named Tomo prior to his reconciling with his wife, and her mother has mysteriously vanished.
From this point on, Tomoya and Tomoyo adjust to the stunning realization that they are now surrogate parents to this child in their own unique ways. Tomoyo easily slides into the role of a parent, bonding easily with Tomo by showering her with love and affection. Tomoya, initially a passive player in this change of events, hopes to prove he has both initative and resolve by finding a way to deal with an old flame of Tomoyo's by himself. Without getting in to too much detail, Tomoya admittedly decides to take some very irresponsible risks in this portion of the story, but the purpose of him doing so is laid out effectively by Maeda. Many may not find fault with it at all.
It's around this point that Tomoyo After shines. Our five main characters (Tomoya, Tomoyo, Takafumi, Tomo, and Takafumi's ex, Kanako) are an endearing group of leads who play off each other very well. Kanako's vulgar frankness interacts nicely with Tomoya's quirky imagination and contrasts effectively with Tomoyo's straight-laced, matter-of-factness. Tomoya and Takafumi's bond as brothers is also portrayed organically, with the two ribbing each other in a good-natured, heartwarming manner. Regardless of their differences, all of the cast members love Tomo and wish only the best for her. The interesting tension this causes about halfway through the story is one of the most compelling parts of the story.
The much-discussed After arc of the story is worthy of its fame. It's thought-provoking, true to the characters involved, and deeply emotional. I have a feeling it will stick with me almost as long as After Story will.
For some much needed levity, the game allows you to play an RPG minigame, Dungeons and Takafumis, a surprisingly complex and lengthy bonus that delivers good humor and (for better or for worse) challenging game design. At level 35, I've yet to finish it :P.
Tomoyo After is another solid entry from Japan's best visual novel company. If you enjoyed Tomoyo's arc in Clannad, then I would recommend this game in a heartbeat.

Dungeons & Takafumis (D&T) is a minigame within Tomoyo After that is straightforwad to play and somewhat difficult to master. D&T is like a tactical RPG, except you can only give orders at the start of a battle. Once the battle starts, you lose all control of your characters - they will move around the map to follow those orders (mostly for the best, but not always). Besides the orders, you control character starting position, equipped gear, and stat growth via allocating growth points and changing jobs.
The relatively small number of options under the player's control makes D&T straightforward to play. The difficulty is that the equipment won at the end of a battle is random. The Random Number God might give you what you need when you need it, or forsake you. The challenge in D&T is to win all battles within an in-game time limit by optimising your orders, starting positions and stat growth, while making the best use of the randomised equipment.

Party Hard has an interesting premise where you play the role of a psycho who simply does not like loud parties. His solution? Kill every one at the party of course! If I was to try an nail Party Hard to a single genre, I would say it's a tactical stealth game, though murder-sim also comes to mind.
The idea of putting the stealth genre into a crowded, open room, as Party Hard has done, is a pretty unique experience. In most other stealth games, the area is sparsely populated with tons of corners and objects to hide around, but in Party Hard you're in a large open room, where every one can see every one else. It makes stealth tactics much more interesting as the player will have to be creative on how he or she approach any given situation., with witnesses littered every where.
In Party Hard, the most basic way of accomplishing your goal of murder is simply to stab someone. It's also recommended that you dump the body somewhere unseen as they'll alert other party goers. The key here is not to get caught, even if someone alert the cops, as long as you don't get pined with the crime, you're still good to go. The game also gives you an assortment of randomly generated environmental traps and dangers, with each stage featuring it's own unique RNG generation. You can activate any of these traps at any given moment in order to help you murder the party. The game also encourages creative play, as each scenario plays out more like a sandbox. For example, there is a stage with a swimming pool. I got creative, and experimented with carrying passed out partiers into the pool to see if they'd drown. Indeed they did, and this is just one example of how you can get creative with the many "kill tactics" available to you. The overall premise of this idea, with how sandboxy the stages are designed, coupled with the random event generation that comes with every play though, the game does a good job at encouraging replay, while keeping things interesting and surprising.
Though the core of Party Hard is pretty enjoyable, and if nothing else, unique and interesting, it's not without it's faults. Your character's movement speed is at a snail's pace, with only a short, and slow regenerating stamina bar to help with it. It also encourages a lot of moving back and forth repetitively in order to dump bodies safely. Couple these 2 slow elements with the fact that when you fail a stage, you have to start at the beginning. Considering that some of the stages can take upwards to, if not over, 20 minutes to complete, the game can feel tedious at times.
Party Hard's overall creative stealth play, with it's interesting random event generation, I found it more enjoyable than tedious. It's overall a very unique and enjoyable experience, though some of the tedium will turn some players off.
Pros:
- Unique stealth gameplay design
- Good visuals and audio
- Lots of dark comedy
- Random event generation keeps the game fresh
Cons:
- Punishing fail state that waste time rather than teach a lesson
- Slow movement pace
- Can be repetitive

I've been enjoying this game since 2012, long before the Steam re-release, and it ranks as one of my all-time favourite racing sims. It's a little known gem that deserves greater exposure than it has achieved to date.
Being based on a modified and evolved version of the rFactor engine gives Stock Car Extreme a great platform to build on and Reiza have done just that. For what it lacks in visual polish, Stock Car Extreme more than makes up for it on the track with cars that feel convincingly realistic. This is a title that really needs to be driven with a racing wheel to get the best experience, with force feedback that conveys the physics so well.
Car and track content is fresh, varied and eclectic with a South American focus (Reiza is a Brazilian developer) therefore offering something a little different from other race sims. The car selection ranges from the V8 touring cars that lend the title it's name to the Mini Challenge series to karts, a prototype, a Camaro and a selection of open wheel cars past and present. Tracks are equally varied with locations from around the world and historic layouts plus a couple of good street circuits.
In summary: Stock Car Extreme is a must-have title for racing simulation fans.

The Witcher 2 was the first Witcher game I heard of, and also the first one I heard very good things about. Yet, Witcher 3 was the first one I actually completed, and thus, decided to revisit the precursor games. So this review will be from the POV of someone who got to experience the brilliance of Witcher 3 first, and because of it, sees the games in a different light than someone who might've been new to the franchise when they played through Witcher 1.
The game picks up a couple of months after the events of the first game, letting you have your old weapons and armor from Witcher 1 if you imported your savefile, which I like. It keeps the games consistent and rewards the returning fans who loved the last game enough to buy the sequel.
Combat was definitely developed beyond the clunkyness and buggyness of Witcher 1, with it now being more responsive and dependent on the individual player's skill in stead of RNG and basic point-and-click mechanics. One thing I didn't like at first was how they changed the Aard and Igni signs to not be an AOE attack initially. Of course I changed my mind when I learned that you could upgrade them to do AOE damage down the line in the skill tree so this is not really a negative thing in my conclusive opinion of the game. They also did a much better job at separating throwables from potions, making potions something you could only do in preparation for battle during meditation.
The locking-on system is a bit weird imho, seen as how you still run around like a chicken without a head even when locked on, instead of being more focused on the locked-on target. If they were to use the system that they later did in Witcher 3, they could have had a different dodging-system when locked on from when not locked on, like for example side-stepping. This is not really a negative point though, so I'm not really that bothered by it. One thing I will say about the combat in Witcher 2 is that it is in its own way very clunky at first and takes an hour or two to get used to. This is not really a problem if you're a fast learner and/or don't mind having the patience to get used to a combat system.
The story in the game has had some big improvements from Witcher 1, with the lore being more consistent and the world feeling a lot more alive and breathing. The characters are very well put together and developed, unlike in a lot of other RPGs, where all the NPCs feel bland and unimportant. In this game a lot of the NPCs, even those that ARE pointless and random background-characters, feel realistic and feel as though that they are a part of the world they exist in, which a lot of other games does not achieve as well. The story of the game itself is in my opinion very good, with a bunch of twists and turns, with a whole lot of depth. The basic overarching story is that Geralt, a witcher that was accused of murdering King Foltest, sets out to hunt down the person that actually murdered the king and by doing so, attempts clearing his own name. Throughout the game you can make a lot of different choices that does impact the game in a big enough way that the choices feel impactful, responsive and makes them feel as though they have real consequence. A lot of the choices you make in the game can change the game itself quite a bit.
In the ways of setting up Witcher 3 it does a wonderful job, almost spoonfeeding you information that'll be important in the third installment at some points. A lot of the choices you make in this game will carry over to the next game if you choose to import your save file when beginning a new save for Witcher 3. The ending of Witcher 2 pretty much explains the beginning of Witcher 3 perfectly, with the omens of the ending in this game being played out in the beginning of the next game.
As a conclusion, I would like to recommend The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings to anyone who is interested in a good RPG with a great amount of depth and around 40-50hrs playtime if doing all sidequests. There is a lot of replay value here seen as how many choices there are that changes the tides of the game.
My final verdict on Witcher 2 is: 9.5/10

After playing The Witcher, The Witcher 2 felt very weird. The graphics are much more realistic, which most people prefer - I on the other hand am more torn between Witcher 1 & 2. The first games more game-like graphics appealed to me quite a bit. The fighting mechanics of the first game, albeit quite easy, were fun. Which is the total opposite for The Witcher 2, in my opinion. The inventory system is also much more tedious in The Witcher 2, as you constantly have to manage the weight of your backpack instead of having inventory slots and an easier access to an overlook of everything in your inventory, à la The Witcher.
The story is much more deep and filled with betrayal after betrayal and it somehow feels much more darker. The choices were also harder than in the first game and affected the story on a whole new level. Your choices even decide to which places you go and who you do quests for. The beginning was not completely engaging, but after a while the story really picks up pace. After all the build-up, the last chapter is truly superb.
The combat on the other hand... After starting the game I quickly became frustrated with the combat system. It was quite hard, but manageable, to fight an enemy. When faced with two enemies, at least the other one could quickly get a backstab at you, and take you down in a hit or two. And more often than not, you were fighting multiple enemies. The parrying system and especially the counter attacking part of it was the worst. It all had to be timed so precisely that I could barely do it in the tutorial, and never tried it again after that. I got the feeling that to survive combat, one had to roll and resort to only using hit-and-run tactics. I almost quit the game in chapter 1 already, but then I decided to set my pride aside and lowered the difficulty to easy - so I mostly just played through the game because of the excellent story. On easy mode the Witcher's opponents become, well, quite easy. Luckily it made the game quite fun though.
Excluding the combat, there were few big things to complain about. One very frustrating bug that comes to mind though, resides in chapter 2. The quests have a very specific order in which they need to be completed in order to get the outcome that I desired - and even though I loaded a saved game from quite a while back and did everything in the order stated on the wiki and the quests got the completed status, the quests were still marked as failed in my journal at the start of chapter 3...
Overall though, the game is very much worth a playthrough; if nothing else, then for the excellent story. I highly recommend playing through The Witcher & The Witcher 2 before starting The Witcher 3, because it gives you a whole lot of immersion compared to directly jumping into The Witcher 3 - especially regarding the characters.
I'd give this game an 6.5/10 if you're more into gameplay, and a 9.5/10 if you're in it for the story - like I was.
If nothing else, then quickly play through the main story to better understand all the characters and events taking place in The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt.

Sending a massive crusading army across Europe and into the Middle East, and than being met by an opposing Jihad force is simply stunning. Than depending on the outcome of the crusade you will either be greatly rewarded by the church for victory, or for failure you may be excommunicated and cast as an enemy to the Christiandom! Another unique feature is the guilds. While their effects and purpose are hard to see at first, they will progressively become more helpful to your nation and will lead to some awesome and elite troops specific to different factions. For example, England can develop a woodsmen guild in Nottingham and once it reaches a certain level, you can recruit Sherwood archers that can camoflauge in the woods and have tremendous range. The powerful Knights Templar are another guild specific to Christian Nations, while eastern nations have the Hashassins guild. If there is one thing that frustrates me during combat, it is that sometimes archers don't fire directly at the enemy when there on walls, but it just takes some practice mastering their line of sight and taking advantage of their range. I also wish there were more historical battles as they provide some awesome scenerios and challenging battles. I recommend going through atleat one play through as the vanilla game, and than trying out the VAST amounts of full and partial mods that have been made for this game. You can even try your own costumizations to the script and combinations of different modification until you find the perfect balance for you. All in all, this a game for the ages and is better than 99% of the garbage that comes out nowadays.

To make my review more valuable to the interested:
I haven't played Terran Conflict. I chose to begin with Albion Prelude for reasons I'm unsure of now, so I can't compare to X3:TC for those coming from there. I can, however, fully support new players starting with X3:AP like I did.
X3:AP is a great sandbox game with just enough guided gameplay in the form of various plotlines. The plotlines have enough information about the universe to give new players a basic understanding of events past and current. The game shines most as a sandbox, though.
The systems in X3:AP include both combat and trading fleet management, ship customization in the form of basic upgrades, computer systems, and weapons, station building with much freedom. Management systems seem to hold their own. I find they do what they need to quite well. All of these items are great and fun to play with, but are tarnished by limitations when you get deeper in to the game.
The most annoying of those limitations comes from the game's engine. Slowdowns occur in heavily populated sectors, especially with large player station complexes or large-scale battles. The slowdowns in large complexes can be bearable, but I've found large scale battles to be impossible to participate in. Even now with updated hardware, the game still stuggles for me. With that issue, you're left fighting these battles OOS (out of sector), commanding your fleets on the sector map.
Other issues that tarnish the gameplay come in the form a major and minor bugs. One major bug is the erratic behavior of friendly ships in war sectors while OOS which will cause you ship casualties if you don't keep them out of those sectors (which is only about 6 sectors, but still an annoyance).
Some things in the game seem to have little value to the experience such as the Unfocused Jumpdrive and covert missions, but the bulk of the game seems to hold it's worth.
Overall, you can find much enjoyable in the game. Most bugs and annoyances you won't realize until you've put plenty of time into the game making a purchase worthwhile. Working your way up from one ship to an army with system of stations producing whatever you desire is an enjoyable experience. Carelessness can always get you killed or your profits lost.

After playing through this game once, I need to get some things off my chest about this game, as I have very mixed feelings about it.
Yes, the game is a low effort port and you will definitely notice it. Yes, playing without a 2 stick controller is just not going to do, so don't try this with keyboard / mouse. But that's not why I'm not recommending this game.
First impressions were very good, the game has something from a lot of games. It's a mix of Space Invaders, Dark Souls, Bayonetta, Furi and all of that in a fast paced action JRPG. Also notice that it's from the makers of Metal Gear Rising Revengeance and Bayonetta. The story starts very intriguing about what it means to be human and life in a post-apocalyptic world of robots, so it seemed like my kind of game and I really wanted to like it.
About the setting:
The game tries to be as realistic as possible and even explain elements of the game (e.g. UI, respawning, saving) in their robot setting, which seems very cool at first, but gets very stale after a while when you start noticing its obvious flaws and limits - from plot to gameplay.
I was constantly left wondering: Why don't they just do that and avoid the whole problem altogether? Why is this even relevant? Unfortunately most of the almost philosophical topics from the start are just never touched on again and then the story doesn't even follow its own rules sometimes for the sake of being more dramatic...
About the gameplay and difficulty:
If you play on normal or easy, it is a very enjoyable experience. You will feel very overpowered, enjoy hack and slay styled combat the way it is supposed to be played and everything is fine.
If you want a challenge and try the game on hard (there is also super hard where you always die in one hit), you just get ♥♥♥♥ed over so much. The game isn't really hard, but unfair and very punishing. With the ridiculous level scaling you will get oneshot by everything a few levels above you and even the cheapest mechanics. With the no autosave mechanic, you will sometimes have to replay whole levels again just to try once more. And good luck getting to your corpse (this alone can take a while) and standing still for 3 seconds in the middle of enemies that already killed you and without your equipment. If you die again, you loose your equipment forever, at which point you can basically reset the game.
After a lot of grinding, because even the available side quests are 20 levels above you and not a valid xp ressource, when you outlevel the enemies even just slightly, the game is basically the same as normal and way too easy. The balancing really just isn't good. There would definitely be a line between super hard and way too easy, but the developers couldn't find it.
About the game world:
The way the story and world is designed feels more like a low effort MMO to me. You will see most of the zones (only 5) in the game very quickly and then get sent to the same places over and over again. Many sidequests are very simple go here, kill that type quests and aren't even voiced. I really just expected more.
For one playthrough the amount of content might be fine, but as you may know, they expect you to play the game up to 5 times to get the full story. Considering that even the first playthrough is very repetitive, down to even most of the bosses repeating and the second playthrough being 90% the same as the first one, this is just low effort design to me. Rehashing the same content as many times as you possibly can is not what I want in a game and I already got tired of it during my first playthrough.
Also the first main ending (A) you get after playing through the whole game once isn't even a motivating ending. You get no explanations, no epilogue, no foreshadowing, no motivation, nothing. They just cut out during a regular scene and you just casually start all over again and to get more info you basically have to play it at least 3 times.
Summary:
Even though I initially enjoyed the setting and most of the gameplay, over the course of the game, as I started noticing all the flaws, limits and the dwindling quality, my motivation was fading. So much of the game seems to be lazily put in and not thought through. The same content just gets dragged out and repeated multiple times. Adding the bad port on top, I unfortunately cannot justify recommending this game. It wasn't the worst game I ever played, but it wasn't good either.

This game is an extension on the Terran Conflict universe with new plot lines and content. Its basically a huge space sandbox which at first feels very overwhelming, however knowing how to do everything is not essential.

You pick a start scenario which sets your race and starting ship(s) and credits plus gives you access to the different plot lines. The main plots have no time limit so you can ignore them untill you feel like doing them and just fly around and explore the vast universe.
The dynamic economy can be exploited for profitsss or you can scavenge the wares dropped from capital ships in the war sectors. After you have made heaps of cash you can build factories  and or a trade fleet and generate a constant income. You can also just be a pirate and loot wares from the ai ships flying around. Or you can do none of the above but you need creditssss!! for more capital shipssss!!
The graphics are great for a game of this age and complexity, good immersion.
I just fly around and shoot with the mouse, keyboard controls can be customized too.
The only downsides of this game are its interface, while it needs to be complex it could have been thought out better. I think it is due to features being continually added over time.

Theres also issues with how the war sectors are scripted which will make your hair fall out but i learned to work around it and now have ended the war anyway.
I recommend this game to people who dont mind a bit of a learning curve. I personally had no problem being drawn in by the universe and having it consume most of my spare time.

Played about a good 50+ hours so far, finished the main game and the Claptastic Voyage, currently busy with TVHM.
Honestly, i really don't get much of the negativity surrounding TPS, it's a fantastic game. The game has a number of flaws (in comparison to B2) but also has a lot of features that redeem it. I'll just list up the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Excellent storyline. Whereas i couldn't be arsed about B2's storyline, TPS does so a lot better. Everybody has a knack for Jack (pun intended) and TPS is focused around his side of the story that lead up to the events of B2. Don't wanna spoil it so i'll keep it short. The story will give you a lot more perspective on Jack, and why he's such a psycho hell-bent on reducing Pandora to rubble, and what morality he bears to it. You'll get to see his reasons for it.
- Plenty of new additions. For example, slag has been removed and replaced with cryo damage. It's essentialy still the same thing, as it boosts damage, but enemies will be slowed or paralyzed for a few seconds, making it a far more effective elemental weapon. A new weapon is also introduced: Lasers, which is pretty much as awesome as it sounds.
- Money is essentialy worthless in B2, with the exception of grinding slot machines. (which rarely give anything good anyway, so its mostly exchanging it for Eridium) Not the case anymore, vendors reguraly have excellent items on stock, even the occassional legendary item. And they dont come cheap. Money is an essential part, and paying a respawn fee is now something you want to avoid. Along with that, there's the 'Grinder', a machine that can turn items and weapons you don't need into something new, with a good chance of them increasing in rarity level. (for example, 3 green items can be turned into a blue one)
- Level scaling is a lot better, with the 'Triton Flats' (an area which you will reguraly be returning to) set to your current lvl as the story progresses. Backtracking, grinding and looting is thus also a lot more viable if you wish to do so.
- I've encountered a lot of bugs in B2, including a pretty gamebreaking one. It's annoying. TPS has a lot less 'rough edges', in the 50+ hours i've spent i have passed by barely any bugs at all.
- A whole new cast of characters with entirely different playstyles. Whereas B2 regurgitated some of the characters from B1 into B2 (Commando being Roland, Gunzerker being Brick, etc.) every character in the game has its very own special skillsets and are extremely enjoyable as well.
-There's lots of new enemies everywhere, which is awesome. Unfortunately though, some of them are mostly 'repackaged' enemies from B2. (Kragoons being Skags, Scavs being bandits, etc.)
Cons:
- It's shorter than B2. Fewer sidequests and a slightly shorter (though more enjoyable) storyline.
- Little new weaponry. There's the lasers they added, which are awesome, but they've mostly ported the arsenal from B2 to TPS. I would've enjoyed seeing some new weapons around. Though, thankfully, there are a good number of new legendaries (quite a lot, actually) to find, and i've encountered a few high-lvl weapons (blues/purples, though i could be wrong and these have been ported from B2 as well) that i haven't seen before. It's still a shame though. For a game that focuses so much on loot and progression, some new flavors would've definetly been appreciated. Claptastic Voyage includes a new rarity level (Glitch) and new weapons which are awesome, but you won't find them in the vanilla game so i don't really think they count.
- They've really tried to bring back that feel of humor from it's predecessors and implemented it into TPS. Yeah, i've laughed heartily a few times, but they've tried to give you the occasional chuckle every now and then. Or at least, that's the aim. Thankfully, none of it feels forced, but it's just not funny most of the time.
- The whole low gravity thing is awesome, but the fact that you have to maintain your oxygen is just annoying. Occasionaly you'll have to run off to a location containing oxygen when you're on your way. Instead of keeping the pace, you're just gonna have to stop every now and then. For absolutely no reason whatsoever. It's not a feature Gearbox, it's just annoying.
- It may not be something for everyone, but the DLC is - aside from the Claptastic Voyage (which is amazing by the way) - pretty little. B2 has huge amounts of excellent DLC (DLC done right), TPS has far less. Of course, this shouldn't affect the rating of the game, it's an add-on after all.
In conclusion, i recommend B:TPS. Though i urge every person new to the series to start out with B2 (you dont need B1 if you dont wanna), if you want some more of it, totally get TPS. It might not be brimmed with content like B2 was, nor is it a huge step up what B2 did for B1, it's still a great addition to the Borderlands franchise.

People are b****ing about this game because it is difficult. Yes, the hard mode is crazy difficult, but
. This game takes some time to get used to, I would say give it at least 3 hours before giving up and bashing the game in the reviews. Once you get the hang of things it becomes much easier. By my 4th or 5th attempt the game seemed significantly easier than it was the previous tries, and that's just solo. The co-op experience is amazing and much easier, probably one of the best co-op survival games out there. Once you get a good group of friends and start making progress the game gets crazy addicting.
I personally have been playing on the 'EXPLORER' mode and will continue to until I can get a better grasp on how the game should be played and patterns in it that will help make progress in the 'SURVIVOR' mode, and if you are hoping to get the most out of this game, I recommend the same.
Basically this game takes time, so do not get it if you are looking for some super lax casual survival stuff that you're not willing to put time into.
All in all the story is intriguing with a giant map, the survival aspects are difficult but realistic, and it is a great game to play with friends. And it's still being updated, with the massive bunker update coming out recently, the devs are clearly putting a lot of effort into making the game even greater than it is. Totally recommend this game, the people hating on it either don't understand what the game is supposed to be or are mad that later in the story you will face supernatural enemies.

If your a survival genre lover I highly suggest not buying this game for it.  Currently it's more of a story telling game with a bit of monsters that drop loot and some resource gathering to build equipment.
I will be reviewing this game as a survival game as this is the reason I bought the game and also the game description.
"The Wild Eight is an UNFORGIVING SURVIVAL GAME set in Alaska full of mystery and danger. Explore, hunt and craft shoulder-to-shoulder with friends or random players online. Unless you are brave enough to survive this nightmare on your own?"
(*Side note* game is not hard at all, u can survive this "nightmare" on your own)
Gameplay 8/10
Very simple, stun enemy and attack and use traps on stronger enemies.  There is some skill involved in getting used to how to survive (Gathering food, resources and priority upgrades) but other than that it's a very straight forward game anyone can pick up and play.
Story
6/10
So far everything is still up in the air, I expect to change this as more content rolls out, by the story is interesting enough for me to come back in the future.
Controls
9/10
The controls in this game is very very smooth, no bugs, simple click and WASD user input.  I choose to not give it perfect as currently running down a hill makes you fly off and die, this includes stairs.  Intended or not by the dev it requires control to go down a set of stairs that no one would normally do so it makes it harder to use the controls in a way.
Content
7/10
As the game is in beta it's understanable for there to be a lack of content, but I believe there is a lot of simple content that could have been added that the game is lacking. A very simple one would be the ability to build inside the hub as it's very limited in storage space making it pointless to really go out and gather resources.  Which this in turn kills some of the content that is being provided by the game itself.
Survival Content
3/10
Sadly there is not much to the survival content in this game.  You do need food to survive, temperature meter, creatures, resources to gather but as a harsh survival game where your lost somewhere, I expected to be able to find weapon recipes, crafting buildings / benchs, being hunted (waves of creatures), upgrades where it's not only a simple stat upgrade.  This entire game, the only time I felt I was in danger was when I lost control going down a set of stairs and died... at no point of this game I felt that I Was playing a survival game, just more of a storyline game.
End game
2/10
There is a huge lack of end game content as once your finished the side quests and main quest there is nothing left.  Orignally I expected the survival aspect of this game but the content for that is very lacking.  I have finished the game and don't plan on playing it at all until the next... maybe 10 patchs?
Overall
5.8/10
I know the score is very low for me to recommend the game but I totally recommend this game outside of the survival content.  If your planning to buy this game for the survival aspect, DON"T.  You will be very disappointed (As someone who plays heavly modded minecraft, The Forest, Don't Starve, 7 Days to die, Savage Lands).
TLDR; Good game, not a good survival game, don't buy if your expecting it to be survival

Some of my friends would say that writing a review for Deus Ex just seems stupid. People
how good this game is right? They don’t need me to be badgering them to play it! But the sad truth is that as the younger demographic come onto the scene, this is one of those gems that they are missing. And can we really blame them? Just one look at the screenshot or the gameplay on YouTube is enough to tell you that this is not a pretty looking game! Is it really worth getting in 2015?
What Deus Ex provides is a lot of mechanical depth. There is a lot of freedom in the way you approach things: you can be a ruthless murderer, a hacker, a stealthy assassin… it’s entirely up to you how to approach the situations you encounter in the game. Also the mechanics, with the exception of the awful crossbow (don’t try it) don’t feel all that dated. Upgrading your abilities and the various augmentations you can make to yourself is implemented really well to the game, and feels quite modern. What I will warn you about though is that you should not expect to be able to shoot accurately when you start the game. If you don’t put points into pistols then you are going to suck with pistols – it’s annoying but mechanically it makes a lot of sense. After all, in order to shoot accurately you have to be a skilled shot!
Unfortunately it does look terrible, which is the point that I’m going to put the challenge on you as the reader to make the decision. This is one of the best PC games of all time, that’s a fact. If it was released nowadays with modern graphics it would be winning awards. So if you think you can cope with the outdated graphics, then I challenge you to play this game. I advise that in the opening section of the game you put those points into pistols and stick to the shadows to begin with. But if you can get through that opening level, then you are in for a treat – because this game is fantastic.
Please do feel free to comment if you’ve tried and you get stuck or whatever. Or if you were able to break through the graphics barrier and are enjoying arguably one of the finest narrative experiences ever created. I’d love to hear the feedback.

After playing through this game once, I need to get some things off my chest about this game, as I have very mixed feelings about it.
Yes, the game is a low effort port and you will definitely notice it. Yes, playing without a 2 stick controller is just not going to do, so don't try this with keyboard / mouse. But that's not why I'm not recommending this game.
First impressions were very good, the game has something from a lot of games. It's a mix of Space Invaders, Dark Souls, Bayonetta, Furi and all of that in a fast paced action JRPG. Also notice that it's from the makers of Metal Gear Rising Revengeance and Bayonetta. The story starts very intriguing about what it means to be human and life in a post-apocalyptic world of robots, so it seemed like my kind of game and I really wanted to like it.
About the setting:
The game tries to be as realistic as possible and even explain elements of the game (e.g. UI, respawning, saving) in their robot setting, which seems very cool at first, but gets very stale after a while when you start noticing its obvious flaws and limits - from plot to gameplay.
I was constantly left wondering: Why don't they just do that and avoid the whole problem altogether? Why is this even relevant? Unfortunately most of the almost philosophical topics from the start are just never touched on again and then the story doesn't even follow its own rules sometimes for the sake of being more dramatic...
About the gameplay and difficulty:
If you play on normal or easy, it is a very enjoyable experience. You will feel very overpowered, enjoy hack and slay styled combat the way it is supposed to be played and everything is fine.
If you want a challenge and try the game on hard (there is also super hard where you always die in one hit), you just get ♥♥♥♥ed over so much. The game isn't really hard, but unfair and very punishing. With the ridiculous level scaling you will get oneshot by everything a few levels above you and even the cheapest mechanics. With the no autosave mechanic, you will sometimes have to replay whole levels again just to try once more. And good luck getting to your corpse (this alone can take a while) and standing still for 3 seconds in the middle of enemies that already killed you and without your equipment. If you die again, you loose your equipment forever, at which point you can basically reset the game.
After a lot of grinding, because even the available side quests are 20 levels above you and not a valid xp ressource, when you outlevel the enemies even just slightly, the game is basically the same as normal and way too easy. The balancing really just isn't good. There would definitely be a line between super hard and way too easy, but the developers couldn't find it.
About the game world:
The way the story and world is designed feels more like a low effort MMO to me. You will see most of the zones (only 5) in the game very quickly and then get sent to the same places over and over again. Many sidequests are very simple go here, kill that type quests and aren't even voiced. I really just expected more.
For one playthrough the amount of content might be fine, but as you may know, they expect you to play the game up to 5 times to get the full story. Considering that even the first playthrough is very repetitive, down to even most of the bosses repeating and the second playthrough being 90% the same as the first one, this is just low effort design to me. Rehashing the same content as many times as you possibly can is not what I want in a game and I already got tired of it during my first playthrough.
Also the first main ending (A) you get after playing through the whole game once isn't even a motivating ending. You get no explanations, no epilogue, no foreshadowing, no motivation, nothing. They just cut out during a regular scene and you just casually start all over again and to get more info you basically have to play it at least 3 times.
Summary:
Even though I initially enjoyed the setting and most of the gameplay, over the course of the game, as I started noticing all the flaws, limits and the dwindling quality, my motivation was fading. So much of the game seems to be lazily put in and not thought through. The same content just gets dragged out and repeated multiple times. Adding the bad port on top, I unfortunately cannot justify recommending this game. It wasn't the worst game I ever played, but it wasn't good either.

ALWAYS ON GRIND
Always on grind. Both the plot quests and randomly generated missions require you to do one thing, grind for money until you can afford to purchase whatever it is to complete the mission - at which point the mission is easy. Missions are either easy because you have the money, impossible because you don't, or impossible because of time limits and you don't happen to have a jump drive or appropriate wares installed at the time.
Flight controls are good and customizable, and the backgrounds are pretty.
The economy, trading, and station building are all about having enough money - and you either spend time with tedious micromanagement or let it run on some form of laconic automatic.
The map interface is clunky and painful. Why is it always so difficult to find certain available goods? The encyclopedia tool helps, but ultimately falls short of explaining why all the stations and factories which supposedly are trying to sell their wares fail to broadcast their location or advertise pricing.
Combat in the smaller M5, M4, and M3 ships is fun, but larger ships are often impossible to get through their shields. Using a larger ship yourself makes combat a non-event after you equip turrets with phased repeater guns for missile defence; hoever, the larger ships are painfully slow.
Modding helps aleviate some of the above problems but fails to correct some of the fundamental flaws in this game.
Bottomline: The game has SETA to accelerate time in the game - because you are so often just waiting to get from point A to B. However, even at 10x speed, waiting isn't fun.

I love this game series... it has everything I want in a game...
Except for functional AI.
The game is supposed to allow you to form fleets and use those fleets to go into battle.  Awesome right?
Nope.  It's not awesome, it sucks.
Why does it suck?
Because the AI of your wingmen/fleet ships sucks.  They circle around you constantly rather than following in a rigid formation.  This causes them to do all sorts of really stupid stuff like crash into you or crash into anything around you or just generally crash.  And when they crash into you, you die and they die, or something dies.
So, you can't use wingmen effectively - which defeats like 50% of the purpose of the game.
Anyway, you can't just make something like this so lazily - but the company did make something like this so lazily.  One of the most important features in the game is absolutely broken and they never bothered to fix it.
Honestly, I could crap better pathing algorithms than this game has and I'm not even a professional programmer.  At least I know I wouldn't ship a game with pathing problems like that.  Why is it so hard to get the ships to track rigid formation targets instead of swarm around your ship like flies?  Well... it's not.
Want cool big ships?  Totally awesome right?  Well, forget about flying with wingmen because they'll crash into you left and right unless you are ordering them around through half a million menus.  Sure, you'd think there'd be a key for "order wing to attack X target" - there is, it works sometimes.  But, sadly, you can't have that wing flying with you because they'll crash into you left and right.  Which means the only TWO KEYS that you have to control any fleet in the same system as you are off limits unless you're flying... and it must be precisely this: an M6 or M7 with no more than ten M4/5s.  Forget trying to have a fleet if you want to fly a capital ship.  Of course capital ships are useless without a fleet....  But, alas, they hired halfwitted monkeys to code the GUI.
Like playing with a mouse?  Find Joysticks too large and cumbersome?  Well, you can't use autoaim then, AT ALL...  That means on your giant ship where the turrets are positioned like a kilometer apart, your shots are going to be aimed at that enemy ship a KILOMETER APART because your turrets are just going to shoot straight instead of interpolating what enemy you're attacking and forcing both wing's turrets to collide at that point in three space.
Why can't you use autoaim with the mouse but you can with a joystick?
I have no clue whatsoever, but I imagine it's just to show you how much you were shafted by a company that apparently spent its entire budget on skybox reflection shaders.
Maybe it's because the maths for screen to point were too hard for the halfwitted monkey GUI programmers.
One of the cool things about this game is you get to build factories.  Sounds fun right?  You get to position them in space and build giant complexes out of them!  Well, thankfully they've made it easy by allowing you to visually see the factory in 3 space before you place it - you can even rotate it around with the number pad and position it and the like.  This would be great if it weren't for the fact that they force you to have a semi-transparent (emphasis on the "semi" more than the transparent) map covering the ENTIRE SCREEN while you place the factory.  It's ok though, you can just press "ALT-H" to hide the hud like in regular mode?  Oh?  It doesn't work?  Well, why should a simple toggle exist to temporarily hide the GUI overlay?  Sure it would come in handy while placing a factory, I mean they did bother to give you a representation of the factory in 3 space before you place it - but why should we let 5th grade programming prevail when we can half halfwitted monkey programming?
But in all seriousness - this is the kind of game I want to play - but there are so many things that make it so inordinantly and unintuitive to play that I have to give it a thumbs down.   They want you to play it like a text game with a graphical componant rather than a graphical game with a textual RTS component.   I'm cool with micromanaging fleets and factories and spending three hours in space just setting up trade routes and supply lines - but damnit I want there to be a purpose to it!  When I want to go dogfight I don't want stupid half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥GUI programming to get in the way and that's what you end up fighting against in X3: the GUI.
The enemies in X3 aren't the enemies you're fighting when you want a little space combat, it's the programmers who seem to lack absolutely any intuition whatsoever when it comes to a user interface/real time combat mechanics.

are the moments when I am compelled to take time out to leave a review for a game. In fact, I think I've written only one or two reviews in the 8 or 9 years I've been on Steam. And yet, NieR: Automata has compelled me to leave one.
From beginning to end and from top to bottom, this game is exquisite. The pacing, the feel of its open world, the music, the twisting and turning story are all among the very best in the class. Told over multiple play throughs from multiple perspectives, and leaning heavily on nihilistic precepts and philosphies, the game takes you on a roller coaster of a ride that not only forces you to question the motives of the protagonists and antoganists, but their very purpose (and yours too from time to time). Side quests aren't your typical filler experiences found in most open world experiences: each one was carefully crafted to add depth and complexity to the story, to the background, to the core philosophical questions the game poses to the player and its characters.
The high quality story telling through the game's interactions brings you in tight with the characters (even the side characters) and doesn't let go. The hardships some characters endure over the course of the game is presented without lots of direct exposition, rather through subtle body language, discouraged commentaries, and painful admissions. Fleeting hope makes you want to grab at it like a lifeline as pain and sadness reaches out to envelope you and your protagonists. The struggle of emotions bears the most satisfying of rewards for those players who endure to the end. The distance some characters have...their reactions to situations...it's all for a deeper reason, all of which will be revealed with time. And it's worth the wait to find out. Nihlism runs deep in the game as I mentioned and several characteers are named after famous philospophers. Reading about them will enrich your overall experience.
In my opinion, it's for every gamer who loved the story and delivery of games like FF7 and FFX but have been perpetually disappointed with the RPG genre ever since. It's for those who love beautiful characters with exquisite animation. It's for those who love great action and awesome combat. It's for those who love a game with meaning that go far deeper than the surface and forces you in the real world to question your motivations and values. Should you have an ear to hear what characters and situations are really saying, this game will resonate with you like a clanging symbol long after your play session ends. It's for those who enjoy the idea or experience of playing a game multiple times from multiple perspectives (think Dishonored), each more rewarding than the last. Hell, the game doesn't even begin until the 3rd playthrough, and by then you will have had enough "holy s**t!" moments to last the rest of the year.
YEP. I went in with ZERO expectations (didn't play any Drakengard games or the original Nier)...and came out the other side championing this game as my Game of The Year already. Sorry, Zelda. Sorry Nioh. Sorry Horizon. Sorry _____ (fill in whatever else is coming this year). If I didn't have another single player game to play this year, this would be enough for me. The mix of highs and lows, the pacing, the character development, the emotions on display from beginning to end have wrapped me around this game's proverbial finger. So much so that after 90 hours, I'm genuinely *excited* to start all over again from scratch. No game I've ever played has so moved me, and with the depth of the characters and knowing the story behind the story, I expect the next time through might be even better. This is a game that was clearly made with more love than most. It takes more risks than most and as a result offers a product rarely seen. If you enjoy single player, story-driven games at all, you do yourself a disservice by NOT playing this game. There's a reason it's Metacritic score is so high and why so many people are talking about this game.
I'd buy this game again in a heartbeat, folks. I've never been more glad than I am now that I took a chance on a game (never played any of the games in the franchise before). I haven't felt this rewarded by a game experience in 20 years (Final Fantasy 7 at launch) and I mean that. The game is probably going to end up in my top 5 all time, and I've been gaming for 30 years.
Support this team and Yoko Taro's work. He is one of the best story tellers we have left. Oh, and do yourself a favor and immediately disable MSAA. Great tips for maximizing your PC performance with the game can be found here:

To summarize, Disgaea 2 PC does everything the PC port of the first game did, but much better. Apart from including DLCs from all the previous versions of the game - for free, nonetheless - all systems are refined, giving you more combat options and less grinding.
- Every character has a passive ability that gives them something unique, giving you a reason to not just roll with the characters with the best base stats.
-There's special equipment that raises weapon aptitude to S and stat aptitudes to over 100% for each weapon type, making your dreams about gun-toting healers and swordfighting witches a lot more viable! (if you can spare an equipment slot)
-There's a lot more cute monsters this time around! 0w0
- The item world has random Mystery Rooms every few floors and you can cause Dark Courts to appear at certain floors, breaking up the monotony of levelling up items with some bonus rewards, shopping, or minibosses. You even sometimes get a chance to buy Rare and Legendary items, which means you don't need to spend ages looking for a Legendary Cosmic Blade!
-The story is made out of several parallel narratives, which leads to an overall smoother pacing.
- There is no damage from ending a turn lifting an ally, and a stack of characters can do special combo attacks, making the lift/throw system more useful than just quickly moving around.
- There are magical monster weapons now making caster monsters more viable in combat.
-The Demon Rank system is removed, anyone can apply for any Dark Assembly bill... no more need to grind Promotion Exams whenever you want to do something!
And to all of the above, add more secret bosses than ever before and no less than TWO alternate overworlds to unlock (the Dark World and the Land of Carnage) that each adds new challenge to the basic story missions, and you easily have enough content to spend hundreds of hours playing.
Has more feels than Clannad After Story

I bought this game for myself and a few friends a while back ago. We played for a few hours, got bored, and stopped. We then kinda forgot about it.
Fast forward a year, we couldn't figure out a game to play together. That's when I remembered Don't Starve Together. We all remembered hating it, but we decided to play anyway since we had nothing else better to do. This game is now one of my favorite games of all time.
Where do I start? Well, for one, this game takes a while to figure out. That's why we hated it, we died 2 days in and assumed the game was supposed to be like that. Turns out, we just sucked. This game is incredibly suspensful, causing even the most minor of victories seem like you brought Hiter back from the dead just to punch him in the face until he dies again. It's so amazingly rewarding even when you do something as stupid as kill a rabit and feed it to your friend to prevent them from dying.
The artstyle of this game is superb. Nearly everying seamlessly changes sprites when your sanity decreases, slowly becoming more and more horrifying. The Character design is amazing, you can play as characters such as a lumberjack who eats wood to not become a beaver, a woman who gains sanity from burning everything, and an Opera singer who is so into the part that she refuses to eat anything other than meat, just to be a true viking.
Also dying is even hilarous. There is a statistics page that logs everything you have ever died to and how long you lived beforehand. I've died to fire, wolves, deerclops, darkness, starvation, and nearly everything. The funny thing though? I died to eating monster meat on my current record. That's right, I voluntairly ate a rotten peice of meat and died durring my longest running game. Monster meat is the most powerful enemy confirmed
Also I should note the Devs are amazing. That's a plus
Overall 10/10, would be the last player left and eat a monster meat in front of my dead friends while they screamed in agony again

Despite this game being Early Access, I would 100% recommend it already.
I've only given this game about an hour of play with two friends but already I am a little bit in love with it.
The game combines elements from Platformers, RPG's and roguelikes to create a fantastic little indie game.
The gameplay is rather simply to fight, craft and quest your way through various randomly generated dungeons. Unlike most platformers this game isn't a rush and hack'n'slash. You have to craft your own weapons, potions and food in order to survive which sounds simple but can get challenging quickly.
Playing with more than one person we quickly found out if we didn't share our resources we would die within minutes. Also, the friendly-fire meant instead of just spamming the attack button we actually had to watch what we were doing/who we were attacking.
The crafting list already has a fair few items on it, I am sure you can find the list somewhere but I rather enjoyed guessing what would work with what, which gave the game a nice survival feel.
The game is hard though. If you're playing with others you will need a way to communicate, and being in Early Access in-game chat isn't implemented yet.
And because this game is still Early Access there ARE bugs, but none that are gamebreaking (that I have encountered), it is fully playable, and enjoyable.
So far, I can't find much to fault about this game at all. The developer has been consistent with his work on the game but has also been consistent with his updates on Kickstarter too (19 since November 19th) which for me is always a good sign for games in Early Access.
For £6.99 you can't go wrong with a game this fun.

Deus Ex is a cyberpunk FPS aRPG and is largely regarded as one of the best games of all time.
Says something about how just how good a game is when the main argument isn't that this was one of the best games ever made, just whether or not it's aged well over time. That Deus Ex is superb, or at least was superb, is completely uncontested.
One of the biggest talking points about Deus Ex is that "the graphics have aged". When games like Jet Set Radio, Vagrant Story and Resident Evil Code: Veronica were released in the same year and still hold up to contemporary standards, the argument doesn't hold. Simply that the standards have risen, and so Deus Ex's mediocre art design, and that their environmental modellers clearly bit off much more than they could chew, can no longer ride on the novelty of 3D graphics. They simply did not have the capabilities to bring their vision to life, and instead of making compromises chose to march forward anyway - and that shows.
Likewise, that Deus Ex's mechanics have aged into something clunky, doesn't hold weight when mechanically beautiful and smooth games like Rayman 2, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 and Banjo Tooie were released the same year and are still incredibly fun to this day. System Shock 2, another FPS aRPG, was released a year prior and controls smooth as butter. Deus Ex's mechanics didn't suddenly become clunky, they just always were.
Regardless of contemporary comparisons, though, the game still has is fair share of problems. After Hong Kong the game easily starts wearing out its welcome and starts dragging on - even though the story itself goes on a rollercoaster ride. It doesn't help that by the end of Hong Kong, they have introduced and established every single mechanic, weapon, augment, tool, and all bar one of the very limited enemy types, and never elaborate or experiment on them beyond that. For all intents and purposes you just largely do the same thing until the end of the game.
Clunky mechanics mean that while the game touts supporting multiple playstyles, a pure Stealth/Pacifist run will outright put you to sleep. Inching along with the world's slowest crawl and using the very limited selection of stealth takedown weapons just isn't fun, it's monotonous and awful. The idea of supporting multiple playstyles that take you through completely different paths through the game also falls apart, because after the first mission or two you'll be outright ransacking every corner of levels -  and are largely expected to, to account for JC Denton's vulnerability and lack of resources.
Despite all of this, Deus Ex is rightfully regarded as an incredibly good game that has earned the right to your time.
It's Blade Runner, bereft of the emotional dialogue, with equal parts near-future Ship of Theseus-induced existentialism, a timeless narrative of class warfare, and a massive dose of utterly ridiculous conspiracy theories treated as fact. The dramatic voice-acting doesn't hold up ("JC, A BOMB") but the usual cool delivery and rapid-fire discussion of the themes delivers on the premise expertly, with Jay Franke doing a fantastic job as JC Denton.
JC Denton is a fantastic example of being a blank slate without actually being a blank slate. The perfect fit for a sounding board for the various political ideologies and conspiracy theories throughout the game, he serves to question and debate the various factions without ever noticeably projecting his own agenda beyond trying to do the right thing.
Deus Ex doesn't need perfect graphics, or even fully realized mechanics to be an excellent game - it has managed to cement itself at the higher end of the Wall of Fame with its expertly-directed dialogue, pleasing mechanical complexity and utterly brilliant and satisfying level design that easily remains just as good to this day.
And this is why you should buy it and play it right through to the ridiculous end.

The short review;
Ultimately I do really like this game. There are some very annoying things about the pacing of the conversations and the main character's personality but it is a really charming world with a good story! I love Daedalic for their enviroments, the cosy and magical atmosphere, interesting worlds and the puzzeling. The mechanics were interesting but unexploited, the story somewhat lacked a connection to the main character. Even if the story was very nice, in the end it sort of lost its meaning.  However, if you like magic and beautiful fairytale-like graphics, this is a game for you.
And now for the long review;
SPOILER WARNING
THOUGHTS ON THE STORY
I must say the story, nay, the main character was a little too heroic for my taste! The story is actually very nice, I would say it is about following your dreams even if critizised by others (which feels very relevant for those working in the game industry - atleast where I'm from). Removing the characters personality from the story I actually appriciated it a lot, the pacing was good, the game opened up successivly revealing new areas with new characters and new quests. I never found the story frustrating or the pacing irritating apart from maybe the end with the stage and everything, the finale.
I did like the twist in the end that sort of turned out not to be a twist at all (?) lol, but it felt a little far-fetched, rather wishing to make a point than actually making it. In the end the good guy turns out to be a bad guy, who turns out to be a good guy? ... So I guess the fable-side to this story is not to believe someone is evil only because people say so, and its' never too late to make things right.
As mentioned above there was a lot of praising of the main character, Jerry, (from others as well as himself, especially from all the female characters who NATURALLY were all in love with him or called him sweetiepie as they watched the children, baked cookies or waited for that new fashionable purse) which really got on my nerves, apart from the grumpy garden owner and the gome maybe (yay for them!). Jerry didn't really feel like he had much character development through the story - he did doubt his wishes to become a magician in the beginning, but not enough to feel like a change in character as the story developed. Very early on he seemed over-confident in himself and it did not really feel like he went though a struggle.
Even though there were some ties in the story to Jerry's past (his father) it still felt very vague and not really reason enough for me to care. However, when I realised Jerry had lost so many years of his life and his mother had been waiting for him I did feel touched and was motivated to change it back. For me that was a big motivator along with the wish to explore and the will to adventure. However, it may just be that his personality irritated me so much that I cannot write much positive stuff in this section, haha. I'm still not sure what Jerry ought to have learned from this, and even if he learned that he CAN be a magician for a living, or something, I never found out which was slightly disappointing.
Also, sometimes it felt like the characters took a little bit too much of the game - in many conversations there were a lot of small-talk that wasn't really related to the story and didn't really fit into the character's personality. Simply sillyness, which can sometimes be fun, but combined with the odd pacing in the conversations (weird pauses and so) it made me very frustrated. The end was also a little bit caotic, that the bad guy was evil, but then only now and not in the past, but then then that scene in the end where the recent and evil version of the evil person who-shall-not-be-named helped Jerry get back... At first I thought that Jerry was the apprentice that turned evil and that he was Zaroff, and that he was brought back in time to see all this to ultimately give up his magical powers to prevent it from happening or something.. just for a brief moment. I was slighly disappointed when that wasn't the case lol.
Graphically it really felt like the game changed in time. As the player got further and further away from Mousewood the graphics gets darker, with the Dwarfs homes and the Moths, and to the west the forest. Also the different worlds in which Jerry found the different spells grew darker, and the growing threat from the Lizards was very nicely portraid.
THOUGHTS ON THE MECHANICS
The game mechanics progress nicely along with the story as the player learns new spells which kept me interested. I did not expect any of the mechanics of the different spells and I must say they feel very unique. It was also combined with several mini-quests (collecting stickers, raindrops and what not) which was a very nice detail for giving the player some extra feeling of progression and raising atleast my awareness.
I felt a little dissapointed that the spells were used to little when the focus was so much on magic otherwise. Much of the game consists of finding, combining and using things to get new things to take you to new places like in Deponia, though slightly less difficult. In comparison to Deponia there were alot of items that stayed with the player through the whole game, and I must say I had a little "Aha!" When I realized I was going to make another magical circle in the end. The was also alot more centered around Mouseville compared to Deponia which was much more stretched out over different scenes and places, so Night of the Rabbit felt much more compact and interesting to me. The world changed more and as a player I was able to interact with it much more over time, strengthening the bond to the world and its inhabitants.
SUM OF THE CARDEMUM
In the end I found myself really wishing for the world which Jerry originally came from to be changed, for me to be able to use the spells I learned to see the world in a different way, maybe that the rocks that once were quiet really weren't and that I could use fox-cunning to create illusions to amuse a child or something to prove that Jerry will continue to use his magic in this world too, and ultimately becoming a Wizard in this world too. Too see that all this affected him somehow. That is what I lacked in the end.

This was my first time playing Deus Ex and since it is widely regarded as a classic PC game which everyone has already played, I give my opinions as someone who isn't influenced by nostalgia (the game was originally released in 2000). That said I can fully understand why the game is heavily praised by many individuals.  The game does an excellent job of letting the player decide how they want to play the game by letting the player choose which categories to spend upgrade points and by deciding which augmentations to install/upgrade.  These upgrades and augmentations don’t just change your character’s performance in combat, but have an effect on how easily your character can traverse certain portions of the level.  This, multi-path structure is what makes the game interesting since many current games will give you the options on how you want to kill things but keep you on a mostly linear path. In keeping with giving the player total freedom, the game also offers multiple endings and while this isn’t unique, this is one of the few games where the choice at the end is a true “moral choice” as opposed to just having a “good/evil” ending.  Criticisms I had with the game are minor.  The game certainly hasn’t aged well graphically and the AI can be truly awful at sometimes but given the age of the game, issues like this are to be expected.  The inventory system is clunky, making it annoying to rearrange/add/drop items but again this is minor.  Finally, the default control layout will absolutely have to be changed for new players.

I bought this on the day it released, with minimal reviews to give me any real idea what I'd be getting into. It was a gamble, but I'm happy to say that it paid off swimmingly.
The game has you in the role of a guy who just wants a good night's rest. But a bunch of obnoxious college kids have been throwing a loud house party next door all night long. You just want it to end so you can get some sleep.
So you grab your mask, a knife, and pay a visit.
The goal is ultimately to kill everyone at the party by any means necessary. Use traps, poison food, tamper with the electronics, set things on fire, cause explosions or simply pick them off one by one. The levels are paritally randomized with different goodies to use on your victims.
However, it isn't as easy as it sounds. The partygoers may be as dumb, but they'll still call the police if they see a body or witness a murder. You want to try and stay out of the spotlight as much as you can, because while the cops may give up looking for you? They'll get more tenacious every time they get called in. You might even have to deal with someone worse if you keep slipping up.
It can be a difficult experience, but it is rewarding when you pull it off. Regretfully, sometimes a level can just be plain impossible to finish without getting caught. But it isn't too hard if you play it carefully.
The only real big negative I have is the lack of a basic tutorial. You'll find newspaper clippings that give you advice, but not enough information to really work with. You'll have to just experiment and figure out most elements for yourself.
But in the end? It's definately worth a try at least.

Another game from Dagestan Technology that was "inspired" by something else; but at the very least, this one tried to be different instead of just blatantly ripping off Meat Boy, like they did with Bloodbath Kavkaz and Hotline Miami.
Sadly, it's still pretty bad. Both the controls and the hitboxes, which are the most crucial elements to this genre of games, are imprecise, to put it mildly.
Combined with a level design that further pushes the fake difficulty by screwing with the player (such as moving the exit door from under your nose to the other side of the level, suddenly spawning a death trap above you or making a fake platform that you wouldn't know about unless you already died to it.)
Basically, it's a rage game that you would play not for the challenge, but to punish yourself or others.
And that's if you even get it to work. I tested it on 3 different computers and only on one of them I could actually play it.
The other two got either a Blue Screen Error immediately after launching of the game; or it played with FPS constantly jumping between 10 to 20, making the game virtually unplayable.
And I'm not the only one that had such problems, so for all intents and purposes, this game is just simply broken.
Another really annoying thing is the complete absence of settings.
Especially the audio ones, since the speed changes of the soundtrack during every death and restart (which happens every couple of seconds,) together with a disc scratching sound effect, will make your ears bleed after a while.
But hey, who needs that when you have hats, right?

A decent time sink game slightly compareable to Mount & Blade. Depending on your chosen player start you have almost nothing and slowly build up to bigger ships, factory complexes and trade empires.
Sadly there's really no real reason or end-game goal to the game, f.ex. like conquering Caldaria in Mount & Blade for yourself or another faction.
The trade system is pretty bare bones (prices only change depending on whether a factory has more or less wares, their "competitors" don't affect them and companies can never go out of business), the stock exchange they added in Albion Prelude is outright broken (you can buy shares at their minimal price and they NEVER EVER go lower than a set value), and there's no real reason to wage war against factions, unless you're aiming for money early game through piracy or want to capture certain unique ships. Once you get one of the end-game destroyers the game quickly loses its charm as there's no real reason to use it on anything, other than to create random havoc.
The war between Terrans and the other races they added in Albion Prelude is extremely lackluster as it never spills outside certain "war sectors". It's completely avoidable, it doesn't affect the market or race politics in any way and there's no way to "win" the war for either side save for a seperate long quest that isn't really about waging war. Even if you wipe the enemies from all war sectors they'll just spawn more units and factories out of thin air once you exit the sector and the same is true for other races as well.
You can't really interact or change the game world in any meaningful way and the world itself is extremely static where nothing mentionable occurs unless the player takes a mission, which usually involves spawning a number of enemies out of thin air, depending on the player's fighting rank. Even in those the failure only affects your reputation and rewards, but doesn't f.ex. lead to full-scale invasion or the invaders setting up shop even if they hypothetically wiped out everything in the area. The other missions like taxi service, transport etc. also consist of hauling people and objects that appear out of thin air. There's no actual cause and effect which makes NPCs offer these missions and there's no competition to try fill their needs either. It's more of a
for the player rather than an actual sandbox with a living world where everything doesn't simply revolve around you.

The "from rags to riches" portion of the game is enjoyable and offers hours of gameplay in form of exploration, battles, space piracy and empire management and you're given free reins on how to approach your goal to glory, but the actual "sandbox" part of the game is virtually nonexistant and you'll see the limits of the game the moment you actually get powerful enough to hypothetically "influence" anything in the universe.

Okay wow, on the surface this was an okay game with some fun familiar gameplay mechanics but going a little deeper, this game delivers some pretty heavy story notes that upon first impression appear to be superficial. I'm impressed Mr Yoko Taro and surprised that I've never discovered your games before this one. There are some heavy philosophical/existentialist themes in this game and without saying more it pulled a very heavy "6th sense" on me; emotionally it went from okay to extremely sad and melancholic.
For anyone wanting to try this game, I can't stress this enough, beating the game once, isn't beating the game at all; it is just a chapter break in the story. They take 'new game+' video game mechanic and completely flip it on expectations.
